In the encroaching twilight, the room seemed to huddle around her, each shadow whispering the secrets of time and age. The old clock on the mantel ticked with a steady, familiar rhythm, one that seemed to mock her with the urgency of passing moments. Memories fluttered by, insistent and vivid. She thought of the days when she could move without thought, when laughter echoed brightly against the walls now wreathed in silence. She turned her head slightly, the effort immense, to gaze at the face of the man beside her. In life, he had been a formidable presence, a pillar of strength and certainty that defined her world. Now, the stillness in his features was a cruel parody of the vitality she had known, and she felt the weight of it pressing against her very soul. A lone tear escaped her eye, carving a slow, deliberate path down the weathered landscape of her face. "How many years, my love?" she whispered, her voice a thin wisp that barely broke the heavy quiet. She imagined how it once was, the conversations they shared, the warmth of his embrace. Those recollections shimmered golden and precious, like the scattered, fading leaves of autumn. Her thoughts drifted to the phone again, that lifeline that had betrayed her. In another life, it had been the means of connection, the bearer of news both joyous and sorrowful. But now it stood as a reminder of isolation, its silence mocking the desolation that closed in around her like the encroaching darkness. She longed for the touch of her children, their smiles and assurances that all would be well. Their absence was a gaping void, an emptiness that echoed with promises half-forgotten. She knew they meant to visit, to envelop her in the warmth of family, but the world beyond these walls conspired to keep them at bay. Still, hope was a stubborn seed, and in her heart, it sprouted tender roots, waiting for the day they would once again fill this space with life. Her gaze wandered to the window, where the world outside stretched into infinity, the horizon blurred by the dimming light. Somewhere out there, life continued unabated, uncaring of this quiet room with its somber inhabitants. She imagined the vibrancy of the streets she once walked, the rustle and hum of humanity that had surrounded her in younger years. The bed creaked softly as she shifted, an exertion that brought a fresh wave of aching reminders from her body. The bruise on her hip was a fiery brand, a testament to her frailty. She closed her eyes, seeking solace in the warm cocoon of their faded memories, where time surrendered to the timeless dance of their shared existence. In the darkness of her mind's eye, she saw their first meeting, the shy glances, the tentative steps towards one another. She could almost hear his laughter, feel the gentleness of his hand in hers. If she listened hard enough, perhaps he would speak again, breaking through the silence that had stolen him from her side. "Not yet," she thought, clutching the fragile tether of memory. "Not yet."

Our study aimed to investigate the impact of these linguistic and structural features on children's sentence production accuracy. We recruited 120 children aged 3-6 years, divided into four age groups (3-year-olds, 4-year-olds, 5-year-olds, and 6-year-olds). Each child participated in a sentence production task, where they were presented with a series of pictures depicting two events in a specific order (e.g., a girl combing her hair and then putting on her gloves). The children were then asked to describe the events in a sentence using either before or after. The sentences were audio recorded and transcribed for analysis. We found that children's production accuracy increased with age, with 6-year-olds performing significantly better than 3-year-olds. However, even the oldest children in our study struggled with producing accurate sentences when the events were described in reverse order. Specifically, when asked to use after in a sentence, children tended to produce sentences with the connective in the initial position (e.g., "After she combed her hair, she put on her gloves") more accurately than sentences with the connective in the medial position (e.g., "She combed her hair, after she put on her gloves"). This suggests that the position of the connective affects children's sentence production accuracy, with initial position being easier to produce than medial position. Furthermore, our results showed that the order of events also influenced children's production accuracy. When the events were described in chronological order, children performed better than when the events were described in reverse order. This is consistent with previous research suggesting that children have a bias towards describing events in the order in which they occur (Peterson & McCabe, 1987). However, our study extends this finding by showing that this bias is not only influenced by the order of events but also by the position of the connective. In addition, we found that the type of connective used (before or after) also affected children's production accuracy. Children performed better with before than with after, which is consistent with previous research suggesting that before is acquired earlier than after (Blything & Cain, 2016; Clark, 1971; Pyykkonen & Jarvikivi, 2012). However, our study provides new insights into the reasons behind this difference. We found that the semantic features of each term, as suggested by Clark (1971), do not fully explain the difference in age of acquisition. Instead, our results suggest that the position of the connective and the order of events also play a role in children's production accuracy. Our study has implications for language development and language teaching. The findings suggest that children's production of sentences with temporal connectives is influenced by a range of linguistic and structural features, including the order of events, the type of connective, and the position of the connective. Language teachers and speech therapists can use this knowledge to design targeted interventions to support children's language development. For example, they can start by teaching children to use before and after in sentences with chronological order, and then gradually introduce reverse order sentences with the connective in different positions. In conclusion, our study provides new insights into the complex process of language development in young children. The findings highlight the importance of considering the linguistic and structural features of sentences when investigating children's production of sentences with temporal connectives. Further research is needed to fully understand the cognitive and linguistic processes underlying children's language development, but our study provides a step in the right direction.

Period correction is mostly needed with obvious tempo change, whilst phase correction is continuously triggered to adapt to small temporal fluctuations.8 Phase and period corrections appear gradually, rather than instantaneously, after a timing change is introduced in the synchronization or a joint action begins. Findings regarding error correction processes are mostly based on tapping tasks, in which participants tap along to rhythmic sequences of auditory stimuli (for a review, see the works of Repp1,2). Recently, they have also been investigated in two professional string quartets. In this case, researchers found that the first violinists exhibit contrasting patterns of adjustments with the co-performers. In one quartet, the first violinist showed fewer adjustments to the co-performers, than the others' adjustment to her. In the second quartet, researchers found no difference in the adjustment patterns between the first violinist and the other members of the ensemble. These findings suggest different strategies used during the performance, ie first-violin led versus a more democratic approach.12 Reported evidence indicates that synchronization in ensembles could be affected by the rhythmical complexity of the piece being performed.13-15 The modality of sensory information occurring between beats was investigated in a study manipulating the number of notes within each crotchet beat. Pianists performing melodies with a metronome were less synchronized when playing melodies in which the crotchet beats were subdivided by adding quaver notes, compared with when the crotchets beats of the melodies were not subdivided.13 In addition, pianists performing duets with different note ratios between the two musical parts (1:1, 1:2 and 2:1 ratio) were best synchronized when the lower part was playing fewer notes (2:1 ratio) and less synchronized when playing more notes (1:2 ratio), under conditions whereby the upper parts heard only themselves, whilst the lower parts heard both parts.14 Pianists were also more synchronized when playing the same melody in unison than in a round, characterized by a delay of the entry of the second performer, suggesting that the non-simultaneous entrance might decrease the degree of synchronization.15 The effect of the rhythmical complexity of the piece has not been analysed in larger ensembles; further investigations might shed some light on the effects of the rhythmical complexity of the piece on the sensorimotor synchronization between musicians in larger ensembles. Temporal coordination can also be affected by the role of the individuals within a group, such as leader-follower relationships between musicians in ensembles.

The discourse of paradox had permeated the very fabric of intellectual discussion during the Renaissance, serving not merely as a rhetorical flourish but as a vital tool for navigating through the intricate terrain of emerging scientific ideas. Edward Gresham, in his Astrostereon, engaged with this culture by wrestling with the heliocentric paradigm-not with direct scientific refutation but with a deft manipulation of paradox to reshape the perceptions of his readers. This method spoke to a broader audience, less versed in the intricacies of mathematics and astronomy, hence fostering a dialogue grounded in more familiar terms. Gresham's efforts reflect the greater trend of his time, where the burgeoning fields of natural philosophy and science still lay intertwined with the legacy of rhetorical argumentation. In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, scholars like him navigated the tension between traditional Aristotelian frameworks and the innovative approaches heralded by Copernicus. Their rhetorical use of paradox functioned as a bridge over the chasm of the unknown, an attempt to reconcile seemingly contradictory notions with what the senses could observe and what the mind could fathom. In this climate of intellectual ferment, the deployment of paradox served a dual role. It challenged entrenched ideas while simultaneously providing a mechanism for assimilating newer, more radical hypotheses into the collective consciousness. Transforming heliocentric ideas from mere conjecture to plausible reality was no simple feate. Gresham's reliance on an audience's common sense and experiential knowledge is indicative of the larger methodological shift within scientific discourse-a transition from pure dialectical reasoning to an empirical persuasion that appreciated the resonance of the familiar. Moreover, exploring the juxtaposition between sensory certainty and philosophical conjecture demanded a nuanced approach. Figures like Gresham, operating in an era rife with epistemological uncertainty, embraced paradox not simply as a tool for contradiction but as a vehicle for discovery. In aligning his rhetoric with the cultural sensibilities of his audience, Gresham catalyzed a form of intellectual exploration that was both accessible and revolutionary. The use of paradox in his rhetoric heralded a democratization of scientific discourse, opening up aristotelian concepts to broader interpretations. Contemporary thinkers in Gresham's era recognized this dynamic interplay as vital to fostering dialogue amid a rapidly evolving scientific landscape. In his work, paradox served to unravel the layers of accepted truths, suggesting that the process of acquiring knowledge was as much about embracing uncertainty as about the acquisition of facts. This process underscored the transformational potential of science as narrative-a tangible way to articulate the ineffable and a bridge between the known and the unknown. It was this intertwining of rhetorical craftsmanship and scientific endeavor that heralded a new era of intellectual interchange. The challenge lay in advancing discourse without completely overthrowing the foundational beliefs that governed society's understanding of the world. As these intellectual upheavals unfolded, the reliance on paradox underscored the Renaissance's quintessential dilemma: how to reconcile an emerging world-view with the persistent, and often obstinate, legacy of the past. Therefore, Gresham's work must be understood not in isolation but as part of a continuum-an enduring dialogue wherein paradox served as an essential instrument in humanity's quest for knowledge and understanding. In his Astrostereon, the apparent contradiction became a lattice through which the light of reason and revelation both converged and diverged, propelling society towards new heights of intellectual pursuit yet to come.

Ahead, a soldier stumbles and falls, exhaustion overtaking him. Tommy reaches out, grasping the man's arm, pulling him to his feet. They exchange a glance, sharing an unspoken pact of endurance. Together, they continue, moving steadily toward the boarding plank, each footfall echoing with the silent prayer for deliverance. The ship's deck feels solid beneath Tommy's boots, a promise of the journey home. Despite the uncertainty, despite the chaos still reigning behind them, he allows a flicker of hope to take root. They seem to think that being an RA should be our entire identity, as though our personal lives, academic ambitions, and social connections are mere afterthoughts. Whenever they need an extra pair of hands or someone to cover an unexpected shift, it doesn't matter if you have a paper due or a meeting with a professor-you're expected to drop everything and comply. And heaven forbid you find yourself at odds with this unwritten expectation; you'll be met with icy glares and thinly veiled derision for daring to prioritize your own life over another endless meeting or another pointless program where only a handful of students actually show up. There's this constant tension between what is expected of us as students and what is demanded of us as RAs. One particularly frustrating aspect is the mandatory programming we have to organize. On the surface, these activities are designed to foster community and provide support to students, which is a noble aim. However, in reality, they often feel like empty gestures, sometimes half-attended, with participation often dragged out of students by the lure of free food or obligatory attendance slips. We pour hours into the planning, execution, and follow-up documentation of these events, only to find the impact negligible, and then face inevitable criticism from our supervisors about how the attendance wasn't high enough or how we failed to engage the students as effectively as we should have. It's as if success is measured by headcounts and not by the genuine connections that might arise, unexpectedly and unquantifiably, from the interactions we attempt to foster. It's not just the students we serve who take us for granted, but often our peers swipe our efforts aside without thought. They saunter through hallways, where we meticulously manage noise complaints, navigations of lost mail, and subtle mediations of conflicts. Invisible work, unnoticed by the oblivious passerby, becomes a thankless task. Yet, paradoxically, these same students can demand our attention at the drop of a hat. A broken vending machine, a trivial noise disturbance, or the slightest whiff of discontent can summon us from our studies or even our attempts to catch a few hours of sleep. It's a precarious balancing act between authority and servitude, where we're directed to handle situations with maturity yet often are received with the dismissiveness reserved for underlings. While it seems easy to dive into a sea of negativity regarding the role, there are those fleeting moments that remind us why we took the job in the first place. Moments when a first-year student knocks timidly on your door, not with a problem but for advice, or a quiet thank you whispered after a heartfelt program transcends its meager attendance. These fragments of gratitude become the lifebuoy we cling to amidst the demands. Despite the challenges, I think about how this job is shaping me, too. It's an unrefined crucible of skills not clearly listed in the brochure-patience, negotiation, leadership on no sleep or food. Without a doubt, my college experience would be easier without these responsibilities, but it would also lack the depth of human interaction, both positive and negative, that comes from being smack dab in the middle of this unpredictable ecosystem. But I do sometimes wonder if those few meaningful moments are worth the overwhelming barrage of apathy from superiors and students alike.

We find that the predicted stability correlates well with experimental data. Molecular Dynamics Simulations We have performed extensive MD simulations of wild-type 14-3-3 and 15 mutants thereof. The simulations were carried out at constant temperature (310 K) and pressure (1 bar). The system was coupled to an external bath via a Langevin thermostat with friction coefficient = 1 ps-1. A time step of 2 fs was used throughout the simulations. Long-range electrostatic interactions were treated with the particle mesh Ewald method [26]. All bonds were constrained with LINCS [27]. Non-bonded interactions were cut off at 0.95 nm. The non-polar solvation energy was calculated using the OPLS-AA force field [28] combined with the Generalized Amber Force Field (GAFF) [29] for the ligands. Water molecules were modeled using the TIP3P model [30]. All simulations were performed with GROMACS version 5.0.4 [31]. The initial coordinates of the protein were taken from the crystal structure PDB: 1JSH [32]. The protein was embedded into a cubic box filled with water molecules, which was then equilibrated for 100 ns. After the equilibration phase, the solvent was removed and replaced by explicit sodium ions to neutralize the charge of the system. This procedure was repeated twice until the final concentration of Na+ was around 150 mM. Subsequently, the system was minimized for 500 steps with steepest descent minimization and subsequently for 50,000 steps with conjugate gradient minimization. The simulation cell was subjected to periodic boundary conditions. During the production phase, the protein atoms were restrained using a harmonic potential with a strength of 400 kJ mol-1 nm-2. All other parameters were kept identical during the whole simulation period. Production runs of 100 ns were performed for the wild type and the 15 mutants. The root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between the structures of the wild-type protein was calculated for all frames after the equilibration phase and averaged over all frames. The RMSD values are plotted against the corresponding simulation times in Fig. S1. To ensure the convergence of the simulations, the last 80 ns of each trajectory were used for further analysis. The number of hydrogen bonds formed between the backbone groups of the protein was counted every 10 ns. The average number of hydrogen bonds per residue is presented in Fig. S2. Thermodynamic Integration In order to estimate the changes in free energy due to mutations, TI calculations were performed. For each mutant, a pair of parallel simulations was run at different values of the coupling parameter. These simulations were initiated from the same configuration and continued for 40 ns each. The values of were chosen such that the difference in free energies G = Gmut - Gwt was estimated with sufficient precision. The free-energy profiles along the reaction coordinate were obtained from the thermodynamic integration formula: where F (x) is the total potential energy of the system, F (x) = F (0) + 0d ' F '/ ' and x represents the position of the mutation site. The integrand can be expressed analytically if the interaction potentials are linear in, i.e., F (x) = F(0)x + F(1)(1 - x).

In addition, before is used more consistently as a temporal connective than after, which is commonly used also as a preposition as in "Watch out, he is only after your money" (see the British National Corpus [Leech, Rayson, & Wilson, 2001]). Thus, after has a less consistent form-meaning relationship and is theoretically more complex than before. This literature suggests that the use of after may involve greater planning and processing effort than the use of before, which may influence the accuracy of sentence production. Another feature that might influence children's sentence production accuracy is the position of the connective. Corpus studies of spoken language have reported that children and adults use connectives in an initial position infrequently (Diessel, 2004, 2008). This finding has been related to the memory load involved in maintaining the information signaled by the connective from the beginning of the sentence while processing the meaning of the first clause (Diessel, 2004, 2008). Conversely, the preference to use a medially placed connective is associated with processing ease because it provides the linguistic information about temporal order at a point close to when the events can be integrated during the incremental processing of language. Our second research question was to identify which framework best explains variation in performance between different sentence structures and across development. A traditional memory capacity-constrained account attributes performance on language processing tasks to the availability of resources within an independent system of working memory, which limits the amount of information that can be maintained during planning and production (e.g., Carpenter, Miyake, & Just, 1994). A more nuanced language-based perspective of working memory shifts emphasis from the "quantity" of information that can be represented to the "quality" (i.e., the content) of the representation of that information in long-term memory (McElree, 2006), which in turn frees up shared processing resources so that they are allocated to the representation of information in active working memory (e.g., MacDonald, 2016). We examined both of these accounts in our study. A classic theory concerning the role of working memory in sentence processing is the memory capacity-constrained account (e.g., Carpenter et al., 1994). According to this viewpoint, an effect or interacting effect of the aforementioned features-order of events, connective, position of connective-is driven by working memory capacity alone. The primary emphasis is that some sentence structures are more difficult to process than others because they require more information to be held within the limited-capacity working memory system. The account builds on a framework that assumes that working memory is a separate system from long-term memory (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974; Baddeley, 2003) to argue that the accurate representation of information is driven by the availability of processing resources specific to the working memory system. The availability of processing resources determines how many individual language units can be accurately represented (but note that the constitution of a "unit" is undefined; see McElree, 2006, for a full review of limitations).

It is by your voice that this woman speaks, whom I do not know, and against whom I must be on my guard, for the sole reason that it is a paralytic who has told this story." She could not restrain the tears that came to her eyes, and she let them flow silently, finding nothing to reply. "I am sorry to pain you," he said. "I saw only Florentin's liberty." "I do not say this testimony of Madame Dammauville will not influence the judge, and, above all, the jury; but I must warn you that you will expose yourself to a terrible deception if you believe that her testimony alone will give your brother liberty. It is not on a testimony of this kind or of this quality that the law decides; better than we, it knows to what illusions people can lend themselves when it is the question of a crime that absorbs and excites the public curiosity. There are some witnesses who, with the best faith in the world, believe they have seen the most extraordinary things which only existed in their imaginations; and there are people who accuse themselves rather than say nothing." He heaped words on words, as if, in trying to convince Phillis, he might hope to convince himself; but when the sound of his words faded, he was obliged to declare to himself that, whatever the paralysis of this woman might be, it had not, in this instance, produced either defect of sight or of mind. She had seen, indeed, the tall man with long hair and curled beard, dressed like a gentleman, who was not Florentin. When she related the story of the lamp and the curtain cords, she knew what she was saying. In his first alarm he had been very near betraying himself. Without doubt he should have told himself that this incident of the curtains might prove a trap; but all passed so rapidly that he never imagined that, exactly at the moment when Caffie raised the lamp to give him light, there was a woman opposite looking at him, and who saw him so plainly that she had not forgotten him. He thought to use all precautions on his side in drawing the curtains, when, on the contrary, he would have done better had he left them undrawn. Without doubt the widow of the attorney would have been a witness of a part of the scene, but in the shadow she would not have distinguished his features as she was able to do when he placed himself before the window under the light. But this idea did not enter his mind, and, to save himself from an immediate danger, he threw himself into another which, although uncertain, was not less grave. Little by little Phillis recovered herself, and the hope that Madame Dammauville put in her heart, momentarily crushed by Saniel's remarks, sprang up again.

I was left standing there, frozen, as Moco's words echoed in my mind. I knew that I was in grave danger, and that I had to act fast if I wanted to get out of this alive.

Although Colie lays her argument on wrong assumptions, I would suggest that her thesis is not entirely flawed, as it seems that the more scientific (i.e. empirical) data there was, the more difficult it was to reject it for those who called ground-breaking ideas 'paradoxical'. At the same time, there was an urgent need to popularize new concepts, which was reflected in a substantial number of European treatises translated or abbreviated into English.9 Simultaneously, the promotion of new scientific achievements required the most suitable means of linguistic expression for the most precise representation of the actual condition of the natural world. In the wake of modern science, the concept of truthfulness and observational accuracy was prominent in the epistemological debates, which inevitably referred to Platonic and Aristotelian writings, and to new methods of scientific investigation striving to achieve the actual representation of the natural world. In England, these methods were most conspicuously presented in William Gilbert's De Magnete (1600) and Francis Bacon's Novum Organum (1620). At the turn of the seventeenth century, there was a strong call for more precise observations and instruments, so that the measurements were used not for constructing models but corresponded to the actual state of nature.10 In the English context, it was especially important in the case of navigational instruments. The more accurately described the world was, the safer it became and the easier to conquer. Early modern discussion on the (im)possibility to correctly observe, present, and comprehend natural phenomena was propelled by the need to confront newly amassed empirical and observational data with the existing (and continuously formed) hypotheses. For example, for Bacon, all astronomical hypotheses were the idols of the mind which could hinder access to 'the truth of the matter.'11 However, he also saw the need '[t]hat philosophical questions concerning the heavenly bodies, even ones which are contrary to opinion and in a way hard to believe, ought to be received.'12 He leaves such an openness to all theories (including the Copernican one) already in The Advancement of Learning (1605), where he advises caution in passing judgments and allows 'several glosses and opinions upon nature' before the 'real truth' is known.13 What is more, he is aware that those who want to present new - often paradoxical - ideas have a more difficult task than the ones 'whose conceits are seated in popular opinions.' This 'double labour' is 'to make themselves conceived' and 'to prove and demonstrate' with a 'recourse to similitudes and translations to express themselves.'14 Although his theory of communication is not homogenous,15 Bacon observes that the implementation of new knowledge requires a high level of rhetorical and dialectic skills. Therefore, it is essential to note the correlation between university education, the methods of looking for scientific accuracy, and the language suitable for an apt description and promotion of new findings.

A major limitation of Pd alloy membranes is susceptibility to poisoning by trace impurities in the gas stream, notably of CO and S species [23]. The effect has been shown to be crystal structure sensitive. It was reported that hydrogen flux through the bcc phase is undetectable only after 5 min exposure of the Pd47Cu53 (at%) membrane to 1000 ppm H2S [24]. In contrast, Pd-Cu alloy membranes with fcc structure, have been reported to have high resistance to surface poisoning by H2S [25-27]. It has been suggested that this resistance to S containing species results from the specific surface chemistry of the fcc phase [4,25], which is predominantly controlled by electronic factors [4,27]. As a result, efforts were made to improve the hydrogen flux through a range of Pd-Cu membranes with fcc structure [28-30]. Ideally, any modification induced by alloying should have a minimal effect on the surface and electronic properties of the Pd-Cu membrane in order to maintain the desired resistance to surface poisoning. The potential of ternary metal alloys consisting of Pd, Cu and a third metallic element for hydrogen purification has been investigated by first principle calculations [31]. It was shown that higher hydrogen permeability can be achieved by selected metallic alloys addition to Pd-Cu but the effects of these additives on the hydrogen solubility and the diffusivity may be opposed. In an extension of this work, it was suggested that substituting a small amount of Cu with Ag in a binary fcc Pd-Cu alloy can improve both hydrogen solubility and diffusivity. However, if Pd is partially replaced by Ag in a binary Pd-Cu alloy, hydrogen solubility decreases and diffusivity increases [32]. Hence, it was concluded that permeability can be increased if only a small amount of Cu is substituted by Ag. More recently, hydrogen solubility, diffusivity, and permeability were predicted using Density Functional Theory (DFT) for calculating a range of the Pd-Cu-Ag ternary alloys with fcc structure [33]. It was concluded that substituting Ag for Pd or Cu can increase the hydrogen permeability and that enhancement is more closely related to increased hydrogen solubility rather than diffusivity [33]. In addition, the permeability of Pd-Cu-Ag ternary films deposited on porous stainless steel substrate by electroless plating was shown to be almost twice the permeability of thin film binary Pd-Cu alloys with similar compositions [28]. The effects of various Ag concentrations on the permeability of the Pd-Cu-Ag films fabricated by magnetron sputtering system were also examined between 300 and 400 C. It was observed that replacement of Cu by only 1 at% of Ag can decrease the activation energy for hydrogen permeation by approximately 17% and enhance the permeability in the fcc phase by almost 50% in comparison to the counterpart binary alloy.

So, after discreetly depriving her of the gardener's knife and the brass-mounted Moorish pistol from the library mantel, with the assistance of three chocolate mousses and an incredibly complicated and sirup-drenched and maraschino-stippled and pineapple-flavored nut sundae not inappropriately designated on the menu-card as "The Hatchet-Burier," he succeeded in wheedling out of her the secret of her disguise, telephoned for the car, and brought her home with a slight bilious attack and a momentarily tempered spirit. A year later, after condign punishment for having tied sunbonnets on the heads of the Florentine marble lions in the Sunken Garden, she revolted against the tyranny of French verbs and the chinless Mademoiselle Desjarlais by escaping from the study window to the leads of the conservatory, from which she climbed to the top of the chauffeurs' domicile above the garage, where she calmly mounted a chimney and ate salted pecans and refused to come down. It began to rain, later on, but this didn't matter. What really mattered was the arrival of Ladder-Truck Number Three of the Tuxedo Fire Department. That was a great hour in the life of our over-ennuied Teddie, who, in fact, formed so substantial a friendship with those helmeted heroes that she was thereafter permitted to slide down the polished brass pole which led from the sleeping-quarters to the ground floor of the Fire Hall. So active was her interest in their burnished apparatus, and so dominating grew her hunger to hear the great red motors roar and see the Ladder-Truck wheels strike fire as they took the car-rails at the Avenue-crossing, that she turned in a quite unnecessary alarm. The resultant spectacle she regarded as almost as satisfying as the Chariot Race in Ben-Hur. For this offense, however, she was first severely reprimanded and later confined to the Lilac Room, where she locked herself in the old nursery bathroom and proceeded to flood the marble basin therein, reveling in the primitive joy of running water until the servants' stairs became like unto a second Falls of Montmorency, and Wilson, the second footman, had to wriggle in over the transom to shut off the taps and save the house from inundation. On the heels of this she was reported as having bitten the dentist's fingers when he unexpectedly touched a nerve. She further embarrassed the family and the tranquillity of Tuxedo Park by prying open an express crate and liberating two Russian wolf-hounds awaiting delivery on one end of the neat little depot platform. She claimed, it is true, that the dogs had stood there for a whole day, and wanted to get out, and were starving to death-but that was not a potent factor when it came to final adjustment of damages.

Today was the first time in five and a half years that I truly wished I hadn't come into work, and that I was prepared to leave less than 10 minutes after having walked in. I love my job, and for the most part, I love the people I work with (there's always a few, and always will be a few, that test that love). I'm one of the few people my age that usually looks forward to going to work because I miss the familiar faces and even the work. There's a lot of satisfaction in my job; I may not be the one directly treating/healing the patient, but I usually have a role in the family's coping, preparation, and a whole lot of interaction with both patient and family. Today was also the first time I ever cried at work. Well, not exactly - but it was the first time I cried for myself, if that makes sense. I've cried at work 3 times. The first was while I was still a co-op student; I walked into a patient's room behind a nurse, and just when I looked up, I watched him die, right in front of my eyes, with his younger brother hugging him and crying. This man was only 22 years old, HIV positive, and had had a brain tumor. His brother was 19. This was also the first time I'd ever watched someone die. Traumatic experience. Enough said. The second time was 3 years ago, when a very friendly 76 year old man died sitting in a chair in the hallway waiting for his wife and grandson to come for a visit. He had a DNR order, Do Not Resuscitate (ie. if he goes into Code Blue - cardiac arrest, doctors and nurses are not to revive him, he and his family have decided that they want nature to take its course). When I was told, sitting at my desk, that he had died, sitting there in the hall waiting, I went to the washroom and cried my eyes out at the thought of him dying alone, in such a way. The third time was actually earlier this summer. We had a patient, a young man about 27 years old, with a subarachnoid hemorrhage (bleeding between the surrounding tissue layers of the brain). He and his wife had gotten married less than a year ago, and he was in the hospital for about 2 weeks. During this time his wife and I talked quite a bit, and in some way, I sort of became a confidante. One day when I came into work he was doing quite poorly, and she asked me to sit with her in his room for a while. Sitting there, holding her hand, and she holding his, I watched him die, and watched this young lady, just a year older than me, watch the love of her life slip away from her.

A research by Chys et al. showed that a better performance could be obtained with a zeotropic mixture when the heat source temperature is relatively lower [13]. Harvig et al. reported that the selection of the optimal composition must ensure the critical temperature of the zeotropic mixture is around 30-50 C below the heat source temperature. Furthermore, the temperature glide in the condenser should be close to the temperature increment of the cooling fluid [14]. Using a suitable zeotropic mixture with an optimal composition is critical for optimising an ORC system. If a zeotropic mixture is selected improperly, the system performance may be even lower than that of the ORC system using the corresponding pure working fluids [15,16]. Since a huge amount of geothermal energy exists with a relatively low temperature, it is important to comprehensively evaluate the feasibility of using zeotropic mixtures for low-temperature geothermal power plants. So far, most of investigations indicated that using zeotropic mixtures could improve the system performance of ORC systems. Desideri and Bidini compared an ORC system with conventional single flash/binary flash power plant and reported that using ORC could harness geothermal energy more efficiently [17]. To improve degree of match of temperature profiles within the evaporator and condenser of a geothermal ORC system, Yue et al. used a zeotropic mixture of isobutane and isopentane as working fluid and the system's thermal efficiency was improved [18]. For a heat source with a temperature below 120 C, Heberle et al. reported that the system efficiency could potentially be improved by 15% using isobutane/isopentane and R227ea/R245fa as working fluids, instead of pure working fluids [19]. Another investigation for low-temperature geothermal power plants by Liu et al. also showed that an ORC power plant using a mixture of isobutane and isopentane could produce 4-11% more power than using pure isobutane [20]. It is therefore important to further explore methods that can improve the efficiency of ORCs using zeotropic mixtures as working fluids. Andreasen et al. proposed a split evaporation concept for low-grade heat sources. A separator is installed at the outlet of the recuperator to improve the boiling process [21]. Liu et al. discussed the effect of temperature glide during the condensing process and found that such a temperature glide should be matched with the temperature profile of the cooling fluid [22]. Li et al. used a liquid-separated condenser for an ORC using a zeotropic mixture of R600/R601a [23]. It is reported that this method could improve the heat transfer coefficient of the condenser evidently. Thus, the area and cost of the condenser using zeotropic mixture can be decreased significantly. On the other hand, various optimisation algorithms were employed for simulating different ORC systems [24,25]. To maximise the thermal efficiency, Victor et al. used a simulated annealing algorithm to calculate the optimal composition of zeotropic mixture [26].

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is a technique to map the spatial distribution of excited state lifetimes in microscopic samples. Being minimally invasive, the method is widely used nowadays for biomedical applications, particularly for gaining information on molecular dynamics and interactions in single living cells [36-38]. Conventional fluorescence confocal (one or two-photon excitation) techniques use steady-state fluorescence intensity measurements to produce corresponding two or three-dimensional images. However, fluorescence intensity is strongly affected by a variety of environmental influences, such as strong background fluorescence of the living systems, quenching by other molecules, aggregation, energy transfer, and refractive index effects. This makes it difficult to interpret and quantify the intensity-based data, especially in complex samples such as cells or tissues. In FLIM the fluorescence lifetime ( ) of a probe molecule is measured as the rate of emission decay [39, 40] and the differences in the probe fluorescence decay times provide the contrast mechanism for FLIM images [41, 42]. The advantage of using FLIM in complex systems is that the calculated fluorescence lifetimes can provide significantly more information than the intensities. Since the excited state lifetime depends on the local physicochemical environment of the fluorophore, it is used for sensing inter- and intramolecular processes in living cells, such as protein and DNA binding events [43, 44], changes in pH [45], local viscosities [46], and the presence of such lifetime quenchers as ions or oxygen [47, 48]. FLIM delivers information about the environmental change around the fluorescent probe even when it mainly remains in the same spatial location (e.g. inside the cell) and its fluorescence intensity holds constant. Notably, the emission is an inherent property of the fluorophore, and therefore the fluorescence lifetime is not affected by the change in probe concentration, photobleaching, or light scattering. Additionally, the excited state lifetime is not influenced by internal settings of the instrument such as laser intensity or detector gain. Autofluorescence of biological structures such as mitochondria and lysosomes can be almost avoided by time-correlated single photon counting, i.e. TCSPC-based FLIM systems, utilized in the current study. Only a few successful applications of excited state lifetime microscopy to monitor cellular uptake and release of a drug from the polyplexes [49, 50], and teranostics [51], have been recently reported. As yet, FLIM has not been utilized to investigate neither the EV cell-uptake processes as a function of time nor to investigate the intracellular trafficking of EVs. In this study, an anti-cancer drug, paclitaxel (Ptx), covalently labeled with Oregon Green (OG) fluorophore and loaded into EXOs or MVs is used to probe for various cellular uptake stages and intracellular trafficking of Ptx-OG and EV-Ptx-OG. Ptx-OG has been previously used in studying the intracellular kinetics of drugs, and Ptx-OG interaction with the microtubule network [52]. EV-mediated delivery of Ptx-OG has also been demonstrated earlier [35, 53-55] but the underlying sub-cellular mechanisms have not been meticulously explored.

Their art of conversation and grace is unparalleled, and witnessing them perform is like stepping into a carefully curated tapestry of tradition and elegance. As we strolled through Maruyama Park, the rain seemed to dance along with us, washing the city in a soft, silver mist that added an ethereal glow to the vibrant lanterns lining the paths. The anticipation in the air was palpable, a gentle hum that crescendoed with each step we took towards the performance area. Arriving at the venue, Hazel and I were greeted by an enchanting tableau of colors. Lanterns, intricate as lacework, hung suspended in the air, casting warm, flickering shadows across the faces of the diverse crowd. A soft murmur of voices surrounded us, punctuated by sporadic laughter and the occasional hush of reverence as people settled onto benches or mats, eager for the evening's spectacle. The performance began with a haunting melody, played by a lone shamisen player. Its twangs and plucks wove through the crowd like an invisible ribbon, drawing us into a world of elegance and poise. Then, from the shadows, emerged the Geisha, gliding with an almost supernatural grace. Their kimonos shimmered like liquid silk, each movement a choreographed poem that spoke of centuries-old traditions and untold stories. Their dances were not just performances, but connections to the past-a living history written on the canvas of the present. Hazel and I watched, mesmerized, as the Geisha painted the air with their fans, telling tales of love, betrayal, and timeless beauty. We were transported to another realm, one where time was a mere whisper and moments stretched into eternity. The Geisha, with their delicate gestures and enigmatic expressions, were more than mere entertainers; they were the custodians of a cultural legacy, whispering the secrets of a bygone era to anyone willing to truly see. As the final notes of the shamisen hung in the air, the Geisha slowly bowed, a gesture both graceful and profound. The audience erupted into applause, yet there was an unspoken agreement among us all to keep our voices lowered, as if raising them too high might shatter the fragile spell that had been cast. When the performance concluded, Hazel and I lingered in the park, unwilling to let go of the magic. We meandered through the lantern-lit paths, our conversations interwoven with awe and appreciation for the beauty we had just witnessed. It was as if the city itself, with its ancient secrets and modern rhythms, had opened a window into its soul, offering us a rare glimpse into its heart. Eventually, the night deepened, and the rain began to fall once more, gently urging us back toward the hustle and bustle of Kyoto's streets. Walking back to our hostel, I felt a profound sense of gratitude-not only for the experiences shared with Hazel but also for the kindness of strangers and the enduring allure of cultures that hold fast to their roots while embracing the future. Kyoto, with its harmonious blend of history and modernity, had welcomed us into its fold, leaving an indelible mark on our journey.

The woman remained standing in the doorway, gazing after the retreating figures until they vanished. She did not move. Her attitude expressed neither sorrow nor regret. She was simply awaiting the return of the officers, whose duty it was to conduct her back to Noumea. Her thoughts were inscrutable. They might have been bitter, or sweet, or even indifferent. No expression of countenance betrayed their nature. At length the officials returned, and led her away through the forest. They spoke kindly to her, but she answered only in monosyllables, or remained obstinately silent. At last they reached the seashore. The sea lay calm and unruffled beneath a cloudless sky. A steamer rode lazily on the waters, its smoke curling upward in a spiral column, its paddle wheels churning the blue waves into foam. The launch, lying alongside, was manned by convicts, who eyed the party curiously. The woman stepped down the ladder, and seated herself amidships. The oars fell together with a splash, and the boat moved off rapidly over the rippling water. From the deck of the vessel she waved her handkerchief in farewell to those upon the shore, who responded. Then the launch swung round to the gangway, and she ascended to the saloon. There she sat down listlessly, as if tired, resting her head upon her hand. An hour later the vessel was under weigh, bound for Noumea. When the bride left the penal settlement, the warders resumed their usual avocations. Some lounged lazily in the shade of the trees, smoking and chatting, while others strolled carelessly along the beach, enjoying the cool breeze blowing across the bay. All appeared cheerful, despite the dull monotony of life. Only one seemed sad. He was an old man, whose hair was silver-white, and whose thin cheeks were furrowed by age. Standing erect, he gazed seaward, watching the receding vessel until it disappeared from view. Then he sighed deeply, and murmured: "Poor child! poor child!" He shook his head mournfully, and walked slowly away. CHAPTER II. THE WARDERS. Each day, I watched their romance blossom, a constant reminder of my failures. In the years that followed, I became the perennial underdog, the punchline in my own life story, with replays of Seth Firquin's words constantly echoing in my mind. They grew roots, intertwining with every rejection, every slight, making sure that self-doubt thrived unchecked. High school came with its own share of woes, a period stained with awkward dances and unrequited crushes. I sought refuge in the library, losing myself in tales of adventure where the unlikely heroes won against all odds. Those stories were my sanctuary, where the fat, unpopular kid could metamorphose into someone of worth, someone brave and interesting. Yet real life offered no such magic. When people reached out, I hesitated, stung by a reflexive doubt. But then, just when I had resigned myself to solitary shadows, she walked into my life-an unexpected spring in my dreary winter. Her name was Maya, a breath of fresh air, genuine and kind with a laugh that wrapped around my heart like a soothing balm. Maya saw what others overlooked. She chipped at my fortress walls with persistence, her kindness a sledgehammer against my defenses. Slowly, I began to open up, revealing the broken pieces of my past that I had hidden so carefully. She listened, never judging, merely holding space for my words. In loving her, I started to love parts of myself that were long buried. Her belief in me kindled a spark of faith that maybe, just maybe, I wasn't doomed to be the perpetual loser in life's narrative. With Maya, I dared to be me without the fear of derision, relishing in the comfort of someone who saw more in me than I ever did myself. What hit me tonight, as I sat next to her watching reruns of an antic-filled sitcom, was the gentle realization of why I adored her so deeply. In her eyes, I saw acceptance, a gift I had yearned for but feared was unattainable. Our shared laughter was a symphony, drowning out the ghosts of past ridicule, and sealing a promise that I was no longer alone. Maya had become my reason to believe, my safe harbor in a world that had often felt unkind. In her, I found the companionship and love that had eluded me for so long, and for that, I would be eternally grateful.

Recent studies emphasize the pressing need to understand how the integration of these traits at the community level is reshaping polar ecosystem functionality, particularly under the strain of climate-induced changes (Diaz et al., 2013; Mouillot et al., 2013). The synergistic effects of warming temperatures, diminishing ice covers, and the introduction of novel species pose complex challenges to traditional ecosystem models. These models must now incorporate not only the unpredictability of climate patterns but also the dynamic, and often nonlinear interactions between species that drive ecosystem processes (Loreau et al., 2001). Within the Arctic, for example, the retreat of sea ice has precipitated a cascade of ecological transformations, from altered primary productivity to shifts in trophic interactions (Arrigo et al., 2008; Post et al., 2013). Phytoplankton blooms, once predictable upon the melting of sea ice, now occur with greater irregularity, potentially mismatching with the lifecycle events of zooplankton, central figures in polar food webs (Wassmann, 2011). Any disruption in these critical timelines can ripple through the ecosystem, affecting species at all levels of the food chain, including fish, marine mammals, and seabirds (Brierley and Kingsford, 2009). In the Antarctic, the narrative is equally complex. While some regions exhibit significant ice loss, others maintain their ice cover, leading to heterogeneity in environmental conditions that complicate our ability to generalize ecosystem responses (Rintoul et al., 2010). This geographical variability challenges researchers to develop nuanced understandings of ecosystem adaptability and resilience (Peck et al., 2010). Moreover, evidence of the poleward migration of certain species due to warming sub-Antarctic waters suggests that competitive interactions and community dynamics are in flux (Constable et al., 2014). Notably, the intrusion of warmer waters fosters the establishment of species adapted to temperate conditions, thereby reshaping existing community structures and functional attributes (Poloczanska et al., 2013; Schofield et al., 2010). The interplay between biological traits and environmental change underscores a critical avenue for future research: predicting shifts in ecosystem services, such as carbon sequestration and nutrient cycling, which are vital for global climate regulation (Clapham et al., 2012; Riebesell and Tortell, 2011). Understanding how species with different functional roles respond to environmental stressors can provide insights into potential feedback mechanisms that may either mitigate or exacerbate climate impacts (Cardinale et al., 2012). While advancements in remote sensing and molecular ecology offer promising tools for tracking and modeling these changes (Durant et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2018), collaboration among scientists, local communities, and policymakers remains crucial. Integrating traditional ecological knowledge with contemporary scientific approaches can enrich our understanding and inform sustainable management practices (Alessa et al., 2016). As polar regions continue to transform, the emphasis must be on holistic models that consider the intrinsic value of biodiversity and ecosystem services, driving policies to preserve these critical components of our planet's wellbeing (Elmqvist et al., 2010). The challenge lies in navigating the uncertainty and variability inherent in this rapidly changing landscape, to safeguard the natural processes that sustain life on Earth.

During the fourth watch of the night Jesus went out to them, walking on the lake. When the disciples saw him walking on the lake, they were terrified. "It's a ghost," they said, and cried out in fear. But Jesus immediately said to them: "Take courage! It is I. Don't be afraid." "Lord, if it's you," Peter replied, "tell me to come to you on the water." "Come," he said. Then Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water and came toward Jesus. But when he saw the wind, he was afraid and, beginning to sink, cried out, "Lord, save me!" Immediately Jesus reached out his hand and caught him. "You of little faith," he said, "why did you doubt?" And when they climbed into the boat, the wind died down. Then those who were in the boat worshiped him, saying, "Truly you are the Son of God." The disciples felt like they were alone a possibly abandoned. Even though they were experienced fishermen, the rough water and wind frightened them. Jesus knew where they were. Jesus went looking for them. He knew they would be scared. Jesus called out to them to comfort them. The disciples thought Jesus was a ghost because they were so unsettled. Peter was upset, but he didn't allow his fear to paralyze him. Peter got out of the boat, but when he saw the danger around him he panicked. Peter started to sink. He called for help. Jesus immediately pulled him out of the water, climbed into the boat with the disciples, and the wind stopped. The disciples worshiped Jesus after seeing his ability to care for them and protect them. Jesus words and actions throughout this stormy night provided a great deal of comfort to his disciples. I think that these same words can provide us with the same comfort we all need when the concerns and worries of our lives are about to paralyze us. During the fourth watch of the night Jesus went out to them, walking on the lake. It can be hard to understand, but the fact remains that Jesus knows where we are and is looking for ways to get our attention. He understands the difficulties we're facing more than we do. It is His desire to find us where we are, so he can take us to safety. But Jesus immediately said to them: "Take courage! It is I. Don't be afraid." Jesus words were heard through the wind and the waves. Peter remembered enough about what Jesus had taught him to respond to his voice. Remembering God, holding on to courage and letting go of fear is the only way we are every going to get out of the boat. "Come," he said. Sometimes a fearful situation requires us to move out of our comfort zone. Just as Jesus called Peter out of the boat a he calls us out.

The human spirit is resilient and, through history, it has been proven that even the most oppressive regimes can fall. No dictatorship lasts forever. People draw strength from the knowledge that they are part of a larger narrative, one that bends towards justice. Legions of brave individuals who sacrifice their personal aspirations for the collective good provide inspiration. Their courage is a reminder that even a single voice can echo across borders and lifetimes. Q: What role do you think the youth of Iran can play in changing the country's future? A: The youth are the architects of tomorrow. They are a potent force for transformation because of their idealism, energy, and vision. In Iran, young people are increasingly questioning the status quo and yearning for freedoms that other parts of the world take for granted. They have access to information and can see the disparities between their lives and those of their peers globally. This awareness is a catalyst for change. As such, they have the potential to drive movements for greater freedom, equality, and transparency. The government's attempts to stifle dissent through censorship and intimidation only amplify the call for change within these young minds. Q: With limited media freedom in Iran, how can stories about human rights violations continue to emerge? A: In today's digital age, suppressing information is becoming increasingly difficult. Despite rigorous efforts to control the narrative, the truth has a way of seeping out. Citizen journalism has become an indispensable tool in bringing stories to light. Social media platforms serve as alternate channels that bypass traditional media constraints. While the government may try to restrict access, virtual private networks (VPNs) and other technological tools help circumvent these barriers. The international community, too, plays a role by providing platforms for voices that cannot be heard within their own country. Q: What message would you like to convey to Iranians who may feel disillusioned or powerless? A: To those who feel disillusioned, I say, remember that the journey toward justice is long and often arduous. Progress can seem slow, but each act of defiance, no matter how small, contributes to the larger cause. Change is rarely immediate, but perseverance is key. You are not alone; countless others share your hopes and dreams. Together, you create a tapestry of resistance and hope that ripples through time and space. It's important to remain engaged, to continue speaking out, and to keep hope alive in your hearts. Remember that every step taken is a step towards a future where freedom and justice prevail.

The purple leaves of Anacampseros rufescens, a succulent species previously reported to exhibit a combination of C4 and CAM-cycling photosynthetic pathways, have long been a subject of interest in the scientific community. The purpose of this study was to investigate the ecophysiological significance of these purple leaves, which are characterized by high concentrations of anthocyanins. In arid regions, succulents often develop purple, red, or pink leaves as a means of coping with environmental stressors such as drought and high temperatures (Barker et al., 1997; Fondom et al., 2009). Manetas (2006) suggests that the production of anthocyanins in leaves may serve as a photoprotective mechanism, shielding the photosynthetic apparatus from excessive light energy. In the case of Anacampseros rufescens, the purple leaves may play a crucial role in regulating photosynthesis under conditions of drought stress. As a C4/CAM-cycling species, this succulent is well adapted to survive in arid environments, where water availability is limited. The purple leaves may serve as a mechanism to reduce water loss through transpiration, allowing the plant to conserve water and maintain photosynthetic activity. Furthermore, the anthocyanins present in the leaves may also provide antioxidant properties, protecting the plant from oxidative damage caused by high levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated during photosynthesis (Noctor et al., 2002). To investigate the ecophysiological significance of the purple leaves, we conducted a series of experiments to examine the effects of drought stress on photosynthesis and antioxidant activity in Anacampseros rufescens. We used a combination of gas exchange measurements, chlorophyll fluorescence, and biochemical assays to assess the responses of the plant to drought stress. Our results show that the purple leaves of Anacampseros rufescens exhibit a significant reduction in photosynthetic activity under drought stress, accompanied by an increase in antioxidant activity. These findings suggest that the purple leaves may play a crucial role in regulating photosynthesis and protecting the plant from oxidative damage under conditions of drought stress. In conclusion, the purple leaves of Anacampseros rufescens are an intriguing example of the complex adaptations that have evolved in succulent plants to cope with environmental stressors. Further research is needed to fully understand the ecophysiological significance of these purple leaves and to explore the potential applications of this knowledge in the development of drought-tolerant crops.

First I started college, then I became a liberal. And when I say "became" I mean it. I wasn't a closeted liberal, I just didn't know how to think about things for myself. I had to learn how to question everything. Everything. It took awhile. Now I don't even like to use the word "liberal." Too easy to label people, too easy to dismiss them. So now I am a progressive. And I still question everything. Especially religion. To be fair, I still do pray sometimes. When I'm stressed, or sad, or sick, or scared. But I don't pray to Jesus. I pray to myself. Or whatever deity is out there that might listen to me. I don't call him/her/it God anymore, because it's too easy to label people. I don't go to church anymore, because I find it boring, and hypocritical, and sexist. I don't volunteer anymore, because I'm lazy and selfish. I don't vote anymore, because all the candidates suck. I don't date anymore, because guys make me nervous and don't understand me. I don't have friends anymore, because everyone sucks. I don't eat anymore, because food makes me fat. See? I'm a total mess. I'm not sure why I'm telling you this. Maybe because I want to be honest about where I am, and maybe you'll relate to it. Or maybe it's because I want to tell you that Christmas doesn't matter to me anymore. I'm not trying to offend anyone who does celebrate it, although I probably will anyway. I just don't see the point. I can't pretend to believe in something I no longer believe in. I can't celebrate a holiday that doesn't mean anything to me. And I can't act like it's fun to buy gifts for people I hardly know. Even though I do enjoy giving gifts, I hate being told what to buy someone. I like giving gifts to people I care about, not random people who I only know from work or school. It feels fake. I wish I were Christian again. I'd probably be a lot happier. I miss having a community, having beliefs, having a purpose. I miss singing hymns. I miss the hope. But I don't want to lie about what I believe. I don't want to fake it. And I certainly don't want to be pressured into doing something I don't believe in. So I guess that's my issue with Christmas. I don't want to do it. I won't do it. I don't have to do it. You can't make me do it. So I'll try to stay away from it as much as possible. I'll smile at the decorations and the songs and the lights. I'll watch the movies and drink hot cocoa. I'll try not to be a Grinch. But I won't sing along with Bing Crosby. I won't put up a tree. I won't wrap presents. I won't hang stockings. I won't bake cookies. I won't decorate gingerbread houses. I won't spend money on gifts I don't need. I won't worry about whether or not Santa brings me presents. Because I don't need presents. I don't need to pretend to believe in something I don't. I don't need to feel guilty about not believing. I don't need to be religious. I don't need to be Christian. I don't need to be anything. I'm okay with that. I'm okay with not believing. I'm okay with not caring. I'm okay with not following tradition.

Majestic, unfurling before me like a grand tapestry woven of vibrant greens and cerulean skies, the expanse of Africa is not just land; it is a living entity, pulsating with the rhythm of life, teeming with unseen perils lurking behind every vibrant flower and beneath every shadow of ancient trees. It's a paradise, Smithy! Gaze upon it while we still can, for it is just as likely to swallow you whole as it is to embrace you in its arms. I could feel the weight of the danger intertwined with the beauty of the sights around me. The beachlands morphed into rugged hills, hills that beckoned and threatened, cloaked in the mystery of their unknowns. Elephant majesties moved through the underbrush, trunks swaying gently, their very existence a defiance against the encroachment of man. There was both ferocity and grace in their movement-like spirits, almost. I swallowed hard, the unbidden gasps of awe caught within the confines of my throat. Before I could gather my thoughts, a sudden, chilling sound shattered the peace-a distant roar, raw and primal. That is when the unsettling realization dawned upon me, the electric atmosphere charged with the intoxicating essence of the wild. It sparked a flame in my chest. Dangerous beauty! All around were whispers of danger, suggesting that steel rails might hew through landscapes rich with life and suffering. My heart, there in that moment, sang a curious melody of fear and eagerness. And yet, I was not alone. My companions, their voices laden with ignorance to the risks ahead, chattered incessantly. "Once we finish the bridge, we'll continue onward toward Nairobi! Just think of the glory, Patterson!" They were bright-eyed fools, eager for promotion and the sweet nectar of notoriety. Ignorance is bliss, was it not? With each jubilant exclamation, I felt the specter of fate loom closer, affirming that with every dream chased, darkness lurked just beneath the surface. John Henry Patterson, keep your chin up; you've accepted this challenge. No man worth his salt would merely stand by while glory beckoned. We reached the Tsavo, and my breath caught as I beheld the roaring waters, the formidable entity whose depths I was to conquer with my vision and labor. "This river will bend to our will," I muttered, an affirmation spoken more for my sake than that of the murky waters. As the sun hung low, casting a golden hue, the river was a thundering beast, willing, but not yet tamed. But the whispers grew louder, the tales of the creatures that roamed these lands-a lion, a hunger, a presence known but unseen. The locals spoke in hushed tones of their nightly adventures; "When the sun falls, it is not safe. The spirits rise with the moon." My men brushed aside these warnings-unfounded legends to them, folklore to ridicule. They laughed as if the very earth below could not feel the tension building in response to their hubris. One fool in particular, a stout man with a bristling beard, swore he could tame a lion with but a glance. "Bring forth the beasts," he laughed, "I fear no specter!" Oh, the folly of man, how blinding it can be! As dusk settled in, it felt like the world had shifted into a new plane-ominous, yet beautiful; inviting, yet fraught with danger. I told myself these tales were merely shadows of fear-after all, we were builders of worlds, constructs of steel and ambition. But in the midnight air, as stars twinkled like the eyes of unknown watchful beings, I couldn't shake the feeling that we were mere players in a stage far grander than ourselves, and my heart raced with both dread and anticipation.

The discovery has raised concerns that the captain may have had a connection to terrorist groups, who often use untraceable SIM cards to communicate. Investigators are treating the call as a potentially significant lead, as anyone buying a pay-as-you-go SIM card in Malaysia is required to provide their identity card or passport number. The captain's estranged wife, Faizah Khan, is also set to be questioned in detail by investigators. As I sat in the cozy parlor of Ellermore, the fire casting flickering shadows across the walls, I found myself drawn into the warmth of their familial camaraderie. The low murmur of voices, punctuated by laughter and light-hearted banter, enveloped me like a soft shawl. Charlotte, or Chatty as her brothers affectionately dubbed her, seemed to radiate an unassailable spirit, her presence a beacon of warmth and laughter that made the room feel like a sanctuary amid the chill of the Scottish evening. Her brothers, boisterous Charley and more reserved James, took turns regaling me with tales of their childhood exploits, their mischievous interludes sparking images of a happy, chaotic household. I could almost hear the echoes of their youthful laughter spilling out into the sun-drenched gardens of their family home, where the scent of blooming heather mingled with the crisp air of autumn. It struck me as remarkable how the sickness that had threatened to overshadow their lives only seemed to have further bound them together in resilience. They spoke of the little ones with such love and pride, and yet it was the forbearance shown by Charlotte that held a special reverence in their voices. "We owe her a great deal," James remarked one evening, as we shared a bottle of whisky on the fringes of night. "She not only cared for little Harry and the rest when they fell ill, but she steadfastly stood where Mother would have. It has been a trying time, yet Chatty always rises above it." His eyes, usually so composed, shone with a gratitude deep as the lochs that surrounded us. Their mother's passing had been a shadow over their formative years, and her absence clearly hewed a contour in their lives that was both a pang and a point of pride. As the week unfurled, the rugged beauty of Scotland outside became a canvas for my unfolding narrative alongside this charming family. I found an unexpected joy in joining them on their excursions, trekking through the highlands, where the heather blossomed in riotous purples and greens against the slate-grey sky. The air was tinged with the saltiness of the sea, a briny whisper that seemed to buoy our spirits as we hiked along steep cliffs. In these moments, Charlotte's laughter harmonized with the bleating of sheep, and her voice, lilting and clear, would rise above the landscape like an aria performed to the rugged concert of nature around us. One afternoon, we found ourselves atop a craggy overlook, overlooking a vast expanse of shimmering water below. I watched as Charlotte, standing with her hair whipping in the wind, appeared both fierce and gentle-a guardian spirit of the wilds around us. Her brothers stood a few paces behind, their teasing banter momentarily forgotten, drawn into the momentous beauty of the scene and the reciprocity of their sister's spirit. "Chatty, don't go too close to the edge!" Charley yelled, the protective note in his voice unmistakable. Yet there was a pride beneath it, too-a recognition of the tenacity that defined her. Charlotte turned, her bright eyes dancing with mischief, and for a moment I glimpsed the depth of her heart-the burden and the joy of bearing familial love and responsibility alike. "Fear not!" she called back, stretching her arms wide as if to embrace the majestic world before us. "I'm here to savor every breath of it." In that fleeting moment, standing against the unrelenting winds, surrounded by her family, she seemed impossibly free.

A wide range of tracer properties has been tested for the identification of sediment sources (Bainbridge et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017; Collins and Walling, 2002; Collins et al., 2017b; Estrany et al., 2010; Grimshaw and Lewin, 1980; Haddadchi et al., 2013; Hatfield and Maher, 2009; Mckinley et al., 2013; Nosrati et al., 2018b; Palazon and Navas, 2017; Walling et al., 1999). Geochemical tracers are, however, the most widely used in published studies to date (D'Haen et al., 2012; Froger et al., 2018; Haddadchi et al., 2014, 2013; Hughes et al., 2009; Koiter et al., 2013; Nosrati et al., 2018b; Olley and Caitcheon, 2000) because of their frequent ability to discriminate strongly among different sources and to apportion sources of fine-grained sediment with reasonable levels of uncertainty (Malhotra et al., 2018). The use of one single tracer to apportion sources is inappropriate given the inherent risk of spurious source-sediment matches (Carter et al., 2003; Collins et al., 1998; Malhotra et al., 2018; Mukundan et al., 2012; Walling et al., 1999; Zhou et al., 2016). In response, so-called composite fingerprinting approaches have been developed based on combining several tracer properties into fingerprints. The use of such "composite signatures" provides a more reliable and consistent means for determining sediment sources (Walling et al., 1999), reduces the likelihood of false source-sediment links and often provides the scope for discriminating more sources (Collins et al., 1998, 2017b). In this study, a composite fingerprinting approach, using statistical validation of different composite signatures, and a multivariate Bayesian un-mixing model, was applied for determining the relative contribution of each of three sub-basins of the Kamish River, in Iran, to downstream target bed sediment samples collected on the main stem. Land managers and policy makers frequently seek information on the contributions of sediment from individual source types, classified for example, on the basis of generic land use categories such as arable or grass, but also including additional sources such as channel banks, since this type of source classification scheme provides a clear means of selecting relevant mitigation measures capable of reducing sediment mobilization associated with tillage methods, livestock management or fluvial scour of channel margins. In larger catchments, however, where land use patterns can be complicated, and the contributions from individual source types more spatially variable, provision of such information exclusive of some form of underpinning spatial information on the general sources of sediment problems, is not necessarily supportive of decision making which is commonly based on limited resources for on-the-ground follow-up and intervention planning. Here, previous work applying sediment fingerprinting procedures has adopted an alternative approach to the classification of potential sources, based on tributary sub-catchments (e.g., Caitcheon, 1993; Collins et al., 1997; Hardy et al., 2010; Nosrati et al., 2018a; Stone et al., 2014; Vale et al., 2016; Wilkinson et al., 2013).

Yet his picture ended up in a trash can... completely unrecognized... at one of the most important TV animation studios in town. I'm not picking on FilmRoman when I point this out. The same could have happened at any studio, even the one this man made billions of dollars for over the years. Think about that for a second and let it soak in. How can we as artists "see further" like Isaac Newton if our collective memory is so short, we don't even recognize the pioneers who made everything we do possible? This is the sort of shortsightedness that's led to stories in the press announcing that hand drawn animation is obsolete. Hand drawn animation is no more replaceable by computer graphics than drawing and painting are replaced by photography. Cartooning is an irreplaceable artform, not an expendable technique. Tonight, we're here to honor the creative achievements of a team of artists who pulled together to make one of the most successful hand drawn animated films of all time. I would bet that just about all of us here tonight have pretty much the same question on our minds... How can the art of hand drawn animation return to the creative peak it enjoyed just a few short years ago? Again, I'm going to give you a second to think about that question and let it soak in. The Board of Directors of ASIFA-Hollywood has been thinking long and hard about that question. We've determined that, as an organization, it's time for us to go beyond just screenings and the Annie Awards. It's time for us to build something that ASIFA-Hollywood's founders, Bill Scott, June Foray and Bill Littlejohn envisioned as a goal for our organization nearly forty years ago... a museum, library and archive devoted to the art of animation... an institution dedicated to documenting, preserving and promoting those broad shoulders we all stand upon. The first step in achieving this goal is the establishment of something the founders of ASIFA could never have imagined... a "virtual archive"... A computer database containing hundreds of thousands of digital files representing animation drawings, model sheets, pencil tests, background paintings, book and magazine illustrations, cartoons, voice over reels, interviews, information and movies... all searchable by keyword. In short, the ultimate artist's clip file. We all know that the major studios in town maintain their own archives to preserve the documents related to their particular productions, ASIFA-Hollywood's archive will be unique, because it will be dedicated to documenting and serving the people who actually make animated films... the artists. ASIFA-Hollywood is in an unique position to be able to pull together a wide range of material for its archive... a much broader scope than any corporate archive could ever hope to encompass.
