The days when she had gone to school at home seemed like bright pictures out of a story-book now, especially the Saturdays when she and Jack used to walk through the woods together. How the red squirrels chattered as they ran along ahead of them, jumping from tree to tree, and then turning to sit up and scold saucily before running away again. How the rabbits dodged behind the fallen logs and under the brushwood piles, and then peeped out at them with their bright black eyes! And how she and Jack used to laugh when they saw them, and try to think of new names to call them by. They had named every rabbit, squirrel, bird and snake in those woods, and now they must all miss Jack and her, and wonder why they stayed away. It almost broke Joyce's heart to think of the disappointment of the two faithful dogs, that used to meet them at the end of the lane, and follow them through the woods. "Oh, dear, dear, dear," sighed Joyce, as she opened her eyes again, and looked down at the bare gravel paths below. It was not a pleasant prospect. Even the beds of gay geraniums and heliotrope had been emptied of their summer bloom, and nothing but stiff rows of dead stalks remained to show where they had stood. It was so unlike anything that she had ever known at home, that it added another dreary touch to the loneliness of her surroundings. She was still gazing disconsolately down, when a sudden movement among the branches below attracted her attention. Parks and Rec, that show just brought a whole new level of appreciation to the art of whiskey sipping, and honestly, I can't say I'm complaining. Those characters made it seem so rich and meaningful, didn't they? Ron Swanson with his love for bourbon-man, that inspired me to explore beyond just the shots of tequila I was used to, you know? It's more about the experience; the whole process of tasting, savoring, and enjoying a drink reflects life, in a sense. So, this whole whiskey journey has turned into a hobby, right? It's not just about getting buzzed anymore. Golly-can you imagine a better way to unwind after a long day than sitting back with a nice glass of Scotch? Yeah, you can feel that warm hug from the inside out, can't you? It's like embracing coziness while sitting in front of a crackling fire, only, well, without the fire hazard, unless it's one of those artisanal candle things people are raving about-commitment level low but ambiance high. And speaking of low commitment, that reminds me, why are people so obsessed with pseudo-deep conversations in bars? You know, the kind where someone's pouring their heart out over a pint of beer like it's confessional Sunday? I swear, you never really know if the person sitting next to you has lived the most riveting life or just learned how to string a few clever phrases together over cheap booze. Either way, it's captivating. Gully, you should get us some of those hilarious little anecdotes; I think we could fill a book with them someday. Now, don't get me started on those wild stories, man! Remember that one guy in the corner? The relentless storyteller-who couldn't hold a drink but could definitely hold an audience? Well, imagine waking up next to that guy's ridiculous tales written down, and you're just left scratching your head, mulling over whether you simply enjoyed the morbid curiosity or had your share of regret mixed in the background. Life's little quirks, I suppose. And it's fascinating; here we are, sipping this high-quality Scotch, yet you knew I'd always find a way back to tequila. That's clarity for you! But let's be real, tequila has its moments-it's got that fire, that excitement, like a legendary night out that rolls like a dramatic series finale. Just like whiskey has its fit evenings, steeped in class and sophistication, tequilas have a spontaneity baked into each bottle with its own folklore! So, what we really ought to hash out here is this base thing, this notion of what drinking means to us-are we bridging gaps in conversation, creating memories, or simply escaping the mundane? I guess it could be all of the above-or none! That's the beauty of it, isn't it? A proverbial can of worms waiting to be opened, like some grand metaphor for adulthood where the rules are few, and the ride is gloriously unpredictable. And even though we chase after that elusive eureka moment in camaraderie or find solace in shared silences, isn't it nuts that we're just scratching the surface? I mean, think about it-drinking still remains one of that few things that brings people together, cuts through the pretense, and lets us feel a tad less alone in this wild world. With that fun thought dancing into the air, I'd say it's high time we poured another drink, wouldn't you agree?

Alan studied the rhythmic movements of Carl's hands, the precision almost hypnotic in its own right, and felt an odd comfort in the familiarity of it all. "How can you work with this noise?" he shouted, trying to be heard over the clamor of machines. Carl shrugged with a smile that suggested he was quite used to it. "Once you find the rhythm, it's just music," he replied, his voice calm. He winked at Alan, with an air that bespoke of hard-earned experience. Alan nodded, though he wasn't entirely convinced. "Guess I'll be doing something quieter," Alan mused, more to himself than to Carl. He glanced at the sheets of leather waiting to be made into shoes, the weight of their task settling upon him. Yet, Alan's mind seemed adrift, distracted by Caleb's secret discovery and what it could mean. His eyes flickered over toward the exit, as if expecting someone to burst through with revelations of his own. "Ever find anything strange around here?" he asked, testing the waters of his curiosity. "Strange?" Carl echoed, furrowing his brow as if considering all the unlikely possibilities, then chuckled again. "Well, every now and then, something does pop up that makes you wonder if the factory is older than it looks... why'd you ask?" "No reason," Alan replied a bit too quickly, trying to mask his curiosity with a nonchalant shrug. He didn't feel like sharing the real reason just yet-not without more certainty of what lay within the lock box Caleb found. Carl returned his focus to the leather, his deft hands moving with practiced ease. Machines clacked and whirred around them, underscoring every word with mechanical resolve. Alan watched Carl work, appreciation turning to determination. Somehow, he knew that whatever secret Caleb guarded, whatever hidden thing lay in that box, it had the potential to change everything he understood. Outside, thunder rumbled again. The growl resonated through the factory, creating shadows where there should have been none, making the air feel thick with the anticipation of a storm long overdue. Alan felt an inexplicable chill-a warning on the wind perhaps, carrying on it questions yet answered. "Hey, Alan," Carl spoke, snapping him out of his reverie. "When's your old man gonna give you the reins?" Carl's tone was light, but Alan heard the sincerity in it-workers liked and respected Sam Parrish, and out of that affection, they extended a bit of goodwill toward Alan too. Alan shrugged again, the weight of what might be hinging on countless hidden factors beyond his reach. "Soon, I guess. Dad seems pretty fixed on it." His gaze wandered back to the entrance, where laughter and conversation filtered in from the outside world. "You'll do good," Carl reassured him, with a firm nod that was both blessing and bond. Silence settled between them again, where the sounds of industry were the only conversation needed. But for Alan, the secrets whispered by Caleb's discovery lay just beneath the surface-unspoken potential, intricate as the machinery around him, ready to spring to life.

Moreover, let's delve into the notion of leadership, irrespective of one's political allegiance. The measure of a leader shouldn't solely be intelligence by academic pedigree but by the resonance of their policies, their ability to unite, and their commitment to truth. Intelligence is a multifaceted construct; it includes empathy, foresight, and the capacity to listen-a trait often overshadowed in the cacophony of politics. Admittedly, my perspective on Bush originates not strictly from academic discourse or partisan hearsay but from observing the consequences of his decisions, the aftermath of his policies, and the enduring ramifications that often felt more detrimental than beneficial. Are these judgments premature or biased? Possibly. But isn't discourse meant to challenge, unravel, and examine these biases until clarity-or at least a semblance of it-is achieved? The crux of our argument dissolves into a deeper philosophical dissertation: what does it mean to be "right" in a world textured by myriad truths? Each conviction seems pegged to personal experiences and circumstantial evidence rather than an absolute repository of truth. Thus, in accusing you of being a conduit for "progressive ideas," I merely note an observable tendency, much as you record my perceived antipathy towards conservatives. Both observations, I wager, emerge from preconceived narratives. However, narrative is subjective. It paints our reality, colors our arguments, and guides our understanding. Absent diverse perspectives, these narratives become monochromatic, ignoring the world's complexity. This is why I choose to engage. To dissect, to navigate through verbal anarchy, searching for insights in adversarial exchanges. Certainly, communication fails when confined within echo chambers. Dialogue becomes paramount. Engagement demands more than an exchange of accusation or defense; it requires vulnerability. An acceptance that my convictions could indeed be flawed-perhaps that's the essence of meaningful discourse. A willingness to admit inadequacy and recalibrate accordingly. In addressing the attributes of socialism vis-a-vis capitalist orthodoxy, perhaps the discussion ought to pivot towards utility: which system, or blend thereof, improves the net welfare? Capitalism fosters innovation and ambition, yet often disregards equity. Socialism, while advocating for fairness, can sometimes stifle individual enterprise. Somewhere between these poles lies a synthesis of the beneficial. In the geopolitical theatre, both ideologies become adversaries, often missing the vital point: governance is about people, not control of resources or ideology. Embracing this could perhaps justify our common endeavor to create structures that work, as opposed to relentless ideological jousting. Ultimately, the discourse is a tapestry woven of countless threads: ideology, bias, truth, and fallacy interwoven. In this weaving, the pursuit is not dominance, but understanding. While this exchange was provoked by differing views of a singular political figure, it echoes larger societal debates. In closing-though my earlier stance was to abandon this dispute-I realize this interplay might just be the lifeblood of democracy. This space of contentious, earnest, chaotic debate is where discovery happens. So perhaps these words aren't wasted, but rather invested in a larger cause: the perpetual quest for meaning, relevance, and perhaps, reconciliation amidst discord.

Fjelldal et al. (2015) clearly showed fewer vertebral and jaw malformations at seawater transfer and harvest in triploid Atlantic salmon fed higher P inclusion in freshwater (9.4 vs. 7.1 g total P kg-1). Results suggest freshwater developmental stages in triploids require higher P inclusion for correct skeletal development. One of the factors that may influence the observed differences in skeletal development and associated nutritional requirement between triploids and diploids is growth rate. Vertebral mineralisation can be compromised during periods of accelerated growth (Hansen et al., 2010). Elevated rearing temperatures for Atlantic salmon juveniles result in faster growth accompanied by poor vertebral mineralisation through disrupted bone and cartilage formation (Ytteborg et al., 2010). Instances of faster growth alongside higher incidence of vertebral deformities in triploid Atlantic salmon have been reported (Leclercq et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2012) and may indicate dietary requirements could be greater for triploids than their diploid counterparts. Higher P and protein diets have been shown to stabilise severity of malformations and sustain faster growth in seawater for triploid Atlantic salmon (Smedley et al., 2016). Faster growth in diploids coincide with increased bone density and expression of igf-I receptor in bone (Wargelius et al., 2005), where local expression may be associated with initiating extracellular matrix (ECM) production. Hence, accelerated growth factors anticipated in triploid freshwater growth may impact regulation of mineralisation of the ECM. Environmental factors that induce accelerated growth in diploid Atlantic salmon such as high temperature, have also led to vertebral fusions and associated upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase 13 (MMP-13) (Wargelius et al., 2010) and downregulation of osteogenic marker collagen typ I 1 (Col1a1) (Ytteborg et al., 2010). MMP-13 is a matrix metalloproteinase which is involved in the degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM) associated with chronic inflammatory responses characterised by bone remodelling and leading to deformity. Collectively, given the known differences in growth performance between diploids and triploids these osteogenic biomarkers may be useful in elucidating mechanisms for triploid associated skeletal deformity and the role of dietary P in homeostatic mechanisms of bone growth. Hydroxyapatite, the key mineral component of bone, synthesis is dependent on phosphate (PO43-) and calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis which is systemically regulated primarily through circulating parathyroid hormone (PTH), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)2D] and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23; Martin et al., 2012). These factors regulate PO43- intestinal absorption, remodelling in bone and excretion in kidney, through sodium-phosphate cotransporter (Npt2a) activity, according to demand and availability. Increased kidney Npt2a activity is observed under periods of dietary PO43- restriction in rainbow trout (Sugiura et al., 2003), however, little research has been conducted on these P-bone homeostasis pathways in salmonids, let alone triploid fish (Fjelldal et al., 2015). In other vertebrates, FGF23 secretions are known to be directly induced through expression of fgf23 from osteoblasts and osteocytes, the mineralising osteogenic cells in bone, and promote renal PO43- resorption with coordination of [1,25(OH)2D] (Martin et al., 2012).

As they approached the cutting-shed, the air was filled with the sweet, heady scent of apricots, and the soft rustle of leaves as the fruit was sorted and prepared for drying. Mrs. Tiffany's eyes sparkled with pleasure as she watched the women and girls at work, their faces intent on the task at hand. Judge Tiffany, too, seemed to relax, his eyes crinkling at the corners as he watched his wife's pleasure. "Ah, yes, Olsen has indeed overloaded that team," he said, his voice low and soothing. "I'll have to speak to him about it. We can't have those horses overworked." Mrs. Tiffany nodded, her eyes still on the workers. "Yes, it's a pity. Olsen is a good man, but sometimes he gets carried away with his enthusiasm." As they watched, a young girl, no more than twelve years old, caught Mrs. Tiffany's eye. She was working with a group of older girls, her hands moving quickly and surely as she sliced the apricots. Mrs. Tiffany's gaze lingered on the girl, her expression softening. "Ah, that's Emily," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. "She's one of our new girls. Her family came out from the city a few weeks ago. I'm not sure how they'll make out, but they seem a hardworking lot." Judge Tiffany's eyes followed his wife's gaze, and he nodded. "Yes, we'll have to keep an eye on them. It's not easy for city people to adjust to country life." Mrs. Tiffany's eyes flashed with amusement. "Oh, I think they'll do all right. They're eager to learn. And Emily, in particular, has a natural talent for this sort of work. She's been a big help already." As they continued to watch, Emily looked up, her eyes meeting Mrs. Tiffany's. For a moment, the two women held each other's gaze, and Mrs. Tiffany felt a pang of recognition. She saw in Emily's eyes a spark of the same determination, the same sense of purpose that had driven her own life. "Ah, I think we should go over and see how they're doing," she said, her voice a little firmer. "I want to make sure they're not overexerting themselves." Judge Tiffany nodded, and together they walked over to the cutting-shed, their footsteps quiet on the dusty ground. As they approached, the women and girls looked up, their faces breaking into smiles as they saw the judge and his wife. Mrs. Tiffany's eyes sparkled with pleasure as she surveyed the scene before her, the warm sun beating down on her face, the scent of apricots filling her nostrils. It was moments like these that made her feel grateful for this life, for the simple pleasures and quiet joys that it brought her.

Consequently, overcoming these challenges necessitates the implementation of comprehensive monitoring and risk assessment protocols throughout the lifespan of the CCS operation. These protocols are designed to provide early detection of potential issues and to mitigate any adverse effects that may arise during the injection process (Meyer et al., 2016). Enhanced monitoring techniques, including advanced geophysical methods and continuous fluid sampling, are essential to ascertain the integrity of geological formations designated for CO2 storage. By employing these methods, operators can gain vital insights into the behavior of the subsurface environment and maintain the operational efficacy of storage sites. In parallel with enhanced monitoring, the development of predictive models is crucial to adequately simulate the long-term storage scenario. These models can help ascertain the interactions between injected CO2 and the surrounding geological integrity, providing an essential framework for anticipating any deviations from expected performance (Kuuskraa and Smith, 2012). Leveraging sophisticated modeling software allows engineers and geoscientists to visualize fluid migration within geological formations, evaluate potential leakage scenarios, and optimize injection strategies to ensure adherence to environmental safety standards. Moreover, the economic viability of CCS projects is closely intertwined with regulatory frameworks governing carbon emissions and storage practices. Stakeholder engagement and a transparent policy approach can significantly enhance public acceptance and investment in CCS technologies. Governments, industry leaders, and environmental organizations must collaborate to create a cohesive policy landscape that encourages research, promotes pilot projects, and facilitates dialogue on regulatory matters. Furthermore, financial incentives, such as carbon credits or subsidies, can stimulate participation in the CCS sector and bolster the deployment of carbon capture technologies across diverse industry applications. It is also imperative to recognize the educational aspect of advancing CCS. A robust outreach initiative aimed at informing both the public and decision-makers about the benefits and risks associated with carbon capture and storage can play a pivotal role in shaping societal perspectives. Fostering awareness around the importance of reducing atmospheric CO2 levels and actively participating in climate change mitigation efforts can galvanize community support for CCS projects. This is particularly vital in regions with potential storage sites, where local populations may have inherent concerns about geological interventions. In addition, advancing CCS technology requires sustained investment in research and development to explore innovative carbon capture methodologies and novel geological configurations for storage. Breakthroughs in materials science may yield advanced sorbents or solvents that enhance CO2 capture efficiency while simultaneously reducing energy consumption, making the carbon capture process not only more effective but also economical. Research into alternative storage formations, such as saline aquifers and basalt formations, may reveal additional avenues for greater CO2 sequestration potential. The global imperative to address climate change propelled by increasing CO2 concentrations champions CCS as a critical component in our collective journey towards a sustainable energy future. The deployment of CCS is poised to mitigate emissions from hard-to-abate sectors, including cement and steel production, thus unlocking pathways to profoundly lower national and global carbon footprints. As we forge ahead, it is crucial to adopt an integrated approach that encompasses technological advancement, policy support, and stakeholder engagement, ensuring that CCS fulfills its promise as a cornerstone of our climate strategies. In this relentless pursuit, the fusion of science, societal will, and strategic foresight will lay the groundwork for effective climate action, transforming ambitions into tangible achievements.

'Useless Beauty' contains a particularly detailed consideration of the human condition for example, including the summation that; "it is thanks to our intelligence, that trifling accident, that we can never feel at home in a world which was not made for such as us, which was never intended to shelter, nourish, and satisfy reasoning beings". De Maupassant writes about life, death, liberation and entrapment, making him an engaging author from an existential viewpoint. The contribution of this article is twofold. First, it introduces the tourism-in-literature approach. This is a method for data collection and interrogation using literary sources, with the assumption that works of literature may both reflect and shape contextual representations and interpretations of tourism and thus be a useful resource for enriched understanding. Overlap is with Tribe's (2008) explanation of 'virtual curating' (albeit with a tighter literary focus), whereby interrogating art adds to representation and interpretation in tourism, whilst also addressing the lack of methodological innovation within the discipline. The tourism-in-literature research approach may complement but is distinctive from literary tourism, described as a leisure activity associated with literary influences (Squire, 1994); a specific type of tourism where people are drawn to locations associated with an author or their writing (Hoppen, Brown, & Fyall, 2014). Likewise literary geography/tourism, which considers the association of narrative space with particular frame settings, appreciating the ways in which text and space, fiction and location, might be understood as inseparable and co-productive (Hones, 2011). Instead, tourism-in-literature is adjacent to that which has been introduced in marketing as the overlapping marketing-in-literature and literature-in-marketing sub-genres (Brown, 1999). These assume that literary and art theory can be a fertile source of ideas and interpretations when analysing marketing (Stern & Schroeder, 1994), that the collective recognition of literary masterpieces can make these useful tools for engagement (Brown, 1999), and hence that adding literary methods to philosophical and historical ones may provide richer insights into reading marketing theory (Stern, 1990). More specifically applying to tourism studies, there is a similar connection between literature and tourism, with travel frequently represented in literature. Towner's (1984) review of the grand tour for example, draws upon descriptions of tourism in contemporary fiction. Meanwhile, Alex Garland's (1996) novel 'The Beach' explores the possibilities of late 20th Century backpacking and is brought by Scheyvens (2002) into her review of backpacker culture. As yet however, such literary analyses have been little adopted within tourism studies and not explicitly in terms of approach. According to Robinson and Andersen (2002) literature in the sense of fiction or creative writing is an important but under-used instrument through which we can explore the nature, development and meaning of tourism. Second, in order to illustrate the application and usefulness of literature-in-tourism, the intersection of existentialism and tourism as represented and interpreted by De Maupassant is considered by this paper.

Monday, May 17, 2004 I woke up to the bright Vegas sunshine streaming through the cracks in the curtains. Lauren was still asleep, snuggled under the covers. I lay there for a few moments, relishing the coziness and the prospect of an entire day ahead in this vibrant city. Eventually, the sound of shuffling and murmurs from the hallway nudged me out of bed. By the time Lauren stirred and groggily joined the world of the living, I was already halfway through my first cup of coffee. We decided to hit the breakfast buffet, which, like everything in Vegas, was excessive and glorious. Towers of pastries, fruit, pancakes, eggs-everything you could imagine and more. We piled our plates high and found a spot by the window where we could watch the city gradually come to life. The early morning sun reflected off the buildings, casting bright spots over the sidewalks and streets. After breakfast, we decided to explore the strip and soak in the sights. The air was warm and dry, a gentle breeze tugging at our hair as we walked. There were people everywhere-tourists snapping photos, street performers entertaining small crowds, and the ever-present hum of conversation. Each hotel was a world in itself, extravagantly themed and larger than life. We wandered into the Venetian, and I couldn't help but marvel at the replica of the Grand Canal, gondolas and all. The day flew by in a blur of colors and sounds. We slipped into shops filled with shimmering trinkets, and I snapped photos of everything-dazzling lights, quirky street art, and the constant parade of people. We stopped for snacks now and then, trying out gelato here, a pretzel there. Vegas was a city of indulgence, and we were more than willing participants. In the afternoon, we ducked into a dimly lit casino, not to gamble, but simply to experience the atmosphere. The sound of slot machines mingled with the shuffle of cards and the occasional cheer from a table. It was a sensory overload of the best kind, an energy that was both electric and intoxicating. As luck would have it, we found a quiet corner and sat for a while, taking everything in. Once the sun started to dip towards the horizon, we headed back to our hotel to freshen up and rest before our evening plans. The city by night was an entirely different creature, and we were eager to see it all. For dinner, we made reservations at a rooftop restaurant. The view was unparalleled, with the sparkling lights of the strip stretching out before us and the mountains silhouetted against the sunset sky. It felt like we were on top of the world as we enjoyed our meal, sharing laughs and recounting the day's adventures. After dinner, we roamed the streets again, now alive with neon lights and music at every turn. We ended the night with a visit to a famous fountain show, joining a crowd of onlookers as the water danced and swayed to classical tunes. The air was cool, and I felt a shiver of contentment, knowing that this was only the beginning of our Vegas escapade.

Engaging in the metaphorical wrestling match that is political commentary, one cannot help but recognize the resilience of certain talking points, as they surface again and again like an indestructible whack-a-mole. The President's assurance that today's challenges would be met with unwavering resolve is a refrain we've heard before, each time adorned with varying degrees of theatrical gravitas. Yet, with the national economy still entrenched in a sluggish recovery and global tensions simmering on high heat, this well-rehearsed composition seems less like an orchestra and more like a steady drumbeat leading us to the edge of a cliff. As we plunge deeper into this political masquerade, it's clear that the art of promising and doing are two distinctly different crafts, much like comparing finger painting to the Sistine Chapel. The clear lack of mention of key figures, essential past promises, or even a simple acknowledgment of monumental tragedies strikes one as selective amnesia. It's as if the President stood before the nation, armed with a map, yet opted to rely on his internal compass - one that suspiciously lacks bearings. A dangerous endeavor when steering the ship of state. Our self-styled Captain navigates these choppy waters with words like "evil" marking the charts, a conveniently ambiguous term deployed to conveniently fill gaps where policy detail should dare tread. Each use of "evil" carries a punch aimed more at emotional strings than intellectual rigor. It's a rhetorical firework, brilliant in its fleeting impact, yet leaving nothing but smoke and a faint echo. In this rhetorical dance, let's nod to Nancy Pelosi, who, seizing the moment with the dexterity of a chess grandmaster, found the address infinitely amusing. Perhaps not in content, but rather in execution, a shadow play of words without the weight of intent. Her restrained laughter, echoed by those with a penchant for the absurd, resonated through the political corridors-an odd anthem for these strange times. Yet these anomalies are deftly punctuated by the President's nod to timeless platitudes: the inherited challenges, those passed from generation to generation, now squared onto his resolute shoulders. Such noble proclamations unfold like a script from a blockbuster saga-a fictive cinematic universe where victory is merely a montage away. However, unlike Hollywood, reality lacks this convenient fast-forward button. As these theatrics unfold, one can only wonder if this is what we've always expected from the political theater-a place where bold declarations echo louder than nuanced dialogues, and the laugh track, whether audible or implicit, is a staple part of the experience. So, as the pundits march forth, with their pens poised to gloss this speech with gilded praise or scathing critique, the rest of us observe, like spectators at a peculiar blend of gladiator sport and Shakespearean tragedy. The pages of reality flip forward, indifferent to the scriptwriters, and we march on, grappling with each multifaceted challenge-aware that beneath the bombast, we remain ever hopeful that the tune itself might change. For now, however, we sit through another act, waiting for the plot to advance, hoping that, in time, the rhetoric will give way to resonant substance. Until then, the laugh track remains at the ready, poised to punctuate the unfolding spectacle with irony and wit.

As she grew older, Rosalie's fascination with her father only intensified. She would watch him with an unwavering gaze, mesmerized by the way he moved, the way he spoke, the way he seemed to command the very air around him. Her mother and sisters would often try to engage her in conversation, but Rosalie's attention would always wander back to her father, her eyes fixed on him as if she feared missing some crucial detail. Her mother would sigh and shake her head, but Rosalie didn't care; she was too busy drinking in the wonder of her father's presence. Everything about him was extraordinary, from the way he strode across the room to the way he laughed, a deep, rumbling sound that seemed to shake the very foundations of the house. Even the way he ate his breakfast was a marvel to Rosalie, the way he devoured his eggs and bacon with a relish that was almost animalistic. Her mother and sisters would nibble at their toast and sip their tea, but her father attacked his meal with a gusto that left Rosalie breathless. And then, of course, there were the stories. Oh, the stories he would tell! Tales of adventure and bravery, of daring feats and narrow escapes. Rosalie would sit at his feet, her eyes wide with wonder, as he regaled her with stories of his own childhood, of the time he had climbed to the top of the highest tree in the forest, or the time he had wrestled a bear to the ground. Her mother would roll her eyes good-naturedly, but Rosalie didn't care; she was too busy basking in the glory of her father's exploits. As she grew older, Rosalie began to realize that not everyone saw her father in the same way. Her friends at school would talk about their own fathers, and Rosalie would listen, amazed, as they spoke of men who were kind and gentle, who helped with the household chores and played games with their children. Rosalie couldn't imagine her father doing such things; her father was a giant, a titan, a god. He didn't do ordinary things; he did extraordinary things, things that left her breathless and awestruck. And yet, despite her father's larger-than-life presence, Rosalie began to feel a growing sense of unease. She would watch him, mesmerized, as he dominated the room, but she would also catch glimpses of her mother, tired and worn, her eyes red-rimmed from lack of sleep. She would see her sisters, quiet and deferential, their eyes cast down as they waited on their father's every whim. And she would wonder, fleetingly, if perhaps her father's extraordinary nature came at a cost, if perhaps his dominance was not quite as natural and ordinary as she had always assumed. But the thought would flit away, lost in the tidal wave of her father's presence, and Rosalie would be left, once again, enthralled and entranced by the wonder of her wonderful father.

"...nor need they be. The court is a place for ceremonies and etiquette, where knights are bound by strict rules and conventions, whereas the field of chivalry is a realm of freedom and adventure, where a knight-errant can roam unfettered, guided solely by his conscience and the code of honor. Besides, my dear housekeeper, I have already tried my hand at court life, and found it wanting. The petty intrigues, the backbiting, the endless flattery - no, no, my heart yearns for the open road, the thrill of the unknown, the clash of steel on steel." The housekeeper sighed, shaking her head in despair. "You are as stubborn as a mule, senor. You will not listen to reason, nor heed the warnings of those who care for you. Very well, go your way, but do not say I did not warn you. You will come to grief, mark my words." Don Quixote smiled, his eyes twinkling with amusement. "Fear not for me, dear housekeeper. I have the blessing of the heavens, and the favor of the ladies. What more could a knight-errant ask for? Besides, I have my trusty squire, Sancho Panza, to guide me and keep me out of harm's way." Sancho, who had been listening to the conversation with great interest, now spoke up. "Ah, yes, your worship, I'll be there to look out for you, never fear. But, if I may be so bold, might I suggest that we take a few precautions before setting out? A bit of food, a flask of wine, a good horse -" Don Quixote waved his hand impatiently. "Enough, Sancho. We shall not be delayed by such petty concerns. Our quest is a noble one, and we must not be swayed by base considerations. We shall set out at dawn, and the road shall provide for us." The housekeeper and niece exchanged a despairing glance. They knew that once Don Quixote had made up his mind, there was no stopping him. They could only stand by and watch as he rode off into the sunset, bound for who-knew-what adventures and misadventures. As the evening drew to a close, Don Quixote retired to his chamber, his mind racing with thoughts of the journey to come. He polished his armor, sharpened his sword, and pored over his maps and guides. Sancho, meanwhile, busied himself in the kitchen, packing a small sack with provisions and muttering to himself about the foolishness of it all. The night wore on, the stars twinkling in the sky above, as the two companions prepared to set out on their latest, and perhaps most perilous, adventure yet.

Our investigation aimed to elucidate the intricate dynamics at play within these mountainous environments, seeking to understand how elevation-associated factors influence litter decomposition rates specifically for these two predominant tree species. The study sites were carefully selected, representing a range of ecological conditions, with each site reflecting varying temperature and moisture regimes as one ascends. At lower elevations, the deciduous European beech predominated, while higher elevations were characterized by the hardy Black pine, known for its resilience to harsher climatic conditions. To quantify decomposition rates, we utilized a standardized litterbag method, allowing for consistent monitoring of mass loss over time. The experimental design incorporated multiple replicates at each elevation, ensuring that fluctuations attributable to microenvironmental differences were minimized. Sampling was conducted at intervals of every three months, permitting us to track changes in litter mass and analyze the associated biotic and abiotic factors affecting decomposition. Preliminary results indicated a clear trend; litter from the Black pine decomposed at a slower rate compared to that of European beech. This finding aligns with existing literature suggesting that litter quality-characterized by factors such as carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and lignin content-exerts a profound influence on decomposition processes (Melillo et al., 1989). The differences observed can be partially attributed to the higher lignin concentrations found in the Black pine needles, which typically make them more resistant to microbial breakdown. Additionally, soil characteristics at varying elevations were scrutinized, particularly focusing on pH, moisture content, and organic matter composition. The interplay between these soil properties and microbial activity was found to be closely interconnected, with microbial biomass often peaking in soils enriched with organic matter at mid-elevations, prior to declining in higher, less fertile zones. This microbial decline was coupled with a noticeable shift in community structure, corroborating findings from studies that highlight the influence of environmental gradients on soil biota (Wardle, 2002). We also explored the potential roles of abiotic stressors in shaping both above- and belowground ecological relationships. It became evident that as one ascends, the severity of winter conditions, including extended snow cover and frost events, could drastically alter the phenology and overall biomass of vegetation. Consequently, these shifts may have cascading effects on litter composition and the subsequent decomposition processes, as certain plant species may either thrive or fail under escalated climatic stress. Further analyses will delve into the nutrient release patterns during decomposition, assessing how these fluctuating rates of nutrient availability may influence the surrounding soil nutrient status and potential plant growth rates in these alpine environments. The interplay of temperature, moisture, and litter quality presents a complex but crucial element in predicting how these high-mountain ecosystems might respond to ongoing climate change. Ultimately, our study aims to contribute to the burgeoning body of knowledge concerning climate impacts on alpine ecosystems, which are not merely remote and pristine but are, in fact, bellwethers for broader ecological changes globally. Understanding these dynamics is imperative for formulating effective conservation strategies that aim to preserve the integrity of mountain ecosystems in the face of escalating climatic uncertainties. As we hone in on the final stages of analysis and interpretation, it is our fervent hope that our findings will illuminate the profound interconnections between climate, soil, and biodiversity within these fragile environments.

This finding indicates that IOR is object-based rather than location-based and it also suggests that it is active as long as the visual input is present. In Hofler, Gilchrist, and Korner (2011) we investigated in three experiments whether and how saccadic IOR supports search when the same display is searched twice for different target letters. In line with the literature on single searches, we observed IOR during each of the two consecutive searches (see Fig. 1 for the results of Experiment 1; Hofler et al., 2011): Saccadic responses were longer when a previously inspected item as compared to a non-inspected item was probed while participants were "in the midst" of the first or the second search. However, at the time when the first search was completed, IOR seemed to be no longer active: Saccadic responses to recently inspected items of the previous search took almost the same time as saccadic responses to previously non-inspected items. This suggests that the completion of a search might lead to the reset of IOR at the end of the first search before it is resumed when a further search in the same environment is required. The finding was underpinned by a further experiment in Hofler et al. (2011) in which the participants were not allowed to complete the first search. Rather, while they were searching for the first target, search was interrupted by prompting the next target such that they had to switch to the next search immediately. As compared to a condition in which they completed the first search, IOR was active across searches in this interrupted-search condition. The finding that IOR is no longer active when a search is completed challenges some results from previous research that addressed the involvement of IOR in single searches (see above). In particular, if IOR relies on the presence of the objects in the display after a search is completed (Muller & von Muhlenen, 2000; Takeda & Yagi, 2000), we would expect that IOR is maintained across two consecutive searches in the same display (because the display does neither change nor disappear across the searches) which was not supported by our previous findings. However, whether or not IOR remains active after a search might also depend on the subsequent task. If a search is completed and no further search follows directly (as is the case in most experiments on this topic in the literature; e.g. Klein, 1988), IOR might remain active after the end of the search because it does not have any detrimental effect. However, when a further search in the same environment is required, a "reset" of IOR after the first search might ensure that the upcoming search can be conducted without compromising search efficiency due to the inhibition of previously inspected items.

The runner's stride broke. Flinging himself sidewise, he rolled bodily down a short, sandy slope, then came up fast and plunged headlong into the shelter of a grotesquely-shaped rock pillar. Aboard the cruiser, someone cursed: the amplifier picked up the echo. Voices rose angrily, only to cut off again as sharply as if slashed with a knife. And now, a new voice. A woman's voice, ragged and not quite steady: "Don't worry, Thigpen. No one's going to hurt you. You've my word for that." A little eddy of dust drifted out from behind the rock pillar; that was all. Again, the woman's voice: "This is Veta Hall, Thigpen. You don't know me, but you've probably heard of the man I'm speaking for: Pike Mawson, the adjudicator on Japetus. He wants to make a deal with you." From the rock pillar, silence only. "You needn't play coy, Thigpen. Mawson knows all about that 'life catalyst' you helped Tornelescu work out. That's why he sent us for you. He's old and crippled; he needs that catalyst himself, so he can find youth again. He'll give anything for it - anything you name. And he doesn't care how many human guinea pigs you killed developing it, or that you cut old Tornelescu's throat. He'll even help hide you from the FedGov men, if that's worrying you." The last eddy of dust from behind the rock faded away. "Please, Thigpen!" the woman begged. "Please surrender! It's suicide if you don't." A pause. "Look: you've heard of Igor Cheng, haven't you? The slaver from the Belt? Well, that's who Mawson sent with me to help bring you in - Cheng and three of his pet Belt killers. Only now that the FedGov's put a price on your head...." The woman's voice trailed off. Then, after a moment, it rose again, with such violence the amplifier screamed protest. "Don't you understand, you fool?" she cried hysterically. "If you come in now, Igor's willing to live up to his bargain with Mawson. But if you give him trouble, he'll kill you for the FedGov bounty. Only if he does that, then he'll have to murder me too, so I can't give him away to Mawson when he claims pushing you off was an accident, or self-defense, or whatever other story he decides on!" Again, silence, broken only by the whish of blowing sand and the ululations of the wind. The woman sighed audibly. "All right, Thigpen. Don't say I didn't try to give you a chance." Emptiness, defeat, had replaced the desperation in her voice. The amplifier clicked off. A moment later a landing ladder ratcheted into view below the cruiser's cylindrical hull.

Currently, the huge amount of data and the demanding hardware and computational requirements make methods based on 2-D matrix probes difficult and costly to implement (Jensen et al. 2016). Ultrasound speckle decorrelation (SDC) has shown the capability in estimating the through-plane flow velocity using a 1-D array transducer (Rubin et al. 2001; Park et al. 2013; Zhou et al. 2018). With the through-plane velocity, the flow volume can be calculated by integrating the velocity over the luminal area when the vessel is scanned in the transverse view. The principle of ultrasound SDC is that the SDC over time follows a specific Gaussian curve. This Gaussian-based relationship has been derived by (Wagner et al. 1983; Chen et al. 1997) and was used in a series of studies, including 3-D ultrasound imaging (Housden et al. 2007), blood flow estimations (Li et al. 1998; Rubin et al. 1999; Tuthill et al. 2012) and investigations of elastic tissue properties (Bamber and Bush 1995; Cespedes et al. 1999). However, the application of ultrasound SDC on estimating blood flow in arteries was limited by the low frame rate of conventional ultrasound (Rubin et al. 2001; Park et al. 2013) and the weak signals coming from blood cells. The imaging frame rate must be high enough to capture the fast signal decorrelation due to rapid flow passing through the rather small elevational dimension of the transmitted acoustic beam. In the last decade, the emergence of plane-wave ultrasound techniques, which can increase the imaging frame rate by two orders of magnitude, has greatly expanded the capability of medical ultrasound imaging. Furthermore, the advent of microbubble contrast agents can also significantly enhance the ultrasound signal from blood. Using high frame rate imaging techniques and microbubbles contrast agents, we have recently demonstrated the feasibility of the SDC method both in vitro and in vivo, showing that the maximum measurable through-plane flow velocity can be well over 1 m/s, which is physiologically equivalent to most flow in the cardiovascular system (Zhou et al. 2018). However, the current SDC method has an intrinsic limitation on differentiating the flow direction in the blood vessel. In other words, it can only estimate the through-plane flow speed but not the direction. In many parts of the cardiovascular system, there is bidirectional flow (reverse flow will occur) during certain periods of the cardiac cycle, especially when diseases exist in the vessel (Sutton et al. 1994; Bukachi et al. 2005; Tahmasebpour et al. 2005; Leow et al. 2015).

Further, it has been proposed that developing an understanding of others requires accurate representation of the self's interoceptive states (Fotopoulou & Tsakiris, 2017; Ondobaka, Kilner & Friston, 2015). Altered interoceptive processing has also been found in individuals with anxiety and depression (Ehlers, 1993; Paulus & Stein, 2006), conditions which have high co-occurrence with autism (Paulus & Stein, 2010). Indeed, anxiety-related concerns are among the most common problems presented by autistic children and adolescents in the clinic (Ghaziuddin, 2002) and empirically, a number of studies have identified higher rates of anxiety disorders and symptoms in autistic children than typically developing children (Gadow, DeVincent, Pomeroy, & Azizian, 2004; Kim, Szatmari, Bryson, Streiner, & Wilson, 2000; Muris, Sterrneman, Merchelbach, Holdrinet, & Meesters, 1998; Simonoff et al., 2008; Sukhodolsky et al., 2008; Weisbrot, Gadow, DeVincent, & Pomeroy, 2005). Of the previous investigations of interoceptive abilities in autistic individuals to date, only one included a measure of anxiety. Garfinkel et al. (2016) investigated the performance of twenty autistic adults on each of the three interoceptive dimensions they delineated, compared to twenty typical adults of similar age and gender. In addition to reduced interoceptive accuracy, they found elevated interoceptive sensibility in autistic, relative to typically developing, participants. No group differences were found in interoceptive awareness. The authors conceptualized the difference between interoceptive sensibility and interoceptive accuracy as an interoceptive trait prediction error. They found that this difference was greater in the autistic than the typical adults, and that it was predictive of anxiety symptoms; that is, the greater the prediction error, the more elevated the anxiety levels, providing a novel explanation for the elevated anxiety levels seen in autism. Consistent with this interpretation, Schmitz, Blechert, Kramer, Asbrand, and Tuschen-Caffier (2012) proposed that individuals who are more prone to anxiety also show an altered interoceptive trait prediction signal. This discrepancy between observed and expected body states triggers the symptoms of anxious affect, worrisome rumination and avoidance behaviors. Yet, the experimental literature on the role of interoception in anxiety has been mixed, and different dimensions of interoception have not been thoroughly investigated. Enhanced interoceptive accuracy has been reported to be over-represented amongst anxiety patients (Dunn et al., 2010; Pollatos et al., 2007). However, other studies show no relationship between interoceptive accuracy and anxiety (Antony et al., 1995; Barsky, Cleary, Sarnie, & Ruskin, 1994; Ehlers, Margraf, Roth, Taylor, & Birbaumer, 1988) or the reverse relationship, with higher anxiety symptoms in those with weaker interoceptive accuracy (De Pascalis, Alberti, & Pandolfo, 1984). It is unclear what is behind these divergent findings, although it is likely that low sample sizes and different measurement protocols play some role. Understanding the nature of anxiety symptoms in autism has been identified as an area that is under-researched and urgently needed for the development of appropriate treatment and intervention (Lord et al., 2005).

Furthermore, this multifaceted construct known as Big Data is not merely a trend; it represents a paradigm shift in the ways organizations and individuals interact with information. The implications of these advancements ripple across a plethora of domains, tantalizing researchers and practitioners alike with innovations that were once deemed inconceivable. Machine learning, artificial intelligence, and data analytics are at the forefront of this revolution, facilitating the processing of vast data sets that can herald new insights and augment decision-making capabilities [20]. In the realm of healthcare, for example, Big Data applications can lead to the emergence of predictive analytics, forecasting infection outbreaks or identifying potential adverse drug reactions, thus placing a premium on patient safety [21]. With wearables and bio-sensors continuously generating data markers on individual health, healthcare professionals are endowed with the means to deliver personalized medicine tailored to the distinctive needs of each patient, thereby enhancing treatment efficacy [22]. This convergence of Big Data with healthcare not only transforms patient engagement but also optimizes operational efficiency by reducing wait times and streamlining resource allocation [23]. On the economic front, Big Data is becoming a crucial asset in financial markets. Financial institutions utilize advanced algorithms processing real-time data to inform trading strategies, manage risks, and detect fraud with unprecedented accuracy [24]. The ability to analyze sentiments derived from social media platforms can also furnish financial analysts with insights into market trends, thus altering traditional models of market prediction [25]. Consequently, organizations that embrace data-driven methodologies can leapfrog their competitors, gaining a tactical advantage in a world characterized by relentless change [26]. In agriculture, Big Data heralds the dawn of precision farming, where farmers utilize data analytics to maximize crop yields while minimizing resource consumption [27]. Satellite imaging, coupled with real-time weather data and soil monitoring, can inform farmers about the optimal timing for planting, irrigation, and harvesting, ultimately promoting sustainability and food security [28]. This analytical approach empowers farmers to make timely decisions that drive both productivity and environmental stewardship. Yet, as we marvel at the endless possibilities offered by Big Data, we must also confront the myriad challenges it presents-especially concerning data privacy and security [29]. The collection, storage, and processing of immense volumes of personal data open Pandora's box regarding ownership and consent; individuals are often unaware of how their information is utilized by corporations, leading to potential abuses of data [30]. Moreover, with cyber-attacks becoming increasingly sophisticated, the necessity for robust cybersecurity measures has never been more urgent [31]. Understanding these risks accentuates the need for regulatory frameworks that will protect individuals' rights while encouraging innovation. Initiatives like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in the European Union exemplify efforts to strike a necessary balance between safeguarding personal information and fostering a data-rich economy [32]. In conclusion, as we navigate through this data-laden era, the interplay of opportunity and responsibility emerges. The potential of Big Data to revolutionize numerous sectors is matched by the imminent dangers its misuse can spawn. Hence, cultivating a culture of ethical data stewardship is paramount as we collectively forge ahead into uncharted territories of intelligence, connectivity, and collaboration, striving to unlock the true value embedded within the torrents of data that surround us.

We constructed an initial search (search #1) to identify studies reporting on individuals discharged from psychiatric inpatient care: (discharge*) AND (mental* OR psychiatr* OR schiz* OR psychos* OR psychot* OR bipolar* OR manic* OR mania* OR personality disorder* OR psychopath* OR affective OR depress* OR neurotic* OR neurosis OR neuroses). We then did search #1 in combination with outcome-focused terms: (suicid* OR overdose* OR self-harm* OR self harm* OR self-injur* OR self injur* OR self-poison* OR self poison* OR parasuic*); (violen* OR aggress* OR assault* OR attack* OR homicid* OR kill* OR murder* OR reoffend* OR re-offend* OR recidiv* OR forensic); (death* OR mortal* OR died OR dying OR fatal* OR dead* OR lethal* OR loss of life); victim*; and accident*. In the literature, adverse outcomes have been examined predominantly as single outcomes in individual studies, with differences in underlying populations, settings, and outcome definitions and measures, rendering between-study comparison of risk estimates problematic. Although the evidence bases for suicide, non-fatal self-harm, and perpetration of violence post-discharge are substantial, reports on being a victim of violence are fewer, and almost no published studies have reported on risks of serious accidental harm or death in this population. We found no published studies that have investigated a broad range of adverse outcomes in a single large cohort. Therefore, comparison of absolute or relative risks for different types of fatal and non-fatal adverse outcomes post-discharge has not been possible. Added value of this study We did a national cohort study of almost 1 64 million Danish people, examining multiple fatal and non-fatal adverse outcomes among people discharged from their first inpatient psychiatric treatment episode, and calculated absolute and relative risks versus matched individuals of the same age and sex without a history of psychiatric admission, according to length of follow-up. As we investigated an array of serious adverse outcomes, direct comparison between multiple risks in a single cohort was possible. People discharged from psychiatric care were at higher risk of all eight adverse outcomes examined versus the comparator cohort. Around one in three people discharged from such care will have experienced at least one of the adverse outcomes examined at 10 years post-discharge, with absolute risks being highest in individuals diagnosed with a psychoactive substance use disorder at first discharge, and lowest in those diagnosed with a mood disorder. Risk of committing homicide was greater than that for becoming a homicide victim, although these absolute risks were minimal. Risks of suicide and self-harm were especially elevated within 3 months of first discharge, whereas risk elevations for accidental death, violent criminality, and being hospitalised due to violence were relatively homogeneous across the 10 year follow-up period. Implications of all the available evidence People discharged from psychiatric inpatient services are prone to experiencing various serious adverse outcomes. A multi-agency approach is thus needed to reduce these risks, and no single preventive measure will suffice.

But the real unemployment rate is actually much higher, and is closer to 11% if you take into account discouraged job seekers and those working part-time involuntarily. (For more information about the real unemployment rate, see this analysis.) So while there may be plenty of available workers, they're not necessarily willing or able to fill every position that becomes vacant. In fact, according to EPI, the "jobless rate" - the percentage of people without jobs who are actively seeking employment - is now 16%, compared to 10.9% in December 2000. A report released by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia two weeks ago found that the high unemployment rate was causing wage pressures to remain subdued. Employers weren't having to offer huge salary increases to attract new employees. What's more, the report said, the sluggishness in pay had become self-reinforcing: "The lack of strong wage gains appears to be contributing to weak spending growth." In other words, lower pay means less money for consumers to spend, which slows down economic activity. If this sounds familiar, it should: It's exactly what happened during the first half of the Clinton administration, when weak consumer spending led to two recessions. Indeed, the current recovery is very similar to the Clinton-era recoveries. According to Porter, the problem then was an imbalance between the supply and demand for labor, just as it is today. Back then, though, the imbalance was caused by the so-called baby boom echo: The big wave of births after World War II meant that each year a large group of young adults entered the workforce. This created a glut of available workers, and kept wages down. Now we have a different kind of baby boom: the aging of the baby-boom generation itself. Because the population is growing older, the pool of available workers is shrinking, and consequently, wages are rising. So far, though, the upward pressure on wages isn't enough to overcome the downward pressure from the sluggish economy. Here's where things get interesting: The baby boom echo ended around 1986. And the Clinton recovery began in earnest in late 1994. Coincidence? Not likely. The reason is simple: When the baby boom echo ends, the labor market tightens up considerably, because the supply of available workers shrinks. At the same time, the demand for labor also tends to increase, because the baby boomers themselves begin to enter the peak earning years of their lives. These twin factors lead to rapid wage growth. This phenomenon helps explain why Bill Clinton's approval rating jumped from the low-30s to the mid-60s within the space of three years. With a booming stock market, rising incomes, and falling deficits, Clinton's approval rating soared. And although the economy slowed down considerably after 1997, wages continued to rise rapidly until the bursting of the dot-com bubble in March 2000. So here we are again. Paul, son of the former Texas congressman and frequent presidential candidate Ron Paul, is attracting attention with an unusual blend of Libertarian policy that hat-tips social conservatism at every turn. Gen. Keith Alexander leads the National Security Agency and routinely justifies his agency's secritive work to members of Congress and federal judges in clandestine meetings outside of public view. Obama said during a lengthy January 17 speech about U.S. signals intelligence gathering - an oration that might be a preview of the government's courtroom defense - that 'the men and women of the intelligence community, including the NSA, consistently follow protocols designed to protect the privacy of ordinary people.' 'They're not abusing authorities in order to listen to your private phone calls or read your emails,' the president insisted. His press secretary, Jay Carney, followed up ten days later with assurance during a daily briefing that 'to the extent that the NSA collects information, it is focused on valid foreign intelligence targets and not the information of ordinary Americans.' 'Look,' he told reporters, 'I mean, terrorists, proliferators, other bad actors use the same communication tools that others use.' Other Democrats who are unsympathetic to Paul's position have been more crass about it. Former Pennsylvania Gov. Ed Rendell told The Washington Times on Wednesday that the lawsuit just made him 'look like a petty politician.' 'Obviously the strategy is to appeal to the base,' Rendell said. Paul's objection focuses on the so-called bulk phone-record 'metadata' that the NSA gathers routinely. The data includes phone numbers, dates, times, and the durations of calls.

Who was he kidding, ten years ago when the opportunity for fatherhood had presented itself his indecisiveness had allowed the chance to slip through his fingers. What right did he have complain about missed opportunities, he at least have been given the opportunity to live. Her name was Victoria and for him at least it had been love at first sight. She was beautiful, funny, warm, passionate and full of life. They had worked in the same office building but in different departments. Before long he was finding excuses to walk by her desk and just to say hello or to exchange a smile in passing. He was somewhat intimidated by her and could not gather the courage to directly ask her out. One Monday however they were discussing that night's football game and without planning to he ended making a bet on the games outcome. If his team won he would buy her dinner, if her team won she would buy dinner. His team won. The following night found them walking hand in hand through the sand on one of Southern California's many beaches. Their conversations flowed easily and the silent moments were warm and comfortable. To his surprise as the sunset she reached up to him and gently kissed his lips. When she saw his look of astonishment she explained that she did not want to wait as long for their first kiss as she had for him to ask her out. So began a long love affair with a woman that in all honesty had been his soul mate that is if there was such a thing. They spent most of their free time together. Drives along the coast. Trips to Vegas. Long nights at one of their homes watching old Bogie and Bacall films. Everything was perfect. He knew that she was waiting for him to propose but she knew that he was gun shy having been briefly married several years before. So she bided her time and waited for him to be comfortable with the idea. And she waited. And waited. And waited. He was afraid of marriage and scared to death of the long-term commitment. He went so far as to buy an engagement ring but he never gave it to her. That is until it was to late. One night she showed up at his door with pizza, beer and a somewhat timid look on her face. She barely spoke over dinner and sat quietly on the couch not really responding to him or the television. Finally he got the hint and her turned off the television, he took her hand in his and asked her what was the matter. He almost hit the floor when she blurted out that she was pregnant. A thousand and one thoughts and emotions went through his head all demanding individual attention. I'm going to be a father. Am I ready to be a father?

Now, let's dive deeper into the implications of the situation. It's crucial for any relationship to balance closeness and independence. When one party feels overwhelmed or pressured, like this guy is experiencing, it usually stems from a lack of space to breathe and grow. This isn't just a romantic principle; it applies to friendships, family dynamics, and even professional relationships. When someone proclaims, "I have to work on myself," it's an innate acknowledgment that they need time to reflect, rejuvenate, and reconnect with their own identity outside the confines of the relationship. Understand that the statement can often be laced with complexities. Often, it's less about the person they are pulling away from, and more about their own internal battles. They may be grappling with self-esteem issues, professional responsibilities, or just the general chaos that life throws our way. The hardest part is recognizing when it's time to step back, refocus, and allow that person the space they say they need without taking it as a rejection. This is where many individuals err; they react rather than respond. Our friend here is in that very predicament, feeling the urge to compensate for her retreat by intensifying his own efforts. Rather than allowing her the freedom she's seeking, he's inadvertently pushing her further away. This could lead to resentment or frustration on both ends-her for feeling trapped and him for feeling rejected. It's important to remember that emotional clarity can only come when we detach from the desire to control the outcome. Furthermore, when you give someone the space they need, it can spark curiosity and attraction. When a person feels confident in their autonomy and independence, they are more likely to appreciate their partner in a profound way. It restores a sense of value to the connection-something that often gets overshadowed by the desperation to maintain proximity. To address this situation constructively, I suggest this gentleman first take a step back and evaluate what his motivations are in the relationship. Is he seeking connection out of genuine affection, or is he attempting to fulfill his own insecurities by forcing the relationship to progress? Then, he should communicate openly with his partner about how he feels, but do so with an understanding of her need for individuality. By framing the conversation with empathy, he can establish a dialogue that honors her request while still expressing that he cares for her and wants to support her growth. The best advice, however, is to occupy this time for himself as well. Focusing on personal growth, hobbies, or goals during this period can be transformative not just for him but for the relationship as a whole. By cultivating his own interests and passions, he can avoid falling into a reactive mindset and instead cultivate a stronger sense of self, which is incredibly attractive. As I often tell my clients, love is not about clinging but about allowing. When you can embrace love with open hands, it means you understand that each individual's path, whether together or apart, is valid. So, embrace her need for space, use this opportunity to become the best version of yourself, and allow the relationship to unfold naturally. Through this process of mutual respect and understanding, you may find that both of you emerge from this phase with a deeper connection and appreciation for one another. Remember, true love flourishes in the soil of freedom.

Face stimuli associated to the receipt of a monetary loss are more likely to be recognized than other faces in a subsequent attentional blink task (Raymond & O'Brien, 2009) and receive enhanced visual processing in a masked recognition task (O'Brien & Raymond, 2012). Stronger reorienting processes for abrupt-onset (exogenous) colored cues linked to a monetary punishment have also been reported (Bucker & Theeuwes, 2016; but see; Rutherford, O'Brien, & Raymond, 2010), as well as increased attentional capture by colored singleton distractors associated to evasion of a monetary loss in a visual search task (Wentura, Muller, & Rothermund, 2014). Recent data reveal that perceptual features associated to receipt of punishment boost primary visual cortex responses (as reflected by the higher amplitude of the C1 potential), relative to reward-associated and neutral ones (Rossi et al., 2017), although evidence for an enhanced representation in visual ventral areas for gain- versus loss-associated stimuli has been found for symbol cues during an economic decision-making task (San Martin, Appelbaum, Huettel, & Woldorff, 2014) and for object categories presented in images of natural scenes (Barbaro, Peelen, & Hickey, 2017). Though evidence for modulatory effects of punishment associations in visual perceptual and attentional tasks, whether it can be observed for specific locations in cluttered naturalistic contexts remains an open question; furthermore, it is unclear whether it has a lasting effect that can modulate LTM-based attention. Here, we aimed to shed light on whether and how punishment-related mechanisms influence the ability of LTM to guide perception in naturalistic contexts. We used a similar experimental approach as in our previous study (Doallo et al., 2013) to disentangle whether spatial expectations from LTM incorporate value signals specifically related to past avoidance of an aversive outcome to magnify experience-based biases upon perceptual decisions on relevant objects in cluttered scenes. Event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded to reveal the time course over which punishment-associated memory-guided attention exerts its effects on the ongoing neural activity in visual cortical areas. We analyzed the P1, N1 and N2pc components. These potentials reflect visual processing (P1 and N1) and target selection (N2pc). The P1 potential, a positive deflection peaking about 100 msec after stimulus presentation, is modulated by visuospatial attention and thought to reflect a sensory gain control mechanism within extrastriate visual cortex (Heinze et al., 1994; Hillyard, Vogel, & Luck, 1998; Martinez et al., 1999). The N1 potential is a negative deflection, subsequent to the P1, which is also modulated by attention. The N1 attention effect is believed to index a top-down modulation of discriminative processing in areas of the ventral visual stream (Hopf, Vogel, Woodman, Heinze, & Luck, 2002; Luck, 1995; Vogel & Luck, 2000). The N2pc is an enhanced negativity at posterior electrode sites contralateral to the location of an attended target, typically emerging 200-300 msec after target onset.

Furthermore, the choice of connectivity metric can significantly impact the interpretation of results, and the field would benefit from a comprehensive evaluation of the strengths and limitations of each approach. For instance, amplitude-based measures, such as amplitude covariance and amplitude correlation, are sensitive to changes in signal power, which can be influenced by various factors, including sensor placement and noise levels (Nolte et al., 2004). On the other hand, phase-based measures, such as phase-locking value and phase-lag index, are more robust to amplitude fluctuations but may be affected by the choice of frequency band and window length (Lachaux et al., 1999). Moreover, the use of different connectivity metrics can lead to distinct network topologies, highlighting the need for a standardized framework for comparing and validating results across studies. Another challenge in resting-state connectivity analysis is the handling of multiple testing corrections, which is essential to account for the large number of possible connections between brain regions. The Bonferroni correction, a common approach, can be overly conservative, leading to a high rate of false negatives (Hochberg and Tamhane, 1987). More advanced methods, such as the false discovery rate (FDR) correction, can provide a better balance between type I and type II errors, but their implementation can be computationally intensive and may require specialized software (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). In addition, the integration of prior knowledge and constraints into connectivity models can improve the accuracy and interpretability of results. For example, incorporating anatomical information from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) or structural MRI can help to inform the specification of connectivity models and reduce the risk of false positives (Honey et al., 2009). Similarly, the use of Bayesian approaches, which incorporate prior distributions on model parameters, can provide a more principled way of handling uncertainty and model selection (Friston et al., 2002). Despite these challenges, the study of resting-state connectivity using electrophysiology has the potential to reveal novel insights into brain function and dysfunction. By leveraging the high temporal resolution of MEG and EEG, researchers can investigate the dynamic reorganization of brain networks across different states, such as sleep, attention, and cognitive load (Buzsaki et al., 2012). Furthermore, the development of more sophisticated connectivity models, incorporating non-linear and time-varying effects, can provide a more nuanced understanding of brain function and its relationship to behavior and cognition (Valdes-Sosa et al., 2011). In conclusion, the estimation of resting-state connectivity using electrophysiology is a complex and multifaceted problem, requiring careful consideration of various methodological and analytical challenges. By acknowledging these challenges and developing more robust and standardized approaches, researchers can unlock the full potential of electrophysiology for understanding brain function and dysfunction. Ultimately, the integration of electrophysiology with other neuroimaging modalities, such as fMRI and DTI, can provide a more comprehensive understanding of brain organization and its relationship to behavior and cognition.
