The lower manufacturing costs of the roll-to-roll fabrication process compared to other technologies make them an attractive technology. Moreover, the efficiency of this developing technology has reached noticeable levels in a short period of time. From the reported efficiency of 3% in 2006 [36,37], cell efficiency has increased to more than 11% in 2015 [12,38]. Table 1 shows the confirmed efficiencies of OPV cells and minimodules compared with the values obtained by cells and submodules of some of the most common PV technologies. Data have been extracted from the most recent biannual report presented on certified efficiencies measured on solar cells and modules [12]. The efficiency values shown in Table 1 are reported at very specific conditions, defined as Standard Test Conditions (STC) [40], which are hardly ever met outdoors in real working situations. Thus, the efficiency really achieved by the PV devices under working conditions may differ substantially from these published values, since the performance of PV modules depends on many factors, like for example: The temperature of the module. For most technologies, the higher the temperature of the module is, the lower is its efficiency. The total incident solar irradiance, as depending on the physical structure of the solar cell the performance can be strongly dependent (and non-linear) with the varying solar radiation. The angle of incidence between the solar radiation and the normal to the module surface. In spite of the anti-reflective coating and the surface texture, as the angle of the incoming radiation increases, the proportion of reflected light increases, decreasing the energy available to be absorbed by the module. The spectral responsivity of the module's active material. Different materials may have different spectral responsivity to the range of wavelengths of the incoming irradiance, converting more efficiently some wavelength bands than others. The performance of some technologies may vary after long exposure to high irradiance levels or temperatures, while others may show seasonal effects on their energy production. This effect is not considered in the present study. Besides the intrinsic characteristics described above, others specifically related to the location and installation of the module also have an impact on the performance of a PV device. These are, for example, the orientation and inclination of the module, its location, possible shadows from the surrounding horizon, and presence of soiling or snow. Studies about the performance of OPV devices under different working conditions are reported by different groups in literature. They are mainly focused on indoor measurements dedicated to the study of the positive effect of high temperatures which typically enhance the performance of OPV [41-44] and on outdoor measurements [45-52]. In these studies the behaviour of OPV devices at different irradiances and temperatures is analysed together with their long term stability.

Endowment heterogeneity is a crucial and common feature in most real life settings, like principal-agent relationships or bargaining situations with a monopolistic seller and competitive buyers. One simple example of how endowment heterogeneity may affect the efficacy of costly punishment is to consider the strategic dilemma faced by someone building a new house, and finding the outcome unsatisfactory. In the absence of a budget constraint, hiring a good lawyer to sue the builder is both an available option, and a credible threat. If resources are scarce, the balance between your resources and the builder's company size will most likely determine the extent to which you can effectively punish the builder. Endowment heterogeneity (rather the mere existence of sanctions, and its technology) thus becomes a relevant determinant of the damage you can credibly inflict to the builder. In this paper, we investigate the effect of endowment heterogeneity on trust and trustworthiness in a controlled laboratory experiment. We give the investor the possibility of punishing the allocator at a cost, and systematically manipulate the distribution of initial endowments. When sanctions are available, trust could increase because the investor may anticipate the allocator will fear sanctions. Arguably, the allocator will be more or less afraid depending on the magnitude of the investor's endowment, relative to the allocator's one. If the investor is much wealthier than the allocator, we say that the investor's capacity of punishment is high because the investor can destroy most of the allocator's payoff investing a relatively small share of her own payoff. Alternatively, the allocator will fear sanctions relatively less if she is wealthier than the investor, and the investor's capacity of punishment of the investor is low.4 As a result, the effect of sanctions on trust and trustworthiness could very reasonably be mediated by differences in initial endowments. Interestingly enough, endowment heterogeneity also changes other features of the trust game by exogenously introducing an unequal distribution of resources. Inequality aversion may generate strong behavioral reactions to non-reciprocal behavior in some endowment distributions, critically affecting the likelihood of punishment. We test four different predictions in our experiment. The first one is related to the existence of social preferences. Both inequality aversion and reciprocity predict an effect of endowment heterogeneity in the trust game, as we will explain below (Coleman, 1990; Rodriguez-Lara, 2014; Smith, 2011; Xiao & Bicchieri, 2010). Secondly, the deterrence hypothesis assumes that punishment increases both trust and trustworthiness, with the effect of punishment being non-decreasing with the difference between the investor and the allocator's endowments (i.e., trust and trustworthiness should increase monotonically with the investor's capacity of punishment, as defined above).5 Our third hypothesis relies on the hidden costs of punishment.

When you see stalwarts like David Gower and Ian Botham in the commentary box, the anticipation that something insightful is about to be discussed envelops the air. Over the years, the way cricket has been presented to us has undergone nothing short of a revolution. From the early days of static angles and grainy footage, the evolution has been akin to a gentle transformation into a vivid, detailed painting-where every stroke, every nuance, is captured and displayed with precision. The advent of technology like Hawk-Eye paved the way for a more analytical approach, allowing armchair critics and aficionados alike to marvel at the intricacies of trajectory and bounce. Snicko, with its auditory prowess, has ended many a debate over dubious edges, capturing even the faintest snicks with a precision that leaves little room for doubt. James Weatherby, whose family served as accountants to members of the Jockey Club, was assigned the task of tracing the pedigrees of all racing horses in England. His research, completed in 1791, resulted in the first volume of the General Stud Book. It listed 186 Arabian, Turk, and Barb horses - the last two being North African breeds - that had been brought into England from the Middle East in the 17th and 18th centuries and used as stallions or broodmares; all modern Thoroughbreds are descended in the male line from just 28 of these stallions. Any horse not traceable to one of the horses listed in the General Stud Book could not run in any race conducted under Jockey Club rules. The book, updated annually, remains today the breed registry for all Thoroughbreds worldwide. The Jockey Club established the practice of declaring certain horses as "stakes" horses before they were entered in any race. This meant that owners put up some money in advance so that there would be prize money for the winner. An owner who races a horse over which he has not declared a stake forfeits half the purse. The system of stakes races replaced the old challenge system of match racing between two opponents to win a private bet. As the racing of stakes horses became more popular with the public, the Jockey Club introduced another type of race in 1845 called a handicap. Each horse was required to carry a certain weight that depended on ability, age, distance of the race, and sex. Handicaps give extra weight to better horses and reduce the weight carried by inferior horses. The theory behind handicapping is that each horse in the field should reach the finish line together. Spectators enjoy trying to pick the winners in such close contests. Today the majority of races are run under handicap conditions. The first recorded Thoroughbred race in North America was held in 1665 on the plains of Long Island. The British settlers of Maryland and Virginia quickly followed suit. By 1750 the Tidewater aristocracy sponsored matches throughout the South. But the American Revolution largely destroyed interest in racing. After the war, Kentucky-bred Thoroughbreds dominated the sport until the Civil War, when again public interest in racing declined precipitously. The sport revived in the late 19th century, particularly in the Northeast, where tracks such as Jerome Park (1866, now defunct), Saratoga (1863), Monmouth Park (1870), and Pimlico (1870) opened. In 1894 the American Jockey Club was formed to supervise racing, but it proved ineffective. In 1897 the rival National Association of State Racing Commissioners was founded with the same objective. The two groups merged in 1908 as the Jockey Club. Although no formal system of classification was established for major races in the United States, certain prestigious races were regarded as equivalent to the English classics. At various times the following races fell into this category: the Travers Stakes (1864) at Saratoga, the Brooklyn Handicap (1887) at Gravesend on Coney Island, the Suburban Handicap (1884) at Sheepshead Bay also on Coney Island, and the Carter Handicap (1895) at Aqueduct. In 1930 the three premier races for three-year-olds were designated as the American Triple Crown: the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness Stakes, and the Belmont Stakes. The Breeders' Cup series of races was instituted in 1984 to provide championship races in various categories.

She was not sure if this was a joke, but she had no intention of obeying - she rarely did anything she was told as a child. An enthusiastic rider, one of her favourite games in summer was to gallop through fields of corn, often seriously damaging the crop. 'I was very naughty, and behaved pretty badly really,' she recalled gleefully. Candida Lycett Green, second left, was the daughter of John Betjeman, left, pictured at their home in Farnborough around 1948 with her brother Paul and mother Penelope - and dog Peter Pudding. This idyllic childhood ended in 1954, when she was sent to boarding school. 'I was a revolutionary at heart,' she said, 'so I hated it.' A half-hearted attempt to study sculpture at Oxford Polytechnic followed, before she joined Richard Ingrams and others including David Dimbleby and Auberon Waugh at the Edinburgh Fringe. Self-deprecating as ever, she claimed she had earned a place in their Town And Gown revue because the producer had heard her singing in the bath. What he was doing in her bathroom, she never attempted to explain. A few months later, in London, during a short-lived stint as a magazine sub-editor, she met Savile Row tailor Rupert Lycett Green. An obsessive gambler who played poker till the small hours, he played backgammon with customers in the window of his shop. His designs ushered in the multi-coloured peacock attire of the Sixties, with gold-embroidered jackets and rainbow ties. His shop did for men what Mary Quant was doing for women, offering 'a young man's view of cut and proportion'. As a child, Candida, pictured, was an enthusiastic horse rider who rarely obeyed her parents' wishes. Candida claimed it was his flair on the dance-floor that won her heart, but it was also his cavalier sense of adventure. He had a sporty Mini Cooper, and drove it so violently that Candida's beehive hairdo would collapse as he took corners. They married and on honeymoon attempted to drive around the world in a Land Rover. It was stoned by locals in Tripoli, held up at gunpoint in Kabul, and overturned in Rajasthan in India. In Damascus, the newlyweds found themselves in a military coup, and in Beirut they were adopted by Ba'ath separatists who took them clubbing at the city's decadent Folies Bergeres club. Back in London, they were more fashionable than ever. Painter David Hockney wanted a Lycett Green suit, and in lieu of payment did a drawing of Candida. Her magazine career, though, was scuppered when the editor caught her working for his rival, Private Eye - although her job was stapling the pages together and handing out advertising on the Tube. But no Betjeman would be deterred that easily from writing. As her family grew - she and Rupert had five children - she did what her father had done and started writing bedtime stories. These became the basis of two children's books about Hadrian the Hedgehog.

Uncertainties associated with global-scale hydrological modelling are usually higher as compared with those related to the regional-scale hydrological models (Hagemann et al., 2013; Gosling et al., 2017; Hattermann et al., 2017). This can be explained by coarser resolution of the input data and usually poor performance of global models (most of them are not calibrated) in the historical reference period (Hattermann et al., 2017), as well as inability of most of the global models to take into account water management infrastructure (Abbaspour et al., 2015). Due to this, it makes sense to verify trends by application of the basin-scale models. Further, there are some continental-scale studies performed with the pan-European models, which are partly calibrated. Donnelly et al. (2016) applied a multi-basin model E-HYPE to the entire Europe, which showed good simulation results, and can be used for climate impact studies after some improvements, regarding input data and additional calibration. Roudier et al. (2016), applying three pan-European models, LISFLOOD (Burek et al., 2012), E-HYPE (Donnelly et al., 2016) and VIC (Liang et al., 1994), found that drought events may increase in Southern Europe, in particular, in Southern France and Spain, and the frequency of flood events may increase in Northern Europe, if the global temperature will increase by +2 C. A study of Alfieri et al. (2015) applied the distributed hydrological model LISFLOOD driven by the high-end climate change scenario in major river basins across the entire European region. They found decrease of runoff in the Southern Europe and increase of runoff in Northern Europe, and no specific trends for the discharges in the Central Europe. However, the abovementioned analyses were focused on the extreme events frequency analysis or on the validation of the pan-European models, and not on the general picture of the hydrological impacts of projected climate change. Regarding the hydrological impact assessments performed with the regional scale hydrological models, it usually focuses on individual regions, often single river basins, and studies encompassing large areas are rare (Aich et al., 2014; Vetter et al., 2016). Recently, a Special Issue in Climatic Change (see editorial Krysanova and Hattermann (2017)) addressed the issue of intercomparison of the regional-scale hydrological models and climate change impacts across twelve large river basins around the globe (including two basins in Europe: Rhine and Tagus), fulfilled by the efforts of the ISI-MIP project (Warszawski et al., 2014) group. Our study aims to close the existing gap and provides an assessment of trends in the long-term mean annual dynamics of river discharge in eight representative European basins triggered by climatic change. For that, an eco-hydrological process-based catchment scale hydrological model was applied, which was calibrated and validated for each case study in advance and accounted for water management operations, where applicable. It used a more elaborated approach, when compared to the previous European-scale studies.

The intricate dance of sister chromatid cohesion is a complex process that relies on the precise coordination of multiple molecular machineries. In addition to the cohesin complex, a plethora of cohesion establishment factors have been identified, each playing a crucial role in ensuring the faithful distribution of genetic information between daughter cells. One such factor is the PCNA clamp loader, which has been shown to interact with cohesin and facilitate its loading onto chromosomes (Mayer et al., 2001). The PCNA clamp loader is a heterotrimeric complex composed of RFC1, RFC2, and RFC3, which is essential for the loading of PCNA onto DNA replication forks (Waga and Stillman, 1998). The interaction between PCNA and cohesin is thought to occur through the PCNA-binding domain of the cohesin subunit Scc1, which is responsible for recruiting cohesin to replication forks (Huang et al., 2011). Another cohesion establishment factor is the replication checkpoint complex, which consists of the three subunits Tof1, Csm3, and Mrc1 (Mayer et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2004). This complex is responsible for monitoring the progression of DNA replication and arresting the cell cycle in response to DNA damage or replication fork stalling (Branzei et al., 2003). The replication checkpoint complex has been shown to interact with cohesin and regulate its activity, thereby ensuring that sister chromatid cohesion is established only after DNA replication is complete (Hanna et al., 2001). The replisome component Ctf4 has also been implicated in sister chromatid cohesion, as it has been shown to interact with cohesin and facilitate its loading onto chromosomes (Hanna et al., 2001). Ctf4 is a DNA-binding protein that is essential for the recruitment of the replisome to replication forks, and its interaction with cohesin may help to ensure that cohesin is loaded onto chromosomes in a timely and coordinated manner. In addition to these factors, the Chl1 helicase has been identified as a cohesion establishment factor, as it has been shown to interact with cohesin and regulate its activity (Skibbens, 2004). Chl1 is a DNA helicase that is essential for the resolution of DNA replication intermediates, and its interaction with cohesin may help to ensure that sister chromatid cohesion is established only after DNA replication is complete. The precise mechanisms by which these cohesion establishment factors interact with cohesin and regulate its activity are not yet fully understood, but it is clear that they play critical roles in ensuring the faithful distribution of genetic information between daughter cells. Further studies are needed to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying sister chromatid cohesion and to identify additional factors that contribute to this process.

And you begin to sift through all the junk you've been fed about how you should behave, how you should look, how much you should weigh, what you should wear, what you should do for a living, how much money you should make, what you should drive, how and where you should live, who you should marry, the importance of having and raising children, and what you owe your parents, family, and friends. You learn to open up to new worlds and different points of view. And you begin reassessing and redefining who you are and what you really stand for. You learn the difference between wanting and needing and you begin to discard the doctrines and values you've outgrown, or should never have bought into to begin with... and in the process you learn to go with your instincts. You learn that it is truly in giving that we receive. And that there is power and glory in creating and contributing and you stop maneuvering through life merely as a "consumer" looking for your next fix. You learn that principles such as honesty and integrity are not the outdated ideals of a bygone era but the mortar that holds together the foundation upon which you must build a life. You learn that you don't know everything, it's not your job to save the world and that you can't teach a pig to sing. You learn to distinguish between guilt and responsibility and the importance of setting boundaries and learning to say NO. You learn that the only cross to bear is the one you choose to carry and that martyrs get burned at the stake. Then you learn about love. How to love, how much to give in love, when to stop giving and when to walk away. You learn to look at relationships as they really are and not as you would have them be. You stop trying to control people, situations and outcomes. And you learn that alone does not mean lonely. You also stop working so hard at putting your feelings aside, smoothing things over and ignoring your needs. You learn that feelings of entitlement are perfectly OK.... and that it is your right to want things and to ask for the things you want... and that sometimes it is necessary to make demands. You come to the realization that you deserve to be treated with love, kindness, sensitivity and respect and you won't settle for less. And you learn that your body really is your temple. And you begin to care for it and treat it with respect. You begin to eat a balanced diet, drink more water, and take more time to exercise. You learn that being tired fuels doubt, fear, and uncertainty and so you take more time to rest. And, just as food fuels the body, laughter fuels our soul. In this paper we use the term 'publication counting methods for a national research evaluation exercise' (in short: publication counting methods) in a broad sense to cover all aspects of bibliographic data into a score for a field (within an institution) used in a performance-based research funding system. We identified five dimensions of publication counting methods for a national research evaluation exercise: (1) unit of assessment, (2) counting method, (3) institution limit, (4) researcher limit, and (5) point scale. The publication counting method is just one of many elements of the broader challenge facing a national research evaluation system, which are not focused on just publications. Nonetheless, publications are the most important criterion. The first dimension reflects the unit of assessment. For instance, in Norway, scientific institutions are assessed, while Poland has changed their unit of assessment from whole institutions, e.g. a faculty comprising researchers from a few fields (the 2013 and 2017 evaluations) to separate fields within institutions (the 2021 evaluation). In this way, the new Polish unit of assessment is similar to the solution used in the Research Excellent Framework (REF) in the United Kingdom. The second dimension, counting method, is related to a fair approach towards multi-authored publications (Sivertsen, 2018). In Norway, square root fractional counting is used, while Poland use a combination of three methods, i.e. whole counting, fractional counting, square root counting. Sivertsen (2016), in a discussion on redesigning publication counting methods in PRFSs, highlights that there is a need for a method which will allow for balancing across different field-dependent co-authorship practices. According to Sivertsen, such a method is square root fractional counting. Having a similar point of view with Sivertsen, we believe also that square-root counting can be useful not only for balancing results across fields but also for analyses carried out for separate fields. All fields have subfields, which have diverse publication practices, for instance, theoretical physics and high energy physics within the field of physics. The third dimension concerns an institution limit, i.e. limiting the number of submitted publications from a single unit of assessment (institution or field, depending on the adopted evaluation model). The number of publications per FTE most often expresses this limit. For instance, in Norway, all publications of an evaluated institution are used, whereas in Poland in the 2013 and 2017 evaluations, only a limited number of publications were included in the calculation. This limit is expressed by the 3N-2N0 formula, where N is the arithmetic mean of the full-time equivalent (FTE) of academic staff members who work in a given scientific unit during the evaluated four-year period, while N0 is the number of academic staff members who were not authors of any publication during the period in question (Kulczycki, Korzen, & Korytkowski, 2017). In the UK Research Excellence Framework 2021, the average number of publications required per FTE in the unit of assessment is 2.5 (Research Excellence Framework, 2018).

Since species influence these functions via their collective traits (Naeem and Wright, 2003), such traits are termed effect traits (Hooper et al., 2005; Suding et al., 2008) (Table 1). When the relationship of traits and functions is soundly assessed we can use the collective trait pattern of a community in combination with community abundance or biomass to indicate ecosystem functioning (Bremner et al., 2006b) Fig. 2). This approach benefits studies on large spatial scales, as measuring functions at those scales is inherently difficult, and in many cases impossible. Another advantage of trait-based approaches is that early responses to changes are visible in the functional structure rather than in the taxonomic structure of a community (Gagic et al., 2015; Mouillot et al., 2013). Recent use in terrestrial ecosystems has demonstrated that trait-based methods enable generalizations of the trait diversity-functioning relationship within and between ecosystems, and aid prediction of the functional consequences of biodiversity loss (Gross et al., 2017). Accordingly, those traits showing a response to a disturbance are termed response traits (Hooper et al., 2005) (Table 1). These traits are highly relevant in assessing species thresholds and the resilience of ecosystems to change (Gutt et al., 2017) and consequently are important indicators for management and conservation (Bremner, 2008). Uses with immediate application potential for polar regions include identifying regions that are most vulnerable to changes (Diaz et al., 2013; Mouillot et al., 2013; Suding et al., 2008), detecting early conservation outcomes in marine protected areas (Coleman et al., 2015), and identifying functional hotspots (Stuart-Smith et al., 2013). Given their high invasion potential (Cheung et al., 2009), polar areas would also benefit from using trait-based approaches to assess the response of ecosystems to species invasions as done in European Seas (Hewitt et al., 2016; Weigel et al., 2016), or to assess the potential of particular species to become invasive (Cardeccia et al., 2015). Similarly, Suding et al.'s (2008) and Hewitt et al.'s (2016) application of trait-based approaches to estimate climate change effects on ecosystem functions is highly relevant to polar regions. The origin of trait-based approaches lies in freshwater (Southwood, 1977; Townsend and Hildrew, 1994) and terrestrial ecology (McIntyre et al., 1995; Olff et al., 1994). They are, however, used with increasing frequency in marine systems: a survey of 233 peer-reviewed studies on marine communities (S1) showed that only 5% where published prior to 2000, and after 2010 the number of publications showed an almost threefold increase despite great challenges in sampling, observation and manipulation of natural assemblages in marine ecosystems (Beauchard et al., 2017). These obstacles are particularly prevalent in polar marine systems, likely contributing to the sparsity of studies, which consider trait-function relationships in these regions. In the Arctic Ocean, only one study from the Canadian Arctic measures a function (benthic remineralization) and relates it to the functional diversity of local benthic communities (Link et al., 2013).

He was also a dreamer, and a student of human nature, and his thoughts were often far removed from the commonplace topics of conversation about him. "You said something just now, Doc., about a woman's not having the nerve to commit murder," he spoke, slowly and thoughtfully. "I wonder how much truth there is in that statement? Do you really think most women are afraid of killing another person?" "Of course they are," Davenport answered promptly. "They may wish to kill, but when it comes to actually doing so, they simply lack the necessary pluck." "Well, maybe," Monroe admitted, "but I've known women who would do almost anything to accomplish what they wished. And then there are the abnormal ones." "There's nothing abnormal about women," Pollard declared. "They're just like us men, only better." "But aren't they sometimes different?" Monroe persisted. "Women are peculiar creatures," Pollard conceded. "Every one is unique, though all women have certain characteristics common to their sex." "Yes," Davenport agreed, "but they are certainly not prone to commit murder." "No," Barry chimed in, "that's why it's such a shock when we hear of a woman being tried for murder." "Or convicted of it," added Pollard. "So we've got a sort of consensus of opinion here," Monroe summed up. "We agree that women are rarely guilty of premeditated murder, because they haven't the nerve to carry out their plans. Is that it?" "That's it," Barry affirmed. "Go on, Monroe, tell us your ideas on the subject." "What are they?" Monroe asked. "I'm no authority, but I've been thinking over this old business of Mellen's death, and I confess I believe Mrs. Mellen did it." "Nonsense!" Pollard exclaimed. "It's ridiculous even to suggest it." "Pneumonia doesn't keep a person from getting out of bed," Monroe reminded him. "Besides, if she did get out of bed, she might have managed to strangle poor Mellen without leaving any marks. Haunted by this uncertainty, might there be one or more of you who have had twinges of feeling that - as the Yale Precision Marching Band chants to opposing goalies in Ingalls Rink - It's All Your Fault: all Yale's fault for having failed to provide you with a single marketable skill? If students in the room have not yet felt this, there may be some in the upper balconies who have, or will. Some while back I met a woman in Southern California (I name no names) who revealed that she had not one but two Yalie sons who had come back home after graduation to a new life, not quite what she expected, of getting up late, eating bizarre amounts of cereal, and watching reruns on TV; and who, when pressed about what they might want to go out and do, glared the unspoken words: Don't Go There. If anyone in this room resonates to this description, I have a message for you: it's going to be all right. Is it any wonder if the end of college should produce a pause before you find the onward way? For the great majority of you, the end of college marks the end of a far longer stretch (for some it began in the days after birth) in which your life has been defined by the fact that you were in school. Since kindergarten or preschool, school was where you spent the day. School was the answer to the question what you were doing with your life. (Remember the convenience of this? Question: what are you doing with your life? Answer: I'm still in school.) A succession of schools set you your annual tasks and challenges. And school said what came next - more school, of course: after fifth grade, sixth; after high school, college. Now, for the first time, you are about to step out of that structured life into the abyss of the undetermined. No wonder if it's disorienting - what else would it be? But another name for life unstructured in advance is freedom, and other words for the life lived in that territory are independence, maturity, and adulthood. Welcome to them. Will it be beyond your power to orient yourself in that world, find your way in it and make something good of it? In bad moments it may seem so; but think back to your arrival here. When you came ashore at your last terra incognita, you may have felt at a loss, but then something kicked in - some mix of courage, spirit, curiosity, and desire - that helped you go forward to meet this unknown place, engage its challenges, and make it your own. Do I doubt that the same thing will happen again when you leave here? I do not; you've done little these last four years to make me think of you as helpless or resourceless.

As we stood before the justice of the peace, Maria's eyes were fixed on the clock, her mind racing with the looming deadline. I could sense her anxiety, but I was trying to keep a sense of humor about it all. I mean, what's a little paperwork, right? We'd already been married in our own way, in our own private ceremony, all those years ago. But I knew this was important for her, for our daughter, for the benefits that came with being a "real" married couple. The justice of the peace, a kind-faced woman with a warm smile, asked us to exchange our vows. Maria's voice was barely above a whisper, but I could feel her sincerity. I repeated my vows, trying to keep my own emotions in check. The cupcakes, a sweet reminder of the Mamas who had come to witness our union, sat on the table beside us. As we signed the papers, I couldn't help but think about the journey we'd been on. From that trip to Healdsburg, to the countless conversations we'd had about marriage, to the decision to finally take the plunge. It was a decision that felt more like a formality than a grand declaration of love. But as we walked out of City Hall, hand in hand, I knew that this was important. This was about more than just paperwork or benefits. It was about our daughter, about our family, about the world we wanted to create for ourselves. It was about being seen, being recognized, being equal. As we hailed a cab to take us back to our daughter's school, I turned to Maria and smiled. "You know, I never thought I'd be one of those people who'd get married in a rush," I said, chuckling. Maria looked at me, her eyes sparkling with amusement. "I never thought I'd be one of those people who'd get married at all," she replied, her voice low and husky. We laughed, our eyes locked, and for a moment, everything felt right with the world. We were married, or at least, we were on paper. And who knows, maybe one day, that paper would mean something more. Maybe one day, we'd be able to live our lives without worrying about benefits and paperwork and recognition. Maybe one day, we'd be able to love each other without apology, without fear of persecution. But for now, we'd take what we could get. We'd take the cupcakes, the Mamas, and the justice of the peace. And we'd keep on loving each other, no matter what the world threw our way.

"And you?" questioned Nickel Plate. "I stayed behind to keep watch and see if I could find any trace of her, but I couldn't." "And then what happened?" "I don't want to lose her." "Oh, dear me! What shall we do without her?" sighed Bumbus. "We shall starve, Master." "I think not," said Nickel Plate. "There's plenty of money in the bank." "But we can't touch it until next year." "That's true," said Nickel Plate, thoughtfully. "But we might borrow some of it." "Borrow!" cried Bumbus. "How can we borrow what isn't ours?" "Bogie Man has promised to lend me some," said Nickel Plate, proudly. "He said he would lend me enough to buy a new horse." "Where did you get the money to pay him back?" asked Bumbus. "I haven't any yet," said Nickel Plate, "but I'll find some way to get it." "What a shame!"

Source Consciousness is the unifying fabric of existence, embodying all experiences, aspirations, and journeys intertwined within the tapestry of life. Imagine a vast ocean, each droplet a unique expression of the same water. In this light, every soul is a singular wave rising and falling upon the surface, each wave distinct yet undeniably part of the greater whole. This idea invites us to reconsider how we interpret our actions, not as isolated events freighted with karmic debt, but as interconnected ripples that influence not just our own immediate surroundings, but also the depths of the collective consciousness. So, what does this mean when we speak of Karma in the context of Source Consciousness? It means that rather than a rigid ledger where good and bad deeds measure our worthiness, Karma becomes a dance of energy-an exchange of vibrations that flows freely throughout the cosmos. Each thought, word, and deed sends forth a signal, reverberating through this intricate web of life. When understood this way, Karma transitions from a heavy burden to an enlightening guide, illuminating the paths we tread with each newfound understanding. Yet, the challenge arises when we cling to the old paradigm-the one rooted in duality, where actions are categorized as either righteous or sinful. This fragmented thinking can lead to guilt, fear, and a misplaced sense of control over the universe. We find ourselves trapped in a cycle of doing good to offset negativity, rather than simply inhabiting our authentic selves. The truth is, letting go of this relentless pursuit of perfection is where true freedom resides. It's about embracing the entirety of our humanity, with all its flaws and wonders. Thus, we ask ourselves: How do we navigate the complex waters of our existence? The answer lies in the cultivation of awareness and compassion, not just towards ourselves, but for others with whom we share this journey. When we recognize that each individual's struggle is not solely a product of their past choices but also influenced by myriad circumstances beyond their control, we can foster a profound sense of connection. In this understanding, we cease to see Karma as a punishing force, but instead as a potent teacher, inviting us to reflect, learn, and grow. Moreover, let's consider the implications of our actions with an expanded view of time. Rather than being beholden to a linear interpretation where past actions dictate future fates, let's entertain the possibility of a more fluid understanding. Think of moments of awakening, transformations, and changes in behavior as a breaking point, where one can redefine their path. In this view, it's not so much about rectifying past deeds but actively creating present and future realities that align with our highest truths. As we delve deeper into this paradigm shift, we can begin to reclaim the power of our choices, understanding that each moment represents a new opportunity to ignite positive energy within ourselves and the world around us. This energy, when shared and nurtured, can spawn acts of kindness, compassion, and understanding, sending ripples that have the potential to touch countless lives. Ultimately, Karma can be perceived not as an absolute law but as a guiding principle-an invitation to explore the questions of our existence, encouraging us to engage more fully with our experiences. Through this lens, our life becomes an exploration of how we express ourselves as part of that vast ocean of consciousness, urging us to embrace the journey not in fear, but with playful curiosity and an open heart. In this way, we transcend the archaic notions of retribution and begin to dance freely amidst the unfolding mystery of our shared existence.

It was a great house, partly Elizabethan, with additions in later days, with two great wings, in one of which was a fine portrait gallery, while the other contained the show apartments of the house, a suite of rooms which were quite worthy to have been occupied by a king, though fact compels us to add that royalty had made but a very slight use of them. King Charles, in one of his hasty rides in the midst of his troubled career, had paused to eat a morsel in the hall, and to wash his royal hands in a dressing-room. This was all, but it was something, and the rooms were beautiful with their faded furniture and heavy old hangings and tapestries, and chairs covered with embroidered work. All this was very much faded, and kept with difficulty from falling to pieces; but it was very imposing, and strangers came from all quarters to see the house. The pictures in the gallery were all portraits now, though it was a tradition that there had once been several old Masters which were sold in the troubles, but of which the frames still remained, blankly filled up by pieces of old brocade, in themselves a sight to see. Some even of the portraits, especially those which had been painted by famous masters, had disappeared too, so that the importance of the gallery in point of art was small. These remains of glory past were separate from the living part of the house. They were kept in order, and shown to strangers, a point of family pride which every Prescott held to be essential. But the existing Prescotts lived in the centre part of the house, which was too large for them, with its great hall and the other beautiful rooms, so airy and spacious, which were the creation of a generation which did not fear expense and loved space. The fine wainscoted room which was used as the dining-room in modern days, accommodated thirty people easily at dinner, whereas the Prescotts numbered but six, and seldom had company. The drawing-room was still larger, with noble broad bay windows, each as big as a modern room. To furnish all this, it may be supposed, was no trifle; and the furniture was shabby; what was old, faded; what was new, not half good enough for the natural splendour of the place. Nevertheless, new and old together harmonised somehow by mere use and wont, and the general appearance was that of a mingled humility and pride, like the character of the family, which thought such great things of itself and yet was able to do only little things and occupy a small position in the world.

Nomi Malone, played with fervent intensity by Elizabeth Berkley, arrives in Sin City with nothing but the clothes on her back and an insatiable hunger for fame. She weaves her way through a kaleidoscope of absurdities, each scene more outlandish than the last. The movie thrusts you into a world where pole dancing is high art, and ambition is as seductive as the neon lights that adorn the Strip. Nomi is the epitome of that longing, crashing through the doors of destiny with the ferocity of a runaway train. As the movie rolls, I find myself enthralled, half-smiling, half-groaning at the sheer audacity of it all. There's a scene where she defiantly declares to her competition, "I am a dancer!" as though that proclamation alone could hand her the keys to the kingdom of glitter and glamour. It's a line delivered with such bombast that it's tough not to chuckle, yet impossible to deny its underlying truth - this girl wants her moment in the spotlight, and she'll do just about anything to seize it. I'm hopping from scene to scene, cringing at the over-the-top dialogue while simultaneously relishing every glorious minute. The performances are a hodgepodge of theatrics, with Gina Gershon as the villainous dance queen Cristal Connors delivering a memorable, if laughable, ode to the ephemeral nature of fame. It's a melodramatic clash of titans, epitomized in an epic catfight that is so absurd, you can't help but wonder if any part of it was meant to be taken seriously. At the half-point of the film, it hit me like a ton of bricks: there's a certain kinship shared between Showgirls and the glittering chaos of actual Las Vegas. Both are built on the premise of alluring dreams wrapped in layers of insanity, one moment intoxicating and the next - utterly preposterous. Nomi is swept into this whirlwind, battling her demons, clambering up the social ladder, and navigating the tumultuous terrain of lust, ambition, and betrayal. The irony is that this train wreck of a film somehow encapsulates a more profound commentary on the price of success - and yet, as it does so, I can't help but laugh. By the time the infamous "I'm a dancer!" line rolls around again, I'm cackling, thoroughly engaged in the spectacle that is Showgirls. The pasties, the shot glasses, the ridiculousness of it all provides a sort of comfort, an affirmation that films don't always need to be critically acclaimed or Oscar-nominated to have a place in our hearts - some are better for their glaring flaws, illuminated against the backdrop of cinematic conventions. The closing credits begin to roll, reverberating through the room as I reach for the remote, still chuckling, a cigar-sized grin plastered across my face. I ponder the arbitrary nature of art, wondering what it says about the viewer's soul. Am I savoring the delicious absurdity of life, or am I merely laughing at an amateur's misguided attempts at greatness? The distinction blurs like the lines between fantasy and reality, much like the characters of Las Vegas itself. As I flip the case over to admire the box art one last time, I remind myself: we all have our guilty pleasures - some are just a little louder than others.

Both isoforms are ubiquitously expressed ER-localised basic leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors consisting of an N-terminal cytoplasmic domain with transcriptional activity, a transmembrane segment, and an ER luminal domain that senses ER-stress [10-12]. In addition to structural similarities, ATF6 and ATF6 also share the same mechanism of activation under ER stress, which is translocation from ER to the Golgi apparatus where they are sequentially cleaved at their luminal and transmembrane domains with Golgi- resident proteases S1P and S2P, resulting in liberation from the ER membrane of their cytosolic N-terminal regions, designated as ATF6 (N) and ATF6 (N) [10,11,13]. These cleaved and activated forms subsequently migrate to the nucleus where they bind as homo- or heterodimers to the promoter of genes containing ER stress response elements (ERSE-I and -II), originally identified in the genes encoding the ER chaperones such as BiP, and induce transcription [10,11,14-17]. Previous work has established that there is a functional redundancy between two isoforms of ATF6 as a single knockout of each ATF6 isoform in mice or fish was without phenotypic effect in the absence of exogenous ER stress whereas their double deficiency was embryonically lethal [18-20]. Despite the presence of an overlapping and compensatory function between isoforms of Atf6, there is some evidence for isoforms having distinct functions which are not redundant and only become apparent under conditions of increased ER stress. For instance, Atf6 ko mice develop liver steatosis when challenged with tunicamycin whereas Atf6 ko mice do not [21,22]. Also, ATF6, but not ATF6, has been shown to have a specific role in the regulation of the PIGF and Wfs1 genes [23,24]. Studies on each isoform have indicated that ATF6 is inducible by increases in ER stress whereas ATF6 is not [18,25-27]. In addition, ATF6 appears to have a higher transcriptional activity than ATF6 [25,26]. Given that ATF6, like ATF6, senses and becomes activated in response to the accumulation of unfolded/misfolded proteins within the ER, it would be logical to expect activation of ATF6 in MCDS. However, only induction and activation of ATF6 has been studied to date [6,7]. Here we make the first direct and systematic comparison of the roles of ATF6 and - under ER stress caused by the expression of a variety of MCDS-causing collagen X mutations in our cell culture model of the disease activated UPR [28]. In addition, we crossed Atf6 and Atf6 knockout mice with Col10a1 p.N617K mouse model of MCDS to investigate the role of each isoform in the MCDS disease mechanism in vivo. We demonstrate that Atf6, like Atf6, is involved in the MCDS disease mechanism. The two isoforms of Atf6 play some distinct roles in modulating the MCDS-mediated ER stress but, also work in concert to finely tune the extent and magnitude of Atf6-mediated UPR response.

So it was that one day a little girl, peering through the open window of her father's car, saw a glimpse of the great gray walls, towering above her like giant walls, and heard the roar of the water as it tumbled down the rapids, and knew that she was looking upon the New River. But to-day the little girl was standing in the doorway of the school-house, looking wistfully out upon another view, and the sun was shining upon the grimy buildings which lined the street below, making them look almost beautiful, and sending long rays of light among the trees beyond. There were patches of green here and there among the red-brown leaves of autumn, and the grass was still green; and the little girl's eyes followed the line of the mountain-side where it rose high above the town, till it met the sky. "It is so beautiful!" she said softly, turning back into the room. "I don't wonder you love it so much, Miss Bessie." "Yes," answered the teacher, with a sigh. "But I shall miss it so much when I leave it!" She put her arm about the child's shoulder, and together they walked slowly down the hillside, passing the rows of houses, and the few shops which gave Wentworth a business-like appearance, and out of the town into the country again. "You will have plenty to do, though," remarked the little girl, cheerily. "And there are lots of pretty things to see in Washington. You will have a good time, won't you?" "Oh, yes, indeed!" answered the young teacher, eagerly. "But I shall feel as if I were leaving my home." "Well, you know you haven't any home now," said the child, naively. "Your father and mother are dead." "Yes, they are," agreed Miss Andrews, sadly. "They died when I was a little girl, and since then I have lived with my aunt and uncle, and my cousin Ruth." "That is nice," commented the child. "My mother is dead, too, and I live with my father. He is a professor in college, and he has to stay there a good deal, and sometimes I am lonesome." "Do you often come here?" asked Miss Andrews, interestedly. "No," replied the child. "This is only our first visit. We came because we wanted to see how people live in the country." "And do you like it?" "Yes, indeed! I think I should like to live in the country better than in the city. It seems more natural and pleasant. Don't you?" "Oh, yes! I love it, although I grew up in a large city myself. My father was a merchant there, and my mother was his partner." "What became of your money when your parents died?" asked the child, curiously. "There wasn't any," answered Miss Andrews, simply. "We didn't have anything except what we earned ourselves. But I was happy enough, and I was taught to be content with what I had." "Were you poor?" persisted the child. "No, I suppose not," replied the young woman. "We managed to get along somehow, and I think we were happier than most rich people. We had each other, and we had our work to do, and we were thankful for that." "How did you make money?" "My uncle was a minister, and my aunt kept house for him. They took me to live with them, and paid me a small salary for teaching school. That is the way I learned to teach."

When she perceived that he was not moved by the sight of her, she watched him more closely; for she said in her girl's heart that the eyes that are blind to a beautiful woman see one of three things: gold, or power, or heaven; but her sight was fixed only on him. Then her throat was dry, her heart fluttered in her maiden breast like a frightened bird, and sometimes, when she would have tried to speak, she felt as if her tongue were broken and useless; the fire ran lightly along her delicate body, her eyes saw nothing clearly, and a strange rushing sound filled her ears; and then, all at once, a fine dew wet her forehead and cooled it, and she trembled all over and was as pale as death - like Sappho, when a certain god-like man was near. Yet the stranger saw nothing, and his look was bright and cold as a winter's morning in the mountains. Almost every day he went out and climbed the foot-hills alone, and when the sun was lowering he came back bringing herbs and flowers, which he dried carefully and spread between leaves of grey paper in a large book; and he wrote spells beside them in an unknown tongue, so that no one dared to touch the book when he went out, lest the genii should wake and come out from between the pages, to blind the curious and strike the gossips dumb, and cast a leprosy on the thief. At night he lay on the roof of the fore-house beside the gate of the court, because it was cool there. Baraka came to him, before midnight, when her mother was in a deep sleep; she knelt at his side while he slept in the starlight, and she laid her head beside his, on the sack that was his pillow, and for a little while she was happy, being near him, though he did not know she was there. But presently she remembered that her mother might wake and call her, and she spoke very softly, close to his ear, fearing greatly lest he should start from his sleep and cry out. 'The ruby mine is not far off,' she said. 'I know the secret place. Rubies! Rubies! Rubies! You shall have as many as you can carry of the blood-red rubies!' He opened his eyes, and even in the starlight they were bright and cold. She stroked his hand softly and then pressed it a little. 'Come with me and you shall know the great secret,' she whispered. 'You shall fill this sack that is under your head, and then you shall take me with you to Egypt, and we will live in a marble palace and have many slaves, and be always together.

We'd sit in tight circles, strumming guitars, crafting dreams bigger than the Parisian night sky, where music was our silent rebellion against the structured ideologies of our parents. My childhood was a world of contrasts-my parents spoke of revolutions, while I dreamt of revolutions in sound, the thumping beats that could unite a crowd, erase borders, and transform a night into something transcendent. In my teens, Paris was a city pulsating with rhythms unknown to the mainstream. The underground clubs and tucked-away venues held a siren's call, and I was mesmerized by the possibilities I found there. Nights would melt into mornings without my realizing, as the beats dictated the course of time, bending reality into something intangible. It was an epiphany; music wasn't just sound, it was a transcendental force capable of altering perceptions. I started my DJ nights in the modest club circuit of Paris. With a second-hand pair of turntables and a collection of records scavenged from local shops, I began to hone my craft. It was all about intuition, feeling the crowd's energy and feeding it back with amplified vigor, the way a dancer harmonizes with an unseen rhythm. It's an unspoken conversation, an exchange that doesn't need languages or words-only beats and the soulful echo they leave in their wake. But Paris, with its roots in tradition and cultural bastions, was hesitant to embrace this new insurgency of sound. I encountered skepticism from club owners and traditionalists alike, but the belief in the music I played-and in the surges of joy and liberation it sparked-never faltered. Even when my parents expressed doubts about the path I had chosen, the music resonating in my veins screamed otherwise. It carried an intensity that matched the fervor of the protests and intellectual debates I'd grown up around. Music was my manifesto, my statement of intent. Then came Ibiza. A sun-drenched island off the coast of Spain beckoned with promises of liberation and limitless creativity. My first residency there was transformative. The island was a place of dreams where DJs were modern-day shamans, leading ecstatic gatherings beneath cascading lights and endless skies. It was where questions of artistic legitimacy vanished, replaced by pure exhilaration and communal bliss. Through determination and a bit of serendipity, I found my sound- a perfect amalgamation of house and electro-pop, tunes built not just to entertain but to elevate. In Ibiza and beyond, the nights became a whirlwind dance of colors and sounds, and I was at the helm, driving the nights into crescendos that even I hadn't known were possible. As my tracks began to soar internationally, my career followed. Collaborations started lining up, each one further propelling the unexpected, yet unfaltering, rise of the DJ to the pop star echelon. This was a revolution of a different kind-a cultural, musical paradigm shift. DJs became the voices behind the microphone, shaping pop culture in ways unforeseen just a few years before. David Guetta's journey isn't just about beats and rhythms; it is about transformation, not just of a man from Paris, but of sound itself-of making a whisper of a genre echo through stadiums and hearts worldwide.

In the context of the escalating global sanitation crisis, the integration of innovative sanitation technologies such as anaerobic digestion (AD) becomes paramount. As the world's population swells and urban areas become increasingly congested, the pressing need for sustainable sanitation solutions intensifies. Households in low-income regions, often lacking adequate infrastructure, find themselves reliant on rudimentary systems that frequently falter under the weight of demand. The provision of decentralized solutions, such as AD, addresses these deficiencies by offering an adaptable, scalable approach to waste management that aligns with local realities. The promise of AD lies not only in its ability to process organic waste but also in its dual benefit: the generation of biogas serves as a renewable energy source. This is particularly vital in regions where energy insecurity poses significant challenges to economic development and daily living. Utilizing biogas for cooking or electricity mitigates dependence on fossil fuels, position ing communities on a path toward energy independence. Moreover, the biogas output can enhance food security by allowing smallholder farmers to invest in crop production and livestock rearing, fostering a more resilient agricultural sector. Despite its virtues, the widespread adoption of AD in sanitation efforts must confront certain barriers, notably the technical and educational hurdles that communities face. Many regions lack the expertise necessary to establish, maintain, or optimize AD systems. Furthermore, public perception often plays a detrimental role; communities may harbor misconceptions about human waste management technologies, fearing health risks when, in fact, these systems can provide safe and effective sanitation solutions. Education and awareness campaigns are thus critical in dispelling myths and fostering community ownership and involvement in sanitation initiatives. The need for integrated approaches is evident. The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) champion initiatives that focus not only on improving sanitation but also on ensuring sustainable management of water resources, supporting the conclusion that sanitation solutions cannot exist in isolation. Improving access to clean water, paired with optimized waste treatment systems, forms an essential bedrock for advancing public health, environmental integrity, and economic growth in vulnerable regions. The link between sanitation and hygiene is crucial; according to WHO, improved sanitation and hygiene practices can significantly reduce the incidence of diarrheal diseases, underscoring the need for comprehensive approaches to achieve long-lasting outcomes. Consequently, one promising avenue involves harnessing local resources and traditional knowledge in the design and implementation of sanitation solutions. Engaging local communities in the process not only fosters a sense of ownership but also ensures that the systems put in place align closely with cultural practices and economic realities. Community-led initiatives can be tailored to meet the specific needs and circumstances of individual regions, enhancing their effectiveness and sustainability. In sum, the integration of anaerobic digestion technology within the framework of decentralized sanitation systems heralds a paradigm shift in addressing the sanitation challenges faced by millions globally. By centering efforts on sustainability, community engagement, and resource optimization, we can establish a foundation that promotes not only public health but also social equity and environmental stewardship. As the world edges closer to the 2030 deadline for the SDGs, the urgency of these initiatives cannot be overstated. Collective action, innovation, and commitment to reimagining our approach to sanitation will be paramount in achieving universal access and eradicating the scourge of inadequate sanitation.

ZnO and doped ZnO fibers are especially interesting for gas sensing and optoelectronic applications due to their high surface to volume ratio. There are several reports in the literature on electrospinning of ZnO, doped ZnO and various metal oxide/zinc oxide composites [27-45]. Al doping has been used to improve the conductivity of ZnO [41-45]. Fibers of bare ZnO [29,30], ZnO doped with cobalt [31], copper [32], cerium [33] and cadminum [34], and ZnO/SnO2 [35,36] and ZnO/In2O3 [37] composites have been used as gas sensors. ZnO/SnO2 [38,39] and ZnO/NiO [40] have been studied as high capacity anodes for lithium ion batteries. Although the excellent controllability of fiber properties and the wide range of attainable materials have made electrospinning the most popular nanofiber preparation method, its industrial applicability is limited due to its modest production rate [46]. Conventionally fibers have been spun from a single needle in which case typical solution flow rates are in the range of 0.1-2 ml/h and fiber productivity around 0.1 g/h and even less in the case of ceramic fibers. Upscaling via multiplication of needles is complicated because the electric fields at the needle tips are altered by the nearby needles significantly affecting the spinning process [47]. Needleless designs relying on self-formation of Taylor cones on polymer solution surfaces have shown improved upscalability, but typically have somewhat less control on the fiber properties [48-52]. Solution blow spinning has recently emerged as a new straightforward method for improving fiber productivity [53-55]. It relies on a high velocity gas flow to draw a polymer solution into fibers. The method has gained significant interest especially in the preparation of nanofibers for biomedical applications. As compared to the needle electrospinning substantially higher solution feed rates can be used and thus productivity is significantly increased. Electroblowing is a combined method of both the conventional needle electrospinning and solution blow spinning, i.e. both high voltage and high velocity gas flow are used to form fibers from a solution [56-58]. The main jet drawing force is the high velocity gas flow and thus high production rates comparable to solution blow spinning can be obtained. Similarly to electrospinning the repulsion between the charges in the polymer jets in electroblowing results in a randomly oriented fiber network with less bundling of fibers as compared to the solution blow spinning [59,60]. Significantly less materials have been prepared by solution blow spinning and electroblowing as compared to electrospinning. Especially reports on preparation of inorganic fibers are scarce. Solution blow spinning has been used to prepare ZnO [61] and via pyrolysis of solution blown zinc acetate/polyacrylonitrile also ZnO encapsulated carbon [62] nanofibers. Alumina fibers have also been solution blow spun and electroblown, though only with relatively large average fiber diameters of 4.12 and 2.75 1/2m, respectively [58]. In this study we used electroblowing to prepare ZnO and conductive aluminum doped zinc oxide (AZO) nanofibers.

Passing down a narrow aisle between the alcoves the visitor noticed that some of the compartments were wholly in darkness; in others where lamps were glowing he could see a table and chairs. In one corner, under a sign lettered ESSAYS, an elderly gentleman was reading, with a face of fanatical ecstasy illumined by the sharp glare of electricity; but there was no wreath of smoke about him so the newcomer concluded he was not the proprietor. As the young man approached the back of the shop the general effect became more and more fantastic. On some skylight far overhead he could hear the rain drumming; but otherwise the place was completely silent, peopled only (so it seemed) by the gurgitating whorls of smoke and the bright profile of the essay reader. It seemed like a secret fane, some shrine of curious rites, and the young man's throat was tightened by a stricture which was half agitation and half tobacco. Towering above him into the gloom were shelves and shelves of books, darkling toward the roof. He saw a table with a cylinder of brown paper and twine, evidently where purchases might be wrapped; but there was no sign of an attendant. "This place may indeed be haunted," he thought, "perhaps by the delighted soul of Sir Walter Raleigh, patron of the weed, but seemingly not by the proprietors." His eyes, searching the blue and vaporous vistas of the shop, were caught by a circle of brightness that shone with a curious egg-like lustre. It was round and white, gleaming in the sheen of a hanging light, a bright island in a surf of tobacco smoke. He came more close, and found it was a bald head. I am not alone: according to statistics compiled by the Canadian Mental Health Association, approximately 2% of the population will suffer from manic depression at some point in their lives, and another 5% will suffer from a major depressive episode. The majority of those who suffer from manic depression have their first episode before the age of 30. Unfortunately there is no cure for this disease, only treatment. And this is where our problems begin. For too long now, mental health has taken a back seat to physical health care needs. We need to look no further than the current situation surrounding the Royal Ottawa Hospital, which has been forced to close beds due to budgetary constraints, leaving patients without a place to stay, and staff without jobs. It is important to note that this is not a unique situation: in October 2003 the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health was also forced to close beds because of budget shortfalls. While it is easy to dismiss these closings as being the result of poor management, it is important to remember that all hospitals in Ontario are facing similar situations. In spite of the recent announcement by Dalton McGuinty's government that they are going to put more money into health care, mental health remains underfunded, and the government continues to treat mental health as a secondary issue. As a result of this lack of funding, the Royal Ottawa Hospital has been forced to reduce the number of acute care beds available to patients from 88 to 48, and the long term care beds have dropped from 90 to 72. These cuts have resulted in the loss of 50 jobs within the hospital, and the closing of 35 beds. One might ask what difference does this make? The answer is simple: every bed that is closed means that there is less room for people who require help. The closure of beds means that fewer people will receive the help that they need. In order to truly appreciate the impact of this situation, it is necessary to understand something of the history of the Royal Ottawa Hospital, and its role in treating mental illness in Eastern Ontario. The Royal Ottawa Hospital, originally known as the Lady Grey Hospital, opened in 1910, as the first psychiatric hospital in Canada that was dedicated exclusively to the treatment of nervous disorders. The purpose of this institution was to provide care for those suffering from mild to moderate forms of mental illness. Over the course of the past century, the Royal Ottawa Hospital has grown to include two campuses, and provides services for both adults and children, as well as providing outreach programs for adolescents. The Royal Ottawa Hospital is also home to the University of Ottawa Institute of Mental Health Research, which conducts research into various aspects of mental illness. The Royal Ottawa Hospital is one of four specialized psychiatric facilities in Ontario, and is the primary facility serving Eastern Ontario, providing services to a catchment area that extends from Cornwall to Deep River, and from Pembroke to Hawkesbury. According to the Canadian Mental Health Association, the average cost of treating a patient in a community-based program is $22 per day, whereas the cost of keeping a patient in hospital is between $500-$600 per day. Given that the average length of stay in a hospital is 10 days, the total cost of treating a patient in hospital is between $5,000 and $6,000. It should therefore follow that it makes economic sense to provide community-based support systems, thereby reducing the amount of time spent in hospital. This is not happening. Instead, the Royal Ottawa Hospital is having to cut beds, and lay off staff, even though it is operating at capacity. Patients are being discharged before they are ready to return to the community, and are then readmitted after relapsing.

Since no snowpack observations are assimilated in operational models, the snowpack stratigraphy may remain skewed during the whole winter season. Thus, freezing precipitation events are considered as a source of errors in numerical snowpack forecasting by French operational services in the Pyrenees. The latest developments in mesoscale Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems offer new opportunities to forecast atmospheric icing and freezing precipitation, since they include advanced cloud micro-physics schemes with a representation of mixed-phase cloud processes and a higher diversity of water species. For instance, Thompson et al. (2009) used the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model at kilometric resolution with an improved microphysics scheme for winter precipitation (Thompson et al., 2004) to predict icing due to freezing rain, freezing drizzle or freezing fog. Forecasting freezing precipitation is still a challenge: in the Integrated Forecasting System of ECMWF (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts), cloud and precipitation physics were recently modified to improve freezing rain predictions (Forbes et al., 2014). Additionally, the high horizontal resolution of mesoscale NWP systems gives a better representation of the topography, which allows to study these events in complex terrain. Drage and Hauge (2008) used MM5 to simulate atmospheric icing in a Norwegian coastal mountainous terrain, in-cloud icing was also simulated by Yang et al. (2012) on Mount Washington (U.S.A.) with the regional mesoscale model GEM-LAM at 1-km grid spacing, and WRF was used by Podolskiy et al. (2012) to simulate rime formation on Mount Zao (Japan) and by Fernandez-Gonzalez et al. (2015) to simulate a freezing drizzle event in the Guadarrama Mountains (Spain), both at 1-km resolution. AROME (Application of Research to Operations at MEsoscale; Seity et al., 2011; Brousseau et al., 2016) is the mesoscale NWP system of Meteo-France, operating at kilometric grid spacing over France (2.5 km from 2008 to 2015, 1.3 km since then). It was recently used to drive snowpack simulations with Crocus at kilometric resolution over the French Alps (Vionnet et al., 2016) and the Pyrenees (Queno et al., 2016). Vionnet et al. (2016) highlighted AROME potential for mountain meteorology and Queno et al. (2016) showed a good representation of the snow cover spatial distribution and benefits in terms of daily snow depth variations, despite strong positive biases in terms of snow depth. More specially, AROME includes a comprehensive cloud micro-physics scheme, and thus, simulates supercooled cloud water, which is of particular interest in regard to the issue of freezing precipitation. The aim of the present study is to assess the potential of AROME associated with Crocus for the detection of freezing precipitation events and the modelling of the formation of an ice layer on the snowpack in the Pyrenees. The original character of the study derives from the use of cloud micro-physical informations from a mesoscale NWP system in mountainous terrain combined to a snowpack model for ground icing. It relies on the first conversion of NEFA to acyl-coenzyme A (Acyl-CoA) in the presence of acyl-CoA synthetase (ACS) (Scheme 1). The acyl-CoA produced is oxidised by acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOD) with generation of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). In the presence of peroxidase (POD), the hydrogen peroxide formed yields a red or blue/purple pigment by quantitative oxidation condensation with TBHB or (MEHA), which can be quantified by UV-spectrometer at defined wavelength. These methods are expensive, time consuming and can only be operated in the laboratory. Therefore, NEFAs are not routinely assessed except within specific clinical study contexts despite their importance in diabetes research and disease management. If H2O2 produced from step 2, acyl-CoA oxidation by ACOD at the presence of oxygen, can be detected electrochemically, it should be possible to determine NEFA concentration electrochemically from the amount of H2O2, similar to the colorimetric method. This could provide a coherent method to current electrochemical based glucose biosensor to develop a multiplex biosensor platform for simultaneous measurement of different metabolic biomarkers. This study will look at the electrochemical detection of H2O2 from the reactions in Scheme 1, using oleic acid (OA) as the NEFA of interest. It was chosen as the NEFA of investigation in this study as it is one of the most abundant plasma NEFAs and it's functional uptake in both muscle and liver are the same as that of total NEFA [18]. Layer-by-layer (LBL) technique is one of the most promising methods for surface modification and biomolecule immobilization because of its simplicity, versatility and wide range of materials that can be used for film assembly [19,20]. The method is mostly based on electrostatic assembly of oppositely charged polyelectrolytes to a charged solid surface. It has been widely used for functional coating, materials encapsulation, biosensing and other applications [21-24]. Since enzymes are also polyelectrolytes, whose charge depends on the isoelectric point (Ip) of the protein and the solution pH, they can be easily immobilized into the LbL film without complex chemical reactions and dehydration. In this way, the electrostatically deposited enzymes can remain good biological activity [25]. However, the commonly used polyelectrolytes in the LbL technique such as poly(allyalmine hydrochloride) (PAH)/poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) (PSS) and poly(dimethyldiallyammonium chloride) (PDA)/polymethacrylic acid (PMAA) are usually electrically nonconductive, which would be a limiting factor for them to be used in bioelectronic devices [23,26]. Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) have attracted great attention as functional materials for preparation of enzyme electrodes and biosensors due to their unique electrocatalytic properties [27-30]. PDA is a strong polycation that can be well adsorbed on carbon or gold electrodes [31,32].

Fall slid into its dormant state and the alleys cooled with the early touch of winter. Yet for us kids, the promise of long summer days lived on in memory. The crisp air tangled with the faint aroma of summer's last laughter, fading echoes skimming across the craggy rooftops. There stood Old Man Withers' house, shrouded in mystery and cloaked in whispered legend. Despite the stories, we all knew the true heart of baseball beat loudest in that forbidden yard, where legends of yore were said to have tossed their gloves and loosed stray balls to the cosmos. "Hey, Smalls!" Timmy had shouted one day, wild excitement in his eyes. "You gonna brave it this time? Gonna be a card-carryin' member of the Mighty Nine?" His voice carried across the distance between us, his challenge marking the air like a dare no kid in their right mind would ignore. Past adventures and neighborhood myths hung in suspense around the elastic tether of the sandlot, and though I had spent endless days embroiled in the gang's antics, I felt the gap still between me and their fervent camaraderie. To them, cliches like teamwork, bravery, and brotherhood were lived truth-not just tales extracted from summer afternoons. That's how it was when you were privileged to play ball with the likes of Benny, Squints, Ham, and Yeah-Yeah. I bit my lip, the silent clamor of the sandlot setting the stage, infusing the chilly air with a hyper-real echo of what summer had been. I wanted in; more than anything, I wanted to be one of them-not just the new kid who miraculously made it through the summer adventures without wilting in the sun. Benny the Jet flashed me a grin, perpetually confident and calm. "We got all winter to by, boys," he declared, optimism marking every word like a beacon against the growing dusk. Benny's gaze met mine. He nodded, as if summoning me to join their hallowed ranks truly now. With a Yankee cap caressed by the late autumn winds, Squints, ever the strategist, mapped out our impending plan. "So how are we gonna get that ball?" he squawked, eyes narrowed behind thick frames, voice a mix of schemer and dreamer. "We go around, through or over?" Challenges laid like a feast in front of us, I realized the crude grandeur of childhood's grand stage; no trophies mattered here-only honor, daring feats, and tall tales spun in the twilight. In this army, we were bound by a singular pursuit: the reclaiming of what was ours, both ball and glory alike. We looked to the creaky fence, plotting our incursion into Old Man Withers' mythic territory. Planning and bickering, our chatter filled the silence, a kind of music all its own. "Let's play," Benny murmured, the words as much an epithet, a summons, as they were a simple suggestion. Through the chill, unyielding in our resolve, we pressed on toward the boundary of the yard where heroes were both born and bested-dreamers on that diamond field of dreams. And together, we knew that with each passing inning, we crafted a legacy uniquely ours, in the endless echo of summer.
