These smallholders typically face multiple constraints, including limited access to inputs and credit, inadequate extension services, lack of market linkages and poor infrastructure (Mottaleb, Rahut, & Ali, 2019; Rigg, Salamanca, & Parnwell, 2016). While these factors contribute to low yields, they also pose formidable barriers to the uptake of new technologies. Consequently, the scaling up of innovations requires carefully designed strategies that take account of the diverse contexts within which farming takes place. In this paper we analyse the case of direct seeded rice (DSR) as an example of a promising technology that can lead to more productive and sustainable rice-based systems. In conventional puddled transplanted rice (PTR), fields are flooded, soil is mechanically tilled and seedlings are raised in nurseries before being manually planted in the main field. PTR is labour intensive, requiring 25-30 person-days ha-1 for transplanting alone (Darai, Singh, & Sidhu, 2016). By contrast, DSR involves sowing pre-germinated seeds directly onto the soil surface without prior tillage or flooding, reducing labour requirements to 10-12 person-days ha-1 (Farooq, Siddique, Rehman, Aziz, & Lee, 2011). Labour savings are particularly important in India where the cost of hiring labour has risen sharply over recent years (Humphreys et al., 2015). With fewer people available to work on farms, especially during peak periods, and many women unwilling to carry out back-breaking tasks such as transplanting, the mechanization of rice establishment methods is becoming increasingly attractive (Kumar & Ladha, 2011). Although the development of DSR started in the 1960s, its widespread adoption was constrained by several issues: (i) the absence of suitable machinery, (ii) the lack of effective weed control options, (iii) poor germination under dry conditions, and (iv) lower grain quality (Mahajan, Chauhan, & Johnson, 2012). However, progress has been made in addressing these problems, resulting in significant improvements in DSR performance compared to PTR, such as higher yields and net returns, and lower water use (Jat et al., 2011; Mahajan et al., 2012; Mahajan, Chauhan, & Gill, 2013). The potential benefits of DSR make it an ideal candidate for SI initiatives. To assess whether these benefits materialize in practice, we present results from a three-year study conducted in four districts of Bihar, covering 900 households across two cropping seasons each year. We compare the performance of DSR relative to PTR using data collected through repeated surveys, supplemented by focus group discussions and key informant interviews. Our analysis covers the economic, agronomic and environmental dimensions of sustainability, assessing both the biophysical and socio-economic impacts of DSR. Given the importance of smallholder inclusion in contemporary SI frameworks, we pay particular attention to how the impacts vary across different farmer groups, disaggregating our findings by gender, education levels, landholdings and wealth status. Finally, we identify lessons learned from this study to inform the design of future SI interventions. 2.1. Study sites We conducted our research in four districts of Bihar - Begusarai, Muzaffarpur, Samastipur and Vaishali - selected because they represent the most common agro-climatic conditions found in Bihar. The region has a sub-tropical monsoon climate, characterized by hot summers and mild winters.

The AMA has told members of Congress that doctors fear a new government-sponsored health insurance program would reimburse them at Medicare rates. "Medicare reimbursement rates have not kept pace with the cost of practice," AMA President Dr. Nancy Nielsen told CNN earlier this week. "Our Medicare rates are back at 2001 rates, and the reality is, that's not where our rent is, that's not where the electricity is. The system for paying doctors is a broken system, and everybody acknowledges it." Other doctors' groups, however, support the idea. The American Academy of Family Physicians, the National Physicians Alliance and other groups put out a statement of support this week for Obama's plan. "Having the choice of a public health insurance plan will help make health care more affordable for patients, foster greater competition in the insurance market and guarantee that quality, affordable coverage will be there for our patients no matter what happens," they wrote in a joint statement.. 9.

Frances nodded thoughtfully, her gaze fixed on the garden below. "She does, in a way, but isn't that what mothers are for? Besides, Aunt Anne never had children, so how would she know?" Donald leaned back, crossing his arms. "Right you are, Frances. She always seems to have a grand opinion on everything, but I reckon she wouldn't last a day in our shoes. Do you remember the time she tried to make us recite poetry after tea?" Frances giggled, a sound like tinkling bells. "Yes, and Lucy quoted 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Bat,' instead of 'Star,' and Aunt Anne nearly fainted with horror. I thought she might never come back after that." "Well, here we are again," Donald said with a resigned sigh. "We must rise to the occasion, I suppose. Even if it means enduring her lectures on the art of proper etiquette or the importance of Latin." Lucy, still cradled in Barbara's affectionate embrace, looked up with wide eyes. "What if we showed her our fort in the backyard? Maybe she wouldn't be so stern if she saw we could build things." Donald chuckled. "Or maybe she'd lecture us on unsafe structures and how children in her day had better toys. But, still, it might be worth a try." Frances turned from the window suddenly, a bright idea alighting in her mind like a bird on a branch. "What if we prepared a performance for her? Like a play or a concert. Something that shows we're not complete heathens." Donald rolled his eyes, but there was a gleam of interest. "A concert, you say? I can play a mean harmonica, you know. And Lucy could sing-or at least try." Lucy clapped her hands, enthusiastic. "I know lots of songs! We could dress up too, just like in the stories." There was a collective nod among the siblings as the seeds of a plan began to sprout. "If we keep her entertained," Frances reasoned, "she might not have time to criticize us. It'll be our secret weapon." Even Donald, who often carried a cynical heart, felt a flicker of hope. "Right then," he declared, standing tall. "We'll need to organize it all quickly. Costumes, music, perhaps some poetry." Lucy wriggled down to join her siblings' huddle. "Barbara can help with our outfits. She always knows how to make things look special." "Capital idea, Lucy," Frances agreed. "And we could rehearse in the afternoons, make sure everything is just right." As the afternoon sun began to set, casting a golden hue over the nursery, the children's spirits soared, buoyed by their bold plan. The prospect of Aunt Anne's visit no longer seemed as daunting. Instead, it shimmered with the excitement of a new adventure. Barbara, peeking in from the doorway, marveled at the whispered excitement. "What are you three plotting now?" she called, a smile tugging at her lips. Donald stepped forward, his chest puffed with pride. "We've decided to give Aunt Anne a proper welcome-a concert and perhaps a theatrical performance. Might you assist us, dear Barbara?" Barbara laughed, delighted by their ingenuity. "Of course, I'll help. But remember, all of you, Aunt Anne only stays for a short while. It's up to us to make her time here as joyful as possible." With determination etched on their faces, they nodded in agreement, pledging silently to make this holiday one to remember-for Aunt Anne and for themselves.

So you see, while the elements of cinema might crave metaphoric storytelling, our current predicament is stripped of all such embellishments. This is raw, unfiltered reality, doused in the gravitas of a dire ultimatum. We aren't playing out some elaborate screenplay's third act climax; we're living in the now, at the mercy of unpredictability. Think for a moment, the ramifications-the chain reactions-this situation could spawn. A city on edge, citizens paralyzed by fear, global news outlets scrambling over each other to capture the next twisted development. Their lenses zooming in, pixels transmitting distant tremors of terror to living rooms worldwide. In moments such as these, the line between audience and participant blurs dangerously. We become unwitting actors in a drama that none of us consented to join. And what of our demands? Simple, yet daunting as they traverse the ether to reach ears that determine fate: a private plane fueled and ready, an uncharted course far from extradition treaties, and an opening of forgotten vaults holding ransom untold. But let us remember, this isn't some garden-variety escapist fantasy crafted from Hollywood's polished veneers. It's a sobering reminder of what realism could look like if it played a more insidious role in the narrative tapestry. Beneath the buzzing cacophony of helicopters cutting through the panoramic skyline, beneath the umbrage of strategic armor and snipers anxiously lingering, you hear the ticking. It crescendos in symphonic strokes of tension, each second dilating into eternity. This isn't just another tedious act of rebellion; it's a clarion call against systemic rigidity-anarchic in method, coherent in cause. Back inside our fortress against folly, nerves fray like wires exposed to stormy weather. Logic clashes with emotion as eyes-fearful, defiant, resigned-speak volumes untethered by scripted dialogue. Humanity's unfiltered face, riddled with faults yet profound in its perseverance, stares back-forcing reflection: Can empathy be extracted from chaos, or are we doomed to be driven by instinct alone? Outside, life doesn't pause; unaware pedestrians continue their partially sanitized circadian routines. Yet, oblivion is partial for a heartbeat-a communal pause ignites whispers of distress. Yet like any spectator snapping from complacency, they too recoil-seeking meaning in senselessness, order in disarray. But reality, unlike fiction, offers no script doctors or last-minute plot revisions. If we survive the complications-should negotiated whispers slither through hashed radio waves, mitigate explosive details-the price of triumph over this unscripted odyssey shall reverberate through corridors of history. If not, our embedded climax shall become another stark cautionary tale that screenplay scribes might find too over-the-top, simultaneously pandering and profound. Either way, as shadows lengthen and night embraces all, a singular truism persists: In the throes of calamity, beneath the exterior woven by capricious storytelling, remains a common denominator too frequently neglected-an innate hunger for order amidst beautifully orchestrated entropy. A beat passes. "So, Stanley," I lean back into the covertly tensed tranquility, "what's the move? Cinema may indulge escapism, but we... we are part of something corpse-cold real. How about we pen our own ending?"

They lived well if plainly, and toiled out in the open unusually hard. Their eyes were steady, their bronzed skin was clear, and their laughter had a wholesome ring. A fiery-haired Scot, a Highlander of the Isles, sat upon a barrel-head sawing at a fiddle, and the shrill scream of it filled the barn. Tone he did not aspire to, but he played with Caledonian verve and swing, and kept the snapping time. It was mad, harsh music of the kind that sets the blood tingling and the feet to move in rhythm, though the exhilarating effect of it was rather spoiled by the efforts of the little French Canadian who had another fiddle and threw in clanging chords upon the lower strings. They were dancing in the cleared space what was presumably a quadrille, though it bore almost as great a resemblance to a Scottish country dance, or indeed to one of the measures of Bretonne France, which was, however, characteristic of the country. The Englishman has set no distinguishable impress upon the prairie. It has absorbed him with his reserve and sturdy industry, and the Canadian from the cities is apparently lost in it, too, for theirs is the leaven that works through the mass slowly and unobtrusively, and it is the Scot and the habitant of French extraction who have given the life of it colour and individuality. Extremes meet and fuse on the wide white levels of the West. It was, however, an Englishman who was the life of that dance, and he was physically a bigger man than most of the rest, for as a rule, at least, the Colonial born run to wiry hardness rather than solidity of frame. Gregory Hawtrey was tall and thick of shoulder, though the rest of him was in fine modelling, and he had a pleasant face of the English blue-eyed type. Just then it was suffused with almost boyish merriment, and indeed an irresponsible gaiety was a salient characteristic of the man. One would have called him handsome, though his mouth was a trifle slack, and there was a certain assurance in his manner that just fell short of swagger. He was the kind of man one likes at first sight, but for all that not the kind his hard-bitten neighbours would have chosen to stand by them through the strain of drought and frost in adverse seasons. As it happened, the grim, hard-faced Sager, who had come there from Michigan, was just then talking to Stukely about him. "Kind of tone about that man - guess he once had the gold-leaf on him quite thick, and it hasn't all worn off yet," he said. "Seen more Englishmen like him, and some folks from Noo York, too, when I took parties bass fishing way back yonder." He waved his hand vaguely, as though to indicate the American Republic, and Stukely agreed with him.

The Olympics consists of 28 sports, 41 disciplines and 306 events. There will be a number of new sports introduced in Rio, with golf and rugby sevens - which made their debuts in 1900 and 1924 respectively - returning for the first time since 1904 and 1924. Meanwhile, kiteboarding was due to replace windsurfing - only for the latter to win it back, ensuring a British medal hope in Nick Dempsey. Canoeing is now canoe sprint and canoe slalom, cycling gets rid of the road time trial and swimming features open-water events. The likes of badminton, handball and shooting all have mixed events for the first time. In athletics, there will be a focus on GB's Mo Farah, Jamaica's Usain Bolt and Kenya's David Rudisha. The Brownlee brothers, Alistair and Jonny, are looking to go gold-silver again in the triathlon, having done so at London 2012. In rowing, Britain's men's eight defend their title, as do Helen Glover and Heather Stanning in the women's pair. Nicola Adams attempts to become the first Briton to defend an Olympic boxing title since Harry Mallin in 1924, and Jade Jones looks to retain her taekwondo crown. Andy Murray hopes to repeat his victory over Roger Federer in the men's tennis singles final four years ago. Justin Rose goes in golf's first Olympic competition since 1904 aiming to emulate George Lyon, who won in Canada that year. There are also plenty of potential stars of the future, such as gymnast Ellie Downie, shooter Amber Hill and diver Tom Daley. There are four levels of protein structure primary secondary tertiary quaternary, and remember when naming these structures. You always start with the smallest and work your way up to the largest. Secondary structure is how the polypeptide chains fold into alpha helices and beta sheets, tertiary structure is when these smaller folded structures come together to create a larger functional three-dimensional shape. And finally, the quaternary structure is when multiple polypeptide chains come together to create a large multi-subunit protein such as hemoglobin or insulin. The function of a protein depends upon its shape and structure, and changes in temperature pH or salinity can change the shape and structure of a protein. Denaturation occurs when a protein's weak chemical bonds break apart, which causes the protein to unfold and lose its shape. Some proteins are denatured naturally during digestion because enzymes in your stomach break apart the bonds in the proteins. The second class of metrics is based on similarity to other targets that are known to be tractable. However, even small differences in sequence can markedly alter ligand binding and thus this method can be highly inaccurate. The third metric is based on analysis of historical data for a target. There is an abundance of experimental data cataloguing measured protein-ligand binding affinities: PubChem [30], BindingDB [31], ChEMBL [32], Binding MOAD [33], PDBbind [34], AffinDB [35], ChemSpider [36] and others. One of the earliest papers on this topic suggested assessing ligandability using the idea of maximal affinity [13]. The idea is that high affinity ligands should have been developed for a highly ligandable target, whereas weaker affinity ligands should have been developed for a target with lower ligandability. This is a logical and effective idea, but there is a caveat. Consider two protein targets for which a similar binding affinity has been reached. If one of the targets requires the testing of ten-times as many ligands to achieve this binding affinity it is arguably a significantly less ligandable target. With this in mind, we attempt to address two important issues with current concepts of ligandability. The majority of studies make a binary distinction between druggable and undruggable targets. Ligandability and druggability are relative concepts, such that separating targets into druggable and undruggable will always be arbitrary. A continuous metric, such as the best-known affinity [13], is more natural and more useful to inform decision making in drug design. One of the reasons that a binary distinction of ligandability has been favoured is that quantification of target ligandability is difficult. Visual inspection of data and personal experience of a given target are not ideal. Experimentally quantifying target ligandability requires careful and unbiased analysis of a large body of data. We discuss an alternative to the concept of maximal affinity, proposing a continuous metric for ligandability based on experimental data. We present a concept of ligandability that is based on the binding affinity achieved for a target as well as the effort necessary to reach this binding affinity. We consider binding affinity data from BindingDB [31] expressed as Ki measurements. Figure 1 shows the pKi values for 1/220,000 compounds, plotted against the molecular weight. The distribution shows a similar picture to previous studies, with a very weak correlation of 0.33 and an apparent ceiling around pKi = 15 (1 fm affinity) [37]. We set out with the goal of devising a metric that quantifies ligandability in terms of the balance of effort and reward. Deriving this metric provides us with experimental ligandability metrics for well-studied targets and allows us to assess our computational predictions of ligandability.

Those same households, she said, also cut back on their trade-book purchases by about 6 percent compared with 2002. "The problem is that you can only grow by attracting new customers, but the industry is not attracting new customers; in fact, it's losing customers," Rappaport said. "That means it's relying more and more on the heavier book-buyer - the more affluent, higher-educated customer - but we're seeing some slack in that area as well. There's only so many books that those people can buy." The root of all evil Why the slippage? One major factor, several experts agreed, is the recent growth of the used-book market, which has been cutting into sales of new books. If you can get a perfectly good used copy of a book for less than half the price - which is easier than ever now, thanks to used-book Internet brokers such as Abebooks.com and, increasingly, Amazon - why buy new? The used-book trend is especially notable among heavy book-buyers, Rappaport said, and in the college textbook market, in which Greco estimates that $1 out of every $3 is now spent on used books, with the trend heading toward $1 out of every $2. But the deeper problem - the root of all evil, from the publishing industry standpoint - is the fact that as entertainment choices multiply, Americans are reading less. According to numbers crunched by Veronis Suhler Stevenson, a New York-based investment bank that specializes in media companies, Americans spent 120 hours a person a year reading consumer books in 1998; by 2003, the number of hours had fallen to 106. By 2006, the projected number of hours we spend reading will be 103. By contrast, according to the VSS findings, television-watching took up 1,551 hours of our time in 1998, and is expected to rise to 1,679 hours two years from now. Internet use is also skyrocketing, from 54 hours in 1998 to a projected 213 hours in 2006. And "Reading at Risk," a new survey released this month by the National Endowment for the Arts using data collected by the Census Bureau, shows that the percentage of Americans who read novels, short stories, plays or poetry - and, in fact, any sort of book - has steadily declined in the past two decades. The drop-off was especially noticeable among young adults, with literary reading among 18-to-24-year-olds dropping from almost 60 percent in 1982 to about 43 percent in 2002. "In 1980, life was very different," Greco said. "You didn't have cable, you didn't have satellite. You didn't have VCRs and DVDs. You didn't have the Internet. These new technologies, while they're wonderful, have diverted people away from a lot of things, including reading."

As I lay on the grass, dazed and rubbing my sore face, I realized that cricket wasn't going to be my ticket to Olympic glory. The ball, once a blur, was now a menacing, hard-edged projectile that seemed to have a personal vendetta against me. I trudged off the pitch, my new specs askew, and slumped against the chain-link fence. The jeers of my classmates still echoed in my ears as I wondered if I was cut out for this sports business after all. But I refused to give up. I devoured books on sports psychology, pouring over chapters on mental toughness and visualization techniques. I practiced my visualization skills in front of the mirror, perfecting my "gold medal" pose and rehearsing my acceptance speech. I even convinced Mum to let me put up a poster of my idol, Eddie "The Eagle" Edwards, on my bedroom wall. Dad, however, remained skeptical. "You're not exactly built for sports, son," he'd say, eyeing my scrawny frame. But I was determined to prove him wrong. I began to scour the local sports clubs, searching for the perfect discipline to showcase my unique talents. One fateful Saturday morning, I stumbled upon a flyer for the Cheltenham Ski Club. Skiing! The thrill of speed, the rush of adrenaline, the stylish outfits - it was the perfect fit. I could already see myself swooshing down the slopes, a vision of elegance and athleticism. I badgered Mum into taking me to the club's open day, where I met the coach, a gruff but kind-hearted Scotsman named Chuck. Chuck eyed me up and down before declaring, "You're a wee bit of a scrapper, aren't ye?" I beamed with pride as he handed me a pair of skis and pointed me towards the makeshift slope. The first few runs were...eventful. I face-planted into a snowbank, got my skis tangled in a fence, and at one point, ended up skiing backwards down the hill. But Chuck was a patient man, and with his guidance, I slowly began to get the hang of it. As the sun began to set on that chilly winter afternoon, I felt a strange sensation - a sense of belonging. I was a skiier, and skiier's were a special breed. We were daredevils, thrill-seekers, and masters of the mountain. And I was one of them. The bus ride home was a blur of excitement and exhaustion. I couldn't wait to tell Mum and Dad about my newfound passion. As we pulled up to our stop, I leapt out of my seat, skis in hand, and bounded up the path to our front door. Mum answered, a look of concern etched on her face. "Eddie, what's all the commotion about?" I grinned, still panting from my exertions. "I've found my sport, Mum. I'm going to be a skiier!" Her face lit up with a warm smile. "Well, isn't that just the most wonderful thing, pet?" And in that moment, I knew that nothing could stop me from reaching the top of the Olympic podium. Nothing, that is, except maybe my lack of coordination, questionable eyesight, and tendency to trip over my own feet...

So I decided to conduct a little experiment. I left the dishes there for a full week, resisting every fiber of my being screaming to tidy them up. I wanted to see if they'd eventually notice, if they'd take the initiative to clean up. My client and I had laughed about this; she promised to try it too with her kids. Day one stretched into day two and nothing changed. In fact, the pile grew. Additional cereal bows adorned the coffee table like uninvited guests. It's amazing really, how quickly it escalates from a single dish to a monumental sculpture of adolescent disregard. By midweek, I noticed a strange thing happening; or more accurately, a lack of happenings. The kids didn't seem to notice the growing clutter. They navigated around the plates with ease and blissful ignorance. Occasionally, I would hear them discussing trivial matters-did you see my phone charger? Can I have a snack? Never once did they mention the evolving art installation on the coffee table. My frustration became intertwined with a strange form of admiration. How could they live in such chaos and remain completely unaffected? My client messaged me with similar results, describing how her own offspring remained blissfully unaware of the mess, stepping over sports gear and remnants of yesterday's homework without a second glance. Each day, we'd compare notes, and each day, we shared disbelief over their oblivion. Kids, we realized, have an unparalleled ability to see what they want to see. And by see, I mean completely disregard everything that doesn't directly impact their immediate desires or needs. By the end of the week, nothing had changed. This was not a lesson learned for our children but rather for us. We came to the conclusion that although they don't notice or share the pressing urgency of a tidy space, it doesn't necessarily signal a failure on our part. Teens are wrapped up in their transitions, caught between childhood simplicity and adult responsibilities. Their focus, more often than not, is internal-do I fit in? Why is growing up so complicated? Is there a new episode of my favorite show? We resolved to change our approach. Instead of battles, we would choose negotiations. Instead of nagging, we'd find a balance between guidance and letting go. In relinquishing control over the small things, we found calm. In humor, we found patience. It was a joint venture into the unknown territory of teen logic. Moments once centered on conflict were now opportunities for conversation. That pile of dishes eventually disappeared-not due to a sudden awakening but because a compromise was reached. We found our peace in acknowledging that their perspective is just vastly different from ours. Letting go of constant battles over cleanliness, we focused on the larger picture, fostering not only a tidier home but also a more harmonious one. And, yes, occasionally it involves a gentle reminder about that ketchup bottle. As for my client, she shared the same sense of newfound understanding. The battle of the plates had become a lesson in empathy, patience, and the art of picking battles wisely. Our plates, once symbols of frustration, became symbols of quiet triumph in the everyday chaos of family life.

After eating lunch we packed up our bags again and headed towards Kalalau Valley, the last 5 miles of the hike. This section of the trail is said to be the toughest part, and it was, but nothing too crazy. We walked through a lot more of the jungle with huge trees, roots, plants, etc. and a lot more steep inclines/declines. About halfway between the two campsites, there is an area called Crawleras Ledge, it's about 200 yards long, straight across the face of the mountain and drops hundreds of feet into the ocean below, very cool. Right after crawleras ledge was probably the worst part of the hike, just a lot of switchbacks and big hills to climb. We arrived at Kalalau Beach around 8pm. 12 hours later. And we were exhausted. We found a spot under a tree to pitch our tent and then cooked dinner and ate, we crashed early. Day 2 a 3 Miles Today was a lot easier, we didn't have as far to go today, we woke up around 9am and made breakfast, then hung out for awhile before taking our day packs and heading to the end of the valley. It took us about an hour to get there, not much elevation change, mostly flat land. When we got there we swam in a freshwater pond which was pretty cold but felt good after sweating so much. Then we sat on the beach for awhile, then went back to our campsite. We made lunch, hung out, met some other people, played cards, ate dinner, then went to bed. Day 3 a 10 Miles The hike back was a lot tougher than the hike there. We woke up around 9am again, made breakfast, broke down camp, and packed everything up. We started hiking back around 11am. The first couple miles weren't too bad, just a lot of uphill. Once we got to Crawleras Ledge, things got harder. Just a lot of ups and downs. Around mile 15, about 2 miles past Crawleras Ledge, my legs gave out on me and I couldn't walk anymore. My calves cramped up and I couldna move them without pain. So I stopped every 100-200 yards for the rest of the hike. I would stop and stretch my legs and try to massage them a bit, they hurt like hell. It took forever to get back, I kept thinking we were almost done, but it seemed like it would never end. By the time we got to the top of the hill leading down to the waterfall, I thought I was done, but once we got to the waterfall I realized we still had another mile to go. So I did what any person would do, I took off my shoes and socks and waded across the river barefoot, and it felt amazing! Then I put my socks and shoes back on and finished the final mile. We got back to the parking lot around 9pm. It was dark. I was tired. My legs were cramping. But I was happy. I had made it. 32 miles in three days. Ia never hiked anything close to that distance before. I was proud of myself. I feel like I accomplished something. And now I want to keep accomplishing things. Numerical simulations based on Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) techniques represent the most promising solution because, if properly validated, they could provide useful information about the physics of the fluid-structure interaction phenomena, such as flow separation, reattachment, spray generation, and so on. Among all CFD approaches, the Reynolds Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) simulation technique is the most used one because it provides reliable solutions within reasonable computational times. However, the RANS approach requires the definition of a turbulence model that is able to simulate the turbulent nature of the flow field around the hull. Unfortunately, no universal turbulence model exists. For this reason, many authors proposed their own models or adopted different turbulence models for different geometries, operating conditions, and flow regimes. An exhaustive review of the literature concerning CFD applications to stepped hulls can be found in [6]. In this chapter, the authors present some numerical investigations carried out using a free-surface RANSE solver to study the hydrodynamics of stepped hulls in calm water and in waves. In Section 9.2, the numerical methodology is presented, while in Sections 9.3 and 9.4, respectively, two validation test cases against experimental data are discussed. Then, in Section 9.5, a parametric investigation aimed at studying the effects of wave height and length on the hydrodynamic performance of a typical stepped hull is reported. Numerical Investigation of Stepped Hulls Zotti I.;Bruzzone D.;Villa D.;CAMPORA U.;MUSCARI R.;CAMBIERI M.;FILIPPI G.;SCAMARDELLA P. In the last few years, the development of lightweight engines and propulsion systems, along with the development of lighter boats built by shipyards with new technology and materials, has forced designers to pay increasing attention to hull design. Outboard engines in particular are characterized nowadays by a very low weight to power ratio and high reliability. These features make them suitable for several installation types, including military, commercial, pleasure, and racing. The new composite materials allow a boat weight reduction of 30% with respect to a traditional hand-made layup. In this scenario in recent years, the high-speed planing craft for military, commercial, and pleasure use, with a very low weight to power ratio has spread even further. The reduction of weight to power ratio involves an increase of maximum speed; as a consequence, naval architects are oriented even more in stepped hull design to reduce the resistance at high speed and ensuring good dynamic stability and seakeeping. The step is a sharp discontinuity located in the bottom surface of the hull; it is transversal and usually V-shaped, with the vertex facing aftward, on the outboard sides of the hull the step terminates with large apertures (also named 'inlets') for incoming air. As pointed out by [1], the stepped hull is characterized by a low hydrodynamic drag-to-lift ratio at high speeds and by a wetted area reduction due to a flow separation, which occurs at step location and then reattaches at the aft body [2]. Moreover, stepped planing hulls have a small variability of trim angle and improve control of the longitudinal attitude because they are sailed always on a n + 1 wetted triangle, where n represents the number of steps. In fact, for a single stepped hull, an additional aft-lift is created, due to the presence of the reattachment line (stagnation line) in the aft-body. This force keeps the running trim of the vessel almost constant with Froude number (at high speed).

We identified 35 studies that reported on the risks of adverse outcomes in individuals discharged from inpatient psychiatric care, with 22 of these studies examining suicide risk, 10 examining all-cause mortality, and 5 examining non-fatal self-harm. Only 3 studies reported on homicide victimisation, and 2 studies reported on homicide perpetration. No studies examined the full range of adverse outcomes investigated in our study. The existing literature suggests that individuals discharged from inpatient psychiatric care are at increased risk of adverse outcomes, but the evidence is limited by the lack of standardisation in outcome definitions, study populations, and follow-up periods. Our study aimed to address these limitations by examining a comprehensive range of adverse outcomes in a single cohort of individuals discharged from their first inpatient psychiatric treatment episode. We used Danish national registry data, which provided a large and representative sample of individuals with a history of inpatient psychiatric care. The use of registry data also allowed for accurate and complete follow-up of the study cohort, reducing the risk of bias and increasing the precision of our estimates. We estimated incidence rates and relative risks for each adverse outcome separately according to follow-up period, ranging from the first 3 months to 10 years or more post-discharge. This allowed us to examine the temporal pattern of risk for each outcome and to identify periods of highest risk. We also compared the absolute and relative risks across the various endpoints examined, providing a comprehensive picture of the range of risks faced by former psychiatric inpatients. Our results showed that individuals discharged from inpatient psychiatric care were at increased risk of all adverse outcomes examined, with the highest risks observed in the first 3 months post-discharge. The risk of suicide was particularly elevated in the short-term, with a relative risk of 15.6 (95% CI 12.3-19.8) compared to individuals of the same age and sex without a history of inpatient psychiatric care. The risk of homicide victimisation was also high, with a relative risk of 10.2 (95% CI 7.4-14.1). In contrast, the risk of all-cause mortality was highest in the longer term, with a relative risk of 2.5 (95% CI 2.2-2.9) 5-10 years post-discharge. The risk of non-fatal self-harm was also elevated, with a relative risk of 4.8 (95% CI 4.1-5.6) in the first year post-discharge. The risk of hospitalisation due to violence was highest in the short-term, with a relative risk of 6.3 (95% CI 4.8-8.3). Our findings suggest that individuals discharged from inpatient psychiatric care are at increased risk of a range of adverse outcomes, with the highest risks observed in the short-term. The comparison of absolute and relative risks across the various endpoints examined provides a comprehensive picture of the range of risks faced by former psychiatric inpatients, and informs service planning and policy. Our results highlight the need for targeted interventions to reduce the risk of adverse outcomes in this population, particularly in the short-term post-discharge.

DTI-based diffusion metrics are then assumed to reflect white matter organization at the center portion of the tract/s of interest middle. However, it is now well documented that such templates at times fail to reflect the 'center' of a tract which can result in questionable anatomical accuracy, the combination of which can result in spurious group differences in tract metrics (see Bach et al., 2014). Thus, some have argued that TBSS based approaches should be interpreted with caution (Bach et al., 2014; Pecheva et al., 2017; Tamnes et al., 2017). With respect to behavioral relevance, in some of the above studies alterations in white matter organization coincided with poorer motor performance in the DCD group. However, the direction of the correlation coefficients have also been mixed/unexpected in some studies (Zwicker et al., 2012). For example, Zwicker and colleagues found that the decreased motor ability observed in children with DCD was associated with decreased mean axial diffusivity in the CST and posterior thalamic radiation. However, developmental studies have typically shown that, where changes are observed, axial diffusivity tends to decrease with age from childhood through to adolescence (for a review, see Lebel et al., 2017). This is likely the result of the increased complexity in fibre orientation that is generally observed with maturation, which would hinder diffusion along the principal axis of the diffusion ellipsoid and reduce axial diffusivity. Accordingly, were white matter properties in motor tracts to contribute to poorer motor outcomes, one might assume microstructure to be disrupted which would generally manifest as increased axial diffusivity in otherwise healthy children. Consequently, the behavioral significance of previously reported white matter abnormalities in DCD is difficult to discern. Finally, in all previous diffusion MRI studies in DCD the diffusion tensor framework has been adopted (i.e., diffusion tensor imaging- DTI), which requires only moderate numbers of encoding directions (a minimum of six) and relatively low b-values (b ~ 1000 s/mm2) (Caan, 2016). Accordingly, DTI remains the most common diffusion MRI modelling method. Nonetheless, the fundamental limitations of the DTI model have been well documented in seminal works (Farquharson and Tournier, 2016; Farquharson et al., 2013; Jeurissen et al., 2013; Jones, 2008; Jones et al., 2013; Tournier et al., 2011). Briefly, DTI relies on a single tensor to estimate fibre orientation within a voxel, meaning that it can only resolve a single fibre orientation per voxel and is unable to represent multiple fibres in a single voxel. Since fibres are thought to cross, fan and/or diverge in up to 90% of white matter voxels (Jeurissen et al., 2013), it is now widely recognized that the DTI framework is prone to creating anatomically inaccurate reconstructions or spurious white matter tracts/streamlines and should therefore be interpreted with extreme caution (Tournier et al., 2011). Hence, while previous studies applying the basic tensor framework have provided important insight into white matter organization in DCD, these data must be interpreted in the context of the abovementioned fundamental limitations.

If you fellows don't know enough to throw on the switch after all these years of running a car, and then expect to sit there and grin your heads off while I break my back cranking, you're mighty much mistaken - that's all I've got to say. You may think it's a joke, but I don't! I'm through with you," and turning on his heel, after flashing a look at his two chums, Bob Baker started off down the road afoot. "Here, where are you going?" called Jerry, after him. "Home!" was the short answer, "and I'm not going out with you fellows again in a hurry!" Ned and Jerry looked at one another. It was the first time in a long while that there had been any serious difference among the three chums. "Oh, come on back!" urged Ned, for he saw that Bob was very much in earnest. "Come on back." "Not on your life!" snapped Bob. "I'm through." "We didn't mean anything," went on Ned, starting after his friend. "But it was so funny to see - " "Ha! Ha! Joke!" sneered Bob. "If it's so funny write it out and send it to the humorous column. You won't get another chance to laugh at me, though." "He's mad, all right," murmured Ned. "Looks so," agreed Jerry. "Oh, I say Bob!" the tall lad went on, "come on back. Honest, I didn't know the switch was off. Come on back. It's a good ways to Cresville, and we've only just started the run. Come on back, and you can steer, and I'll crank up. And if we get a puncture Ned and I'll put on a new tire, and you won't even have to get out of the car. I mean it!" The figure, stalking down the road in anger, was seen to hesitate the merest trifle. But Bob did not turn around. "That almost fetched him," said Jerry. "Say something, Ned." "We'll stop at the first place we come to, and get a bite to eat, even if it isn't noon," shouted the lad who had discovered the disconnected switch. "That ought to do the business," he added, in lower tones. It seemed to be, for Bob halted, appeared to be considering the matter at length, and then turned around. "Does all that go?" he demanded. "Sure," chorused Ned and Jerry. "And about me not having to help sweat putting on a tire?" "That's right," Jerry assured him. Bob came slowly back. "All the same," he spoke as he climbed into the tonneau, "it was no fun cranking a car with the switch off." "We agree with you," said Jerry, winking at Ned with the eye concealed from his offended chum. "But it wasn't intentional," he added, soothingly, as he went to the crank. "Go ahead, Bob, you can steer if you want to."

He would come out on the lawn in the morning, and sit down beside her on the bench, and talk about all manner of things except those that concerned themselves, and she would listen hungrily. When he left her, she would go into the house, or into the park, and walk up and down until her excitement subsided, and then she would set herself to some task, any task, in order to calm herself. The next day he might not speak to her. These flashes of light were followed by darknesses of depression, and Honora's spirits rose and fell accordingly. She did not know what to expect from day to day, and her mind was never free from anxiety. The newspapers, too, were full of the progress of the campaign, and she found herself reading articles and editorials on political subjects which hitherto had been closed books to her. A new interest possessed her, and she wondered why she had never felt it before. From time to time she received notes from Susannah Price, who kept her informed of events in Ripton. One of these contained a curious piece of news: Mr. Isham had suddenly sold his place and gone away, no one knew where. The town was agog with speculation, but Mrs. Price had heard nothing definite, save that he had taken rooms in New York. This intelligence had the effect of reawakening Honora's fears concerning the real object of his visit to Highlawns, and she was haunted by the thought that she had not sufficiently warned Hugh of the man's treachery. She took to scanning the faces of the tradesmen who came to the door, wondering whether Isham might not send emissaries to spy upon them. Another thing disturbed her: the absence of letters from Mr. Larrabbee. Why didn't he write? She had no means of knowing that he was in Europe. And what was happening to Hambleton? Had Hugh forgotten that he had promised to help him? What was going to become of poor Hambleton? At last, when she could endure the suspense no longer, she resolved to ask Hugh point-blank, and seized upon an opportunity when he appeared unexpectedly at luncheon one day. "Mr. Larrabbee hasn't written lately," she said. Hugh started, and glanced across the table at her. "No." "I wish you'd let me see his letter, Hugh." "It was very short," he replied, "and it didn't concern you." She had never known him to be deliberately rude to her before, and her hand trembled as she put down her fork. Her face was very pale, but she persisted. "What is going to happen to Mr. Hambleton?" she asked. He stared at her. "What do you mean?" "Haven't you forgotten him, Hugh?" she demanded. "I'm afraid you have. You haven't done anything for him since we've been here. I can't think how you could forget your promise to him!" "You're right," he exclaimed, with a sudden contrition. "I had forgotten him." "Well, I haven't," said Honora. "No, I don't suppose you have," he answered, looking at her curiously. "You seem to remember everything, Honora." She was silent for a moment, striving to control her voice. "Don't you care any more what happens to him, Hugh?" she asked. "Yes, I care," he said, quickly. "Do you want to hear the truth?" he asked. "It isn't a pretty story." "Go ahead," she replied, "I'm used to the truth."

Of data-derived models, linear interpolation of observed total suspended solids (TSS) concentrations (Box C) has the most intense data requirement but the least predictive capacity. The sediment budget is the defining concept for modelling all major sources and delivery of sediment at a basin scale (Trimble, 1993). In some northern hemisphere agricultural systems, surface erosion dominates sediment sources (Walling and Collins, 2005) and the effectiveness of best management practices (BMPs) is well represented in existing models (e.g., Zhang and Zhang, 2012). However, gully and streambank erosion can also be important sources at basin scale (Prosser et al., 2001b). Many sediment models omit these processes while providing in-depth treatment of surface erosion (de Vente and Poesen, 2005), which can jeopardise remediation priorities (Boomer et al., 2008). The environmental and land management drivers of sources and sinks can provide powerful constraints on predictions of sediment loads away from monitoring stations provided they are appropriately conceptualised. Representing the spatial patterns in sediment sources is key to effectively reducing losses of fine sediment from agricultural watersheds, as it is for reducing phosphorus losses (Gburek and Sharpley, 1998). Sediment sinks such as deposition in reservoirs and floodplains are also important since they can have large impacts on sediment delivery through stream networks (Prosser et al., 2001b; Trimble, 1993). For example, while accelerated sediment loads causes severe pollution impacts in some coastal waters, the net effect of human activity has been an overall decline in sediment yield to the global ocean, with accelerated erosion being outweighed by sediment trapping within reservoir impoundments (Syvitski and Kettner, 2011; Walling, 2008). The mean-annual SedNet sediment budget model (Box A; Fig. 1), has been applied to identify river basin sediment sources across the large area (> 420,000 km2) draining to the Great Barrier Reef (GBR; McKergow et al., 2005b), and to assess the relative effectiveness of source management in reducing river loads (Cogle et al., 2006). A large component of total phosphorus and total nitrogen is also delivered to the GBR attached to fine sediment (Kroon et al., 2012). However, this mean-annual model does not estimate load time-series for input to hydrodynamic and biogeochemical models of receiving waters. Time-series are important for understanding ecosystem impacts such as Crown-of-thorns starfish (COTS) outbreaks on the GBR, which are triggered by elevated river pollutant loads in large flood events and are a major cause of declining coral cover (De'ath et al., in press). In this paper we describe a major variation of the SedNet model called dynamic SedNet, abbreviated to D-SedNet.

There are various types of such money-back guarantees. These include, for example, a coupon to participate in another tour, as in the case of whale watchers in Hawaii who do not see whales. In the case of the Amami rabbit, which is an endangered and iconic wildlife species in Japan, tour participants to Amami Oshima, Japan who do not see rabbits can receive 50% of their money back. Although the money-back guarantee is expected to increase tour numbers, such risk could also result in the failure of the nature-based tourism business model. In other words, the money-back guarantee could significantly reduce tourism revenue, depending on the tour fee, refunding ratios (e.g. 50% guarantee), and the number of tour participants. However, the tradeoffs around the money-back guarantee have not been discussed in this context. Estimating demand for wildlife viewing without the guarantee offered by tour operators could, therefore, mislead stakeholders, such as wildlife managers and policymakers. To address this, we examine the case of the Amami rabbit tours in Japan to investigate tourist preferences for wildlife viewing, while taking into account money-back guarantees. In business and marketing, the money-back guarantee is a well-known refund mechanism (Desmet, 2014; Suwelack, Hogreve, & Hoyer, 2011) used to reduce the likelihood of consumers being dissatisfied. It also improves their perception of the purchased goods as high in quality and reliability (Boulding & Kirmani, 1993; Heiman, McWilliams, & Zilberman, 2001; Moorthy & Srinivasan, 1995). Although it remains challenging to understand exactly how a money-back guarantee affects human behavior and decision-making (d'Astous & Guevremont, 2008), scholars have shown that such guarantees can significantly influence consumer decision-making (Boulding & Kirmani, 1993; Erevelles, Roy, & Yip, 2001). Despite its widespread use and reports (Evans, Dana Clark, & Knutson, 1996; Meynecke et al., 2017; Scott & Lemieux, 2010), no studies have quantitatively examined how the design of a tour with money-back guarantees can affect customers' participation decisions and tour guides' revenue. This study thus makes several unique contributions to the literature. First, we statistically model consumers' preference towards the design of tours with money-back guarantees and their participation decisions as a function of the tour price and the money-back guarantee ratio. The estimated model then allows us to calculate how consumers' participation decision and tour guides' revenue are affected by the price, money-back guarantee ratio, and sighting probability. We then identify the revenue-maximising design under various levels of sighting probabilities. No prior studies on money-back guarantee have considered how tour guides could change the tour design to attract participants. Using the case of the Amami rabbit tours in Amami Oshima, Japan, the main objective of this study is to investigate the preferences of tourists for wildlife viewing by taking into account money-back guarantees. We apply the discrete choice model as the valuation method to assess tourist willingness-to-pay for Amami rabbit-viewing.

We then provide discussion and conclusions. ## Literature Review ### Paratransit Management in Developing Countries In developing countries, paratransit is operated under two different types of ownership: individual and cooperative. Individual ownership refers to when each driver owns his/her own vehicle and operates independently, while cooperative ownership indicates that multiple drivers jointly own one or more vehicles, and share the profits and losses (Gannon and Liu, 1997). In general, paratransit is operated under the individual-ownership model, but cooperative ownership is becoming increasingly common due to its advantages over individual ownership, such as reducing operational costs and increasing revenues (Gannon and Liu, 1997). Several studies have focused on paratransit management in developing countries. Cervero and Golub (2007) reviewed various cases of paratransit management in developing countries and summarized them into four categories based on the degree of intervention by authorities: laissez-faire, partial regulation, full regulation, and deregulation. They argued that, although the optimal approach depends on local contexts, the most appropriate option might be a combination of all four approaches. In addition, they mentioned that, in order to make the transition from a laissez-faire to a regulated regime, it is necessary to develop a political consensus among stakeholders through dialogue, negotiation, and compromise. Joewono and Kubota (2007c) conducted a comparative study of paratransit management in Indonesia, Thailand, and Vietnam. They concluded that paratransit services should be integrated with formal transport modes to create a seamless transportation system. In order to integrate paratransit services, they recommended the following measures: (i) setting up a legal framework that allows for the integration of paratransit services; (ii) establishing a coordinating body that oversees the coordination of paratransit services; (iii) providing financial support for paratransit operators; and (iv) creating a favorable business climate for paratransit operators. According to Gannon and Liu (1997), the following factors determine whether paratransit will operate under the individual- or cooperative-ownership model: * Vehicle cost: If the vehicle cost is high, the cooperative-ownership model may be preferred because it allows drivers to pool resources and share the cost of purchasing and maintaining vehicles. * Operating cost: If the operating cost is high, the cooperative-ownership model may be preferred because it allows drivers to share the cost of fuel, maintenance, and insurance. * Market demand: If the market demand is high, the individual-ownership model may be preferred because it allows drivers to respond quickly to changes in demand. * Competition: If competition is intense, the cooperative-ownership model may be preferred because it allows drivers to cooperate and compete against larger companies.

The authors found that patients with left dorsolateral prefrontal damage frequently named the digit instead of the letter. These patients seemed to understand the instructions and did not have problems in repeating them. However, they failed to maintain the instruction active over time. Interestingly, the same problem emerged also in healthy subjects who were distracted during the task performance. Thus, it appears that, depending on certain conditions, we can all be prone to behave in an automatic fashion, disregarding our own intentions. Although the literature concerning this phenomenon is still scarce, recent studies have started to investigate the effect of specific factors, such as cognitive load, on capture errors. For instance, it has been shown that performing a secondary task interferes with performance in a primary task, increasing the rate of capture errors (Risko, McLaughlin, Foulsham, & Kingstone, 2012). Moreover, it has been demonstrated that capture errors can be reduced through practice of the target task (Levy, Pashler, & Boer, 2006). Goal Neglect and Capture Errors Giorgia Cona;Sergio Della Sala;Maria Serena Panzeri In many everyday situations, people act disregarding their explicitly intended goals, automatically following other lines of actions that were not part of their original plan. An example of this not infrequent situation could be the following: one morning you get up with the clear intention to do something, for instance to electronically pay your bills. When you turn on your computer and click the browser icon, your emails get in your way. Your original idea fizzles and another goal takes charge. You start reading and replying to emails, including some which are clearly much less important than having the power cut off due to lack of payment (which, by the way, will end any further possibility of reading your emails). This "unwanted" behaviour seems to be automatically triggered by cues in the context that drag us to other lines of action interfering with our original aims and goals. In the given example, the sole glance at the browser icon is enough to make you disregard your original plan. This replacement of some goals with others happens in countless situations of everyday life and most of us live with it, without further consequences. In human psychology, such occurrences have been described as "slips" or "capture errors", referring to errors that occur when a more salient or practised behaviour takes place when a similar, but less salient, action was intended (Norman, 1981, 1983; Reason, 1990). This term has been widely used in different fields including client usability, and in both medical and legal psychology. In one case, for example, two police officers claimed to have shot a suspect while supposedly intending to use their taser (Shoichet, Morris, & Lavandera, 2015). Even if the importance of such mistakes has long been recognized, there is not much research performed to elucidate which variables - regarding the subject and the action context - predispose to this kind of error in normal subjects. Patients with frontal lobe pathology show slips and capture errors at multiple levels. In anarchic hand, for example, objects in the environment may draw out compulsive, unwanted actions from the affected hand (Della Sala, Marchetti, & Spinnler, 1991; Riddoch, Edwards, Humphreys, West, & Heafield, 1998).

Furthermore, fMRI-Neurofeedback allows for simultaneous monitoring of other brain regions that may change during learning, thereby providing important information about neural mechanisms of change. The first studies on fMRI-Neurofeedback were conducted in healthy subjects and focused on self-regulating brain regions involved in pain perception (deCharms et al., 2005; Yoo et al., 2008). Subsequently, fMRI-Neurofeedback was applied in patient populations with various disorders including chronic pain (DeCharms et al., 2005), depression (Young et al., 2017), anxiety (Zilverstand et al., 2015), Parkinson's disease (Subramanian et al., 2011), tinnitus (Hallam et al., 2015), stroke (Sitaram et al., 2014) and ADHD (Alegria et al., 2017; Kucyi et al., 2016). In ADHD, fMRI-Neurofeedback studies so far have targeted different brain areas, such as the right anterior insula (Kucyi et al., 2016), the right caudate nucleus (Alegria et al., 2017), and the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Liu et al., 2017). In all three studies, participants successfully learned to increase BOLD signal in the respective target region, albeit at varying degrees. Alegria et al. (2017) reported enhanced caudate activation in ADHD adolescents relative to controls and increased connectivity between caudate nucleus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) following fMRI-Neurofeedback. This study also reported improved task performance and decreased reaction times in the ADHD group compared to controls after fMRI-Neurofeedback (Alegria et al., 2017). Liu et al. (2017) found increased functional connectivity from the DLPFC to the striatum, posterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus. They also observed significantly higher ratings of sustained attention ability in the ADHD group after fMRI-Neurofeedback. Kucyi et al. (2016) reported enhanced insular activation after fMRI-Neurofeedback, but no changes in symptoms or task performance. Although these preliminary findings suggest that fMRI-Neurofeedback is feasible in ADHD, none of these studies included an active control condition. Alegria et al. (2017) compared ADHD adolescents with healthy controls who received the same number of sessions as the clinical group, but did not find any differences between groups, suggesting that the effect could have been due to repeated exposure to the task rather than to neurofeedback. Therefore, the aim of this pilot study was to test whether there is a differential improvement in ADHD symptoms in adolescents receiving real vs. sham fMRI-Neurofeedback. Sham fMRI-Neurofeedback is a valid placebo control condition because it provides feedback on brain activity from another person, hence participants do not receive feedback on their own brain activity and thus cannot train it (Sulzer et al., 2013). We also explored whether there were any differences between groups regarding functional connectivity patterns of the basal ganglia and the fronto-parietal network, given that they play a crucial role in inhibitory control and motor planning, functions that are impaired in ADHD (Castellanos et al., 1996; Rubia, 2011, 2018b; Vaidya et al., 1998).

The reason why he adopted this course is not far to seek. In a word, he wished to be polite. He could not bear to shock people's feelings. He was fond of saying, "I am afraid I should be too much of a boor if I said what I think." And yet Gaetan had been brought up as a Catholic, like all the members of his family since time immemorial. His mother died when he was nine years old, and his father, occupied with public affairs, gave him little attention. But he was educated by a Jesuit tutor, and in spite of the progress of the revolutionary spirit in France he received the first communion, the sacrament of penance, confirmation, and matrimony. All these things happened to him without his understanding them very clearly, but he performed the ceremonies mechanically, as he would have done had he been baptizing a child, marrying a couple, or burying a corpse. It never occurred to him that such rites might be mere formalities, meaningless gestures. On the other hand, he had a great respect for priests, whom he called "the clergy," and he believed that they ought to be respected because they were the representatives of God. As a boy he thought that they wore white linen bands round their necks, and that they ate fish every day except Fridays, when they fasted. He also imagined that they spent most of their time in singing psalms, and that they prayed continually. These ideas were not so remote from the truth as may appear to modern readers. They are found in the catechism books used in the schools of the period, and they were taken seriously by many of those who read them.

As we delve into the realm of climate governance, it becomes increasingly apparent that the dominant discourses and metaphors employed by powerful elite sources play a crucial role in shaping public perception and policy outcomes. Our analysis of influential climate policy-science reports from prominent international climate governance institutions between 1992 and 2012 reveals a fascinating narrative of how these discourses have evolved over time. One of the most striking features of our analysis is the prevalence of economic metaphors in climate policy discourses. The language of markets, costs, and benefits has become increasingly dominant, reflecting the growing influence of neoliberal ideology on climate governance. The 1992 UNCED report, for instance, emphasized the need for "sustainable development" and "environmentally sound economic growth," while the 2012 Rio+20 report spoke of "green economy" and "low-carbon growth." This shift towards economic metaphors has significant implications, as it frames climate change as a problem that can be solved through market mechanisms and technological innovation, rather than a fundamental transformation of societal values and practices. Another key theme that emerges from our analysis is the notion of "urgency" and "crisis." The 1992 UNCED report warned of the "imminent threat" of climate change, while the 2012 Rio+20 report spoke of the "window of opportunity" to address the crisis. This rhetoric of urgency serves to create a sense of emergency, which can be used to justify policy measures that might otherwise be seen as draconian or unpopular. However, it also risks creating a sense of fatalism, where the public feels overwhelmed by the scale of the problem and disempowered to take action. In addition to economic metaphors and the rhetoric of urgency, our analysis also reveals a significant emphasis on the concept of "resilience." The 2007 IPCC report, for instance, emphasized the need for "adaptation" and "resilience" in the face of climate change, while the 2012 Rio+20 report spoke of "building resilience" and "enhancing adaptive capacity." This focus on resilience reflects a shift towards a more pragmatic, technocratic approach to climate governance, where the emphasis is on managing the impacts of climate change rather than mitigating its causes. Our analysis also highlights the importance of "partnerships" and "collaboration" in climate governance. The 1992 UNCED report emphasized the need for "international cooperation" and "global partnership," while the 2012 Rio+20 report spoke of "multi-stakeholder partnerships" and "public-private partnerships." This emphasis on partnerships reflects the growing recognition that climate change is a complex, multi-faceted problem that requires the involvement of a wide range of actors, from governments and corporations to NGOs and local communities. In conclusion, our analysis of influential climate policy-science reports between 1992 and 2012 reveals a complex and evolving landscape of discourses and metaphors. The dominant themes of economic metaphors, urgency, resilience, and partnerships reflect the growing influence of neoliberal ideology and the increasing recognition of the complexity of climate change. However, they also raise important questions about the power dynamics at play in climate governance, and the extent to which these discourses serve to empower or disempower different actors and interests. As we move forward in the fight against climate change, it is essential that we critically examine the language and metaphors we use, and work towards a more inclusive and equitable approach to climate governance.

Legros foresaw grand pageants and courtly gatherings swathed in his creations-the very thread linking courtly pomp to the tailored manifestations of his imagination. As the day waned, golden light poured through the workshop's tall windows, illuminating the animated figures within, each seam and stitch charting a course toward destiny. In the light of this debate we have chosen to focus on reports from prominent international organisations involved in the building of a climate governance regime because although they may not govern entire policy fields on their own, international organisations often set and implement key rules within them; create, channel, and disseminate knowledge; shape dominant discourses; frame problems and solutions; influence negotiations through their ideas and expertise; and oversee the implementation of projects on the ground (Newell et al., 2012: 96). This grants them an important, and often underestimated, degree of autonomy and power to shape outcomes (Newell et al., 2012). In the final reckoning, policies are ideas about how the world should be, and "ideas do not exist apart from language" (Marx, 1953, cited in Prawer, 2011: 272). Because the sources we analyse are important sources for journalists, they have the power to define the language used to describe possible responses to climate change within the public sphere. The wide attention paid to the Stern report on the economics of climate change (Stern, 2006) and the ensuing discussions about the relative financial costs of mitigation versus unmitigated climate change highlight just how central economic frames are to discussion of climate policy. We argue that there is nothing intrinsic to anthropogenic changes in the chemical composition of the atmosphere which demands that decisions about whether and how to respond should be made solely through economic frames. Rather, we suggest that focusing attention on climate change as an economic problem is a conscious political act, performed primarily through language. This is not to deny the relevance of economics to climate policy making, but it has been argued that justice and ethics (e.g. Vanderheiden, 2008) and democratic decision-making principles (Machin, 2013; Carvalho and Peterson, 2012) are equally important frames for governance of climate change. Suggesting that climate change is primarily an economic problem reduces the policy space for these alternative framings and the resultant marginalisation of these less expert, technical frames undermines efforts being made elsewhere to build strong positive public engagement (Machin, 2013; Carvalho and Peterson, 2012). Given the importance attributed to the communication of climate change, we suggest a better understanding of how institutional narratives are shaping downstream framings of climate change can offer guidance as to where in the communication process interventions should be directed. The cultural circuits model provides a longitudinal analysis of how environmental discourses evolve as they are received and re-communicated through the cultural filters of producers and consumers (Carvalho and Burgess, 2005: 1460). The model identifies media professionals as the producers of environmental discourses; "groups of media professionals...produce stories from source materials which will define the days news" (Carvalho and Burgess, 2005). These media professionals produce texts, in line with linguistic, visual and genre norms which help define the public sphere (Carvalho and Burgess, 2005: 1458).

Many studies have shown the important role of the surface area of reacting minerals - the fluid-solid interface - in determining rates and extents of reaction in porous rocks (Helgeson et al., 1984; Velbel, 1985; Haggerty and Gorelick, 1995; Kieffer et al., 1999; Colon et al., 2004; Luquot and Gouze, 2009; Noiriel et al., 2009; Gouze and Luquot, 2011; Navarre-Sitchler et al., 2013). The observation of surface area, and its distribution among specific mineral phases in a porous medium, however, has been complicated by the difficulty in interrogating the interior properties of a rock. Conventionally, the approach for characterising surface area in field settings has been to measure overall surface area using, e.g., N2-BET, and correlate mineral specific surface area to modal composition (Helgeson et al., 1984; Velbel, 1985; Zhu, 2005; Kampman et al., 2009). Observations of the rates of reactions in rock cores with simple mineralogy - pure quartz, calcite - and well established rate laws have also been used in Kieffer et al. (1999), Colon et al. (2004), Noiriel et al. (2009), and Luquot and Gouze (2009) to infer the evolution of surface area in sandstone and carbonate rocks. Neutron scattering has been used by Navarre-Sitchler et al. (2013) to characterise surface area heterogeneity and its evolution with reaction in low-porosity igneous rocks. That technique had the advantage that features with length scales from microns to nanometers are simultaneously characterised across a sample domain with a length scale of order 1 cm. Recent work by Peters (2009), Landrot et al. (2012), Golab et al. (2013) and Hezel et al. (2013) have described the distribution of surface area from observations of rocks using X-ray and electron imaging. In those works they pioneered the combined use of these observations, registering 3D X-ray imagery of rocks at the microscopic scale with 2D electron image mapping of minerals to produce 3D maps of the mineral distribution within a rock. The success of these techniques suggested that there was an opportunity to derive these statistical descriptions of the pore space from direct imagery of the mineral phases in situ of the rocks themselves. In this work we endeavoured to apply those techniques to develop a statistical description of the heterogeneity in the mineral surface area available for reaction from direct observations of a Berea sandstone and five carbonate rocks. The rock samples were dominated by pore-network structures, absent fractures, dissolution features, and vuggy conduits for flow. The description of these structures will be key to a full description of reactive processes in porous media, but is outside the scope of this work. In this paper the materials and methods employed for the research are reviewed in Section 2. This includes brief summaries of the use of conventional petrological characterisation tools and more detail about the techniques used for processing X-ray images. The results are presented in Section 3.

SusPtrit has naked grains (i.e. not covered by hulls) of amber color. Initial multiplication of seed material from these mapping populations was carried out both under greenhouse and field conditions, resulting in healthy grains. After a few rounds of multiplication, however, in each mapping population some of the lines produced very poor quality grains, that looked dark-discolored and shrivelled, and showed poor germination rate. Both naked- (hulless) and covered- (hulled) seed lines seemed to be affected by this condition. Growing the plants in the greenhouse, under controlled temperature and humidity and sulphur fumigation to control pathogens, did not solve the problem. The poor quality condition of the grains was initially presumed to be due to infection by a seed borne pathogen, but no fungal or bacterial agent was identified as causal organism after samples were analysed by a seed laboratory certified by ISTA (International Seed Testing Association) standards ('NAK', Nederlandse Algemene Keuringsdienst voor zaaizaad en pootgoed van landbouwgewassen Grain discoloration in barley and wheat is reported in literature under several terms: kernel discoloration (KD, term that will be mostly used in this study), weather staining, kernel blight, dark smudge, black stain and more (Jacobs and Rabie, 1987; Li et al., 2003; Mathre, 1997). Dark discoloration at the embryo end of the grain is particularly referred to as black point, and is considered as a type of kernel discoloration by some authors (de la Pena et al., 1999; Li et al., 2003) but as a distinct phenomenon by others (Walker et al., 2008). Kernel discoloration in general is a problem for the barley grain industry because it negatively affects the quality of malting barley, consequently downgrading it as feed and leading to significant economic losses (Li et al., 2003; Miles et al., 1987). Also seed germination rate and seedling emergence and vigour are negatively affected (Li et al., 2003, 2014). There is no consensus on the causes of kernel discoloration. Early reports linked it to a number of fungal pathogens, mainly Alternaria alternata, Bipolaris sorokiniana, and Fusarium graminearum (Li et al., 2003; Mathre, 1997). Other studies, however, provided no evidence of association between discoloration and fungal infection, with no differences in the amount of mycelium observed in black-pointed and normal barley or wheat grains (Jacobs and Rabie, 1987; Williamson, 1997). A general agreement is that environmental conditions play a key role in grain discoloration. QTL mapping studies have been performed for black point (BP) and KD in barley (Canci et al., 2003; de la Pena et al., 1999; Li et al., 2003; Tah et al., 2010; Walker et al., 2008), with several genomic regions identified. KD, therefore, is a complex and poorly understood trait, governed by multiple genes and under strong influence of environmental factors. In the present study, we set out to investigate whether the poor grain quality character in the three SusPtrit-derived mapping populations had a genetic basis.

The quest for a stable foam in oil-saturated porous media has been a long-standing challenge in the field of enhanced oil recovery. As mentioned earlier, oil can have a detrimental effect on foam stability, making it crucial to understand the impact of oil on foam behavior. These studies have provided valuable insights into the mechanisms by which oil affects foam stability, but more work is needed to fully understand the complex interactions between oil and foam. One approach to mitigate the impact of oil on foam stability is to develop surfactants that can effectively stabilize foam in the presence of oil. Surfactants are molecules that reduce the surface tension between oil and water, allowing foam to form and stabilize more easily. However, not all surfactants are created equal, and some may be more effective than others in stabilizing foam in oil-saturated porous media. Recent studies have focused on the development of novel surfactants that can effectively stabilize foam in the presence of oil. For example, researchers have explored the use of block copolymers, which are molecules composed of two or more different blocks that can interact with oil and water in different ways. These molecules have been shown to be effective in stabilizing foam in oil-saturated porous media, and may offer a promising solution to the problem of foam stability in oil displacement applications. In addition to the development of novel surfactants, researchers have also explored the use of other techniques to improve foam stability in oil-saturated porous media. For example, some studies have investigated the use of nanoparticles to stabilize foam, which can provide additional benefits such as improved foam mobility and reduced foam breakdown. Other studies have focused on the use of electric fields to enhance foam stability, which can be particularly useful in situations where the oil-saturated porous media is highly heterogeneous. Despite these advances, there is still much to be learned about the behavior of foam in oil-saturated porous media. Further research is needed to fully understand the complex interactions between oil, foam, and surfactants, and to develop effective strategies for stabilizing foam in these challenging environments. However, with continued advances in our understanding of foam behavior and the development of novel surfactants and techniques, it is likely that foam will play an increasingly important role in the field of enhanced oil recovery. In conclusion, the development of stable foam in oil-saturated porous media is a critical component of enhanced oil recovery. While oil can have a detrimental effect on foam stability, researchers have made significant progress in understanding the mechanisms by which oil affects foam behavior and in developing novel surfactants and techniques to mitigate these effects.
