However, with continued advances in our understanding of foam behavior and the development of novel surfactants and techniques, it is likely that foam will play an increasingly important role in the field of enhanced oil recovery.

Professor Oxford explains: 'The mutated version isn't any nastier - it just means the vaccine isn't as effective because it doesn't recognise it.' Some viruses mutate faster than others - for example, swine flu (H1N1) hardly changes at all, whereas H3N2 can change quite significantly within a few months. 'This is a problem every year, but particularly so this year because the flu strain is mutating more rapidly than usual,' adds Professor Oxford. 'If someone gets the mutant strain they may still get sick, but if they've had the vaccine, they will probably suffer less severe symptoms and recover more quickly.' CAN WE MAKE ANOTHER VACCINE NOW? No. It takes five months to develop a new vaccine, so even if the mutated strain were targeted now, it wouldn't be ready until April. And by then, flu season will be over. There is also another problem. If the vaccine were changed now to target the mutated strain, it would mean that anyone who'd already had the original vaccine would need another dose. This is impractical, since most people don't want two jabs. SO WHY NOT HAVE TWO DIFFERENT TYPES OF JABS? The idea of having two jabs to protect against two versions of H3N2 is not practical, according to Prof Oxford. 'People do not like having injections,' he says. 'And if you start making a fuss about the vaccine, fewer people take up the offer.' He adds: 'It's important to remember that although the vaccine isn't perfect, it is still worth having. Even if you're unlucky enough to catch the flu after vaccination, your illness should be milder than if you hadn't been vaccinated.' WHO'S MOST AT RISK FROM FLU? Flu is caused by several different viruses and spreads through coughs and sneezes. Symptoms include fever, chills, headaches, aches and pains, sore throat, runny nose and cough. Most people will feel better within a week, but it can lead to serious complications such as pneumonia, especially among older people, pregnant women and those with chronic illnesses. These groups are offered the free NHS jab. Pregnant women are urged to get the flu vaccine to avoid birth defects. Researchers have warned that women who come down with the infection during pregnancy are four times more likely to have a child with brain damage. Scientists found babies born to mothers who contracted flu were 36 per cent more likely to have spina bifida, a condition where the spine fails to form properly, leaving part of the spinal cord exposed. They were also nearly twice as likely to suffer cleft palate, where the roof of the mouth fails to close completely. The researchers believe the problems arise due to high temperatures brought on by flu affecting how a baby develops in the womb. WHAT ARE MY CHANCES OF CATCHING IT? Currently, the risk is low. Figures released by Public Health England show that between December 21 and January 4, 43.9 GP consultations out of 100,000 were for flu-like illness. This compares with 107.2 out of 100,000 at the peak of the 2008/09 flu pandemic. But Dr Richard Pebody, head of seasonal flu surveillance at PHE, warns: 'We are currently seeing a rise in flu activity and urgent treatment with antiviral medications is recommended for those with flu in intensive care. 'Flu vaccination offers the best protection against the virus and it's not too late to get vaccinated.' WILL ANTIBIOTICS HELP ME? Antibiotics kill bacteria and cannot treat viruses such as flu.

They provide a basis for the justification of decisions and actions and thus shape agendas for action. Foresight activities and scenario-based methods have long been used as tools for managing uncertainty in business and military planning, and have become increasingly popular in public policy making in recent decades (Da Costa et al., 2008; Georghiou, 1996; Havas, Schartinger, & Weber, 2010; Sardar, 2010). Foresight is understood here as a range of methodological approaches that aim at systematically exploring alternative socio-technical futures through participatory processes. Foresight has been applied in various areas of public policy, including environmental, health and technology policy, and particularly in science and technology policy. While foresight exercises often include the exploration of both positive and negative visions of the future, other anticipatory practices, such as horizon scanning, focus primarily on identifying risks and threats (Kuusi, Cuhls, & Steinmuller, 2015). Both foresight and horizon scanning have gained importance in recent years as part of efforts to strengthen evidence-informed decision making in policy. As such, they complement other anticipatory practices, such as impact assessment or cost-benefit analysis, which seek to estimate the effects of proposed policies, rather than explore alternative futures. Foresight and horizon scanning can be seen as part of a broader shift towards "anticipatory governance" that seeks to incorporate knowledge about potential future developments into present-day decision making (Barben et al., 2008; Guston, 2014; Owen, Macnaghten, & Stilgoe, 2012). In contrast to traditional forecasting techniques, which attempt to predict the future based on past trends, foresight and horizon scanning take account of uncertainties and contingencies. As a result, they produce not singular predictions, but rather sets of possible futures that may occur depending on certain conditions. The papers in this special issue build on these perspectives and advance our understanding of how socio-technical futures feature in the governance of innovation in three respects: First, the articles broaden the scope of inquiry beyond established methods and tools, such as foresight or horizon scanning. Second, the articles highlight the importance of practices that go beyond formalized methods, such as storytelling or the use of metaphors. Third, the articles analyze how socio-technical futures shape the governance of innovation by studying how they influence policy agendas, actor networks, regulatory frameworks, or the design of technological artifacts. The article analyzes the influence of anticipatory practices on policy debates concerning the development of self-driving cars in Germany. Drawing on interviews with key stakeholders, it examines the role of expectations and visions of self-driving cars in shaping the policy agenda, actor networks, and regulatory framework. The findings show that the vision of self-driving cars as a solution to traffic congestion and safety issues was central in driving the policy debate and mobilizing support from different actors. However, the study also highlights the importance of other factors, such as economic interests and institutional dynamics, in shaping the policy process. Overall, the article contributes to the literature on anticipatory governance and the role of socio-technical futures in shaping policy debates. This paper discusses the role of foresight as a tool for shaping socio-technical futures in the context of the European Union's Horizon Europe program. It argues that foresight can help to anticipate potential challenges and opportunities associated with emerging technologies, and suggests that a multi-level approach that combines top-down and bottom-up initiatives can enhance its effectiveness. The paper also emphasizes the importance of involving a wide range of stakeholders in the foresight process to ensure that diverse perspectives are taken into account.

Each thought tumbles over the other, like a chaotic procession of feelings marching through the corridors of my mind. The fear is palpable, a cold, creeping fog that wraps itself around my chest, squeezing tighter with every heartbeat. What have I become? Who am I in this shifting landscape of friendships and choices? I didn't ask for this emotional upheaval, this tumult that feels like a tornado ripping through the previously calm plains of my life. The weekend is creeping closer, an imminent specter that sends shivers down my spine. What if it's the last time I genuinely enjoy my time with Tyler-our ridiculous inside jokes, late-night conversations that last well into dawn, the immense comfort of his presence reminding me that I'm not alone in this sprawling city? The thought of that possibility makes my stomach churn. Will this weekend become a funeral for the friendship that has shaped so much of who I am? There's a gnawing question at the back of my mind-am I overanalyzing everything? All these feelings, all this worry, do they stem from my insecurities or a genuine concern for the bond I hold dear? Each day, the distance grows-not in miles yet, but in shadows that extend between us. I've felt it more acutely since we decided to part ways. It's a strange and unwelcome deja vu, invoking memories of high school friendships forged in innocent youth, only to fade into distant echoes as we grew older and more complicated. And then there's David, who remains the steady foundation amidst my swirling doubts. He is the tether that keeps me grounded, the voice of reason that I desperately need. I think of him sitting across the table, how he'll offer a listening ear or a well-timed joke to ease the mounting tension in our conversations. But does he know the true extent of my turmoil? I'm not sure. Sometimes, I catch myself veiling my darker thoughts in humor, hoping it'll mask the cracks beginning to splinter my facade. I find myself playing scenarios in my head like a movie on a continuous loop-behind the laughter, the shared moments, the easy camaraderie, will I uncover an undercurrent of resentments and worries? Part of me fears that if I open up, if I let slip the fragile emotions gnawing at me, I'll disrupt the delicate balance we've managed to maintain. I need to talk to Tyler about my feelings; perhaps I owe him the honesty of my turmoil. Yet, with each passing hour, I feel a tightening knot in my chest. Maybe this is what growing up is-learning to navigate the muddy waters of emotional complexity and discern how to maintain connections when they feel just out of reach. Perhaps I am becoming the monster I once feared-obsessed with preserving what's left of my happiness at the cost of others. Is that the price of admission to adulthood? The realization is frightening, illuminating darkened corners I'd rather leave untouched. As the sun dips low on this strange day, I recognize that I may have to confront my ugly reflections sooner rather than later. The fear is daunting, but the looming prospect of losing Tyler is scarier still. Perhaps, in this whirlpool of anxiety and discomfort, I will find the courage to finally speak the truths that have long begged for release.

Inadequate characterisation of tephra layers may lead to erroneous correlations, especially in areas with many active and thus potential source volcanoes. Miscorrelations can have serious implications for derived age models, e.g., in palaeoenvironment reconstructions. In this paper, we present a critical review of the late Quaternary tephrostratigraphic record as it is known from scientific literature for the Andean Southern and Austral Volcanic Zones, which span the approximate latitude range 33-55 S (Fig. 1). They comprise 74 volcanic centres thought to have been active during post-glacial times (Global Volcanism Program, GVP, http://volcano.si.edu/; Large Magnitude Explosive Eruptions database (LaMEVE), http://www.bgs.ac.uk/vogripa; Crosweller et al., 2012; Siebert et al., 2010), ranging from clusters of (monogenetic) cones to central stratovolcanoes and large volcanic complexes. They include some of the most historically active volcanoes of the Andes, such as Villarrica and Llaima, both of which have erupted several times per decade in recent history, with relatively limited regional impact (Dzierma and Wehrmann, 2010; Van Daele et al., in press). They also include several volcanoes that have had historical Plinian-style eruptions with significant regional or even hemispheric impact, e.g., the 1932 Cerro Azul (Quizapu; Hildreth and Drake, 1992), 1991 Cerro Hudson (Wilson et al., 2012), 2008 Chaiten (Watt et al., 2009) and 2011 Puyehue-Cordon Caulle (Collini et al., 2013) events. This region is of particular interest not only for its frequent volcanic activity, but also because of the potential for investigating the (pre-)historical regional record of large earthquakes (similar to the 1960 Mw 9.5 Valdivia earthquake) using turbidite deposits in lakes (Arnaud et al., 2006; Moernaut et al., 2007; Bertrand et al., 2008a). In addition to being volcanically and tectonically active, southern South America is the only landmass to cross the southern westerly wind belt, which is a significant control on global ocean circulation and so climate (Kilian and Lamy, 2012). High-resolution palaeoenvironmental archives have therefore been sought from the many fjords, lakes, and areas of peatland in southern Chile and Argentina (Kilian and Lamy, 2012). The predominantly post-glacial records obtained have provided significant insights into, for example, interhemispheric climatic linkages and the dynamics of both Holocene climate and the regional deglaciation (e.g., Lamy et al., 2010; Moreno et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2013). At the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM; ca 25-16 ka in the study region; Hulton et al., 2002; Glasser et al., 2008; Kaplan et al., 2008) the Southern and Austral Volcanic Zones were largely glaciated, so this region is a good case study to investigate the potential coupling between deglaciation and volcanism, namely a possible increase in eruption rates during deglaciation and early post-glacial times (Huybers and Langmuir, 2009; Watt et al., 2013a).

As I sit here in my comfortable American home, surrounded by the familiar sounds of English being spoken and the hum of air conditioning, I can't help but feel a pang of guilt. Guilt for complaining about the heat and the language barrier when I first arrived in the Philippines. Guilt for taking for granted the luxuries I have here. But most of all, guilt for not doing more when I was there. I think back to the faces of the children we met, their bright smiles and curious eyes. I think about the mothers who worked tirelessly to provide for their families, despite the odds against them. I think about the fathers who toiled in the fields, their sweat and labor yielding little more than a meager harvest. And I think about the GK workers, selfless and dedicated, who poured their hearts and souls into making a difference. As I reflect on my experience, I realize that it wasn't just about the physical poverty I witnessed. It was about the emotional poverty that plagues so many. The feeling of hopelessness, of despair, of being trapped in a cycle of poverty with no way out. It was about the lack of confidence, the lack of self-worth, the lack of dignity. But it was also about the resilience, the strength, and the determination of the human spirit. It was about the GK workers who refused to give up, who refused to accept that poverty was a permanent state. It was about the mothers who fought to provide for their families, who worked tirelessly to give them a better life. And it was about the children, who despite the hardships they faced, still managed to smile, still managed to laugh, still managed to dream. As I settle back into my life here, I know that I can't just forget about the Philippines. I can't just forget about the people I met, the experiences I had, and the lessons I learned. I have to do something. I have to spread the word, to share my story, to make a difference in my own way. I know it won't be easy. I know there will be times when I'll feel overwhelmed, when I'll feel like I'm not making a difference. But I also know that every small step counts. Every conversation I have, every article I write, every donation I make, is a step towards creating change. As I look back on my journey, I realize that it's not just about the Philippines. It's about me. It's about my own growth, my own transformation. It's about recognizing my own privileges, my own biases, and my own limitations. It's about becoming a better person, a more compassionate person, a more empathetic person. And so, as I close this chapter of my life, I know that it's not really an ending. It's a beginning. A beginning of a new journey, a journey of self-discovery, of growth, of making a difference. A journey that will take me to places I've never been, to meet people I've never met, and to experience things I've never experienced. But most of all, a journey that will allow me to make a difference, one small step at a time.

3. Wireless LANs: A New Dimension in Networking The concept of wireless LANs is not new, but the technology has only recently become practical and affordable for widespread use. Wireless LANs offer the potential to revolutionize the way we access and share information. By providing mobility and flexibility, wireless LANs can increase productivity, improve communication, and enhance collaboration. Wireless LANs can be used in a variety of settings, including: * Office buildings: Wireless LANs can provide employees with the flexibility to move around the office and stay connected to the network without being tied to a specific desk or location. * Education: Wireless LANs can enable students to access course materials and collaborate with classmates from anywhere in the classroom or campus. * Healthcare: Wireless LANs can provide medical professionals with real-time access to patient records and medical information, improving patient care and streamlining communication. * Manufacturing: Wireless LANs can enable factory workers to access production data and communicate with colleagues in real-time, improving efficiency and productivity. * Public hotspots: Wireless LANs can provide public access to the internet and other network resources, making it easier for people to stay connected while on-the-go. 4. IEEE 802.11: A Standard for Wireless LANs The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) has developed a set of standards for wireless LANs, known as IEEE 802.11. The 802.11 standard defines the physical and data link layers of a wireless LAN, including the protocols and procedures for data transmission, error detection and correction, and network management. The 802.11 standard is designed to provide a common framework for wireless LANs, allowing devices from different manufacturers to communicate with each other seamlessly. The 802.11 standard is divided into two main parts: the physical layer (PHY) and the medium access control (MAC) layer. The PHY layer defines the physical characteristics of the wireless link, including the frequency band, transmission rate, and modulation scheme. The MAC layer defines the rules for accessing the wireless medium, including the protocols for data transmission, error detection and correction, and network management. The 802.11 standard is designed to be flexible and adaptable, allowing it to be used in a variety of wireless LAN applications. The standard supports multiple frequency bands, including the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, and multiple transmission rates, including 1 Mbps, 2 Mbps, 5.5 Mbps, and 11 Mbps. The standard also supports multiple modulation schemes, including frequency shift keying (FSK), phase shift keying (PSK), and quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM). 5. Wireless LAN Architecture A wireless LAN consists of several key components, including: * Wireless network interface cards (WNICs): These are the devices that connect devices to the wireless network. WNICs are typically installed in laptops, desktops, and other devices. * Access points (APs): These are the devices that connect the wireless network to the wired network. APs are typically installed in a central location, such as a building or campus. * Base stations: These are the devices that provide the wireless link between the APs and the wired network. Base stations are typically installed in a central location, such as a building or campus. * Network management system: This is the software that manages the wireless LAN, including the configuration of the APs, WNICs, and base stations. The architecture of a wireless LAN is designed to provide a flexible and scalable network that can support a variety of devices and applications.

The early years of his life were marked by a distinct absence of convention. Educated by experience rather than instruction, he absorbed knowledge from the very world he traversed. Whether mingling with the common folk or observing the nuances of more rarified circles, Ferdinand's education was that of a practical philosopher-one who measures the scope of his wisdom not by dusty tomes but by the weight of lived experience. And it was precisely this education that emboldened him to set out upon the journey that would define his legend. Fathom's exploits were as varied as they were daring. Unfettered by the constraints that encumbered men bound to station or meticulous upbringing, he navigated the labyrinth of society with an agility unmatched by his peers. He was at once a tactician and a diplomat, a master of subtlety whose words danced with eloquence, capable of eliciting the glint of admiration or the shadow of suspicion. His path was neither straight nor narrow, but it was unmistakably his own, marked by an audacious spirit that reveled in the conquest of circumstance. As the chronicle of Ferdinand's life unfurls, it becomes evident that he bore no illusions about the nature of his enterprise. The world was a canvas upon which he could inscribe his destiny, each encounter a stroke in the grand tableau of his existence. He was as much a creation of his own will as of the situations he molded to his favor. While others might have been daunted by the prospect of self-creation, Ferdinand embraced it with fervor, transforming each obstacle into an opportunity for self-expression. In this endeavor, Ferdinand Count Fathom stands as a testament to the indomitable human spirit. His legacy, intertwined with the very fabric of his exploits, challenges the reader to ponder the boundaries of identity, merit, and the inexorable pursuit of one's own truth. Through the annals of his adventures, he emerges not merely as a figure of history but as a beacon of resilience, urging us to question the narratives we construct and the legacies we leave behind. And so, this tale unfurls, with its myriad twists and turns yet to reveal.

They found spatial clustering of areas of high heat vulnerability in Central and East London that coincide with areas of potentially high heat exposure. Taylor et al. (2015) examined the risk of mortality in London during hot weather events by combining data on population age and distribution, UHI, and dwelling characteristics to calculate the spatial variation in heat-related mortality risk across London. Spatial variation of heat-related mortality was found to reflect background mortality rates due to population age, while dwelling characteristics were found to cause a larger variation in risk than the UHI. This research, however, did not consider future climate, socio-demographic or adaptation scenarios. Jenkins et al. (2014b) utilised high spatial resolution probabilistic projections of urban temperatures with projections of demographic change as part of a risk assessment at the ward scale in London. They found that reducing indoor temperatures by 1-2 C reduced both annual heat-related mortality and residential overheating compared to no-adaptation in future scenarios, however limited consideration was given to the nature and feasibility of potential adaptation actions. A range of actions including land-use planning, building design, community resilience, and emergency planning and response must be considered together for cities to manage long term heat-risk. Research on the effectiveness of localised adaptation actions in London is growing, including solar shading; building insulation and ventilation (Porritt et al., 2012); roof insulation and window upgrades (Mavrogianni et al., 2012); green roofs (Virk et al., 2015, 2014); and occupant behaviour (Mavrogianni et al., 2014). However, evidence on the effectiveness of adaptation actions in lowering heat-related mortality is limited (Frontier Economics, 2013), and quantifying the effectiveness of specific adaptation options into an associated temperature based increase in resilience at the city scale remains a significant challenge (Jenkins et al., 2014b). There is limited research on existing and future heat-risk that actively considers the effectiveness of specific adaptation actions in managing that risk through time at the city scale (Stone et al., 2014). There is a need to continue developing, trialling, critiquing and demonstrating how pathways approaches can be utilised in informing and motivating adaptation planning (Wise et al., 2014; Haasnoot et al., 2012; Barnett et al., 2015; Kingsborough et al., 2016). Adaptation pathways have not been applied to long-term planning for urban heat-risk at the city scale, and a lack of demonstration in this context limits decision-makers' confidence in their utility. This paper explores the potential for adaptation strategies to manage future heat risk under a long-term population growth and climate change scenarios. This research adopts a framework for adaptation planning and the development of adaptation pathways developed by Kingsborough et al. (2016); generates quantified estimates for the effectiveness of a range of adaptation options; and utilises an updated probabilistic spatial heat-risk assessment model developed by Jenkins et al. (2014b) to demonstrate how adaptation pathways in response may manage long-term heat-risk in London.

[Footnote 1: See Chapter XVIII.] Roger Armstrong was the son of the third child of a Scotch-Irish family that had settled on the banks of the Ohio, and there established their home, which became the starting point of the later migrations into the Mississippi Valley. The lad's grandfather, Sandy Armstrong, was born in Ireland, came over to America with his parents, and grew to manhood among the Pennsylvania Germans. He married a girl from Virginia, and removed westward, building his log cabin on the banks of the Ohio, in the neighborhood of Wheeling, where he lived during the remainder of his life. His children were numerous, and all of them had become grown men and women before the outbreak of the Revolutionary War. Two sons fought under Washington, one being wounded at the battle of Germantown. Both returned safely to their homes after the close of the war, and continued to live in the vicinity of Wheeling. One of these was the father of Roger Armstrong, whom we have mentioned. He married a young lady from Maryland, and removed farther westward, settling near St. Louis, where he bought land, and commenced farming. His wife died soon afterward, leaving her husband with a boy and a girl. Several years later he married again, and shortly afterward moved still farther westward, establishing himself on the bank of the Missouri River, where he began clearing off timber and preparing his farm. He had a large family of boys and girls, the eldest of whom was Roger Armstrong. As has been said, the lad was born in Maryland, and spent his childhood in the vicinity of Wheeling, where he attended school, and received such instruction as could be obtained at that early day. When quite young he went to St. Louis, and there attended school until the death of his step-mother. Afterward he accompanied his father to the Missouri, and assisted in the preparation of the new farm. Here he lived, working hard and doing well, until the spring of the year 1804, when he set forth on an expedition that led him far beyond the limits of the then territory of the United States. At the time of which we write he was eighteen years of age, tall and slender, with light hair, blue eyes, and fair complexion. He was considered a bright lad, and fond of reading, though somewhat headstrong. Roger's companion, Richard Wade, was also the son of a pioneer. His father was an Englishman who left England when quite a young man, and came to America. He was an industrious mechanic, and did good work wherever he went. He settled first in Philadelphia, where he learned his trade as a carpenter, and where he met and married a young lady from New Jersey. They remained in Philadelphia for many years, rearing a family of four sons and two daughters. In the course of time the father took up his residence in Baltimore, where he opened a shop, and worked at his trade, making chairs, and other wooden articles. Soon afterward he removed to Fredericktown, in the State of Maryland, and purchased a tract of land, where he built a house, and commenced farming. All of the members of his family, except the youngest daughter, had attained maturity when he made this removal. The oldest son, whose name was John, remained in Baltimore, following the same calling as his father. A second son, Robert, entered the army, and served through the Revolutionary War, receiving promotion at its close, and retiring from active service with the rank of captain. Afterward he located in Fredericktown, where he followed farming, and died some years ago.

His visits were less frequent, and when he met the young girl, whose very life was bound up in his, his manner had in it a reserve that chilled her heart as if an icy hand had been laid upon it. She asked for no explanation of the change; but, as he grew colder, she shrunk more and more into herself, like a flower folding its withering leaves when touched by autumn's frosty fingers. One day he called on Edith. He was not as cold as he had been, but he was, from some cause, evidently embarrassed. "Edith," said he, taking her hand - it was weeks since he had touched her hand except in meeting and parting - "I need not say how highly I regard you. How tenderly I love you, even as I could love a pure and gentle sister. But - " He paused, for he saw that Edith's face had become very pale; and that she rather gasped for air than breathed. "Are you sick?" he asked, in a voice of anxiety. Edith was recovering herself. "No," she replied, faintly. A deep silence, lasting for the space of nearly half a minute, followed. By this time the maiden, through a forced effort, had regained the command of her feelings. Perceiving this, Edwin resumed - "As I said, Edith, I love you as I could love a pure and gentle sister. Will you accept this love? Will you be to me a friend - a sister?" Again there passed upon the countenance of Edith a deadly pallor; while her lips quivered, and her eyes had a strange expression. This soon passed away, and again something of its former repose was in her face. At the first few words of Florence, Edith withdrew the hand he had taken. He now sought it again, but she avoided the contact. "You do not answer me, Edith," said the young man. "Do you wish an answer?" This was uttered in a scarcely audible voice. "I do, Edith," was the earnest reply. "Let there be no separation between us. You are to me what you have ever been, a dearly prized friend. I never meet you that my heart does not know an impulse for good - I never think of you but - " "Let us be as strangers!" said Edith, rising abruptly. And turning away, she fled from the room. Slowly did the young man leave the apartment in which they were sitting, and without seeing any member of the family, departed from the house. There was a record on his memory that time would have no power to efface. It was engraved too deeply for the dust of years to obliterate. As he went, musing away, the pale face of Edith was before him; and the anguish of her voice, as she said, "Let us be as strangers," was in his ears. He tried not to see the one, nor hear the other. But that was impossible.

As the demand for wood pellets continues to rise, the need for innovative solutions to address the challenges associated with their production and transportation becomes increasingly pressing. One such solution is the application of torrefaction technology, which involves the thermal decomposition of biomass at temperatures between 200-300 C to produce a dry, brittle, and porous material. This process has been shown to significantly reduce the moisture content of biomass, making it easier to store and transport, while also increasing its energy density and grindability [14]. Torrefaction has been found to be particularly effective in addressing the issues of moisture absorption and mold growth, which are major concerns in the production and transportation of wood pellets. By removing the majority of the biomass's moisture content, torrefaction can prevent the growth of mold and bacteria, reducing the risk of spoilage and contamination [15]. Additionally, the resulting torrefied biomass is more resistant to degradation, allowing it to withstand the rigors of transportation and storage without degrading in quality. The use of torrefaction in the production of wood pellets has several other benefits, including the ability to increase the energy density of the final product, making it more efficient to transport and store. This can lead to significant cost savings, as well as reduced greenhouse gas emissions from transportation [16]. Furthermore, torrefaction can also increase the grindability of biomass, making it easier to mill and combust, which can improve the overall efficiency of power generation [17]. Despite the many benefits of torrefaction, there are still several challenges associated with its implementation. One of the main concerns is the high energy requirements for the torrefaction process, which can be a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions. Additionally, the cost of torrefaction equipment and facilities can be high, making it a significant investment for biomass producers [18]. In order to overcome these challenges, researchers and industry experts are working together to develop more efficient and cost-effective torrefaction technologies. For example, some studies have focused on the use of alternative energy sources, such as biomass gasification, to power the torrefaction process [19]. Others have explored the use of different torrefaction temperatures and times to optimize the process and reduce energy requirements [20]. As the demand for sustainable and renewable energy sources continues to grow, the role of torrefaction in the production of wood pellets is likely to become increasingly important. By addressing the challenges associated with torrefaction and developing more efficient and cost-effective technologies, the industry can help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and meet the growing demand for biomass-based energy.

Understanding the nuances of corporate entrepreneurship demands a meticulous exploration of how internal communication channels facilitate or hinder the engagement of intrapreneurs. Language and rhetoric play pivotal roles in shaping the perceptions and motivations of employees; the manner in which management conveys the importance of innovation can significantly influence individual attitudes towards risk, creativity, and initiative (Bherwani & Rao, 2021). When management actively engages in a dialogue centered on change, not merely as a directive, but as a shared vision to which all can contribute, it nurtures an environment ripe for entrepreneurial exploration (Burgelman, 1983). This alignment of communication strategy with organizational values is essential; employees are more inclined to embrace entrepreneurial behaviors when they perceive the corporate narrative as inclusive and empowering. Moreover, fostering an entrepreneurial mindset among employees necessitates addressing their concerns and limitations candidly. An effective strategy may involve creating forums where employees can voice their ideas and reservations without fear of reprisal or judgment. Empirical evidence suggests that such environments not only encourage more individuals to step forward with innovative proposals but also forge stronger connections among team members, enhancing collaborative efforts towards common goals (Kearney et al., 2019). Thus, it becomes incumbent upon managers to cultivate spaces for constructive feedback and dialogue, ensuring that employees feel heard and valued. In tandem with supportive communication, resource allocation emerges as a critical factor in facilitating CE. The allocation of financial, temporal, and human resources directly impacts employees' capacity to engage in entrepreneurial activities. When organizations commit resources explicitly earmarked for innovative endeavors, they signal to employees that such initiatives are not only welcomed but expected (Rogers et al., 2020). This kind of investment fosters a sense of ownership among employees as they recognize that their contributions are integral to the organization's trajectory. Conversely, scant resource allocation can evoke feelings of disillusionment, leading employees to perceive the system as resistant to change, thus preventing them from undertaking intrapreneurial initiatives. Additionally, the significance of leadership styles cannot be understated in the realm of corporate entrepreneurship. Transformational leaders, in particular, have been shown to be instrumental in empowering employees by motivating them to transcend their self-interest for the sake of the organization (Bass & Riggio, 2006). These leaders inspire a collective sense of purpose, crucial for engendering a culture of innovation. On the other hand, a more transactional leadership style, focused primarily on rewarding compliance and performance metrics, may inadvertently stifle entrepreneurial spirit amongst employees, as they may be less motivated to diverge from established protocols (Chin et al., 2013). To complement leadership dynamics, the structural attributes of an organization also play a salient role in influencing CE. Structures that are overly hierarchical can inhibit the flow of ideas, while more flat organizational designs tend to encourage open communication and cross-pollination of ideas across departments (Floyd & Lane, 2000). This becomes increasingly imperative in the modern landscape, where agility is key. Organizations positioned to rapidly pivot in response to market signals can harness employees' innate creative capabilities effectively, cultivating a continuous stream of innovation. While the factors influencing CE are multifaceted, it is the interplay between these elements-communication, resource allocation, leadership styles, and organizational structure-that ultimately shapes the environment conducive to intrapreneurial endeavors. As organizations navigate the complexities of the 21st century, the strategic embrace of corporate entrepreneurship promises not just renewal and growth but additionally, a reinvigorated sense of purpose among employees as they become active participants in the journey of innovation and change. Future research must delve into the intricacies of these relationships, painting a clearer picture of how to harness the full potential of human ingenuity within organizational confines.

I thought you were both ahead of that." He turns his gaze to the manuscript, skepticism etched on his face. "Do you really think you should be getting involved again?" She shoots him a look, her defenses rising. "It's not about getting involved, Hutton. It's about closure-finding my connection to my past." The bubbles of the dish soap foam and drift like fragile memories on the water's surface. "Besides, Edward's writing was always transformative for me. It shaped a part of who I am." Hutton steps closer, his expression softening. "Susan, I just want to make sure that you're not dredging up old wounds for a few sweet words on a page. It's only a novel, after all." "Is it really?" she counters, glancing again at the sealed box. "To him, it might be much more. The hours he spent wrestling with words, the pieces of his heart he stitched together on paper..." "In the end, it's just a book, right?" Hutton interjects, insistently. An unfamiliar tension crackles in the air between them. "Maybe. But it's also a bridge. A door. Something I closed off for two decades." She takes a deep breath, her voice steadier now. "What if he's finally ready to talk? Or to understand how the choices we made shaped both of our lives?" Hutton looks away, his jaw clenched. "Just... just remember what you both went through. You were so unhappy." "I know!" she snaps. The porcelain dishes clink together in the sink with the intensity of her agitation, echoing shadows of their past arguments. "And I've carried that unhappiness with me. Maybe he has too. What if this is an opportunity?" Hutton leans in a fraction closer, peering into her eyes, searching for the answer he wants to find there. "You really think a few pages of text could change anything?" Susan raises the box defensively, her hand trembling only slightly. "I don't know, Hutton! But maybe it's not just about changing things. It's about acknowledging them." She finally moves away from the sink, wiping her hands on a towel, steeling her resolve. "We've both moved on, but that doesn't erase the reality of what had been. It's just... part of me." A silence hangs over them, heavy and laden with unspoken sentiments. Hutton flicks his gaze back toward the manuscript, his brows knitting together. "And what about us, Susan? What does that mean for us?" The question lingers, curling up between them like steam from a boiling kettle, ready to spill over. "What if it's not just about Edward?" "Are you trying to open old wounds of your own?" he quips, though there's a trace of somber acknowledgment threading through his tone. As the sun began to set on the Rooney estate, Michael and his family made their way to the grand ballroom, where the wake was in full swing. The room was filled with the city's elite, all gathered to pay their respects to the deceased patriarch, James Rooney. Michael's father, Sullivan, was a man of great influence, and it seemed that everyone wanted to pay their respects to him. As they entered the ballroom, Michael's eyes scanned the room, taking in the sea of familiar faces. He spotted Mrs. O'Malley, the owner of the local bakery, chatting with Mrs. Flynn, the wife of the city's mayor. He saw the union leader, Mr. Kelly, shaking hands with Sullivan, and the city's newspaper editor, Mr. Johnson, sipping a glass of whiskey at the bar. Michael's eyes lingered on the coffin, where the deceased James Rooney lay, his face pale and still. Michael felt a shiver run down his spine as he gazed at the pennies on the man's eyes. He had always found it fascinating, the way the coins seemed to stare back at him, like two cold, dead eyes. As the night wore on, Michael's father, Sullivan, made his way around the room, shaking hands and accepting condolences. Michael followed him, trying to stay out of the way as his father worked the room. He spotted his friend, Jimmy, standing by the punch bowl, and made his way over to him. Jimmy was a scrappy kid from the wrong side of the tracks, but he was a good kid, and Michael liked him. They had grown up together, exploring the city's alleys and rooftops, getting into all sorts of trouble. "Hey, Mike," Jimmy said, as Michael approached. "What's the haps?" "Not much, Jimmy," Michael replied. "Just trying to stay out of trouble." Jimmy chuckled. "Good luck with that, pal. You know how it is." Michael nodded, knowing exactly what Jimmy meant. Trouble seemed to follow him everywhere, like a shadow. As the night wore on, Michael found himself getting restless. He had always been a restless kid, always looking for the next adventure, the next thrill. And tonight was no exception. He excused himself from Jimmy and made his way to the door, where he slipped out into the night air. The city was alive and pulsing, the sounds of jazz music and laughter drifting through the streets. Michael felt a thrill run through him as he hit the pavement, the cool night air filling his lungs. He loved nights like this, when the city seemed to be his own personal playground. He walked for a while, taking in the sights and sounds of the city. Moreover, some case-control studies have reported much higher and statistically significant odds ratios (Ghanizadeh, 2008; Shilon et al., 2012). Summarizing, the exact extent to which ADHD in children and adolescents is associated with an increased risk of UPIs, even after controlling for comorbid conditions, is still unclear. Perhaps even more importantly, meta-analytic evidence on possible beneficial or harmful effects of ADHD medications on the risk of UPIs is lacking. To the best of our knowledge, no randomized controlled trials have aimed to assess the effects of ADHD medications and the risk of injuries, possibly due to the relatively low incidence of injuries. Hence, studies using observational data can offer useful information on the association, provided appropriate methodologies are applied. Whilst case-control studies aimed at addressing the effect of ADHD medication on risk of UPIs are hampered by the "confound by indication" bias (pharmacological treatment is more common in children with severe compared to mild forms of ADHD), self-controlled case series (SCCS) studies or other methodologies that take into account individual differences have a suitable design to explore this issue. Gaining insight into the magnitude of the association between ADHD and risk of UPIs in children and adolescents, as well as on a possible beneficial or harmful effect of ADHD medications, is highly relevant from a clinical and public health standpoint. In particular, meta-analytic evidence of a significant association between ADHD and increased risk of injuries and of a protective role of ADHD pharmacotherapy could inform the debate regarding the discontinuation of medication during week-ends or school holidays (Ibrahim and Donyai, 2015). Furthermore, findings of a protective effect of medication would contribute to the current, controversial scientific debate around the actual benefits and risks of ADHD medications (Banaschewski et al., 2016). Of note, a recent meta-analysis by Amiri et al. (Amiri et al., 2017) pooled 35 studies published until 2014 and found a pooled odds ratio in children of 1.96 (95% CI = 1.6, 2.4), indicating that ADHD is significantly associated with a risk of injury. However, several methodological sound studies have been published in the past three years, which could not be included in this previous meta-analysis, and some other important (for example, the above mentioned Canadian survey by (Dudani et al., 2010) were not included. Additionally, the Amiri et al. study did not control for gender effects, which are a crucial confounder due to the association of both risk of UPIs and ADHD to male gender (Gaub and Carlson, 1997; Peden et al., 2008). Finally, and importantly, the meta-analysis by Amiri et al. was not aimed to assess the impact of ADHD medications on the risk of UPIs. The present meta-analysis extends in important ways the meta-analysis by Amiri et al. including studies in children and adolescents published until June 2017, controlling for gender and, importantly, exploring the effects of ADHD medication by pooling self-controlled studies.

Here were two men who had been together for nearly three decades, and yet they were still fighting for the right to call themselves husband and husband. It seemed almost absurd, in this day and age, that they should have to fight for something as fundamental as the right to marry. But as we talked, I began to realize that their struggle was about more than just a piece of paper. It was about dignity, about respect, about being recognized as equals in the eyes of the law. Stahl and Seneca were not asking for special treatment, just the same rights and privileges that heterosexual couples take for granted. As I left their studio and walked back out into the chilly spring air, I couldn't help but feel a sense of hope. Maybe, just maybe, this small town on the Delaware River was a harbinger of things to come. Maybe the rest of the country would follow New Hope's lead and recognize that love is love, no matter what gender. Of course, not everyone was pleased with the council's decision. I spoke to a few residents who expressed concerns about the implications of gay marriage, who worried about the impact on traditional values and the sanctity of marriage. But even they seemed to acknowledge that the tide was turning, that the world was changing, and that maybe it was time to adapt. As I left New Hope and headed back to the city, I couldn't help but feel a sense of optimism. Maybe, just maybe, this small town on the Delaware River was a sign of things to come. The one and only masterpiece I can't help but cling to is "The Bell Jar." Sylvia Plath's words wrap around my brain like ivy; they're haunting yet beautiful, surreal yet painfully real. It feels like finding a kindred spirit hidden within the pages. I adore the blend of prose with poetry, the way Plath dances between darkness and determination. If I could, I'd shove it into the hands of everyone I know, but alas, not everyone resonates with that kind of raw emotion. Dreams What do you dream about? Typically, my mind wanders through bizarre landscapes-a mix of the surreal and the completely nonsensical. Some nights it's a cacophony of colors and laughter, while other nights I find myself falling through endless tunnels or staring into the depths of an inky void. And more often than not, I wake up confused about whether those dreams meant anything at all. Do you have recurring dreams? Yep! There's one about swimming in an ocean made of chocolate. Seriously, the sweetness and richness are overwhelming. When I wake up, I always wish I could dive back in. Goals What's your biggest dream? To embrace my creativity fully and let it breathe, to feel the pulse of the world vibrate through my fingertips when I create something-be it through writing, art, or sound. I want to travel, immerse myself in different cultures, and gather inspiration from the people, their stories, and their landscapes. The world has so much to offer, and I crave every experience. Short-term goals? To ace my French class and learn to cook something complicated-and not burn it to a crisp this time! Cooking disasters are a tale of their own; my last souffle was an absolute tragedy. Hobbies When not trapped in books or enveloped in music, what occupies your time? Journaling! It's my therapy, my sanctuary. I pour my soul-my daydreams, dark thoughts, and all those fleeting moments-into those pages. Sometimes my handwriting resembles the scribbles of a mad scientist, but it feels liberating. I also dabble in photography; capturing a fleeting moment or a serene sunset can feel like alchemy. The right angle can transform the mundane into something breathtaking. Friendships What qualities do you value in friends? Honesty and creativity, hands down. I adore friends who can challenge me, forcing me outside my comfort zone. Laughter is a must; I want people who can find humor even in the darkest sides of life. Someone who appreciates late-night talks about everything and nothing. Who would you consider your best friend? Oh, that would be Mira. We bond over shared guilty pleasures in music and a history of chaotic adventures (and mishaps). She understands my dreams and ambitions, all the while accepting my quirks. It's a mutual love affair of weirdness and acceptance. Family How do you feel about your family? They're my foundation, my chaotic support system. We're not perfect, but isn't that what makes it interesting? There's love, there's strife, but at the core, we're a bunch of misfits navigating this rollercoaster together. Do you get along with your siblings? Mostly, although my younger brother has an uncanny ability to push my buttons. I'd be lying if I said I didn't enjoy our sibling rivalry from time to time. Nevertheless, the fate and transformation of HOCs during water treatment processes are complex and depend on a variety of factors, including pH, temperature, presence of other organic and inorganic compounds, and operational conditions of the treatment plant (Mons et al., 2011). Recent advancements in analytical techniques have allowed for a more detailed characterization of these compounds and their transformation products. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), commonly using ozone or UV radiation in combination with hydrogen peroxide, have been employed as an alternative method to conventional treatment strategies (Zwiener and Frimmel, 2000; von Gunten, 2018). These methods aim to exploit highly reactive hydroxyl radicals to effectively break down HOCs, yet their efficiency also varies with the chemical structure of the target compounds and the matrix of the treated water (Rivas et al., 2011). Despite the potential of these advanced treatments, the incomplete degradation of HOCs remains a salient concern. Some degradation products may retain or even surpass the toxicity of the parent compounds, posing additional risks to both human health and aquatic life (Richardson and Ternes, 2018). This necessitates ongoing monitoring and evaluation of water treatment protocols to safeguard public health while minimizing environmental impact. The complex interactions between hydrophobic organic pollutants and natural organic matter further complicate these treatment processes, as these interactions can impede the removal efficiency or lead to the formation of yet unidentified by-products (Lloret et al., 2012; Mitch et al., 2012). Increasing urbanization and industrial activities contribute to the introduction of HOCs into water systems, highlighting the urgency for regulatory frameworks and policies aimed at preventing contamination at the source (Diamond et al., 2015). Public awareness and stakeholder engagement are essential in promoting ecologically responsible practices that mitigate the discharge of both natural and synthetic organic pollutants into water bodies (Gordon et al., 2003). The development of engineered solutions, including novel sorbents and filtration technologies, holds promise for enhancing the removal of challenging contaminants during water treatment (Nguyen et al., 2011). The implications of climate change further underscore the need for adaptive management strategies. Fluctuations in hydrological conditions, driven by shifting precipitation patterns and extreme weather events, can exacerbate the mobilization and distribution of HOCs in aquatic systems (McNeill et al., 2012). As such, integrating real-time monitoring systems and predictive models within water management frameworks can provide valuable insights into potential pollution events and allow for timely mitigation measures (Crittenden et al., 2012). In conclusion, while significant progress has been made in understanding and treating hydrophobic organic compounds in water systems, challenges persist in transforming fundamental research into practical applications. Collaborative efforts spanning scientific research, engineering innovation, policy development, and community involvement are imperative to ensure water quality and safety in the face of evolving environmental pressures (Kummerer, 2009). Future research should continue to elucidate the mechanistic pathways of HOC transformation and removal while exploring sustainable treatment technologies that can be integrated into existing infrastructures (Shannon et al., 2008). By advancing these efforts, we can work towards a more comprehensive and effective water management system capable of navigating the complexities of both current and emerging aquatic contaminants.

The unique characteristics of coral mounds, shaped by the framework-forming cold-water corals, have been extensively studied along the continental margins of the Atlantic Ocean and its adjacent marginal seas. These features are not only widespread but also exhibit a remarkable degree of variability in their morphology, dimension, and distribution. The height of coral mounds can range from a few meters to over 300 meters, while their lateral extension can vary from a few tens of meters to several hundred meters. The shape of these mounds can be circular, oval, arcuate, V-shaped, elongated, or irregular, often influenced by the prevailing current regime. The development of coral mounds is a slow process that occurs over geological timescales, often spanning thousands to millions of years. The growth of these mounds is primarily driven by the proliferation of framework-forming cold-water corals, such as Lophelia pertusa, and their ability to trap suspended sediments from the near-bottom waters. The corals require vigorous and turbulent bottom currents to secure a food supply and provide a sufficient lateral supply of sediments that contributes to mound aggradation. The relationship between coral mounds and bottom currents is crucial, as it determines the availability of food and sediment for the corals. As a result, coral mounds are often found in the vicinity of contourite drifts, which are deposits of sediment that have been transported by bottom currents. The interplay between coral growth and sedimentation is a key factor in the formation of these unique features. The discovery of new coral mound areas continues to expand our understanding of these enigmatic structures. Recent studies have revealed the presence of coral mounds in previously unexplored regions, such as the Mediterranean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the geological and biological processes that shape these features. Further research is needed to fully understand the complex interactions between coral growth, sedimentation, and bottom currents that shape the morphology and distribution of coral mounds. The study of these features can provide valuable insights into the geological and biological processes that have shaped the seafloor over millions of years.

Just then two men in uniform standing apart from the rest, advanced. They wore the costume of boarding officers, the dark-blue uniforms being garnished with brass buttons and on their heads were caps with bands across the front bearing the word in gilt letters, "Inspector." One of these men was tall and muscular, with a bushy black beard, deep gray eyes and a heavy mass of dark-brown hair. His companion looked like a mere boy, with a handsome face, a pair of keen eyes and a dashing, aggressive air that showed he was of a bold, intrepid character. He walked right up to the inspector. "So you want to see the Bradys, do you?" he asked Gibson, quietly. "Yes, I would," asserted the inspector, glaring at him in surprise. "Then look, for we are the Bradys!" exclaimed the boy. He took off his cap and his companion stripped off a wig and false beard. Every one in the room glanced at them in amazement. No one suspected their identity before. Old King Brady was now seen to have white hair and a clean-shaven face, in which a daring, determined character was shown. Even the Collector was astonished. When he recovered his composure, a smile crossed his face, and he rose and warmly shook hands with the pair, saying: "Well, this is an agreeable surprise." Old King Brady smiled, took a chew of tobacco and replied: "You got our chief to assign us on this case and requested us to be here at two o'clock, and here we are." "Ready for work?" "Yes, sir. Instruct us." "Well, all I can tell you is that this country is being flooded with precious stones upon which no duty is being paid, and I want you to find the party who is doing the crooked work." "Have you any clews upon which we can work?" "None, whatever. You'll have to get them yourselves from the importers in John street, Broadway and Maiden Lane. They may give you some points." "We shall follow your suggestion." The two detectives started for the door, then paused. Harry Brady, the boy, then said: "Mr. Gibson has some doubts about our ability to work for the Custom House. Since he has flung defiance at us, we'll accept his challenge." "How? growled the inspector, in ugly tones. "Well, we'll meet you officers and the Collector on board the steamer Campania, of the Cunard line, in one hour, when she reaches her pier from Quarantine. If we don't show up more smugglers than you do, we'll give up this assignment." "I'll go you!" eagerly exclaimed the jealous inspector. "And I'll be there to see that you get fair play," grimly said the Collector. The Bradys silently bowed and withdrew. When they reached the street, Old King Brady laughed and said: "They're all jealous of us. But we'll show them a trick or two, Harry."

Her sweet face continued to haunt me, and, in the despairing and romantic mood of a Manfred, I spent many a night on the mountains around Heidelberg, watching the stars rise, and brooding over my unrequited love. Thus my brother's letter was far from being a source of pleasure to me, though it was kindly meant on his part (for he was ignorant, so I subsequently learned, of my own love for Daphne). His invitation, translated into the language of my thoughts simply meant, "Come and be more unhappy than you are!" Deep down in my heart I had cherished the belief that something unforeseen would happen to break off George's engagement. The sands of that hope were now fast running out. The 25th of the month would remove Daphne from me forever. For several days I fought with my despair, but at last I resolved to be present at the wedding. "I may as well play the stoic," I muttered, "and accept the inevitable. Perhaps the fact of seeing Daphne actually married to another will cure me of this folly." Curiosity, also, to see how Daphne would behave on the occasion was an additional motive for going; and, poor fool that I was, I thought of the trembling handclasp, the blush, and the sweet glance that a woman seldom fails to bestow on the man who has once expressed his love for her. Christmas Eve, midnight, found me on board the packet-boat steaming out of Calais Harbour. The sea was singularly smooth, and there was in the air that which gave promise of a heavy fall of snow ere long. Wrapped in my cloak, I leaned over the side of the vessel, listening to the silver carillon of the church-bells pealing forth from every steeple and belfry in the town the glad tidings that the sweet and solemn morn of the Nativity had dawned. Faintly and more faintly the chimes sounded over the wide expanse of glimmering sea, till they were finally lost in the distance. At first my thoughts were gloomy. To play the stoic is never a very pleasant task. Yet I was not totally abandoned to despair. A ray of hope played over my mind, and, as the distance that separated me from Daphne diminished, this hope gradually became stronger and stronger. Nil desperandum should be my motto. The wedding had not taken place yet; weddings have been broken off at the very altar: why should not hers be? Foolish though it may seem, I began to nurse the pleasing idea that Fate might yet transfer Daphne to my arms. As if my wish had become a certainty, I trod the deck of the Channel steamer with exultant step, refusing to go below, although the wintry flakes were falling now in steady earnest. Such is the power of hope over the human mind; or is it something more than a poetic fiction that coming events cast their shadows before?

The night was a wonderland of deep spaces and glittering stars. Somewhere far away a native tom-tom throbbed like the beating of a fevered pulse, quickening spasmodically at intervals and then dying away again into mere monotony. The air was scentless, still, and heavy. "It's going to be deuced warm," said Tommy. "Have a smoke?" said Monck, proffering his case. The boy smiled with swift gratification. "Oh, thanks awfully! But it's a shame to hurry over a good cigar, and I promised Stella to go straight back." "A promise is a promise," said Monck. "Have it later!" He added rather curtly, "I'm going your way myself." "Good!" said Tommy heartily. "But aren't you going to show at the Club House? Aren't you going to dance?" Monck tossed down his lighted match and set his heel on it. "I'm keeping my dancing for to-morrow," he said. "The best man always has more than enough of that." Tommy made a gloomy sound that was like a groan and began to descend the steps by his side. They walked several paces along the dim road in silence; then quite suddenly he burst into impulsive speech. "I'll tell you what it is, Monck!" "I shouldn't," said Monck. Tommy checked abruptly, looking at him oddly, uncertainly. "How do you know what I was going to say?" he demanded. "I don't," said Monck. "I believe you do," said Tommy, unconvinced. Monck blew forth a cloud of smoke and laughed in his brief, rather grudging way. "You're getting quite clever for a child of your age," he observed. "But don't overdo it, my son! Don't get precocious!" Tommy's hand grasped his arm confidentially. "Monck, if I don't speak out to someone, I shall bust! Surely you don't mind my speaking out to you!" "Not if there's anything to be gained by it," said Monck. He ignored the friendly, persuasive hand on his arm, but yet in some fashion Tommy knew that it was not unwelcome. He kept it there as he made reply. "There isn't. Only, you know, old chap, it does a fellow good to unburden himself. And I'm bothered to death about this business." "A bit late in the day, isn't it?" suggested Monck. "Oh yes, I know; too late to do anything. But," Tommy spoke with force, "the nearer it gets, the worse I feel. I'm downright sick about it, and that's the truth. How would you feel, I wonder, if you knew your one and only sister was going to marry a rotter? Would you be satisfied to let things drift?" Monck was silent for a space. They walked on over the dusty road with the free swing of the conquering race.

I don't think that's the goal for anyone who's seeking to truly understand themselves and their place in the world. If we glide through life without a single scar, without a single bruise of the heart, we miss out on the chapters of growth that are often disguised in these complexities. In my personal journey, I've encountered friends who, at first blush, seemed like the perfect companions. But as time unfolded, their true hues emerged, as did mine. Some relationships blossomed into lush gardens, others turned into thorny paths, prickling every step of the way. Initially, it was easier to point fingers, to assess blame, to see myself as a victim of their inconsiderations or cruelty. But a deeper dive into self-reflection has taught me that these were merely stepping stones and mirrors reflecting parts of myself I had yet to acknowledge or accept. To navigate the murky waters of toxic relationships, it is pivotal to first recognize their structure. Toxicity isn't always overt; it isn't always raised voices or dramatic fallouts. Sometimes, it's the quiet undermining, the subtle dismissals, the persistent yet gentle erosion of self-worth that infiltrates our interactions unnoticed. And these are the opportunities to pause and question: Why does this discomfort persist? What is it in me that resonates with this toxicity? These questions have guided me toward contemplating the areas in myself requiring nurturing and awareness. Sometimes the universe conspires to place toxic individuals in our path to act as unintentional teachers. They hold a mirror up to the parts of us that are unresolved, inviting us to embrace or transform these aspects. Through these challenging interactions, we either step into our power or shy away from it-either way, we're catapulted into the next phase of our personal development. From this perspective, I want us all to embrace the essence of conflict as a natural part of our expedition. It cultivates resilience, patience, and wisdom when addressed consciously. I remind myself often that the darkest nights produce the most radiant stars. Every toxic relationship that I've endured has ultimately transformed into a testament of my growth, resilience, and capacity for forgiveness-towards others and myself. As we explore our shadow-self in these situations, learning becomes a cyclical process. By understanding where the pain originates, we gain a clearer perception of why we engage with toxicity, either as the giver or the receiver. It's a spectrum, and we've likely oscillated across it. The real lesson is found in our response to these realizations, these insights. We either choose to perpetuate old patterns or embark on the sometimes uncomfortable journey of change. Let's extend this dialogue to encompass compassion, not just for ourselves, but for those who inadvertently bring these lessons into our lives. An invitation remains open to transform toxicity into understanding, judgment into empathy, and fear into love. That's the direction Life as we grow it endeavors to guide us toward. So, each encounter is an opportunity. On this platform, together, we'll discuss difficult topics, support one another's growth, and perhaps find solace in the shared recognition that toxic interactions, though painful, serve as potent catalysts for profound personal evolution. Let's embrace our beautiful mess, for in its midst lies the raw material of transformation.

It's not like there was a support wagon out front telling me to put my feet up while they took care of the baby. When S wasn't home, I was completely on my own. I watched a lot of Woody Allen movies at the beginning with a sleeping baby on my lap. And I figured out mothering day by day. Then the time came for her to learn to eat. I come from a really allergic family, so I did what the American Academy of Pediatrics said and breastfed and gave nothing else for the first six months. The first day we tried cereal, she made faces but ate it. And so it went with the baby foods - sweet potatoes, squash, oatmeal, applesauce and so on. The first foods. The least allergenic ones. Then she stopped. Yes, my daughter stopped eating entirely at about age 10 months. At first I didn't worry too much - or else I consoled myself with the platitudes that prevent you from dying of panic. Pickiness, some said. Give her a hot dog! She'll eat that. The doctor and everyone else I asked said, "Well, give her time; she can still nurse to sustain her caloric needs, you don't really need to worry about it until after she's one." She turned one. She still wouldn't eat. Not only wouldn't she eat - she would cry about it. Really cry. And scream. If you went near her with food she would freak out as if you were offering her a hot poker. I called the doctor again. And again. He said, finally: Make an appointment for her at the feeding clinic at Best Kid's Hospital in the Country. They'll get it sorted out and make you feel better about what you're doing. Best Kid's has a waiting list a mile long to get a splinter evaluated, much less a developmental delay. I made the appointment - I filled out their ridiculous Great American Novel of paperwork - and we went, jazzed to the nines, terrified of what they'd say. Because now she was thirteen months old. The nursing was doing her okay - she wasn't ill - but she was thin. Not gaining. Not growing. Not good. My baby, a plump, rosy, juicy 75th percentile for weight until age 10 months - now 5th percentile. She just was not getting enough calories - human milk is not complete nutrition, calorically speaking, after age one. Still 95th for height - which she has maintained her whole life. She's tall, like her dad. Up until the appointment, I'd tried everything. This is how we learned about the food allergies. Sometimes, the stuff I'd encourage her to eat gave her hives all over her face when she spit it out.
