What can you expect anymore? They've forgotten the grit it used to take-it's all about the shine now, the brass on the uniform and not the soul within it. I understand your frustrations; I've seen it in my own way, living beneath the weight of expectation, and yet, here I stand, a cog trying to fit where none was forged for my shape. Moreover, I noticed the gap between your time served and the uniforms of those marching out there. We've all experienced that disconnection: the unyielding trench of sergeant and private, yet here we are, bound together by circumstance. Maggio gave me a nod, a silent affirmation that spoke volumes. Though his eyes shifted, watching the routine of men like clockwork, I could tell he understood. They all did, in some way. They had their roles, and I had mine, or so it was supposed to be. The chatter of training echoed around us as the sun dipped low, casting long shadows against the dust-strewn ground. The heat of the day still retained a grip, but I could sense the coolness creeping in-the faint promise of night. Warden leaned back in his chair, hands steepled under his chin, assessing me like I was some file he was meant to review. Yet I marked him with a measure of respect; he was trying to understand the chaos within a solitary soldier ready to serve but uncertain of his footing. "What exactly do you see in this life, Prewitt? You've left one rank behind for another far more chaotic. Do you think you'll find your clarity here?" "I didn't leave to seek clarity, sir. I sought to distance myself from expectations that felt too narrow," I replied, words rolling off like ink spilling across parchment, marking territory where I stood. "Fort Shafter was my place of noise, and if the bugle had become my cage, this rifle company is merely another chance to spread my wings-however wounded they may be." "Ah, so the boy wants to fly. What'll happen when the winds come, Private? You think this sky is yours to claim?" His tone was an edge, a low growl dragging through the noise around us. I felt the gaze of the company upon us, waiting for my next words, a trial of sorts to determine if I was worth the space I occupied. "I guess that's up to me to find out, isn't it?" I shot back, a satisfaction curling in my chest; defiance had its beauty. There was silence, a pause where words were heavy in the air, each man in this company baring witness to my answer. Warden's brow relaxed slightly. "Always a better response, Prewitt. The word 'try' is weak. Here in this company, we do-we become." His gaze moved across the room, the men appearing as shadows against the fading light. "Now, what will you do to carve your name here amongst us?" "I will learn what I must. I'll be all in, whatever it takes." And there it was, a fragile thread of conviction sparkling amidst doubt. I felt the shift as the company absorbed my declaration; I wouldn't merely dress the part-I would embody something bigger, something worthy of the weight I willingly took on. Here I would not be a lost note, but a song molded from hardship and passion, harmony after the discord of Fort Shafter. The silence stretched, filled with unspoken resolutions, all of us connected now by the subtle pulse of shared purpose.

There seemed to be a green valley, lush and vibrant with plant life. Admist of the green scenery shimmered the glint of a gold that was purer than the sun that never seemed to go way. Nights seemed to be nonexistent in this village of my dreams. Every afternoon (if the concept existed), the men would haul back.. something. Something with that glint that drove G's eyes mad with ecstasy. The substance would then be hoarded in warehouse. The more happy G got, the more sadness I felt in the men's eyes. They were frequently directed with hatred at G's domineering figure, but then moved sadly to the black pistol-case that hung at his waist. Days. Weeks. Months? The sun that flooded the valley seemed to be weaker day by day, as more of the mysterious golden substance was taken. I communicate with the men, but they only answer in sighs. Maybe they didn't want Gene to get the wrong idea. Gene disapproved of my meeting with the others. But he had no power over what I did secretly. It was my dream, not his. I befriended a hotheaded youth named B. I see in him a reflection of myself, only without a past in academics, a warm home, or food that I have long taken for granted. Days. Weeks. Months? The resignation seemed to turn to anger. Winds howled. What seemed to be once day was now only night. For some reason, I yearned to the men, as if I were destined to be one of them. They also approached me more, probably as a result of my contact with B. On the bleak morning of one of these days, the tension broke. B, with a strength of mind that could not be contained by his meager, malnutritioned body, stared into G's face when the daily retrieval party was to be formed, cursing at him in a language that G wouldn't understand. But to me, it was the most pure form of hatred I had ever seen in life. I shuddered when hearing his words before even understanding what they meant. But I knew instantly what I had to do. I eyed the rest of the villagers. In my eyes I said: "Come closer. It is about to be all over." Men, from age of fifteen to fifty, slowly picked up the branches near them, coming closing, forming a circle that wouldn't break. For once, G's nonchalant smirk faded. He held a not-so-steady pistol up to the young man, who stared into the blackness that will at any second be his death. In growls and grunts to each other in foreign languages, the two backed up steadily. B was stopped short by the wall of the warehouse standing behind him. Gene is about to back into a mob that is slowly forming. He senses this, and gave a pleading look to me, who was standing, silent, melancholy.

There may be a direct link from SHGs to increased awareness and use of public entitlement schemes if the organizing institution has a mandate to increase awareness and utilization of certain public entitlement schemes within their SHGs. Even without this mandate, government organizations and NGOs that support the formation of women's SHGs indirectly help create larger networks and greater communication within those networks, owing to the intrinsic modality of the groups. Greater communication can lead to greater flow of information. Women could learn about public entitlement schemes from their group members even if the group is not organized with an explicit objective to increase awareness about public entitlements. A second channel to increased information may be via increased mobility among women in SHGs. To attend the group meetings, the women need to leave their homestead, increasing their mobility (albeit within their own village). Women that are part of SHGs, because of regular interactions not only with group members but also with external agents that facilitate these groups, may become more adept at communicating. Often, this experience of being in a group and interacting with other women can in itself boost women's self-confidence. Family members (mostly husbands) of women in SHGs may also feel more confident about the ability of these women to leave the homestead and engage with the outside world, perhaps even going outside the village (with their group). The ability to hold public entities accountable, the second demand side constraint identified above, is more complex. One can view this as a culmination of factors - improved social networks, greater mobility and greater self-confidence - that may lead to greater political participation, which in turn may lead to greater accountability. Women in SHGs meet regularly for their group meetings, which exposes them to the practice of meeting in groups and may make them more likely to attend village council meetings (the gram sabha and the mahila gram sabha, described in Section 5). The collective voice of the group, along with increased self-confidence, gives them further encouragement to raise issues at these meetings and demand their rights. Drawing on these conceptual underpinnings, we examine whether SHG membership increases political participation, awareness, and utilization of public entitlements among its members. We enrich this analysis by examining whether SHG membership leads to increased social networks, self-confidence and mobility. To assess the impact of SHG membership on political participation and awareness and use of government entitlements, this paper draws on cross-sectional data collected in 2015. The data used here is from the baseline survey of an evaluation of the impacts of layering nutrition-sensitive interventions, including those that foster greater awareness and use of government health, nutrition and food security programs, on an NGO's existing agricultural-livelihoods program platform.

They had heard that they could get a better view of Warwick Hall from there as they passed it. "It is so far away," explained Joyce, "that we can't make out much about it except from a distance." "I hope it won't look as bare and bleak as Miss Cynthia says it does," said another girl. "She told me that there wasn't anything pretty around it but the peacocks, and that they were so noisy that nobody could study when they screamed." "Oh, I don't believe it!" exclaimed the third girl. "Miss Allison wouldn't send me to a place like that." "I am sure that it is lovely," added the fourth. "My mother went to school there herself, and she has always talked so enthusiastically about it that I feel as if I know every nook and corner of the dear old place already." The boat whistled just then, as it turned a bend in the river, and the four girls leaned forward eagerly, scanning the shore ahead. There, rising above the trees, were the high towers and pointed gables of Warwick Hall. The setting sun sent a flood of light across the water, touching everything in its path to gold. As the boat drew nearer, the terraced gardens sloping down to the river came into view, and the four girls saw that they were bright with flowers. A flock of white pigeons circled around one of the towers, and a peacock strutted slowly along the balustrade, spreading its tail in the sunlight. "There! What did I tell you?" cried Betty Lewis, the last speaker. "Isn't it beautiful? And isn't it picturesque?" "Yes, indeed," agreed the others, as they watched the vision fade slowly behind them. "It certainly looks romantic enough to suit anybody." "But oh, girls, think of having to stay cooped up there for six whole months!" groaned Helen Adams. "The time will simply drag, I know." "No, it won't," contradicted Betty. "We'll have lots of good times, and the time will pass before we know it." "Well, I wish that it would pass now, before I begin to be homesick," sighed Helen. "I'd give anything in the world to be back in my own room again." "You've no idea what a comfort it is to be able to say 'my own room,'" put in Mary Stewart. "I never realized how nice it sounded until I began living in hotels. You're lucky, Helen, to be going straight from your own house to a home of your kind aunt's. I shall have to live in a hotel till Aunt Susan comes back from Europe." "I'm glad that I haven't any relations here," said Joyce. "It makes me feel independent to know that I can do exactly as I please, and that there is nobody to boss me." "That's because you're used to doing as you please," answered Mary. "I'd love to have somebody boss me occasionally, - somebody belonging to me, you know, - a mother or sister or something of that sort. But I suppose that I ought not to complain. Although the bias to look at the eyes relative to other facial features is a well-established finding, there is limited understanding of the mechanisms that drive this effect. One obvious consideration is the extent to which eye looking is under top-down volitional control compared to the extent to which it is an automatic and reflexive process, triggered bottom-up by the stimulus (Laidlaw et al., 2012). The argument for automatic and reflexive responding is supported by existing findings. For example, Kliemann, Dziobek, Hatri, Steimke, and Heekeren (2010) used an emotional recognition task with a short viewing period (150 ms) to try to understand initial and reflexive viewing patterns to the face. Adults were significantly more likely to orient their gaze upward towards the eyes (when initially fixated on the mouth) than adjust their gaze downwards away from the eyes (when initially fixated on the eyes). In another study, Laidlaw et al. (2012) used a novel paradigm to directly test volitional and automatic aspects of eye bias. Participants were explicitly asked not to look at either the eyes or mouth. Those who were told not to look at the eyes made more errors (i.e. fixations to the eyes) than would be expected with a random fixation pattern. In contrast, participants demonstrated strong suppression of mouth looking when told to ignore the region. The data suggest volitional control of mouth looking in the absence of full volitional control of fixations to the eyes. This finding was replicated by Laidlaw and Kingstone (2017) who also showed that face discrimination suffered when fixations to the eyes were avoided during initial viewing, and that covert viewing of the eyes was not sufficient to confer an encoding advantage. In the current study we examine the nature of these automatic and volitional components of eye looking further. It is notable that Laidlaw et al. (2012) found that participants who were told not to look at the eyes spent significantly longer looking to the eyes in the early viewing period (first 1000 ms) than the late viewing period (fixations starting after 1000 ms). This suggests that the unconscious bias to look at the eyes may be more difficult to inhibit during the relatively early period of face viewing and it could be inferred that faster automatic processes are superseded by slower volitional processes. Following previous work using first fixations to measure attentional priority (Fletcher-Watson, Findlay, Leekam, & Benson, 2008), our paradigm offers a more fine-grained analysis of this time course by measuring the location of the first fixation to the face. Laidlaw and colleagues' (Laidlaw et al., 2012; Laidlaw & Kingstone, 2017) methodology also required participants to avoid looking at features. Given the known challenges of thought suppression (Wenzlaff & Wegner, 2000), instructing participants within a negative frame i.e. not to look at the eyes, may be more challenging than positive instruction to look to the mouth.

The hall was a bustling cauldron of voices, a veritable symphony of accents ringing through the air like the clang of hammers on anvil. I recall how the clamor enveloped me as we stepped inside, my heart racing like it was rehearsing for its grand debut. Rows of wooden benches creaked under the weight of their occupants, each person a portrait of passionate conviction, with faces painted by the hand of democracy itself. Old men shuffled papers, their gnarled fingers pacing across the creased pages, while younger folk stood in clusters, exchanging fervent whispers and pointed gestures that seemed to dance in the dim light. "Now, pay attention, Willyum," my Pa said, nudging me with his elbow. His breath brewed with the aroma of cheap cigars, but I didn't mind much. This was my first taste of democracy, the raw, unfiltered essence of it. The very air crackled with the anticipation of ideas flaring to life, commissioning the spirits of conversation to prance about like wild stallions in a meadow. "Here comes Fixem!" someone in the back shouted, and suddenly, the din hushed into a collective murmur. There he stood - the Honorable Wallace Fixem, tall and ostentatious in his tailored coat, as if he had borrowed it from the pages of a magazine. His presence commanded respect, not merely by merit of position, but by the sheer charisma pulsing from his being. With every step towards the front, the crowd parted like the Red Sea, anticipation rippling through the throng. "Good evening, ladies and gentlemen!" he boomed, and I felt my chest swell with the weight of that honorific. "It is indeed a pleasure to stand before you today, amidst such a distinguished gathering of our esteemed community!" I glanced at my Pa, who wore a look of feigned moderation, his eyes alight with concealed skepticism. "It's all show and no go," he muttered under his breath, suspicious of the sincerity woven into Fixem's silken words. But I, caught in a rapture of youthful naivete, was entranced by the spectacle before me, every flamboyant gesture punctuating a vision of a better world as Fixem spun tales of hope and reform. As he spoke of roads and railways, of bridges spanning over troubled waters, I could almost imagine the promises blossoming into reality. Yet, amidst those soaring possibilities, I caught sight of my fellow attendees, their faces veiled in bemusement or outright disillusionment. An elderly gentleman in a flat cap tightened his grip on a flyer, crumpling it as he muttered something under his breath that sounded suspiciously like "pie in the sky." Another voice, this one youthful and vibrant, broke through the murmured discontent. "What about the rights of the working man?" a girl protested, squeezing her way to the front of the hall. Her eyes sparkled with indignation, and for a split second, the gaze of Fixem bore the weight of uncertainty, as though he was momentarily confronted with the very fabric of his polished rhetoric. "Aren't we here to address the real issues?" She was fervent, unyielding, and in that instant, I felt the burgeoning spirit of the crowd shifting, like the turning of a tide. Debate stirred in the room, and my heart raced anew, thumping in rhythm with the discontent of a community on the brink. Here I was, at the intersection of intrigue and tumult, a mere boy ensnared in the throes of history unfolding.

The poignancy of his question caught me off guard. I paused, choosing my words carefully, desperately wanting to offer wisdom where I felt I had none. The instabilities in his relationship seemed to bleed into his academic life, and he slipped further behind. His brisk laughter and endless talking were his defenses, his scribbles the heart of a storyteller finding his voice. As the final bell rang, heralding winter's approach and the end of my internship, I knew I'd never forget Calvin-his journey was just beginning.

As we continued our tea, the conversation turned to the topic of my father's recent offer. He had been approached by a wealthy merchant who wanted him to take on a position as a chaplain on one of his ships. My father was torn, as he loved the sea and the idea of traveling, but he also felt a strong sense of duty to his family and the parish. "I must say, I'm not sure what to do," he said, looking at my mother for guidance. "On one hand, it would be a wonderful opportunity to see the world and spread the word of God to those who need it most. On the other hand, I would be leaving my family behind, and I'm not sure if it's right to do that." Aunt Deb, who had been quiet until now, spoke up. "I think it's a terrible idea, your father. You're a clergyman, not a sailor. You have a duty to your parish and your family. Why would you want to leave them behind?" I couldn't help but disagree with Aunt Deb's opinion. I had always been fascinated by the sea and the stories of adventure that came with it. I had spent countless hours poring over books about explorers and pirates, and I longed to experience it all for myself. "I think it's a wonderful opportunity, Father," I said, trying to reason with Aunt Deb. "You would be doing God's work, and you would be seeing the world. It would be an adventure like no other." But Aunt Deb was not swayed. "It's not just about seeing the world, Dick," she said sternly. "It's about doing what's right. You should stay here and help your family, not gallivant off to sea." I knew that Aunt Deb was right, but I couldn't help but feel a sense of restlessness. I wanted to see the world, to experience all the things that lay beyond our small village. I knew that my father was torn, and I hoped that he would make the right decision. After tea, I decided to go for a walk in Leighton Park to clear my head. As I walked, I thought about my father's offer and the arguments for and against it. I knew that I would have to support him, no matter what he decided. As I walked, I stumbled upon a small pond and decided to go fishing. I had always loved fishing, and it was a way for me to clear my head and relax. But as I was casting my line, I felt a sudden jolt and found myself struggling to get free. I looked up to see a swan attacking me, its beak snapping wildly. I tried to shoo it away, but it was too aggressive. I was starting to get worried, but then I heard a voice behind me. "Hey, Dick, need a hand?" It was Mark Riddle, one of my friends from school. He had always been a bit of a troublemaker, but he was also very brave. I nodded, and Mark came over to help me. Together, we managed to fend off the swan and get me out of the pond. I was shaken, but grateful to Mark for his help. As we walked back to the village, I couldn't help but think about my father's offer again. I knew that I would have to support him, no matter what he decided. But I also knew that I couldn't shake the feeling that I was meant for something more.

Following a report on this invention by Paul Delaroche, a leading scholar of the day, the French government bought the rights to it in July 1839. Details of the process were made public on 19 August 1839, and Daguerre named it the Daguerreotype. The announcement that the Daguerreotype "requires no knowledge of drawing...." and that "anyone may succeed.... and perform as well as the author of the invention" was greeted with enormous interest, and "Daguerreomania" became a craze overnight. An interesting account of these days is given by a writer called Gaudin, who was present the day that the announcement was made. However, not all people welcomed this exciting invention; some pundits viewed in quite sinister terms. A newspaper report in the Leipzig City Advertiser stated: "The wish to capture evanescent reflections is not only impossible... but the mere desire alone, the will to do so, is blasphemy. God created man in His own image, and no man- made machine may fix the image of God. Is it possible that God should have abandoned His eternal principles, and allowed a Frenchman... to give to the world an invention of the Devil?" At that time some artists saw in photography a threat to their livelihood (see Artists and Photography ), and some even prophesied that painting would cease to exist. The Daguerreotype process, though good, was expensive, and each picture was a once-only affair. That, to many, would not have been regarded as a disadvantage; it meant that the owner of the portrait could be certain that he had a piece of art that could not be duplicated. If however two copies were required, the only way of coping with this was to use two cameras side by side. There was, therefore, a growing need for a means of copying pictures which daguerreotypes could never satisfy. Different, and in a sense a rival to the Daguerreotype, was the Calotype invented by William Henry Fox Talbot, which was to provide the answer to that problem. His paper to the Royal Society of London, dated 31 January 1839, actually precedes the paper by Daguerre; it was entitled "Some account of the Art of Photogenic drawing, or the process by which natural objects may be made to delineate themselves without the aid of the artist's pencil." He wrote: "How charming it would be if it were possible to cause these natural images to imprint themselves durably and remain fixed on the paper!" The earliest paper negative we know of was produced in August 1835; it depicts the now famous window at Lacock Abbey, his home. The negative is small (1" square), and poor in quality, compared with the striking images produced by the Daguerreotype process. By 1840, however, Talbot had made some significant improvements, and by 1844 he was able to bring out a photographically illustrated book entitled "The Pencil of nature." (See note HERE). Compared with Daguerreotypes the quality of the early Calotypes was somewhat inferior. (See comments on Claudet).

A palpable tension hung in the air, resonating with the clamor of conflict and the dissonance of diplomatic strife. As clashes continued to reverberate through the beleaguered city of Aleppo, the voices of dissent grew louder, not only on the battleground but within the chambers of the international community. With the United Nations in a state of heightened anxiety over the unfolding humanitarian crisis, analysts dissected the implications of the General Assembly's vote and the profound ramifications of Kofi Annan's departure as the figurehead of peace efforts. Annan's resignation, a deeply significant moment, marked yet another blow to a process already beleaguered by fruitless negotiations and increasing violence. The tensions, both political and military, bore down heavily on the populace in Aleppo, where civilians remained caught in the crossfire of their government's relentless pursuit to quash resistance. Reports of daily atrocities continued to emerge, painting a vivid portrait of the war's ugly reality. Human Rights Watch characterized these incidents as emblematic of war crimes; armed confrontations proliferated beyond mere skirmishes into a dark tapestry woven with threads of desperation and defiance. Meanwhile, the Free Syrian Army's temporary gains in Aleppo were a stark reminder of the volatile nature of the conflict. Unable to maintain their hold on the TV building, rebel forces were consistently outgunned and outmaneuvered by troops loyal to Assad, who prepared to retaliate with fervor. Sniper fire echoed down the blood-stained streets, forcing civilians to scurry for cover, while artillery explosions shattered the fragile calm at the heart of the city. This relentless cycle of violence echoed the tenacity of the opposition, who continued to assert themselves even in the face of seemingly insurmountable odds. In Damascus, state-run media narratives sought to shape public perception, framing the rebels as mere mercenaries rather than freedom fighters. The government's portrayal of the insurgents reinforced a steadfast belief in their own righteousness, as they fought to preserve what they termed "the integrity of the nation." Citizens, bombarded by relentless propaganda, grappled with the duality of their reality; the specter of liberation loomed large yet was shadowed by an oppressive regime unyielding in its defenses. As debates roiled within the United Nations, it became increasingly evident that consensus remained a distant dream. Western diplomats rallied around the resolution, citing the urgent humanitarian needs as justification for stronger interventions. In contrast, Russia and China maintained a steadfast commitment to supporting the Assad regime, casting doubt on any efforts to contain Syria's descent into chaos. Their firm standing demonstrated a broader geopolitical struggle, where alliances would test the limits of international diplomacy. In the streets, tenuous pockets of normalcy persisted amidst the pandemonium. Markets opened, albeit cautiously, as vendors attempted to peddle goods in an environment fraught with uncertainty. The resilient spirit of the people was remarkable; children played in the rubble where their homes once stood, clinging to fleeting moments of joy as their future slipped further from their grasp. Community initiatives flourished, offering solace in the form of makeshift schools and clinics, enabling residents to reclaim a semblance of their disrupted lives. Yet, dark thoughts lingered-how much longer could this fragile hope endure? At what point would the tides of conflict sweep away the last remnants of peace? The question weighed heavily, not just on the weary minds of Aleppo's citizens but on those watching from afar, engaged in discussions that drifted aimlessly through the corridors of power without the decisive action they demanded. As the morning light filtered through the haze of despair, it illuminated the harsh reality: the road ahead would be fraught with challenges, yet it remained a road toward potential change.

I wanted to share my journey with you, as it has truly transformed my understanding of relationships and has brought me back from the depths of despair. When my ex and I broke up, I felt like a shell of my former self. The pain was palpable; it was not just the loss of a partner but the shattering of a future I had envisioned. I remember those long nights when I would toss and turn, ruminating over every argument, every moment of tension that had brought us to that point. It felt relentless. But what I discovered during this tumultuous period was not just heartache, but a profound opportunity for growth. Initially, I was mired in sadness, convinced that I would never be whole again. I would sit on the couch with my head buried in a pillow, crying over missed calls and fleeting memories. Yet, as the weeks turned into months, I started realizing something crucial - the only person responsible for my happiness was me. I began reaching out to friends and slowly started rebuilding my life. I took up a new hobby, one that I had previously shelved due to the demands of my relationship. I found joy in the little things that had once been overshadowed. I signed up for cooking classes, which, believe me, was not just a culinary adventure, but allowed me to immerse myself in a new world where I could learn and create something beautiful. At the same time, I embarked on a journey of self-acceptance, diving into books about emotional intelligence and resilience. I began journaling - vitally important for processing my thoughts and feelings during this challenging time. As time passed, I could feel my self-worth rebuilding brick by brick, like a wall growing stronger with each passing day. I learned to let go of the anger I had toward my ex and focused instead on forgiving myself for mistakes I believed I had made. I created an intention to move forward rather than backward, and that is when things began to shift in my life. One day, while I was volunteering at a local shelter, I received a message that would change everything. It was my ex. At first, I was shocked, heart racing as I read their words. They wanted to reconnect, to talk about what went wrong. I was cautious but also intrigued; could this be a new beginning? I took a deep breath and remembered my journey of personal growth. I decided to approach the conversation without expectations, having worked so hard to reshape my own narrative. When we met, something magical happened. Instead of rekindling old arguments, we shared what we had learned - not just about each other but about ourselves. This was a conversation grounded in respect, understanding, and vulnerability. I could see how much I had changed during the time apart, and I realized they had too. We weren't the same people who had broken up; we were now individuals with fresh perspectives and experiences. Through honest communication, we both expressed a desire to move forward, together yet as two whole people - a relationship rooted in mutual growth rather than a reliance on one another for validation. It was exhilarating. We rekindled our romance, but now with a different foundation. We built trust and intimacy, creating a secure pair bond that felt more alive than ever before. This journey had taught us both that love is not simply about finding someone but about becoming the right partner for each other. So, to everyone going through hardship after a breakup, remember that this is not the end but rather a step in your personal evolution. You can catalyze change, and in doing so, you just might attract the love you seek.

The irony dripped from Sam's words, a sardonic twist curling his lip as he stuck out his hand for the cash. Ben rifled through his pocket, retrieved a crumpled twenty and a fiver, and slapped them down with a look of disdain that matched Sam's own. "Consider it your tithe for today," Ben muttered, glancing back at the boys, who leaned against their mud-splattered truck, eyes trained on the flat expanse of road behind them. "I'm just maintaining the peace," Sam shrugged, pocketing the money with the practiced ease of a man who'd been caught in this struggle of power and survival more times than he liked to count. "Keep the peace, keep the quiet. That's all folks around here want." "Tell that to the guys out for a lynching," Ben replied, the bitterness sharp in his voice. He spat on the ground, the dust greedily soaking it up, and turned to leave, motioning for the boys to follow. They trudged to the truck, kicking up small puffs of dust with each step, an air of tension hanging over them like a low, dark cloud. Wasn't easy living in these parts; every day was a delicate dance between coexistence and conflict, between survival and surrender. "You think they'll really come after us?" one of the younger ones asked, nervous eyes darting between Ben and the horizon, as if expecting an army to crest the hill any moment. Ben paused, hand resting on the door handle, gaze fixed on some unseen point far off in the plains. "Anger fuels people in ways you can't predict. They might. But we'll be ready if they do." A low hum of agreement swept through the group, boots scuffing the dirt as they piled into the truck. The engine turned over with a rough growl, a mechanical promise of power and escape that belied its age and wear. For a moment, as they pulled away from Sam's isolated outpost, it was the only sound on the wind. Minutes stretched into an uneasy silence, the road nothing but a pale ribbon carving through the endless sprawl of sagebrush and scraggly pine. Clouds loomed on the horizon, swollen with an impending storm that would turn this ochre landscape to something fierce and formidable. Nature had always been the true ruler here; men were just transient, fleeting shadows on her vast stage. "Where we headed now?" murmured the boy from before, fiddling with a frayed thread on his jacket. The question etched lines of worry into his young forehead, a glimpse of the man he might become if this land and life didn't chew him up first. Ben tipped his hat lower against the sun's glare. "We head north. Find safer ground, where folk remember what it means to share the land instead of hoardin' it. Places like that still exist. You just gotta know where to look." The boy nodded slowly, as if trying to believe it, searching Ben's face for that surety he desperately needed. And Ben, feeling the weight of their hopes, kept his eyes on the road, steering them toward whatever lay ahead.

As he continued to pace, the sounds of the neighborhood seemed to grow louder, more distant, and more irrelevant. The jazz music started up again, and this time it was followed by the wail of a siren in the distance. The boy on the sidewalk looked back at him with a mixture of curiosity and fear, and John felt a surge of anger towards him. Why should he be the only one to feel this pain? Why should his father's death be a personal affront to him alone? He quickened his pace, his feet carrying him farther and farther away from the house. He didn't want to go inside, didn't want to face the inevitable. He didn't want to lose his father, didn't want to be left alone in this world. But he knew he couldn't stay out here forever. Eventually, he would have to go back in and face the reality of his father's passing. As he walked, the sounds of the neighborhood grew fainter, and the silence of the street became more oppressive. He felt like he was walking through a tunnel, with the darkness closing in around him. He couldn't shake the feeling that he was being pulled towards some unknown fate, some dark and foreboding future. He stopped at the corner of the street, his eyes fixed on the Gallant house. He could see his mother sitting in the rocking chair, her head still bowed, her hand still pressed to her eyes. He could see the doctor sitting in the chair beside her, his eyes fixed on some point beyond the window. And he could see his father, lying in the bed, his chest rising and falling with labored breaths. John took a deep breath, his heart pounding in his chest. He knew he couldn't stay out here any longer. He had to go back inside, had to face what was happening. He took a step forward, then another, his eyes fixed on the door. He could feel the weight of his father's death bearing down on him, could feel the darkness closing in around him. But he knew he had to go on, had to face the unknown, had to find a way to carry on without his father. As he approached the door, he felt a strange sense of calm wash over him. He took one more step, then pushed the door open and stepped inside. The room was quiet, the only sound the soft hum of the phonograph in the background. His mother looked up at him, her eyes red and puffy from crying. The doctor looked up, his eyes expressionless. And John looked down at his father, his eyes fixed on the still, pale face. The room was silent, the only sound the soft hum of the phonograph, the only movement the slow, labored breathing of the dying man. John felt a sense of numbness wash over him, a sense of detachment from the world around him. He knew that his father was dying, knew that he was going to be gone soon. But he couldn't feel it, couldn't process it. All he could do was stand there, frozen in shock, as the darkness closed in around him.

As I lay awake, my mind racing with the absurdity of it all, I couldn't help but wonder what other unentitlements the good people of this great nation would soon be demanding. Free cars? Free housing? Free meals at the local diner? It's not as if we haven't already seen the likes of it. After all, we've got people clamoring for free healthcare, as if the very notion of personal responsibility has gone the way of the dinosaur. And don't even get me started on the so-called "living wage." What's next? A constitutional amendment guaranteeing everyone a minimum of 40 hours of leisure time per week? I mean, come on, folks, if you want to earn a decent living, you've got to put in the effort. My grandfather used to work 12 hours a day, six days a week, and he didn't complain. Well, not too much, anyway. But I digress. The point is, we've created a society where people expect something for nothing. And it's not just the young folks, either. I've seen grown adults, people in their 40s and 50s, who still believe the world owes them a living. They're like giant, entitled babies, crying and whining because they didn't get their way. And then there's the media, fanning the flames of discontent with their sensationalist headlines and biased reporting. They're like a bunch of vultures, circling overhead, waiting for the next big story to swoop in and feast on. And we, the public, are the ones who suffer for it. Take this whole gas price debacle, for example. It's a crisis, they say. A crisis, I tell you! But what's the real story here? Is it the price of gas, or is it the fact that we've become a nation of gas-guzzling, SUV-driving, energy-hungry consumers who can't seem to get enough? I mean, have you seen the size of some of these vehicles on the road? They're like small tanks, for crying out loud! And don't even get me started on the environmentalists. They're the ones who want us to believe that we're destroying the planet, that we're running out of oil, that we need to switch to alternative energy sources. But what's the real agenda here? Is it to save the planet, or is it to control our behavior, to tell us what we can and can't do? As I lay there, wide awake, my mind racing with the absurdity of it all, I couldn't help but wonder what the future holds. Will we continue down this path of entitlement and dependency, or will we finally wake up and take responsibility for ourselves? Only time will tell, I suppose. But one thing's for sure: I'll be awake, watching and waiting, as the world spins further and further out of control.

Lawsuits in those cases are pending in several federal appeals courts across the country. The Hobby Lobby and Conestoga claims are in yet another Obamacare category: for-profit corporations claiming a religion-based exemption. These suits follow the high court's decision two years ago that narrowly upheld the key funding provision of the health care law, a blockbuster ruling affirming that most Americans would be required to purchase insurance or pay a financial penalty, the so-called individual mandate. The constitutional debate now shifts to the separate employer mandates and whether corporations themselves enjoy the same First Amendment rights as individuals. Three federal appeals courts around the country have struck down the contraception coverage rule, while two other appeals courts have upheld it. That "circuit split" made the upcoming Supreme Court review almost certain. David Green and his family are Hobby Lobby's owners and say their evangelical Christian beliefs clash with parts of the law's mandates for comprehensive coverage. They say some of the drugs that would be provided prevent human embryos from being implanted in a woman's womb, which the Greens equate with abortion. Those drugs include Plan B contraception, which some have called the "morning after" pill. The large retailer says it already provides coverage for 16 federally approved forms of contraception - such as condoms and diaphragms - for its roughly 13,000 employees, who Hobby Lobby says represent a variety of faiths. The White House has said it believes a requirement on contraception coverage is "lawful and essential to women's health" and expressed confidence the Supreme Court would ultimately agree. Obamacare's supporters say it does not require individual company owners to personally provide coverage they might object to but instead places that responsibility on the corporate entity. "Throughout our nation's history, corporations have been treated differently than individuals when it comes to fundamental, personal rights of conscience and human dignity," said lawyers for the Constitutional Accountability Center, a progressive public-interest legal group. "The First Amendment's free exercise guarantee has always been viewed as a purely personal liberty." But lawyers representing the Hahns say they deserve freedom from what they call state intrusion into private moral decisions. "The question in this case is whether all Americans will have religious freedom and will be able to live and do business according to their faith," said Matt Bowman, senior legal counsel with the Alliance Defending Freedom. "Or whether the federal government can pick and choose what faith is, who are the faithful, and where and when they can exercise that faith." A key issue for the justices will be interpreting a 1993 federal law known as the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, requiring the government to seek the "least burdensome" and narrowly tailored means for any law that interferes with religious convictions. Can companies, churches, and universities be included, or do the protections apply only to "persons?"

The majority were young men, and the older ones looked like the younger ones once did. Stukely himself was not more than twenty-eight, but he had a greyish beard, and his face was deeply lined. He wore a dark suit, which was cut close to the throat, and a black necktie, and he talked very little, except when any one spoke to him. He moved about among his guests with a glass of cider in his hand, and every now and then went out to look at his horse, which had just come in from a run, and was standing restlessly in the yard. Once or twice he disappeared into the darkness, and returned in a few minutes with another bottle of cider. This was generally the signal for a fresh round, and then the men would talk louder than ever. One of these was a tall, slight fellow with a sallow face and deep-set eyes, who wore a flannel shirt, a belt round his waist, and high boots. His name was Kinsman, and he had come up from Manitoba last spring, having worked his way across the continent on a freight car. At first glance, he seemed the least like the others, but there was nothing about him that suggested the city slum or the factory district. He had lived too much in the open air, and, moreover, his mouth was set firmly, and his eyes were clear and bright. When he took a drink, he drank slowly, and with evident enjoyment, and then he would go to work again on a sawmill engine which he had built for Stukely, and which lay, ready for transportation, in a corner of the barn. It was only when he stopped for breath that he spoke, and he seemed to take no notice of anything that passed around him until the conversation turned upon a subject that interested him. "That's so," said Kinsman, "but I never heard of a man being drowned before." "Never?" asked one of the company. "Why, there's a fellow up near Moose Jaw who was killed by a buffalo bull last winter, and I know a chap in Saskatchewan who lost his scalp a month ago. You can't move without running against accidents." Kinsman shook his head. "I've seen a good deal of the country," he continued, "and I've never known anyone to get hurt yet. But if you want a story, here's one. I was working in Winnipeg last summer, and we were building a bridge over the Assiniboine. Well, one day I was sitting on a pile of lumber waiting for my dinner, when I saw a Chinaman walking along the bank of the river with a basket on his shoulder. He was dressed in a sort of smock frock, and he had on a pair of heavy boots and a straw hat. By-and-by he came up to me, and asked if I could tell him how to cross the river. I told him it wasn't safe, because there were alligators in the water. He didn't seem to understand, and asked me if I meant crocodiles. Then I pointed to a big log which floated a few yards from the shore, and told him to walk on that. Well, he got on to it, and started to cross the river. Pretty soon he fell off, and the current caught him, and dragged him under. We ran down to the edge of the water, but we couldn't see him anywhere. I don't suppose he'd have been missed, only he'd left his basket behind, and there was a dollar and a quarter inside it.

My own thoughts do incline toward his; but, as you say, when one sees men like my Lord Falkland, who have hitherto stood among the foremost in the ranks of those who demand that the king shall govern according to law, now siding with him against them, one cannot but feel how grave are the difficulties, and how much is to be said on either side. How is one to choose? The king is overbearing, haughty, and untrue to his word. The Parliament is stiff-necked and bent upon acquiring power beyond what is fair and right. There are, indeed, grievous faults on both sides. But it seems to me that should the king now have his way and conquer the Commons, he and his descendants will henceforth govern as absolute monarchs, and the liberty of the people will be endangered; while on the other hand, should the Parliament gain the upper hand, they will place on a firm basis the liberties of Englishmen, and any excesses which they may commit will be controlled and modified by a future parliament, for the people of England will no more suffer tyranny on the part of the Commons than of the king; but while they cannot change the one, it is in their power to elect whom they will, and to send up men who will govern things moderately and wisely."

A few miles away rose the white walls and red roofs of a great ranch house; nearer, a straggling line of blue smoke indicated the haciendado's "corral" or quarters. But the traveler did not awake until the sun was high overhead, and then only to rise lazily, yawn, stretch himself, and again pursue his desultory way. The hacienda he approached was one of the largest in Santa Clara County, extending its domains on either side of the canada del Raimundo, and possessing a frontage of nearly three miles on the main road. Its owner, Don Ramon Alvarado, had been one of the richest landholders in the State, and had lately sold the greater portion of his estate to an American company, retaining only sufficient for the working of his cattle and horses. This part included the canada del Raimudo, and the wooded hillside above it, whose summit commanded a view of the whole valley of San Jose. To this hill Don Ramon had removed after selling his rancho, and built a new adobe house, which, although smaller than his former habitation, was scarcely less picturesque. Yet he was seldom there; having engaged himself to the new proprietors as mayordomo, or superintendent, he preferred living in the old quarters, near the scene of his labors, and not far from the actual dwelling-house of the American director, Mr. Slinn, whom he served with the same grave courtesy and precision he would have shown to an original purchaser. Indeed, he could not help regarding Slinn as a tenant, and looking upon the sale of the property as only a financial transaction, without prejudice to his own seignorial rights. Nor was he entirely wrong. Although the new proprietors had introduced certain radical changes in the method of working the estate, they had retained many of the usages of the old system, partly from necessity, partly from custom, and partly from the influence of Don Ramon himself. So the old patriarchal rule was still exercised over the peons, who were clothed and fed like children, and treated with parental kindness, albeit with the severity of a parent. The old festivals were still celebrated with bull baits and fandangos, and even the mission priests were allowed to visit the estate and minister to their flock. Only one thing was withheld - the hand of Dona Isabel, the daughter of Don Ramon. Whether this was because she was the last representative of an old Spanish family, or whether it was because her dark eyes and thin aquiline profile were supposed to exercise an unhallowed fascination over the simple-minded Americans, certain it is that the reputation of being a coquette preceded her wherever she went, and woe betide the unfortunate swain who dared to lift his eyes to her! The prohibition extended even to the newly-imported Cornish miners who worked the coal-mines of the company, and who were supposed to combine with their insular taciturnity the brutal passions of their race. Meanwhile Dona Isabel lived alone with her father and sister upon the hill, attended only by an Indian woman and a Chinese cook, and visited solely by the good fathers from the Mission Dolores. She rode on a mustang almost as wild as herself, accompanied only by her maid, and sometimes joining the vaqueros in their sports with a fiery zest that delighted while it half-terrified them. Her little coquetries with these handsome metifs passed for innocent amusement, and were accepted as such by her indulgent father, and even by her confessor.

How could I know whether or not I was pregnant without taking a pregnancy test? What if I didn't think I was pregnant and therefore didn't bother to take a pregnancy test until after I missed my period? Would I then need to wait another month to see if I missed my second period before I knew whether or not I was pregnant? I was beginning to feel anxious about being pregnant and not knowing it. In fact, the more I thought about it, the more convinced I became that I must be pregnant. I began to sweat. Maybe I should take another pregnancy test. Just to make sure. But what if the first test was faulty? Or what if there was something wrong with the second test? Should I buy three different brands of pregnancy tests and take them all simultaneously? I began to hyperventilate. I needed to go back and reread the chapter. A few minutes later, I felt calmer. There was no reason to panic. Even though I had already taken a pregnancy test and gotten a positive result, there were several other signs of pregnancy listed in the chapter. I quickly scanned through the list. Morning sickness: check. Frequent urination: check. Fatigue: double check. Sore breasts: check. Nausea: check. Mood swings: triple check. I was definitely pregnant. I closed the book and went to bed. I closed the book and went to bed. Chapter 5: Your Third Month "If you haven't already done so, consider cutting down on your work hours, especially if you have a stressful job. By putting in fewer hours at work, you'll have more time to rest and relax and less stress to cope with. Not only will you enjoy your pregnancy more, but you'll also give your growing baby the healthiest environment possible.a At this point, I was feeling completely overwhelmed.

You've experienced firsthand how the industry is evolving globally. Could you share some of the trends and challenges you've observed in music tech during your travels? Certainly, there are so many exciting trends appearing right now. One major trend I've noticed is the burgeoning interest and investment in artificial intelligence within the music industry. During my visit to Europe, particularly in places like Valencia, there was a significant discussion about how AI is being integrated into different phases of music production-from composition and songwriting to performance and even audience engagement. This technology is not only creating new opportunities but also raising questions around authenticity and the value of human touch in creative processes. In India, I observed a different kind of trend. There's an immense wave of new platforms emerging, tailored to local content that cater to specific regional languages and cultures. This localized approach to music tech allows for more personalized and meaningful listener experiences. Moreover, it was incredible to see how traditional elements are being blended with modern technology to create innovative musical expressions. But with these advancements come challenges. One of the main hurdles is ensuring that technology doesn't overshadow the artistry. There's also a significant conversation happening around digital rights management and fair compensation for artists. As the landscape evolves, it's crucial that those behind the music-composers, performers, producers-can reap the benefits of their work, which is something that the industry still struggles with. I also wanted to mention the rise of immersive music experiences as a notable trend, especially during my chats in the U.S. with industry professionals in cities like Los Angeles and Nashville. VR (Virtual Reality) and AR (Augmented Reality) are opening up new ways for artists and fans to connect, offering more interactive and engaging concert experiences. However, this also means that the industry needs to address accessibility issues and ensure that these technologies are available to a broader audience. These global insights highlight the exciting but complex nature of the current music tech landscape. There's no one-size-fits-all solution, and it can be fascinating to see how different regions adapt to and adopt these technologies based on their unique cultural and economic circumstances. Can we delve deeper into your thoughts on how these trends will shape the future of music distribution and consumption? I'd love to hear your take on whether these technological advancements could potentially democratize the industry more, especially for emerging artists. Absolutely, I think technology holds the potential to democratize the industry significantly. By lowering barriers to entry and providing powerful tools for creation and distribution, more artists than ever have the means to reach a global audience. I've seen firsthand how even small-scale musicians in remote areas can now share their art with the world, thanks to platforms that allow easy access to music production tools and widespread distribution networks. Yet, democratization comes with its set of challenges and complexities. While technology enables broader access, it also saturates the market, making it difficult for individual voices to rise above the noise. It will be essential for platforms to develop ways to help artists sustain their careers in this vast digital sea. The next few years will likely be pivotal in defining how these advancements and trends continue to unfold.

Why shouldn't they catch a few halibut or ling from the trawl-boat and sell them to the hotel? And if they did get caught, what then? They'd just have to take their punishment like men - that's all. In any case, it wasn't going to be easy to catch anything. There were plenty of big fish about, but they were all too clever for the boys' snares. It was no use setting traps, because the fish could swim under the stones and into the holes. And there was only one chance of catching a big fish, and that was by means of a deep-sea line. Such a line was made of a strong cord, fastened to an iron sinker and attached to a stout rope which ran through a pulley fixed to a cross-piece of wood standing upright in a hole bored in the beach. A boy sat on the cross-piece and lowered the line by pulling the rope; another stood by to draw up the fish when it was hooked. But though these boys knew how to set a deep-sea line, they hadn't got one to set. So they had decided to steal one. Martin Bruvold, who lived next door to Peer Troen, had heard something about it and had offered to help. He had seen the deep-sea line hanging up inside the boat-shed, and had promised to keep watch outside while Peer went in and fetched it. But he had also managed to give himself away, and now his father had discovered the plot, and was watching the shed himself. Luckily the door was not locked, so Peer was able to slip in unseen and carry off the line. His first thought was to hide it somewhere safe, but it wouldn't fit into the wheelbarrow, and Martin was already running off with the tub. Then suddenly Peer remembered the big rock pool close beside the house. He put the line down in it and covered it up with seaweed. Now Martin must be told to wait there for him. It was not likely that anyone would think of looking in that particular pool. As a matter of fact, it was rather too shallow for a deep-sea line. But Peer didn't care about that. What mattered was that the line should be hidden where nobody else would find it. Martin waited impatiently until the coast seemed clear. Then he hurried back and joined Peer again. They looked carefully round, and seeing no one, made for the beach. Just as they reached it, however, Martin stopped short. "What's the matter?" asked Peer. "Nothing," replied Martin, "only I'm afraid we're being followed." "Nonsense!", said Peer scornfully. "You've been dreaming." "I tell you I saw someone coming down behind us!" "Well, let 'em come!" retorted Peer. "We'll soon see who's afraid of whom!" Martin hesitated. He wasn't sure whether he had really seen anybody or not. After all, he might have been mistaken. Perhaps it was only a shadow cast by the clouds passing overhead. Besides, Peer was his friend, and he oughtn't to let him down. He started walking again. But almost immediately he stopped once more. This time he couldn't doubt the evidence of his senses. Someone was certainly following them. Peer turned sharply round. No one was in sight. "There isn't a soul near us," he declared. "If there was, we'd know it." Martin shook his head. "But we do know it," he insisted. "Just look at that cloud. It's moving. It's the same cloud we passed under just now.

The importance of Salah in our daily lives cannot be overstated, my dear brothers and sisters in Islam. It is a pillar of our faith, a cornerstone upon which our entire existence as Muslims is built. And yet, we often take it for granted, neglecting its significance and importance in our lives. We get caught up in the hustle and bustle of our daily routines, and before we know it, the time for Salah has passed us by. We make excuses, we procrastinate, and we delay, but ultimately, we are only cheating ourselves. The Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wasallam, has warned us about the consequences of neglecting our Salah. He has told us that the first thing we will be questioned about on the Day of Judgment is our Salah. Will we be able to stand before Allah subhanahu wa'ta'ala and proudly say that we fulfilled our obligation to Him? Or will we hang our heads in shame, knowing that we failed to perform our Salah with the regularity and sincerity that it deserves? The Quran is replete with verses that emphasize the importance of Salah. In Surah Al-Baqarah, Allah subhanahu wa'ta'ala says, "Guard strictly your (habit of) prayers, especially the Middle Prayer; and stand before Allah in a devout (frame of mind)" (2:238). In Surah An-Nisa, He says, "Verily, the prayer is enjoined on the believers at fixed hours" (4:103). These verses leave no room for doubt or ambiguity. Salah is not a suggestion, it is an obligation, a commandment from Allah subhanahu wa'ta'ala that we must fulfill. And yet, we continue to make excuses. We say we are too busy, too tired, too distracted. We say we will pray later, but later never comes. We say we are not in the right state of mind, that we are not feeling spiritual enough. But Salah is not just about feeling spiritual; it is about obedience, about submission to the will of Allah subhanahu wa'ta'ala. The people of jihad, who are fighting in the way of Allah, are still obliged to pray. They are in the midst of battle, surrounded by the chaos and uncertainty of war, and yet they still find time to perform their Salah. They know that their Salah is a source of strength, a source of comfort, a source of guidance. They know that it is their connection to Allah subhanahu wa'ta'ala, their lifeline in times of turmoil. So what excuse do we have, my dear brothers and sisters in Islam? What excuse do we have to leave our Salah, to neglect our obligation to Allah subhanahu wa'ta'ala? We have no excuse, no justification, no rationalization. We must take our Salah seriously, we must prioritize it, we must make it a central part of our daily lives. Let us not wait until it is too late, my dear brothers and sisters in Islam. Let us not wait until we are standing before Allah subhanahu wa'ta'ala, regretful and remorseful, wishing we had done things differently. Let us take control of our Salah, let us take control of our lives. Let us make a commitment to ourselves, to our faith, and to our Lord, to perform our Salah with regularity, with sincerity, and with devotion.

Squires, Andrew; Brett, David John Lionel. / Investigating the impact of thermal gradients in solid oxide fuel cells using infrared thermography. In: Journal of Power Sources. 2014; Vol. 245. pp. 545 - 551. abstract = "Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are considered to be a promising future power technology due to their high efficiency and fuel flexibility [1]; however, the widespread adoption of such devices has been inhibited by, amongst other things, the long term mechanical instability of the stack [2-5]. The cermet anode Ni-YSZ (yttria stabilised zirconia) is widely used in the construction of such cells with the intimate contact of metallic, ceramic and pore phases in the composite material providing a 3-dimensional distribution of triple phase boundaries (TPBs) in the electrode, maximising its electrochemical performance. However, the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch between the anode and electrolyte phase (often a thin YSZ layer) has been widely reported to be the main cause of thermomechanical failure of SOFCs [6,7]. Thermal imaging has previously been performed on pellet SOFCs by Brett et al. [8] who utilised the technique to evaluate heat transfer coefficients, and Pomfret et al. [9,10] who used a filtered CCD camera to investigate the carbon formation caused by employing methanol and ethanol as direct fuels for SOFCs. Additionally, Sch{\"o}ttl et al. [11] used thermal imaging to investigate the thermal gradients imposed by passing a cold gas stream onto an open cathode SOFC. However, to date, the difficulty in obtaining optical access has limited the use of thermal imaging on larger form factor SOFCs. Thermal gradients in SOFCs are present due to a wide range of conditions, including thermal cycling to/from operating conditions [12], and under operation due to load following and localised electrochemical reactions [13]. These gradients can exacerbate degradation arising from the thermal expansion co-efficient mismatch between the metallic and ceramic phases [14]. The balance-of-plant is greatly increased by the need to minimise thermal gradients, reduce the prospect of thermally induced failure and prolong the stack lifetime. Finite element analysis (FEA) has indicated that thermal gradients of the order of 104 K m-1 may exist under internal reforming conditions [15] and that thermal gradients drastically increase the prospects of cell failure [16] by causing differential stress across the cell (indeed, these models also predict the presence of thermal gradients under steady state conditions [17-19]). Limited reports of experimental procedures investigating the effect of thermal gradients in operating SOFCs exist; however, it has been reported that large temperature gradients and localised hot spots are observed due to internal reforming on small form factor SOFCs [20,21]. Stresses in SOFCs arise due a range of conditions, including sintering during the manufacture of the cell and under operational conditions (caused by both thermal and physical effects) [22,23].

On the right hand, and beneath you, lies a broad expanse of olive groves and vineyards, stretching away into the distance, until they mingle with the horizon. There, too, you see orchards and corn-fields, and gardens, and cottages, and villages, and hamlets, and farm-houses, and villas, and palaces, and churches, and convents, and castles, and towns, and cities, and rivers, and lakes, and mountains, and forests, and plains, and hills, and valleys, and a thousand other objects of beauty and delight. What a contrast! But turn now to the north-east. Yon dark line of distant mountains bounds the view. It is the Sierra de Estrella. On the summit of the highest peak rises a huge, white mass, which looks like a castle. It is the Convento de Nossa Senhora da Assuncao, built there by a pious king, three centuries ago, in fulfilment of a vow made to the Virgin Mary, if she would vouchsafe to preserve him from shipwreck, during a stormy voyage to Africa. From thence a bold range of heights stretches south-west, until it terminates in that lofty cliff, rising abruptly from the river below. That river is the Mondego. It flows directly under the cliff. At its base stands a large building, which seems to be a fortress, with high walls and battlements, and towers, and bastions, and embrasures, and drawbridges, and portcullises, and massive gates, and sentinels pacing their rounds, and cannon pointed in all directions. It is a fortress. But, though its architecture proclaims its antiquity, it is not a castle. Its history does not date back to the days of chivalry. It is a prison. In times past, indeed, when the Marquis de Pombal was minister, and the Duke of Lafoes prime-minister, it was the royal palace. For, strange to say, these two great statesmen, who were also rival courtiers, persuaded the young queen Donna Maria I., that her own palace was haunted by evil spirits, and induced her to leave it, and occupy this gloomy pile, where, for several years, she held her court. The monarchs of Portugal never had any liking for it, and after the death of the marquis, the queen returned to her own abode. This prison is called Peniche de Coimbra. The city, which you see immediately opposite, is Coimbra. The river, flowing from the south, forms there a semicircular bend, so that the city stands on a tongue of land, washed on both sides by the stream. A bridge connects it with the fortress. It is a noble structure, consisting of twenty-one arches, each eighty feet wide, resting on piers of solid granite, and extending in length nearly half a mile. This bridge was commenced in the reign of King John III., more than three hundred years ago, and finished in that of his successor, Sebastian. The architect was Filippo Terzi, a Florentine. It cost three millions of dollars, and is said to be the most magnificent work of the kind in Europe. The city itself is surrounded by walls and ramparts, with bastions and watch-towers, and fortified gates, and deep ditches filled with water. Within these defences rise numerous churches and convents, and hospitals and colleges, and palaces and dwellings, the whole covering a space of about two square miles.

He is tasked with observing not only the summit but the footpath, the flora beneath, the interplay of sunlight and shadow on the rocks. Only by acknowledging the entirety is his understanding complete. Like this traveler, Yosef is urged by his father to immerse himself entirely in the world of his brothers, not neglecting the sheep or any collective aspects of their experience in the fields. Yaakov's teachings lie subtly between the lines. When he says, "bring me word," he is not necessarily asking for facts or simple reassurances. He's asking for insight into context, for a vision that extends beyond the scope of immediate concerns. In this way, perhaps he seeks to nurture within Yosef an aptitude for discernment, equipping him with the variant skills necessary for shepherding not only sheep but the complex flock that is family and community. Returning to our analogy of the automobile, imagine it again, crashing into that tree. Suppose the driver was en route to a significant gathering, carrying heirlooms or messages of peace-objects whose importance is not immediately discernible in the aftermath. Suddenly, the wreckage assumes a new dimension of significance. Similarly, Yaakov is not fixated on the vitality of life alone but on the harmonious functioning of a world intricately composed. In nurturing this mentality, we learn that every element of creation, every tiny mechanism and creature, possesses innate value in the broader scheme. Our responsibility, therefore, is not merely to ask if everyone is fine but to delve into the microcosms making up their lives. This fosters empathy, a crucial trait for any leader, which Yosef one day must learn to embody. As the parishad unfolds, we observe how interconnected relationships can be, each person and decision symbolizing a thread in the grander weave of history. This capacity for thorough examination roots in the appreciation of minutiae, safeguarding against the unforeseen consequences ripple through time when such details are overlooked. Yaakov's message, though seemingly mundane, teaches us to cherish both the grand and the granular. Through prioritizing the welfare and wholeness of those around us, beyond mere survival, we can hold together the diverse threads of a family, a community, a nation. Recognizing in ourselves and others the delicate interplay of every lived experience draws us closer to an ideal unity, a cosmic harmony where all play their part, no longer mere spectators but active contributors to the world's music. In Yosef's task, there is a quiet but profound assertion-for real peace and prosperity to be reached, one must care deeply, observe meticulously, and act with benevolence for all, weaving together lives anew with the sincerest intent.

"Rubbish nothing!" Dawson cried. "You want to see some of 'em?" He began pointing out the spires of several London churches that could be seen above the skyline. "See that one? St. Paul's Cathedral. That's the tallest building in London. And here's Westminster Abbey, and Big Ben, and the Houses of Parliament." "You're crazy, mate!" Freddy said with a laugh. "Look at these things, for Pete's sake. They're just church steeples. You can't compare them to skyscrapers." "Just watch me," Dawson retorted. "Steeple or no steeple, they're still higher than the Empire State. But don't take my word for it. Ask anybody. Anybody at all." "Oh, shut up, you madman," Freddy said impatiently. "Can't you see I'm enjoying looking at the sights? Besides, I don't believe a word you say." "Well, you'll find out soon enough," Dawson said with a grin. "And when you do, you'll remember this moment." "You mean that?" Freddy demanded. "Then why don't you prove it right now?" "Prove what?" "That you're telling the truth, you nut!" "Okay, I will." Dawson turned toward the stewardess who was passing by. "Say, lady, how high is the Empire State Building?" he called out. She stopped in her tracks and looked at him. Then she smiled and nodded. "Fifteen hundred and two feet, sir," she replied. "Thank you, miss," Dawson said politely. He turned back to Freddy Farmer. "There you go. Fifteen hundred and two feet. Now if you'll kindly tell me how high St. Paul's Cathedral is, maybe I'll believe you." "St. Paul's Cathedral?" Freddy repeated, as though the name meant nothing to him. "Yes, St. Paul's Cathedral," Dawson said with a straight face. "How high is it?" "Don't know," Freddy said after a pause. "How should I know?" "Because I'm going to ask somebody else," Dawson said, and turned toward the stewardess again. "Excuse me, Miss," he said, "but how high is St. Paul's Cathedral?" The girl smiled and shook her head. "I'm sorry, sir, but I've never been to London," she said. "Never mind, thanks anyway," Dawson said, and turned back to Freddy. "So there you are," he said. "You see, I told you so. A simple matter of facts. The Empire State isn't the highest building in the world. It's only the tallest." "Huh!" Freddy muttered. "A silly distinction. Anyway, you didn't prove anything. Maybe the girl would have known if you'd asked her about St. Paul's instead of asking about some cathedral." "Sure, sure," Dawson said with a chuckle. "Now let's get back to the important business of enjoying ourselves. There's plenty of time later to enjoy the rest of the trip. Come on, Freddy. Let's go in and see what the hotel has for us." With that, Dawson reached out and caught hold of Freddy's sleeve. He pulled the English youth along with him through the lounge door and out into the main corridor of the plane. "Hey, what about our luggage?" Freddy suddenly called out. "In the baggage compartment," Dawson replied. "We'll pick it up later. Right now I'm hungry. How about you?" "Hungry? Of course I am!" Freddy cried.

Will it emerge from its perilous journey around the sun, or will it succumb to the intense heat and gravitational forces that threaten to destroy it? For months, astronomers have been tracking ISON's progress, monitoring its trajectory and predicting its fate. Some have expressed doubts about the comet's chances of survival, citing its fragile composition and the intense heat it will face as it approaches the sun. But others remain hopeful, pointing to the comet's size and speed as factors that could help it withstand the sun's fury. As the comet enters the sun's outer layers, it will be exposed to temperatures of several million degrees. This is a daunting prospect, to say the least, and many experts believe that ISON may already be disintegrating before it even reaches the sun's surface. But Professor Tim O'Brien, associate director of Joderell Bank Observatory, remains optimistic. "It's like throwing a snowball into fire," he said. "It's going to be tough for it to survive. But luckily, it's a big object and it moves fast, so it won't spend too much time close to the Sun. There is a lot of uncertainty." If ISON does survive its encounter with the sun, it will be an incredible sight to behold. The comet is expected to appear at its brightest yet, low in the sky at dawn in the UK during December. It will be a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for stargazers to catch a glimpse of this celestial wonder. But even as the world waits with bated breath for the outcome of ISON's encounter with the sun, scientists are already planning for the next step in the comet's journey. "If it survives, it will be a great opportunity for us to study it in more detail," said Professor Mark Bailey, from Armagh Observatory in Northern Ireland. "We'll be able to learn a lot more about its composition and its origins." As the clock ticks down to the moment of truth, astronomers around the world are holding their breath. Will ISON emerge from its encounter with the sun, or will it succumb to the intense heat and gravity that surrounds it? Only time will tell.
