At the end of January, city officials unveiled new crimefighting measures, including a reward of $20,000 for information solving a homicide and $500 for locating illegal guns, plus funding for the witness assistance program and increasing police presence. At the news conference announcing the measures, Nutter put it this way: "To every criminal out there: I just put a $20,000 bounty on your head." A violent trend. City officials say it's too early to determine whether Philadelphia's homicide rate will continue to rise this year. Last year, as the city was besieged by teen mob attacks, Nutter made it clear he would not tolerate the violence. He raised some eyebrows last summer when he took to the pulpit to call out the predominantly black youths involved in the attacks. "You damage yourself, you damage another person, you damage your peers, and quite honestly, you damage your own race," said Nutter, who is black and has two children. In an attempt to stop the mob violence, Nutter moved up the weekend curfews for teens in two Philadelphia neighborhoods that bore the brunt of the seemingly random attacks. "There is no excuse for young people being out so late at night by themselves and then making bad decisions and literally assaulting other citizens," Nutter said. "I will not tolerate that." Philadelphia may have the worst homicide rate of the country's most populated cities, according to the most recent complete data (see fact box on left), but it pales in comparison with less-populated U.S. cities. Based on statistics from 2010, Philadelphia's homicide rate is about 20 killings per 100,000 people, according to FBI statistics. By comparison, cities with smaller populations have murder rates far worse than Philadelphia, including New Orleans at 49.1, St. Louis at 40.5 and Baltimore at 34.8. Criminal justice professor Jerry Ratcliffe says it's important to put Philadelphia's homicide data into a broader perspective. "Nobody likes to have these homicide statistics," said Ratcliffe, director of the Center for Security and Crime Science at Temple University. "You're talking about 34 homicides. That's in a city of 1.5 million people." While the daily body count is a disturbing trend for the city and triggers rampant media coverage, it doesn't mean Philadelphia is on track to become the murder capital of the country, Ratcliffe said. "I don't want to belittle the numbers, but it's really too difficult to assess the safety of the entire city based on little over a month of data," he said. "The real test will be this spring or summer when we (normally) see the violence peak." Sending a message. Therefore, size-frequency distributions can be used to assess the functioning of present-day ecosystems subjected to anthropogenic impacts (Queiros et al., 2006; Reizopoulou and Nicolaidou, 2007; Basset et al., 2012; Macdonald et al., 2012) and can represent sensitive indicators of oxygen depletion in the fossil record (Rohl et al., 2001; Twitchett, 2007; Caswell and Coe, 2013). The sedimentary record in the Gulf of Trieste, an area with natural gradients in primary productivity and affected by the 20th century anthropogenic eutrophication (with oligotrophization occurring since 1990s, Mozetic et al., 2010, 2012; Djakovac et al., 2012) and inter-annual hypoxia (Giani et al., 2015), represents a unique historical archive for assessing shifts in size structure of macrobenthic species affected by the 20th century anthropogenic eutrophication. Some macrobenthic organisms in the northern Adriatic Sea are able to survive short-term hypoxic events (Riedel et al., 2012) and to rapidly re-colonize the sea-floor with high densities in the wake of hypoxic events. One of these species is the bivalve Corbula gibba (Hrs-Brenko, 2003; Mavric et al., 2010; Nerlovic et al., 2012). The abundance of this species in living assemblages is used as an indicator of ecological status of living benthic communities (Simonini et al., 2009; Dauvin et al., 2012; Zettler et al., 2013; Chatzinikolaou et al., 2018; Moraitis et al., 2018), and its abundance in death assemblages in sediment cores can be used to trace past benthic dynamics under oxygen depletion (Tomasovych et al., 2017; 2018a). However, it is unclear whether this species responded to hypoxia and other disturbances that occurred in the 20th century also in terms of its size structure. Finally, this species was geographically widespread in shallow-water benthic communities since the Miocene in the Central Paratethys, Mediterranean, and Atlantic (Dominici, 2001; Zuschin et al., 2007, 2014; Scarponi and Kowalewski, 2007; Schneider, 2008; Scarponi et al., 2013, 2017; Amorosi et al., 2014; Harzhauser et al., 2017; Ruman et al., 2017; Rossi et al., 2018). Assessing its indicator potential on the basis of actualistic studies thus can have large importance in ecological and environmental analyses of Cenozoic molluscan assemblages (Senes, 1988; Senes and Ondrejickova, 1991). Death assemblages from sediment cores provide a unique opportunity to assess size structure of molluscan assemblages prior to the 20th century eutrophication. Death assemblages observed in sediment cores tend to be time-averaged to decades, centuries, or millennia (Kosnik et al., 2015; Tomasovych et al., 2016; Kowalewski et al., 2018). They can be insensitive to short-term, seasonal or yearly changes that occur at finer temporal resolution but will detect major, long-lasting changes in the composition and structure of communities (Tomasovych and Kidwell, 2010), and allow identification of significant changes in composition, size or production of molluscs prior to major anthropogenic impacts (Kidwell, 2007; Smith et al., 2016; Bizjack et al., 2017; Harnik et al., 2017; Martinelli et al., 2017).

I'd rather you went in somebody else's boat than mine, then," was the ungracious response. "Why, Hank!" exclaimed Colin in surprise, "what a thing to say!" The old sailor nodded sagely. "The skipper don't know much more about boat-whalin' than you do," he said, "that was all done away before his time. He's willin' to tackle anythin' that comes along, all right, but a whalin' boat is just about the riskiest thing that floats on water." "How's that, Hank?" asked the boy. "I always thought they were supposed to be so seaworthy." "They may be seaworthy," was the grim reply, "but I never yet saw a shipwright who'd guarantee to make a boat that'd be whaleworthy." "But I'm sure I've read somewhere that whales never attacked boats," persisted Colin. "Mebbe," rejoined the gunner, "but I don't believe that any man what writes about whalin' bein' easy, has ever tried it in a small boat." "Well," said the boy, "isn't it true that the only time a whale-boat is smashed up is when the monster threshes around in the death-flurry and happens to hit the boat with his tail?" "Not always." "You mean a whale does sometimes go for a boat, in spite of what the books say?" "I never heard that whales cared much about literatoor," the sailor answered with an attempt at rough humor, "an' anyway, most o' them books you've been readin', lad, are written about whalin' off Greenland an' in the Atlantic." "What difference does that make?" queried Colin. "Isn't a whale the same sort of animal all the world over?" "There's all kinds of whales," the gunner said, as though pitying the boy for his lack of knowledge, "some big an' some little, some good an' some bad. Now, a 'right' whale, f'r instance, couldn't harm a baby, but the killers are just pure vicious." "You mean the orcas?" the boy queried. "Only just the other day Captain Murchison was talking about them. He called them the wolves of the sea, and said they were the most daring hunters among all things that swim." "Sea-tigers, some calls 'em," the other agreed, "an' they're fiercer than any wolves I've ever heard about, but I never saw any of 'em attackin' a boat. I have seen as many as twenty tearin' savagely at a whale that was lyin' alongside a ship an' was bein' cut up by the crew. The California gray whale - the devil-whale is what he really is - looks a lot worse to me than a killer. He's as ugly-tempered as a spearfish, as vicious as a man-eatin' shark, as tricky as a moray, an' about as relentless as a closin' ice-floe." "There she blo-o-ows!" came the cry again from the crow's-nest.

I stepped inside, pushing past her gently, and made my way to the living room where FB was lounging in a recliner, his eyes fixed on the TV but clearly not absorbing a thing. His expression was a dark storm cloud, and I could almost see the resentment bubbling beneath the surface. "FB," I began, keeping my voice calm but firm. "We need to talk." He didn't look at me right away, and I could understand why. When someone holds onto their anger like a lifeline, admitting they're in the wrong feels like pulling the rug out from under themselves. Eventually, he turned to face me, his lips pressed into a thin line. "What's there to talk about?" he muttered, his tone dripping with defensiveness. "You've already made your point clear." "Yes, and I'm about to make it again," I snapped back. "You're upset because you can't gallivant off to Arizona with your brother, and it's somehow all our fault? You've got responsibilities, FB. Commitments. Ones that don't just disappear because you'd rather spend time elsewhere." He opened his mouth to protest, but I held up a hand. "Let me finish. My daughter, your wife, needs you here. She has medical appointments that she cannot miss. You know this. We all know this. This isn't some surprise that sprang up overnight." The silence in the room was thick, tense. FB's gaze flickered to my daughter, who stood in the doorway, her arms wrapped protectively around herself. Her eyes were pleading, filled with a complexity of emotions that made my heart ache. She needed him to be more than just present physically; she needed his support and understanding. "FB, your family is supposed to help out," I continued, my voice softening. "But not by enabling you to shirk your duties. We're here to back you up, to stand beside you, not in your stead. You need to be the husband she can rely on, the father your children can look up to." He sighed heavily, the weight of my words evidently sinking in. It was a slow realization, one that crept up on him like a thief in the night, stealing away the indignant anger and leaving something more vulnerable in its wake. "You're right," he said finally, the fight draining out of his posture. "I just... I miss him. I miss the way things used to be." "I get that, I really do," I replied gently. "But life isn't about clinging to the past. It's about making the present work, no matter how tough it gets. You can still plan a trip with your brother- just not at the cost of everything else." My daughter sniffled softly, stepping forward to rest a hand on FB's shoulder. The simple action spoke volumes, bridging the gap that had, for the longest time, felt insurmountable. She leaned in, resting her head against his. "We'll figure it out," she murmured. And in that moment, there was hope-hope that maybe, just maybe, he'd embrace them, along with all the chaos and unpredictability life had to offer.

This elasticity captures the willingness-to-pay for faster deliveries. Second, we need to estimate the responsiveness of exports to changes in administrative barriers to trade. This elasticity shows how much exporters adjust shipments to changes in administrative burdens. Both elasticities can be estimated using the same data set as the one used to calculate the value added of trade.4 In our empirical application, we use firm-level data from Hungary covering both imports and exports. For imports, we construct a unique dataset matching imported products with the corresponding Hungarian product.5 Using this information, we estimate the total welfare loss due to administrative barriers to trade at $12 million, about 0.6% of GDP. Interestingly, this number does not include any indirect effects through lower prices, nor the benefits of reduced delays in customs clearance. Moreover, the figure represents the average cost across all sectors and countries of destination. Administrative barriers to trade tend to be especially costly for small firms. We therefore also analyze the effect of administrative barriers to trade on the relative competitiveness of small and large firms. Our results indicate that while small firms tend to operate in markets with lower trade volumes and higher tariffs, they are also significantly disadvantaged by high administrative barriers to trade. This is consistent with the view that smaller firms are less likely to be able to afford the compliance costs associated with international trade. We thus identify the direct costs of complying with administrative barriers to trade as a significant factor contributing to the relative disadvantage of small firms vis-a-vis large ones. We conclude by discussing policy implications of our analysis. The most obvious solution to reduce the administrative costs of trade is to make them less cumbersome. Countries can learn from each others' experiences, and develop common standards for shipping documents and inspection methods. To complement these efforts, however, it is important to recognize that even if governments take steps to streamline administrative processes, exporters will still face costs in terms of delayed shipments. Thus, it is essential to support private sector initiatives aimed at improving supply chain management. Such efforts could focus on making it easier for businesses to cooperate internationally. For example, firms could create online platforms to share information on potential buyers/suppliers, logistics providers, and customs authorities. These platforms should be designed so as to help match the right partners based on their location, size, and specific needs. Additionally, there is scope for policy makers to promote the development of specialized financial instruments tailored to the needs of SMEs involved in international trade. Finally, since the benefits of trade facilitation may vary substantially across industries and destinations, it is crucial to tailor policies to the particular circumstances faced by different groups of firms. We study the role of trade facilitation in shaping the patterns of international trade. We develop a simple theoretical framework showing how trade facilitation affects consumer surplus, producer surplus, and trade volumes. We then test the predictions of the model using detailed micro-data on the exports and imports of Hungarian firms. We show that administrative barriers to trade impose substantial welfare losses on consumers and producers alike. We further demonstrate that these costs disproportionately impact small firms, highlighting the importance of trade facilitation for fostering a level playing field between large and small firms.

Now, your turn," Tilda said, drawing her voice to a whisper as if to match the gentleness of the odd peace around them. The sick woman did not respond, her eyelids flickering slightly, seeming to hover in a realm just beyond the veil of conscious thought. Undeterred, Tilda continued her lilting game, her young spirit unbowed by the inertia of the long whitewashed room. "I love my love with a B, because he's bold," Tilda persisted, casting her eyes toward the ceiling where the evening shadows began to transform the stark walls into something mysterious and almost enchanting. The hospital ward was a strange place indeed, where sorrow and healing tread carefully around one another, whispering secrets only the sick and the innocent could hear. Tilda found herself ruminating on such thoughts often now, as she lay, day after monotonous day, her young limbs restless beneath the starchy bedsheets. For Tilda, the world outside beckoned like a kaleidoscope in perpetual motion-a far cry from this static, sanitized existence. Her senses longed for the bustling sights and sounds of the showground, the vibrant tapestry of life she had once known. The clatter of hooves and the sharp crack of a ringmaster's whip; the vibrant pennants flapping defiantly against a blue sky; the gasps of an audience caught in the thrall of a trapeze artist's gravity-defying arc. But here, all was muted and dim, the echoes of merry calliopes nothing more than ghostly fragments of memory that stirred somewhere deep within her. It was not only the longing for the circus that tugged at Tilda's young heart. In those early morning hours, she found herself forging an unspoken connection with her somnolent roommate. How strange it was-to know nothing about the woman, not even her name, yet to feel inexplicably drawn to her, as if some invisible thread bound them together in shared adversity. Tilda imagined stories about her, tales of hardship and resilience, perhaps similar to those told by the show-folk around campfires on cold nights. She turned her eyes to the sketch of a tree etched into the paint over time, the simple lines teasing the mind with imaginings of freedom beyond these walls. "I love my love with a C, because he's clever," Tilda murmured, smiling at the rhyme that formed neatly in her mind. As she spoke, the woman finally stirred again, her eyes fluttering open, fixing once more on the girl with a clarity that held an unspoken appeal, like a lighthouse beckoning a lost ship in a stormy sea. Without exchanging words, they shared a moment of understanding, two lost souls adrift in an ocean of bedsheets and antiseptic. Whatever stories the woman's past held, they remained locked behind her weary eyes, a secret kept tightly bound within her gaunt frame. Yet Tilda was not deterred. She knew, with the resolve of any true show-folk, that the heart speaks its own language, one that needs no words. So she stayed, offering solace with the rhythmic cadence of her simple game, and the wonder of what might lie beyond these sterile confines if only given the chance.

The atmosphere at Harrah's poker tables was electric, a blend of tense concentration and boisterous laughter that made it clear we were in for one hell of a night. We found our seats, and I settled in, dollar bills neatly stacked beside my chips, ready to dive into the unspoken battle of bluffs and bold bets. Despite the blaring music and the flashing lights from all angles, the poker game had an almost sacred atmosphere among the players. Conversations were hushed, gestures were considered, and most eye contact was avoided to keep anyone from reading too deeply into the minds of their opponents. I threw myself into the game, with every card, every chip, and every daring move blending into a tapestry of strategy. The evening spun out in a quick whirl, snap decisions, shallow breaths, and moments where time either rushed ahead or dragged to a stop depending on the hand I was dealt. Every now and then, one of my friends' hoots of victory or groans of defeat would rise above the din, pulling me from my reverie for just a heartbeat before returning my focus to the delicate dance of poker. Things took an unexpected turn when, after many rounds, I found myself sitting with a startlingly large stack of chips in front of me. I was riding high on a wave of luck and nerve, blindsiding the table with my newfound prowess. It was the kind of high that comes unexpectedly on such nights, leaving you a bit breathless and wondering how long it will last. As the game wore on, the charm of each chip, the weight and promise of them, intensified the night's sense of impending victories or losses. Our cocktail waitress made frequent appearances, balancing trays of our bright, potent drinks, fueling our energy for whatever the night promised. It was nearly three in the morning when exhaustion finally brushed against the edges of my adrenaline-fueled state. My friends, equally energized and exhausted, began to show signs of weariness, rubbing their eyes or stretching in their seats. We decided to cash out. The clamor of chips being exchanged for crisp bills signaled our dwindling hours in Harrah's; the night was far from over, but it was clear we needed a change of scenery. Back on the streets of New Orleans, the air was balmy, buzzing with the lively hum of festivities that seemed to surge and ebb like ocean waves. Colorful beads swung from balconies, the stark outline of wrought iron fences decorated against the glow of streetlights, while music, laughter, and voices of people drifted along the streets like a living organism. The group moved with a reckless, lively intoxication, the spell of adventure far from broken. We danced through the streets, the cobblestones beneath our feet and the beat in our hearts driving us forward. Our exuberance seemed echoed in the crowds that filled the night, all caught in their own moments of merriment. Our night was a wild journey that had no hint of slowing, a testament to the whirlwind of camaraderie, laughter, games, and boundless thrill that carried us forward.

In his rage and disappointment at finding himself, as he chose to consider it, outwitted by a man upon whom he had always secretly looked down, the true feelings wherewith he had regarded an alliance welcomed by his cupidity, but resented by his pride, escaped without let or hindrance. "What did we want with a person called Stubbs? What the deuce could we want with him or any of his kind but their money?" demanded he, pacing the room, black with wrath. "I never should have let the fellow set foot within these doors if I had dreamed of this happening. I took him for an honest man. What? What d'ye say? Humph! Don't believe a word of it; he must have known; and as for his expecting to pull things round, that's all very fine. It's a swindle, the whole thing." Then suddenly the speaker stopped short and his large lips shot out as he faced his daughter: "Does Leonore say she hasn't a penny?" "She says she will have to give up everything to the creditors. I suppose," said Susan, hesitating, "everything may not mean - I thought marriage settlements could not be touched by creditors?" "No more they can, that's the deuce of it." "Then -?" She looked inquiringly, and strange to say, the fierce countenance before her coloured beneath the look. If he could have evaded it, General Boldero would have let the question remain unanswered, although it was only Sue, Sue who knew her parent as no one else knew him - before whom he made no pretences, assumed no disguises - who had now to learn an ugly truth; - as it was, he shot it at her with as good an air as he could assume. "She has no settlement, damn it." "No settlement?" In her amazement the open letter fell from the listener's hands. She recollected, she could never forget, the glee with which her father had rubbed his hands over the "clinking settlement" he had anticipated from Leonore's wealthy suitor, nor the manner in which it had insinuated itself into every announcement of the match. No settlement? She simply stared in silence. "If you will have it, it was my doing," owned General Boldero reluctantly; "and I could bite my tongue off now to think of it! But what with four of you on my hands, and the rents going down and everything else going up, I had nothing to settle - that is, I had nothing I could conveniently settle, and it might have been awkward, uncommonly awkward. I could hardly have got out of it if Godfrey had expected a quid pro quo. And he might - he very well might. A man of his class can't be expected to understand how a man of ours has to live decently and keep up appearances while yet he hasn't a brass farthing to spare.

In contrast, electrical measurements have been used as an alternative to radiation based densitometry for in-situ quantification of liquid hold-up in structured packed beds. Both electrical capacitance [17] and electrical resistance measurements [18] have been demonstrated to produce liquid hold-up measurement accuracies similar to radiation based techniques while also having the benefit of drastically reduced costs, orders of magnitude higher acquisition rates, and safer installation and use. It has been suggested that electrical measurements may be scalable and appropriate for industrial field service [17]. Tomography systems based on electrical measurements have been deployed in various industrial field service applications to characterize and quantify two-phase fluid flows both with and without fixed structural internals. Electrical Resistance Tomography (ERT) systems have been used to investigate the mixing characteristics in a packed-bed external loop airlift bioreactor [19], the effect of particles and liquid load on the phase distribution in trickle bed reactor [20], and gas distribution and void fraction in a packed bubble column with different packing materials [21]. Son et al. used ERT to measure the liquid distribution in pilot-scale packed column, in order to study the effects of the liquid load, gas factor, and liquid properties on the liquid distribution under various offshore conditions [22]. Similarly, electrical capacitance tomography (ECT) systems have been used to investigate pulse flow and pulse velocity in co-current trickle bed reactors [23] and solid phase distributions in a gas-solid fluidized bed [24]. Hamidipour used a twin-plane ECT to study the hydrodynamics of gas-liquid co-current down-flow and up-flow packed beds by cross-correlating each plane's tomogram to axial dispersion residence time distribution and modelled liquid hold-ups and pseudo-interstitial velocities for pulsed flow in the system [25]. Operators of industrial scale mass transfer operations that are highly dynamic in nature, such as post combustion CO2 capture systems with varying gas inlet flows and varying product recovery constraints, would benefit from real time in situ hydrodynamic data of the column internals. This information could be used to reduce settling time between plant states, increase process agility, troubleshoot reactors that are operating outside of design specifications, and allow for more efficient operation at off-design conditions. When considering the development of this type of measurement system, several practical considerations make electrical capacitance tomography (ECT) a strong choice for the measurement technology. Absorption mass transfer operations (e.g. aqueous amine based post combustion CO2 capture) are gas phase dominant, therefore electrical capacitance measurements preferred over conductivity measurements which would prefer a continuous liquid film path between each sensor array contact. The in-situ process probes would be low cost to manufacture, safe to operate, free of moving parts, and could be coated to increase corrosion resistance as they would not be required to directly contact the fluid or packing.

Despite the large number of studies employing flexible meshes for fluvial flooding (Castro Gama et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2009; Sanders et al., 2010; Schubert et al., 2008), none explicitly assesses the role of different mesh configurations, let alone for large-scale applications. While for these bespoke studies an efficient mesh was usually created first, such fine-tuning is too time-consuming for large-scale inundation modelling which may encompass several larger catchments. What is rather needed are fast approaches to generate flexible meshes over large areas covering a grand variety of topological properties. To make maximum use of the potential of flexible meshes, a resolution sufficiently fine to provide locally relevant results has to be determined a priori. How various degrees of mesh refinement impact large-scale inundation modelling results is hardly researched until now and thus additional insight is needed. In contrast to flexible meshes, there is a multitude of studies investigating various aspects of regular grid refinement. For instance, it was found that spatial resolution impacts the accuracy of inundation estimates (Savage et al., 2016a), water depth estimates and floodplain drainage flow (Savage et al., 2016b), and channel flow through near channel storage effects (Horritt and Bates, 2001a). Hardy et al. (1999) concluded that grid resolution impacts simulated discharge linearly and water depth in a less structured way due to the impact of the geographical surrounding of each observation location. Comparable results were obtained by Fewtrell et al. (2008) in a small urban environment. In this study, we will add considerations for large-scale (potentially even global-scale) flood hazard models using a fast set-up of flexible meshes. We present a first benchmark and sensitivity analysis to advance our understanding how model accuracy scales with flexible mesh discretization in large-scale studies. Eventually, we want to better understand (a) how different configurations of flexible meshes influence model accuracy, (b) how results differ between flexible meshes and regular grids, and (c) what lessons can be learned for future applications. The analysis was performed by employing GLOFRIM, a globally applicable framework for integrated hydrologic-hydrodynamic modelling (Hoch et al., 2017b). GLOFRIM is an openly accessible, modular, and extensible tool facilitating model coupling, currently allowing for spatially coupling PCR with DFM or LISFLOOD-FP (LFP; Bates et al., 2010). What was decisive to apply GLOFRIM was the requirement to guarantee identical spatially varying model forcing for all discretizations as well as the need to include all river reaches and floodplains in the analysis. Three different 1-D/2-D flexible meshes of the lower Elbe basin (Fig. 1) were forced with identical output from PCR at 30 arc-minutes spatial resolution. All flexible meshes were created based on the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) method (Renno et al., 2008). We decided to use HAND as it requires only little input data and is fast in computing topographical gradients with respect to the channel network.

Bottom-up metamodelling is an iterative process, since different versions of metamodels and exemplar models are continuously evolved in an interleaved manner until the final version of the metamodel is obtained [1]. Our proposed approach does not require a metamodel that is refined to follow the best practices or patterns proposed for metamodel development. The only requirement is that the metamodel must include all the types and the relationships that are present in the example models. The term "draft" which characterizes the metamodels needed as part of this approach implies firstly the optional need of having metamodelling best practices applied to the metamodel. Secondly, it can be "draft" in terms of not being a final one that covers all the concepts of the domain, but an intermediate one that covers a subset of the concepts, as soon as these are the only concepts appearing in the example models. This draft metamodel, following the iterative flexible MDE principles, should reach a final version that covers all the envisioned concepts and relationships. Related to that, it is necessary to highlight that our proposed approach focuses only on the inference of the types of the untyped nodes in the example models created (or evolved) as part of a flexible MDE approach (see "Example models definition" phase in Fig. 1). The way that the draft metamodel is inferred (or evolves) is outside the scope of this work and it is an interesting area of future research; the draft metamodel should fulfil the aforementioned requirement, though. In previous work [10,11], an approach to tackle the error of type omissions was proposed. The algorithm, that is based on Classification and Regression Trees (CART), is trained on the elements of the example models only, trying to identify similarities based on different sets of criteria and predict the types of untyped nodes without requiring the existence of a metamodel. This work contributes a novel approach in addressing the challenges associated with type omissions, but this time taking into account a draft metamodel constructed by language engineers, using constraint programming principles for suggesting the possible types. More specifically, the syntax and the constraints defined in the draft metamodel are automatically transformed to a set of facts and rules that are then applied to the example models to reduce the number of possible types of untyped nodes. Beyond the requirement for a metamodel, another important difference with the previous approach is the fact that in this work, the correct type for each node is always included in the set of suggested types. In the previous work, the suggested type is not guaranteed to be the correct one.

African Nations Cup: Zambia shocks Ivory Coast Zambia upset favorites Ivory Coast to win the Africa Cup of Nations Sunday night. The Copper Bullets won 8-7 in a penalty shootout after the game ended 0-0 after extra time. Goalkeeper Kennedy Mweene converted the decisive spot kick, sending his effort into the bottom corner before racing away to celebrate with his teammates. Ivory Coast missed three penalties during the shootout, with Gervinho and Kolo Toure both seeing their efforts saved and Didier Ya Konan firing wide. Zambian President Michael Sata was quick to congratulate the national team, who dedicated their victory to those killed in a plane crash in Gabon 19 years ago. "On behalf of the government and people of Zambia, I wish to congratulate our gallant soccer team for making history by becoming the new champions of Africa," Sata said. "This is no small achievement for any country, let alone a relatively small country like ours." Sata added: "We mourn with the families of those who perished in the Gabon disaster 19 years ago, and we also remember our great coach Godfrey Chitalu. May the souls of our departed heroes rest in peace." Zambia's success comes almost two decades since the entire Zambian team died when their plane crashed shortly after takeoff from Libreville airport en route to Dakar for a World Cup qualifier against Senegal. All 30 passengers and crew were killed, including 18 players and five officials. Meanwhile, Ivory Coast goalkeeper Boubacar Barry refused to blame his teammates for the loss. "What happened? We played very well, but we did not win. It's a shame," Barry said. "I'm sorry for my team-mates, especially those who couldn't convert their penalties." Sunday's final was the fourth consecutive time Ivory Coast has lost a major championship match, having failed to win the 2006 Africa Cup of Nations final against Egypt despite dominating the match and losing in the semifinals in 2008 and 2010. Barry said: "It hurts, but we have to accept it. That's sport. We have to move forward now."

Brazil is in a deep recession and political crisis, while protests marred the arrival of the Olympic torch in Rio on Wednesday. A New Zealand jiu-jitsu athlete claims he was kidnapped in Rio, while Chinese state media criticised security after women fencers were robbed and shooting team members found "unauthorised payments" on their credit cards. Brazil has drafted in 85,000 security personnel from 55 countries who will be stationed at the sport venues, Olympic Village, airports and main roads - almost twice as many as were at the 2012 London Olympics. There is also 200km of security fencing being used. More than 500,000 tourists are expected to come to the Games and organisers say more than one million of the 7.5 million tickets remain unsold. There have also been issues with the Olympic Village and the sailing venue. Australia initially refused to move into the village, in the Barra da Tijuca neighbourhood, citing electrical problems, gas and water leaks among other issues in their building. When they did eventually move in, the team were evacuated for a small fire and returned to their rooms to find essential equipment had been stolen. At the sailing venue in Guanabara Bay, a taskforce removed 25.4 tonnes of floating rubbish during last year's Olympic test event. But Rio officials admit they have failed to keep up promises to clean the water and the Associated Press says swallowing just three teaspoons of water from the bay is likely to lead to illness. This is not the first time a host city has been criticised for its preparations, but the IOC says Rio is now "ready to welcome the world". Brazil is at the centre of an outbreak of Zika virus, that is spread by mosquitoes and can lead to birth defects. It is so serious the World Health Organisation has recommended pregnant women avoid travelling to the Games - but mosquitoes are rare in August and in June it recommended the Games not be moved or cancelled. That advice has not stopped a number of the world's top golfers and tennis players withdrawing, citing Zika fears. Competitions will take place across 32 venues in Rio, with football matches also scheduled for the cities of Belo Horizonte, Brasilia, Manaus, Salvador and Sao Paulo. There are 306 events in 28 Olympic sports but none are bigger than the 100m sprint final and the world's fastest man Usain Bolt. The Jamaican is aiming for an unprecedented triple triple, as he tries to win the 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay titles for the third time - and his battle with American sprinter Justin Gatlin is likely to be a highlight of the Games. USA swimmer Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian of all time, will be looking to add to his 18 gold medals. American tennis player Serena Williams could win her fifth Olympic medal, while Team USA's star-studded basketball team will be aiming for their third consecutive gold.

To address these research questions, it is imperative to analyze the existing structures and dynamics within the Finnish energy retrofit marketplace, while also considering the sociocultural dimensions that influence household decisions regarding energy upgrades. Finland's unique geographical context poses both challenges and opportunities, particularly in terms of energy consumption patterns dictated by its cold climate and long winters. As households grapple with the dual pressures of rising energy costs and the need to mitigate carbon emissions, understanding the peculiarities of the market landscape becomes increasingly crucial. One significant aspect is the role of government initiatives and incentives aimed at catalyzing energy retrofitting. The Finnish government has implemented various policies that aim to lower the barriers to entry for homeowners considering retrofits. These include financial grants, tax incentives, and subsidies for energy-efficient technologies. However, the effectiveness of these initiatives can vary widely; often, potential adopters are either unaware of existing programs or find the application processes convoluted and time-consuming. Therefore, enhancing the visibility and accessibility of these schemes is not only a policy recommendation but a necessity to motivate households to engage in comprehensive energy retrofits. Moreover, the importance of knowledge dissemination cannot be overstated. Several studies highlight the critical gap in information as a barrier to adoption (Hyysalo et al., 2013). Households often feel overwhelmed by the myriad of technologies available and the complexity involved in choosing the most suitable options for their homes. Educational campaigns and community workshops focusing on energy literacy can empower residents with the knowledge required to make informed decisions, thus demystifying the retrofit process. Bringing in local actors, such as energy consultancies and educational institutions, to provide tailored advice could facilitate a more streamlined path toward comprehensive retrofitting. In addition to information sharing, the concept of social influence plays a pivotal role. The clustering of retrofitting activities within certain neighborhoods - often referred to as social proof - can create a ripple effect, whereby homeowners observe their neighbors opting for energy improvements and feel compelled to follow suit. Leveraging this phenomenon by fostering community engagement and showcasing successful retrofit projects can amplify the momentum necessary for wider adoption. This could involve creating platforms for shared experiences, enabling residents to discuss their journeys, challenges, and successes. Another key consideration is the interplay between technology and market dynamics. The rapid evolution of energy-efficient technologies presents both opportunities and challenges; while confronting the stability and longevity of emerging solutions, households may fear investing in technologies that quickly become outdated. As such, product evolution must be accompanied by robust warranties and after-sales support to nurture consumer confidence. It is essential to develop a responsive market ecosystem where manufacturers, installers, and service providers can guarantee not only high quality but also the longevity of their solutions. In examining the character and quality of energy retrofits specifically in Finland, it becomes clear that a multifaceted approach is required to create an interconnected, supportive environment conducive to comprehensive retrofitting. Hence, the integration of policy, outreach, community dynamics, and technology must culminate in a cohesive strategy that promotes not just the uptake of individual technologies but rather a holistic transformation of the residential energy landscape. As we consider how the Finnish market adapts to these evolving needs, the potential for significant contributions to national energy targets becomes increasingly apparent.

Parson Ives had been very handsome in his youth, and though worn by years (he was forty years older than his child), and by the grief of bereavement, he was yet famous for his good looks. Betty wore a short dark green riding-habit and a broad felt hat. She was as much at home on horseback as on foot, and seldom in the mornings wore a less business-like costume. The other two occupants of the coach were to ordinary eyes less interesting. Mistress Mary Jones was a faded woman, who had once been pretty, a spinster, a great friend of Betty's, and one of her father's parishioners. She was an excellent woman in her way, albeit somewhat given to terrors both real and fanciful. Her opposite neighbor was a man past the prime of life, owner and breeder of large herds of cattle near Wancote, a man who, after attending the Newbury markets, often returned home by this very coach, and was believed to carry large sums of money in the flap-pockets of his many-caped riding-coat. Mr. Barnes had a fixed mask-like countenance, his bushy eyebrows almost met in a wrinkle that told of thought and deep calculation. He was clean-shaven, and his chin was swathed in a huge neckcloth of white muslin; he wore his hat low on his brow. "I like not to be out so late on the high road," said he very suddenly, so that both Mr. Ives and Mistress Mary Jones started, and Betty, whom nothing ever startled, turned her great blue eyes inquiringly on him. "Why, sir?" she asked. "Why, my good young lady, because the Newbury sales are just over, and it is well known that the stock reared on Belford home farm has sold well" "Are the roads not safe then, sir?" asked Mr. Ives rather anxiously. "I do not quite say that, for it is many a long day since the coach was attacked between Newbury and Wancote; but rumour has been busy." "Ha!" cried Betty, sitting upright eagerly. "It is said that Wild Jack Barnstaple has been heard of in the neighbourhood." "Heaven help us!" shrieked Mary Jones. "Be calm, I entreat you, my dear madam, and have pity on my unfortunate toes! Zounds! it is torture enough to be subject to periodical gout, without such an infliction as the stamp of a lady's fashionable heel on the tender place." "But you say Wild Jack is in the neighbourhood! Oh Heaven! what will become of us!" Betty's blooming cheek had turned just a faint shade paler, but the rosy colour came rushing back, her eyes flashed. Suddenly stooping forward she said in a low voice: "Mr. Barnes, you may confide in me. Do you carry much money?" He answered in a tone of assumed ease, "Paper to the value of nearly a thousand pounds."

Le Glorieux paused mid-somersault, momentarily mesmerized by the Duchess's droning voice, which carried the weary weight of countless tales from a bygone era. Her stories, woven with threads of nostalgia and melancholy, painted pictures of grand banquets, opulent tapestries, and gallant knights who had once graced these very halls. Yet, while the duchess's voice rolled on, a different kind of music reached his ears-a melody of clattering hooves echoing in the cobblestone courtyard, the trumpeting heralds announcing the arrival of esteemed guests for Lady Clotilde's departure. The court jester's curiosity overcame decorum, and with a final, joyous handspring, he propelled himself towards the window. Careful to remain unseen by the dowager, Le Glorieux gently peeled back a corner of the heavy curtain. Through the gap, he watched as servants scurried about like ants, bustling with urgency; crates and satchels were being loaded into gilded carriages bearing the emblem of Brittany. Outside, the castle courtyard was a hive of activity. Horses snorted impatiently, knights adjusted their brightly polished armor, and groomsmen rushed, tending to last-minute preparations. It was a grand spectacle, but within its chaotic choreography, Le Glorieux sought a familiar face-Lady Clotilde herself. She was a vision of grace amidst the clamor, issuing instructions while maintaining the serene composure characteristic of nobility. Her deep auburn hair was secured beneath a delicate lace veil, and her sapphire gown shimmered in the autumn light, evoking an image of regal elegance. The jester's eyes sparkled with delight as he returned to the present moment, resolving to pay his respects to the Lady Clotilde before she departed the castle's embrace for the pursuits awaiting her in Brittany. For though she held no official title, her kindness was renowned, extending even to him-a mere fool. He felt a peculiar fondness for the lady, who had often been the audience for his antics, indulging him with mischievous glances and gentle laughter. He skittered through hidden passages and stairwells, taking pleasure in the castle's labyrinthine complexity. His destination was the grand entrance hall, where Lady Clotilde would surely pause before commencing her journey. At last, breathless yet exuberantly alive, he arrived just in time to see her stepping through the towering arched doorway. Catching sight of her, Le Glorieux beckoned with an exaggerated flourish, his every motion infused with exuberance. Lady Clotilde, spotting the familiar figure, graced him with a warm smile. A small congregation had gathered, drawn by the lively atmosphere, yet Clotilde's attention remained on the jester. "Noble Lady, I bid thee farewell," he intoned grandly, executing a dramatic bow. "May your voyage be as bright and fair as your spirit." She chuckled, a sound akin to silver bells softly chiming. "And may your days be filled with merriment, dear Glorieux. Look after our duchess, won't you?" With an impish wink, he promised to do so, attempting to mask the pang of sadness that her absence would bring. Then, with a playful twirl, Le Glorieux disappeared into the throng once more, blending into the tapestry of vibrant life that defined the castle on this brisk autumn day.

Notably, in all known structures of c-di-GMP-binding effector proteins or enzymes, the c-di-GMP is bound either as a monomer or intercalated dimer. Biophysical studies suggest the possibility of higher order oligomeric forms of c-di-GMP, but they have yet to be observed in any biological context (Gentner et al., 2012). While the roles played by c-di-GMP in controlling cellular processes in unicellular bacteria are becoming clear, the function(s) of c-di-GMP in multicellular, nonmotile bacteria such as Streptomyces are unknown. The complex Streptomyces life cycle involves two distinct filamentous cell forms: the growing or vegetative hyphae and the reproductive or aerial hyphae, which differentiate into exospores for dispersion through a massive synchronous septation event (Flardh and Buttner, 2009). In the model species Streptomyces venezuelae, there are three GGDEF proteins, two proteins with HD-GYP domains, and five proteins containing both a GGDEF and an EAL domain (Figure 1A). Altered expression of the GGDEF proteins, CdgA and CdgB, and deletions of the EAL proteins, RmdA and RmdB, have a significant impact on Streptomyces growth progression, suggesting that c-di-GMP plays a role in controlling developmental processes in multicellular bacteria (den Hengst et al., 2010; Tran et al., 2011; Hull et al., 2012). Interestingly, cdgA and cdgB have recently been identified as direct regulatory targets of the developmental master regulator BldD (den Hengst et al., 2010; Tran et al., 2011). Mutations in the bld loci block the formation of aerial hyphae, resulting in a "bald" phenotype, and also affect the production of antibiotics (McCormick and Flardh, 2012). BldD sits at the top of the regulatory cascade controlling development, serving to repress expression of sporulation genes during vegetative growth (den Hengst et al., 2010). In Streptomyces coelicolor, BldD controls the expression of at least 167 genes, including 42 genes ( 1/225% of the regulon) that encode regulatory proteins (Elliot et al., 2001; den Hengst et al., 2010). Among these BldD targets are many genes known to play critical roles in Streptomyces development, including other bld regulators (e.g., bldA, bldC, bldH/adpA, bldM, and bldN), several whi (white) regulators required for the differentiation of aerial hyphae into spores (e.g., whiG and whiB), and genes encoding critical components of the cell division and chromosome segregation machineries such as FtsZ, SsgA, SsgB, and the DNA translocase SffA (den Hengst et al., 2010; McCormick, 2009). How BldD activity is regulated, however, has been unknown. Here we show that BldD is a c-di-GMP-binding effector protein, thus revealing a link between c-di-GMP signaling and the development of multicellular bacteria. Specifically, structural and biochemical analyses show that the second messenger c-di-GMP activates BldD DNA binding by driving a unique form of dimerization that is mediated by a tetrameric form of c-di-GMP.

Citizen science has grown dramatically in popularity in the last two decades as a result of more projects being readily available for participants; technological advances such as data entry on portable devices allowing easier data collection and entry by non-experts; greater recognition that scientists can capitalize on citizen scientist availability and enthusiasm to increase capacity; increased research funding shortfalls; and the need to meet an outreach-related component (Dickinson et al., 2010; Silvertown, 2009). The social component of citizen science offers countless tangible and intangible benefits including facilitating behavior change towards environmental issues, developing long-term community-based conservation programs to benefit ecosystem services and habitats, increasing opportunities for adults and children to interact with nature, increasing scientific literacy, bridging communication gaps between scientists and researchers, and providing additional avenues to inform policy makers on conservation and environmental issues (Bell et al., 2008; Danielsen et al., 2005; Dickinson and Bonney, 2012; Kleinke et al., 2018; Schmeller et al., 2009; Schultz, 2011; Theobald et al., 2015; Trumbull et al., 2000). Data accuracy is one of the main concerns that scientists have with citizen science programs (Danielsen et al., 2005; Law et al., 2017), and several studies have assessed the quality of citizen science data in an attempt to comprehend the underlying problems and develop effective future protocols (Birkin and Goulson, 2015; Burgess et al., 2017; Callaghan et al., 2017; Kremen et al., 2011; McDonough MacKenzie et al., 2017; Rudisser et al., 2017). In general, the findings indicate a disparity between citizens' self-assessed and actual identification skills, suggesting the importance of evaluating this difference before launching data collection. However, the general consensus is that researchers do not yet fully understand the error potential in citizen science data possibly because data accuracy does not have a reliable definition and there are few consistent metrics on data accuracy (Dickinson et al., 2010). A study assessing citizen science journal articles revealed that only approximately half of the published articles reported having accurate data from citizen scientists but the studies examined did not necessarily define data accuracy (Aceves-Bueno et al., 2017). Burgess et al. (2017), while identifying broad barriers for publishing citizen science data, note that not all projects are suited for citizen scientists and such thoughts on suitability for citizens has also been reiterated by Kleinke et al. (2018) in their study on a pollination services project. Some of the suggested barriers include insufficient awareness among scientists about projects suitable for citizen science, data quality inconsistency, bias among scientists for certain data sources (such as age and educational levels of citizen scientists) and the extent of time commitment required by the project. Given the importance of pollinators, there are a few well-known citizen science projects, including the Great Sunflower Project (Domroese and Johnson, 2017), Pollination Investigators (Kleinke et al., 2018) and the Urban Pollination Project (Potter and LeBuhn, 2015).

"A child - is she only a child?" The trumpets sounded, the practice was resumed; this time, fortunately, no command, no responsibility. The four batteries executed their evolutions together; this immense mass of men, horses, and carriages, deployed in every direction, now drawn out in a long line, again collected into a compact group. All stopped at the same instant along the whole extent of the ground; the gunners sprang from their horses, ran to their pieces, detached each from its team, which went off at a trot and prepared to fire with amazing rapidity. Then the horses returned, the men re-attached their pieces; sprang quickly to saddle, and the regiment started at full gallop across the field. Very gently in the thoughts of Jean Bettina regained her advantage over Mrs. Scott. She appeared to him smiling and blushing amid the sunlit clouds of her floating hair. Monsieur Jean, she had called him, Monsieur Jean, and never had his name sounded so sweet. And that last pressure of the hand on taking leave, before entering the carriage. Had not Miss Percival given him a more cordial clasp than Mrs. Scott had done? Yes, positively a little more. "I was mistaken," thought Jean; "the prettier is Miss Percival." The day's work was finished; the pieces were ranged regularly in line one behind the other; they defiled rapidly, with a horrible clatter, and in a cloud of dust. When Jean, sword in hand, passed before his Colonel, the images of the two sisters were so confused and intermingled in his recollection that they melted the one in the other, and became in some measure the image of one and the same person. Any parallel became impossible between them, thanks to this singular confusion of the two points of comparison. Mrs. Scott and Miss Percival remained thus inseparable in the thoughts of Jean until the day when it was granted to him to see them again. The impression of that meeting was not effaced; it was always there, persistent, and very sweet, till Jean began to feel disturbed. "Is it possible" - so ran his meditations - "is it possible that I have been guilty of the folly of falling in love madly at first sight? No; one might fall in love with a woman, but not with two women at once." That thought reassured him. He was very young, this great fellow of four-and-twenty; never had love entered fully into his heart. Love! He knew very little about it, except from books, and he had read but few of them.

The Roe and Doe rulings affected laws in 46 states. For the justices, Roe reflected earlier cases involving the right to privacy. That "right," wrote Justice Harry Blackmun in the main opinion for the court, is "broad enough to encompass a woman's decision whether or not to terminate her pregnancy." But the ruling was a qualified one, and that fact has been used by abortion opponents in their efforts to narrow the scope of other abortion provisions. Blackmun noted that the state's "important interests in safeguarding health, maintaining medical standards, and protecting potential life" are compelling enough to justify regulation "at some point in pregnancy." That "qualified right" found its form in the controversial "trimester analysis" laid out by the justices in Roe: permitting no government regulation during the first three months of a pregnancy; allowing limited regulation in the second trimester to protect the woman's health and safety; and granting government the power to ban abortions during the third trimester - a time when, medical consensus has concluded, the fetus is capable of living on its own. That reasoning has outraged abortion opponents and puzzled many legal scholars. "The better argument for the result reached in Roe v. Wade," said Edward Lazarus - a former law clerk for Blackmun and an author of "Closed Chambers: The Rise, Fall, and Future of the Modern Supreme Court" - "is that it's necessary for the equality of women, rather than grounding it in the privacy right." After Roe, the high court affirmed the right to abortion in subsequent cases: striking down provisions requiring a husband's consent for a first-trimester abortion; requiring parental consent for an unmarried woman under 18; striking down efforts to expand on laws requiring women to give informed consent before having an abortion; striking down a 24-hour waiting period; and striking down a law requiring doctors to inform women of the risks and of assistance available if she were to carry the fetus to term. Remote sensing datasets like MODIS and Landsat can play pivotal roles in conjunction with advanced machine learning algorithms, enabling the creation of robust models to predict canopy height across vast and inaccessible Arctic landscapes. A key prerequisite for effective model development is the establishment of a reliable ground truth dataset, representative of diverse Arctic ecosystems. As such, efforts to compile and standardize in situ vegetation measurements, integrated with remote sensing data, are essential for calibrating and validating these predictive models. Existing databases, while helpful, often lack the granularity needed to dissect the complexities of Arctic vegetation dynamics thoroughly (Raynolds et al., 2019). Furthermore, a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between vegetation height, biomass, and climatic factors is crucial for accurately modeling changes over time. The Arctic is experiencing a rapid climatic shift, with consequences that ripple through the ecosystem. Higher temperatures are facilitating the northward advance of shrubs, prompting changes in community composition and ecosystem function (Tape et al., 2006; Elmendorf et al., 2012). It is often observed that taller shrubs can outcompete lower-growing species for light and space, potentially altering the successional pathways of these ecosystems (Gough et al., 2013). This dynamic warrants close monitoring and further investigation, emphasizing the need for a unified approach to biodiversity assessments that incorporates both ground and airborne observations. Integrating community ecology with remote sensing technology not only empowers researchers to create a clearer picture of current vegetation states but also aids in prognosis for future shifts. For example, by examining changes in shrub dominance and canopy height, we can infer potential impacts on permafrost stability due to altered snow accumulation patterns and subsequent thermal regimes. This is crucial, as permafrost thaw can lead to significant carbon release, creating feedback loops that exacerbate climate change (Vickers et al., 2018). Improvements in the temporal resolution of remote sensing platforms, such as the advent of high-resolution satellite systems, present significant opportunities to monitor seasonal and interannual variability in tundra vegetation more adeptly. By examining NDVI time series, it is possible to unravel patterns of shrub growth in response to environmental conditions, providing insights into how interdependent biophysical processes evolve over time. Moreover, correlating NDVI with climate data offers the chance to explore packing density and biomass in relation to moisture conditions, further refining our models of vegetation-hydrology interactions (McGuire et al., 2012). As remote sensing techniques continue to advance, the integration of socio-economic considerations cannot be overlooked. Communities dependent on traditional Arctic knowledge can provide invaluable perspectives to enhance our understanding of land cover changes and their implications for local ecosystems and livelihoods. Engaging with Indigenous peoples and incorporating traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) into scientific assessments may improve our grasp of plant community dynamics and their response to climate variability. Such collaborative approaches hold immense potential to foster adaptive management strategies aimed at sustaining not only Arctic habitats but also the cultural and economic frameworks of communities that thrive within these shifting landscapes. Ultimately, the challenges posed by climate change on Arctic tundra vegetation demand innovative and comprehensive methods to monitor and analyze canopy height and associated ecological shifts. A multidisciplinary framework that marries advanced technology with empirical ecological research will equip scientists and policymakers alike with the knowledge necessary to confront these pressing environmental issues effectively.

The European iron and steel industry's reliance on fossil fuels is a significant contributor to its high carbon footprint, with the majority of its CO2 emissions coming from the 30 integrated steel plants that produce 60% of the European steel output. The blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) route, which is the dominant method of steel production, is particularly emissions-intensive, generating two and a half times more emissions per tonne of crude steel produced compared to scrap recycling. As the steel scrap recycling rate is not sufficient to meet the increasing demand for steel, ore-based steel production is expected to remain dominant until at least 2050. To achieve the EU's emission reduction targets for 2020, 2030, and 2050, the 30 integrated steel plants will need to implement breakthrough technologies for CO2 emission abatement. Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is a key technology that can contribute significantly to deep emission cuts in this industry. A hybrid approach that combines CCS with biomass (bio-CCS) could provide even further emission reductions. However, the average 2017 price of European emission allowances of 5.80 tCO2-1 and the absence of bio-CCS specific incentives make its application in Europe unrealistic for the moment. Despite this, the likely overshoot of the remaining CO2 budget for limiting global warming to below 2 C, in combination with the slow transition to low-carbon iron and steel making technologies, is increasing the need for the deployment of significant CO2 emission reduction measures like bio-CCS in Europe in the near future. Bio-CCS offers a way to generate energy that is carbon neutral/negative, making it suitable for co-application during energy conversion or with energy-intensive industrial processes. Scenarios for the decarbonization of the iron and steel industry generally involve CCS, either on its own or in combination with a top gas recycling blast furnace process. However, due to the technical role that fossil fuels play in the iron ore reduction process, only a limited biomass substitution is feasible. Therefore, additional measures such as bio-CCS deployment would be needed to achieve high levels of CO2 reduction across an integrated steel plant. The use of bio-CCS in the iron and steel industry could also provide a way to generate negative emissions, which would be essential for compensating for CO2 emissions from sectors that may have a hard time reaching carbon-neutrality, such as agriculture, aviation, or industry. The key role of negative emission technologies is to generate negative emissions that would compensate for CO2 emissions from sectors that may have a hard time reaching carbon-neutrality.

Next came the vassals who held land in consideration of their personal service in war. They were the baron's body guard, and his chief dependence for aid when attacked by his enemies. After these were ranged the vassals who held land by the tenure of husbandry. Their services consisted in ploughing and sowing the demesne lands, making hay, reaping corn, mowing meadows, &c.; and they were considered inferior to the military tenants. These again were succeeded by the cottagers, who held small portions of land by doing certain works, such as carrying letters, acting as messengers, carting wood, &c., and who were accounted lowest of all. The peasants, however, who had no land, were not permitted to attend this court, but received their orders through the bailiff. The ceremony commenced by the reading of the charter of enfeoffment, which was done by the clerk of the court. The charter contained the conditions upon which the lands were granted, and the services required in return. When this was concluded, the various classes of vassals advanced before the steward, and swore fealty to their lord, and did homage to him, according to their respective tenures. Some, kneeling down, put their hands between those of the steward, and swore allegiance to their liege lord. Others performed the same ceremony to the esquire, and others again to the bailiff. All the feudal services were thus renewed, and the rights of the lord secured. At the conclusion of this ceremony, the vassals returned to their places, and the esquires, pages, and domestics, who had been waiting in the lower end of the hall, were summoned to perform their duties. These were the servants of the household, who had no interest in the soil, and whose occupations were confined to domestic affairs. They were divided into three classes - officers, servants, and labourers. The first class consisted of the seneschal or steward, the chamberlain, the constable, the marshal, the porter, the chaplains, the physician, the almoner, the knights, and squires of honour. The second class comprehended the carvers, cupbearers, sewers, ushers, marshals of the hall, pantlers, butlers, cooks, bakers, brewers, cellarers, yeomen of the chamber, grooms of the chamber, pages, huntsmen, falconers, farriers, minstrels, and clerks. The third class comprised the valets, kitchen boys, scullions, grooms of the stables, carters, sumptermen, gardeners, and the like. These also renewed their engagements, and were admitted to serve in their respective capacities during the will of the master of the house. The court being ended, the steward gave notice to the assembled multitude, that the lord of Sudley would hold open house for one week, at which time he expected all his friends to do him the honour of calling upon him. He then ordered the gates to be thrown open, and invited all to enter, and partake of the hospitality of the castle. The invitation was gladly accepted, and every one pressed forward to gratify his curiosity, and feast his eyes with the splendour of the interior. It was about noon when the multitude entered the great hall, where tables were laid out for their entertainment. On the elevated part of the floor, a table was spread for the use of the baron, his family, and principal guests. The steward sat at the upper end, and the esquire at the lower.

To the right, a snug chamber suggested itself as the reading nook, furnished with well-worn armchairs that invited a languorous retreat into the pages of some long-forgotten tome. Somewhere in the labyrinth of literature, a record player softly crooned an old jazz standard, its velvet notes weaving seamlessly with the susurrus of turning pages. It was then that the proprietor, R. Mifflin himself, emerged from a fog of tobacco smoke, an enigmatic figure with twinkling eyes and a beard as untidy as the sprawling stacks. He approached with the leisurely gait of one accustomed to the unhurried tempo of the bookshop life. "Good evening," he greeted, his voice carrying the warmth of one who truly cherished his domain. "It seems you've found your way to our haunted refuge." "I have," replied the young man, grinning at the proprietor's use of the word 'haunted.' "Though I must say, it's a pleasant kind of haunting." "Indeed," Mifflin chuckled, a sound like the creak of a well-loved binding. "A ghost or two of literary genius never fails to enrich the atmosphere. "There's something romantic about the idea of just stumbling upon the right book." Mifflin nodded sagely, "Ah, serendipity is a fine guide. Just remember, if you find yourself in a quandary, I'm never far from the thickest smoke." With a nod of thanks, the visitor ventured further into the shop's recesses, each alcove revealing new literary delights. He paused at a section dedicated to adventure stories, his eyes dancing over titles that promised daring exploits and faraway lands. It occurred to him that the world outside-wet, cold, and indifferent-seemed a distant reality here amid the quiet companionship of books. In a cozy alcove at the rear of the shop, an old wooden desk had been transformed into a makeshift tea station, complete with steaming kettle and chipped porcelain mugs. Nearby, a ragtag assortment of books on herbal lore and forgotten brews looked on approvingly. He poured himself a cup, savoring the earthy aroma that mingled with the ever-present tobacco smoke, creating an olfactory tapestry as complex as any story. As he took a sip and gazed around, he couldn't shake the feeling that he was on the brink of discovery-not just of a book, but of a world unseen, an unfolding narrative of which he was now a part. Here, within the walls of Parnassus at Home, the spectral whisper of past readers and stories lingered, promising adventures yet untold. The young man felt an unfamiliar thrill-a sense that, in losing himself among these shelves, he might find something truly extraordinary.

I felt like a child in an adult world where everything seemed alien and confusing. I wanted my parents. I had no idea why they werent there, I just wanted them to be there. They came each day and held my hand, but I wanted to go home. The next few days were spent in my room watching the clock tick away towards discharge. I tried to read but the pain prevented me. I tried to sleep but the pain prevented me. It was clear that whatever was wrong with me was serious. My family were told to prepare themselves for the worst. The worst was something I did not want to hear. The doctors didnt seem too sure either. This was a new case, the symptoms were similar to a condition called pericarditis but the severity was different. Pericarditis is inflammation of the membrane surrounding the heart. There are many causes of pericarditis including infection, autoimmune diseases, drugs, trauma and cancer. It is also thought to be caused by stress, which seems ironic given that mine was due to stress. My symptoms were similar to those who suffer from this condition but the fact that I had been admitted to hospital twice previously with this symptom made it difficult to diagnose. Fluid around the heart and lungs is known as pleural effusion. Effusions can occur with other conditions such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, malignancy and bacterial infections. I had none of these. The only conclusion reached after extensive testing was that I had developed a viral infection. A virus, a simple virus that was causing me so much pain. Why had I not caught a cold before? I remember being shocked at the news, but relieved. Relieved that I might actually get better soon. I went home with instructions to rest and take paracetamol for any pain. I slept all weekend, feeling the effects of the steroids they had injected into my spine. The following Monday I returned to college. I sat in class, nodding off every five minutes, I missed lectures, I missed classes, I missed deadlines. I was too tired to function properly. I was unable to concentrate, I was depressed. I didnt care anymore. I just wanted to go back to bed. I fell asleep during tutorials and lectures. My mind was in a fog, my body was weak. I went to the doctor and asked him if he could give me some sort of sleeping pill. He said that I needed to stop taking the steroids, that they would make me feel worse in the long run. He gave me some valium instead. Valium, I had heard of it before. I imagined it to be a magic pill that would allow me to fall asleep without having to endure the agony of lying awake. I took the pill and waited. It worked, I finally got some rest. I still felt drained though, I wasnt myself. I was falling behind with my essays and assignments. I couldnt focus. I felt lost, confused, overwhelmed. I wasnt coping. I went back to the doctor. He referred me to a psychologist. I didn't know what that meant exactly. Was she going to talk to me about my problems? Would she be able to help? What would she say? I was nervous. I imagined her sitting across from me in a room with a desk and a chair. She would ask me questions, then tell me what was wrong with me. She would give me advice, and tell me how to fix it. I would walk out of that room cured. Or maybe I would walk out of that room with a diagnosis. I wasnt sure which option I preferred. She flew to Hong Kong last Sunday to help Snowden, and accompanied him on Monday on his flight to Moscow, where she continues to advise him. Sarah's parents are said to be 'very proud' of her for taking on such a high-profile role. A friend of the couple told me yesterday: 'They're very supportive of her work.' Sarah, who graduated from Oxford University in modern languages, has spent much of her adult life abroad, but returns frequently to visit her parents. In recent years she has been based in Germany, where she worked for a time in Berlin as a translator and editor for the German Institute for International and Security Affairs. She met Assange when he visited Berlin in December 2009 to give a talk about whistleblowing. After the event, they went out together for dinner and drinks. She became part of his inner circle, travelling to Iceland with him, where he began working with local activists on a video exposing U.S. military action in Iraq. Sarah is believed to have helped edit the footage, which showed two American helicopters shooting at civilians, including journalists. It was released online in April 2010 under the title Collateral Murder. As the pair grew closer, Sarah moved back to Britain, living first in London before moving to Norfolk, where she worked as an unpaid volunteer for WikiLeaks. By then, she had become one of Assange's closest confidantes, and was often seen at his side. In September 2011, Assange invited her to join him at Ellingham Hall, a Georgian mansion near Bungay, Suffolk, rented for him by Vaughan Smith, owner of the Frontline Club, a private members' club for journalists in London's Paddington. Assange was living under house arrest pending possible extradition to Sweden to face sexual assault allegations. At the time, Sarah denied they were romantically involved, insisting: 'We are just friends.' But her mother let slip to a neighbour that Sarah was Assange's girlfriend. She added that she hoped the relationship would survive. Asked if she knew what was happening to her daughter in Moscow this week, Mrs Harrison replied: 'I am afraid I don't know anything about it.' Mr Harrison declined to comment. Neighbours say they are typical of their generation, keeping themselves to themselves and never gossiping about their famous son-in-law or his legal battles. Their daughter has kept a similarly low profile until now. One friend, who asked not to be named, described her as 'quiet and shy', adding: 'She's always been interested in politics and human rights issues.' Another acquaintance said: 'Sarah's a good egg. She's got a good heart and is very intelligent. She wants to make the world a better place.' Despite her closeness to Assange, Sarah has always avoided the limelight, saying little publicly about him or her role within WikiLeaks. However, she did write a letter to the Daily Telegraph defending the website against claims that it endangered lives by publishing secret documents. Her only other known public statement came in January 2011, when she issued a message on Twitter urging supporters to donate money to WikiLeaks. Since then, she has slipped off the radar, although some reports suggest she may still live with Assange at the Ecuadorean embassy in Knightsbridge, where he has been staying since June 19 last year. This week, however, she was thrust into the spotlight by her association with Snowden, who is wanted by the FBI for leaking top-secret information. She was pictured boarding the plane in Hong Kong, wearing sunglasses and carrying a brown leather handbag. On arrival in Moscow, she tried to keep a low profile, hiding behind a pillar as she waited for Snowden to emerge from the aircraft.
