This ongoing debate highlights the complexity of semantic memory organization within the brain, as researchers strive to delineate the cognitive functions attributed to the left and right ventral temporal lobes. The dichotomy becomes particularly salient when examining the nature of conceptual knowledge as mediated by these regions. Traditional models often posit the left ventral temporal lobe (lvTL) as central to language-related semantic processing, while the right ventral temporal lobe (rvTL) is thought to be more involved in the perception of visual and emotional aspects of semantic knowledge (Lambon Ralph et al., 2009; Wright et al., 2017). However, the reality is considerably more nuanced, as evidenced by the clinical presentations of SD that reveal both interindividual variability and overlapping cognitive deficits. For instance, in L > R cases, the profound anomia observed is indicative of the stringent reliance on the lvTL for lexical retrieval, wherein patients struggle to name objects or perform verbal tasks that presuppose a robust semantic network. Furthermore, the lexical-semantic deficits manifest in a plethora of semantic categories, suggesting that the lvTL is not solely responsible for linguistic constructs but rather plays a critical role in encompassing a broader spectrum of conceptual knowledge (Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006). In stark contrast, R > L patients exhibit a diminishment in facial recognition capabilities, illuminating the rvTL's role in integrating social and emotional cues intrinsic to comprehending semantic meanings related to people and their interactions. The right hemisphere's contribution to these facets of memory cannot be undervalued as it offers insights into how emotional associations and contextual factors influence semantic retrieval. Intriguingly, the existence of these asymmetrical atrophy patterns in SD not only elucidates the specialized functions of each temporal lobe but also raises essential questions regarding the interconnectivity between these regions in healthy individuals. The apparent disjunction in semantic processing may signify a division of labor, wherein the lvTL engages in the linguistic aspects of semantics, while the rvTL engages in processing more holistic or contextual elements. This characterization posits a collaborative model of semantic processing in which the seamless integration of information across both lobes is essential. Moreover, the cognitive disarray triggered by asymmetric brain atrophy in SD presents a unique opportunity to study the dynamic interplay of neural circuits involved in semantic knowledge storage and retrieval. Functional imaging studies in healthy individuals, paired with longitudinal observations of SD patients, could provide deeper insights into the interactions between the lvTL and rvTL, as well as their contribution to the overarching neural network that encompasses semantic cognition. Investigators may employ advanced neuroimaging techniques, such as diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), to assess white matter integrity connecting these lobes, thus enabling a clearer picture of how structural changes influence functional outcomes. Preliminary findings from such studies suggest that individuals with robust connections between the lobe exhibit improved performance on semantic tasks, highlighting that the integrity of these neural pathways is critical for optimal cognitive function (Patterson et al., 2007). Ultimately, understanding the nature of semantic dementia not only offers a window into the specific vulnerabilities of our cognitive architecture but also sheds light on broader paradigms of cognition and memory disruption. In pursuit of this elucidation, ongoing research continues to navigate the intricacies of how brain pathology can disrupt established cognitive frameworks, offering new vistas for understanding cognition in both health and disease. Each discovery propels us closer to a comprehensive understanding of the neural substratum of conceptual knowledge, shedding light on the multifaceted interactions that characterize our cognitive landscapes.

As the nature of international trade evolves, the debate around economic unions has become increasingly entangled with concerns about income inequality, job security, and cultural identity. The rise of global value chains has led to a growing sense of disconnection between the winners and losers of globalization, with many workers in traditional manufacturing industries feeling left behind. The shift towards service-oriented economies has also created new challenges, as the benefits of trade are often concentrated among high-skilled professionals, while low-skilled workers face increased competition from automation and outsourcing. The growing importance of regulatory harmonization has also raised concerns about the erosion of national sovereignty and the influence of multinational corporations on policy-making. In general, a good summary must be able to represent the core idea, and effectively convey the meaning of the source (Zhuge, 2015). In this paper, we aim to understand what this means in a data context: what a dataset summary must capture in order to help data practitioners select the data to work with more confidence. This is currently a gap in the human data interaction literature. The data engineering community, on the other hand, has created some standards and best practices for publishing and sharing data, including DCAT,3 schema.org,4 and SharePSI)5). However, none of these initiatives offer any guidance on what to include in a dataset summary. Sometimes text summaries are generated automatically using so-called natural language generation (NLG) methods. These methods are commonly bootstrapped via parallel corpora of data and text snippets, but an extensive exploration of the qualities of these training corpora is missing (Wiseman et al., 2017). Overall, this leads to summaries that vary greatly in terms of content, language and level of detail, which are often not fit for purpose (Koesten et al., 2017; Neumaier et al., 2016). We have undertaken two complementary studies in dataset selection and summarisation. Both studies build on previous research of ours from Koesten et al. (2017). In that work, we have reported on the results of a series of interviews with 20 data practitioners, which have helped us define a general framework for dataset search, built around the three themes mentioned earlier: relevance, usability and quality. The first study presented in this paper takes the next step: we analysed 69 data-search diaries by students who were asked to document in detail how they go about finding and selecting datasets. The students wrote 269 diaries, which we analysed qualitatively starting from the framework from Koesten et al. (2017). This resulted in a list of dataset selection attributes. In the second study, we carried out lab and crowdsourcing experiments with overall 80 data-literate participants, who created a total of 360 summaries for 25 datasets. We analysed the summaries thematically to derive common structures in their composition, which led to a list of dataset summary attributes. We grouped these attributes into four main types of information: (i) basic metadata such as format and descriptive statistics; (ii) dataset content, including major topic categories, as well as geospatial and temporal aspects; (iii) quality statements, including uncertainty; and (iv) analyses and usage ideas, such as trends observed in the data. We found a core set of attributes that were consistently prevalent in the two studies, across different datasets and participants. We used them to define a template to design more meaningful textual representations of data, which resonate with what people consider relevant when describing a dataset to others, and when trying to make sense of a dataset they have not used before. Our summary template is primarily meant as a tool for data publishers, but also for data scientists and engineers.

The diversity of C/EBP isoforms is further increased by numerous PTMs of amino acid side chains; in addition to phosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues, lysine acetylation and methylation also occurs, as does methylation of arginine. Enzymes responsible for PTM of C/EBP include CARM1/PRMT4, G9A/EHMT2, and CREBBP/KAT3A, all of which also serve as epigenetic histone code writers. The decoration of C/EBP by PTM alters its capacity to engage in protein-protein interactions (PPI) and to direct cell fate, suggesting that the signal-dependent C/EBP modification index reflects integration of various upstream signaling events to adjust its interactome and to determine its gene regulatory and epigenetic capacity (Leutz et al., 2011). The combination of translational modifications and PTMs may thus encrypt the dynamic interactome, with C/EBP being the keystone for a wide range of functional outcomes (Lee et al., 2010b; Sebastian et al., 2005; Sterneck et al., 1997; Stoilova et al., 2013). The C-terminal third of C/EBP,,, e contains highly conserved DNA-binding and bZip domains that may dimerize within an extended trans-regulatory bZip network including C/EBP, AP-1, and ATF transcription factors. The N-terminal two-thirds region of the C/EBP primary structure is predicted as an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Miller, 2006). Phylogenetic analysis, nevertheless, suggests that the C/EBP N terminus also contains several highly conserved short peptide regions (CRs) that are enriched in amino acids with hydrophobic and bulky side chains. These CRs are discontinuous and separated by less conserved and family-specific regions of low complexity characterized by a predominance of small and polar amino acids (Leutz et al., 2011; Tsukada et al., 2011). Experimental studies involving a large number of deletions and CR/IDR shuffling mutants suggested a highly modular, context-dependent functionality of N-terminal C/EBP CRs (Kowenz-Leutz et al., 1994; Lee et al., 2010b; Leutz et al., 2011; Williams et al., 1995). Screening for interaction partners using N-terminally derived C/EBP peptides further supports the notion that many C/EBP interactions may occur in a modular and dynamic fashion that relies on molecular recognition features (MoRFs) and short linear peptide motifs (SLiMs) in combination with adjacent PTMs (Dunker et al., 1998; Leutz et al., 2011; Tompa et al., 2014; van der Lee et al., 2014; Wright and Dyson, 1999). Based on previous observations of the modular structure and biological functionality of C/EBP peptide regions, we developed a novel technique to systematically explore the C/EBP interactome. Briefly, C/EBP was deconstructed into small linear peptides of 14 amino acids immobilized on a solid-phase matrix. The starting point for each peptide was shifted by four amino acids, creating a tiled peptide array covering the entire amino acid sequence of C/EBP. PTM-containing peptides were included according to recorded modifications and their position in the primary C/EBP structure.

The Benders' method of operation was simple. When unsuspecting visitors stopped at the cabin, they would sit them down and serve them food at a table. Then either Ma or Kate would distract them, usually by offering another serving of food. While the victim's head was turned, John Jr. or Pa would strike them with a hammer. The blow wouldn't kill the person, but stun them enough to make them easy prey for a quick slash across the throat with a knife. The body was then dropped through a trap door into the cellar where it was later stripped and buried somewhere on the property. Most of the bodies were found buried in a long trench near the orchard. Others were discovered buried in the garden, which was always freshly tilled but never produced any crops. After the killings, the Benders would take whatever money and goods the dead possessed and sell them in towns nearby. One victim, Dr William York, disappeared after leaving Independence, Kansas, to visit his brother in Fort Scott. His brother organized search parties and offered rewards for information leading to his whereabouts. Two months later, York's abandoned wagon was found in Drum Creek Township. Several days later, York's brother received a letter allegedly written by York saying he was in St Louis and needed money. Suspicious, the brother asked local storekeepers if anyone had recently purchased supplies that matched those missing from his brother's wagon. He was told that two men fitting the description of John Jr. and Pa Bender had bought such items. After learning this, the brother returned home and began organizing a group of vigilantes to investigate the Benders. On May 5, 1873, the vigilante party arrived at the Bender cabin to find it empty except for an eerie rocking chair still moving slightly. They searched the grounds and found what appeared to be bloodstains on the porch. Using the handle of a broken shovel, they probed the soft soil in the garden until they felt resistance. Digging further, they uncovered human remains. By the end of the day, eight more bodies were unearthed. All bore similar injuries. The vigilantes tracked the Benders down and caught up with them near the town of Thayer. Legend has it that the gang escaped after a gunfight with the posse. According to other accounts, the vigilantes killed four people resembling the Benders, and assuming they were the fugitives, left the bodies unburied. However, none of the bodies was ever positively identified as being members of the murderous family. The Bender family was never seen again and nobody knows for sure what happened to them.

Its fate would hinge upon the intricate web of trust that underpins the entire financial system. Trust - that delicate yet indispensable currency - would be shaken to its core. A failing bank, perceived as unable to meet its obligations, could catalyze an avalanche of fear that spreads like wildfire through the markets. Suddenly, depositors, investors, and other banks would reassess their positions and their relationships, choosing caution over confidence. In this environment, every whisper could become a shout, every rumor a harbinger of doom. But let us not lose sight of the broader picture. The dynamic between banks and depositors is merely a symptom of a far larger organism: the economy itself. As the gears of this machine grind together, they are lubricated by the very money that flows through our hands, banks acting as intermediaries in a game of systemic trust and borrowed hope. We are all complicit in this grand ballet, each transaction a step, each investment a move in the intricate choreography of finance. Yet, consider the implications of this dance. The very act of lending and borrowing intertwines our fates, making us, in a sense, codependent. If a bank falters, its reach extends into the savings of everyday individuals, the mortgages of families, and the working capital of businesses. A financial crisis, therefore, transforms from a single institution's failure into a contagion that can sweep through an entire economy, unraveling livelihoods and eroding trust. The interconnectedness that makes our system efficient also makes it precariously fragile. Take, for example, the tale of Lehman Brothers, which once towered as a titan in investment banking. Its collapse in 2008 sent shockwaves far beyond Wall Street, triggering a global financial crisis that spiraled through the lofty towers of the financial elite and into the homes of the working poor. The fallout was catastrophic; millions lost their jobs, homes, and sense of security. The reverberations of that singular event underscored how fragile the edifice of trust really is. In the aftermath, governments scrambled to intervene. Fiscal policies were concocted, and multitrillion-dollar bailouts were authorized with the urgency of a fire brigade responding to a conflagration. Central banks slashed interest rates and injected liquidity into the banking system. The lesson was clear: while banks play a pivotal role in the economic continuum, they are also the potential harbingers of chaos. Our collective reliance on them is a Faustian bargain, the promise of prosperity tethered to the specter of ruin. So, what of the individuals caught in this web? The ordinary people who simply wish to save, invest, and provide for their families? Is their financial future always dependent on the whims of these sprawling institutions? The answer is complicated. Yes, we must interact with banks and financial systems, but we also wield the power of choice. As depositors, we have the ability to seek out credit unions or community banks, institutions less likely to engage in the reckless behaviors that can lead to ruin. It is, after all, our hard-earned money at stake, and the more we understand the mechanics of the system, the better equipped we are to navigate its treacherous waters. Thus, informed citizens can advocate for greater regulation, demanding transparency and accountability from those who hold the keys to our economic safety. Education becomes our shield against misinformation and fear. By understanding the vulnerabilities inherent in banking, we can forge a financial future that prioritizes stability over speculation and security over blind trust. In this way, we lend strength not just to our own accounts but to the very economy that sustains us. And perhaps, in doing so, we can mitigate the inherent fragility that lies in every bank's vault.

Col Shaw, who had served in Bosnia and Kosovo, had been evacuated from the first Gulf War in 1991 suffering acute stress having exacerbated a pre-existing depression and spent time recuperating in hospital. The inquest heard evidence from Major William Common, who was critical of the workload placed upon Col Shaw. He said he had first met Col Shaw in July 2010 when he was posted to Warminster to take over from him as deputy commander. Lieutenant Colonel Robert Shaw was commander of the Warminster Garrison in Wiltshire. 'I worked reasonably closely with Robert Shaw who I found to be a thoroughly decent, approachable, genial, charming man,' Maj Common said. 'We spoke almost every day and on occasions would have wide-ranging discussions about life in general and family. 'I understood Robert Shaw to be a reasonably happy person but I was aware of difficulties with both his mother and mother-in-law, who appeared to be particularly demanding. 'It was clear to me that Robert found it difficult to meet the competing demands of his role as CO and deputy garrison commander. 'He always worked a full day and was often still in his office when I left yet he seemed to find it hard to programme routine activities like writing timely appraisal reports of his civilian and military staff. 'His grasp of the critical garrison-wide PFI contract, Project Allenby/Connaught, was never more than minimal.' Major Common added: 'Fundamentally Robert Shaw was a decent officer who I was proud to serve with but was of limited ability.' He said that the supporting staff posts were left vacant and the arrival of Colonel Peter Merriman as commander of Warminster Garrison in 2011 saw an increase in Col Shaw's workload. Maj Common said Col Merriman was 'determined' to set up a new officers' training course and build a new larger gymnasium. Maj Common said his last meeting with Col Shaw was on May 21 when he was shocked by his appearance. 'Robert was standing over his desk pouring over some papers. He looked tired and depressed and would neither meet my gaze or engage in conversation,' he said. 'I was shocked by his demeanour as in our three years he had always been open, friendly and welcome. He seemed to me to be on the verge of a nervous breakdown.' 'It was completely unfair and totally unreasonable to expect Robert Shaw to provide unit level support services, including meeting additional demands, without adequate staff' Major William Common. It was not at the mountains nor at the river that Bessie Andrews looked, but at the grimy cabins of the miners, scattered along the hillside, and she thought with a sigh how little successful she had been in winning the hearts of their occupants. She had come from Richmond in a flush of happiness at her good fortune in getting the school, and determined to make a success of it, but she found it "uphill work" indeed. Her story was that of so many other Southern girls coming of families old and one time wealthy, but ruined by the Civil War. The father, who had gone forth to battle in the strength of his young manhood, left his right arm on the bloody field at Gettysburg, and came home, at last, to find himself quite ruined. He could get no laborers to cultivate his fields, rank with the weeds of four years' neglect; his stock had been seized by one or other of the armies, for both had fought back and forth across his land, with a necessity of need that knew no law; his people had been freed, and, excepting two or three of the older house-servants who had grown gray in the family's service, had drifted away no one knew whither. For three years he struggled to bring order out of this desolation, but the task was greater than his strength. So the plantation was sold for a mere fraction of its worth before the war, and the family had moved to Richmond, in the hope that life there would be easier. There, ten years after the city fell before Grant's army, Bessie Andrews was born; and there, some twelve years later, her father died, gray before his time, bowed down with care, so broken by his grim battle with the world that disease found him an easy victim. So Bessie Andrews had never known the luxury and kindliness and easy hospitality of the old plantation life, but its influences and traditions lived still in her blood. She was a gentlewoman, with all a gentlewoman's shrinking from the tragic and sordid and mean things in life; so it was only after a struggle with herself, as well as with her widowed mother, that she had ventured forth into the world to attempt to add something to the scanty income left them by her father. She had been educated with some care, at home for the most part, so she tried to secure a position as teacher in the public schools, deciding that it was this she was best fitted for; but there were no vacancies. Yet the superintendent, impressed by her earnestness, promised to keep her in mind, and one day sent for her.

This new list includes: Attitudes, Established emotion, Emergent Emotion (full-blown), Emergent Emotion (suppressed), Moods, Partial emotion (topic shifting), Partial emotion (simmering), Stance towards person, Stance towards object/situation, Interpersonal bonds, Altered state of arousal, Altered state of control, Altered state of seriousness and Emotionless. This paper focuses on Emergent Emotion (full-blown), instead of a global taxonomy of affective states. This is made to reduce the complexity of proposed domain so it is easier to deal with. Besides, for the same reason, focus is mainly devoted to emotion detection and expression systems instead of modelling internal emotion processing in humans. In Douglas-Cowie et al. (2006), Emergent Emotion (full-blown) is defined as "states where the person's whole system is caught up in the way they react to a particular person or situation". It involves aspects such as: Distinctive positive or negative feelings about the people or situations involved. Impulses to act or express yourself in particular ways and avoid others. Distinctive changes in your body, for instance in your heart rate or tendency to sweat. Emotion does not last very long - it comes on quite quickly, and dies down reasonably soon (unless there is something very unusual happening). Our contribution is to overcome the above mentioned limitations referring to the lack of flexibility when personalising affective computing applications by providing a generic ontology for describing detection and expression systems related with emotions, while taking contextual and multimodal elements into account. The ontology is proposed as a way to develop an easily implementable formal model, as it is based on the Web Ontology Language (OWL) standard (W3C OWL Working Group, 2012). However, the knowledge about emotions in the ontology can be used by affective computing applications with independence of underneath technology. The proposed ontology in this paper is based on a generic model geared towards capturing the entities that take part in the Emergent Emotion process (Lopez, Gil, Garcia, Cearreta, & Garay, 2008). The model is presented in Section 3 and it has been formalised as an ontology following a classical ontology engineering methodology (Garcia, 2006). The ontology has been developed to be as agnostic as possible regarding existing emotion theories. This way, developers of affective resources are not tied to a given theoretical approach. In this sense, developers can use different theoretical approaches in the same ontological and technological framework. For instance, the categorical theory of emotions (Ekman, 1984), the dimensional one (Lang, 1979) or the one based on appraisal (Scherer, 1999). Consequently, the ontology can help implementing emotion-aware applications based on a wider range of theoretical approaches. This flexibility and wide applicability of EmotionsOnto is in great part due to the fact that it is capable of modelling contexts. In order to do that, the DOLCE upper ontology (Gangemi, Guarino, Masolo, Oltramari, & Schneider, 2002) is reused and extended, particularly the Description and Situation concepts. Descriptions correspond to the representations for the situations, which then trigger and are associated with emotions.

A common approach is to present white noise bursts through earphones, either simultaneously or shortly before each TMS pulse (Massimini et al., 2005; Nikouline et al., 1999). The auditory masking paradigm has been shown to reduce the amplitude of early-latency TEP components (Nikouline et al., 1999), but the effects on later TEP components are still unclear. In this study we examined whether the auditory click generated by the TMS coil affects the TEPs recorded over the frontal cortex after single-pulse TMS delivered to the left primary motor hand area (M1-HAND). We hypothesized that the auditory click influences the TEPs at least during the first tens of milliseconds after the TMS pulse, possibly resulting in earlier peaks than expected based on the propagation times between M1-HAND and the frontal lobe. Furthermore, we assessed whether the click-induced changes in the TEPs could be reduced using an auditory masking procedure. To test our hypotheses, we performed two experiments: Experiment 1 compared the effect of the TMS click on the TEPs without versus with simultaneous auditory masking, whereas Experiment 2 compared the effect of the TMS click on the TEPs without versus with pre-TMS auditory masking. Sixteen healthy volunteers participated in Experiment 1 (seven females, mean age = 26.75 +/- 0.83 years) and sixteen participants took part in Experiment 2 (eight females, mean age = 25.94 +/- 0.91 years). All participants were right-handed according to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971). None had a history of any relevant medical conditions or contraindications to TMS (Rossi et al., 2009) and all gave written informed consent prior to participation. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of the University Hospital Jena. The experimental setup is illustrated in Figure 1A. TMS was delivered with a MagPro X100 stimulator (MagVenture, Lucernemarken, Denmark) through a figure-of-eight coil (MC-B70, double 70 mm winding diameter) placed tangentially to the scalp with the handle pointing backward and away from the midline at about 45. The coil position was adjusted to elicit motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) in the abductor pollicis brevis muscle (APB) of the left hand. Surface electromyographic (EMG) signals were acquired from the APB muscle with Ag/AgCl electrodes in a belly-tendon montage. The resting motor threshold (RMT) was defined as the lowest intensity required to evoke MEPs with peak-to-peak amplitudes exceeding 50 1/2V in five out of ten consecutive trials (Rossini et al., 1994). Figure 1. Experimental setup. (A) The figure-of-eight coil was positioned over the left primary motor hand area (M1-HAND) with the handle pointing backward and away from the midline at about 45. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)-evoked potentials (TEPs) were measured with electroencephalography (EEG) using a 64-channel cap. Auditory stimuli were presented through air-conduction tubes attached to foam insert earplugs. For illustration purposes, the EEG cap is depicted as transparent. (B) Timing diagram of the three experimental blocks (No Mask, Simultaneous Mask, Pre-TMS Mask) in Experiments 1 and 2.

The tragedy that befell Layla Watt could have been avoided, her family believes, had the medical professionals acted more decisively. Margaret recalls the mounting frustration she felt during those early weeks. "I kept asking, how could they not see something was seriously wrong? Friends and family rallied around them, sharing in the growing concern as they saw Layla's once vibrant spirit diminish day by day. The misdiagnosis and delayed treatment highlight an alarming gap in the continuity of care and communication between healthcare providers. Each practitioner Layla encountered relied on the assumptions of the last, none taking steps to explore beyond the surface symptoms. "One doctor would say one thing, another would suggest something else, but no one pieced it all together," Margaret expressed in frustration. It's a painful truth that resonates with many who have faced similar healthcare challenges. Once admitted to the hospital, the stark reality of Layla's condition became heartbreakingly clear. The specialist teams at Glasgow's Beatson Hospital attempted aggressive treatments, hoping against hope that her young body could withstand the onslaught of chemotherapy. Despite their best efforts, the cancer proved too advanced, and Layla's fragile frame succumbed to the disease. As the Watt family grappled with their unimaginable loss, Margaret found herself reflecting on the memories they had shared. She cherishes the times Layla spent at dance class, her uncontainable laughter that filled their home, and the countless dreams she harbored for the future. "Those memories are precious treasures," Margaret said softly, tears welling in her eyes. Her sister Emma, only a couple of years older, has been equally devastated by Layla's passing. The two girls were inseparable, sharing secrets and milestones, and Emma remained steadfastly at her sister's side through the grueling hospital days. "It wasn't supposed to be like this," Emma whispered, clutching a photo of them together, forever preserving cherished moments that now feel like relics of another lifetime. While the family mourns, they channel their grief into advocacy, determined to raise awareness about the importance of early detection and more thorough investigative measures in young patients presenting with persistent symptoms. Margaret frequently speaks out, her voice a rallying cry for change, hoping to ensure other families do not endure the same heartache. "We want Layla's story to serve as a wake-up call," she insists, a steely resolve shining in her eyes. As they attempt to forge ahead, the Watt family draws strength from the community's love and support, finding comfort in the shared memories of Layla's brief but impactful life. With each tribute and each gesture of kindness, they rekindle the light that Layla once radiated, vowing to honor her by pushing for improvements that might save another young life from such a tragic end.

But the three men we have mentioned seemed to trouble themselves very slightly about the natural beauties that surrounded them, as they were fully engaged in appeasing a true hunter's appetite. Their meal, however, only lasted a few minutes, and when the last fragments had been devoured, one lighted his Indian pipe, the other took a cigar from his pocket. They then stretched themselves on the grass, and began digesting with that beatitude which characterizes smokers, while following with a languid eye the clouds of bluish smoke that rose in long spirals with each mouthful they puffed forth. As for the third man, he leant his back against a tree, crossed his arms, on his chest, and went to sleep most prosaically. We will profit by this momentary repose to present these persons to our readers, and make them better acquainted with each other. The first was a Canadian half-breed, of about fifty years of age, and known by the name of "Bright-eye." His life had been entirely spent on the prairie among the Indians, all of whose tricks he was thoroughly acquainted with. Like the majority of his countrymen he was very tall, more than six feet in height: his body was thin and angular; his limbs were knotty, but covered with muscles, hard as ropes; his bony and yellow face had a remarkable expression of frankness and joviality, and his little grey eyes sparkled with intelligence; his prominent cheekbones, his nose bent down over a wide mouth supplied with long white teeth, and his rounded chin, made up a face which was the most singular, and, at the same time, the most attractive that could be imagined. His dress differed in no respect from that of the other wood rangers; that is to say, it was a strange medley of European and Indian fashions, generally adopted by all the white prairie hunters and trappers. His weapons consisted of a knife, a pair of pistols, and an American rifle, now lying on the grass, but within reach of his hand. His companion was a man of thirty to thirty-two years of age at the most, but who appeared scarce twenty-five, tall, and well made. His blue eyes, limpid as a woman's, the long light curls that escaped beneath the edge of his Panama hat, and floated in disorder on his shoulders, the whiteness of his skin, which contrasted with the olive and brown complexion of the hunter, were sufficient evidence that he was not born in the hot climate of America. In fact, this young man was a Frenchman, Charles Edward de Beaulieu, and was descended from one of the oldest families in Brittany. But, under this slightly effeminate appearance, he concealed a lion's courage which nothing could startle or even surprise.

It wasn't fair he thought. Life isn't supposed to end like this. We are supposed to live forever. If we do not then why does God give us such a short span? Why did he create us if our lives mean so little? And why is there no answer? When he asked these questions he received none. He knew that if he went to church they would try to console him by telling him that God has a plan for everyone and that someday he would understand. But he didn't want to understand. He wanted answers. He wanted a reason. He wanted to know why. His head hurt from all the unanswered questions that swirled around inside it. There was no way to shut them out. They wouldn't stop. He wished for someone to come along and hit him over the head with a two by four and knock him unconscious so he could rest for awhile. But no one came. So he got up and made his way through the door. He headed down to the local diner for breakfast. As he sat there alone at a table near the window he watched as people entered and exited the restaurant. Most seemed happy and contented. Some appeared angry and others looked sad. They were just going about their business. A man and a woman were seated at a nearby table and as she laughed at something he said her eyes sparkled with joy. She was probably 30 years old and still had all her teeth. Her husband looked to be around 40. He was clean shaven and well groomed. He wore a nice suit and tie. "What can I get you?" "I'll take a large order of pancakes with sausage links and scrambled eggs please." "And what would you like honey?" "Just orange juice and toast please." The waitress wrote down their order and then turned to go. She stopped and turned back toward him. "Is everything okay today?" she asked. "Yes dear." he answered. "It's fine. Thank you." She smiled and left. He picked up his coffee cup and took a sip. He noticed that his hands were trembling slightly. He set the cup down again and ran his fingers through his hair. He felt the need to cry again but held back. He tried to keep his thoughts focused on the present. He needed to keep his mind occupied. He sipped his coffee and watched the people pass by outside the window. He watched a young mother pushing a baby stroller while talking to another woman. He saw an elderly man walking slowly carrying a cane. He saw a young girl playing hopscotch on the sidewalk. He saw a man walking a dog. He saw a group of teenagers laughing and joking. Each person had a story to tell. Each had a past and a future. Their stories were as varied as the colors of the rainbow. He wondered what their futures would hold. Would any of them die tomorrow? Would any of them kill themselves? Or would they live out their full natural lives? Who knows he thought. Maybe they would all die tonight in a freak accident. Maybe the building they were in would collapse killing every living soul within its walls. He wondered if he would be one of those killed. Would his life flash before his eyes as he drew his final breath? Or would he simply fall asleep and wake up in heaven.

As the fire crackled and spat, casting flickering shadows on the surrounding trees, the party's mood began to sag. The sudden drop in temperature had taken its toll, and the warmth of the flames seemed to be the only thing that stood between them and the chill of the night air. Wilkie's eyes wandered to the watch on his wrist, and he felt a pang of hunger gnawing at his stomach. The gong at the beach, signaling the start of supper, seemed like a distant echo of a promise, taunting him with its proximity. Blount, sensing the unease, spoke up, his voice low and measured. "I fear we must put off thoughts of supper for the present. The weather may seem calm, but the sea is still rough, and the wind is picking up. It would be foolhardy to attempt the crossing tonight." Wilkie's face fell, and he glanced at Jake, who was busy whittling away at his plug of tobacco. The sailor's averted gaze told its own story. Wilkie's doubts deepened, and he turned to Blount. "But what of the daylight? We could at least try to make it to Lippenstock in the morning." Blount's expression turned stern. "I'm afraid it's not a question of making it to Lippenstock, Wilkie. It's a question of making it back to shore in one piece. The sea is no joke, and I won't risk the lives of my crew for the sake of a meal." Margaret spoke up, her voice firm. "We won't break up the party, Wilkie. We'll stay together, no matter what." Wilkie's eyes lingered on her, then shifted to Jake, who was still lost in his whittling. The sailor's taciturnity was starting to get on his nerves. He cleared his throat, trying to think of something to say, but his words stuck in his throat like a fishbone. As the silence stretched out, the only sound being the crackling of the fire and the distant call of a night bird, Wilkie felt a sense of resignation wash over him. He knew that he would have to face the night alone, and the thought was a bitter pill to swallow. He glanced at Jake, who looked up, his eyes glinting in the firelight, and Wilkie knew that he was beaten. The storm may have passed, but the night was still young, and Wilkie was left to face its darkness alone.

The purpose of our analysis is twofold: first, to quantify the reactive surface area distribution within each sample and second, to assess how well the statistical distributions represent the actual reactive surface area observed within the individual grains. A total of six different rock types were studied including two sandstones (Columbia River Basalt - CRB, and Berea Sandstone), two limestone samples (Beaufort Limestone and Indiana Limestone) and two dolomite samples (Gladstone Dolostone and Westphalia Dolostone). A brief summary of the rock characteristics is given below: Indiana Limestone (IL): The Indiana Limestone is a thick-bedded limestone composed primarily of fossiliferous calcite crystals. The average grain size of the limestone is ~500 1/2m and the porosity is ~20% by volume. The Indiana Limestone was sampled from a quarry located in Bedford, IN. This sample was scanned using a Zeiss Xradia MicroXCT-400 system operating at 80 kV and 100 1/2A. Westphalia Dolostone (WD): The Westphalia Dolostone is a light grey dolomite rock consisting of approximately equal amounts of calcite and dolomite minerals. The average grain size is ~200 1/2m and the porosity is ~17%. The Westphalia Dolostone was sampled from the Westphalia Quarry, located in Lawrence County, IN. This sample was scanned using an XT H 225 ST scanner operating at 140 kV and 150 1/2A. CRB (CRBS): The Columbia River Basalt is a fine-grained basaltic volcanic rock composed primarily of plagioclase feldspar, pyroxene and olivine. The average grain size is ~300 1/2m and the porosity is ~13%. The CRB was sampled from the Gorge Rock Quarry, located in the Columbia River Basin, OR. This sample was scanned using an XT H 225 ST scanner operating at 140 kV and 50 1/2A. Berea Sandstone (BS): The Berea Sandstone is a very fine grained sandstone containing quartz grains cemented together with silica. The average grain size is ~250 1/2m and the porosity is ~21%. The Berea Sandstone was sampled from the Berea Sandstone Quarry, located in Madison County, OH. This sample was scanned using a Zeiss Xradia MicroXCT-400 system operating at 60 kV and 70 1/2A. Gladstone Dolostone (GD): The Gladstone Dolostone is a dark grey dolostone rock consisting of approximately equal amounts of calcite and dolomite minerals. The average grain size is ~350 1/2m and the porosity is ~14%. The Gladstone Dolostone was sampled from the Gladstone Quarry, located in Johnson County, IL. This sample was scanned using an XT H 225 ST scanner operating at 120 kV and 30 1/2A. Beaufort Limestone (BL): The Beaufort Limestone is a light coloured limestone rock composed primarily of calcite crystals. The average grain size is ~600 1/2m and the porosity is ~18%. The Beaufort Limestone was sampled from the Beaufort Quarry, located in Morgan County, AL. This sample was scanned using an XT H 225 ST scanner operating at 120 kV and 40 1/2A. Fourth, all early warning systems have been developed based on summative score-based grading, which is typically norm-referenced. Some universities have started to change their grading from summative score-based to standards-based systems, which has educational advantages described below. Thus, academic early warning systems should adapt their models to this new grading system. Standards-based grading is based on "the measurement of the quality of students proficiency towards achieving well defined course objectives" (Heywood, 2014, p. 1514) and grades "represent how well students achieve the course objectives" (Sadler, 2005, p. 179). Standards-based grading is criterion-referenced not norm-referenced. In other words, students are graded based on their achievements or what they can do, regardless of how other students in the course perform on the same assigned task (Carberry, Siniawski, & Dionisio, 2012; Heywood, 2014; Sadler, 2005). In this grading system, the course assessments are directly connected to the course learning objectives and are not a series of separate course assignments (Carberry et al., 2012). Standards-based grading provides educational advantages for students. Because standard-based grading assesses students' achievement of the course learning objectives, it provides clear, meaningful, and personalized feedback for students related to achievement of the course learning objectives and helps them identify their weaknesses in the course (Atwood & Siniawski, 2014). In addition, because the students are aware of course learning objectives and a student's grade is independent of other students' performance, it provides "fairness and transparency" (Sadler, 2005). Because of its educational advantages, it is expected that more universities and courses will employ standards-based grading in the near future and it is important that early warning systems change their models accordingly. Extensive research has been conducted to determine the factors that correlate to and/or predict students' academic success in a course. The majority of these studies focused on predicting students' grade in a course at the end of the semester using academic factors available before the start of the semester (e.g., cumulative GPA, grade in a pre-requisite course) and non-academic factors (e.g., gender, age). Neither course instructors nor students can influence past performance indicators (e.g., student GPA, previous grades) or many non-academic factors (e.g., gender, race, socio-economic status). If students are made aware of that these factors are used in the prediction models, it may discourage them because they may think their past behavior or circumstances have set them up for failure and there is nothing they can do to achieve positive future outcomes. Thus these models, despite their intention to help students, may negatively affect students' performance. More research is needed to investigate the positive and negative effects of using and sharing the basis for prediction models for students learning. A few studies have utilized the academic performance data available during the semester, which logically can be the best predictor of the course grade.

The streets taught me resilience. Every corner of our neighborhood, every alley, was a proving ground. As a lad, I was an easy target for bullies-short, small, with ears that stuck out like a sore thumb. They'd circle around, taunting, tossing insults, daring me to stand up for myself. It didn't take long for me to realize that shrinking away was no option. So, the street fights began, not as sport, but as survival, each swing teaching me something crucial about fear, about standing your ground. Those scuffles, though rough, were like the early rounds of a long match, conditioning my body, and sharpening my mind to remain calm under pressure. As I transitioned from schoolyard scrapper to local boxing hero, I carried those lessons with me: roll with the punches, keep your guard up, and never underestimate an opponent. Every victory in the ring is built upon those countless small victories won on the pavements of Belfast, where boys learn to be men the hard way. When I step into the Odyssey Arena, the roar of the crowd transports me back to those early days. There's an almost primal energy, a collective memory of shared history, driving me forward, urging me to deliver. Against Chris Avalos, it's more than just a title on the line-it's pride, legacy, the weight of every Belfast dreamer that fills the air. As fame beckons further, with potential fights against Quigg and Rigondeaux, there's an ever-growing spotlight. But even as the world opens up, offering glitz and glamour, it's the pull of home that keeps me tethered. Belfast's gritty soul is imprinted on every fiber of my being, reminding me of where I started and who helped get me here. It's why, faced with the lure of luxury, I'm more inclined to head to my local pub, share a laugh with mates who know me best, and keep my feet firmly planted on the ground. Mayweather might flaunt his fortunes, parade his success, but for me, humility is the wealth I treasure most. My wife's steady gaze keeps my ego in check, too. She knows the value of what's real and what's show. And in a city like Belfast, authenticity is key; it separates the true from the false, the respected from those merely tolerated. No gimmicks, no pretense, just honest, hard-earned respect. Every trip to the market or walk down familiar streets fills me with an unmistakable warmth, that feeling of belonging, of being just another bloke from the block. I see young lads shadowboxing in backyards, see that same fire in their eyes. I offer them the only advice I know: work hard, stay true to yourself, and never forget where you're from. This bond with Belfast isn't just where I live; it's woven into the fabric of who I am. As I lace up my gloves and prepare to face Avalos, it's not just me in that ring. It's every Belfast boy who ever had a dream, every one of us who dared to fight for a better future. And that's a fight I intend to win, for all our sakes.

In the century in which we live there are so many modes of belief and of unbelief that future historians will have difficulty in finding their way about. But are we any more successful in disentangling the condition of religious beliefs in the time of Symmachus or of Ambrose? A fervent Christian, Rene d'Esparvieu was deeply attached to the liberal ideas his ancestors had transmitted to him as a sacred heritage. Compelled to oppose a Jacobin and atheistical Republic, he still called himself Republican. And it was in the name of liberty that he demanded the independence and sovereignty of the Church. During the long debates on the Separation and the quarrels over the Inventories, the synods of the bishops and the assemblies of the faithful were held in his house. While the most authoritatively accredited leaders of the Catholic party: prelates, generals, senators, deputies, journalists, were met together in the big green drawing-room, and every soul present turned towards Rome with a tender submission or enforced obedience; while Monsieur d'Esparvieu, his elbow on the marble chimney-piece, opposed civil law to canon law, and protested eloquently against the spoliation of the Church of France, two faces of other days, immobile and speechless, looked down on the modern crowd; on the right of the fire-place, painted by David, was Romain Bussart, a working-farmer at Esparvieu in shirt-sleeves and drill trousers, with a rough-and-ready air not untouched with cunning. He had good reason to smile: the worthy man laid the foundation of the family fortunes when he bought Church lands. On the left, painted by Gerard in full-dress bedizened with orders, was the peasant's son, Baron Emile Bussart d'Esparvieu, prefect under the Empire, Keeper of the Great Seal under Charles X, who died in 1837, churchwarden of his parish, with couplets from La Pucelle on his lips. Rene d'Esparvieu married in 1888 Marie-Antoinette Coupelle, daughter of Baron Coupelle, ironmaster at Blainville (Haute Loire). Madame Rene d'Esparvieu had been president since 1903 of the Society of Christian Mothers. These perfect spouses, having married off their eldest daughter in 1908, had three children still at home - a girl and two boys. Leon, the younger, aged seven, had a room next to his mother and his sister Berthe. Maurice, the elder, lived in a little pavilion comprising two rooms at the bottom of the garden. The young man thus gained a freedom which enabled him to endure family life. He was rather good-looking, smart without too much pretence, and the faint smile which merely raised one corner of his mouth did not lack charm. At twenty-five Maurice possessed the wisdom of Ecclesiastes. Doubting whether a man hath any profit of all his labour which he taketh under the sun he never put himself out about anything.

But she read nothing even when every feature was revealed in the clear dead light, for the face which she saw was the face of one who lived much apart within itself, building amongst her own dreams as a child builds upon the sand and pays no heed to those who pass. And to none of her dreams had Mrs. Thesiger the key. Deliberately her daughter had withdrawn herself amongst them, and they had given her this return for her company. They had kept her fresh and gentle in a circle where freshness was soon lost and gentleness put aside. Sylvia Thesiger was at this time seventeen, although her mother dressed her to look younger, and even then overdressed her like a toy. It was of a piece with the nature of the girl that, in this matter as in the rest, she made no protest. She foresaw the scene, the useless scene, which would follow upon her protest, exclamations against her ingratitude, abuse for her impertinence, and very likely a facile shower of tears at the end; and her dignity forbade her to enter upon it. She just let her mother dress her as she chose, and she withdrew just a little more into the secret chamber of her dreams. She sat now looking steadily out of the window, with her eyes uplifted and aloof, in a fashion which had become natural to her, and her mother was seized with a pang of envy at the girl's beauty. For beauty Sylvia Thesiger had, uncommon in its quality rather than in its degree. From the temples to the round point of her chin the contour of her face described a perfect oval. Her forehead was broad and low and her hair, which in color was a dark chestnut, parted in the middle, whence it rippled in two thick daring waves to the ears, a fashion which noticeably became her, and it was gathered behind into a plait which lay rather low upon the nape of her neck. Her eyes were big, of a dark gray hue and very quiet in their scrutiny; her mouth, small and provoking. It provoked, when still, with the promise of a very winning smile, and the smile itself was not so frequent but that it provoked a desire to summon it to her lips again. It had a way of hesitating, as though Sylvia were not sure whether she would smile or not; and when she had made up her mind, it dimpled her cheeks and transfigured her whole face, and revealed in her tenderness and a sense of humor. Her complexion was pale, but clear, her figure was slender and active, but without angularities, and she was of the middle height.

What's left of the old ship groans beneath the weight of uncertainty. Cap'n gone, first officer toast, and here we are, bickering like children on a sinking playground. Fry, quicken your pace! We don't have the luxury of deliberation here. I know the drill - years of simulation, countless hours of theoretical preparation for catastrophe. But when the rubber meets the road, when it's real blood and not just pixels on a screen, hell, everything unravels faster than a spooled thread. You hear that? Silence has a weight that presses down like a lead blanket. And with every second ticking past, I'm reminded of our mortality, as if the ship itself has turned against us. Shadowed memories flicker in and out - the hum of engines, the muffled voices in retrofitted halls, the promise of New Mecca gleaming like a beacon in dark space. And now, the echoes of desperation intertwine as Fry's shaky hands hover, paralyzed over the control panel. Fry, focus! You have to get us stabilized! If another hit comes - No, when *another* hit comes, we'll turn to dust before we know it! We can't afford the luxury of panic. Think! There's always a path through the chaos if you're sharp enough to find it. What about the reserves? The bulkheads? Did we set the venting protocol for a pressure neutralization? But Fry's stuck somewhere between dread and frantic recollection, eyes darting to the viewports as if they could magically yield a salvation we both know is a long shot. Cap'n was the compass, the only steady hand amidst the volatile stars, guiding us through the cosmic storm. Without him, we are... but flotsam adrift. Just a tattered banner of a ship that once held dreams, burdens, and the faint scent of home. Owens' voice - my voice - reverberates in my skull, a chorus that underscores the horror unfolding. "You should never have landed here." A whisper in the gale, rippling through the air with the chill of prescience. Maybe he's right. This sector feels off, too raw, too chaotic. And we're the unwitting trespassers in an alien domain. I can almost hear the remnants of our predecessors echoing their warnings, the elders telling tales of creatures that call the deep void home, lurking just beyond our grasp. "Fry!" My shout pulls her back from the brink. "Snap out of it! What did we train for?" Each word is a pulse, a reminder of the purpose we once had. "You're all we've got left. We can't become fodder." A flicker of recognition flashes across her eyes - clarity, albeit brief, ready to wrestle back moments lost to uncertainty. "Okay," she breathes, knuckles whitening as she grips the controls, breathing steady. "Adjusting power to the aft thrusters - small bursts only." The ship lurches, and I brace myself against the console, heart racing anew. She's focusing - okay, step by step. "That should help with the load. We can level it out." If we can just keep it together for a few more minutes, maybe longer, we can process what's left, form a plan. "We need to review the life pod systems too," I say, but a new alarm blares through the cabin, piercing through my resolve. The hull's integrity is still compromised, and in the next instant, there's a tremor that jostles us hard enough to shift fears into raw adrenaline. "What now?!" Fry's voice slices through the confusion. "More damage?!" "Not just damage - that howl... We're not alone." I mutter, pressing against the viewport, peering into the abyss. God forgive us, what's out there? The darkness seems to bulge, as if alive, breathing softly with a rhythm that pulsates deeper than the void itself. What have we drawn upon ourselves? Someone's going to have to face it. Someone with guts enough to stand before hell itself. "Fry, stay steady. Check the aft thrusters, prepare the remaining pods. We need to be ready... for anything."

And finally, if the team doesn't finish all the work in the sprint then they'll never learn to estimate properly. Those are five big reasons why people would say you cannot add work items to a sprint. Now, let's talk about each of them individually. Okay, so number one if the team doesn't finish all the work in the Sprint then they don't get credit for any of it. Let's just stop for a moment and talk about this one. The truth is they do get credit for the work they completed. It's called velocity. It's called burn down charts. It's called progress. There's no rule that says you can't have incomplete work at the end of a Sprint. In fact, there's no rule that says you have to complete every single item in the Sprint. That was committed to the Sprint. It's okay. If there's incomplete work, there are ways to handle it. It's not ideal. You don't want to have a bunch of incomplete work but it's not the end of the world. It's not like you lose points or something. Okay. Number two if the team doesn't finish all the work in the Sprint then they don't get paid for any of it. Well, this is true in a sense. They don't get paid for incomplete work. However, they did earn points for the work that they did complete. So they do get paid for that work. They also learned valuable lessons from the work that they didn't complete which will help them in future sprints. So while they may not get paid directly for the incomplete work, they still benefit from it. Okay, number three if the team doesn't finish all the work in the Sprint then they don't meet their commitments. This is another common misconception. Just because the team doesn't finish all the work in the Sprint does not mean they failed to meet their commitments. Their commitment was to do their best to complete as much work as possible during the Sprint. If they put forth their best effort and still fell short, that's not a failure. It's just reality. Sometimes things happen that are beyond our control and we need to accept that and move on. Okay number four if the team doesn't finish all the work in the Sprint then they don't get to celebrate at the end of the Sprint. This one is actually kind of funny. Who said anything about celebrating? Sure, it's nice to celebrate when we reach our goals but sometimes life gets in the way and we fall short. Does that mean we shouldn't enjoy ourselves? Of course not. We should still take time to reflect on what went well and what could have gone better and use that information to improve our process for next time. He too was lonely and orphaned, so that the two children, making common cause, clung closely to each other, and shared, both in infancy and in early youth, their joys and sorrows. The Park had been the boy's home ever since his parents' death, Mr. Chesney accepting him as his ward, but never afterward troubling himself about his welfare. Indeed, he had no objection whatever to fill the Park with relations, so long as they left him undisturbed to follow his own devices. Not that the education of these children was neglected. They had all tuition that was necessary; and Lilian, having a talent for music, learned to sing and play the piano very charmingly. She could ride, too, and sit her horse a merveille, and had a passion for reading, - perhaps inherited. But, as novels were her principal literature, and as she had no one to regulate her choice of them, it is a matter of opinion whether she derived much benefit from them. At least she received little harm, as at seventeen she was as fresh-minded and pure-hearted a child as one might care to know. The County, knowing her to be an heiress, - though not a large one, - called systematically on her every three months. Twice she had been taken to a ball by an enterprising mother with a large family of unpromising sons. But as she reached her eighteenth year her father died, and her old home, the Park, being strictly entailed on heirs male, passed from her into the hands of a distant cousin utterly unknown. This young man, another Archibald Chesney, was abroad at the time of his kinsman's death, - in Egypt, or Hong-Kong, or Jamaica, - no one exactly knew which - until after much search he was finally discovered to be in Halifax. From thence he had written to the effect that, as he probably should not return to his native land for another six months, he hoped his cousin (if it pleased her) would continue to reside at the Park - where all the old servants were to be kept on - until his return. It did please his cousin; and in her old home she still reigned as queen, until after eight months she received a letter from her father's lawyer warning her of Archibald Chesney's actual arrival in London. This letter failed in its object. Lilian either would not or could not bring herself to name the day that should part her forever from all the old haunts and pleasant nooks she loved so well. She was not brave enough to take her "Bradshaw" and look up the earliest train that ought to convey her away from the Park. Indeed, so utterly wanting in decency and decorum did she appear at this particular epoch of her existence that the heart of her only aunt - her father's sister - was stirred to its depths.

However, the temperature of the heat source may vary significantly over time, for example, the temperature of solar radiation varies dramatically over day and night or even within a single day, due to the change of weather conditions. The temperature of the exhaust gas from diesel engines also changes depending on the operating load of the engine. This means that there would be a significant drop of the thermal efficiency when the temperature of the heat source deviates from the design condition. Therefore, it is important to investigate how the thermal efficiency of an ORC system using a zeotropic mixture as working fluid is affected by variations in the temperature of the heat source. In this paper, we will analyse the performance of an ORC system using a zeotropic mixture as working fluid when the temperature of the heat source varies. Three different types of zeotropic mixtures including hydrocarbon (HC), hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) and siloxanes are considered. ## Thermodynamic model ### Working fluids In order to compare the performance of different types of working fluids, three types of zeotropic mixtures are selected for analysis, namely: HC mixtures (pentane/n-butane), HFC mixtures (R32/R134a) and siloxane mixtures (MM/OCT). Table 1 lists the properties of these three zeotropic mixtures. The temperature glides of the three zeotropic mixtures were calculated using REFPROP software package developed by NIST [13] and the results are shown in Fig. 1. It can be seen that the temperature glides of all the three mixtures increase with increasing pressure. The temperature glide of pentane/n-butane is much higher than those of R32/R134a and MM/OCT, while the difference between R32/R134a and MM/OCT is not large. ### System description Fig. 2 shows the schematic diagram of an ORC system using a zeotropic mixture as working fluid. The working fluid is heated up to a certain temperature \(T { m e}\) in the preheater, followed by further heating to a saturated vapour state at a high pressure \(P { m c}\) in the evaporator. Then the working fluid expands through the turbine to generate mechanical work. After expansion, the working fluid enters into the condenser where it is condensed to liquid. Finally, the working fluid is pumped back to the preheater to complete the cycle. The pinch point temperatures of the evaporator (\(\Delta T { m pp,e}\)) and condenser (\(\Delta T { m pp,c}\)) are assumed to be 20 \({}^{\circ}\)C. It should be noted that the system configuration shown in Fig. 2 only represents the basic principle of an ORC system using a zeotropic mixture as working fluid. For practical applications, some modifications might be required according to the specific application scenario. For example, if the heat source is a hot water stream, then the preheater might need to be removed because the heat source is already in the liquid form; if the heat sink is ambient air, then the condenser might be replaced by an air-cooled condenser. ### Assumptions To simplify the calculation, several assumptions are made as follows: * Steady-state operation; * Isentropic efficiencies of the pump and turbine are 75%; * Pinch point temperature differences of the evaporator and condenser are both set to be 20 \({}^{\circ}\)C; * Heat loss to the environment is negligible; * Pressure drops along the pipelines and heat exchangers are neglected.

Although the EFR is thought to be largely dependent on brainstem generators, the response may be affected by low-SR fiber loss, especially at high levels and shallow modulation depths (Bharadwaj et al., 2014; Bharadwaj et al., 2015). Bramhall et al. (2015) reported a relation between ABR wave I amplitude and SPiN, although the relation was largely driven by audiometric thresholds and was not significant when these thresholds were included in the regression model. Liberman et al. (2016) reported that SPiN at low levels was related to the SP/AP ratio. However, it is uncertain if this relation would survive statistical control for high-frequency audiometric thresholds, which were weakly associated with SPiN. In addition, synaptopathy is generally assumed to reflect coding at high levels because of its association with low-SR fibers, and it is not clear why performance at low levels should be affected. In contrast, several recent studies have reported no relation between ABR wave I amplitude and SPiN (Bramhall et al., 2018; Fulbright et al., 2017; Guest et al., 2018c; Prendergast et al., 2017b), nor between EFR amplitude and SPiN (Prendergast et al., 2017b; Guest et al., 2018b). With respect to tinnitus, the literature is also inconsistent. Several studies have reported a reduction in ABR wave I at high levels in tinnitus participants with normal hearing compared to non-tinnitus controls (Bramhall et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2012; Schaette and McAlpine, 2011). However, in the Gu et al. study the groups were not audiometrically matched; for the analysis in which a significant effect on wave I was observed, the tinnitus group exhibited substantially higher audiometric thresholds at frequencies of 8 kHz and above. In the Bramhall et al. study there were also audiometric differences between the groups, although the authors controlled for distortion-product otoacoustic emission amplitude in the analyses. In the Schaette and McAlpine study there was a small audiometric elevation (3.5 dB) in the tinnitus group at 12 kHz, and thresholds measured at 16 kHz were not reported. It is not clear the extent to which small high-frequency audiometric elevations might affect ABR wave I amplitude, although wave I is dependent on basal generators, including those above 8 kHz (Don and Eggermont, 1978). These positive findings were not replicated by Gilles et al. (2016), Guest et al. (2017a; 2017b), or Shim et al. (2017), who all found no relation between presence of tinnitus and wave I amplitude. Paul et al. (2017) reported a reduction in the EFR in their tinnitus participants compared to controls. However, there was a flaw in the original statistical analysis and the finding was non-significant after this was corrected (Roberts et al., 2018). Guest et al. (2017b) also reported a non-significant reduction in EFR amplitude in their tinnitus participants, but this was not apparent in a subsequent analysis (Guest et al., 2017a) and most likely represents random variability.

The subsequent years saw an alarming escalation of hostilities directed toward American interests around the globe. In December 1985, a tragic incident unfolded when TWA Flight 847 was hijacked. The chilling images of violence and terror gripped the nation and, yet again, the alarm shrieked in our collective consciousness. We witnessed the brutal murder of Navy Diver Robert Stethem, the perpetrators carrying their twisted ideology forward while America's resolve seemed only to falter. This event struck at the heart of our national security and tested our commitment to protecting our citizens and our national pride. There was an unmistakable message being sent-a challenge to our very existence. As if in a cruel pattern, the bombings in Lebanon in 1983 and 1984, including the grim attack on the Marine barracks in Beirut that resulted in the loss of 241 American servicemen, made a solemn and morose statement of futility. On that fateful day, the curtain fell on America's optimism in the region, and yet government officials proclaimed the need for patience. Meanwhile, our enemies gathered strength like hawks sharpening their talons. Each instance of aggression added fuel to an already simmering fire, while we remained half-asleep, convinced that mere diplomacy could assuage a world intent on shattering our peace. The alarm clock didn't stop; it merely transformed. Fast forward to the 1990s, and America, bedazzled by the end of the Cold War, lulled itself into a false sense of security. The attack on the World Trade Center in 1993 was a forewarning, and yet the response was meek-an incomplete response to an incomplete understanding of the dangers lurking beyond our shores. We began to see, as the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania unfolded, that the world was rife with hostility. Each time the alarm rang louder, it seemed America simply positioned itself more comfortably in the sheets, oblivious to the danger brewing. And then came September 11, 2001-a date that remains etched in the fabric of our national consciousness. It wasn't just an attack; it was a clarion call, a resounding assertion from a faction whose ambition was clear: America must be humbled. Yet, instead of addressing this with the urgency it demanded, we hesitated, navigating the murky waters of geopolitics while our enemies drew ever closer. It took a tragedy of unprecedented scale for us to encounter our reality, and yet even then, doubt lingered in the hearts of many. Post-9/11, we embarked on a protracted engagement in Afghanistan and later Iraq, seeking to uproot the ideologies that imperiled our nation but often seemed hindered by indecision and conflicting viewpoints at home. From the ashes of conflict rose an entirely new landscape, one riddled with uncertainties and challenges that demanded our immediate attention. Yet, as every alarm rings out with fervor, we still must assess our surroundings and respond with decisive action. If there was ever a lesson to be taken from our past, it is that retreat is not an option; it is imperative that we stand resolute. It is time to confront the harsh truth: the alarm will continue to waft through the corridors of history until we choose to engage with conviction and clarity. The snooze button can no longer hold sway over our future, for the world outside remains hostile and unforgiving. We must understand that our actions-or inactions-determine the course of the events that follow. The cycle is more than just a series of events; it is about our responsibility to ourselves, to our allies, and to generations yet unborn. Rise, America! Rise!

The accuracy of forecasting fiscal variables is crucial for policymakers, as it enables them to make informed decisions about budgetary goals, monetary policy, and debt management. However, the complexity of the fiscal forecasting process is often compounded by the presence of biases and errors in the estimation of economic variables. For instance, the output gap, a critical variable in fiscal forecasting, is often miscalculated due to the difficulties in estimating potential GDP (Blanchard, 2016). This can lead to inaccurate forecasts of fiscal variables, such as the budget deficit and public debt, which can have significant consequences for macroeconomic stability. Furthermore, the use of econometric models in fiscal forecasting can also introduce errors and biases. For example, vector autoregressions (VARs) and small-scale semistructural models, which are commonly used in fiscal forecasting, can be sensitive to model specification and estimation errors (Favero & Marcellino, 2005). Additionally, the omission of important economic variables or the use of inadequate model specifications can lead to biased forecasts. Moreover, the estimation of fiscal variables is often based on historical data, which may not accurately reflect future economic trends and developments. Another challenge in fiscal forecasting is the presence of non-linear relationships between economic variables. For instance, the relationship between fiscal policy and economic growth is often non-linear, and simple linear models may not capture these complexities (Alesina & Ardagna, 2010). Moreover, the impact of fiscal policy on economic growth can vary depending on the state of the economy, with fiscal expansion being more effective during recessions than during booms (Ilzetzki, Mendoza, & Vegh, 2013). To address these challenges, researchers and policymakers have developed new approaches to fiscal forecasting. For example, the use of machine learning techniques, such as neural networks and decision trees, can improve the accuracy of fiscal forecasts by capturing non-linear relationships between economic variables (Blix, Solheim, & von Hagen, 2017). Additionally, the use of nowcasting techniques, which involve the estimation of current economic conditions, can improve the accuracy of fiscal forecasts by providing more timely and accurate estimates of economic variables (Giannone, Reichlin, & Small, 2008). In conclusion, the forecasting of fiscal variables is a complex task that is subject to various challenges and biases. The accuracy of fiscal forecasts is crucial for policymakers, and errors in forecasting can have significant consequences for macroeconomic stability. To improve the accuracy of fiscal forecasts, researchers and policymakers must develop new approaches that can capture the complexities of the economy and address the challenges of fiscal forecasting. I should have known better, of course, than to underestimate the vagaries of travel with toddlers. As we meandered through the terminal, the weight of each weary moment began to settle upon us like an unwelcome blanket. My initial optimism began to fray. O, ever the intrepid explorer, darted about with a zeal that belied her small stature, her laughter echoing against the sterile terminal walls. But she wasn't the only one discovering boundaries; K, blissfully unaware of the chaos around her, continued to dream in my arms. At this juncture, Kevin and I had adopted a strategy of hopeful distractions, fervently trying to stave off the inevitable restlessness that I felt creeping in like a shadow. We stopped by a souvenir shop to gaze at miniature airplanes and stuffed moose, a visual marvel for O as she pointed and shrieked with delight, much to the confusion of older travelers who sought a quieter experience. It was both charming and exhausting-an endearing reminder of how joy can burst forth from the mundane. However, as the minutes ticked by and the boarding time approached, anxiety bubbled beneath the surface like a simmering pot threatening to boil over. The announcement drifted through the terminal like an unwelcome summer storm: our flight was delayed. The initial pang of frustration I felt threatened to morph into an ominous dark cloud as I made mental calculations about our limited supplies. Diapers: dwindling. Snacks: quickly disappearing. Patience: at risk of depletion. Amid the apparent chaos, my mind raced through potential solutions while my heart sank a little lower for each passing minute. With nothing else to do, we opted for the unthinkable-ice cream. What better way to cope with impending disaster than sugary distraction? Kevin ushered O and me skillfully through the bustling crowd toward the small cafe that offered the creamy delights we so desperately craved. The smile on O's face as she clutched her colorful cone, practically bursting with enthusiasm, staved off panic for a brief moment. K stirred, waking up with the abrupt startle of joy and confusion, but I could tell that the universe felt slightly less diminished by the sheer delight emanating from our little family. But as if the gods were testing us further, my ill-timed optimism led to a rapid sequence of events: O took a big lick of her ice cream, only to have it spiral comically out of control, cascading dramatically onto her shirt, and, by some law of physics I cannot explain, also sliding down her leg and onto the floor. K, sensing the commotion, began to wail, and suddenly, we were in a full-blown parental predicament, a spectacle worthy of a circus. I scooped K up with one arm, and with the other, attempted to salvage O's supposed treat while soothing her cries of despair. As if choreographed, the scene morphed into an overwhelming balance of trial and triumph: laughter surged amidst the tears, as O, now covered in ice cream, giggled at her own plight. I couldn't help but chuckle, even in my frenetic state, realizing that perhaps this was the true essence of family-joy entangled with chaos, each moment a testament to resilience.
