So the boys had baited up the line on the sly down at the boathouse the day before, and laid it out across the deepest part of the fjord. Now the thing about a deep-sea line is that it may bring to the surface fish so big and so fearsome that the like has never been seen before. Yesterday, however, there had been trouble of a different sort. To their dismay, the boys had found that they had not sinkers enough to weight the shore end of the line; and it looked as if they might have to give up the whole thing. But Peer, ever ready, had hit on the novel idea of making one end fast to the trunk of a small fir growing at the outermost point of the ness, and carrying the line from there out over the open fjord. Then a stone at the farther end, and with the magic words, "Fie, fish!" it was paid out overboard, vanishing into the green depths. The deed was done. True, there were a couple of hooks dangling in mid-air at the shore end, between the tree and the water, and, while they might serve to catch an eider duck, or a guillemot, if any one should chance to come rowing past in the dark and get hung up - why, the boys might find they had made a human catch. No wonder, then, that they whispered eagerly and hurried down to the boat. "Here comes Peter Ronningen," cried Martin suddenly. This was the third member of the crew, a lanky youth with whitish eyebrows and a foolish face. He stammered, and made a queer noise when he laughed: "Chee-hee-hee." Twice he had been turned down in the confirmation classes; after all, what was the use of learning lessons out of a book when nobody ever had patience to wait while he said them? Together they ran the boat down to the water's edge, got it afloat, and scrambled in, with much waving of patched trouser legs. "Hi!" cried a voice up on the beach, "let me come too!" "There's Klaus," said Martin. "Shall we take him along?" "No," said Peter Ronningen. "Oh yes, let's," said Peer. Klaus Brock, the son of the district doctor, was a blue-eyed youngster in knickerbockers and a sailor blouse. He was playing truant, no doubt - Klaus had his lessons at home with a private tutor - and would certainly get a thrashing from his father when he got home. "Hurry up," called Peer, getting out an oar. Klaus clambered in, and the white-straked four-oar surged across the bay, rocking a little as the boys pulled out of stroke. Martin was rowing at the bow, his eyes fixed on Peer, who sat in the stern in command with his eyes dancing, full of great things to be done.

The intricate dance of protein dynamics and their interactions with ions, water, and other small molecules fundamentally influences channel function. To truly elucidate the relationship between structure and function, we must not only appreciate the role of pore dimensions but also the molecular forces governing these alterations. Advanced computational modeling techniques, including molecular dynamics simulations and free-energy calculations, have gained traction, promising to bridge this gap. These methods allow for the exploration of channel behavior over time, capturing the subtle fluctuations that often elude static structural snapshots. Recent advancements in this domain have showcased the importance of allosteric modulation-the phenomenon where the binding of an ion or molecule at one site influences the properties of a distant site. Notably, the identification of allosteric sites within ion channels not only aids in functional annotation but also heralds new therapeutic avenues for drug design. Efforts to characterize these sites have been bolstered by high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy, which permits visualization of conformational states previously obscured in crystallographic studies. Such advances enhance our understanding of how states transition between resting, activated, and inactivated forms. Furthermore, as we continue to expand our catalog of ion channel structures, it is imperative to employ integrative approaches that combine functional assays, structural data, and computational predictions. Employing techniques like patch-clamp electrophysiology alongside structural investigations has begun to furnish a more holistic picture of channel behavior in live cell models. This synergistic approach allows for real-time observation of ion flow, capturing dynamic states that would otherwise remain invisible. Indeed, such methodologies permit the dissection of complex gating mechanisms and underlie the diverse functional repertoire of ion channels. Encouragingly, the evolving realm of artificial intelligence and machine learning offers new opportunities to enhance our understanding. Algorithms trained on vast datasets of ion channel activity can be employed to predict functional outcomes based on structural variations, potentially accelerating the identification of novel targets for pharmacological intervention. These technologies, while still in their infancy, promise to unveil the underlying principles governing ion selectivity and conductance, illuminating how these processes are intricately intertwined with channel architecture. As we look towards the future, a collaborative effort across disciplines-structural biology, biophysics, computational modeling, and therapeutic development-will be critical to overcoming existing limitations. This consolidation of expertise can yield unprecedented insights into how conformational dynamics relate not merely to ion permeation, but also to broader physiological outcomes, elucidating the roles of these channels in health and disease. Moreover, tackling the challenges posed by complex channelopathies-a class of disorders invariably linked to ion channel dysfunction-requires a profound understanding of these proteins at multiple levels. Such insights would propel us towards innovative treatment strategies, underscoring the premise that detailed structural knowledge can translate into clinical applications. The ongoing pursuit of ion channel science stands as a testament to the intricate foldings and unfoldings not just of proteins, but of our understanding itself. In this endeavor, it remains crucial to acknowledge that the conformational landscape of ion channels is shaped both by intrinsic properties and extrinsic influences, driving the elegance of cellular signaling and homeostasis. Through continuous exploration, we shall unravel the intricate web connecting structure, dynamics, and function within the vibrant world of ion channels-a quest that promises to expand our foundational knowledge and inspire future research directions in cellular physiology.

The other reason was that, oddly enough, my mother, before my birth, had dreamed of him so persistently and with particulars so unvaried that she gave my father no option but to change the settled habits of our family and bestow upon me the name, which he despised, of a patriarch whom he underrated. Her dream, repeated, she told me, with exact fidelity and at regularly recurring periods, was that she could see St. Francis standing on a wide sea-shore between sand-dunes and the flood of waters - standing alone there with an apple in his hand, which he held lightly, as if weighing it. By and by, said my mother, she saw three women come slowly over the sandhills from different points, one from the south, one from the north, and one from the west; but they converged as they drew near to St. Francis, joined hands, and came directly to him. The midmost of the three was like a young queen; she on the side nearest the sea was bold and meagre; the third was lovely, but disfigured by a scar. When they were come before St. Francis, after reverences, they knelt down on his right hand and his left, and the queenly woman in front of him. To her, courteously, he first offered the apple, but she laughingly refused it. She of the scar, when it was held before her, covered her face with her hands and shrank away; but the hardy woman craned her head forward and bit into the apple while it was yet in the saint's hand. Then the young queen would have had it if she might, but was prevented by the biter, and the two clamoured for it, silently, by gestures of the hands and eyes, but with haste and passion. At this point, said my mother, her dream always ended, and she never knew who had the apple. She fretted greatly because of it, and was hardly recovered after I was born. My father, who disliked all women except my mother, and, Catholic as he was, had scant respect for the mendicant orders, hated this dream, hated to be reminded of it, hated the name which he had been persuaded into giving me, and, as a consequence, I believe, never loved me. For unnumbered generations of our family we had been Antonys, Gerards, Ralphs, Martins; the name of Francis was unknown to the tree; he never ceased to inveigh against it, and foretold the time when it would stand out like a parasite upon its topmost shoot. "Your Italian ecstatic," he told my mother, "began life by running away from his father and only came back for the purpose of robbing him. He taught more people to live by singing hymns than ever were taught before, and preached the virtues of poverty, by which he intended the comfort it was for the blessed poor to be kept snugly idle by the accursed rich.

However, there are few imaging studies investigating how ATX improves inhibitory function in ADHD patients. Inhibitory control can be measured using various tasks, such as the stop-signal task (SST), go/no-go task (GNGT), and Stroop task. The SST requires participants to respond to a "go" signal as quickly as possible while withholding responses when a "stop" signal occurs shortly after the presentation of a go signal. The GNGT requires participants to respond to target stimuli (go trials) while withholding responses to non-target stimuli (no-go trials). The Stroop task measures interference between color names and font colors (e.g., the word "red" printed in blue ink). Although these tasks measure similar cognitive processes, some differences among them should be noted. First, the SST and GNGT require inhibition of motor responses whereas the Stroop task involves inhibition of verbal responses. Second, the SST and GNGT involve both proactive and reactive inhibition, whereas the Stroop task involves only reactive inhibition. Third, the SST requires subjects to inhibit an already-initiated action, whereas the GNGT and Stroop task require subjects to withhold actions not yet initiated (for reviews see Aron, 2011; Friedman and Miyake, 2004). In the present study, we used the SST and Stroop task to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying improved inhibitory control induced by ATX treatment in adolescents diagnosed with ADHD. We hypothesized that ATX would improve inhibitory control performance through its influence on the NA system, resulting in changes in activation patterns in the prefrontal and parietal cortices. To test our hypothesis, we examined whether ATX affected inhibitory control-related brain regions identified by previous research on healthy adults performing the SST and Stroop task (Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Cai and Leung, 2009; Chikazoe et al., 2007; Garavan et al., 1999; Konishi et al., 1999; Menon et al., 2001; Nee et al., 2007; Roberts and Hall, 2008; Rubia et al., 2003; Sharp et al., 2010; Swick et al., 2008; Xue et al., 2008). Specifically, we focused on two regions known to play key roles in inhibitory control: the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and presupplementary motor area (pre-SMA)/anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) (Swann et al., 2012). Previous studies have demonstrated that the IFG plays a role in reactive inhibition, while the pre-SMA/ACC is involved in proactive inhibition (Aron, 2011; Aron et al., 2004; Chikazoe et al., 2009; Jahfari et al., 2011; Kennerley et al., 2006; Wessel et al., 2013). Furthermore, it has been suggested that the right hemisphere is dominant for inhibitory control (Aron et al., 2004; Chikazoe et al., 2007; Hampshire et al., 2010). Based on these findings, we predicted that ATX-induced improvements in inhibitory control would be associated with increased activity in the right IFG and pre-SMA/ACC. In addition, because the SST and Stroop task differ in terms of what types of inhibitory control are required, we expected to observe differential effects of ATX on activity in the IFG and pre-SMA/ACC across the two tasks.

Her eyes sparkled with excitement, and a flurry of thoughts raced through her mind. A year in the North-a year spent amidst the bustling streets and vibrant lives of her relatives she had heard so much about. "Three months with Aunt Clara, followed by Aunt Elizabeth, Aunt Gertrude, and finally Aunt Marie! What adventures await me," she mused, momentarily lost in daydreams of snug parlors, holiday gatherings, and the myriad of faces that filled her mother's stories. "Patty?" her father's voice cut through her reverie, drawing her back into the warm light of her father's office. "What do you think about this plan?" he asked, leaning forward, his brows furrowed with expectation. The soft glow of the lamp amplified the warmth in his dark eyes, urging her to answer. "I think it sounds wonderful, papa! I've always dreamed of seeing new places and meeting my aunts. And to think of being a housekeeper-of having a home to call my own! It fills me with joy!" Despite her bubbling enthusiasm, however, a flutter of apprehension weighed upon her heart. "But will you be alright here by yourself for so long?" He chuckled, the sound deep and comforting. "Oh, Puss, don't you worry about your old father. I'll manage just fine," he assured her, waving a dismissive hand. "Trust me. It will be good for both of us. And besides, I'll have plenty to keep me busy. Selling lumber doesn't happen overnight, you know." His smile stretched wide, illuminating his earnestness. "And you will be gaining so much-both in life and learning." Patty pondered this, imagining herself in the well-furnished rooms of her aunts' homes. Each with their quirks and eccentricities, like stories waiting to unfold. Would they seek her guidance on their knitting patterns? Would they tell tales of their youth that felt achingly familiar? A giddy sense of wonder enveloped her. "What if I forget my Southern accent?" she asked playfully, mimicking the genteel drawl she had so often heard nestle among her neighbors. "I might end up sounding like a Northern lady-how dreadful!" Her father's laughter filled the room once more, echoing the gentle warmth he had always wrapped around her. "Patty, my sweet girl, I highly doubt you'll lose your charming Southern twang. And even if you do, remember it's not about how you sound but rather the person you are inside that matters most. Your kindness, your humor, your spirit-that's what'll make you who you are, no matter where you live." "But wouldn't it be fun to throw in a few Northern expressions?" she chimed, a mischievous glint in her eye. "I could be the perfect blend of manners and style! A Connecticut belle with a Virginian heart!" "Indeed! A true Renaissance woman!" he teased back, matching her joviality. They shared a chuckle, an affection only such a bond could fuel. As their playful banter settled into a comfortable silence, Patty could feel the underlying undercurrent of change washing over her, like the swell of the tide gently tugging at the shore. Life was preparing to unfold a new chapter, and she was resolutely determined to greet it with open arms and unfettered joy. The shimmery prospect of traveling North captivated her, yet deep down lay the comforting stability of her roots in Virginia, where her father would always be. "Promise, Papa," she said half-seriously, "you won't turn the house into a lumberyard while I'm away?"

An ancient model of recovery can be found in the Yoga Sutra of Patanjali, one which is also embodied in the Four Noble Truths of the Buddha. In its briefest form, this model is an outline of the stages in the healing process, presented here as four questions: 1. What is the nature of the pain that all humans experience? 2. What is the cause of that pain? 3. What will be experienced when the pain is removed? 4. How can the pain be removed? Yoga tells us that before searching for a cure it is important to look deeply into the nature and causes of illness. It is also important to get an idea of how things will be when symptoms have been removed, because otherwise we may have illusions about what recovery will be like. For example, eliminating anxiety is not the outcome of treatment for panicathe outcome is the ability to manage anxious feelings. If we rewrite the four questions of the ancient model, focusing on panic attacks, they might read: 1. What is panic disorder? 2. What causes it? 3. What will life be like for the person who has overcome panic attacks? 4. How is recovery accomplished? Looking for a Cause Biologically oriented physicians have tended to attribute panic symptoms to problems of the nervous system. Jacob DaCosta, a Civil War physician, set the tone when he wrote, "It seems to me most likely that the heart has become irritable from its overreaction and frequent excitement, and that disordered innervation keeps it so." This focus on biochemistry and physiology led to the development of tranquilizers. Not long afterwards, Freud identified a form of anxiety that appeared in discrete, time-limited episodes. "An anxiety attack of this sort," he wrote, "may have linked to it a disturbance of one or more of the bodily functionsasuch as respiration, heart action, vasomotor innervation, or glandular activity." Nearly one hundred years later, this focus on the emotional component of panic has resulted in the psychiatric diagnosis called Panic Disorder. More recently, clinicians have been exploring the role of disturbed breathing in panic attacks. As early as 1950, the physician R. L. Rice maintained that anxiety attacks were often the result, not the cause, of disturbed breathing; now psychotherapies for panic that include breath training are state-of-the-art. (Even so, very little training in this area is available to clinicians.) Those who are familiar with yoga will recognize the classic body-breath-mind triad in these three points of view. But if a single cause for panic disorder exists, it has yet to be discovered. Instead, these three areas seem to interact with one another, forming feedback loops that grow larger if not addressed in some way. For example, if someone is afraid of going to public places, then self-esteem plummets, fears increase, opportunities for relationships are limited, and panic-prone factors such as the fear of being labeled "incompetent" grow.

The more I observed, the thicker the web became, until my movements were constricted by the weight of injustice and complacency. I could no longer sit by as a passive observer, allowing the world to unravel into chaos and brutality before my very eyes. I decided that it was time to act, to cut through the tangled strands of inaction and despair with the sharp blade of determination. Yes, I was but one voice in a cacophony of narratives, but I held onto the belief that a single note could resonate in ways unforeseen, sparking a symphony of change. I began to write, my pen scribbling furiously over pages, a torrent of thoughts pouring out like a deluge, each word a tiny act of rebellion against a towering monolith of ignorance. My manifesto, a call to arms not in the traditional sense of weaponry but as a demand for awareness, connectivity, and compassion, became a vessel through which I voiced my dissent. Our society, as I saw it, was enshrouded in a fog of misinformation, willing to be led astray by those who thrived in the shadows. This corporate hegemony, this unyielding beast that dictated the rhythms of our existence-from the subtle whispers of ads infiltrating our minds to the more blatant acts of political puppetry-had grown too powerful. It fed on the fear of the uncertain, manipulating narratives to convince us that dependency on its offerings was the only path to success, to happiness. My writing was not an attack but rather an awakening, a gentle but firm nudge to remind us of our shared humanity, our collective power to rewrite the story. I hoped for it to be a spark, igniting conversations around dinner tables and within classrooms, encouraging dialogue rather than discord. The transformation wouldn't be easy; the beast we aimed to dismantle had thrived for centuries, learning and adapting with each generation. Yet, as insurmountable as the challenge seemed, history was peppered with the triumphs of resistance, of the few leading the many toward enlightenment, toward freedom. And so, I pressed on, fueled by a belief in the inherently good nature of people, their incredible capacity for empathy and innovation. The narrative offered by the establishment was not the only one, and with every keystroke, every spoken word, I sought to craft a new narrative of equity and justice. My friends joined me in this quest, each contributing their unique perspectives and skills, forming a mosaic of ideas bound by a common purpose. Together, we laid the foundations of a movement, dreaming of the day when the walls around us would crumble, revealing a world where prosperity was not synonymous with exploitation but with dignity, respect, and care for all. Thus, the manifesto was not merely my story but our story, a testament of defiance against the status quo, illuminating a vision for a world anew, held in the tender hope that others would join in this journey, adding their voices to the growing chorus.

"If you want a song on demand, YouTube is the place to go, but if you want to discover music you would go to Pandora or 8tracks," he said. Like Spotify and other services, 8tracks also offers a mobile app that allows users to stream music free to their phones. A brief guide to online music. Owning music "a lot of work' Apple's iTunes is still the world's most popular music vendor, with more than 225 million accounts. One reason streaming music is catching on is the rise of online or mobile apps built on large music providers, such as Apple, that have already secured copyrights on songs, says Eliot Van Buskirk, editor and chief of Evolver.fm, an independent music publication. "You can now build apps on top of apps, and everything is legal and no one is getting sued. In terms of music fans, it is a bit confusing because there are so many options," he said. "I think downloading came from a time when our mp3 players didn't have Wi-Fi connections and our computers did not connect that fast." They have begged, borrowed and stolen points this season and Lowton - like their entire back five - did a superb job. In summer it was a perfect bower of lilies and roses, the great white shafts of the one rising above the broad branches, heavy with flowers, of the other (for in those days there were no standards), and the whole air sweet with the mingled perfume. Liddy Joscelyn, Mrs. Selby's little sister, thought there was no flower-garden in the world like it; but then she had not been away from home since she was twelve, and had not seen much, and there was nothing like it about the White House. That, place, too, had changed in these years. Ralph Joscelyn was the one upon whom the change had told most. It was not that he was much altered in personal appearance, nor yet that he had entirely mended and corrected his ways. Perhaps indeed the alteration visible in him was more due to the fact that there was nobody about the place who crossed him, no one who opposed any strenuous opposition to his will, or dissented from his opinions, than any real alteration. But it was a quieter life which the homestead led, subject to much fewer storms than of old; and Mrs. Joscelyn lived a far less anxious life. The loss of her youngest boy so long ago - though it might not be really the loss of him, since who could tell what day he might re-appear again? - was not a thing, as everyone said, that she could be expected to get over. But the ten years had calmed her, and, what was more, Liddy had calmed her. Lydia had been sent for to her school when her mother was in the depths of this trouble, and she had never been suffered to go back again, her presence being the only consolation which the gentle and unhappy woman was the better for. And after ten years of Liddy's constant company, Mrs. Joscelyn was a very different woman. Joan, who had been so sympathetic with her mother through that last family trouble, without understanding her in the others, understood still less the effect produced by her little sister, who smoothed down everything without any apparent trouble, more by understanding it, so far as appeared, than from anything she did. When Joan's reign terminated, Lydia became the dominant spirit in the house. She was so at fourteen; how much more at twenty! It was not a good thing for the butter and the cheese. The dairy produce of the White House fell off wonderfully. It was no longer half the quantity, and still less was it equal in quality, to the butter of Joan's time. Old Simon never ceased shaking his head over it till his dying day, and went out of human consciousness moaning to himself that "A' things was altered, and no t' half o' t' money coming in." It was he that had always been the salesman, and he felt it deeply.

Here they acquired the knowledge, and tested their ability, to join the National Organization of Girl Scouts; later when they had two Patrols, according to rules, they were enrolled and became known as the Girl Scouts of Dandelion Troop. It was during their first camping season that they went to Blue Beard's cave, one of the local points of interest, and discovered a man who had been injured by two escaped convicts, who, after robbing him, managed to get away. The poor man was unconscious and would have died in that dark and seldom-visited cave on the top of the mountain had it not been for the timely assistance given him by the scouts and their Captain. Back in the mountain camp Mr. Gilroy, the convalescing guest of Dandelion Patrol, explained how he came to visit Blue Beard's cave that day. Thus the girls learned that he was a great admirer of scout work and had been a patron of the Boys' Scout Organization. The junior scouts who had rescued him now decided to enlist his interests in the Girls' Scout Organization, as well. Mr. Gilroy continued his visit at the Dandelion Camp for a few days after he felt completely restored to normal strength, and, during this visit, became deeply interested in Mrs. Vernon's plans and propositions for her girls. Because of the first aid rendered him in his hour of extremity, Mr. Gilroy insisted upon having the Scout Patrol visit his Adirondack Estate the following summer. To this unexpected proposition the girls gladly agreed, providing their parents and Mrs. Vernon would consent and advance the necessary money to defray the costs of the trip. Hence the second summer of the Dandelion Troop of Girl Scouts was spent on the shores of First Lake, one of the Fulton Chain of lakes. There was a boys' camp a mile away, and Mr. Gilroy divided his time and interest between the two camps. The girls won such favor, however, that their host invited them to accompany him the following summer on a camping trip through the Rocky Mountains. Mrs. Vernon, who had founded Dandelion Troop, was the Captain of the scouts; Juliet Lee was their Leader; and Joan Allison was the Corporal. Since that first enrollment, when there were but four girls, namely: Julie and Betty Lee; Joan Allison, and Ruth Bentley, there were now two flourishing Patrols. In Patrol Number One were the first four girls, and Hester Wynant, Amy Ward, Edith and Judith Blake and Anne Bailey. Patrol Number Two was larger, but the members were younger. It was Patrol Number One that had spent the second summer in the Adirondacks. There were but five girls of Patrol Number One who went to the Rockies for the third season. They were: Julie and Betty Lee, Joan Allison, Ruth Bentley and Anne Bailey. Hester Wynant could not go because she had been needed at home.

He walks over to the bed and grabs a pair of sunglasses from the nightstand. He puts them on and walks over to the window again. He looks through the blinds once more and sees that it's still there. He walks over to the closet and pulls out a shotgun. He loads it and quietly opens the bedroom door. INT. JACK'S CABIN - MAIN ROOM - MORNING Jack peeks his head out of the doorway. He scans the room for any sign of life. Finding nothing, he proceeds to move closer to the main entrance. As he approaches the door, he hears a noise behind him. He spins around and fires a shot in the direction of the noise. He quickly checks the chamber of the gun. He reloads it and moves forward again. He reaches the door and slowly opens it. He steps outside and finds nothing. He closes the door and walks over to the table in the backyard. He sets the shotgun down and picks up the newspaper. He unfolds it and reads it. He throws it onto the ground and goes back inside. He walks over to the couch and collapses onto it. He picks up the remote control and flips on the TV. He scrolls through the channels and finds a news report. He watches as the reporter speaks.... as the body count rises in the latest outbreak of violence. Three bodies have been found this week alone. All three cases seem to be related to the latest strain of the virus known as "The Black Death". The victims all suffered from extreme paranoia and delusions before succumbing to their injuries. The police have yet to determine what caused these deaths, but they believe it may have been due to a combination of factors including stress, lack of sleep, and poor diet. In addition to the physical symptoms, the victims also experienced severe mental deterioration which led to their eventual demise. Authorities warn citizens to take precautions against contracting the disease, such as washing hands frequently, avoiding contact with sick people, and staying away from areas where the virus has spread. They advise anyone who feels ill to seek medical attention immediately.

The only sound is the hum of their engine and the rustling of the wind through the open window. TRISH (exhaling slowly) Well, that was fun. DARRY (eyes fixed on the rearview mirror) Yeah, real fun. With the death of his partner and friend he became sole owner of the firm of Callister & Mansfield, and was soon worth a million dollars. His wealth increased rapidly, until it reached nearly three millions, and then came the crash. The tide of prosperity turned, and he found himself almost penniless. The crash took place in February, 1880, and at once Mr. Callister was forced to retire from active business life. He sold his mansion on Fifth avenue and moved into a smaller house on Thirty-ninth street, and from that moment commenced to live like a miser. For four years he kept up appearances, but in reality his income was limited to about six thousand a year. Then he began to sell off his stocks and bonds, and in another two years he had become a millionaire again. In June, 1883, he married again, and his second wife was Miss Edna Ferris, whose father was president of the First National Bank of New York city. She was a woman of thirty-five, and her husband was forty-eight. They lived together happily, and during the last eighteen months or so had begun to feel that they would like to see their daughter married. In the meantime Frank Mansfield had grown up, and though he had gone through college, had done very little towards establishing himself in any particular business. At the age of twenty he was still living with his mother in a modest boarding-house, and his principal source of income consisted in the allowance made him by Mrs. Mansfield. This amounted to fifty dollars per month, and he spent every cent of it in drinking and gambling. On the evening of Christmas Day, 1884, Frank went to a gaming-house in Twenty-third street where he played poker for high stakes, and lost heavily. When he left the game at midnight, he was broke, and the next morning, after a night of debauchery, he felt very bad indeed. He could not find his breakfast, and did not dare to ask for it, fearing that his landlady might suspect something wrong, and he finally set out for work without eating anything. At ten o'clock he entered the banking room of Webster National Bank, and reported for duty. He was looking pale and haggard, and had evidently passed a miserable night. He sat down at his desk, and waited impatiently for eleven o'clock, when the bank opened. As soon as the doors swung open he hurried out, and walked rapidly up Broadway, wondering how he should pass the day. Finally he determined to call on Edna Callister, and see if she could give him some money. He knew that her father was worth over a million dollars, and he thought that he might be able to borrow a few hundred dollars from him. It was a bold step for him to take, considering his present position, but he believed that Mr. Callister would help him. He remembered how the old gentleman used to treat him in former days, and he was confident that he would receive a welcome from him. The interview which followed between the two men has already been related, and as Frank listened to his host's bitter denunciation of his conduct, he was filled with rage and shame. What right had this old skinflint to speak to him in that way? Why didn't he remember that he had been his father's closest friend, and why couldn't he offer to help him instead of abusing him? As he listened to the old man's tirade, he grew more angry every minute, and when the latter had finished, he rose to his feet, and looked straight into the old man's face.

Furthermore, detailed mechanistic studies have indicated that ITZ interferes with essential viral processes by modulating host cell lipid metabolism, a critical element for the formation and function of the membranous replication organelles of many +RNA viruses (van der Schaar et al., 2016). Such findings underscore the multifaceted potential of ITZ as an antiviral agent, particularly for enteroviruses and other related +RNA viruses, where therapeutic options remain scarce. The inhibition of host factors pivotal for virus replication not only mitigates viral proliferation but also reduces the likelihood for resistance development, as the virus must adapt to changes within a complex host cellular environment rather than targeting a direct viral enzyme or protein. Despite these promising developments, further work is required to fully elucidate the spectrum of ITZ's antiviral efficacy and its underlying molecular mechanisms. Notably, comprehensive studies must address the pharmacokinetics and optimal dosing strategies in the context of viral infections, as existing data predominantly stems from its antifungal and anticancer use. Additionally, as ITZ can modulate the activity of key host enzymes such as CYP3A4, the risk of drug-drug interactions necessitates careful consideration and systematic evaluation in future clinical settings. In parallel, research continues to identify additional candidates for drug repurposing, leveraging high-throughput screening methodologies to pinpoint compounds with broad-spectrum antiviral potential. These efforts converge with the necessity to enhance our repertoire of antiviral therapies that can efficiently address emergent viral threats and address longstanding infectious challenges like those posed by enteroviruses. Collaborative endeavors, encompassing virology, pharmacology, and clinical science, remain central to these pursuits, promising to expedite the translation of promising compounds from bench to bedside. Moreover, as our understanding of viral-host interactions deepens, novel antiviral targets will invariably emerge. New developments in structural biology, genomics, and host-pathogen dynamics are poised to inform the next generation of antiviral strategies, offering fresh avenues for therapeutic intervention and broadening the scope for innovative applications of existing drugs. In conclusion, while ITZ's antiviral capabilities offer a compelling glimpse of its potential diversification beyond antifungal and oncological contexts, the ongoing research is vital to confirming its utility and safety as a broad-spectrum antiviral agent. The collective progress in drug repurposing and the identification of host-targeted treatments stand as pivotal components of the broader scientific initiative to mitigate viral disease burden. These efforts illuminate a path toward improved health outcomes by harnessing existing pharmaceuticals for new antiviral roles and by fostering the development of overarching strategies to combat the perennial challenge posed by viruses across the globe.

Breast cancer research continues to evolve as technological advancements shed new light on the complexities of the disease. The advent of personalized medicine and genomic profiling has opened avenues for tailored therapeutic interventions, which aim to improve patient outcomes and reduce the incidence of dire prognoses. Personalized treatment plans, rooted in the unique genetic makeup of individual tumors, are being increasingly adopted, offering hope in the battle against breast cancer. One of the pillars of personalized medicine is the identification of biomarkers that can predict disease progression and response to treatment. Biomarkers such as estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status are critical in determining treatment strategies [14]. ER-positive tumors, for instance, often respond well to hormone therapies, underscoring the importance of proper biomarker assessment in clinical settings [15]. Emerging biomarkers continue to be evaluated for their potential to refine treatment protocols, promising more precise and effective interventions for patients [16]. Innovative therapies are on the rise, with immunotherapy garnering significant attention for its role in harnessing the body's immune system to combat malignancies. Agents such as checkpoint inhibitors are being studied for their efficacy in treating breast cancer, particularly in cases where traditional therapies prove insufficient [17]. Furthermore, combination therapies that include immunotherapeutic agents and other modalities are undergoing rigorous clinical trials, highlighting the potential for multifaceted approaches in oncology [18]. The integration of big data analytics into oncological research is another transformative development, enabling researchers to decipher complex datasets with machine learning algorithms. Such analyses facilitate the identification of novel drug targets and treatment pathways, providing a comprehensive understanding of tumor biology [19]. Predictive modeling, empowered by artificial intelligence, holds promise for anticipating disease progression and therapeutic responses, thus enhancing personalized care [20]. Patient advocacy and awareness continue to play a vital role in the fight against breast cancer, fueling efforts geared towards early detection and prevention. Public health campaigns stressing the importance of routine screenings and lifestyle modifications aim to mitigate risk factors that predispose individuals to breast cancer [21]. Regular mammography, although subject to debate regarding frequency and age, remains a critical tool in early detection initiatives, ensuring timely interventions and better prognoses [22]. Despite the significant strides made in breast cancer research and treatment, challenges persist, particularly in resource-limited settings where access to advanced diagnostic tools and therapies is often constrained [23]. Global health strategies emphasizing the equitable distribution of resources and technology are essential in narrowing the gap in cancer care disparities [24]. International collaborations among research institutions can expedite the dissemination of cutting-edge advancements and standardize care across diverse populations [25]. In conclusion, the fight against breast cancer is multifaceted, with advancements in technology, medicine, and public health advocacy synergistically contributing to improved patient outcomes. Continued investment in research and international cooperation will be paramount in overcoming the challenges that remain. As we advance, the hope is to inch ever closer to a world where breast cancer is no longer a formidable threat but a manageable condition, characterized by effective prevention, early detection, and personalized treatment trajectories.

As I pulled into the parking lot, I was immediately struck by the sheer size of the campus. I had no idea where to go or where to park, and I started to feel a sense of anxiety wash over me. I mean, who wants to be late to church, right? I finally found a parking spot and made my way to the entrance, but as I walked in, I was greeted by...silence. No one was there to welcome me, no one was there to direct me, and I felt like I was just kind of...lost. I looked around and saw a few people scattered here and there, but no one seemed to notice me or my family. I started to think to myself, "Is this really what I want to expose my family to?" But then, something changed. A gentleman approached me with a warm smile and said, "Hey, welcome to Grace Church! I'm so glad you're here. Can I help you find anything?" And just like that, my entire experience shifted. He showed me where to take my kids, helped me find a seat, and even introduced me to a few people in the community. And let me tell you, that one interaction completely changed the trajectory of my experience at Grace Church. Now, I know what you're thinking - "Chris, that's just one story, what's the big deal?" But here's the thing: that one interaction, those first 11 minutes, completely set the tone for my entire experience at Grace Church. And I'm not alone. Studies have shown that 82% of first-time guests will decide whether or not to return to a church within the first 11 minutes of their visit. That's a staggering statistic, and it highlights just how crucial those initial moments are in setting the tone for a person's discipleship journey. So, what does this mean for us as volunteers at Grace Church? It means that we have a unique opportunity to make a lasting impact on the lives of our guests. We have the power to create an environment that is warm, welcoming, and inviting. We have the power to show our guests that we care about them, that we're invested in their lives, and that we want to help them grow in their faith. And it all starts with those first 11 minutes. As volunteers on the Connect Team, we have a critical role to play in creating an environment that is conducive to connection and community. We are the first point of contact for many of our guests, and we have the power to set the tone for their entire experience. So, what can we do to make the most of those first 11 minutes? Well, that's what we'll be exploring in future episodes of this podcast. We'll be talking to members of our Connect Team, sharing tips and strategies for creating a welcoming environment, and discussing why serving is such a vital role in our discipleship journey. But for now, I want to leave you with a challenge. I want to challenge you to think about your own experiences at Grace Church. Think about the times when you felt welcomed and valued, and think about the times when you felt overlooked or ignored. And then, I want to challenge you to ask yourself: how can I be a part of creating a welcoming environment for our guests? How can I use my gifts and talents to make a difference in the lives of those around me? And how can I play a role in helping our guests take their next step in their discipleship journey? Thanks for tuning in to this first episode of the Connecting Volunteers podcast. I'm so excited to be on this journey with you, and I can't wait to see the impact that we can make together.

Let me ask, how do you decide which direction to specialize in? How did you find your niche, Nathan? Nathan: That's a great question, Ryan. I think it comes down to personal interest and where you naturally gravitate in terms of your creative instincts. For me, I've always been fascinated with nature-the way light filters through leaves or how wind moves across a field. That led me down the path of creating organic environments. There's something incredibly rewarding about capturing the untamed beauty of a forest or the rugged cliffs of a coastline. It requires observation and a real sense of how organic forms come together to create complex ecosystems. Ryan: That's fascinating. So, tell me, what do you think are indispensable skills for an environment artist today? Nathan: Flexibility is key, now more than ever. With technology advancing so rapidly, tools and techniques change almost overnight. You need to be adaptable and willing to keep updating your skill set. Software knowledge is critical-mastering tools like Unreal Engine or Unity is almost a given nowadays. But beyond that, understanding lighting and composition can dramatically elevate your work. It's about making something that isn't just technically proficient, but visually stunning too. And, of course, a keen sense for storytelling-every environment you create should contribute to the narrative of the game. Ryan: How have your experiences influenced the environments you create? Nathan: Traveling has been a big influence. Visiting different places opens up endless possibilities and brings authenticity to my work. Whether it's the sun-drenched landscapes of the Mediterranean or the dense, shadowy forests of the Pacific Northwest, firsthand experiences enrich the textures and stories of the spaces I create. Each trip adds a reference library to pull from when constructing worlds-observing little details like how rain changes the color of stone or the way shadows stretch at different times of the day. Ryan: That's amazing. So, what's your process when starting a new environment project? Nathan: Preparation is crucial. I start with research and gather references to build a mood board capturing the essence of the environment I want to create. After collecting images, sketches, and even textures that represent different elements of the scene, I dive into the blocking phase-establishing the basic shapes and layout to ensure everything aligns with the intended vision. Then it's about detailing, texturing, and adding lighting to bring the space to life. I also make a point to iterate frequently, the first draft is rarely perfect, and small adjustments can make a big impact. Ryan: Can you share one of your most challenging projects and what you learned from it? Nathan: Certainly! There was a project where I had to recreate a historic environment-complete with architecture no longer existing in its original form. The hardest part was working with incomplete data while maintaining accuracy and authenticity. I discovered the value of consulting with historians and using historical texts to reconstruct the world visually. It was a deep dive into history, demanding patience and attention to detail. But it taught me that good art, especially in games, requires more than just artistry; it requires research and passion. Ryan: That's inspiring, Nathan. Thank you for sharing your experiences and your journey with us. Is there any parting advice you'd give to aspiring environment artists? Nathan: Always stay curious and never stop learning. There's no single path in this industry, and being open to new ideas and techniques will keep your work fresh and exciting.

A typical composition of ferritic ODS steels is Fe-14Cr-3W-0.4Ti-0.25Y2O3 (wt%) [1]. There are some enduring uncertainties regarding the specific mechanism(s) of NC formation. Various possible routes have been proposed, which include: a supersaturated solid solution containing Y, Ti and O is produced by room temperature MA that decomposes and re-precipitates as NCs during high temperature consolidation [12]; MA simply fragments Y2O3 to such a fine scale that to most characterisation techniques it appears "dissolved" and precipitation is more akin to coarsening to a scale where Y2O3 can again be resolved [13], and the Y2O3 becomes amorphous during MA and the subsequent precipitation is better described as (re-)crystallization [14]. All these mechanisms are supported by some experimental evidence, and one may predominate under certain conditions or certain alloys, or all may operate but to differing extents. Despite these uncertainties, MA followed by HIP to full density is the most well-established route to manufacture ODS alloys reported in the literature. However, very high pressures (200 MPa) and long soak times (4 h) during HIP are normally required to achieve high density, bulk ODS alloys [15,16], which can result in excessive grain coarsening and a high manufacturing cost. Thus, more cost-effective processes for the manufacture of ODS steels are under exploration, in particular those that offer the potential for scale-up beyond the laboratory scale. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) is a relatively new sintering-based technique [17] in which the powder to be consolidated is loaded into an electrically and thermally conductive graphite mould and a large DC pulsed current (1000-5000 A) is applied under a uniaxial pressure. When current passes through the graphite mould (and the powder if it is electrically conductive), the powder is heated both from the outside (the mould acts as a heating element) and inside (due to Joule heating from the intrinsic electrical resistance of the powder material). SPS is characterised by very fast heating (up to 2000 C/min) and cooling rates and short holding times (minutes) to achieve near theoretical density [17]. Thus SPS occupies a very different time-temperature-density space in powder consolidation maps when compared with conventional methods, such as hot pressing sintering and HIP with ramp rate of 50-80 C/min and a few hours holding time. Although SPS has been studied for a rapidly growing number of materials [17], there are only a small number of studies on the fabrication and microstructural characterisation of ODS steels processed by SPS, briefly reviewed below.

As Chris Graham struggles to come to terms with his diagnosis, he is determined to raise awareness about the devastating impact of familial Alzheimer's on his family. He hopes that by sharing his story, he can help dispel the myth that Alzheimer's is solely a disease of old age. 'People think it's just about forgetting where you put your keys or what day it is, but it's so much more than that,' he said. 'It's a cruel and unforgiving disease that robs you of your memories, your identity, and your dignity.' Mr. Graham's diagnosis has also had a profound impact on his family, particularly his three children, who are still coming to terms with the fact that their father has a terminal illness. 'It's hard to explain to them what's happening, but I want to be honest with them,' he said. 'I want them to understand that I'm not going to be around forever, and that they need to make the most of the time we have together.' Despite the challenges ahead, Mr. Graham remains determined to make a difference. He has become an advocate for Alzheimer's research, and is working with charities to raise awareness and funds for a cure. 'I know I won't be around to see a cure in my lifetime, but I want to make sure that my children and grandchildren don't have to go through what I'm going through,' he said. Mr. Graham's story is a powerful reminder of the devastating impact of Alzheimer's on families. 'We need to work together to find a cure for this devastating disease, and to support families like Chris's who are affected by it.' As Mr. Graham faces the challenges of living with Alzheimer's, he is determined to stay positive and make the most of the time he has. 'I'm not going to let this disease define me,' he said. 'I'm going to keep fighting, and I'm going to keep raising awareness until we find a cure.' His bravery and determination are an inspiration to us all, and a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there is always hope.

The intricate regulation of c-Jun by ubiquitin ligases not only underscores its significance in cellular dynamics but also highlights a strategic interplay between oncogenic and tumor suppressive mechanisms in the context of neoplastic transformations. Indeed, this balance is pivotal in maintaining homeostasis within cellular environments, as unchecked c-Jun activity can precipitate aberrant cellular proliferation, fostering a conducive milieu for tumorigenesis (Schmidt et al., 2014). The activity of c-Jun is further modulated by post-translational modifications beyond phosphorylation, including acetylation, which has been shown to fine-tune c-Jun's transcriptional potency and influence its interaction with co-activators (Wen et al., 2019). Moreover, the complex relationship between c-Jun and growth factors emphasizes a broader ecological downturn of signaling pathways that converge upon key oncogenic nodes. For example, the activation of the MAPK signaling cascade, through extracellular stimuli, can result in sustained activation of c-Jun, thus linking environmental cues to cellular responses that inform proliferation and survival (Zhang et al., 2015). Such insights reveal that aberrant signaling mechanisms not only enhance c-Jun's induction but also redefine cellular fate decisions that are critical in cancer development. The potential of targeting c-Jun, both directly or through its E3 ligases, has spurred interest in therapeutic modalities aimed at reversing malignant phenotypes. Current strategies examining the inhibition of Fbw7 have painted a compelling picture; blocking Fbw7's activity could inadvertently lead to the accumulation of c-Jun, consequently heightening the oncogenic signal (Harris et al., 2019). Conversely, small molecules or peptides that mimic the phosphodegron could inadvertently enhance degradation, presenting tantalizing therapeutic opportunities. Therefore, a holistic comprehension of c-Jun's signaling apparatus remains essential for innovative treatment designs targeting aberrant c-Jun-driven oncogenesis. Furthermore, the role of c-Jun in metabolic reprogramming within the tumor microenvironment has more recently gained traction, with studies revealing its involvement in metabolic pathways that support cell survival in the often nutrient-poor conditions characteristic of solid tumors (Tao et al., 2021). This novel facet of c-Jun biology speaks not only to its historical function as a transcription factor but also as a central player in the broader metabolic landscape, influencing pathways such as glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation to adapt and thrive under duress. Interestingly, the context of c-Jun activity can vary considerably depending on the cell type and environmental factors, pointing to the importance of contextual regulation in the pursuit of understanding tumor biology. For instance, findings from various models demonstrate that in certain contexts, particularly within specific immune cells, c-Jun may exert anti-inflammatory effects, thus suggesting a dual function dependent on cellular context (Wang et al., 2014). This context-dependency also raises fascinating questions concerning the timing and nature of c-Jun engagement with oncogenic programs-potentially revealing novel window periods ripe for targeted interventions. Thus, as research continues to shed light on the multifaceted nature of the c-Jun regulatory network, it becomes increasingly clear that a stratified approach to understanding its roles in both physiology and pathology is essential. Whether regarded as a canonical oncoprotein or viewed through the lens of its regulatory associations, c-Jun exemplifies complexity, integration, and adaptability-qualities that are hallmarks of successful cellular signaling pathways. More comprehensive explorations of c-Jun's partnerships and regulatory networks are anticipated to not only enhance our grasp of its fundamental biology but also unlock new avenues for therapeutic exploration within cancer and beyond.

The man who came with the barrow told us the mail had set him down the morning before at the "Royal George"; that he had inquired what inns there were along the coast, and hearing ours well spoken of, I suppose, and described as lonely, had chosen it from the others for his place of residence. And that was all we could learn of our guest. He was a very silent man by custom. All day he hung round the cove, or upon the cliffs, with a brass telescope; all evening he sat in a corner of the parlor next the fire, and drank rum and water very strong. Mostly he would not speak when spoken to; only look up sudden and fierce, and blow through his nose like a fog-horn; and we and the people who came about our house soon learned to let him be. Every day, when he came back from his stroll, he would ask if any seafaring men had gone by along the road. At first we thought it was the want of company of his own kind that made him ask this question; but at last we began to see he was desirous to avoid them. When a seaman put up at the "Admiral Benbow" (as now and then some did, making by the coast road for Bristol), he would look in at him through the curtained door before he entered the parlor; and he was always sure to be as silent as a mouse when any such was present. For me, at least, there was no secret about the matter; for I was, in a way, a sharer in his alarms. He had taken me aside one day and promised me a silver fourpenny on the first of every month if I would only keep my "weather eye open for a seafaring man with one leg," and let him know the moment he appeared. Often enough when the first of the month came round, and I applied to him for my wage, he would only blow through his nose at me, and stare me down; but before the week was out he was sure to think better of it, bring me my fourpenny piece, and repeat his orders to look out for "the seafaring man with one leg." How that personage haunted my dreams, I need scarcely tell you. On stormy nights, when the wind shook the four corners of the house, and the surf roared along the cove and up the cliffs, I would see him in a thousand forms, and with a thousand diabolical expressions. Now the leg would be cut off at the knee, now at the hip; now he was a monstrous kind of a creature who had never had but one leg, and that in the middle of his body. To see him leap and run and pursue me over hedge and ditch, was the worst of nightmares.

For the case of P2P microgrids, the existing literature has focused on the behavior of prosumers using a microgrid [22,23]. As in [24,25], this paper takes a bottom-up perspective of potential prosumers and assesses the value that these potential prosumers anticipate gaining from participation in a P2P microgrid before joining it. To ensure the authenticity of this bottom-up approach, this work presents an exemplary real-world case involving potential microgrid prosumers in Bangladesh. Those participants are users of so-called solar home systems (SHSs), which are DC standalone energy systems. More than five million of these systems are installed throughout the country [26]. Bangladesh was chosen from among other countries in the Global South, such as India and Tanzania, that also have a high potential for the installation of P2P microgrids and first initiatives implementing such systems [24,27]. The results from this case in Bangladesh can also be generalized to other countries because the electricity access demand profiles are very comparable across different countries, as described by the World Bank's multitier energy access framework [28]. Measures targeted at increasing user motivation that have been discussed in the literature are mainly centered around so-called "prosumer management" [29] systems. These management systems mainly involve assessing the situation from a top-down perspective and identifying the criteria that a prosumer needs to fulfill to be eligible for participation in the microgrid [29]. In this work, the complementary perspective is taken, with the goal of identifying the criteria that a microgrid needs to fulfill to qualify as an attractive option for a potential prosumer who is presently using only a standalone system. This approach was chosen because in P2P microgrids, communities depend on each user's motivation to share electricity. This motivation can be fragile if it is not assessed and adequately addressed. Sustainable microgrid development can be difficult to achieve. A delicate balance between incentivizing asset creation and promoting community-wide energy access needs to be found. Energy justice can decrease [30], and asset inequality can increase [31]. In general, benefits can be stronger for certain user groups [32,33]. It is acknowledged that the sustainable operation of these systems needs to account for potentially contradictory goals [19]. Therefore, design criteria that reflect different aspects of sustainability need to be fulfilled to ensure sustainable long-term development. In summary, our key contributions in this paper are threefold and follow research questions Q1-Q3. First, we analyze fundamental drivers for users to engage in microgrid development. Second, we outline targeted measures on how to stimulate users to participate in microgrids. Third, we give design criteria to ensure sustainable peer-to-peer microgrid advancement. To our knowledge, this work presents the first systematic assessment from the user perspective to identify the key drivers of success for P2P microgrid initiatives. The original research presented here is complemented by the presentation of experience from the practical application of the proposed measures.

His estates were confiscated, and sold to one Richard Lambert, a merchant of London, whose daughter, as will appear hereafter, became afterwards the wife of William Lilly, the astrologer, who has left his memoirs behind him, and who was an actor in the scenes which I shall describe. Lambert was a stanch Republican, and one of the most active in promoting the sale of the forfeited estates of the Cavaliers, although he did not despise the opportunity of making his own advantage by purchasing them. He was considered one of the wealthiest men in the city, and lived like a nobleman. As soon as he had purchased Arnwood, he sent down agents to take possession, and direct what repairs should be made before he removed there with his family, intending to make it his country residence. These agents were Mr Corbould and Mr Heatherstone, both well known to Lambert, the former having served his apprenticeship with him, and become a partner in his business; the latter was a distant relation. They arrived at Arnwood, and took up their temporary abode at the house of Mrs Beverley, the widow of the late owner, who still remained in possession until her jointure should be paid. Her two sons were away serving in the Royalist army, and she had nothing left but her furniture and plate, which had been reserved when the sequestrators came down to examine into the affairs of her husband. Mr Corbould and Mr Heatherstone immediately commenced repairing the mansion-house, and in the meantime made themselves very comfortable in the apartments allotted to them, and fared sumptuously upon the remains of the stock of deer in the park, which were daily killed for their use. Mr Corbould was a widower without encumbrance, and about forty-five years old; he was a tall, good-looking man, with dark hair slightly tinged with grey, and remarkably mild blue eyes. Although he was not exactly what you would call a handsome man, yet he was pleasing in appearance, and gentlemanlike in his manners. Mr Heatherstone was about twenty-eight years old, rather below the middle height, stoutly built, fair-complexioned, and possessed of a countenance which indicated great shrewdness and intelligence. He was a bachelor, and had been brought up to no profession, but had always been employed by Mr Lambert in various ways connected with trade. He was remarkable for his humour, and the jokes which he constantly indulged in, even during the gravest consultations. It may easily be imagined, that in such a lonely situation, surrounded by woods and fields, these gentlemen were thrown much together, and that a degree of intimacy took place between them. Indeed, they had been acquainted previously, as they had often met at Mr Lambert's table; and as they sat together over their wine, they naturally spoke freely to each other, and imparted their hopes and wishes. One evening, after they had dined, they were sitting smoking their pipes, and drinking their port wine, when Mr Heatherstone observed, "Corbould, do you know that I think Mr Lambert intends giving us a hint that he means to marry us?" "I cannot say that I have perceived any such intention," replied Corbould; "but if he does, it can only be in general terms, for he knows little about women." "Very true; but he knows something about his daughters; and depend upon it, if he does marry us, it will be to one or the other of them." "I presume so; but really, Heatherstone, I hardly think that such is his intention.

They had blundered upon their rich find by pure chance. For in the southwest, close upon the Mexican border, in the most lonesome corner of the most lonesome county of thinly settled Arizona, turning back from a long and fruitless prospecting trip, they had paused for one last, half-hearted venture. One idle stroke of the pick in a windworn bare patch had turned up - this! So Pete Johnson's thoughts were of millions; not without a queer feeling that he wouldn't have the least idea what to do with them, and that he was parting with something in his past, priceless, vaguely indefinable: a sharing and acceptance of the common lot, a brotherhood with the not fortunate. Riding to the northwest, Pete's broad gray sombrero was tilted aside to shelter from the noonday sun a russet face, crinkled rather than wrinkled, and dusty. His hair, thinning at the temples, vigorous at the ears, was crisply white. A short and lately trimmed mustache held a smile in ambush; above it towered such a nose as Wellington loved. It was broad at the base; deep creases ran from the corners of it, flanking the white mustache, to a mouth strong, full-lipped and undeniably large, ready alike for laughter or for sternness. The nose - to follow the creases back again - was fleshy and beaked at the tip; it narrowed at the level bridge and broadened again where it joined the forehead, setting the eyes well apart. The eyes themselves were blue, just a little faded - for the man was sixty-two - and there were wind-puckers at the corners of them. But they were keen eyes, steady, sparkling and merry eyes, for all that; they were deep-set and long, and they sloped a trifle, high on the inside corners; pent in by pepper-and-salt brows, bushy, tufted and thick, roguishly aslant from the outer corners up to where they all but met above the Wellingtonian nose. A merry face, a forceful face: Pete was a little man, five feet seven, and rather slender than otherwise; but no one, in view of that face, ever thought of him as a small man or an old one. The faint path merged with another and another, the angles of convergence giving the direction of the unknown water hole; they came at last to the main trail, a trunk line swollen by feeders from every ridge and arroyo. It bore away to the northeast, swerving, curving to pitch and climb in faultless following of the rule of roads - the greatest progress with the least exertion. Your cow is your best surveyor. They came on the ranch suddenly, rounding a point into a small natural amphitheater. A flat-roofed dugout, fronted with stone, was built into the base of a boulder-piled hill; the door was open. Midnight perked his black head jauntily and slanted an ear. High overhead, a thicket of hackberry and arrow-weed overhung the little valley.

A survey by led by the University of Manchester published in August reported that more than a quarter of rheumatoid arthritis patients prescribed anti-inflammatory medication failed to take it properly within six months of the treatment's start. Meanwhile an analysis of patients' urine samples by the University of Leicester revealed in April that least one in four people with high blood pressure has abandoned their medication or takes too little to combat their risk of heart problems. Researchers are now trying to fathom why so many patients fail to take medicines that can so powerfully enhance their health. Unwanted side-effects must play an important part. But Leila Collins, a chartered counselling psychologist who has worked with patients on their ability to stick to medication says that lack of lasting willpower is an important factor. One basic problem is that patients' willpower fades over time as their powers of resolve fade and they begin to feel better thanks to the medication. So their resolution to keep to the prescribed regimen disappears before they get to the end of the course of drugs,' says Collins, who practises in North London and Hertfordshire. 'Some doctors are very good at putting the fear of God into patients, saying things such as "Take your medicines or I won't be responsible for the what happens to you."' But psychological research has found a range of less draconian, and rather surprising, ways in which people can boost the strength of their willpower. According to Professor Baumeister, one simple way to preserve your banks of mental energy is by not wasting it agonising over needless decisions. He cites the case of president Obama, who generally only wears blue or grey suits so that deciding what to wear is one decision he doesn't have to make. 'Likewise, you don't want to waste willpower making decisions about breakfast. Having a set morning routine is much better,' says he says. Another trick is to take short and simple exercise. A study performed at the University of Exeter, two years ago, set out to discover what might help people to resist the temptation of fattening foods. The investigators asked volunteers either to rest for 15 minutes or to spend the time going for a walk. They were then all asked to perform a series of dull but demanding computer tasks. Next to their keyboards was positioned a bowl of chocolates. At the end of the test, the researchers reported in the journal Appetite that the volunteers who had gone for a walk ate half as much chocolate as those who had simply rested. The researchers believe that light exercise energises people sufficiently to revive their brains' flagging resources and thus bolster their will power. Another scientifically backed way to boost willpower is to replenish your brain with fuel and rest. Glucose can help with this, according to a study in the journal Psychological Science in 2008.

If there is insufficient water in the steam generators then the heat will be transferred to the atmosphere through the steam generator relief valves. As long as there is water in the steam generators to act as a condensing medium, the steam flow through the relief valves will not cause them to open. Heat can also be rejected to the environment if the PHTS is depressurized and the moderator heat exchanger valves are opened. This would allow moderator to boil and steam to be released to the environment. If all other heat sinks are unavailable, heat could be dumped to the containment atmosphere by depressurizing the PHTS. However, this action requires operator intervention and would result in high radiation doses due to the release of fission products and radioactive noble gases. The CANDU design employs a single containment structure, which is a large reinforced concrete structure lined with a thin carbon steel membrane. The containment includes the reactor building, which houses the nuclear components, the vacuum building, which contains the shield tanks, and the service area. The service area contains various support facilities such as the control room, the diesel generator room, etc. There are no penetrations between the reactor building and the vacuum building; however, there are many penetrations between these buildings and the service area. The containment is designed to withstand the internal pressure loads resulting from a LOCA. Containment venting systems are available to reduce containment pressure in the event of a severe accident. These include the filtered containment venting system (FCVS) and the passive autocatalytic recombiner (PAR) system. The FCVS was added after Fukushima to provide an additional means of reducing containment pressure. It uses a portable fan unit to draw air from the containment dome space and discharge it to the exhaust stack after passing through a filter. The PAR system is located inside the containment and uses catalytic plates to recombine hydrogen with oxygen in order to reduce the potential for combustion. In this perspective, the left vOT region would be functionally equivalent to the orthographic word lexicon of cognitive dual-route models of reading (Coltheart et al., 2001; Coltheart, 2004). Initial evidence for this came from Kronbichler et al. (2004), who showed that activation in left vOT was affected by the lexical frequency of written words with reduced activation for high relative to low-frequency words. This was interpreted as reflecting easier access to frequently relative to rarely used whole-word representations. Although other early neuroimaging studies failed to find a sensitivity to lexical frequency in left vOT regions (Fiez et al., 1999; Fiebach et al., 2002), more recent studies consistently replicated this effect (Hauk et al., 2008a, 2008b; Graves et al., 2010). Other studies have also shown that left vOT exhibits reduced activation to familiar compared to unfamiliar orthographic forms of the same phonological words (e.g., TAXI vs. TAKSI; Kronbichler et al., 2007, 2009; Bruno et al., 2008; Van der Mark et al., 2009; Twomey et al., 2011). These "orthographic familiarity" effects are also interpreted as reflecting orthographic whole-word coding in left vOT. In addition, Schurz et al. (2010) found a lexicality (words vs. pseudowords) by length (short vs. long letter strings) interaction effect on activation in left vOT. Specifically, a length effect (= higher activation for long relative to short letter strings) was present for pseudowords but absent for words. The absence of a length effect for familiar words is expected when letter strings are assimilated by whole-word representations. Specific support for orthographic whole-word coding in left vOT was also provided by an fMRI priming study (Glezer et al., 2009), which found that the priming effect on vOT activation present for word repetition (coat-coat) disappeared when the prime differed in just one letter from the target word (boat-coat). In contrast, for pseudowords the priming effect was dependent on the number of shared letters. In the debate around the VWFA it has also been questioned whether left vOT is restricted to visual (word) processing as assumed by the original VWFA hypothesis (Dehaene et al., 2002). Instead, it has been argued, the region might have a polymodal function (Price and Devlin, 2003). Interestingly, a similar interpretation has recently been presented by Dehaene and Cohen (2011) who have suggested that the VWFA might be a "meta-modal" reading area. This was based on studies showing the left vOT activation in congenitally blind individuals during reading of Braille (e.g., Buchel et al., 1998; Reich et al., 2011). Examples are: packages UFZ (Niswonger et al., 2006), HYDRUS-1D (Seo et al., 2007) and metaSWAP (Van Walsum and Supit, 2012; De Lange et al., 2014). Comparisons between different soil hydrological models and crop growth models have been given by several authors like Baroni et al. (2010), Eitzinger et al. (2004), Wolf (2002), Bastiaanssen et al. (2004), Kramers et al. (2005), Vanderborght et al. (2005), Kersebaum et al. (2007), Bonfante et al. (2010), Bonfante et al. (2011), Rallo et al. (2012), Rotter et al. (2012), Ahuja et al. (2014), Groenendijk et al. (2014), Oster et al. (2012), Camargo and Kemanian (2016). These comparisons served different purposes but generally concluded that each model works best in the domain and for the purpose it was designed for. We choose to work with the numerical model SWAP (Soil-Water-Atmosphere-Plant) (Kroes et al., 2017), which simulates the soil moisture flow in the one-dimensional vadose zone and is capable of simulating detailed crop growth. The original version of this model was called SWATR (Feddes et al., 1978). The most-cited publication about the successor of this model, called SWATRE, was written by Belmans et al. (1983). Developments continued, and recently SWAP version 4.0.1 (Kroes et al., 2017), was released (swap.wur.nl), which includes the WOFOST 7.17 model for crop growth (Boogaard et al., 2014). Supit (1994) was the first to publish a detailed system description of the WOFOST model. Recent versions are published on the internet (wofost.wur.nl) and an overview of 25 years WOFOST modelling is given by De Wit et al. (2018). A global sensitivity analysis of an earlier version of SWAP has been presented by Wesseling et al. (1997). These authors concluded that knowledge of the boundary conditions was more important than knowledge of the soil parameters. Shafiei et al. (2014) present parameter uncertainty of the SWAP model and its effect on model prediction within the generalized likelihood uncertainty estimation (GLUE) framework for two irrigated agricultural fields in a dry region of Iran. Parameter uncertainty analysis of soil hydraulic parameters showed that in spite of similarity of soil texture in both the considered fields, the estimated parameters (i.e. posterior distribution) exhibit different behaviors.
