In this study, we investigated how water quality and macrophyte composition vary across seasons and years at a regional scale, and if patterns of variation could be related to specific pond characteristics. We addressed the following research questions: (1) What are the seasonal and annual variations in water quality and macrophyte composition? (2) Can the observed patterns of variation be explained by differences between ponds? (3) Do the responses of water quality and macrophyte composition to seasonal and annual variations differ? To answer these questions, we analysed data collected during a three-year monitoring campaign in 20 natural ponds located in Northeast Germany. The studied ponds were chosen to cover a wide range of characteristics, i.e., different sizes, surrounding land uses, and varying degrees of isolation from other water bodies. This allowed us to capture the variability among ponds, which is expected to be much larger than the variability within individual ponds. We used linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) to analyse the effects of seasonality and inter-annual variability on the water quality and macrophyte composition of the studied ponds. The study area is situated in the northern part of Brandenburg, Germany (53 14'48"N, 13 17'24"E). It is characterized by a flat topography with elevations ranging from 30 m to 100 m above sea level. The region was covered by glaciers during the last ice age, which shaped the present-day landscape. Most of the soils developed under periglacial conditions over the course of the past 12,000 years. As a result, soil texture is dominated by sand and gravel deposits, with peaty gley soils occurring locally. The mean annual temperature ranges from 8 C to 9 C, while the average precipitation varies from 500 mm to 600 mm (Patzold et al., 2008). The 20 studied ponds (Fig. 1a) are distributed over a total area of about 400 km. They are located in a predominantly agricultural landscape and have a maximum depth and a maximum size of 5.18 ha. The ponds differ in terms of their shape, size, hydrology, vegetation structure, and degree of connectivity to other waterbodies. Sixteen ponds are connected to streams via inlets and outlets, whereas four ponds lack any direct connection to other waterbodies. Some ponds are surrounded by forests, others are bordered by agricultural fields or grassland. Three of the studied ponds are classified as nature reserves. In addition, two ponds are protected as special conservation areas according to the Habitats Directive (Council Directive 92/43/EEC). One pond is listed as a cultural heritage site and another one is used for recreational fishing. Detailed information on each pond is given in Table 1. The studied ponds were selected based on previous field surveys conducted by the local administration. From the set of potential ponds, we selected those that had not been modified substantially (e.g. by dredging) during the past 50 years. Furthermore, we chose ponds that exhibited a high diversity of shapes, sizes, and surrounding land use types. The resulting selection represents well the variety of natural ponds in the study region. Dubbed the Charlotte's Web Medical Hemp Act of 2014, the bill is named after Charlotte Figi, a young Colorado girl whose parents have campaigned nationwide for easier access to medical marijuana after successfully controlling their daughter's seizures with cannabis oil. Since her story became known, a growing number of parents have flocked to Colorado, hoping for similar success. The Charlotte's Web cannabis strain, developed by the Realm of Caring nonprofit organization in Colorado Springs, is in high demand, in part because of the attention it's received in the media. Many families wait months for a batch to be grown and processed into cannabis oil. Perry's bill, however, would apply to any cannabis strain with a THC content of less than 0.3%. Charlotte's Web and similar strains not only have minimal THC, they have high levels of cannabidiol, another chemical. A growing body of anecdotal evidence suggests that cannabidiol can effectively control seizures, though there are no published studies to support its use. It's easy to find critics who say parents should follow a more traditional route. "There is no evidence for marijuana as a treatment for seizures," Rep. John Fleming, R-Louisiana, a physician, claimed during a congressional hearing last month. "We hear anecdotal stories, and that's how myths come about." Fleming and others point out that a pharmaceutical version of cannabidiol oil, called Epidiolex, is being tested in clinical trials. But many children aren't able to get into the trials. Haleigh Cox is disqualified because she has type-1 diabetes. Others aren't willing to wait several months to be enrolled. "With Epidiolex, there just aren't enough seats at the table," said Mark Knecht, a father from Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania, whose story helped inspire Perry's bill. His daughter Anna, 11, has epilepsy and suffers anywhere from a handful of seizures a day to more than 100, despite her four anti-convulsant medications. Knecht, the chief financial officer of a large Christian medical nonprofit, says Anna has been evaluated at several top hospitals but couldn't land a spot in the Epidiolex trial. Twenty-three states and the District of Columbia have laws on the books allowing medical marijuana for a variety of conditions. But even as states rewrite their regulations, federal law remains the same: Marijuana is illegal to grow, sell or use for any purpose. Under the 1970 Controlled Substances Act, marijuana is listed on Schedule 1, meaning it has "no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse." To backers of reform, the Catch-22 is familiar: Marijuana is restricted in large part because there is little research to support medical uses; research is difficult to conduct because of tight restrictions. A series of memos from the Justice Department has said that arresting individual medical marijuana users is not a priority, and a 2013 memo added that federal prosecutors should not target large commercial operations except on a case-by-case basis.

The child had declared with angry tears and stampings of her small foot, that it was not true, that her mother was good and dear and beautiful; but they had paid no heed to her. The father had sternly commanded silence and sent her away; and the mother had not returned. So she had sobbed her heart out in the silence of her own room, where every object reminded her of the lost mother's touch and voice and presence, and had gone about the house in a sullen silence unnatural to childhood, thereby making herself more enemies than friends. Of her father she was afraid. She shrank into terrified silence whenever he approached, scarcely answering his questions, and growing farther away from him every day, until he instinctively knew that she hated him for her mother's sake. When a year had passed he procured a divorce without protest from the innocent but crushed wife, this by aid of a law that often places "Truth forever on the scaffold, Wrong forever on the throne." Not long after, he brought to his home as his wife a capable, arrogant, self-opinionated woman, who set herself to rule him and his household as it should be ruled. The little girl was called to audience in the gloomy study where sat the new wife, her eyes filled with hostility toward the other woman's child, and was told that she must call the lady "Mother." Then the black eyes that held in their dreamy depths some of the gunpowder flash of her father's steely ones took fire; the little face darkened with indignant fury; the small foot came down with fierce determination on the thick carpet, and the child declared: "I will never call her mother! She is not my mother! She is a bad woman, and she has no right here. She cannot be your wife. It is wicked for a man to have two wives. I know, for I heard Mary Ann and Betsey say so this morning in the kitchen. My mother is alive yet. She is at Grandfather's. I heard Betsey say that too. You are a wicked, cruel man, and I hate you. I will not have you for a father any more. I will go away and stay with my mother. She is good. You are bad! I hate you! I hate you! I hate you! And I hate her!" - pointing toward the new wife, who sat in horrified condemnation, with two fiery spots upon her outraged cheeks. "Jemima!" thundered her father in his angriest tone. But the little girl turned upon him furiously. "My name is not Jemima!" she screamed. "I will not let you call me so. My name is Dawn. My mother called me Dawn. I will not answer when you call me Jemima." "Jemima, you may go to your room!"

People considered at risk of flu are offered a free jab every year. They include: the over-65s; pregnant women; patients with certain medical conditions including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (including emphysema) and diabetes; those living in a care home; carers and healthcare workers. Children aged two to four are also offered vaccination (as a nasal spray). Turning to the second dimension - the structural assumptions imposed - the identification procedures employed in previous studies typically rely on strong assumptions regarding the form of the utility or motivational function meant to represent preferences. For instance, the ring-test is based on the assumption of linear preferences; the studies by Cabrales et al. (2010), Blanco et al. (2011) and Iriberri and Rey-Biel (2013) employ identification procedures based on the piecewise linear model originally introduced by Fehr and Schmidt (1999) as a description of self-centered inequality aversion and later extended by Charness and Rabin (2002) to allow for other forms of distributional concerns and thereby assume piecewise linearity; and Andreoni and Miller (2002), Fisman et al. (2007) and Cox and Sadiraj (2012) check consistency with - and estimate parameters of - standard or modified constant elasticity of substitution (CES) utility functions. Summing up the above discussion we conclude (i) that there is neither an agreement in the literature on what the relevant set of distributional basic motivations - defined as the manner in which people care about the (material) well-being of others - is, nor on how to delimitate distributional types; and (ii) that existing studies employ identification procedures that rely on strong structural assumptions as, for instance, linearity, piecewise linearity or standard or modified CES forms. By using a systematic approach based on a small set of primitive assumptions on preferences, the present paper offers an improvement in both dimensions. It shows (i) that this set of assumptions naturally results in a well delineated, mutually exclusive and comprehensive distinction between nine archetypes of distributional concerns; and (ii) that this set gives rise to a simple non-parametric experimental test - the Equality Equivalence Test (EET) - that discriminates between the archetypes according to core features of preferences rather than properties of specific modeling variants or functional forms. Kevorkian had sprung onto the national scene right about the time I was starting medical school. He fascinated my parents, and during the rare occasions I attended a cocktail party with them, the conversation among their friends seemed to always turn to him. He invoked strong emotions in so many people he had never met. "During your interview for medical school, right there in that building, when they asked you, 'Why do you want to be a doctor?' what did you answer?" I asked. "What did you answer?" he replied somewhat harshly. Throughout the two-and-a-half hour interview, he fluctuated wildly between being downright combative and hostile to being sweet and fatherly. It was almost as if he desperately wanted me to understand all the decisions he had made in his life. By this point, I knew he was just asking me rhetorically, so I waited patiently for him to collect himself. "I told them all the stuff they wanted to hear. Oh, I want to heal people and I want to join medicine, because it is the noblest of all professions... noble, yeah right." "Is medicine a noble profession?" I continued. "What do you think?" he once again fired back. I waited. "No, it is not," he finally answered. Dr. Jack Kevorkian is as opaque a person as I have ever met. But despite his crazed rants - often about the Ninth Amendment to the Constitution, complete with a defense of James Madison and trashing of Thomas Jefferson (that guy... he just took all the credit!) - Kevorkian still knows how to make a point. Not surprisingly, he strongly advocates assisted suicide, or euthanasia, or what he calls "patholysis." Terms matter to Kevorkian, and this is the term he prefers when describing the "medical procedure" he performed on at least 130 people, by his own count. "Path means disease or suffering," he said to me. "And lysis, means destruction," I said. "Exactly," he answered. Patholysis, he repeated. The destruction of suffering. As we walked around campus, Kevorkian drew a lot of attention. Many stopped to say hello, ask for an autograph or take a picture. He spent time with every person, asking about them and their role at the university. It was about an hour into the interview when I realized Kevorkian was trying to make a broader point. It started when I cited a study about the people he had "patholysed." "It says here that in at least five of the people, there was no evidence of any disease on autopsy." I let that hang in the air for a second. He seemed a little stunned that I had found this study. He shook his head slightly, and looked again at his lawyer, with no intention of addressing the point I had just made. "Recently, I had three former CEOs of companies - perfectly healthy - who called me up and told me they wish to die." He let that sink in. It was my turn to be stunned.

Proteins were mostly assigned to a single bin, but for some proteins with functions in diverse biological processes it was necessary to correspondingly assign to multiple bins. While initially focused on metabolic processes, the MapMan framework rapidly evolved to include regulatory processes such as transcription factors and signaling pathways as well as biotic and abiotic stress responses. The ontology was exploited as the foundation for the MapMan application, which allows quantitative omics data to be visualized on functional pathways (Thimm et al., 2004). It also allows users to investigate enriched pathways and to functionally explore differentially expressed genes and accumulated metabolites. Although MapMan was originally developed for use with the model species A. thaliana, it was later adapted to other species by similarity transfer and manual curation (Ling et al., 2013). This proved to be infeasible as a long-term approach, due to the rapid increase in the number of species for which genomics data were available. The tool Mercator was therefore developed to allow automatic annotation of plant protein sequences with MapMan terms (Lohse et al., 2014). Mercator relied on sequence similarity and, when appropriate, protein domains from InterPro (Mulder and Apweiler, 2007) and CDD (Marchler-Bauer et al., 2013) that had been manually assigned to the bins. However, this approach resulted in many annotations to abstract levels, partly due to the absence of appropriate bins for the new species. In terms of describing proteins, the most commonly used framework is the Gene Ontology (GO), which is widely used across all life forms. The GO framework defines terms and their relationship to each other as a means to formalize protein description (Gene Ontology Consortium, 2014). The terms are partitioned in three specific categories (named "Biological Process," "Molecular Function," and "Cellular Component"). These GO terms are arranged as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), where a child term may have more than a single parent. Generally, a single protein can expect to be annotated with a multitude of GO terms originating from each category. While GO is beneficial for a rich annotation, it can pose difficulties when it is used to visualize omics data because the multiple annotations lead to a strong redundancy (Jantzen et al., 2011). The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) ontology is a collection of databases covering many different aspects of biology (Kanehisa et al., 2017). Of these, the KEGG Orthology (KO) database is the closest equivalent to the MapMan framework, using a similar hierarchical structure of protein function terms. KO encompasses genes from both eukaryotes and prokaryotes, and while it was traditionally focused on metabolism, it has been expanded to include a wider range of biological processes. Other frameworks such as PlantCyc (Schlapfer et al., 2017) and Plant Reactome (Naithani et al., 2017) focus primarily on metabolic processes, and, while highly detailed within their area of focus, do not cover a broad range of biological processes and thus cannot easily be compared with MapMan.

Why, one glimpse of that combination was enough to make me clap my hand over my roll and back away from the spot! Just then, though, I notices another gent steppin' up for a squint at the monstrosity, and I can't help lingerin' to see if he gets the same kind of a shock. He's sort of a queer party, too, - short, stoop shouldered, thin faced, wrinkled old chap, with a sandy mustache mixed some with gray, and a pair of shrewd little eyes peerin' out under bushy brows. However, Fickian theory is unable to describe the moisture diffusion process when significant mass loss due to chemical decomposition occurs simultaneously with moisture absorption [33]. Other models have also been documented to describe the moisture diffusion kinetics, such as the Langmuir model [34]. Fig. 1 depicts 3 moisture uptake vs. time curves that are representative of (a) a classical Fickian diffusion three-stage curve with no mass loss, (b) a diffusion curve affected by mass loss taking place, and, (c) a 'true' diffusion curve when mass loss takes place without affecting the moisture uptake measurements. For the assessment of moisture absorption characteristics, the gravimetric methodology has been largely employed by many researchers in both fully immersed and humidity-exposed conditions [3,15,20,33,35,36]. However, interpretation of gravimetric data becomes challenging when swelling, polymer relaxation and chemical decomposition processes take place at the same time as moisture absorption [37]. Dimensional changes due to swelling differentiate the 'free-volume' [20]. Chemical decomposition results in significant mass loss. This mass loss, which stems from the initial dry mass of the material, masks the mass gain due to moisture absorption [33]. Here an innovative method of probing moisture absorption in polymer composites via Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) [38,39] is presented. Impedance spectroscopy is efficiently employed to capture moisture ingress independently of mass loss. Preliminary experiments of the present work were published in [40]. Conventional EIS has been extensively used to study corrosion of metallic materials [41] and metal coatings [42]. Dielectric property measurements have been applied to monitor curing of polymer matrix composites [43,44], environmental degradation [45], damage [46-48] as well as the dispersion of nano-particles in polymer matrices [49,50]. Impedance spectroscopy measurements have been used to study moisture movement in mortar based construction materials [51,52] in addition to the more recent use in medical applications for moisture monitoring of wound dressings [53]. EIS is very sensitive to the presence of water due to the charge associated with the dipoles of water molecules [39,54]. Impedance measurements are expressed by the dielectric properties of the interrogated polymer composite coupled with the dielectric properties of the absorbed moisture [55]. The amount of moisture absorbed can be correlated directly with changes in the dielectric properties of the system. Impedance measurements involve the imposition of an AC potential field in a capacitor-like form. This field polarizes both the polymer and the water molecules (dipole polarization of the polar groups) inducing a frequency dependent displacement. Maffezzoli et al. have used dielectric measurements to monitor water uptake characteristics in epoxy resin materials exposed to hygrothermal environments. Permittivity changes were used to determine moisture diffusion coefficient values and were evaluated against conventional gravimetric measurements. However, quantitative measurements of water uptake were not feasible. In the same work, an embedded dielectric sensor was adopted to record permittivity changes of samples that had to be removed from the aging medium for measurement [56].

At the bottom was a small line: 'Lady Candidates need not apply.' I read it and was very upset. For the first time in my life I was up against gender discrimination. Though I was not keen on taking up a job, I saw this as a challenge. I had done extremely well in academics, better than most of my male peers. Little did I know then that in real life academic excellence is not enough to be successful? After reading the notice I went fuming to my room. I decided to inform the topmost person in Telco's management about the injustice the company was perpetrating. I got a postcard and started to write, but there was a problem: I did not know who headed Telco. I thought it must be one of the Tatas. I knew JRD Tata was the head of the Tata Group; I had seen his pictures in newspapers (actually, Sumant Moolgaokar was the company's chairman then). I took the card, addressed it to JRD and started writing. To this day I remember clearly what I wrote. 'The great Tatas have always been pioneers. They are the people who started the basic infrastructure industries in India, such as iron and steel, chemicals, textiles and locomotives. They have cared for higher education in India since 1900 and they were responsible for the establishment of the Indian Institute of Science. Fortunately, I study there. But I am surprised how a company such as Telco is discriminating on the basis of gender.' I posted the letter and forgot about it. Less than 10 days later, I received a telegram stating that I had to appear for an interview at Telco's Pune facility at the company's expense. I was taken aback by the telegram. My hostel mate told me I should use the opportunity to go home and see my parents. I agreed and telephoned to inform my father, who is himself an engineer, that I was coming home. He was thrilled. He arranged for the train tickets and even came to receive me at the station. From there he took me straight to the company's personnel department. The security guard was dumbfounded when he saw that it was a young girl who had come for the interview. He could not believe his ears when I said that I was there with regards to a letter from the Personnel Department. There was a special enclosure for female candidates on the premises. Was this done for me?' I do not know. But I was escorted into the room. A few minutes later, since the company had not sent any recruitment executive, a worker was sent to escort me to Mr. Moolgaokar's chamber. Obviously he was instructed to accompany me directly to Moolgaokar's room. We entered the room and for the first time in my life I saw JRD. A pleasant smile brightened up his face as he extended his hand. 'Unfortunately our Chairman was away and so his son-in-law, who is also an employee of the Tatas, has kindly agreed to interview you,' he said. 'Tatas have always believed that talent in India is not limited to the urban areas. In fact it is the rural folk that need nurturing, else they would get lost in the maze of poverty,' he said. 'It seems you are running away from the rural masses,' he smiled. I was nervous now, sweat was pouring from my brow, and a thousand fears ran through my mind. What would happen if I failed to get a decent job? This is not Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation, is it?

He began to take an interest in his studies, and in a short time he was one of the best scholars in the school. He also took to athletics, and it was soon evident that he was a natural athlete. He was a capital runner, a good cricketer, and an excellent swimmer. In fact, he was a marvel of strength, agility, and endurance. I, on the other hand, who had been considered a good all-round fellow, began to fall off. I was no longer the best at cricket, and my running, which had been my strong point, was no longer superior to that of others. It was the same with my studies; I was no longer at the top of my class. It seemed as if he had absorbed all my energies, and was using them for his own benefit. "I remember one day," continued Captain Mallett, "we were to have a great athletic meeting, and I was training hard for the mile race. I was confident of winning, but on the day of the meeting, I felt strangely languid and tired. I ran badly, and was beaten by a long way. The winner was, of course, my old enemy. From that day on, I began to think that there was something in the Mal Occhio. I don't mean that I believed he had the power of casting a spell over me, but I did think that he had a sort of unconscious influence, which affected me unfavorably. I have seen him since, and I have always felt the same thing. I have tried to shake it off, but I couldn't. I have even tried to make friends with him, but he has always refused. He seems to bear me a grudge still, and I am convinced that he would do me an injury if he could." Bertha's eyes were wide with excitement as she listened to Captain Mallett's story. She had never heard anything so strange and fascinating in her life. "And what is he doing now?" she asked, her voice barely above a whisper. "He is a successful man," replied Captain Mallett. "He has made a fortune in business, and is now a prominent figure in society. But I have heard that he is not popular. People seem to fear him, and I have been told that he has a reputation for being ruthless in his dealings. I don't know if it's true, but I do know that I would not like to be in his power." The conversation was interrupted by the entrance of the tea-tray, and the guests began to move towards the table. Bertha, however, remained seated, lost in thought. She was wondering if Captain Mallett's story was true, and if the Mal Occhio really existed. She looked around the room, half-expecting to see the man of whom Captain Mallett had spoken, but he was not there. Still, she felt a shiver run down her spine, and she couldn't shake off the feeling that something strange and ominous was lurking in the shadows, waiting to pounce.

These findings underscore a critical paradigm shift in the way hydrological systems are viewed in light of climate volatility. Adaptation strategies are urgently required to address the inevitable transformations that hydraulic regimes will experience. Policymakers must prioritize the integration of climate projections into water management plans to ensure sustainable usage and preservation of water resources amidst changing circumstances. A multifaceted approach-incorporating various stakeholders, from governance bodies to local communities-will facilitate the development of resilient infrastructures capable of withstanding environmental stressors. In particular, the nexus between water availability and agricultural practices is vital, as farming activities consume a considerable proportion of global freshwater resources. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) notes that agriculture will be significantly threatened by climate change, impacting crop yields and increasing competition for dwindling water resources (IPCC, 2014). Implementing sustainable agricultural practices, such as precision irrigation and drought-resistant crop varieties, can mitigate adverse impacts while enhancing food security. There lies an opportunity for synergy between climate adaptation and agricultural innovation; investing in research and development could lead to more resilient crop systems that can endure prolonged droughts or excessive rainfall. Moreover, the implications of altered hydrological cycles extend beyond agriculture. Urban areas, particularly those heavily reliant on consistent water supply, could face unprecedented challenges. Urban sprawl without adequate water management systems may exacerbate flooding, while prolonged droughts threaten water availability, necessitating the execution of integrated urban water management frameworks. Retrofitting existing infrastructures to accommodate stormwater harvesting and groundwater recharge will be crucial in urban environments, rendering them less vulnerable to the extremes of water availability linked to climate change. Concurrently, protecting and restoring natural ecosystems, such as wetlands, plays a pivotal role in bolstering resilience against climate extremes. Wetlands act as natural buffers, absorbing excess water during floods and storing it during dry periods. Thus, conserving these ecosystems not only supports biodiversity but also reinforces the water management framework by enhancing the natural regulation of hydrological cycles. Through conservation efforts, the detrimental effects of climate change can be mitigated, fostering an environment where natural processes can restore balance amid alterations in river flow patterns. Nonetheless, the challenge of equitable water distribution and access remains an urgent concern. As climate change exacerbates water scarcity, vulnerable communities may bear the brunt of these changes, leading to conflicts over resources and increased social disparities. Addressing these inequalities must be central to any water management strategy, ensuring that marginalized populations are not left to suffer the consequences of shifts in hydrological conditions. Collaborative governance, transparent policymaking, and ongoing public engagement will empower communities, fostering a collective responsibility toward sustainable water management. As our understanding of climate-induced changes in hydrology deepens, academia must bridge gaps in knowledge with actionable insights for policymakers. This entails rigorously testing and refining hydrological models while translating complex scientific findings into accessible concepts for stakeholders. Partnerships between scientists, local governments, and civil societies can foster innovative solutions that address both mitigation and adaptation strategies. In conclusion, the intersection of climate change with water resource management requires immediate and sustained action across all levels of governance. The integration of scientific research with practical frameworks will be crucial in navigating the complexities of future hydrological dynamics. With effective strategies in place, societies can transition toward a more resilient and sustainable future, capable of weathering the storms of climate change.

As the controversy surrounding Kaci Hickox's quarantine continues to unfold, medical professionals and civil liberties advocates are weighing in on the issue. Dr. Irwin Redlener, director of the National Center for Disaster Preparedness at Columbia University, expressed concern that the mandatory quarantine policy could have unintended consequences. "By quarantining someone who is not symptomatic and has tested negative for Ebola, we may be creating a disincentive for healthcare workers to volunteer to help combat the outbreak in West Africa," he said. "We need to strike a balance between protecting public health and protecting the rights of individuals." Meanwhile, the American Nurses Association (ANA) has issued a statement supporting Hickox and calling for a more nuanced approach to Ebola protocols. "Nurses are on the front lines of this crisis, and we need to ensure that they are treated with dignity and respect," said ANA president Pamela Cipriano. A major problem found in industrial flare operations is the lack of devices for monitoring and providing a feedback response to optimize combustion efficiency and pollutant emission indices (i.e., the mass of a particular species or class of species emitted per unit mass or energy of gas sent to the flare). As a result, a number of petrochemical companies have been found to be in violation of flare performance standards [8,9]. The EPA has identified over-assisting, in the form of over-steaming or over-aeration, as the primary cause of regulatory noncompliance of flares [10]. Part of the challenge in defining a properly operated assisted flare is due to a lack of published data regarding combustion efficiency and emission indices. The EPA's latest AP-42 publication on industrial flares [11] relies solely on data from a 1983 study by McDaniel [12] when reporting on emission indices for total hydrocarbons (THC), oxides of nitrogen (NOx), and soot for elevated flares. The scope of McDaniel's study was limited to one design of a steam- and air-assisted flare burning 80% propylene and 20% propane. McDaniel [12] recommended a steam-to-fuel gas mass flow rate ratio of 0.4 for a combustion efficiency of at least 98%, while the air flow rate for the air-assisted flare was not provided due to the proprietary nature of the flare stack design. An emission index of 3.34 g THC/kg fuel, where THC is expressed as a methane equivalent, was reported [11]. The average NOx emission indices for air- and steam-assisted flares were calculated to be 1.25 g NOx/kg fuel and 0.66 g NOx/kg fuel, respectively [12]. Soot concentrations were reported as 40 1/2g of soot per L of combustion products for lightly smoking flares, 177 1/2g/L for average smoking flares, and 274 1/2g/L for heavily smoking flares [11]. Since McDaniel [12] was unable to determine the dilution ratio of the sampling system, the soot concentrations describe the mass of soot per volume at the sample location, and are not emission indices, so not particularly useful in determining environmental loading of BC. In a recent industrial-scale study, Torres et al. [13] conducted an investigation to characterize flare emissions at an outdoor facility with uncontrolled ambient conditions and burning a mixture of 80% propylene and 20% natural gas. A key finding from Torres et al. [14] was that the combustion efficiency of steam-assisted flares with steam-to-fuel gas mass flow rate ratios of 0.5 - 1.0 exceeded 95%. For air-assisted flares, studies done by Torres et al. found that the combustion efficiency remained above 96.5% at air-to-fuel gas mass flow rate ratios below 24 [7]. Torres et al. [15] reported NOx emission indices that ranged from 10% to 120% of the values reported by EPA AP-42 [11].

Furthermore, they showed that the macropores facilitate the diffusion of the encapsulated insulin from the MPs into the aqueous environment [39]. In this study, we aimed to develop a novel strategy to enhance the encapsulation efficiency of MPs. The concept of the proposed approach was inspired by the enhanced permeability and retention effect (EPR) observed in tumor tissue [40,41]. It was shown that the EPR effect could lead to an increased accumulation of nanoparticles (NPs) in tumors compared to normal tissues [42]. Therefore, we hypothesized that it would be possible to increase the encapsulation capacity of MPs by taking advantage of the EPR effect. In addition, the incorporation of macroporous structure was also expected to improve the encapsulation efficiency of MPs. We believe that the combination of these two factors would allow for achieving higher encapsulation efficiency than previously reported values [39] without any modification on the existing system. To achieve this goal, we designed and fabricated macroporous MPs loaded with insulin via O/W emulsion/solvent extraction method. The resulting MPs were characterized with respect to their morphology, porosity, pore size distribution, encapsulation efficiency, and in vitro release profile. The influence of macroporosity on the encapsulation efficiency was investigated by comparing the results with those obtained from the MPs without macropores. Finally, the release mechanism of insulin from the MPs was analyzed using a mathematical model. The schematic illustration of the fabrication steps is presented in Figure 1. First, an insulin solution was prepared by dissolving 10 mg of lyophilized human insulin powder (Novo Nordisk Pharma Ltd.) in 500 1/2L of ethanol. Then, 2 mL of poly(d,l-lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA; Mw = 45 kDa, Sigma-Aldrich) dissolved in chloroform (Sigma-Aldrich) was added dropwise to the insulin solution under constant stirring. After complete dissolution of PLGA in the insulin solution, the mixture was transferred to another vial containing 50 mL of water/ethanol (50% v/v). Subsequently, the emulsion was homogenized using an ultrasonic probe sonicator (Vibra cell VCX130, Sonics & Materials Inc.) at 60 W power output for 30 s. The emulsified mixture was then extracted with 200 mL of de-ionized water for 4 h to remove the organic solvent. The resulting suspension was centrifuged at 15,000 rpm for 10 min to collect the MPs. The supernatant was discarded and the collected MPs were washed three times with de-ionized water. The final pellet was lyophilized overnight (Labconco FreeZone 6 Plus) to obtain the dry MPs. The MPs with no macropores were prepared following the same procedure except for the absence of 0.3 g of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS; Sigma-Aldrich). Figure 1 Schematic illustration of the fabrication process of MPs. PLGA: Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid); SDS: Sodium dodecyl sulfate; MP: Microparticle. The morphology of the MPs was evaluated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Hitachi SU8230, Japan). Before SEM imaging, the samples were sputter coated with platinum (JEOL JFC-1600 Auto Fine Coater). The surface area and average particle size of MPs were determined using a dynamic light scattering (DLS) instrument (Malvern Zetasizer Nano-ZS90, Malvern Instruments Ltd.).

'We estimate there are more than 500,000 counterfeit electrical products on sale every day,' he says. And while we may think we're being savvy shoppers by buying cheaper, unbranded alternatives, the reality couldn't be further from the truth. These knock-offs contain inferior components such as poor-quality plastic casings, wiring and circuitry which overheat easily, causing fires. In addition, they lack the fuses that make official chargers safe. 'They don't have any protection built into them,' says Mr Curtler. 'When you overload them they will burn out.' The problem is that, as with the case of Katie Vines, you won't know until it's too late. Katie had just returned home from hospital with her newborn when she received the chargers she'd ordered online. She immediately plugged one into the mains and attached her phone. But within seconds, the charger exploded, sending sparks flying across the room. 'I screamed and ran downstairs to get my boyfriend Chris,' recalls Katie. 'I was really scared because I had Aimee upstairs in her cot. I didn't know if the house might catch fire. We unplugged it straight away.' The couple threw the broken charger away and put the second one in a drawer. But several months later, when Katie's own charger broke, she decided to try the spare. This time, the explosion was even louder and stronger. 'The charger literally blew apart and I had to throw it out of the window,' she says. 'Chris called the police. He was worried that something similar might happen to someone else.' The police came round and took the charger away. Katie was horrified when they told her that they believed the device had come from China. 'You hear stories about these things blowing up and you never expect it to happen to you,' she says. 'Now I'm always checking the wires on our plugs to make sure they aren't frayed and I never leave them switched on when we're not at home.' With the boom in the smartphone market, the number of people unwittingly putting themselves at risk is increasing all the time. The sale of fake Apple iPhone chargers alone grew by 139 per cent between 2011 and 2012. In fact, according to the Intellectual Property Office, almost half of all counterfeit items seized at UK borders last year were electrical goods, such as chargers and hair-straighteners. But despite the danger, experts say that people remain oblivious to the risks. 'Many consumers think that because a product looks genuine, it is,' says Mr Curtler. 'But it's not always obvious that a product is dangerous until it explodes or catches fire. By then it's too late.' It is not known whether the charger involved in the Sheffield fire was unbranded. However, experts point out that even branded chargers can pose a hazard if used incorrectly. Earlier this week, Apple issued a warning to customers not to charge their iPhones with third-party power adaptors following the death of a Chinese woman, Ma Ailun, who was electrocuted when she answered a call on her handset while it was charging. A coroner ruled that Ms Ma, 23, had been using an unofficial charger. Apple responded by offering to exchange any third-party USB adapters for its own brand for less than half price.

Furthermore, chlorination remains a widely utilized method, renowned for its ability to inactivate a broad spectrum of pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, and protozoa. The process involves adding a chlorine solution to water, providing both an immediate and residual disinfectant effect. This method is particularly suited for urban and peri-urban areas, where more infrastructure supports widespread distribution and storage. However, challenges such as taste alterations and the formation of potentially harmful by-products necessitate careful management and ongoing research to maximize its benefits and mitigate drawbacks. The integration of combined flocculation/chlorination techniques represents another innovative approach to address water quality issues. This dual-stage process initiates with the addition of a flocculant to clump together fine suspended particles, facilitating their removal. Subsequently, chlorination ensures the effective disinfection of the clarified water. Such a comprehensive treatment process underscores the necessity of adapting technology to fit local conditions, ensuring that solutions are both practically viable and culturally acceptable. Moreover, developing a sustainable water management framework requires concerted efforts from policymakers, scientists, and community leaders. Collaborations between governmental agencies, non-governmental organizations, and local communities can foster the development and implementation of tailored water strategies. Community engagement is crucial, as it enables residents to partake in the stewardship of their local water resources, promoting practices such as watershed protection, pollution prevention, and conservation efforts. Education and awareness campaigns are integral components of this endeavor, empowering individuals with knowledge about the significance of water quality and the role they can play in its preservation. By instilling a sense of responsibility and providing accessible tools for water monitoring and purification, these initiatives can contribute significantly to public health advancements. As we continue to grapple with global water challenges, it is imperative that diverse innovative solutions are explored and implemented with urgency. The ever-evolving landscape of technology offers promising prospects, yet at its heart, the commitment to safeguarding water remains an enduring mission. By weaving together traditional wisdom and modern ingenuity, society can work towards unlocking universal access to clean and safe water-a fundamental pillar for prosperity and well-being across the globe. Ultimately, addressing water quality issues requires a holistic perspective that considers environmental, social, and economic dimensions. By fostering collaboration and innovation, we can build a resilient framework to ensure the sustainability of this precious resource for current and future generations. The road ahead may be challenging, yet with unwavering dedication, the vision of a world where every individual enjoys their fundamental right to clean water is within reach.

This thesis presents research investigating the effect of borehole design and construction on the yield and water level response of pumped boreholes in fractured rock aquifers, and provides insights into modelling approaches to predict these responses. Borehole design and construction methods vary significantly across different countries and regions, reflecting differences in geological setting, climate, and regulatory requirements. Despite this variation, the majority of boreholes are constructed using similar techniques and materials, such as steel casing, slotted screens, and grout. Although these materials have been used successfully for decades, there remains little published information regarding their suitability and performance in fractured rock aquifers, where they may experience high stress, high strain rates, and high temperatures. A series of laboratory experiments were undertaken at Cardiff University to investigate the mechanical properties of steel pipe under conditions representative of those encountered when drilling boreholes in fractured rock aquifers. The results suggest that the structural integrity of steel pipes may be compromised if they are installed in fractured rock aquifers with high confining stresses (>10 MPa) and are exposed to rapid temperature changes (>1 C/min). If the structural integrity of the steel pipe is compromised, then significant borehole deformation will occur, leading to reduced hydraulic efficiency and increased energy consumption. These findings highlight the importance of considering the effects of fracture closure and thermal expansion/contraction when designing and constructing boreholes in fractured rock aquifers. Borehole construction practices also influence the hydraulic efficiency of a borehole by controlling the amount of gravel pack material used to fill the annulus between the borehole wall and the screen, and the permeability of the resulting gravel pack. This study investigated the hydraulic conductivity of gravel packs formed from crushed limestone and sandstone. Results indicate that the hydraulic conductivity of gravel packs made from crushed limestone was up to three orders of magnitude lower than that of gravel packs made from crushed sandstone. Differences in hydraulic conductivity between the two materials reflect differences in particle size distributions, and highlight the importance of selecting appropriate gravel pack materials to maximise hydraulic efficiency. When designing and constructing boreholes in fractured rock aquifers, it is critical to consider the interaction between the borehole and the surrounding fractures and matrix blocks. Poorly designed and constructed boreholes can lead to inefficient extraction of water and increased energy consumption. A numerical model was developed to investigate the effect of borehole design on the yield and water level response of pumped boreholes in fractured rock aquifers. The model was calibrated against data collected from a monitored borehole located near Newport, South Wales. The results show that the yield of the borehole was sensitive to the diameter of the steel casing and the length of the screen. However, the model did not reproduce the observed decline in yield with decreasing groundwater level below the screened interval, suggesting that other factors, such as the presence of additional inflow horizons and the geometry of the fractures intersected by the borehole, are influencing the yield and water level response of the borehole. The results presented in this thesis demonstrate the importance of considering the effects of borehole design and construction on the yield and water level response of pumped boreholes in fractured rock aquifers. Future work should focus on developing better models that capture the complex interactions between boreholes and fractured rock aquifers, and improving our understanding of the factors that control the yield and water level response of pumped boreholes in fractured rock aquifers.

By the late 19th century, these technological advancements laid the groundwork for exploring cinematic experiences. Esteemed inventors continued to face the challenge of creating a seamless and continuous depiction of motion pictures. Thomas Edison and his assistant, William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, became central figures in this quest. Edison's invention, the Kinetoscope, premiered in the early 1890s. It was a device that allowed individuals to view moving pictures through a peephole. Dickson developed a camera called the Kinetograph, which used Eastman's celluloid film to capture a series of images. Though the Kinetoscope did not project images onto a screen, it was pivotal in fostering public interest in motion pictures. At the same time in France, Auguste and Louis Lumiere, two brothers with a keen interest in photography and science, were devising their own apparatus. By 1895, they had invented the Cinematographe, an engrained testament to human ingenuity. Their breakthrough lay in achieving both recording and projecting capabilities within a single machine. Capable of projecting moving images to large audiences, their device marked a significant leap in the cinematic realm. Their ability to reproduce real-life scenarios, such as the renowned "Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat Station," astonished viewers and ignited global enthusiasm for motion pictures. Simultaneously, inventors like Georges Melies explored film's artistic potential, transcending its initial technical achievements. Melies, originally a magician, saw motion pictures as a platform for storytelling and illusion. His innovative techniques, including double exposure, time-lapse photography, and hand-painted color, mesmerized audiences. Films such as "A Trip to the Moon" in 1902 showcased narrative cinema, paving the way for motion pictures as an art form. In the United States, Edwin S. Porter, an Edison Studios employee, further explored narrative structures in film. His acclaimed work, "The Great Train Robbery" in 1903, employed dynamic editing techniques, cross-cutting, and on-location shooting to enhance dramatic tension. Such innovations encouraged filmmakers to experiment with film language and mechanics, guiding the nascent industry toward storytelling and diverse thematic exploration. By the early 20th century, motion pictures had become an essential cultural and artistic medium. The establishment of film studios in Hollywood transformed the industry into a burgeoning enterprise. Visionary filmmakers, actors, and technicians collaborated to create films that captivated audiences worldwide. Silent films gave way to sound films with the advent of synchronized dialogue and the Vitaphone system, further expanding the film industry's reach and influence. The marriage of technological innovation and creative expression in motion pictures continues to evolve. Digital technology, green screen special effects, and CGI have expanded filmmakers' abilities to craft intricate narratives and dazzling visuals, captivating modern audiences in new and profound ways. The pioneering spirit that characterized motion study analysts like Muybridge and Marey persists in today's technologically advanced and artistically rich film industry, wherein motion pictures remain an extraordinary combination of art, science, and entertainment, continuously reshaping human cultural landscapes and narratives.

This network includes the left angular gyrus (AG), left hemispheric language areas, such as the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), the middle (MTG) and superior temporal gyrus (STG), as well as the supramarginal gyrus (SMG; Klein, Moeller, Glauche, Weiller, & Willmes, 2013, 2014; Menon, 2014; Peters & De Smedt, 2018). Regions of this arithmetic network are typically engaged whenever we solve simple arithmetic problems (e.g., 2 * 8; 5 * 6) by directly retrieving the answer from memory (Delazer et al., 2003, 2005; Grabner et al., 2009; Ischebeck et al., 2006, 2009). However, arithmetic fact retrieval is also prone to errors that are not random. Indeed, false answers are frequently operand related (Campbell, 1994, 1997), i.e., solutions to problems differing by one operand (e.g., the answer 42[6 * 7] to the problem 6 * 8). This pattern indicates that arithmetic fact retrieval is influenced by interferences that affect the correct retrieval of arithmetic solutions. A well-established task that is particularly suited to examine interference during arithmetic fact retrieval is the operand-related-lure (OR) task. In this task, single-digit multiplication problems are simultaneously presented with a correct or incorrect solution on a computer screen, and participants have to decide whether the presented solution is correct or not. Importantly, incorrect equations are divided into problems presented with a solution that is related to the correct result (operand-related-lure, belonging to the same multiplication table; e.g., 7 * 2 = 16[8 * 2]) or with a solution that is not related to the correct result (operand-unrelated-lure; e.g., 7 * 2 = 13). Behavioral studies have revealed an OR interference effect, consisting of lower accuracy and longer response times (RTs) in the operand-related compared to the operand-unrelated condition (e.g., Domahs et al., 2007; Zbrodoff & Logan, 1990). It has been argued that this behavioral effect reflects the associative interference characteristics of the arithmetic fact network as well as the cognitive resources (i.e., semantic control) that are needed to overcome them (Campbell, 1987; Zbrodoff & Logan, 1986). To date, only a handful of studies have investigated the neural correlates of the OR interference effect. All of them have used event-related potentials (ERPs) to better understand the temporal brain dynamics associated with the interference effect (e.g., Domahs et al., 2007; Jost, Hennighausen, & Rosler, 2004; Niedeggen & Rosler, 1999). For instance, Niedeggen and Rosler (1999) provided evidence that the OR interference effect is associated with a negative brain potential in healthy adults, peaking between 300 and 500 msec. after the solution onset (i.e., thereafter called N400 effect). Furthermore, an amplitude difference was found in the late positive component (LPC), which was characterized by a positive peak between 540 and 620 msec. after solution onset. Whereas the difference in the LPC effect was present at all electrodes, the difference in the N400 effect was observed over posterior electrodes of the right hemisphere.

Yet, while these insights furnish a foundational understanding of the attraction dynamics inherent within multi-sided platforms, they fall short of elucidating the intricate web of competitive interactions that shapes the very viability of these organizational forms. The once clear demarcation between competitors and collaborators is increasingly blurred as firms navigate the challenges posed by rapidly changing user preferences, technological advancements, and market entry barriers. The interplay of these factors necessitates a more nuanced examination of how firms position themselves strategically within their respective ecosystems, not merely as standalone entities, but as integral components of a complex marketplace where the actions of one platform can significantly influence the fortunes of others. In this regard, the concept of platform envelopment emerges as a critical consideration for firms seeking to augment their competitive edge in the digital arena. As elucidated by Eisenmann et al. (2011), platform envelopment occurs when a multi-sided platform leverages its existing user base, technological capabilities, and resources to encroach upon and potentially absorb the functionality of a rival platform. The confluence of enhanced capabilities and existing infrastructure allows firms to diversify their value propositions, often leading to a rapid escalation of competition-as seen in cases where tech giants extend their reach into adjacent markets. Amazon's foray into grocery delivery with Amazon Fresh exemplifies this phenomenon, posing a significant challenge to established retailers and meal delivery services alike. Consequently, multi-sided platforms must cultivate not only a robust internal landscape characterized by user engagement and retention, but also a keen awareness of the external competitive landscape. This awareness can manifest in various strategic maneuvers: platforms may choose to engage in aggressive marketing campaigns to attract users from competitors, foster strategic partnerships to broaden their service offerings, or even pursue mergers and acquisitions as a means of consolidating market power. The complexities of these competitive interactions underscore the necessity of a holistic strategic framework that integrates both internal platform governance and external competitive positioning. Furthermore, as the proliferation of multi-sided platforms intensifies, the implications for regulatory scrutiny and antitrust considerations become increasingly salient. Policymakers are often faced with the daunting task of unraveling the nuances of digital markets, determining when platform behaviors stifle competition or lead to anticompetitive practices. The infamous case of the European Union's scrutiny of Google's dominance in various sectors provides a pertinent illustration of the challenges regulators face in navigating this multifaceted landscape. Such interventions weigh heavily on the strategies firms employ to foster user engagement and can compel platforms to rethink elements of their business model-including pricing strategies, data use policies, and user engagement tactics. Thus, the journey to successfully navigate the competitive dynamics of the multi-sided platform landscape is both complex and fraught with challenges. Firms must adopt a dual focus: while seeking to enhance user offerings and cement their user base, they must also remain vigilant, adapting to the competitive maneuvers of rivals and anticipating shifts in user preferences. As digital ecosystems continue to evolve, the platforms that will ultimately thrive are those that adeptly balance these considerations-the ones that prove not only resilient in the face of competition but also innovative in their approach to fostering sustainable user engagement across myriad interconnected user groups. The true test lies in their ability to remain adaptable, continuously reassessing the intersection of competition and collaboration in an ever-changing digital economy.

In short, had he been brought forth in the fabulous ages of the world, the nature of his origin might have turned to his account; he might, like other heroes of antiquity, have laid claim to divine extraction, without running the risk of being claimed by an earthly father. Not that his parents had any reason to disown or renounce their offspring, or that there was anything preternatural in the circumstances of his generation and birth; on the contrary, he was, from the beginning, a child of promising parts, and in due course of nature ushered into the world amidst a whole cloud of witnesses. But, that he was acknowledged by no mortal sire, solely proceeded from the uncertainty of his mother, whose affections were so dissipated among a number of admirers, that she could never pitch upon the person from whose loins our hero sprung. Over and above this important doubt under which he was begotten, other particularities attended his birth, and seemed to mark him out as something uncommon among the sons of men. He was brought forth in a waggon, and might be said to be literally a native of two different countries; for, though he first saw the light in Holland, he was not born till after the carriage arrived in Flanders; so that, all these extraordinary circumstances considered, the task of determining to what government he naturally owed allegiance, would be at least as difficult as that of ascertaining the so much contested birthplace of Homer. Certain it is, the Count's mother was an Englishwoman, who, after having been five times a widow in one campaign, was, in the last year of the renowned Marlborough's command, numbered among the baggage of the allied army, which she still accompanied, through pure benevolence of spirit, supplying the ranks with the refreshing streams of choice Geneva, and accommodating individuals with clean linen, as the emergency of their occasions required. Nor was her philanthropy altogether confined to such ministration; she abounded with "the milk of human kindness," which flowed plentifully among her fellow-creatures; and to every son of Mars who cultivated her favour, she liberally dispensed her smiles, in order to sweeten the toils and dangers of the field. And here it will not be amiss to anticipate the remarks of the reader, who, in the chastity and excellency of his conception, may possibly exclaim, "Good Heaven! will these authors never reform their imaginations, and lift their ideas from the obscene objects of low life? For the next three hours, the women pruned, weeded, and cleaned up the garden. They were all surprised by how much more productive they were as a group than alone. Afterward, they sat around a table eating lunch and discussing their plans for future gardening sessions. The women decided to meet once a week during the spring and summer months. At the end of each gathering, they would choose where to go the following week. Before leaving, they made sure to hug each other goodbye. Real Simple: How to be happier. The Wonder Weeders' weekly get-togethers soon became a source of inspiration and strength for everyone involved. The women grew closer and began sharing more intimate details about their lives. They talked about everything from the loss of their parents (all but one had experienced) to the problems they were having with their adult children. When one woman was going through a difficult divorce, the others helped her move out of her home. "It's not like being a part of a book club, because there is something very earthy about working side by side in the dirt," says Susan. "You don't feel self-conscious about saying whatever comes into your head." There are also practical advantages to being part of such a committed group. When Joy was diagnosed with cancer in 2004, her fellow Wonder Weeders stepped in to maintain her garden while she underwent treatment. And after Joy passed away last year, the women spent several days clearing out the undergrowth behind her house and creating a path leading to a memorial bench overlooking the ocean. "She would have been thrilled," says Terry. Real Simple: 10 ways to de-stress. The women are quick to say that the Wonder Weeders is not a support group, nor does it resemble any sort of organized club. It is simply a bunch of friends who enjoy getting together and making beautiful things. That doesn't mean that there haven't been disagreements among them. But whenever conflicts arise, they are able to resolve them quickly. "There is a kind of implicit trust among us," says Terry. "I think we know that if someone else feels differently than we do, we need to respect that person's opinion." Now that the women are getting older, they joke about calling themselves the Wonder Weederettes. Their bodies ache more easily, and they tire faster. Still, they continue to push themselves, sometimes working past dark, even when they're exhausted. "The fact that we've been doing this for so long is proof that our friendship is really strong," says Maria. "And I'm convinced that it will endure forever." Determine when you want to meet (once a week works best), then decide whether you'd prefer to rotate houses or concentrate on one location for the entire season. You should also discuss whether you want to bring your own tools or use those belonging to the hostess. Make it fun. Keep the mood light by playing music and serving refreshments. If you're feeling ambitious, consider planting a vegetable garden and holding a potluck dinner using the produce. Set goals. Decide ahead of time which projects you plan to tackle. This will ensure that you stay focused and accomplish as many tasks as possible. Keep it casual. Don't worry too much about rules or a rigid schedule. The goal is to relax and have fun, so let the conversation flow freely. Be flexible.

Joseph Smith's reflections on his own prophetic calling reveal a profound connection between his experiences and those of the Apostle Paul. Both figures stand as celestial messengers, chosen in moments of divine intervention, tasked with proclaiming truths that would alter the spiritual landscape of their respective eras. Joseph's admiration for Paul is grounded not only in the challenges each faced, but also in the resolute faith that propelled them forward amidst adversity. In exploring these parallels, one can appreciate the weight of their missions, the disdain from the establishments of their time, and the unwavering assurance of their personal revelations. Paul, a Pharisee and persecutor of Christians, experienced a transformative moment on the road to Damascus. He encountered the Savior in a blinding light, which gave him a commission to preach the very gospel he once sought to destroy. Such a radical shift must have been accompanied by deep introspection and turmoil, akin to what Joseph Smith faced in his youth. Like Paul, Joseph was thrust into the spotlight, facing skepticism and derision for his extraordinary claims-claims that arose from divine encounters rather than human ambition. In his discourse, Joseph mused about the profound misunderstanding that often accompanies divine calling. He pointed out that both he and Paul endured ridicule, their revelations deemed nonsensical by many. Yet, it was the reality of their experiences that sustained them. Joseph drew strength from Paul's resolute declaration of his truth, finding in it a mirror of his own insistence on the legitimacy of his vision. The Savior had spoken to both men, singularly empowering them amidst doubt, leading them along paths that were fraught with peril but illuminated with purpose. This struggle against ridicule formed a notable cohesion between their narratives. Both men launched campaigns of preaching that were met with fierce opposition, yet remained undaunted. Paul's discourse to King Agrippa resonates with Joseph's declaration of faith-neither man was dissuaded by the hostility that sought to undermine their convictions. Joseph likened himself to Paul in that he, too, was standing firm in the face of adversity, fortified by the unshakeable knowledge of what he had seen. Moreover, Joseph's experience echoed Paul's enduring desire to fulfill a divine mandate, a desire that compelled him to traverse vast geographical and cultural landscapes. Both prophets expanded the reach of the gospel, willing to endure persecution for the sake of truth. The letters of Paul express a similar vulnerability-his trials, his tribulations, and yet, his unwavering faith. Joseph Smith clung to this parallel, finding in it a source of comfort; he understood that the pain of conflict served to sharpen his resolve, much like the trials Paul faced refined his mission. As we delve deeper into the Acts of the Apostles, particularly chapters 16 through 21, we will encounter Paul's fervent missionary journeys, characterized by divine direction and the opposition of those hesitant to embrace innovative truths. It mirrors Joseph's own experiences as he unveiled the restoration of Christ's gospel in the latter days. Each step taken by Paul is akin to every revelation received by Joseph-both are testimonies of unwavering devotion to the divine will, living proof that when one aligns themselves with heavenly purpose, the burdens they bear only serve to deepen their commitment. In contemplating the legacies of Joseph Smith and Paul, we discern a shared narrative of divine calling intertwined with human understanding. Each man's mission not only reshaped their lives but also altered the trajectory of belief for countless others. The foundation they laid-built upon revelations received, faith exercised amidst hostility, and the undying pursuit of truth-inspires generations, reminding us of the remarkable journeys that began with the humble act of being called.

Years before the grandparents of these lads had left Virginia at the solicitation of the great hunter and backwoodsman, Daniel Boone, who had discovered the richness of the Kentucky country, and was trying to induce settlers to occupy it, despite the savage Indians who resisted their advance. They had settled on the Ohio, and, with other hardy souls, started to develop homes in the wilderness; and here the two sons of David Armstrong, Bob and Sandy, met with many strange adventures that have been narrated in the first volume of this series.[2] Later on, a terrible flood, such as the Ohio valley had never before known at that early day, when its banks were lined with primeval forests, had swept the cabins of many of the settlers away, and so discouraged them that a party decided to build a floating house on a raft, and go further down the river, looking for new homesteads in the wilderness, this time in the valley of the mighty Mississippi. This houseboat had managed to run the gauntlet of all sorts of perils from hostile Shawanees and jealous French trappers, who resented the invasion of what they believed to be their territory by the daring English settlers. In the end the mighty Mississippi had been reached, and at first the Armstrongs had tried to establish their new home below the junction of the two rivers. It was, however, just before the breaking out of the Revolutionary War, when, over the entire country, settlers were taking sides, either in favor of the colonists or the king; and, as fortune would have it, the sentiment in the little community around the Armstrongs seemed to be so saturated with what they called "loyalty" to the far-distant sovereign that by degrees things became utterly unbearable to old David and his stalwart sons. Conditions had altered so much that in these dark days the French, who had all along been looked upon as enemies, now became warm friends of the colonists. This came about not so much through change of sentiment on the part of the French as a desire to strike back at King George by lending assistance to his rebellious colonies; but, whatever might be the reason, the Armstrongs were content to accept the new order of things, and make the best of them. Further research has also explored the role of parental influence on the development of childhood fears and anxiety. Parents' own anxiety levels and fear responses have been shown to impact their children's fear acquisition, with anxious parents more likely to transmit their fears to their children (Creswell, Apetroaia, Murray, & Cooper, 2010; Murray et al., 2008). Moreover, parents' verbal threat information and reinforcement of avoidance behaviors can contribute to the maintenance of childhood fears (Field, 2006a; Rachman, 1977). Additionally, research has highlighted the significance of peer influence on fear acquisition, with children's fear responses influenced by their peers' fear reactions and verbal threat information (De Jong, Muris, & ter Horst, 2003; Ollendick & King, 1991). The neural mechanisms underlying childhood fears and anxiety have also been investigated, with research suggesting that the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex play key roles in the processing of fear-related stimuli (Blair, Colledge, Murray, & Mitchell, 2001; Blair, Smith, & Livingston, 2011). Furthermore, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have demonstrated that children with anxiety disorders exhibit altered neural activity patterns in response to fear-related stimuli, compared to non-anxious children (Blair et al., 2011; Monk et al., 2008). The development of novel prevention and treatment methods for childhood fears and anxiety is a critical area of research. Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) has been shown to be an effective treatment for childhood anxiety disorders, with CBT programs targeting cognitive restructuring, relaxation techniques, and exposure to feared stimuli (Hofmann et al., 2010; Kendall et al., 2008). Moreover, research has explored the potential benefits of early intervention and prevention programs, such as parent-child interaction therapy (PCIT) and anxiety prevention programs, in reducing the risk of childhood anxiety disorders (Cartwright-Hatton et al., 2010; Rapee, 2002). In conclusion, childhood fears and anxiety are prevalent and debilitating conditions that can have long-term consequences for children's mental and physical health. Research has made significant progress in elucidating the mechanisms involved in the aetiology of childhood fears and anxiety, including the role of cognitive models, environmental factors, and neural mechanisms. The development of novel prevention and treatment methods, such as CBT and early intervention programs, offers hope for reducing the burden of childhood anxiety disorders. Further research is needed to continue to advance our understanding of childhood fears and anxiety and to inform the development of effective prevention and treatment strategies.

As a result, in order to increase Li recovery, some novel methods have been designed to simplify the Li recovery process by preferentially separating Li from other metals (e.g. Co, Ni, Mn), i.e. selective extraction of Li from spent LIBs. Organic acids like oxalic acid [19] and tartaric acid [20], for example, have been investigated and have shown good selectivity for Li over the other metals during waste LIBs leaching. Through this selective leaching process, Li can be enriched into the leaching solution in the form of soluble lithium-related salts (lithium oxalate and lithium tartrate), whereas the other metals (e.g. Co) are left in the leaching residue. Similar research has also been reported on the utilization of mild phosphoric acid as a leaching agent to selectively dissolve Li as LiH2PO4, whilst Co, Ni, Mn mainly remain in the solid phase as their respective phosphate precipitates [21,22]. In this case, Li can be directly extracted as Li3PO4 from the leaching solution - via an increase in pH - although final product purity only approximately 97%. In order to increase Li recovery, certain amount of reducing agents (e.g. 3-5 vol% H2O2) have to be consumed in the acid leaching process. Another interesting method is called oxidizing leaching [23,24], through which considerable amount of Li could be selectively leached out in the presence of acid and oxidizing agents (chlorine and sodium persulfate), whereas the other metals such as Co, Ni and Mn remain in solids at higher valences. In general, Li-rich leaching solutions with trace impurities can be obtained via selective acid leaching processes, and effectively shorten the overall Li recovery process. Nonetheless, these technologies involve high levels of organic or mineral acid consumption and additives - H2O2, chlorine or sodium persulfate. Another distinct disadvantage of these acid-based leaching processes is that significant quantities of alkali compounds are needed to neutralize the acidic leaching solution as Li recovery is best carried out under alkaline conditions (ca. pH 10-12) in order to ensure the high recovery and purity of final products. Nevertheless, this behavior of Li containing active materials with carbon has been exploited in reduction roasting [30,31], which results in the transformation of LiNixCoyMnzO2 into Li2CO3, Ni, Co and MnO in the presence of graphite or lignite at ca. 650 C for 3 h Li2CO3 produced via this method was then selectively extracted as LiHCO3 by leaching with carbonated water at ambient temperature. Like the sulfidation roasting process, reduction roasting needs to be conducted at temperatures above 600 C as C is otherwise too stable to react with LiCoO2 (e.g. 300 C) as previously demonstrated by TGA-DSC analyses for the mixtures of LiCoO2 and C in air and argon atmospheres [25,30]. It is worth noting that only ca. 85% Li could be selectively extracted by the carbonated water leaching from the reduction roast produced, this resulted in LiHCO3 solution containing 4.4 g/L Li under optimum conditions.

He shook his head, his eyes clouding over as he reflected on the paucity of top-class defenders on display. 'It's a global problem, not just an English one,' he said. He went on to lament the dearth of defenders with the ability to read the game, to anticipate and intercept, to marshal a backline with authority. 'These days, it's all about athleticism and pace,' he said. 'Defenders are being coached to be more like midfielders, to press high up the pitch and win the ball back quickly. He spoke of the great defenders of the past, men like Franco Baresi and Paolo Maldini, who could defend with elegance and sophistication. 'They were artists, not athletes,' he said. 'They could defend with their brains as much as their bodies.' The conversation turned to the Premier League, and the manager's thoughts on the current crop of defenders. He was scathing in his assessment, suggesting that many of the top clubs were relying on imported talent to shore up their defences. 'It's a short-term fix, but it's not a long-term solution,' he said. 'We need to start producing our own defenders, defenders who understand the English game and can adapt to its unique demands.' He spoke of the need for a cultural shift, a recognition that defending is an art that requires patience, dedication, and a deep understanding of the game. As the plane touched down, I couldn't help but think of Wenger's boast about the Premier League's attacking prowess. It's a boast that rings hollow when set against the backdrop of a defensive landscape that is as barren as it is bleak. The top clubs may have the financial muscle to attract the world's best attackers, but they seem powerless to stem the tide of mediocre defenders that flood the league. It's a problem that requires a collective effort, a recognition that defending is not just a necessary evil, but an art that requires nurturing and development. Until that happens, the Premier League will continue to be a league of thrilling attackers and mediocre defenders, a league that is as exciting as it is unbalanced.
