Marie's mother looked in and smiled to see her girl fingering her pretty things. "Aren't you two nearly ready to leave the inspection and come to tea?" "Julia doesn't like my caps, mum." "Yes, I do," said Julia; "all I'm asking, Mrs. Amber, is, when is she going to wear them?" Marie's mother came in and sat down and thought. "Ah," she said, shaking her head and looking pinched about the lips, "I don't know. You modern girls buy all these extraordinary things. You ape rich women; but you'll never be able to pay the everlasting cleaners' bills for those caps." "She'll soon give up wearing them, Mrs. Amber." "I'm sure I shan't," Marie denied. "When I was a girl," said Mrs. Amber, smoothing her lap reminiscently, "I remember I wanted a grand trousseau. But girls lived at home more in those days; they didn't go out typing and what not, earning money for themselves. So I couldn't buy what I wanted and my dear mother had too much sense to buy it for me. I had strong, useful things, twelve of everything, and they've lasted to this day. However, Marie thinks differently and she has earned the money to act differently, so let her be happy in her own way while she can." "Won't she be happy when she's married?" Julia asked, while Marie angrily hid her treasures away in tissue paper. "I hope so," said Mrs. Amber; "I'm sure I hope so. But things are all so different when you're married. You girls had better come to tea." Julia linked her arm strongly in Marie's as they followed the elderly woman out. "Marie, love," she whispered, "I'm a grouser. You know I wish you all the luck in the world and more. You know I do?" "I have it," said Marie, smiling. "And I hope you'll have it, too, before long." On the sitting-room table tea was spread; the room was red in the firelight; and the flat was so high up in the block that the street noises scarcely ascended to it. The girls sat down on the hearthrug, and Mrs. Amber seated herself before her tea tray and flicked away a tear. "A week to-day," she said, "I shall be the loneliest old thing in London. I shall be all by myself in this flat when Marie's gone." There were five cups and saucers on the tray, and in a moment the door-bell rang, and Marie sprang up to answer it. "That's Osborn!" she cried in a flutter. She returned demurely between two young men, one of them holding her hand captive. Osborn had brought his friend Desmond Rokeby to talk over details of the great event next week. He kissed Mrs. Amber on the cheek, and turned to Julia with a certain diffidence.

Mention of the girl's desire to get the bananas also creates a strong pull towards their real location because the girl wants to go where they are and not where she thinks they are (Perner, Rendl, & Garnham, 2007). Omitting the girl's desire is, however, a risky undertaking. Without knowing what she wants, children may make her do anything, for example, go to the now empty box to put something else in there. They will make her go to where she believes the bananas are only if they assume that she wants to get the bananas. Because there is no indication of children making this assumption, it is essential that a Duplo true belief (DTB) control task is administered. Rubio-Fernandez and Geurts' (2013, 2016) findings were impressive. Nearly all children (mean age of around 3 1/2 years) made the doll go to the full box in the DTB condition (91% in Experiment 1 of the 2013 study1 and 100% in Experiment 1 of the 2016 study). In contrast, 80% of children made the doll go to the empty box in the DFB condition, whereas only about 22% gave the correct answer to the SFB question (deceptive content task in Experiment 1 of the 2013 study). The data have important consequences for theories explaining early sensitivity to beliefs. First, the fact that children move the doll to the believed location of the bananas as early as they show anticipatory looking in the false belief task (Clements & Perner, 1994) speaks against an implicit knowledge of belief because intentional actions are typically carried out consciously. Second, the data question the explanation that the spontaneity of looking behavior accounts for earlier evidence over the elicited responses in the SFB task (Baillargeon et al., 2010) because children's responses in the DFB task are also elicited. Third, the data speak against the pure processing load account by Baillargeon et al. (2010) that the SFB task requires children to understand the story plus the experimenter's question. Although no specific question is asked, the experimenter nevertheless elicits a response with a range of more general questions. The data also support some proposed explanations. First, the fact that the belief-related responses decline drastically with the mention of the bananas' location or the girl's desire (Rubio-Fernandez & Geurts, 2013) goes well with the claim that the lure of reality cannot be suppressed (Setoh et al., 2016). Second, these effects could also be due to children's difficulty in switching from their own perspective, enforced by mentioning the bananas' location or the girl's desire, back to the girl's perspective (Rubio-Fernandez & Geurts, 2013; Helming et al., 2016), as opposed to children needing to inhibit their representation of reality. Given their theoretical importance, the Duplo results warrant a careful replication, especially given that the employed experimental design has some weaknesses to be ironed out.

His knitted "wrist-warmers" slipped down over his mottled, deeply-veined hands when he stooped to roll the log into the fire. He let go with a grunt. The next instant a mighty sneeze seized him, and Georgina, who had been gazing in fascination at the shower of sparks he was making, saw all of his teeth go flying into the fire. If his eyes had suddenly dropped from their sockets upon the hearth, or his ears floated off from the sides of his head, she could not have been more terrified, for she had not yet learned that one's teeth may be a separate part of one's anatomy. It was such a terrible thing to see a man go to pieces in this undreamed-of fashion, that she began to scream and writhe around in her high-chair until it nearly turned over. She did upset the silver porringer, and what was left of the bread and milk splashed out on the floor, barely missing the rug. Mrs. Triplett sprang to snatch her from the toppling chair, thinking the child was having a spasm. She did not connect it with old Jeremy's sneeze until she heard his wrathful gibbering, and turned to see him holding up the teeth, which he had fished out of the fire with the tongs. They were an old-fashioned set such as one never sees now. They had been made in England. They were hinged together like jaws, and Georgina yelled again as she saw them all blackened and gaping, dangling from the tongs. It was not the grinning teeth themselves, however, which frightened her. It was the awful knowledge, vague though it was to her infant mind, that a human body could fly apart in that way. And Tippy, not understanding the cause of her terror, never thought to explain that they were false and had been made by a man in some out-of-the-way corner of Yorkshire, instead of by the Almighty, and that their removal was painless. It was several years before Georgina learned the truth, and the impression made by the accident grew into a lurking fear which often haunted her as time wore on. She never knew at what moment she might fly apart herself. That it was a distressing experience she knew from the look on old Jeremy's face and the desperate pace at which he set off to have himself mended. She held her breath long enough to hear the door bang shut after him and his hob-nailed shoes go scrunch, scrunch, through the gravel of the path around the house, then she broke out crying again so violently that Tippy had hard work quieting her. She picked up the silver porringer from the floor and told her to look at the pretty bowl. The fall had put a dent into its side.

The words were lost in the howling wind, but the man didn't falter. His boots sank into the dust, sending miniature avalanches down the slope as he clawed his way up the rocky outcropping. The cruiser's hatch slammed shut, and a figure emerged, clad in a black enviro-suit, its visor glinting like polished onyx. The amplifier's bellow continued to echo across the wasteland, the words indistinguishable but the tone unmistakable - a cold, calculated menace. The suited figure leapt from the hatch, landing with a soft thud on the dusty surface. It moved with a fluid grace, its movements economical and precise, as it gave chase. The man, Thigpen, didn't look back, his eyes fixed on some point beyond the rocky outcropping. His breathing was ragged, the breather-mask fogging with each desperate gasp. The cruiser's engines died, and an oppressive silence fell over the scene, broken only by the wind's mournful wail and the soft crunch of boots on dust. The suited figure closed in, its pace unwavering, as Thigpen's strength began to flag. His legs stumbled, his arms flailing wildly as he struggled to maintain his footing on the treacherous slope. A boulder loomed ahead, its surface worn smooth by the relentless wind. Thigpen lunged for it, his hands closing around its base as he hauled himself up and over. The suited figure followed, its movements eerily silent, as it cleared the boulder with ease. Beyond, the rocky outcropping gave way to a narrow defile, its walls closing in like a vise. Thigpen stumbled into the defile, his back against the wall as he faced his pursuer. The suited figure halted, its visor glinting with an unblinking intensity. The amplifier's silence was more menacing than its bellow, and Thigpen knew he was trapped. The defile's walls seemed to close in, the air thickening with the weight of his own desperation. For a moment, the two figures faced each other, the only sound the wind's mournful sigh and the heavy, labored breathing of the man behind the breather-mask. Then, with a sudden, fluid motion, the suited figure drew a weapon from its hip, its muzzle trained on Thigpen's chest. The words, when they came, were cold, detached, and final: "You should have stopped when you had the chance, Thigpen. Now, it's too late."

This is global terrorism hitting everywhere, and they have chosen Iraq to be a battlefield. And we have to take them on," Mowaffak al-Rubaie said Sunday on CNN's "Late Edition with Wolf Blitzer." "If we don't prevail, if we don't succeed in this war, then we are doomed forever," he said. "I understand and sympathize with the mothers, with the widows, with the children who have lost their beloved ones in this country. "But honestly, it is well worth fighting and well worth investing the money and the treasure and the sweat and the tears in Iraq." Nearly 160,000 U.S. troops remain in Iraq, and the war has cost U.S. taxpayers about $600 billion, according to the House Budget Committee. The conflict is now widely unpopular among Americans: A CNN-Opinion Research Corp. poll out Wednesday found only 32 percent of Americans support the conflict. And 61 percent said they want the next president to remove most U.S. troops within a few months of taking office. In the weekly Democratic radio address Saturday, Sen. Bob Menendez of New Jersey said President Bush "took us to war on the wings of a lie." Menendez said that the war has depleted the resources and morale of the U.S. military; diverted national attention away from the war in Afghanistan, where al Qaeda is regrouping; and hurt the hunt for Osama bin Laden. The Iraq war has not made Americans safer, Menendez said, but has instead hurt the U.S. economy. The senator called for a "responsible new direction" regarding Iraq. CNN learned last week, from several U.S. military officials familiar with the recommendations but not authorized to speak on the record, that senior U.S. military officials are preparing to recommend to Bush a four- to six-week "pause" in additional troop withdrawals from Iraq after the last of the "surge" brigades leaves in July. "If the conditions on the ground dictate that we have to have a pause, then we will have to have a pause," al-Rubaie said. The return of all five brigades added to the Iraq contingent last year could reduce troop levels by up to 30,000, but still leave approximately 130,000 or more troops in Iraq. Al-Rubaie emphasized Sunday that any drawdown of U.S. troops "has to be based on the conditions on the ground." "It depends on the development and the growth and the equipment and the capabilities of the Iraqi security forces, and the preparedness of the Iraqi security forces," he said. "This should not be a purely political decision. It should be also a technical, military and intelligence decision." But there has been too much "foot-dragging on key governance questions in Iraq," Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon said on CNN on Sunday. "It seems to me you put off those troop withdrawals, you send exactly the wrong message to the Iraqis."

Others exhibited in preference scenes taken from the life of Heracles, the Theban, through flattery to Candaules, himself a Heracleid, being descended from the hero through Alcaeus. Others contented themselves by decorating the entrances of their dwellings with garlands and wreaths in token of rejoicing. Among the multitudes marshalled along the way from the royal house even as far as the gates of the city, through which the young queen would pass on her arrival, conversation naturally turned upon the beauty of the bride, whereof the renown had spread throughout all Asia; and upon the character of the bridegroom, who, although not altogether an eccentric, seemed nevertheless one not readily appreciated from the common standpoint of observation. Nyssia, daughter of the Satrap Megabazus, was gifted with marvellous purity of feature and perfection of form; at least such was the rumour spread abroad by the female slaves who attended her, and a few female friends who had accompanied her to the bath; for no man could boast of knowing aught of Nyssia save the colour of her veil and the elegant folds that she involuntarily impressed upon the soft materials which robed her statuesque body. The barbarians did not share the ideas of the Greeks in regard to modesty. While the youths of Achaia made no scruples of allowing their oil-anointed torsos to shine under the sun in the stadium, and while the Spartan virgins danced ungarmented before the altar of Diana, those of Persepolis, Ebactana, and Bactria, attaching more importance to chastity of the body than to chastity of mind, considered those liberties allowed to the pleasure of the eyes by Greek manner as impure and highly reprehensible, and held no woman virtuous who permitted men to obtain a glimpse of more than the tip of her foot in walking, as it slightly deranged the discreet folds of a long tunic. Despite all this mystery, or rather, perhaps, by very reason of this mystery, the fame of Nyssia had not been slow to spread throughout all Lydia, and become popular there to such a degree that it had reached even Candaules, although kings are ordinarily the most illy informed people in their kingdoms, and live like the gods in a kind of cloud which conceals from them the knowledge of terrestrial things. The Eupatridae of Sardes, who hoped that the young king might, perchance, choose a wife from their family, the hetairae of Athens, of Samos, of Miletus and of Cyprus, the beautiful slaves from the banks of the Indus, the blond girls brought at a vast expense from the depths of the Cimmerian fogs, were heedful never to utter in the presence of Candaules, whether within hearing or beyond hearing, a single word which bore any relation to Nyssia. The bravest, in a question of beauty, recoil before the prospect of a contest in which they can anticipate being outrivalled.

She had been knitting all afternoon while she listened to the wireless, which was still going in a corner of the room. The window curtains were drawn against the December dusk; a bright wood fire burned cheerfully on the hearth, and an electric lamp stood on a small table near Mrs. Clinton's elbow, so that she could see to count her stitches. She looked very pretty and comfortable, with her grey hair and delicate complexion, and her hands moving quickly among the wool, and she smiled at her husband. "What is it?" she asked, not too anxiously, because she knew there must be nothing very serious wrong, since he was able to sit down to tea. He shook his head. "It's that girl," he said. "She'll do me yet. I've had a letter from her." He took a letter out of his breast-pocket and waved it at her. "Read it," he said. She laid down her knitting and took the letter. "Oh dear!" she said. As Claire's migraines became more frequent and debilitating, she began to feel like she was losing control of her life. She would have to cancel meetings, miss deadlines, and struggle to even get out of bed. Despite her best efforts to manage the pain, she felt like she was stuck in a vicious cycle of suffering. But then, one day, she stumbled upon an online forum where women were sharing their experiences with menstrual migraines. It was like a lightbulb moment for Claire - she realized that her migraines were not just random occurrences, but were actually linked to her menstrual cycle. With this newfound understanding, Claire began to take steps to manage her migraines. She started tracking her cycles, taking notes on when her migraines occurred and what symptoms she experienced. She also started taking magnesium supplements, which are said to help regulate hormones and reduce the frequency and severity of migraines. And, as an added precaution, she began taking over-the-counter medication, Migraleve, 24 hours before her period to help prevent a full-blown migraine. The results were nothing short of miraculous. For the first time in years, Claire was able to go without a migraine. She was able to focus on her work, spend time with her loved ones, and enjoy her hobbies without the constant fear of a debilitating headache. It was a newfound sense of freedom, and Claire was grateful to have finally found a solution to her long-standing problem. But Claire's story is not unique. According to the National Migraine Centre, a staggering 50 per cent of women suffer from menstrual migraines, yet many of them do not make the connection between their cycle and their migraines for years. And, unfortunately, many GPs are not equipped to diagnose and treat menstrual migraines properly. Online forums are filled with women sharing their stories of frustration and disappointment with their healthcare providers, who often dismiss their symptoms or prescribe ineffective treatments. Professor Anne MacGregor, a leading specialist in headaches and women's health, says that the most common cause of menstrual migraines is a drop in oestrogen levels towards the end of the cycle. This hormone surge, which occurs at the start of the cycle, triggers ovulation and the release of an egg. But for some women, this drop in oestrogen can trigger a migraine. "It's a complex issue, and there's still much to be learned," says Professor MacGregor. "But with the right treatment and support, women can manage their migraines and live a more fulfilling life." As Claire's story spread, she began to receive messages from women all over the world who were struggling with menstrual migraines. They shared their stories, their frustrations, and their hopes for a cure. And Claire, now empowered by her own experience, was determined to help them. She started a support group, where women could share their experiences and advice, and connect with others who understood what they were going through. It was a small but powerful step towards a brighter future, one where women could live without the fear of migraines and enjoy their lives to the fullest. And for Claire, it was a reminder that sometimes, all it takes is a little bit of understanding and support to find the solution to a long-standing problem.

The blind on a window of the house next door was pulled to one side, emitting a shaft of light across the path he paced. A head - the head of the little girl his father had so often petted as he strode up the walk when he came home from work - shut off the light. He heard a scuffle of feet and she was pulled from the window. Mrs. Sprockett's husband, in his shirt sleeves, came over and stood on the sidewalk. "Is Maude in there with your mother?" he asked. John looked at him, without a word. "Beg your pardon," said Mrs. Sprockett's husband, backing away. "She didn't say - didn't leave any word - and the baby - and - " The crying of the Sprockett baby could be heard faintly. "I didn't think - I - I - " and Mrs. Sprockett's husband turned awkwardly and went back to the house. Everything was quiet, so quiet that it startled him. A mocking bird warbled in a tree by the porch. He remembered his father saying one night that there was no music sweeter than its song. Fragments of memory came to him vividly. His father pulling him from under a bed the night he was punished for stealing apples at the corner grocery store. His father reading David Copperfield to him and their mutual rejoicing when Betsy Trotwood lectured David's firm stepfather. His father closing his eyes and leaning back and a soft smile on his lips as his mother played "Annie Laurie." These thoughts carried him away so that he stopped quickly when they left him. For a moment he could not realize that death was taking his father. He felt he had been out of his head, walking out there, that it was all a horrible nightmare. He almost began to laugh and dash up to the door to find things as they always had been. He staggered back with an impulse to shout in his agony as realization came back to him. A wild hope seized him. He had been walking there for hours, for days it seemed, and the door had not opened. Perhaps the doctor was wrong, after all. Perhaps his father had rallied strength and would live. His heart beat exultingly. Perhaps - And then the door opened. He knew that his father had left them nothing but what was in the house. He had not spoken to his mother about it. He had been beside her bed until after dawn when, with a gentle sigh, she had slipped off into a merciful sleep. Mrs. Sprockett, who left them only for a few minutes in the morning, he thanked with a guilty feeling of having not appreciated what she had done. The doctor had spoken to him kindly. "My boy," he said, "this comes to all of us. Your father passed as gently as he lived. Remember, there's no sorrow nor suffering where he has gone and - be good to your mother."

On the one hand, the growing prevalence of NCDs in emerging economies is viewed as a negative consequence of socio-economic development, with economic growth and rapid urbanisation associated with a rise in 'modern' lifestyles (drinking, smoking, unhealthy diets, and physical inactivity) and an ageing population. On the other hand, the chronic disease epidemic in the global South is understood to be a serious threat to the sustainability of development through both its negative impact on the productivity of working age populations and the double burden of disease it places on health systems already overstretched by infectious, maternal and perinatal diseases. Predictably perhaps, many of the solutions put forward by these actors are health strategies successfully used in North America and Europe and which are deemed commensurate with the economic context of LMICs (Yach et al., 2006; Lim et al., 2007; Alwan et al., 2010; WHO, 2013). They include tools such as epidemiological surveillance systems as well as public health and clinical interventions that are 'highly cost-effective cheap, feasible and culturally acceptable' such as tobacco taxation, media campaigns for healthy diets and multidrug regimens for people at risk of cardiovascular diseases (WHO, 2010, p.47). There has been no lack of academic attention given to the issue of NCDs in the global South from the public health community (Alleyne et al., 2011; Clark, 2014; Marrero et al., 2012; Stuckler and Basu, 2013). In contrast, critical social science engagements are comparatively rare, although interesting work has recently begun to emerge. For example, political scientists have examined the reasons behind the relative neglect of NCDs in global health policy and funding compared to issues like AIDS, pointing to the expert and advocacy networks involved and the ways issues are framed (e.g. Magnusson, 2007; Jonsson, 2014; cf. also Shiffman, 2009). Similarly, historians and others have started to explore the globalisation of chronic diseases and particular public health strategies like tobacco taxes over the last 50 years (e.g. Brown and Bell, 2008; Reubi, 2013; Weisz, 2014b). Another important part of this emerging body of work is the research carried out by anthropologists and geographers into the way ideas and practices associated with NCDs have been translated, resisted and re-appropriated when travelling to the global South. To illustrate, Livingston (2012, 2013) has pointed to the absence of pain relief medication and the very different understandings of pain in cancer wards in Botswana; while Lawhon and Herrick (2013; cf. also Herrick, 2013) have shown how alcohol control policies in Cape Town have been recast as an instrument to fight criminality rather than improve health. Others have looked into how the ideas and practices associated with NCDs have transformed subjectivities and notions of patienthood in the global South (e.g. Bunkenborg, 2003; Whyte, 2013; Whitmarsh, 2013; cf. also Whyte, 2012).

This intriguing body of research not only sheds light on the dietary practices of these extinct hominins but also presents a complex picture of their interactions with available resources in their environments. In essence, Neanderthals were skilled utilization experts of their ecological niches. They hunted large herbivores, such as mammoths and woolly rhinoceroses, skillfully wielding their stone tools. However, their reliance on significant vertebrate sources, supplemented by a hunting-then-cooking strategy, is telling of a broader adaptability to circumstances that were often unforgiving and variable. While robust skeletal remains support the idea of powerful physique and muscular strength, as depicted in various artistic portrayals, the culinary habits of Neanderthals highlight another dimension of their existence. This approach to cooking-a strategic deployment of fire and rudimentary materials-may well have provided nourishment that exceeded what their digestive systems could otherwise achieve with raw foods alone. Cooking not only serves to soften fibrous materials but can also increase the bioavailability of nutrients, thus enriching the caloric intake from their sustenance. The evidence of marrow extraction and fat consumption indicates that Neanderthals possessed nuanced knowledge about nutrition and the benefits derived from multiple food sources. As perceived through the lens of evolutionary biology, such dietary versatility could have been pivotal for their survival. The evidence for cooking, coupled with the striking absence of marks typically associated with bone gnawing, suggests a well-developed culinary tradition, if rudimentary by our modern standards. However, this endeavor raises an important question: how did their food choices and preparation methods impact their evolutionary success relative to Homo sapiens? The nuanced diversity in their genes also illuminates how particular taste adaptations likely influenced their food preferences. It is plausible that foodstuffs considered bitter by our modern sensibilities were not only palatable but potentially favored by Neanderthals. This genetic predisposition, coupled with their diminished enzymatic efficiency for starch digestion, perhaps shaped their foraging strategies, steering them towards different types of flora and fauna that would sustain them. Furthermore, the impact of environmental shifts cannot be underestimated. Changes in climate and ecosystem might have led to the reduction of key food resources, forcing Neanderthals to navigate a landscape increasingly devoid of the large game they adeptly hunted. These evolutionary pressures could account for their eventual decline, as competition with modern humans for limited resources could have exacerbated their precarious situation. And so, the intrigue does not end there; as researchers delve deeper into the annals of paleogenetics, questions loom large over how Neanderthals adapted, thrived, and ultimately vanished from the Earth. The complexity of their lives, rooted in a blend of cunning, endurance, and perhaps even a rich social structure, evokes a profound reflection on our shared heritage with these ancient cousins. Could the decline of their unique culinary and dietary practices signal a broader narrative of adaptability in the face of changing circumstances? The saga of Neanderthals, underscored by their adventurous taste for life and survival, beckons the pursuit of further exploration into our primal connections-one plate of history at a time.

The biochemical and structural transformations that barley grains undergo during malting are pivotal not only for the brewing and distilling sectors but also for understanding the complex relationships underpinning grain quality. Recent advances in molecular plant breeding have opened new avenues for improving grain attributes that are integral to malting. Notably, specific weight (SW) serves as a key target trait for these improvements, necessitating a closer examination of the factors influencing single grain density (SGD) (Rasika et al., 2018). This exploration includes understanding the compositional elements that may correlate with, or even dictate, the SGD of barley grains, as the interplay of these variables has significant repercussions for the malting industry. As previously mentioned, the endosperm comprises both the aleurone and starchy components, with the latter playing a central role during malting. The aleurone layer, rich in enzymes and proteins, is particularly crucial for the effective breakdown of starches into fermentable sugars. The orchestration of enzyme activity during germination is finely tuned and hinges on the physical characteristics of the grain itself (Cochrane et al., 2006). Research has elucidated the potential for variants in the composition of the endosperm to impart variances in the dimension and density of individual grains, thereby influencing overall swathes of crop yields and qualities (Haaland et al., 2017). Key variables such as starch granule composition and protein profile can exert considerable influence over SGD. Higher protein concentrations, for instance, alter the hydration capacity of grains and can result in denser individual grains. This suggests that not only the chemical composition of the grains, but their physical interactions during grain development must also be meticulously studied (Tsai et al., 2019). Thus, diverging from the traditional focus on genetic or phenotypic selection alone could yield valuable insights that bolster breeding programs. Moreover, it's essential to consider the environmental factors that contribute to grain quality. Field conditions, including soil type, nutrient availability, and climate, significantly impact the final quality parameters of barley grains (Morgan et al., 2020). For instance, variations in nitrogen inputs can lead to differences in both protein content and SW, underscoring the importance of agricultural practices in shaping grain characteristics. Integrating these agronomic aspects with compositional studies positions researchers to develop comprehensive management strategies aimed at optimizing both grain yield and quality. Emerging biotechnological tools, such as genome editing and marker-assisted selection, are becoming increasingly relevant in this context. By identifying genetic loci that govern SGD and its associations with other quality traits, breeders can more effectively make targeted improvements while minimizing the years required for traditional selection methods (Kearsey and Farquhar, 2017). Additionally, understanding the genetic mechanisms that regulate the synthesis of major constituents within the endosperm could pave the way for the development of barley varieties with superior malting properties and overall grain quality. A multi-faceted approach, incorporating both the biochemical depth of grain composition and the practical dimensions of crop management, will undoubtedly foster advancements in barley breeding and ultimately enhance the sustainability of the malting industry. Future directions should encompass a holistic examination of barley attributes, integrating molecular genetics, agronomy, and processing demands to cultivate barley cultivars that meet evolving market standards. As the malting industry adapts to changing consumer preferences and environmental challenges, it is imperative that research continues to illuminate the complex interactions that govern grain quality.

The intersection of technological innovation and sustainable development has become a critical area of focus in the pursuit of mitigating climate change and planetary boundaries. The recognition of the need for transformative innovation has led to a shift towards green industrial policies, with emerging economies like China taking a leading role in strategic environmental sectors. This has sparked a debate about the role of the state in driving innovation and the importance of bottom-up, citizen-led contributions to systemic change. In this context, the concept of "indigenous innovation" has gained traction, particularly in China's Medium-Long Term Plan for Science and Technology (2006-2020). This approach seeks to align R&D investments and incentives in strategic emerging industries with the country's efforts to address environmental imperatives. However, questions remain about the effectiveness of top-down approaches in driving sustainable development, and the need for more inclusive and participatory approaches that involve local communities and civil society. Furthermore, the role of consumer practices and citizen action in driving political change cannot be overstated. Changing consumer behaviors and cultural framings of sustainability are critical in enabling or constraining transitions towards more sustainable development pathways. The importance of everyday routines and practices in shaping sustainability outcomes has been highlighted by scholars, who argue that transitions must be grounded in the lived experiences of people and communities. The recognition of the need for more inclusive and participatory approaches to sustainable development has led to a growing interest in the concept of "co-innovation". This approach emphasizes the importance of collaboration and co-creation between different stakeholders, including government, industry, civil society, and local communities. Co-innovation has the potential to drive more effective and sustainable solutions, by leveraging the knowledge and expertise of diverse stakeholders and fostering a sense of shared ownership and responsibility. In addition, the role of international cooperation and global governance in driving sustainable development cannot be ignored. The Paris Agreement on climate change, for example, represents a critical milestone in global efforts to address the climate crisis. However, the agreement's success will depend on the ability of countries to work together to implement and scale up sustainable development solutions, and to share knowledge and expertise in areas such as clean energy and green technologies. Ultimately, the pursuit of sustainable development requires a fundamental transformation of our economic and social systems. This will require a shift towards more circular and regenerative economies, which prioritize the well-being of people and the planet over profit and growth. It will also require a rethinking of our values and priorities, and a recognition of the intrinsic value of nature and the environment. As the IPCC report starkly warns, the window for action is rapidly closing, and the consequences of inaction will be severe and irreversible. The time for transformative innovation and collective action is now.

As usual in research, the reason for this unsettled debate derives at least partly from differing theoretical perspectives, each of which can account for some published results but is challenged by other findings. There are two principal perspectives concerning asymmetry of atrophy effects in SD currently on the table, which we shall label ATL Representations and ATL Connections. These terms derive from the conceptual framework of the hub-and-spoke model of semantic memory (Chen, Lambon Ralph, & Rogers, 2017; Lambon Ralph, Jefferies, Patterson, & Rogers, 2016; Patterson, Nestor, & Rogers, 2007; Rogers et al., 2004), which suggests that the large and very distributed brain network for semantic memory includes (a) modality-specific input and output components, in brain regions posterior and anterior to the ATL, and (b) a trans-modal ATL centre in which representations are abstracted away from the modality-specific features of concepts, enabling the generalisations that are so crucial to semantic cognition. This centre is the hub, and the connections between modality-specific regions and the hub are the spokes. The ATL Representations and ATL Connections accounts are not mutually exclusive, and evidence for both perspectives has been presented in the literature to date. According to the ATL Representations interpretation of ATL asymmetry, the left and right sides of the semantic hub differ in semantic structure in the sense of what they preferentially represent: the left is mainly responsible for the semantics of words and the right for the semantics of nonverbal (perhaps especially, but not exclusively, visual) things, including objects and faces (Gainotti & Marra, 2011; Mesulam et al., 2013; Snowden, Thompson, & Neary, 2012). Evidence suggesting differential semantic representation of verbal and visual materials comes from, amongst other sources, an elegant study by Snowden et al. (2012, see also Snowden et al., 2018), which compared performance for objects versus people on both written-word and picture based tests. L > R patients had lower scores on the word based tests and R > L on the picture based tests, irrespective of the content (object vs person) (see also Butler, Brambati, Miller, & Gorno-Tempini, 2009). There is also evidence that the right ATL may play a more important role in processing other nonverbal aspects of semantic knowledge, such as sound recognition (see Gainotti (2017) for review). By the ATL Representations account then, pronounced anomia in L > R cases and prosopagnosia in R > L cases arise straightforwardly from the preferential representation of verbal versus visual semantic information in the left versus right ATL, respectively. According to the ATL Connections view of the impact of asymmetry of ATL atrophy, more pronounced anomia is seen in L > R SD cases because, although the representations in the left and right ATL do not differ significantly in what they represent but rather form a system integrated across the two sides, the left ATL has stronger connections to left-lateralised frontal speech production systems.

It's no secret that Prince was a perfectionist - but some of the stories that emerged after his death highlighted the star's ruthless attitude towards his bandmates. "He did like to push the band with fear," said Michael B Nelson, who played trombone for the New Power Generation. One night, months into 1993's Act I tour, Nelson missed a high B during his solo on a song called The Flow. "The next day, [Prince] came by and said, 'You're gonna play that solo right tonight?'" he told Rolling Stone. "I said, 'I'll do my best.' And he says, 'Uh, you did your best last night.' And he walks away." That night, when it came to the solo, Prince walked up to him with his "golden gun" microphone (pictured above) and held it to his head. "I was like, 'Oh, my God.' And he kept doing it. And it was like a week of him doing this, and I'm freaking out. It wasn't showbiz at that point. It was, 'Don't you ever do that again'." Five days before his death, Prince celebrated Record Store Day by cycling to his local record store and snapping up a few bargains. According to Bob Fuchs, the manager of Electric Fetus, the star bought six CDs: Prince then set off on his bike, waving to fans at a nearby hair salon before visiting a local coffee store. According to barista, Alya Al-Hilwani, he preferred a mocha, with no whipped cream. In summer 2015, the Minneapolis house that featured as Prince's childhood home in the film Purple Rain went up for sale. It turns out that Prince bought it himself. Minnesota Public Radio checked property records and discovered the owner of the 1913 house, at 3420 Snelling Avenue, Minneapolis, was NPG Music Publishing - one of Prince's companies. The initial asking price was just $110,000, but Prince paid $117,000 in cash to secure the property. After his death, Prince's estate put it up for sale, saying "the costs of repair and ongoing maintenance" were such that keeping hold of the house was "not in the Estate's best interest". Incredibly, Prince was the biggest-selling artist in the US last year, in terms of album sales. He shifted more than 2.2 million albums in the months after his death, partly because his music was unavailable on the major streaming platrforms. He was the only artist to sell more than one million digital and physical albums in 2016; and sold a total of 5.4 million digital songs, putting him ahead of Drake and Adele. When his music finally became available on Spotify, Apple, Amazon and Google Play this February, it was streamed 17 million times in one week - with Purple Rain alone racking up 1 million plays. Prince had many aliases as a songwriter - Alexander Nevermind, Joey Coco and Jamie Starr, to name but a few.

As the sun set over the battered city of Zawiya, the sounds of gunfire and explosions slowly faded into the distance, replaced by the mournful cries of the wounded and the bereaved. The streets, once filled with the defiant chants of protesters, were now eerily quiet, the only sound being the soft hum of medical helicopters hovering above the city. The doctors at the field hospital in Martyrs Square were working tirelessly to treat the injured, their faces etched with exhaustion and concern. The hospital's director, a bespectacled man with a kind face, spoke to a CNN correspondent, his voice laced with sadness. "We've seen some terrible things today. The injuries are severe, and the death toll is rising. We're doing everything we can to save as many lives as possible, but it's a difficult task." As the night wore on, the city's residents began to emerge from their homes, their faces drawn and their eyes red from crying. They gathered in small groups, whispering and pointing at the destruction that surrounded them. The once-peaceful city was now a scene of utter chaos, the buildings pockmarked with bullet holes and the streets littered with debris. The government's forces, who had been accused of launching the attack on the city, were nowhere to be seen, their whereabouts unknown. The people of Zawiya were left to wonder if they would ever be held accountable for their actions. As the night wore on, the city's residents began to make their way to the city's central square, where a makeshift memorial had been set up for the victims of the violence. The air was thick with grief and anger, the people's faces twisted in a mixture of sadness and outrage. The city's leader, Moammar Gadhafi, had spoken earlier in the day, his words laced with a mix of anger and desperation. He had accused the protesters of being brainwashed by al-Qaeda, and had called on their mothers to take them home. But the people of Zawiya knew the truth - they were fighting for their freedom, and for their right to live in a country where they were not afraid to speak their minds. As the night wore on, the city's residents began to sing, their voices rising and falling in a haunting melody. It was a song of defiance, a song of hope, a song of freedom. And as the people of Zawiya sang, they knew that they would never be silenced, that they would never be defeated.

But ain't it more dangerous for aviators hanging over water than the shore?" "Hi! step out of the way, Larry, if you don't want to get run over!" exclaimed the other, suddenly gripping his companion's sleeve. "No need to scare a feller like that, Elephant." "Well, that machine don't belong around here, anyway; and I guess they're tourists doing the lake road course. Lots of 'em come this way just for the view, which they say can't be beat," the other went on, in a low tone; for the touring car had drawn very close by now. Two men sat in it, one apparently the chauffeur, and the other occupying the commodious seat in the tonneau. The latter was a keen-faced man, with a peculiar eye, that seemed to sparkle and glow; and Larry immediately became aware that he was experiencing a queer sensation akin to a chill, when he returned the gaze of this individual. Still, the other could look very pleasant when he chose to smile, as was the case immediately after the car came to a halt within five feet of where the two Bloomsbury high school boys stood. "Looks like you had had pretty good luck, boys," he remarked, smoothly. "Pretty middlin'," Elephant said, indifferently, as though this were an everyday occurrence with him; when to tell the truth, he and Larry had not done so well all season as on this particular day. "Guess you know where the old fishing hole lies," laughed the stranger, pleasantly. "Quite a collection too - black bass, perch, 'slickers,' as we used to call the pickerel, and even some big fat sunfish. Many a happy hour have I spent just as you've been doing. And I'll never forget how fine those same fish tasted after I'd cleaned them myself for the frying-pan." "That's what we do, sir," replied Larry, now beginning to think the stranger rather a nice spoken man.

Within the past four decades, LULC Change have become a major challenge to the foothill forests of the Pakistan's Himalayan Mountains (Ahmad et al., 2018). Driven by urbanization and population pressure, LULC Change in Pakistan are mostly discernible in the subtropical and moist temperate forest regions (Mannan et al., 2018b). Similar studies have attributed these changes to agricultural expansion, uncontrolled and illegal logging with a net negative impact on both natural and artificial forest regeneration (Qasim et al., 2013; Ullah et al., 2016; Mannan et al., 2018). Meanwhile (Mannan et al., 2018), observed an estimated 5.70 Gg C yr-1 of forest carbon to have been lost from subtropical forests of Pakistan between 1990 and 2017 while (UN Habitat, 2010) and (Rukya et al., 2014) observed an increasing trend in local temperatures, a drop in the number of rainy days, amount of rainfall, and increase in occurrence of landslides within the same period. A similar study by (Lu et al., 2018) observed an estimated 3.5 million km2 of forests to have been lost in the United States between 1700 and 2005 and which resulted in the loss of about 10607 Tg C. The Himalayan forests of Pakistan are under constant threat resulting from agricultural expansion, urbanization as well as uncontrolled and illegal logging. The conversion of these forests does not only cause a loss in forest biomass and carbon stock but also alters forest structure, forest ecosystem and forest composition (Joshua et al., 2017). Given that successful studies on LULC change must include remote sensing (RS) and Geographical Information System (GIS), modeling and simulation analyses using different scenarios also provide future LULC Change prediction (Qasim et al., 2013; Mukete et al., 2017). These RS and GIS approaches have received a wide range of acknowledgement among researchers especially with an inclusion of the Markov Chain (MC) and Cellular Automata (CA) function. Here, the MC model gives appropriate results in Land-use simulations and which can be quantitatively converted into spatially explicit results by using the CA function (Pontius and Millones, 2011; Wang et al., 2012). The forest biomass and carbon are directly linked with LULC Change (Saeed et al., 2018). The conversion of forest land to specific land uses (e.g. Agricultural Land, Built up, Barren Land) results in the loss of forest biomass and carbon stock at both national and international level (Joshua et al., 2017). LULC Change can alter the forest structure, forest ecosystem and forest composition that results the forest biomass carbon loss (Joshua et al., 2017). Reducing emission from Deforestation and Forest Degradation) REDD + Pakistan has reported that if the deforestation is brought to zero level, the potential earning will be estimated from 95 million $ to 316 million $ (REDD+, 2011). The natural forests of Pakistan are facing deforestation at accelerated rate, the deforestation is estimated about 31658 ha (-0.75%) annually (FAO, 2009), while (REDD+, 2011) reported 27000 ha annually degraded from Himalayan pine forest of Pakistan.

Laboratory experiments are also limited in that they cannot replicate true environmental complexity; ecological or behavioural responses to, for example changes in predation pressure or resource competition and escape. It also remains difficult to establish the recovery potential of communities in laboratory simulations. The third widely used approach is the study of natural CO2 emission sites as analogues for CCS leaks (e.g. Caramanna et al., 2011; Pearce, 2006). This approach, while having many merits, has limitations, including (1) most studied sites are long-term phenomena and thus no base-line (pre-release) data exists, (2) the release rate cannot be controlled or "turned off" to study the rapidity with which more typical local conditions are re-established, (3) many sites are within volcanic settings (Hall-Spencer et al., 2008) and therefore may be contaminated with H2S and have atypical temperatures. Although these analogue studies are often insightful, they are of limited geographical distribution; for example the shallow, warm and clear water situations described by Caramanna et al. (2011) and Hall-Spencer et al. (2008) do not directly translate to colder deeper and turbid sites on other continental shelves. If offshore implementation of CCS in Europe is to become a more established mitigation strategy, it will almost certainly be used in colder, more turbid, shelf seas, such as the North Sea, so that more appropriate analogues, with closely similar fauna, seabed sediments, irradiance and temperatures need to be studied before the findings can be directly utilized by policy makers. Whilst some injections of small amounts of CO2 directly into the water column have been performed (Barry et al., 2013), the injection of significant and quantified amounts of CO2, in a controlled way, directly into marine sediments from below would effectively mimic the final stages of a leakage from storage reservoirs. This would allow for the first time a study of the vertical movement of CO2 through the sediments, into the water column and of the biochemical transformations and impacts that occur as the CO2 passes through a vertically structured marine sediment ecosystem, thereby mimicking the shallowest stages of migration and emission at the seabed. An initial scoping study developed a set of criteria for a successful experiment, namely an injection of between one and ten tonnes of CO2, at approximately ten metres below the seafloor, continuing over a period of several weeks. The main driver for these calculations was the need for a release large enough to impose changes and detectable signals onto a natural system, but small enough to avoid a large-scale pollution event. Clearly a short-term, small-scale release of CO2 is not a full analogue for a CCS leak. However, it does encompass many of the processes and systems that are important to understand and guide both monitoring and impact assessment within the marine environment.

The allegations against Amish bishop Sam Mullet and his followers are nothing short of shocking, with claims of rape, beatings, and kidnapping making headlines. The recent beard cutting attacks, which have been linked to Mullet's group, have brought the usually private community to the forefront of national attention. But insiders claim that the true extent of the abuse and control exercised by Mullet is far more sinister. According to a former member of the Bergholz Clan, Mullet rules the group with an iron fist, using fear and intimidation to maintain control. The former member, who wishes to remain anonymous, described a culture of fear and submission, where members are forced to live by Mullet's rules or face punishment. "He would take the wife from the man," the former member said. "The wife would have to go and live with Sam. The husband of that wife would have to go to the chicken coop or out in the barn in the middle of the winter, sometimes day and night." The allegations are eerily reminiscent of the Peoples Temple, a cult led by Jim Jones that ended in tragedy in 1978. The former member of the Bergholz Clan drew parallels between the two groups, warning that the situation could end in a similar catastrophe. "I'm not surprised if I have to call the sheriff some day and say there are a lot of dead people lying around here," the former member said. "That would not be a surprise to me nor would it be a surprise to the sheriff of that county. I have enough inside information that I have no question if something is not done, there will be people that get hurt." The allegations of abuse and control are supported by other former members, who have spoken out about the cult-like behavior of the Bergholz Clan. One woman, whose husband had his beard cut off by the gang, described the atmosphere of fear and intimidation that pervades the group. "I heard many stories about the brainwashing, the beatings, the locking up, and the women he is using," she said. "I believe that Sam Mullet is a very powerful and manipulative person, and he uses his power to control people." As the trial approaches, it remains to be seen what evidence will be presented against Mullet and his followers. But one thing is clear: the allegations of abuse and control are serious and disturbing, and the community is demanding justice for those who have been affected.

The excitement in his little eyes reminded me of the first time we delved into the magical world of Harry Potter together. I remember him getting enthralled with every page, most especially with the rich, vivid illustrations. Jim Kay, the illustrator, really has a way of bringing J.K. Rowling's enchanting story to life, and for a child, this experience is nothing short of spellbinding. Each time we settle onto the couch, the anticipation is palpable. He wriggles with excitement, his little fingers tracing each line of vibrant colors and fantastical scenes, before we begin to read. It's become a cherished ritual, these story sessions. The delightful giggles, wide-eyed wonder, and endless questions are precious, creating memories we'll both treasure as seriously as a vault full of galleons in Gringotts. Now, as we perused the sneak peeks of the fourth book's illustrations, his questions came in rapid succession. "Who's that, Mommy?" he'd ask, pointing at the formidable image of a dragon that took up a full page. "Is it a nice dragon?" "Ah, that's a Hungarian Horntail," I explained. "Very dangerous, but fascinating. You'll discover more when we read about the Triwizard Tournament." His eyebrows furrowed momentarily, before a grin spread across his face, the prospect of discovering a new element in the story clearly thrilling. As each new picture came to light from the Pottermore archives, I could sense his imagination working overtime, spinning tales and fantasies beyond even those I'd anticipated. Imagining what lay ahead, I couldn't help but bask in the warmth of his enthusiasm. It's this joyfulness and curiosity that I hope to nurture further; that spark which illuminates his love for stories, and his ability to journey in his mind to far-off lands and magical places. But what is most rewarding about these reading sessions isn't simply revisiting the beloved narratives of my own childhood. Rather, it's witnessing how these whimsical tales ignite his sense of empathy and understanding about the world around him. Harry's bravery, Hermione's wit, Ron's loyalty-they aren't just characters in a story but lessons wrapped in enchanting prose, reminding us all of the virtues we hold dear. As we prepared to step back into the real world after this lively exploration, he was already thinking ahead. "When we get the book, can we read all night, Mommy?" he asked earnestly, his expression one of pure earnestness. "We'll read it until your eyes grow heavy, and sleep calls you to dream of adventures," I promised, ruffling his hair gently. And honestly, I am just as eager. To dive back into Hogwarts with him, to rediscover magic through his innocent lens, this is truly priceless. So we wait excitedly for the release day, like loyal members of the magical community queuing outside Flourish and Blotts for a new chapter. We'll eagerly flip each page, relish every illustration, and embark on this cherished literary journey, hand in hand. Through it all, it's about sharing the magic-not just the spells and charm but the magic of imagination, the magic of storytelling, and most importantly, the magic of sharing it together.

These findings have been interpreted as reflecting the use of schematic event representations in higher-level language comprehension (Sass et al., 2009), or the need to construct a coherent representation of an object's function from multiple sources of information (Kalenine et al., 2009). However, alternative explanations cannot be ruled out. For instance, participants may have retrieved thematic information for familiar objects without accessing schematic event representations, as suggested by previous research on lexical decision (Chrysikou, Simpson, Hamidi, & Thompson-Schill, 2010). Thematic responses may have been supported by the retrieval of semantic information at the level of abstracted meaning (e.g., the concept 'dog') rather than specific exemplars (e.g., 'Labrador retriever'; de Zubicaray et al., 2013). It remains possible that activation in pMTG and AG reflects the recruitment of executive functions to support semantic retrieval in the face of interference from other related items (Jefferies & Lambon Ralph, 2006). The role of pMTG and AG in semantic processing therefore requires further investigation. A second aim of this study is to examine the time course of semantic processing in ATL and temporoparietal regions. While many neuroimaging studies have reported differential activation in ATL and temporoparietal regions during semantic tasks, few have considered the timing of these effects (Binder et al., 2009; Mirman et al., 2017). The temporal profile of neural activity provides insights into the relative contributions of different brain regions to semantic processing. Earlier studies of semantic memory have typically employed passive viewing paradigms, in which participants simply observe pictures or words on screen (Thompson-Schill, D'Esposito, Aguirre, & Farah, 1997). In contrast, MEG enables researchers to measure neural responses evoked by actively engaging in a task, which better reflects real-world semantic cognition (van Kemenade, Lemhofer, & Baayen, 2012). Studies of the time-course of semantic processing have demonstrated early involvement of occipito-temporal cortex in visual perception and later involvement of ATL in semantic processing (Nobre, Allison, & McCarthy, 1994; Pourtois, Grandjean, Sander, & Vuilleumier, 2004; Schyns, Bonnar, & Gosselin, 2002; Simanova et al., 2015). However, it is not clear whether ATL responds earlier than temporoparietal sites when semantic processing involves the retrieval of conceptual knowledge. Recent work has begun to address this issue, reporting an early peak in the left ATL around 150 ms after picture onset, followed by a later peak in right temporoparietal cortex around 250 ms (Simanova et al., 2015). However, the precise timing of semantic activity in ATL and temporoparietal regions has yet to be established. We sought to address these issues using MEG, which measures magnetic fields produced by electrical currents flowing through the brain. Unlike fMRI, MEG can measure responses to fast-paced stimuli with millisecond resolution, making it ideally suited to studying the time-course of cognitive processes. MEG also provides excellent spatial resolution, allowing us to localise semantic processing within individual brain regions (Bastiaansen, Van der Linden, Ter Horst, Petersson, & Hagoort, 2008; van Atteveldt, Formisano, Goebel, & Blomert, 2004).

The young aviator laughed heartily at this whimsical remark; but he knew Perk was really feeling deeply moved, and would hardly have missed coming back home again for all the wealth in the world. They had left Chicago in the early morning, and when they passed over Cincinnati, it must have been noon. Now, Birmingham lay behind them, and the afternoon was advancing rapidly toward evening. It was high time they began to look around for some sort of accommodations for the night; and perhaps also for a decent meal. "Say, how about stopping off somewhere soon, and getting something to eat?" asked Perk, presently. "It seems to me I could bite the head off a tenpenny nail right now, and chew it into splinters besides." "We ought to reach Atlanta before long, don't you think?" queried the pilot. "Well, we could find a hotel there easy enough; but it'd be more interesting if we could put up at a farm-house, where we'd get genuine Southern cooking, and perhaps meet with some real characters." "Now, that's jest what I was thinking, pardner," declared the other. "Why, we might run across some good old darkey who used to know me when I was a kid. You see, I'm pretty well acquainted with this section of the Southland, 'cause my folks lived here until I was ten, and then went West, where dad met up with trouble, and died. My mother followed him inside six months, and I was left alone in the world, with a hundred dollars, and lots of pluck, to start life on." "Then you came East, and finally joined the Mounties, where you served several years, and became a sergeant?" "Right-o! And since I quit the Force, and struck out to make my fortune, I've met up with more adventures than I ever dreamed possible. But here, let's stop talking shop, and keep our eyes peeled for a likely looking farm-house where we might strike paydirt. This is the land of cotton, you remember, and in another month there'll be busy times down here, picking the fluffy stuff, and ginning it, ready for market. In fact, I've seen the niggers hard at work already in the fields, singing those weird songs that always gripped me tight when I was a youngster. Ah! that sounds good, and makes me feel hungry. Let's drop down a bit, and see if there isn't a good place close by." "Listen to that, will you?" cried Jack, thrilled by the distant chorus that came floating up to them. "The very thing you mentioned, Perk. Seems to me they're singing 'Swing low, sweet chariot!' That song has always gripped me too, whenever I heard it sung. Yes, I see the house below, and it's a fair-sized affair. If we're lucky, we may strike oil there." "How about dropping straight down, instead of circling first?" suggested the other. "Might scare the women-folks half to death to see a biplane swooping down on them, eh, what?" "Perhaps you're right, Perk. Anyhow, it's worth trying. We'll land in yonder field, and walk over to the house. Then you can take hold, and ask for lodgings. Perhaps they've never seen an aeroplane before, and are wondering what under the sun it can be." "Sure, that's so, suh.

In 1995, he took over at Leicester City who were languishing in the bottom half of the First Division. His first full season saw Leicester win promotion to the Premiership. However, it wasn't until after the turn of the century that O'Neill really made his name. With the Foxes being perennial relegation candidates in the top flight, he somehow managed to keep them in the Premiership before selling off their better players to fund his own rebuilding program. When they were relegated in 2001, Leicester fans didn't know what hit them. It took him only one year to get them back into the Premiership and this time, Leicester finished third behind Arsenal and Chelsea to qualify for next season's UEFA Cup. That summer, he also won the InterToto Cup, thus securing qualification for the next season's UEFA Cup competition. Unfortunately, Leicester's form fell apart spectacularly towards the end of the 2003/04 season and O'Neill left the club in March 2000 with the Foxes in the relegation zone. Then came Celtic. In his first season in charge, he guided the Bhoys to a Scottish Premier League title and a League Cup double. Last season, he led the Glasgow side to a treble, consisting of the SPL title, the Scottish Cup and the League Cup. This season, despite losing several key players to other clubs, he still managed to lead Celtic to the league championship again, with the final game of the season against Rangers yet to come. There's no doubt that O'Neill is one of the best managers around today, but can he handle the pressure of managing a club like Liverpool? Will he be able to live up to the expectations of the Anfield faithful if he gets the job? Can he bring success to a club which hasn't won anything since 2001? Personally, I don't think so. Martin O'Neill is a great manager, but I'm not sure if he can handle the pressure that comes with managing such a huge club like Liverpool. A lot of people say that he is too arrogant for the job. Also, he doesn't have any experience of European football. If he does decide to manage Liverpool, he'll probably need a couple of seasons to rebuild the squad and get used to the whole situation. What if he fails? I would hate to see the man sacked after failing to deliver trophies. Besides, I think he'll enjoy life in Scotland more than England. He's already said that he wouldn't leave Celtic unless something major happens. Also, he seems to be enjoying himself in Glasgow. His family loves living in Scotland and the Celtic board are prepared to give him whatever he wants. And finally, he's a Celtic fan. Let's face it, he won't leave Celtic unless he's given a blank cheque to buy the entire Premiership, including its players, referees and coaches. Frank Rijkaard Another man who has never managed outside Spain, Frank Rijkaard has done wonders with Barcelona. Despite inheriting a team that had just lost to Real Madrid in the Spanish Super Cup Final and the UEFA Supercup Final, Rijkaard steered Barca to the La Liga title in his first season in charge. Last season, he repeated the feat with the Catalans winning the league title by a whopping 12 points ahead of second-placed Real Sociedad. They also reached the quarter-finals of the Champions League where they were knocked out by eventual winners AC Milan on penalties.

I couldn't understand why they died and I was still alive. The days became months and even years. I lived my life in fear and dread, waiting to die. For years I believed the media hype that women were not being infected with HIV/AIDS. I thought I was the only one. I was so lonely that I decided to reach out. I posted a flyer in a hospital seeking other women with HIV/AIDS to come to a support group at my home. To my surprise, within days the telephone began ringing off the hook. I would get phone calls late at night from young girls and women - some were in their hospital beds, others isolated in their homes, too afraid to disclose their HIV status to anyone. Within weeks, the support group became so large, it outgrew my living room and we began to meet in the basement of a church. There were professional women, teachers, physicians, secretaries, bus drivers. I began to go with women to their doctor's appointments, advocating that they receive the appropriate care. Women needed so much, but our stories were not being told; we were not the face of AIDS. Women needed shelter from abusive husbands, they needed clothes and food for their children or they just needed someone to talk to. We shared our stories of frustration about not finding services and support for women living with HIV/AIDS. Gay, bisexual black men at high risk for HIV. Women talked about physicians who refused to treat them or who did not know how to treat the different manifestations of HIV/AIDS in women. Women talked about having their HIV status disclosed in public places. We talked about other things beyond HIV. We talked about love and we laughed a lot. Even as we lost our friends, we didn't talk about dying. We talked about learning to live with HIV. In less than two years, the support group became a nonprofit organization called The Women's Collective. In 1996, it provided services to 50 women in the District of Columbia, which has one of the of the highest incidence of HIV in the country. The core of our mission is peer-based, woman-focused and family-centered. Back then, I worked full-time and I was able to get enough funding to hire a part-time person. Today the Women's Collective has 20 full-time staff and a host of volunteers. We provide a wide range of services including case management services, helping women find health and other types of services. The goal is to keep woman in care. We provide AIDS-prevention education, counseling and testing services, and therapeutic counseling services. Women and their children can come in and use our computers for schoolwork or work on a resume. They can come in and get hot food. We have a food and clothes pantry so they can take stuff home.

During this period of hypomania, I found myself immersed in a whirlwind of productivity and frenetic energy. It's almost as if my mind had been gifted this euphoric spark that ignited every thought into a blazing obsession. Ideas flowed freely, cascading like water over a dam, and I plunged headfirst into projects that had long been buried under the mundane responsibilities of daily life. I'm talking about the kind of creativity that leaves you breathless, revitalized, and simultaneously out of touch with reality. I wrote, I painted, I organized everything in sight; a flurry of activity that felt as if I were riding a rollercoaster, with each ascent accompanied by an exhilarating rush of happiness, and each descent reminding me that balance was just a whisper away. But in the back of my mind, I couldn't shake the growing concern-a quiet fear that the thrilling high wouldn't last, that the impending crash lurking just beyond the horizon was waiting to catch up with me. I was fully aware of the pattern, the cyclical nature of this condition, yet while I was thriving in that moment, logic seemed to dissipate like mist. It was a beautiful illusion, akin to a dream that I knew would one day end, but in that moment, I clung to it as tightly as I could. I let this energy carry me swiftly through each day, a blur of late-night inspiration and early morning wakefulness. The truth is, it felt good. Good to feel alive, to feel motivated, and to feel connected to something greater than myself, even if it was fleeting. I was almost jealous of that sense of drive, that electric buzz coursing through my veins. Thus, I neglected to acknowledge the telling signs that others, including my girlfriend, were genuinely concerned about my well-being. Conversations often felt strained, and my tendency to plunge into new ventures left little room for shared moments. I became engrossed entirely in my own universe, one where the external worries faded and my internal chaos took center stage. Yet, amidst this internal excitement, I confronted the void left by Zelda, my dear cat. The heartache of her absence was a contrasting weight upon my heart, deepening as days turned into weeks and the search stretched longer. I'd sometimes catch myself staring out the window, wondering if she was still wandering, possibly even under the stars I once shared with her, calling her name into the night in hopes she could hear me. I sought solace in small distractions, attempting to suppress thoughts of my furry companion. Those days when I felt a breeze drifting through the open windows, a glimmer of her might wash over me, teasing my memory and reminding me of her gentle purrs and playful antics. As time wore on, the hypomanic phase was surely beginning to wane; I could sense the energy transforming, shifting slowly into the usual bittersweet clarity that accompanies reality. It became apparent that I couldn't sustain this constant state forever; I never could. I needed to regroup, refocus on the good habits I once cultivated-exercise, nutrition, maintaining a healthy rhythm in my life before I spiraled too far out of reach. As I sat in deep contemplation, the gradual return towards normalcy did not feel like a defeat but a reawakening. I decided it was time to write letters, to acknowledge the friends I had neglected, and to confront the vulnerabilities I had danced around. Life was ready to ground me once again, but not without its lessons first.

But proving it day in and day out, that's the real challenge, isn't it? Each morning, I rise and dress myself in the armor of parental duty, fortified by my caffeinated arsenal of coffee and sheer will. My days unfold like a series of intricate dance steps-one part grace, two parts fumbling. Amidst the whirls of school drop-off chatter and the endless grocery lists that threaten to consume all reason, there lies the nagging dread that perhaps I'm not enough. I pore over the many books stacked haphazardly on my bedside table, promises of wisdom amid tales of motherhood, hoping to find the secret key that unlocks this challenge. Each page I turn is steeped in advice from learned sages, women who have walked this path before me, yet I can't shake the feeling that I'm skipping crucial steps in this perfect choreography. Maybe I'm watching too much from the sidelines, my instinct tethered tightly by this incessant anxiety buzzing in my chest. As P grows, her laughter fills the air, a sound so pure it lifts me, soaring above the chaos. Yet, there are moments when I catch a glimpse of fear lurking in my periphery-fear that swirls around the topics of friendship and acceptance. Is she too nerdy? Should I let her wear mismatched socks? The world is a complex place, brimming with peanut-shaped obstacles, and I watch as her little heart navigates this labyrinth with a mix of bravery and innocence. Would that I could wrap her in a cocoon, shielding her from everything that could possibly harm her, physical or otherwise. And with each passing day, I learn the art of letting go. It's nauseating to relinquish the reins, yet liberating, too. Sometimes, in my quieter moments, I find the strength to trust-not just in her journey, but in my own instincts as a mother. Of course, there are mishaps along the way. Friendly playdates that turn turbulent, the mishandling of a school project that leaves us both in tears. My competitive nature, already woven into my DNA, rears its head and commands, "You must be perfect!" But perfection, I am learning, is little more than a mirage, flickering in its distance, enticing yet elusive. I try to remember the nights when I'd cradle her small body, rocking her to sleep while whispering absurd stories about brave little hedgehogs who conquered their fears. Those are moments of pure magic, stitched with the invisible thread of love. Whether I'm doing it right, whether I'm "enough"-all of it fades away in the presence of her joyous laughter and sparkling eyes. When the sun dips below the horizon, her giggles turn into sleepy sighs, and my heart swells with gratitude for another day of this uncharted existence-the unpredictable adventure of motherhood. Each night, as I tuck her in, I tell her she can be anything she wants to be, and pray that in that declaration, I am laying down the foundation of faith and confidence that will hold her steady when the world feels too much. My insecurities inch into the corners of my mind, but I remind myself that nurturing her spirit, her curiosity, her essence is far more important than quieting my own anxieties. So here's to the dance of motherhood: the stumbling steps, the laughter amidst the falls, the beauty of shared mistakes-all interwoven in a tapestry that is simply ours.

Gunda Lehman's eager face, Marie M. Belloc's bright blue eyes, and the gentle hands of the other girls who had bid her farewell all flooded her thoughts. She felt a pang of guilt for leaving them, for abandoning them to the care of another teacher. She had always been close to her mother, and the thought of losing her was unbearable. The train pulled into the station, and Miss Aldworth gathered her belongings, her heart heavy with emotion. As she stepped off the train, she was enveloped in a warm, familiar scent - the smell of English air and damp earth. She took a deep breath, feeling a sense of comfort wash over her. She hailed a cab and gave the driver the address of her mother's townhouse, her mind numb with fatigue. The cab ride was a blur, and before she knew it, they were pulling up in front of the townhouse. Miss Aldworth paid the driver and stepped out onto the pavement, her eyes scanning the familiar facade. The house looked smaller than she remembered, the once-green shutters now faded and worn. She felt a pang of sadness, wondering what lay ahead. As she entered the house, she was greeted by the sight of her mother, pale and frail, but with a warm smile on her face. Miss Aldworth's heart swelled with emotion as she rushed to her mother's side, embracing her tightly. "Mother, I'm here," she whispered, her voice trembling. "I'm here to take care of you." Her mother's eyes filled with tears as she looked up at her daughter. "I'm so glad you're here, Marcia," she whispered back. "I've been waiting for you." As they sat together on the couch, holding hands and weeping together, Miss Aldworth knew that she had made the right decision in leaving her students behind. She would return to them one day, but for now, she was needed here, by her mother's side.
