In an unususal twist, the attorney representing the church before the Supreme Court is also a church member - Margie Phelps, a daughter of the pastor. She held her own under sometimes withering questioning from several justices, especially over whether the church's "speech" is personal or public in nature. "Suppose someone believes that African-Americans are inherently inferior, and they are really a bad influence on this country," Justice Samuel Alito said. "And so a person comes up to an African-American and starts berating that person with racial hatred. Now is this just any old old African-American on the street? That's a matter of public concern?" Chief Justice John Roberts said, "Does it make a difference, which seems to me to be the case here, that Mr. Snyder was selected not because of who he was, but because it was a way to get maximum publicity for your client's particular message?" Ginsburg jumped in, noting Westboro had picketed the Maryland state Capitol the same day, just before going to the Snyder funeral. "This is a case about exploiting a private family's grief," she said, "and the question is: Why should the First Amendment tolerate exploiting this Marine's family when you have so many other forums for getting across your message," such as standing in front of the Supreme Court. Into these forts there came men, women, and children, from all parts of the country, each bringing as much food as possible, and each willing to lend a hand to the common defence and the common support. On the 30th of August, the Indians attacked Fort Mims, one of the largest of the stockade stations, and after a desperate battle destroyed it, killing all but seventeen of the five hundred and fifty people who were living in it. The news of this terrible slaughter quickly spread over the country, and everybody knew now that a general war had begun, in which the Indians meant to destroy the whites utterly, not sparing even the youngest children. Those who had remained on their farms now flocked in great numbers to the forts, and every effort was made to strengthen the defences at all points. The men, including all the boys who were large enough to point a gun and pull a trigger, were organized into companies and assigned to port-holes, in order that each might know where to go to do his part of the fighting whenever the Indians should come. Even those of the women who knew how to shoot, insisted upon being provided with guns and assigned to posts of duty. There was not only no use in flinching, but every one of them knew that whenever the fort should be attacked the only question to be decided was, "Shall we beat the savages off, or shall every man woman and child of us be butchered?" They could not run away, for there was nowhere to run, except into the hands of the merciless foe. The life of every one of them was involved in the defence of the forts, and each was, therefore, anxious to do all he could to make the defense a successful one. Their only hope was in desperate courage, and, being Americans, their courage was equal to the demand made upon it. It was not a civilized war, in which surrenders, and exchanges of prisoners, and treaties and flags of truce, or even neutrality offered any escape. It was a savage war, in which the Indians intended to kill all the whites, old and young, wherever they could find them. The people in the forts knew this, and they made their arrangements accordingly. Now if the boys and girls who read this story will get their atlases and turn to the map of Alabama, they will find some points, the relative positions of which they must remember if they wish to understand fully the happenings with which we have to do. Just below the junction of the Alabama and Tombigbee rivers, on the east side of the stream, they will find the little town of Tensaw, and Fort Mims stood very near that place. The peninsula formed by the two rivers above their junction is now Clarke County, and almost exactly in its centre stands the village of Grove Hill.

Lynn's wild eyes dart around the room, seeking a means of escape, but blood courses through her veins and uncertainty floods her thoughts. Parker returns to the kitchen table, his breath steady but a quiet storm brewing beneath the surface. "Where is Val?" he repeats, this time with a steel edge to his voice. "How should I know?" she gasps, her defiance softening with each passing second. She shifts her weight, wincing at the rough rope binding her wrists. "He's gone, Parker! He's not coming back for you, or for me!" With an impatient glare, he paces the room, the timber floor creaking underfoot, a chill settling into the air. Shadows loom large on the walls, beige paint dimming beneath the ghost of fear that has seeped into the very atmosphere. He stops abruptly, turning to face her-eyes piercing, as if ready to dig deeper than mere words. "He was your lifeline," Parker asserts, the disdain lacing his voice. "Now he's left you with nothing." "I told you-I don't know where he is!" The scream echoes off the walls, a discordant cry in the tense stillness, hanging like smoke in the air. Parker advances, his size dwarfing her slight frame-part predator, part interrogator. Lynn swallows hard, realizing that this is no mere conversation but rather a game of survival. "Do we really want to play this?" he asks, his tone lowered, the edges sharp and lethal. Without waiting for her answer, he drags a chair forward and sits down across from her, elbows resting on the table, fingers steepled. Time drips like molasses as they square off; each breath heavy with implication. "You know something," he insists, his eyes narrowing, "and I'm not in the mood for games, Lynn." His words slither like smoke into the air between them, pricking at her guarded heart. To him, she's little more than a detail in a puzzle-fractured, broken, but still potential. They sit in silence, and the air thickens, each second stretching taut with tension. "I don't know where he is. I swear." The tremor in her voice betrays her resolve, but she steels herself, a spark igniting within her declaration. "You think you can bulldoze your way into my life, frighten me into submission? That's not how it works." Parker smiles-a quick flash of amusement. "You've got spirit," he concedes, leaning back slightly. "I like that. But spirit won't save you." His eyes sharpen, returning to the lethal focus of before. Lynn's wheels turn quietly, thoughts racing as she sizes him up. "Maybe he wasn't everything you think he was. Maybe Val left because he was afraid of you?" The audacity shifts in the atmosphere, leaving her bewildered, yet resolute. But Parker simply laughs, a raw, low chuckle that cuts through the heaviness. "I don't fear anyone. Certainly not a washed-up dealer like Val." The room clicks back into a fragile silence, Parker's gaze unrelenting as he contemplates his next move. Each moment crystallizes-a calculation in which both the hunter and the hunted weigh options, aware that to falter now could mean the end. As a fleeting smile flickers across his lips, Parker reaches forward, and the tension spikes: "Then tell me what you do know."

"You have never done anything of the sort." "Well, then, why should you complain to me?" continued Mrs. Somerton. "Why should you try to prevent me from punishing my son? I am sorry that I cannot take a firmer line with him, but it seems to me that he requires very strict discipline. His father's death, and the loss of all his fortune, have made him wild and reckless, and I fear he will turn out a bad character. He needs a strong hand, and I intend to supply it. Therefore, please leave me to manage my own affairs." "And I say, madam," replied the captain, "that you have no right to punish him as you did this afternoon. I heard him crying upstairs, and came down to inquire into the cause of it. And I found him lying on the floor, his face buried in his hands, and tears rolling down his cheeks. When I questioned him, he told me that you had beaten him because he had stolen a loaf from the pantry. Now, I maintain that the lad was not guilty of the crime. It was his cousin who stole the bread, and he only took it because he wanted to give it to his friend. Besides, even if he were guilty, you surely could have punished him less severely than you did." "He is a liar!" shouted Mrs. Somerton. "His cousin confessed to me that it was he who stole the loaf, and I know that the boy was lying when he denied it. Moreover, if you think that I ought not to beat him, you had better tell me how else I am to make him behave himself. He is too wilful for me to reason with him, and, besides, I won't stand any nonsense from him." "It is not right to beat him," persisted the captain. "I agree with you that he wants firmness, and that he requires to be kept in order, but he is young yet, and still very impressionable. Besides, I feel certain that he loves you, and that you love him. Why, therefore, should you treat him so harshly?" "Because he is a wicked boy," she retorted. "He is always getting into trouble, and he deserves every stroke of the whip he gets. There is nothing good in him, and I sometimes wonder whether he is my child at all. Perhaps he is not."

Do you see similarities between your father and Bush? No. My father was once asked [by Barbara Walters] what the most important of his presidency was, and he talked about the deficits. Is it true that you were invited to give the eulogy at your father's funeral, but that Nancy turned you down because she didn't want you talking about stem-cell research? To the casual eye Donald appeared of slight build, but his old friend knew of the steel-like muscles of those arms and the strength of the long, straight legs. The mind of the older man flashed back to a football game in Donald's High School days, with the State championship at stake. Donald had been sent into the game at the eleventh hour, and with defeat staring the home team in the face he had torn through the opposing lines like a madman for agonizing gains until his dark head flashed across the line to victory. Donald came embarrassedly to his feet. "Well, I guess I'll be moving." "Here, boy, take this," the sheriff said awkwardly, thrusting a roll of bills into Donald's hand. The young man's face flushed. "It's awfully good of you, Jim, but I - " "It's all right, Don," interrupted the older man, summoning a smile. "I'm just giving you a loan." Donald looked at him soberly. "I'll pay you back when-I-I-earn it." His face very serious, the sheriff placed a hand on Donald's shoulder. "Now, listen, Don. Your father and I talked here in the office for an hour before he bailed you out, and we agreed that the best thing was to let you go on your own. No, I am not going to give you a lecture, for you are not wholly to blame. He had recently returned from India, where he had amassed a considerable sum of money. The suddenness of his return, and the lavish expenditure of his wealth, attracted attention, and excited suspicion. His appearance was so prepossessing, however, that none ventured to question his right to the possession of his property, until after the occurrence of a fatal accident, when suspicion gave way to certainty. "He appeared to take a particular interest in me, and seemed anxious to gain my confidence. This he effected by his flattering attentions, and the promise of pecuniary assistance, to extricate me from difficulties in which I had involved myself through his persuasion. A few days after our meeting, I found myself pledged to accompany him to France. We reached Paris, where we spent three weeks in dissipation. My companion was a gambler, and my purse was soon exhausted. To retrieve my losses, I determined to sell my watch and ring. The former I took out of my pocket, intending to dispose of it, when I perceived a figure familiar to my eye, standing close behind me. The figure belonged to a man whom I knew well, though not intimately. He was a stranger in Paris, having come there expressly to seek me. I had often seen him at the house of a common acquaintance, whose name was Davenport, and who had frequently mentioned him as being a gentleman of high rank and large landed possessions, but who was said to live a life of seclusion, owing to the ill-health of his wife. The stranger accosted me with much apparent cordiality. "I asked him how he came to know me, and what he wanted? "His answer was abrupt and significant. 'What I want is your watch!' "I started back with astonishment, and looked at him more closely. His countenance was pale and haggard, but otherwise there was nothing remarkable in his appearance. He wore a plain suit of black, and had a travelling cap on his head. "There was something so mysterious in the tone and manner of his reply, that I involuntarily placed my hand upon my watch, and demanded an explanation. "He replied by drawing from his pocket a small piece of paper, on which were written these words: 'If you value your safety, deliver up your watch immediately.' "I did not hesitate. I handed it over to him without making further inquiry. I did not even look at the note again. The moment I had given up the watch, the man disappeared."

James Weatherby, whose family served as accountants to the members of the Jockey Club, was assigned the task of tracing the pedigree, or complete family history, of every horse racing in England. In 1791 the results of his research were published as the Introduction to the General Stud Book. From 1793 to the present, members of the Weatherby family have meticulously recorded the pedigree of every foal born to those racehorses in subsequent volumes of the General Stud Book. By the early 1800s the only horses that could be called "Thoroughbreds" and allowed to race were those descended from horses listed in the General Stud Book. Thoroughbreds are so inbred that the pedigree of every single animal can be traced back father-to-father to one of three stallions, called the "foundation sires." These stallions were the Byerley Turk, foaled c.1679; the Darley Arabian, foaled c.1700; and the Godolphin Arabian, foaled c.1724. American Thoroughbred Racing The British settlers brought horses and horse racing with them to the New World, with the first racetrack laid out on Long Island as early as 1665. Although the sport became a popular local pastime, the development of organized racing did not arrive until after the Civil War. (The American Stud Book was begun in 1868.) For the next several decades, with the rapid rise of an industrial economy, gambling on racehorses, and therefore horse racing itself, grew explosively; by 1890, 314 tracks were operating across the country. The rapid growth of the sport without any central governing authority led to the domination of many tracks by criminal elements. In 1894 the nation's most prominent track and stable owners met in New York to form an American Jockey Club, modeled on the English, which soon ruled racing with an iron hand and eliminated much of the corruption. In the early 1900s, however, racing in the United States was almost wiped out by antigambling sentiment that led almost all states to ban bookmaking. By 1908 the number of tracks had plummeted to just 25. That same year, however, the introduction of pari-mutuel betting for the Kentucky Derby signaled a turnaround for the sport. More tracks opened as many state legislatures agreed to legalize pari-mutuel betting in exchange for a share of the money wagered. At the end of World War I, prosperity and great horses like Man o' War brought spectators flocking to racetracks. The sport prospered until World War II, declined in popularity during the 1950s and 1960s, then enjoyed a resurgence in the 1970s triggered by the immense popularity of great horses such as Secretariat, Seattle Slew, and Affirmed, each winners of the American Triple Crown - the KENTUCKY DERBY, the Preakness, and the Belmont Stakes. During the late 1980s, another significant decline occurred, however. Thoroughbred tracks exist in about half the states.

In these experiments, the surfactant, air and oil are generally mixed in a column to produce a fixed volume of foam. The foam is then observed for a period of time and the rate of foam height decay or the half-decay time (i.e. the time taken for foam to reach half of its original height) has been considered as the measure of the foam stability. Results from these experiments have shown that light oils are more detrimental to the stability of foam. While many of the conclusions drawn from these experiments may be valid for bulk foams, direct translation of the outcomes to foam flow in porous media may be inadequate due to the complexity of the interaction between foam and oil within confined geometries. Different observations have been reported in literature about oil-foam interaction in porous media. Some investigators have reported that the presence of light oil prevents the formation of stable foams [25,26] while others have argued that stable foams can be produced if an appropriate surfactant or foaming agent is selected [27,28]. The negative effect of oil may manifest itself in porous media by prolonging foam generation and reducing foam propagation velocities [28-30]. While the type of oil plays a significant role on foam destabilisation in the bulk scale tests, Jensen and Friedmann [31] demonstrated that the oil saturation was more influential upon the stability of foams than the type of oil in porous media. This observation was also reported by Mannhardt and Svorstol [28] in their study of the effect of oil saturation on foam performance in porous media. Foam quality is also a variable affecting displacement through porous media. Minssieux [25] studied the influence of the foam quality on oil displacement in a sandstone core following the gas-surfactant co-injection method. The author observed a higher oil recovery as the foam quality decreased. Osei-Bonsu et al. [16] also observed more stable foam formation during oil displacement in a Hele-Shaw cell as the foam quality decreased. Ma et al. [18] studied the effect of foam quality on gas diversion by foam in a layered micromodel in the absence of oil. They observed more gas diversion from the higher permeability region (bigger pores) to the lower permeability zone as the foam quality increased until a point beyond which increasing foam quality decreased gas diversion. The dynamics of oil-foam interaction especially in porous media is not fully understood and is a topic of ongoing research. There are many open questions regarding the nature and the dynamics of foam generation and propagation in porous media that need to be addressed such as how exactly the confined pore geometry of porous media influences the dynamics of foam-oil interaction or how the properties of foam affects its sweep efficiency in oil saturated porous media.

The dynamic interplay between signaling cascades and cellular behavior is central to understanding organismal adaptation in diverse environments. Within the bacterial realm, the intricate regulation of c-di-GMP levels serves as a quintessential example of how single molecules can orchestrate a myriad of physiological responses, allowing bacteria to thrive amidst fluctuating conditions. The synthesis and degradation of c-di-GMP are meticulously controlled by the concerted action of DGCs and PDEs, ensuring that cellular responses are appropriately tailored to specific stimuli (Hengge, 2009). Beyond mere signal propagation, the second messenger can also act as a pivotal regulator that shapes developmental fates and population dynamics among microbial communities. Particularly fascinating is the c-di-GMP's influence on biofilm formation-a critical survival strategy for many bacteria. Biofilms, structured communities of microbial cells encased in a self-produced polymeric matrix, are notoriously resilient to environmental stresses and antimicrobial agents. c-di-GMP mediates this transition from a planktonic to a sessile lifestyle predominantly through its interaction with various effector proteins. These proteins, once activated, can elicit changes in gene expression that promote the production of exopolysaccharides, which are essential for biofilm architecture and stability. The evolutionary significance of this capability is underscored by the fact that biofilm formation not only enhances bacterial survival but also facilitates horizontal gene transfer, thereby fostering genetic diversity within microbial populations. Moreover, the c-di-GMP signaling pathway illustrates a remarkable complexity in its regulatory networks. While the presence of the GGDEF domain signifies a potential for c-di-GMP synthesis, a diverse array of sensory motifs allows DGCs to integrate multiple environmental inputs such as nutrient availability, osmotic pressure, and mechanical stimuli. As health systems strive to keep pace with the elusive nature of Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite's ability to circumvent conventional treatments continues to complicate control efforts. This has necessitated a multipronged approach, integrating not only IPTp-SP as a prophylactic measure for pregnant women but also embracing innovative strategies like vector control and public health education to diminish the incidence and severity of malaria. The deployment of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) has been pivotal, offering protective barriers against nocturnal mosquito encounters. Distribution campaigns, often supported by international coalitions, aim to blanket entire communities, prioritizing vulnerable demographics such as children under five and expectant mothers. Despite these endeavors, distribution efficacy remains patchy due to logistical hurdles, cultural resistance, and intermittent funding. Moreover, education campaigns emphasize the importance of early diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) have become more accessible, allowing for immediate detection and subsequent administration of artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs). These efforts hinge on national health policies, infrastructure capabilities, and the adaptive utilizations of technological advancements to enhance disease surveillance and treatment disbursement. Further complicating malaria control is climate variability, influencing transmission dynamics. Changes in rainfall patterns, temperature fluctuations, and humidity can expand malaria's geographical range, thereby challenging previously malaria-free regions. As vector habitats grow, so does the imperative for responsive and localized control measures, underpinned by real-time data collection on weather and transmission trends. In this evolving landscape, the research community persists in its quest for novel interventions. Vaccine development stands at the forefront, with efforts to bolster the immune system's capacity to combat malaria. The RTS,S/AS01 vaccine, one of the frontrunners, offers partial protection, yet it demands rigorous evaluation and substantial support to optimize delivery and efficacy. Collaboration, both within and between nations, has become indispensable. The sharing of data, resources, and expertise among countries can fortify the foundation upon which successful eradication strategies rest. Furthermore, empowering local health workers through training and support builds resilience within communities, pivotal in sustaining long-term gains against the disease. However, amidst these scientific and strategic advancements, the human element remains undeniably critical. Engagement with local populations through culturally sensitive health messaging fosters trust and compliance, intertwining the success of biomedical interventions with social acceptance. Advocacy efforts also play an essential role, galvanizing global support and funding dedicated to malaria control initiatives. In summary, the fight against malaria in sub-Saharan Africa is complex and multidimensional, demanding comprehensive approaches tailored to tackle both the biological complexities of the parasite and the systemic challenges of healthcare delivery. With coordinated global and local efforts, the pathway to eventual eradication becomes clearer, albeit necessitating unwavering commitment and continuous innovation to navigate the hurdles attendant in this ongoing battle against malaria. The strides made thus far instill hope, highlighting the determined pursuit of a future where malaria's grip on affected populations is ultimately relinquished.

Last month a report by the Nuffield Council on Bioethics called for all adults to be automatically considered donors unless they opted out - something that is already the case in Spain and Austria. Under current law, only those aged over 16 can choose to become registered donors, although this is not always followed through when the time comes. A survey carried out last summer found that more than half of Britons (54 per cent) wrongly thought you could register to be an organ donor before the age of 16. Many people also assume that if they die in hospital, doctors will ask relatives whether or not they want them to donate their organs. This is not the case. Relatives are often left feeling they should make the decision themselves. However, NHS Blood and Transplant has launched a campaign to raise awareness of the need for consent to be made clear before someone dies, so that medical staff can honour their wishes. 'It is vital that anyone thinking of becoming a donor signs up to the NHS Organ Donor Register,' says. Dr David Briggs, director of organ donation and transplantation for NHS. Blood and Transplant. 'There are currently around 8,000 patients waiting for a transplant, including nearly 1,000 children, and sadly, despite the efforts of transplant teams across the country, every week two people die because they cannot receive the transplants they need.' Declan was born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, which meant his left ventricle was too small to pump blood properly from his heart to the rest of his body. When he was just four days old, he underwent open-heart surgery to correct the problem. His condition was stable until he was nine months old, when his lungs collapsed during a viral infection. For the next few weeks, he was kept alive by a mechanical ventilator, and then had another operation. At the end of March this year, he went into hospital again. Two weeks later, he suffered catastrophic internal bleeding during surgery. His parents were told the following morning that there was nothing more doctors could do for him. After giving permission for him to be taken off the life-support machine, they were asked if they would like to donate his organs. 'We'd been warned that there was a risk of brain damage if he suffered bleeding, but we hadn't expected this to happen,' recalls Paula. 'When the consultant asked us if we would consider donating Declan's organs, we knew straight away what our answer would be. We couldn't say no.' Declan was placed on a ventilator once more and transferred to a specialist intensive care unit where he was sedated and put on a drug that would stop his heart beating. He was then moved to the operating theatre, where surgeons removed his organs. Paula says: 'The hardest part was seeing Declan lying there with tubes coming out of him. But I'm glad I did it. There's no question in my mind that it was the right thing to do.'

We live in a time when shock value drives engagement, and perhaps that is the currency The New York Times sought to earn with this particular piece. But let's delve deeper: what is the impact of such a narrative on society? On expecting mothers? On partners who find their voices stifled by the prevailing discourse of choice? Stories like these seep into the public consciousness, validating decisions that remain grotesque to many and providing a platform to dismiss the moral weight that accompanies the termination of potential life. While society is busy debating the rights and wrongs, the nuances of human experience-of potential, of promise cut short-fall by the wayside. I can't help but wonder how Amy Richards feels beyond the bravado-infused veneer of her article. Has she truly reconciled her actions with her conscience? Is this self-publication her means of grappling with her choices, an attempt to assert control over a narrative she's not quite comfortable with? Only she knows the answers to these questions, cloaked behind her choice of words and omissions. Defenders of her story might argue that her expression is an exercise in liberation, an extension of her autonomy as a woman. They might say she shines light on topics shrouded in judgment and secrecy. Yet, this "liberation" feels hollow when entangled in the web of consumerist fears and trivial comparisons. This isn't a tirade against the difficult decisions parents must sometimes make. My heart holds empathy for those caught in circumstances far beyond their control-poverty, illness, absence of support. But to parade one's elective procedure as empowerment when drenched in such superficial reasoning? It feels more of an affront than a declaration of independence. Perhaps it's time we steer this conversation back to humane complexities, away from divisive tropes, acknowledging both choice and consequence. There is morphine for a tortured body, but there is no opiate for agony of the spirit, the sharp-toothed pain that stabs at a lonely heart with its invisible lancet. In the darkness of his room, with all the noisy traffic of a seaport city rumbling under his windows, Hollister lay on his bed and struggled against that terrifying depression which had seized him, that spiritual panic. It was real. It was based upon undeniable reality. He was no more captain of his soul than any man born of woman has ever been when he descends into the dark places. But he knew that he must shake off that feeling, or go mad, or kill himself. One of the three. He had known men to kill themselves for less. He had seen wounded men beg for a weapon to end their pain. He had known men who, after months of convalescence, quitted by their own hand a life that no longer held anything for them. And it was not because life held out any promise to Hollister that he lived, nor was it a physical, fear of death, nor any moral scruple against self-destruction. He clung to life because instinct was stronger than reason, stronger than any of the appalling facts he encountered and knew he must go on encountering. He had to live, with a past that was no comfort, going on down the pathway of a future which he attempted not to see clearly, because when he did envisage it he was stricken with just such a panic as now overwhelmed him. To live on and on, a pariah among his fellows because of his disfigurement. A man with a twisted face, a gargoyle of a countenance. To have people always shrink from him. To be denied companionship, friendship, love, to know that so many things which made life beautiful were always just beyond his reach. To be merely endured. To have women pity him - and shun him. The sweat broke out on Hollister's face when he thought of all that. He knew that it was true. This knowledge had been growing on him for weeks. To-night the full realization of what it meant engulfed him with terror. That was all. He did not cry out against injustice. He did not whine a protest. He blamed no one. He understood, when he looked at himself in the glass. After a time he shook off the first paralyzing grip of this unnameable terror which had seized him with clammy hands, fought it down by sheer resolution. He was able to lie staring into the dusky spaces of his room and review the stirring panorama of his existence for the past four years. There was nothing that did not fill him with infinite regret - and there was nothing which by any conceivable effort he could have changed. He could not have escaped one of those calamities which had befallen him.

When she refused his offer, the Thaines carried the day, and the Quakers again became exiles. Jean Aydelot followed them to Pennsylvania and married Mercy Pennington, who was promptly disowned by the Quaker Church for this marriage to one outside its membership. In spite of all this heresy, however, the Aydelots became one of the leading families in the development of the colonies. Their descendants fell heir to the traits of their French-English forbears: freedom of belief, courage to follow a cause, a touch of the wanderlust, the mercurial French mind, and the steady poise of the followers of the Inward Light. A trace of bitterness had come down the years, however, with the family history; a feud-like resentment against the family of Jerome Thaine of Virginia. Francis Aydelot had crossed the Alleghanies and settled in Ohio in frontier days. Here his life, like his narrow, woods-bound farm, was clean and open but narrowed by surroundings and lack of opportunity. What had made for freedom and reform in his ancestors, in him became prejudice and stubborn will. Mrs. Aydelot was a broad-minded woman. Something of vision was in her clear gray eyes. Love of beauty, respect for learning, and an almost statesman-like grasp of civic duty and the trend of national progress were hers, too. From such ancestry came Asher Aydelot, the healthiest, happiest country boy that ever waked the echoes of the old Ohio woodlands, or dared the currents of her mad little rivers, or whistled fearlessly as he scampered down the dusty pike road in the soft black summer nights. Asher was just fifteen when the Civil War swept the nation off its feet. The Quaker spirit of Mercy Pennington made fighting repulsive to his father, but in Asher the old Huguenot courage of Jean Aydelot blazed forth, together with the rash partisanship of a young hot-blood whose life has been hemmed in too narrowly by forest walls. Almost before Cloverdale knew there was a war, the Third Ohio Regiment was on its way to the front. Among its bearded men was one beardless youth, a round-faced drummer boy of fifteen, the only child of the big farmhouse beside the National road. In company with him was his boyhood chum, Jim Shirley, son of the Cloverdale tavern keeper. An April sun was slipping behind the treetops, and the twilight mists were already rising above the creek. Francis Aydelot and his wife sat on the veranda watching Asher in the glory of a military suit and brass buttons coming up the pike with springing step. "How strong he is! I'm glad he is at home again," the mother was saying. "Yes, he's here to stay at last. I have his plans all settled," Francis Aydelot declared. "But, Francis, a man must make some plans for himself. Asher may not agree," Mrs. Aydelot spoke earnestly.

In 2006, malaria was present in 109 countries and territories. I is for Immunity Travelers from malaria-free regions such as Europe and the United States, with little or no immunity, who go to areas with high disease rates, are particularly vulnerable. It is essential to take precautions by taking anti-malarial drugs prescribed by your doctor. J is for Julius Wagner-Jauregg Julius Wagner-Jauregg, a Viennese doctor, was the first to intentionally infect syphilis patients with malaria parasites. By controlling the subsequent malaria-related fever with an anti-malaria drug, the effects of both syphilis and malaria could be minimized. Jauregg received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1927. K is for Killer Malaria is a life-threatening disease but it is preventable and curable if the right steps are taken. Education in recognizing the symptoms has reduced the number of cases in some areas by 20 percent. Recognizing the disease in the early stages can stop the disease from becoming a killer. L is for Laser gun U.S. scientists say they are developing a laser gun that could kill millions of mosquitoes in minutes. The laser fires at mosquitoes once it detects the audio frequency created by the beating of wings, the lead scientist on the project told CNN. The project is being funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. M is for Mosquitoes Malaria is caused by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquitoes. The mosquitoes bite between sunset and sunrise and parasites from the mosquito are then injected into the person's skin and transported to the liver. About 170 species of such parasites exist, but only four cause malaria in humans. N is for Nets The distribution of mosquito nets with insecticide is a very effective method of malaria prevention, and it is also one of the most cost-effective methods. These nets can often be obtained for around $3. Earlier this month, actor Ashton Kutcher won a Twitter race against CNN to reach 1 million followers. Kutcher had pledged 10,000 mosquito nets to charity if he beat CNN, and 1,000 if he lost. CNN agreed to do the same. O is for Obstacles In many endemic areas, access to health facilities, as well as drug costs, still present major obstacles. Humanitarian agency Medecins Sans Frontieres estimates that the cost of treating a malaria-infected person in an endemic country was between $0.25 and $2.40 per dose in 2002. P is for Pandemic For malaria to become a pandemic (plague) in an area, several factors have to be present: high human population density; high mosquito population density; high rates of transmission from humans to mosquitoes and from mosquitoes to humans. Q is for Quinine Quinine was the first effective treatment for malaria in the 17th century. Since the 1940's, many other anti-malarial drugs have appeared on the market and have taken precedent over quinine. But quinine is still being used to treat malaria in some cases.

A number of computational and theoretical studies of both model nanopores (Allen et al., 2003; Beckstein et al., 2001, 2004; Beckstein and Sansom, 2003; Dzubiella et al., 2004; Hummer et al., 2001; Kalra et al., 2003; Peter and Hummer, 2005; Trick et al., 2014; Vaitheeswaran et al., 2004) and of ion channel structures (Anishkin and Sukharev, 2004; Beckstein and Sansom, 2006; Jensen et al., 2010; Zhu and Hummer, 2012) have indicated that the unusual behavior of water molecules within sub-nanometer radius pores such as those found in membrane ion channels plays a key role in determining their ion permeability. This has resulted in the concept of hydrophobic gating (Aryal et al., 2014b; Beckstein et al., 2001) whereby expulsion of water or dewetting of a narrow hydrophobic region of a pore results in its functional closure to ion permeation. The degree of dewetting is dependent on the radius, hydrophobicity, and flexibility of the channel (Beckstein and Sansom, 2004). Thus, an ion channel pore might appear sterically wide enough to accommodate water and/or ions, but instead may be functionally closed (i.e., non-conductive to ions) by a central hydrophobic region. If the radius of such a hydrophobic region is less than about 4-5 A, this can promote dewetting thereby presenting a significant energetic barrier to ion and water permeation. Of course, the absence of dewetting does not necessarily imply that there are no barriers to ion permeation, as the presence of water is not the sole determinant of ion permeability, but it is now clear that the ability of a pore to become hydrated represents a reliable indicator of permeability. This concept of hydrophobic gating has received experimental support from a number of studies of synthetic nanopores (Powell et al., 2011) and ion channels (Aryal et al., 2014a). It is therefore timely to exploit the concepts underlying hydrophobic gating to develop a more accurate and refined tool for annotation of channel structures. In particular, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have greatly enhanced our understanding of a wide range of membrane proteins and are now sufficiently robust and computationally inexpensive to allow their routine application to almost any membrane protein structure as soon as it is determined (Stansfeld et al., 2015). This offers the possibility of using MD simulations of water within a novel ion channel structure as a simple computational tool to aid annotation of its functional state. In the current study, we compare the insights yielded by MD simulations of three different levels of complexity as applied to the crystal structure of the serotonin 5-HT3 receptor (5-HT3R) (Hassaine et al., 2014), a key member of the family of pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGIC) whose functional state was unclear from its structure, but which recent simulation studies have suggested may be functionally closed (Yuan et al., 2016).

I is for Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) One of the most effective methods for preventing malaria transmission is the use of insecticide-treated bed nets. These nets act as a protective barrier against mosquitoes, which typically bite at night. By sleeping under an ITN, communities can significantly reduce transmission rates. The WHO recommends the use of these nets in high-risk areas, and extensive distribution projects aim to provide them to those who need them most, especially vulnerable populations like pregnant women and children. J is for Jaundice In more severe cases of malaria, patients may exhibit jaundice, characterized by yellowing of the skin and eyes. This occurs due to the breakdown of red blood cells and can indicate a severe infection requiring immediate medical attention. Jaundice is a clear signal that the body's defenses are overwhelmed, and swift intervention is crucial to prevent fatal complications. K is for Knowledge Public knowledge about malaria's transmission and prevention is vital in combating the disease. Education campaigns aim to enlighten at-risk populations about symptoms, prevention strategies, and the importance of seeking medical advice promptly. Grassroots initiatives often involve local leaders and health workers in order to strengthen community outreach and engagement. L is for Life-saving treatments Access to life-saving treatment makes a considerable difference in malaria management. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) have become the frontline treatment for uncomplicated malaria, drastically reducing mortality rates when administered promptly. Ensuring that these treatments are available in clinics and hospitals throughout endemic regions is imperative for controlling outbreaks. M is for Mosquitoes Mosquitoes are not just carriers of malaria but the very link in the transmission cycle. Specifically, the female Anopheles mosquito holds the responsibility for spreading the parasite. Their breeding habits are influenced by environmental factors such as stagnant water and humidity, making climate change a crucial concern in malaria transmission dynamics. Understanding these patterns is key to targeted mosquito control measures. N is for Nutritional status A person's nutritional status can influence their susceptibility to malaria. Malnourished individuals, especially children, may have weakened immune systems and are more vulnerable to severe forms of the disease. Health interventions that enhance nutritional intake are essential components of malaria prevention strategies. O is for Outreach programs Malaria outreach programs play a pivotal role in educating communities. These programs facilitate health talks, distribute mosquito nets, and promote environmental management to reduce mosquito breeding sites. By equipping local residents with tools and knowledge, these initiatives empower them to take charge of their health. P is for Prevention Effective prevention strategies include a multifaceted approach that encompasses vector control, community education, and prompt access to healthcare services. Regular insecticide spraying, waste management, and public health campaigns on preventive measures, such as wearing protective clothing during peak mosquito hours, are all crucial in reducing malaria incidence. Q is for Quinine Quinine, derived from the bark of the cinchona tree, was one of the first treatments for malaria and remains relevant in certain contexts today. Though more advanced treatments have emerged, quinine is occasionally utilized in severe cases where other medications may not be effective. Understanding the historical context of such treatments enriches the modern fight against malaria. R is for Research Ongoing research into malaria focuses on vaccine development, drug discovery, and innovative control strategies. Global partnerships among scientists, governments, and organizations aim to accelerate progress in combating this age-old threat. The pursuit of a malaria vaccine has begun to yield promising results, bringing hope to countless lives affected by this enduring disease. S is for Surveillance Robust surveillance systems are essential for tracking malaria incidence and guiding intervention strategies. These systems help identify outbreaks swiftly, allocate resources efficiently, and assess the effectiveness of prevention measures. Countries with strong malaria surveillance can respond more decisively, minimizing the disease's impact on public health.

They also leave their onboard electronic jamming equipment turned on, so that it interferes with British radar systems. And they carry out mock attacks on civilian targets. All this is designed to sow confusion and panic among the public and politicians alike. Just imagine how much more alarming it would have been if these latest intruders had been Russian Tupolev Tu-160 Blackjack bombers, capable of carrying up to six nuclear weapons. No wonder our armed forces are feeling demoralised, frustrated and angry. Our own Air Chief Marshal Sir Stuart Peach - who heads Nato's Military Committee - told me earlier this month that he believed Russia had broken international law by flying its aircraft near Britain without permission. He said: 'If you're going to have a secure Europe, then you need to respect each other's sovereignty.' Yet the Russians are getting away with murder because our Government is refusing to defend us properly. There are only ten Typhoon jets available for such scrambles, and they are based far apart across the country. As one senior officer put it to me: 'We don't know where the next one will come from.' One of those Typhoons was grounded after a technical fault this week, leaving just nine in action. There are plans to base two squadrons permanently on readiness at RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk, but the Treasury has refused to pay for the extra pilots needed. The Russian incursions are not a new phenomenon, but they are increasing in frequency and intensity. When I asked a former RAF chief why he thought this was happening, he replied bluntly: 'Because we let them get away with it.' Last year, the Prime Minister announced a 178billion programme to upgrade our defences, including a fleet of new F-35 Lightning stealth jets. But the money is being spread thinly across too many different projects, and our current level of investment is less than half that of France or Germany. Britain's nuclear deterrent is in crisis, too. Our ageing Vanguard-class submarines will soon reach the end of their useful lives, and the replacement Dreadnought-class boats won't be ready until 2028. Meanwhile, we have lost almost half our Trident missiles, due to the failure of a 1 billion storage facility. This week, a Labour MP called for a Commons inquiry into the scandal, saying it was 'a serious matter that needs investigation'. What does she think it takes to build a missile? That's right - a big bang! So, while Britain continues to dither and procrastinate, Putin carries on flexing his muscles. His regime is desperate to restore Russia's old superpower status, and to turn back the clock to the days when it ruled Eastern Europe like a colonial master. The West must stand firm against him. If we fail to do so, the consequences will be catastrophic.

The quest for sustainable energy solutions continues to drive innovation and research in the field of solar energy. As the world grapples with the challenges of climate change and energy security, the importance of harnessing solar energy cannot be overstated. One of the most promising applications of solar energy is in the development of solar air heaters, which have the potential to provide a reliable and efficient source of heat for various industries and households. In recent years, researchers have made significant strides in improving the performance of solar air heaters through various modifications and innovations. For instance, the use of black painting on the rear of the absorber plate has been shown to increase the efficiency of the heater by up to 10%, as reported by Taki et al. [4]. Similarly, the optimal orientation of the solar air heater has been found to play a crucial role in its performance, with south, south-east, and south-west orientations yielding better results, as demonstrated by Badescu [5]. The heat transfer area of solar air collectors has also been found to be a critical factor in determining their thermal efficiency. Fatih et al. [6] demonstrated experimentally that increasing the heat transfer area can enhance the thermal efficiency of solar air collectors, while Singh et al. [7] showed that baffled solar air collectors can achieve higher thermal efficiencies due to increased air flow paths. In addition to these modifications, researchers have also explored the use of innovative materials and technologies to improve the performance of solar air heaters. For example, Ammari [8] developed a mathematical model to determine the thermal performance of slat solar air heaters, which was found to outperform traditional heaters. Bouadila et al. [9] conducted an experimental study on a single pass solar air heater containing a storage medium in a spherical capsule, which showed promising results in terms of thermal performance. The use of spiral tubes and corrugated tubes has also been shown to enhance the heat transfer performance of solar air heaters, as reported by Bouadila et al. [10] and Goodarzi et al. [14], respectively. Furthermore, the integration of graphene nanoplatelets into solar systems has been proposed as a potential solution for improving their efficiency [11-13]. In conclusion, the development of sustainable energy technologies is crucial for a bright energy future. Solar air heaters have the potential to play a significant role in this effort, and ongoing research is focused on improving their performance and efficiency. By exploring innovative materials and technologies, researchers can help to overcome the challenges associated with intermittent solar energy and provide a reliable source of heat for various applications.

He said you'd let me have 'em half price." "So I will, my - boy. This is the cheapest place in the city." "Well, old man, trot out your best suits. I want 'em in the style, you know." "I know that from your looks," said the old man, a grin illumining his wrinkled face, as he glanced at the rags Sam wore. "Oh, you needn't look at these. My best clo'es is to home in the wardrobe. What have you got for shirts?" A red-flannel article was displayed; but Sam didn't like the color. "It ain't fashionable," he said. "Here's a blue one," said the old man. "That's more like, how much is it?" "Fifty cents." "Fifty cents! Do you want to ruin me? I won't give no fifty cents for a shirt." "It's worth more. It cost me forty-five." "I'll give thirty-five." After some haggling the price was accepted, and the article was laid aside. "Now show me some of your nice suits," said Sam. "I've got a place, and I want to look like a gentleman." "Have you got any money?" asked the old man, with the momentary suspicion that he might be throwing his time and trouble away upon a penniless purchaser. "Yes," said Sam. "What do you take me for?" "How much have you got?" "What do you want to know for?" "I want to know what clo'es to show you." Sam was about to answer five dollars, when a shrewd thought changed his intention. "I've got four dollars," he said. Even this was beyond the expectations of the dealer. "All right, my son," he said. "I'll give you some nice clo'es for four dollars." "You'd better if you want me to come here again. If you do well by me I'll get all my clo'es here." A young man of fashion could not have spoken more condescendingly, or with an air of greater importance than Sam. He was right in thinking that his patronage was of importance to the old man. "I'll dress you so fine the gals will look at you as you go along the street," he said. "Go ahead!" said Sam. "Do your best by me, and I'll send my friends here." Without going into details, it may be said that our hero selected everything to his satisfaction except a coat. Here he was rather particular. Finally, he espied a blue coat with brass buttons, hanging in a corner. "Take down that coat," he said, "I guess that'll suit me." "That costs too much. I can't give you that and the rest of the things for four dollars." "Why can't you?" "I'd lose too much." Opposition confirmed Sam in his determination to own it. "Give it to me; I'll try it on," he said. Putting it on, he surveyed himself with satisfaction, in a small, cracked mirror.

The conversation, punctuated by the rhythmic clinking of pickaxes and the occasional shout of discovery, continued to weave dreams as wild and vast as the Sierra wilderness itself. The motley assembly of prospectors, trappers, and wanderers entertained themselves with visions of future splendor that belied their rough present. "You know," remarked Dick, sweeping his hand across the panoramic view of tangled green, "I've been thinkin' of a grand hotel, right on this here spot. Folks from the city'd come up, breathe the pine air, take in the mountain sunsets, and spend their gold - our gold - right back at us." The idea warmed the group, eliciting nods and murmurs of agreement. "An' think of the ladies," chimed in young Billy Hodges, barely old enough to have whiskers, but already dreaming alongside the older men. "Dressin' up in their Sunday best, strollin' down Main Street with parasols and dainty shoes - why, we'd have a regular civilized place." "An' we'd need a new church," added Maryland Joe, looking thoughtfully at the clearing sky above. "A place t'give thanks for all these blessings, and maybe have decent weddings too." Talk of institutions and settlements could not dissipate the dusty air of pragmatism entirely. The undertone of these flighty ambitions was a landscape as ruthless as it was beautiful. They all knew the brittle boundary between fortune and despair, each man respectful of the capricious nature that had been both benefactor and bane. Yet amid these dreams of opulence, the pressing reality was that work must continue. As the sun dipped beyond the jagged outline of pine-covered ridges, casting long shadows over the valley, tools were set down and a fire lit. Dinner was a simple affair - tinned beans warmed over flames, coffee served in battered tins warm to the touch. The talk that accompanied supper was more subdued, mellowed by the pending night and labor's exhaustion. Once fed and refreshed, the bond of communal desire returned, now focused less on personal gain and more on the thread of shared purpose. Dartmouth Jake, named so after a college left behind back East, raised his cup. "Here's to Devil's Ford, fellas," he declared, gesturing towards the surrounding darkness steeped with possibilities yet to be unearthed. "May she yield her treasures plentifully, and let us not forget our own good fortune in all of it." The fire crackled approvingly, echoing the scattered grunts and affirmations from the assembled. The prospects seemed endless as the night deepened, painting the mountains with starlight, leaving only the immediate warmth of the fire to hold back the vast coolness beyond. In the hazy glow, these men, drawn together by the whims of chance, fancied themselves lords of their newly minted fiefdom. Here, in the cusp of two worlds, where the wild met dreams, every man allowed himself to heed the whisper of providence hinting at an extraordinary destiny. For tomorrow awaited, as uncertain and promising as today's imaginings-a fragile, golden thread spun from hope's own loom.

These innovative methodologies, grounded in both theoretical developments and practical implementations, have significantly advanced our understanding of IDPs and IDRs. In particular, the incorporation of advanced mathematical modeling-such as the Gaussian ensemble model-allows for a more accurate representation of the flexible conformations that these proteins assume in their native environments (20). This model recognizes the presence of multiple conformational states, each contributing to the overall spectral profile observed in NMR experiments. As such, it aids in establishing a more comprehensive visualization of the dynamic landscape that IDPs and IDRs navigate during their biological functions. Furthermore, the integration of machine learning techniques into the analysis of NMR data has proven to be a revolutionary step. By applying algorithms trained on vast datasets of protein dynamics, researchers can identify subtle patterns within complex relaxation data that were previously obscured by noise. These patterns enable more precise characterizations of dynamic regions, informing on how these intrinsically disordered entities interact with their biological partners (21). The increasing computational power available today facilitates such analyses, permitting the exploration of conformational ensembles in silico that correlate with experimental results obtained in vitro. Moreover, the synergy between NMR spectroscopic techniques and other biophysical approaches, such as circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy and fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET), has yielded highly complementary insights. CD spectroscopy conveys information regarding the overall secondary structure content of proteins while FRET techniques elucidate spatial relationships and conformational changes occurring over various distances. This multimodal approach allows scientists to build a detailed narrative of the dynamic behavior of IDPs and IDRs, linking their structural attributes directly to their functional roles in cellular processes, such as signaling and regulation (22). The implications for therapeutic developments are profound. Many IDPs are associated with various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, cancer, and diabetes (23). Understanding their dynamic properties at an atomic level not only enhances our knowledge of their pathological mechanisms but also aids in the design of small molecules or biologics that can modulate their activity. This presents new avenues for drug development targeting IDPs, notably when considering the binding dynamics, as the transient nature of these proteins often complicates traditional drug-discovery approaches. Additionally, the role of post-translational modifications (PTMs) in influencing the dynamics of IDPs and IDRs cannot be overstated. PTMs such as phosphorylation, acetylation, and methylation can dramatically alter the conformational equilibria, thus modifying binding affinity and specificity (24). Advances in mass spectrometry, coupled with NMR, enable the investigation of these modifications in real-time, providing a clearer picture of how they affect the function of IDPs within cellular contexts. As research continues to unravel the intricate webs of interactions that govern protein dynamics, a more nuanced understanding of IDPs emerges-one that underscores their significance not merely as structural anomalies but as pivotal players in the grand orchestration of cellular machinery. In conclusion, the amalgamation of cutting-edge experimental techniques, sophisticated analytical methods, and collaborative efforts across disciplines is essential for the exploration of IDPs and IDRs. This convergence is set to propel the field forward, opening new frontiers in our understanding of protein science and its vast implications for health and disease. As the narrative continues to unfold, the fascination with the flexible, amorphous world of IDPs promises to yield rich insights, challenging preconceived notions and fostering innovative therapeutic strategies in the years to come.

In recent years, Approach-Avoidance Tasks (AAT) have been used to study behavioural responses in a range of fears (Heuer, Rinck, & Becker, 2007; Lange, Keijsers, Becker, & Rinck, 2008; Rinck & Becker, 2007; Roelofs et al., 2010). In the AAT, participants respond to a stimulus presented on screen by pulling it toward them or pushing it away using a joystick. The task builds on the premise that stimuli appraised as negative produce automatic avoidance tendencies characterised by pushing objects away from oneself, while stimuli appraised as pleasant produce automatic approach tendencies characterised by pulling the objects closer (Chen & Bargh, 1999; Solarz, 1960). These approach-avoidance tendencies have been found to differentiate high and low fearful individuals (Klein, Becker, & Rinck, 2011; Rinck & Becker, 2007; Roefs et al., 2011). For example, spider-fearful participants were faster to push spider pictures away, indicative of avoidance, than to pull them closer with this effect not observed in non-fearful participants (Rinck & Becker, 2007). Using a modified approach-avoidance task it is also possible to experimentally manipulate behavioural response tendencies in order to begin to study the possible causal effect on fear-related cognitions and behaviours (for reviews see Vandenbosch & De Houwer, 2011; Woud, Becker, & Rinck, 2011). In a modified AAT, participants are trained to repeatedly pull toward (training approach tendencies) or push away (training avoidance) neutral stimuli using a joystick with the direction of response required determined by some characteristic of the stimuli (e.g. push brown pictures, pull blue pictures). The premise being that repeatedly training approach tendencies by pulling the stimulus closer is hypothesised to lead to more positive appraisals, while training avoidance tendencies would lead to more negative appraisals (Chen & Bargh, 1999; Solarz, 1960). Two studies have investigated the effects of manipulating behavioural-response tendencies on fear-related responses about novel animals in children (Huijding et al., 2009; Huijding, Muris, Lester, Field, & Joosse, 2011). Children were instructed to repeatedly pull toward (approach) or push away (avoid) pictures of Australian marsupials, quokka and quoll. In the first study, the approached animal was rated more positively while disliking of the avoided animal increased (Huijding et al., 2009). Greater avoidance and fear of the avoided animal relative to the approached animal was reported in girls only. No significant effects were observed on a measure of implicit attitudes, the Implicit Association Test (IAT, Greenwald, McGhee, & Schwartz, 1998). In a second study (Huijding et al., 2011), training increased self-reported liking of the approached animal and disliking and fear of the avoided animal. Children sought out more negative information about the avoided animal and more positive information about the approached animal. Once again, no significant effects were observed on implicit attitudes. Associative learning is one possible mechanism explaining how verbal information operates (Field, 2006a). Telling a child a dog is dangerous may evoke a mental representation of threat that becomes linked in memory with the concept of dogs (Muris & Field, 2010). Few studies have investigated interactions between possible pathways to fear learning.

As Mary Gifford stepped into the dairy, the warm scent of milk and butter enveloped her, transporting her back to a time when life was simpler, when her own mother's gentle hands had guided hers in the daily chores. She sighed, her thoughts drifting to her sister, whose impulsive nature had always been a concern. Lucy's words still lingered in her mind, "I may be young, but I have my wits about me, and no soft speeches catch me in a net." Mary's heart swelled with a mix of worry and admiration for her sister's spirit, yet she knew that innocence and naivety often walked hand in hand. As she began to pour the milk into the pans, her stepmother's shrill voice pierced the air once more, "And where's that lazy wench, Lucy? I'll have her know I won't be ignored!" Mary's hands moved with a practiced ease, her mind wandering to the tourney at Whitehall, and the thrill of excitement that had danced in Lucy's eyes. She couldn't help but wonder what secrets lay hidden behind her sister's determination to attend the grand event. The sound of footsteps echoed from the hallway, and Mary's son, little Thomas, toddled into the dairy, his bright eyes fixed on his mother. "Mama, Mama!" he exclaimed, reaching up to grasp her apron strings. Mary smiled, her heart overflowing with love for her child, and the memories of her own mother, who had passed away too soon. She lifted Thomas into her arms, cradling him close as she continued her work. As the afternoon wore on, the sun began its slow descent behind the hills, casting a warm orange glow over the countryside. Mary's thoughts returned to Lucy, and the promise she had made to return within the hour. She glanced out the window, her eyes scanning the rolling hills, but there was no sign of her sister. A faint sense of unease crept up her spine, and she quickened her pace, her hands moving with a newfound urgency as she finished the chores. As the last of the milk was set to cream, Mary handed Thomas over to the waiting servant, and stepped out into the fading light. The air was filled with the sweet scent of blooming wildflowers, and the distant sound of laughter carried on the breeze. Mary's heart skipped a beat as she spotted a figure emerging from the trees, her golden hair shining like a beacon in the dying light. But as the figure drew closer, Mary's sense of relief was short-lived, for it was not Lucy who approached, but a stranger, his eyes fixed intently on the house.

The introduction of bioenergy with CCS could theoretically achieve carbon-neutral steelmaking (considering that bioenergy can substitute over 40% of fossil-based CO2 emissions (Mandova et al., 2018) and that CCS can capture over 60% of the CO2 emissions that occur on-site (IEAGHG, 2013)) without a significant retrofit of a steel plant. However, this carbon-neutral iron and steelmaking opportunity is currently being impeded by the challenges raised by any deployment of bio-CCS. Deployment of bio-CCS has so far been stagnant, with only a few small demonstration-scale bio-CCS projects currently being operational (e.g., the Illinois Industrial CCS Project) (Global CCS Institute, 2018). Any bio-CCS application within fully fossil fuel-based processes would necessitate simultaneously overcoming barriers to both bioenergy and CCS implementation. Issues related to the actual implementation and cost of CO2 capture, transport and storage, uncertainties in the long term response of the environment to CO2 storage, public acceptance and the ability to prolong reliance on fossil fuels, are the main arguments limiting CCS progress (Fuss et al., 2014). As of 2018, there are only 30 MtCO2 stored annually worldwide (Global CCS Institute, 2018). CCS deployment will therefore have a hard time reaching the annual CO2 storage volumes required by, for instance, the International Energy Agency (IEA) 2 C scenario of 400 MtCO2 by 2025 (IEA, 2014). Insufficient policy support to create a business case for CCS, for example, in the EU Emission Trading System (ETS) (Purvis and Vaghi, 2015), makes the required CCS expansion unrealistic over the next decade. On the same note, sustainable biomass supply constraints, concerns associated with competition between bioenergy and food production, the complexity of emission accounting, as well as direct and indirect land use change, are major arguments against increased bioenergy use (Sanchez and Kammen, 2016). There is currently no commercialised application of bio-CCS in the iron and steel industry, even though bioenergy and CCS indepently, are commercialised (e.g., charcoal utilisation in Brazilian mini blast furnaces (Machado et al., 2010) and a CCS facility in Abu Dhabi with an annual capture capacity of 0.8 MtCO2 (Global CCS Institute, 2018; IEA, 2014)). The suitability of bio-CCS is highly dependent on geographic location, which diversifies opportunities for large-scale bio-CCS application across steel plants. Factors such as industrial plant structure, the availability of CO2 storage and transport options, sufficient sustainable biomass resources, supportive regulatory frameworks, etc. (Gough and Upham, 2011), differ for individual plants across different countries and regions. There is currently no comparison of bio-CCS opportunities for individual integrated steel plants, or evaluations of bio-CCS as a strategy for carbon-neutral iron and steelmaking available for the iron and steel industry in Europe. A few studies previously focused on either bioenergy or CCS for iron and steel production in Europe, but to our knowledge, no other studies have considered combining the two technologies.

Extracellular recordings of field EPSPs also report impaired LTP in synapses of the dentate gyrus (DG) and perirhinal cortex, due to enhanced GABAergic transmission (Belichenko et al., 2009; Belichenko et al., 2015; Contestabile et al., 2013; Fernandez et al., 2007; Kleschevnikov et al., 2012; Kleschevnikov et al., 2004; Morice et al., 2008; O'Doherty et al., 2005; Roncace et al., 2017). Although weaker LTP at hippocampal CA1 and DG synapses has largely been ascribed to enhanced GABAergic signalling (Contestabile et al., 2017), some studies report compromised glutamate release in response to closely spaced pairs or trains of stimuli at DG synapses (Kaur et al., 2014) and CA1 synapses (Andrade-Talavera et al., 2015; Siarey et al., 2005), that may contribute to the weaker LTP. Altogether, the electrophysiological studies indicate that synaptic dysfunction in DS is not the same at all brain synapses, and both glutamatergic and GABAergic transmission can be altered. The contribution of individual HSA21 genes to the changes in synaptic function in DS is incompletely understood (Gupta et al., 2016). One way to explore this gene-phenotype relationship, that is faster and less costly than using mouse models, is to overexpress individual orthologous genes in Drosophila and examine their consequences (Chang and Min, 2009; Cvetkovska et al., 2013). Drosophila is an established model of genetic disorders due to its short lifespan, well defined neural circuits, genetic tractability, conservation of molecular mechanisms driving cellular and physiological processes, and the existence of Drosophila orthologues for ~ 75% of disease causing human genes (Androschuk et al., 2015; Perrimon et al., 2016; Ugur et al., 2016). One candidate HSA21 gene for such a study is Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule (DSCAM). DSCAM is a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily with four Drosophila homologues, Dscam1-4 (Tadros et al., 2016), of which Dscam1 is the prototypical member and the most studied. In both Drosophila and mice, Dscam is highly expressed throughout the central and peripheral nervous system (Barlow et al., 2002; Barlow et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004), in a highly regulated spatiotemporal pattern (Saito et al., 2000; Yamakawa et al., 1998), and is locally translated in dendrites and growth cones (Alves-Sampaio et al., 2010; Jain and Welshhans, 2016).

Codeine is given for mild to moderate pain and is the tenth most prescribed drug in the UK. But that is not the only issue with this particular enzyme. There is another group of people who produce too much CYP2D6, so codeine is broken down too quickly in their bodies. This creates a fast 'hit' which then rapidly wears off, explains Dr Martin Johnson, a GP and pain specialist for the Royal College of General Practitioners. 'These so-called rapid metabolisers experience a quick morphine hit when the drug is broken down. The effects of the dose then wear off too quickly, so they start clock-watching until their next dose. In some rare cases this fast-acting effect has caused respiratory depression (when breathing stops), particularly in children, and even deaths.' This is why children recovering from surgery are now no longer given codeine-based pain relief, and why children's cough medicines no longer contain the drug. Dr Johnson suggests that there may be even more fast metabolisers than non-metabolisers - and that put together they could amount to about 30 per cent of the population. 'Patients often keep taking codeine in the vain hope that it will work eventually - but all they experience are the side-effects, such as constipation (it slows down gut movement in the intestine) and none of the pain-relieving benefits,' says Dr Johnson. 'They might return to their GP for a higher dose and still not get any relief. 'Then there are all the people who buy over-the-counter codeine products, who also get no pain relief. 'There could be huge numbers of people on medication that doesn't work for them, or works too quickly to control pain effectively.' Yet there are alternatives, including paracetamol, ibuprofen, diclofenac and other anti-inflammatories. Exercise can help with pain too - particularly for people with arthritis. Common issue: It is estimated that between seven and ten per cent of the population cannot break down codeine. Codeine is not the only drug metabolised by CYP2D6. There are some 25 others including the opioid painkiller tramadol, certain antidepressants known as selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, which include Prozac and Zoloft, and antipsychotic drugs used to treat mental illness. Beta-blockers prescribed for high blood pressure and the breast cancer drug tamoxifen, taken by 13,000 women, also fall into this category. Dr Debenham says it's a big issue. The combustion of sewage sludge results in ashes that can contain up to 10% of total nitrogen (TN) and further 20-30% of organic nitrogen (ON) (Rigby et al., 2016). It is therefore possible to recover some of the nitrogen contained in sewage sludge via the thermal treatment thereof and subsequent separation of the ash fraction. Considering the EU-wide incineration of sewage sludge at 540 Tg a-1 (on dry matter basis) (Eurostat, 2016), this could result in 54 Tg a-1 nitrogen being available for further valorization. In order to valorize the nitrogen recovered from sewage sludge ashes, it must be converted into a reactive form. The conventional route for this purpose involves gasification of biomass followed by catalytic ammonia synthesis. However, this process requires large amounts of energy and is cost-ineffective when compared to the Haber-Bosch process (Steenari et al., 1999). Moreover, it also requires complex catalyst systems for the synthesis of ammonia and hence the possibility of the development of alternative processes for the conversion of nitrogen into a reactive form should be explored. This study focuses on two promising routes for the conversion of nitrogen into a reactive form: nitridation and ammonolysis. Nitridation was reported to occur during the combustion of urea (Petersen et al., 1986) and nitrogen-containing compounds (Kunzru et al., 1974; Kuroda et al., 1984; Noguchi et al., 1992). During the nitridation of carbonaceous materials, elemental nitrogen reacts with surface oxygen groups present on the material's surface forming stable nitrogen species (e.g. -NH, -NCO, -CN, and -C=N-) (Ahn and Chiang, 1995; Burchill et al., 1969; LePage et al., 1990; Lizzio and Jenkins, 1992; Liu and Chiang, 1994; Mochida et al., 1997; Smith and Jenkins, 1997). Although the majority of these studies focused on the nitridation of coal, there are reports on the formation of nitrogen functional groups during the combustion of sewage sludge (Jenkins et al., 2005; Rigby et al., 2016). Ammonolysis, which is the reaction between an amide group and an alcohol, is another promising route for the conversion of nitrogen into a reactive form. The products of the ammonolysis reaction are either amines and/or nitriles depending on the structure of the starting compound (Huang and Chen, 2006; Jia et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2007). Recently, ammonolysis was reported to occur during the pyrolysis of urea (Gokalp et al., 2016). As both the nitridation and ammonolysis reactions involve the formation of nitrogen functional groups, it would be interesting to explore whether any of them occurs during the combustion of sewage sludge and if so, what kind of nitrogen functional groups are formed and how the composition of the ashes produced from the combustion of sewage sludge may affect the extent of these reactions.
