As he inhaled the smoke of his cigarette, he gazed out into the darkness, the trees blurring together in a greenish haze. "I suppose it's the price one pays for the game," he said, his voice low and reflective. "But it's a confoundedly high price, all the same. I've had to shake hands with people I'd rather not have touched with a pair of tongs, and smile at their wives' bonnets till my face ached." He laughed, a short, bitter laugh. "And the things one says! 'My dear fellow, I shall do my utmost to...' - when one knows perfectly well it's all moonshine. Still, I suppose it's the way of the world." Lord Fontenoy nodded sympathetically, his eyes fixed on the darkness outside. "You're not the first to feel like that, George. We've all been through it. But it's worth it, in the end." Sir George's eyes flashed towards him, a spark of irony in their depths. "Worth it? Ah, yes - for the sake of the party, of course. But for one's own sake? I'm not so sure. Sometimes I think I'd rather be a clerk in a counting-house, with a fixed income and a quiet conscience." Lord Fontenoy's face softened into a gentle smile. "You're tired, George. You've worked like a demon these last few weeks. You'll feel differently when you've had a good night's rest and a day or two in the country." Sir George shook his head, his fair hair rumpled and disordered. "No, it's not that. It's the feeling of having sold one's soul - not for a mess of pottage, either, but for a chance of getting into the House. And what's the House, after all? A lot of old fogies and windbags, with a sprinkling of clever men who know how to work the machine." He paused, his eyes fixed on the glowing end of his cigarette. "I wonder sometimes what the country would do if we all told the truth - if we said, 'Look here, we can't do this, and we won't do that.' Would they believe us, do you think?" Lord Fontenoy's smile grew wider. "My dear George, you're in a very advanced stage of election-fever. You'll get over it. And as for the country - well, it's not so easily shocked as you think. It's used to our little ways." The carriage rolled on, the darkness outside growing thicker, the silence between the two men deepening.

In a subsequent study, Klein and MacInnes (2001) demonstrated that IOR was no longer present when the search display was removed after the search was completed. This suggests that IOR is not a permanent tag attached to the object itself, but rather a temporary mechanism that is linked to the visual representation of the object in the current display. This finding is in line with the idea that IOR is a functional mechanism that serves to guide search towards unexplored regions of the visual environment, rather than a permanent memory of previously inspected objects. Further research has also shown that IOR can be modulated by top-down factors, such as attention and expectations. For example, if participants are instructed to search for a specific object, IOR is stronger for objects that are similar to the target object (Wang & Klein, 2010). This suggests that IOR is not a purely bottom-up mechanism, but can be influenced by higher-level cognitive processes. In addition, IOR has been found to be affected by individual differences in visual working memory capacity. Individuals with higher visual working memory capacity tend to show stronger IOR effects, suggesting that IOR is closely linked to the ability to maintain and update visual representations in working memory (Unsworth, Schrock, & Engle, 2004). Despite the wealth of research on IOR, there are still many open questions regarding its underlying mechanisms and functional role in visual search. For example, it is still unclear how IOR is implemented at the neural level, and how it interacts with other attentional mechanisms, such as attentional capture and attentional filtering. One promising approach to addressing these questions is the use of neuroimaging techniques, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and electroencephalography (EEG). These techniques allow researchers to examine the neural activity associated with IOR and its relationship to other attentional mechanisms. For example, a recent fMRI study found that IOR was associated with activity in the frontal eye fields, a region involved in attentional control and eye movement planning (Snyder, Alain, & Kingstone, 2001). In conclusion, IOR is a powerful mechanism that plays a crucial role in guiding visual search towards unexplored regions of the visual environment. By inhibiting previously inspected objects, IOR increases search efficiency and reduces the time it takes to find a target object. While much is known about the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying IOR, further research is needed to fully understand its functional role in visual search and its relationship to other attentional mechanisms.

He was dressed with extreme care, and had evidently studied the art of being well dressed. His manner was cold, but courteous; and as he spoke, he laid his hand on my arm with a sort of confidential familiarity, which, though not pleasing to me, was certainly flattering. After we had conversed for about half an hour, the other guests arrived. There were only three besides myself. One was a literary gentleman, celebrated for his wit and his bon ton; another was a Mr. Savarin, a man of great wealth, who lived in London solely for the purpose of enjoying its luxuries, and who had acquired the reputation of a consummate judge of wines. The third was a young man of fashion, and the same whom I had introduced at Almack's. We went downstairs to dinner, and entered a room lighted up with wax candles, and filled with the rich perfume of flowers. In the centre stood the dinner-table. There is no part of an epicure's establishment where he is likely to be more fastidious than in his cook; and accordingly, the first question asked by a person invited to dine with a professed gourmand is "Who is your cook?" Lord Guloseton's chef d'oeuvre was a Frenchman of the name of Anselme, who had formerly officiated in the family of a Russian prince. The dinner consisted of ten courses. Each course contained five dishes. Thus there were fifty dishes altogether. The order of succession was as follows: 1st Course. Turtle Soup, stewed lampreys, turbots au gratin, salmon cutlets, crawfishes. 2nd Course. Olives farcies, cotelettes de volaille, truffled sausages, fillets of partridge, mayonnaise of fowl. 3rd Course. Souffle of fish, larks en caisse, oyster pie, mutton cutlets, fritters of anchovies. 4th Course. Fillets of beef, curried rabbits, lobster salad, fricandeau of veal, croquettes of ham. 5th Course. Blanquette of chickens, stewed carp, sweetbread pie, fried smelts, ragout of ducks. 6th Course. Vol-au-vent, perch a la Chambord, woodcocks, lamb cutlets, minced collops. 7th Course. Quails en compote, hare soup, venison pasty, braised beef, stewed eels. 8th Course. Fillets of pork, stewed pigeons, roast snipes, hashed mutton, goose liver pie. 9th Course. Maccaroni, stewed leverets, roast teal, potted shrimps, jugged hare. 10th Course. Ragout of artichokes, stewed trout, green peas, cauliflowers, potatoes. With regard to this bill of fare, it will be observed, that the dishes are of a lighter description than those usually served up at our English tables. Some had come alone, others in large family groups. One mother sat with her three young daughters; another arrived with her husband and teenage son. Their ages ranged from eight to 80. All wore their loved ones' medals. Many carried photographs. A few were in tears long before proceedings began. So, too, were many of those watching on screens outside. This was not an easy day. As David Cameron said later, we should not forget the 6,000 servicemen injured during the conflict or the thousands more suffering psychological damage. Nor should we ignore the terrible cost borne by Afghan civilians. Most of us can only guess at the scale of sacrifice involved. Not the Queen. She knows better than anyone how much blood has been spilt over the centuries. Her own grandfather, King George V, lost three cousins in World War I. She herself has sent countless condolence letters to the families of fallen heroes. And she has seen almost every inch of the globe scarred by conflict. Here she was, once again, paying tribute to those who have fought under her flag. The ceremony began with a fanfare from the State Trumpeters of the Household Cavalry. Then the service itself got underway with a hymn, Eternal Father Strong To Save. It contains the lines: 'Oh hear us when we cry to thee / For those in peril on the sea.' Or land, in this case. Or air. The service was led by the Bishop of London, the Rt Rev Richard Chartres. He paid tribute to those who had served in Helmand Province and beyond, adding: 'The courage shown by British forces has won admiration across the world.' He spoke of the importance of reconciliation and forgiveness but added: 'There must also be justice.' Among the other speakers was Sergeant Johnson Beharry VC, the first living recipient of the Victoria Cross since 1965. He received his award for twice saving colleagues while driving through ambushes in Iraq. 'I know what it feels like to lose friends,' he said. 'We remember them today and always.' The most poignant moment came towards the end. After the final hymn, the National Anthem and the Blessing, the organ fell silent. A trumpeter played Reveille. Then the Queen led the way outside to lay a wreath at the foot of the cathedral steps. Behind her came the families of the dead, each placing flowers beside the Queen's wreath. The procession went on for ten minutes. At its head was the widow of Lieutenant Colonel Rupert Thorneloe, who became the most senior Army officer to die in action since the Falklands. His wife Sally was heavily pregnant at the time of his death in July 2009. On the same day, Trooper Joshua Hammond of 2nd Royal Tank Regiment was blown up by a roadside bomb. Now aged nine, his daughter Daisy placed a flower next to the Queen's wreath. Then she stood back and saluted. As the last of the mourners left the scene, the Band of the Grenadier Guards struck up the theme tune from Downton Abbey. It seemed oddly appropriate. Like Downton, this was a grand spectacle involving people from every walk of life. And like Downton, it had ended in tragedy.

What is your name, Missy?" asked Life, becoming very sedate all at once; for, rough as his manners were, he had a kind heart, and would not trifle with the feelings of any one. "My name is Grace Morgan," replied the lady, looking behind her once more, as though she dreaded some peril in that direction. "Be you afeerd of sunthin', that you keep lookin' over yender?" inquired the cavalryman in kindly tones. "What is it? Tell me all about it." "You say you are a Union man?" she inquired doubtfully. "Bet your life on't! I'm orderly sergeant of the fust company of the Riverlawn Cavalry. What's it all about?" asked Life, very tenderly for him. "Stephen Halliburn, who lives about half a mile over there, is my guardian. About twenty Confederate soldiers, or guerillas, I don't know which, are plundering his house and stable, and they say they will have his money if they have to pull his house down to find it," answered Grace, trembling, and glancing frequently behind her, as though she were in mortal terror of the approach of the enemy. "Oh, ho, Grace! That's what's the matter, ain't it? We'll soon fix the gorrillas, or the soldiers, whatever they may be," replied Life, as he looked earnestly in the direction of the road, a few rods distant from the spot. "But I can't carry this chest any farther. I am worn out bringing it so far; for I have been so frightened that all the strength has gone out of me," said Grace, as she placed the box on a rock near her. "I am terribly afraid that Mr. Halliburn will be killed or badly hurt; for he is a Union man, and speaks out just what he thinks." "We will do what we can for him," added Life, still looking in the direction of the road, and listening for sounds from the north. "But you are only a single man; and what can you do against twenty ruffians?" asked the Kentucky girl, who still trembled, and did not seem to believe that the stalwart cavalryman could do anything to aid Mr. Halliburn. "About fifty on us," added Life quietly, still looking and listening. "I'm a scout sent out ahead of half the fust company marchin' this way. I left my horse in the road, to come over this way and take a look, for I had an idee I heerd sunthin' on the left." "Perhaps you heard the ruffians who are plundering my guardian," replied Grace, brightening up when she learned that fifty Union soldiers were in the neighborhood. "He is a dear good man, and I love him as though he were my father. I would not have left him if he had not insisted that I should do something with the chest, which contains all his money and papers. I can't carry it any farther, for it is very heavy."

Soon I had no fear of its depressing effect, for Mary Stuart was one of those women near whose fascinations peace does not thrive. When I found her at the chateau, my martial ardor lost its warmth. Another sort of flame took up its home in my heart, and no power could have turned me to the wars again. Ah! what a gay, delightful life, tinctured with bitterness, we led in the grand old chateau, and looking back at it how heartless, godless, and empty it seems. Do not from these words conclude that I am a fanatic, nor that I shall pour into your ears a ranter's tale; for cant is more to be despised even than godlessness; but during the period of my life of which I shall write I learned - but what I learned I shall in due time tell you. While at the court of Guise I, like many another man, conceived for Mary Stuart a passion which lay heavy upon my heart for many years. Sweethearts I had by the scores, but she held my longings from all of them until I felt the touch of a pure woman's love, and then - but again I am going beyond my story. I did not doubt, nor do I hesitate to say, that my passion was returned by Mary with a fervor which she felt for no other lover; but she was a queen, and I, compared with her, was nobody. For this difference of rank I have since had good cause to be thankful. Great beauty is diffusive in its tendency. Like the sun, it cannot shine for one alone. Still, it burns and dazzles the one as if it shone for him and for no other; and he who basks in its rays need have no fear of the ennui of peace. The time came when I tasted the unutterable bitterness of Mary's marriage to a simpering fool, Francis II., whom she loathed, notwithstanding absurd stories of their sweet courtship and love. After her marriage to Francis, Mary became hard and callous of heart, and all the world knows her sad history. The stories of Darnley, Rizzio, and Bothwell will be rich morsels, I suppose, for the morbid minds of men and women so long as books are read and scandal is loved. Ah, well, that was long ago; so long ago that now as I write it seems but a shadow upon the horizon of time. And so it happened that Francis died, and when the queen went back to Scotland to ascend her native throne, I went with her, and mothlike hovered near the blaze that burned but did not warm me. Then in the course of time came the Darnley tragedy. I saw Rizzio killed. Gods! what a scene for hell was that! Then followed the Bothwell disgrace, the queen's imprisonment at Lochleven, and my own flight from Scotland to save my head.

The S-s-U- Gyp B phenotype is characterized by a lack of Gyp B protein expression on the erythrocyte surface, due to a deletion in exons 2 to 5, and these erythrocytes were relatively resistant to invasion by some strains of P. falciparum (Tarazona-Santos et al., 2011). A well-known but rare Gyp C polymorphism, the Gerbich negative phenotype (a deletion in exon 3) (Colin et al., 1989; Wilder et al., 2009), renders erythrocytes partially resistant to invasion, since the parasite is unable to utilise the merozite ligand EBA140 (Maier et al., 2003). Binding regions have also been identified in the more recently defined erythrocyte receptors, Band 3, CR1 and BSG. The combined 5ABC and 6A ectodomain regions of band 3, encoded by exons 17 and 18 respectively, interact with the MSP1-42kDa processed product through the 19 kDa C-terminal domain (Li et al., 2004). PfRh4 binds to complement-control-protein (CCP) repeats 1-3 in the ectodomain portion of CR1 (Tham et al., 2011) encoded by exons 2, 3, 4 and 5 (Vik and Wong, 1993). BSG also termed the Ok blood group antigen, has two splice isoforms, BSG-L (long) and BSG-S (short). BSG-S has two immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF) domains, which are both required for binding to Rh5 (Crosnier et al., 2011). Wright et al. (2014) described the crystal structure of Rh5 in a complex with BSG and the BSG protein structure was encoded by exons 4, 5, 6 and part of exon 7. Erythrocytes are the most abundant cells in human blood and potentially act as decoys for viruses and bacteria, to bind and clear them, while they are a host for the malaria parasite, these pathogens present opposing selection pressures (Gagneux and Varki, 1999). While variation in the parasite invasion ligands and their erythrocyte receptors have been the subject of frequent study, there have been very few studies of variation in parasite ligands and their cognate receptors in the same individuals, yet it is exactly these kinds of studies that may reveal genes of interest. Furthermore, most of the previous merozoite ligand and erythrocyte receptor diversity studies were conducted in individuals who either had uncomplicated malaria or no malaria at all at the time of sampling. In this paper, we examine individuals with severe malaria due to its various syndromes including impaired consciousness (also referred to as cerebral malaria), severe malarial anemia and respiratory distress (Marsh et al., 1995) and under the hypothesis that this distinct disease phenotype could skew the population towards a particular ligand-receptor genotype. We examined this using the merozoite ligand - erythrocyte receptor interactions. Individuals and their infecting P. falciparum parasite population were genotyped to determine whether the polymorphisms in erythrocyte receptors (Gyp A, Gyp B, Gyp C, band 3, CR1 and BSG) and their merozoite ligands (EBA175, EBL1, EBA140, MSP1, Rh4 and Rh5, respectively) show a skewed population genetic summary statistic when analysed at the same time point.

In 2007, Kimberly Hoskin got a $124 ticket for driving her sister's car, which wasn't insured in Missouri, and then had to pay an additional $100 fine when she missed a court appearance because of an emergency appendectomy. The court, she said, rejected her medical excuse and issued a warrant for her arrest. She paid a total of $224 in fines because she was in the middle of a job search and didn't want an outstanding warrant to prevent her from getting a good job. "Why is it that all the people in court are black?" Kimberly Hoskin said of defendants in municipal court. "I've had so many police officers make a U-turn, follow me, run my plates, find out everything is OK, then turn around and go back in the direction they were going. "There's nothing we can do. In Ferguson, the police do what they want to do. Ferguson does what it wants," said Kimberly Hoskin, 35, who now works the overnight shift on a General Motors manufacturing line. City officials and police declined to respond to CNN's requests this week for comment about the Hoskin family's assertions. Last September, the City Council repealed administrative fees imposed by police when overseeing the release of a towed vehicle, the mayor said. The city also no longer has a specific offense for failing to appear in court, which eliminates certain additional fees and court costs, the mayor said. The Justice Department's report details how Ferguson operated a vertically integrated system - from street cop to court clerk to judge to city administration to city council - to raise revenue for the city budget through increased ticketing and fining. Ferguson's budget increases were so sizable that city officials exhorted police and court staff to levy more and more fines and tickets against violators, who turned out to be largely African-American, the Justice Department said. The demands for revenue were so intense that the police department had "little concern with how officers do this," even disciplining officers who failed to issue an average of 28 tickets a month, the Justice Department report said. Officers competed "to see who could issue the largest number of citations during a single stop," the Justice Department said. One apparent winner was an officer who issued 14 tickets at a single encounter, according to the federal investigation report. Many police stops of civilians "have little relation to public safety and a questionable basis in law," the report said. Ferguson police chief mum on federal report. Indeed, Ferguson enjoyed so much success in issuing tickets and fines that Ferguson, population 21,000, was ranked in the top eight of the 80 municipal courts in St. Louis County by having more than $1 million in revenue in 2010, the report said. When Ferguson court revenues exceeded $2 million in 2012, the city manager responded to the police chief in an internal email: "Awesome! Thanks!"

"Communications and sensors still attempting to establish contact with the intruder, but we are receiving nothing coherent. The cloaking technology they employ is beyond current Starfleet capabilities." "Maintain open channels," Captain Kirk commanded firmly. "If we can get even a whisper of intent from them, we need to know. Spock, any insightful assessments on what might be transpiring?" Spock's sharp features tightened with concentration, an index finger raised thoughtfully to his chin. "The level of aggression exhibited by the Amar leads me to deduce that whatever entity resides within this 'power field' perceives hostility. It is logical to assume they react out of defensive posturing. However, we cannot ascertain their motivations until we bridge that communication gap." Kirk nodded, the weight of command pressing upon him: a delicate dance balancing diplomacy and survival. "Scotty, how close are we to warp readiness?" "We'll be ready to engage in a matter of minutes, Captain," came the cheery Scotsman, his fingers flying with the practiced ease of a true engineer. "Engine alignment is green across the board, but I suggest we keep our options open for a slow approach instead of going in full throttle. We have no idea what we're dealing with." "I concur," Spock interjected. It was a statement laced with an urgency that Kirk recognized. "Disruptors and torpedoes should not be the only tools in our arsenal. Should fear guide our actions, we run the risk of being perceived as a threat." The crew, tense as a coiled spring, awaited their captain's direction. "Prepare to shadow them then. Evasive maneuvers ready as needed. I'm not keen on being the large, shiny target floating through uncharted realms." His eyes drifted to the vast display showing the oncoming alien ship. "Our mission is to observe and ascertain, not incite a war." Suddenly, the tactical display flickered, revealing an increasing number of Klingon vessels lining up behind the Amar, eager for an engagement that might spell disaster for all of them. Kirk turned sharply. "Are they preparing to assist the Amar? What is their status?" "Sir," Uhura replied, her tone laced with concern, "it appears the Klingons are moving toward a coordinated strike. Their weapons are powering up - they seem eager to eliminate the intruders." Scotty stepped back from his console, eyes glimmering with worry. "But if they attack first, it could trigger a conflict that envelops Federation space. We cannot hold all power points when two factions engage recklessly!" Kirk felt the puzzle pieces shift into sharper focus. "We need to intervene, but carefully. Spock, gather data on that luminescent cloud as we approach. I want to know everything about its properties and capabilities. We may yet intervene diplomatically." He could feel the air of uncertainty, charged with the potential for catastrophe. All lives aboard the Enterprise depended on each decision made in this polarized standoff. "Stand by weapons systems, but relays remain set to non-lethal protocols - at least until we know precisely what we're facing." As the hum of the Enterprise thrummed beneath him, Kirk allowed himself a moment of introspection, reflecting on the challenges that lay ahead. There would always be unseen enemies and convoluted motives in the depths of space.

Efforts to mitigate health inequalities in Scotland could thus benefit from a multifaceted approach addressing both stigma and the structural factors that underpin socioeconomic disparities. Initiatives aimed at alleviating poverty-based stigma should focus on raising awareness and promoting social inclusion, emphasizing the role of education and community engagement in challenging stereotypes and fostering understanding. Public health campaigns can educate individuals about the harmful effects of stigma, encouraging empathy and reducing prejudice. These campaigns should also highlight success stories to inspire hope and demonstrate the potential for change, emphasizing that poverty should not define one's identity or limit one's potential. Furthermore, public policies must be aligned with strategies that promote economic equity. This requires a critical examination of existing policies to ensure they do not inadvertently perpetuate stigma or inequality. For instance, revising welfare policies to become more supportive and less punitive can help break the cycle of poverty and its associated stigma. Similarly, investing in education and job training programs tailored to those from deprived backgrounds can provide the tools necessary for social mobility, enabling individuals to improve their socioeconomic standing and health outcomes. Implementing universal health care policies that guarantee access to high-quality care irrespective of socioeconomic status is essential. Access to preventative health services, mental health support, and routine medical care can equitably improve health outcomes, reducing the burden of disease more prevalent in impoverished communities. Healthcare providers should receive training to recognize and address their own potential biases and ensure they are equipped to offer compassionate, stigma-free care to all patients. Critically, interdisciplinary research is needed to further explore the links between stigma, socioeconomic factors, and health outcomes in Scotland. Such research should prioritize the voices and experiences of those affected by poverty, using qualitative methodologies to deepen our understanding of the psychosocial dynamics at play. By developing a more nuanced comprehension of how stigma operates at individual, public, and structural levels, policymakers can be better informed to create effective interventions. Engagement with local communities is paramount. Community-led initiatives can empower individuals, offering platforms for shared experiences and collective action against stigma. These grassroots movements can galvanize support, influencing public opinion, and pushing for legislative changes that address the root causes of stigma and inequality. Collaboration between government entities, non-profit organizations, educators, and affected communities can foster innovative solutions tailored to Scotland's unique sociocultural landscape. To enhance the effectiveness of these strategies, regular evaluation and adaptation are necessary. By monitoring the outcomes of existing policies and interventions, decision-makers can identify areas of success and areas requiring improvement, ensuring that efforts remain flexible and responsive to the needs of Scotland's diverse population. Ultimately, addressing health inequalities in Scotland demands both a dismantling of the stigma surrounding poverty and a robust commitment to systemic reform. By approaching the issue from a holistic perspective that recognizes the interplay of structural and psychological factors, it is possible to craft a more equitable society where health outcomes are not determined by socioeconomic status. In so doing, Scotland can aspire to be a leader in reducing health inequalities, offering a model that other nations plagued by similar issues might follow.

He is a quiet man of middle age, an old white-headed bachelor with a droll twinkling expression, speaking seldom, and then in a curious silent fashion, as though the drowsy heat of the tropics had soaked him through and through. With his white hair, his white clothes, his white moustachios, his white eyelashes, over eyes that seem to hide away among quiet mirthful wrinkles, he carries about him the sort of silence that goes with a miller, surrounded by the white dusty quiet of his mill. As we sit together in the hush of his snuggery of an evening, surrounded by guns, fishing-lines, and old prints, there are times when we scarcely exchange a dozen words between dinner and bed-time, and yet we have all the time a keen and satisfying sense of companionship. It is John Saunders's gift. Companionship seems quietly to ooze out of him, without the need of words. He and you are there in your comfortable arm-chairs, with a good cigar, a whisky-and-soda, or a glass of that old port on which he prides himself, and that is all that is necessary. Where is the need of words? And occasionally, we have, as third in those evening conclaves, a big slow-smiling, broad-faced young merchant, of the same kidney. In he drops with a nod and a smile, selects his cigar and his glass, and takes his place in the smoke-cloud of our meditations, radiating, without the effort of speech, that good thing - humanity; though one must not forget the one subject on which now and again the good Charlie Webster achieves eloquence in spite of himself - duck-shooting. That is the only subject worth breaking the pleasant brotherhood of silence for. John Saunders's subject is shark-fishing. Duck-shooting and shark-fishing. It is enough. Here, for sensible men, is a sufficient basis for life-long friendship, and unwearying, inexhaustible companionship. It was in this peace of John Saunders's snuggery, one July evening, in 1903, the three of us being duly met, and ensconced in our respective arm-chairs, that we got on to the subject of buried treasure. We had talked more than usual that evening - talked duck and shark till those inexhaustible themes seemed momentarily exhausted. Then it was I who started us off again by asking John what he knew about buried treasure. At this, John laughed his funny little quiet laugh, his eyes twinkling out of his wrinkles, for all the world like mischievous mice looking out of a cupboard, took a sip of his port, a pull at his cigar, and then: "Buried treasure!" he said, "well, I have little doubt that the islands are full of it - if one only knew how to get at it." "Seriously?" I asked. "Certainly. Why not? When you come to think of it, it stands to reason.

As we walked out of the medical school, the sun beating down on us, I couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. Kevorkian's words still lingered in my mind, the image of his classmates' faces frozen in my memory. "Dead, dead, dead," he had repeated, his voice a monotone drone. I glanced at my notes, trying to refocus on the task at hand. We had a long way to go before the interview was over, and I had a feeling that Kevorkian was just getting started. As we walked, he pointed out various landmarks around the University of Michigan campus, his eyes squinting slightly in the bright sunlight. "That's where I used to play chess," he said, nodding toward a small park. "I was quite good, you know." I nodded politely, trying to keep up with his rapid-fire commentary. We eventually made our way to a small cafe on State Street, where Kevorkian ordered a cup of black coffee and I opted for a glass of water. As we sat down at a small table, he leaned in close, his eyes glinting with a mischievous spark. "You know, Sanjay, I've been thinking a lot about my life lately," he said, his voice low and conspiratorial. "And I've come to a realization." I leaned in, my pen poised over my notebook. "What's that?" I asked, trying to keep my tone neutral. "I've been living a lie," he said, his voice dripping with conviction. "A lie of convenience, of societal expectations. I've been playing by the rules, trying to fit in, but it's all been a sham." I raised an eyebrow, intrigued despite myself. "What do you mean?" I asked, my voice softening. "I mean, I've been pretending to be something I'm not," he said, his eyes glinting with a hint of madness. "I've been pretending to be a doctor, a healer, when all along I've been a revolutionary. I've been fighting against the system, against the status quo." I nodded slowly, trying to process what he was saying. "And what do you hope to achieve with this revolution?" I asked, my voice measured. He leaned in closer, his eyes burning with intensity. "I want to change the world, Sanjay. I want to change the way people think about death, about life. I want to show them that there's more to life than just existing." I nodded, my mind racing with the implications of his words. As we finished our drinks and prepared to leave, I couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. I had never met anyone like Dr. Jack Kevorkian before, and I wasn't sure if I was ready for what he had to say. But I knew that I had to hear him out, to understand the man behind the headlines, the man who had become a symbol of controversy and debate. And so, I nodded, and followed him out of the cafe, into the bright sunlight, ready to face whatever lay ahead.

This has been happening for several years now, so they know I will eventually find the cash. I do this by borrowing from friends and family. If they're not available then I turn to credit cards. Right now, I owe 15,000. I am, of course, ashamed to be in this situation, especially when people assume we must be rolling in it. But I'm not alone. Many of those parents at Ed's school are struggling too. There's no doubt that the cost of living is rising faster than incomes. Even if you're earning a good wage, there's often little left after paying the mortgage and bills. Some families have fallen behind with their school fees. I'm told that others borrow against their homes to cover them. One mum recently confided that she'd borrowed from her elderly mother-in-law, who'd taken out a loan secured against her house. This woman works full-time and her husband earns around 150,000. They live in a beautiful house worth more than 2 million, yet they can't even manage to pay the school fees. Our financial problems started eight years ago when I became pregnant with our daughter Ruby. I gave up my job as a TV researcher and decided to become a freelance writer. I knew it would be hard to juggle work and childcare, but I hadn't anticipated how difficult it would be to make ends meet. With two children under three, it seemed impossible to write anything longer than a shopping list, let alone a feature article. By the time Ruby was six months old I realised I wasn't making any money, but we still had bills to pay. So I applied for a credit card and began using it to fill the gap. It didn't take long to reach the limit of 5,000. Then I took out another card and maxed that one out too. When we moved to London five years ago, I did some freelance work for magazines including Tatler and Marie Claire. I was earning around 500 per month and contributing what I could to the household budget. But my husband's business was badly affected by the recession and his income dropped significantly. I continued to use credit cards to pay for groceries and petrol. Now I have debts totalling 15,000 spread across four cards, with interest rates ranging from 19.9 per cent to 29.8 per cent. It takes me nearly a fortnight each month to pay off the minimum amounts on each card. I simply don't have enough money to pay off the balances. In desperation, I've turned to a debt charity for advice. I feel guilty asking for help, but I'm running out of options. I'm also worried about the impact our finances are having on Ed. He knows he goes to a posh school, but he doesn't understand why we can't afford to give him pocket money like most of his friends. I hate the thought of him feeling deprived or embarrassed. That's why I try to hide our money troubles from him. It's also why I keep up appearances by wearing designer clothes and accessories. If I look successful then maybe I'll feel it too. Meanwhile, my husband and I are trying to reduce our spending wherever possible. Last weekend, I cancelled our Sky subscription. I haven't told anyone else about this yet, but I'm planning to pull Ed out of school at the end of the summer term. He's only nine and I want him to spend his last few years of childhood enjoying himself rather than worrying about exams. I know it's not a decision everyone will agree with, but I think it's the right thing to do.

"Hey, what do you think you're doing?" he snaps, but Queen merely raises an eyebrow at him. "I'm just checking to see if there's anything interesting here," she says casually, her fingers dancing over the screen. "You might have a hidden life, you know." "Hidden life?" Slim scoffs, snatching the phone back. "What do you expect to find-dark secrets? Secret parties? I just work, come home, and sleep." "Must be a wild ride," she quips, smirking. "You sure know how to live on the edge." Slim chuckles despite himself. "What can I say? I'm a thrill-seeker." "Right." Queen's tone is laced with mockery as she leans back in her seat, crossing her arms. "And what kind of thrills are we talking about? A Friday night binge-watching Netflix or maybe an extra hour at the office?" "Hey! There's nothing wrong with Netflix," he protests. "Actually, the last season of that show everyone talks about? I'm into it." Her expression shifts as she studies him, genuinely interested. "Is it good? I've been meaning to catch up." "Yeah, but there are a lot of twists. You've gotta pay attention," he warns, careful as he navigates his way through traffic. "I can pay attention when I want to," she replies with a glint of mischief in her eye. "It's just usually I'm more interested in what's in front of me than what's on the screen." His lips twitch again, fighting off a smile. "Like, you know, scrambled eggs?" "Touche," she laughs, the tension momentarily melting away. "But really, if we're talking about hidden lives, I want to know more about you." "Like what?" Slim asks, shifting gears expertly as he glances at her. "Why the sad face?" she probes, leaning in slightly, her tone sincere. "It's not really your style in your profile pic." He pauses, the air thickening between them. It's always there, the shadow of the things left unsaid, the little bursts of confessions waiting to erupt. "Just, you know, sometimes life hits harder than expected." Queen nods. "I get that. And here I thought I had a monopoly on having a rough day." "No one wins that game," he replies, somber now. "But my big thing? I just want to make sure it means something, you know?" "Like you care about the murdered souls, right?" "Something like that." She sits back, eyes assessing, weighing the heaviness of his words. "So are you a saint or a vigilante? You know, that champion of justice type?" "Neither." Slim shakes his head, a hint of a smile betraying him despite the weight. "Just a guy trying to figure it all out." "For all the lawyering you do, it sounds like a lot of emotional baggage to carry around," she observes carefully. "Everyone's got their cross to bear," he mutters, barely above a whisper. "True," she concedes, her gaze piercing. "But don't think I can't see you backpedaling. What's beneath all this righteousness?" He shrugs, unimpressed by her detective work. "You think you're clever, huh?" "My mom always said I had a knack for reading people," she beams. "That's why I survived the chaos at home." "Is that so?" Slim's curiosity piques, the previous tension fading slightly. "Care to share?" But she shakes her head, veiling her thoughts behind a smirk. "Maybe later." "Yeah, we'll see," he replies, wondering if 'later' would ever come.

Even though it was a 4-1 margin, this was not only a Lakers team that went through what was then considered easily the better conference, but which went into the Finals with its power forward, effectively, unable to play and its backup guard and top sixth man also limited. Add to that the intrigue of the inevitable splintering, and it's easy to see why the Lakers lost. But they weren't far away from winning, and a healthy, more cooperative team would be the favorite against the East's best, no matter who it is. Jackson had seen this coming almost from the beginning. Yes, Phil could see the future on occasion, too. Not that this one wasn't hard to divine. Jackson had gone through the "It's my team. No, it's my team. No, it's my team. No, it's MY team" thing with Bryant and O'Neal during the 2000-01 season and resolved it pretty well. At least they did in putting together a historic 15-1 run through the playoffs. It was Shaq's time and he was winning his second of three straight Finals MVPs. Jackson knew it was Shaq's time, but he also knew time always won, especially with the big guys. After he was 30, Wilt never averaged 30 points again and only was above 25 one season. After hitting 30, Bill Russell never again averaged more than 15 rebounds. Kareem Abdul-Jabbar played a dozen more seasons after hitting 30 and averaged at least 25 points just twice. Jackson knew it would be coming for O'Neal, and he began to talk to him about eventually turning it over to Kobe, doing, in effect, what Abdul-Jabbar did with Magic Johnson. Not that it was so voluntary, warm and fuzzy with Abdul-Jabbar. He resented Magic, but he also understood. He had a chance to still win and prolong his career if he let his pride and ego - and there never was one any bigger - go a little and allow Magic to step into the spotlight. Abdul-Jabbar won his last league MVP award in 1980. But he was on four championship teams after that. Kareem didn't like Magic being the star, but he understood. Shaq and Kobe just don't get it. Look, when O'Neal and Bryant were blasting away at one another at the beginning of last season, both were right. Shaq is lazy about practice and overweight and doesn't care all the time. Bryant is selfish and self-centered and condescending toward his teammates. So what. That doesn't describe half the rest of the NBA? Or most of corporate America? People are about themselves. That's what great leadership is for - to get them to work together toward a common goal. It's what separated Jackson from his peers. Well, that and the Native American paraphernalia and Zen garden in his living room, as well. But that's another story.

As the night wore on, we found ourselves tangled in a web of laughter, playful arguments, and a few too many slices of pizza. It's funny, really, how a group of friends can turn the mundane into something memorable, all because of the unpredictable chemistry we share. It's as if the world outside fades to a distant hum, and in that small corner of Ryan's "pad," every worry, every burden gets pushed aside. It's like we're suspended in this bubble where nothing else matters-just us, a game board, and the easy banter that flows like water. I never knew much about Monopoly, to be honest. Nate always told me it was a game of strategy; I just found it to be a tedious cycle of buying and selling and pretending to be a business mogul. Perhaps that's why Ryan and Kevin launched into their wrestling match amidst our board game, completely ignoring the colorful money that was just moments ago held in our hands. Ryan grabbed Kevin like he was a rag doll, laughing loudly, and for an instant, it felt as though childhood had resurrected itself in all of us. Such a simple, silly display, but it carried the weight of those endearing memories we often forget as we trudge toward adulthood. Meghan, while feigning annoyance, eventually got caught up in the fray as well. Before I knew it, we were all on the floor, everyone tangled in legs and laughter, the gameboard abandoned, the tiny plastic tokens sliding across the floor like the dreams we had left behind as we grew up. When did it become so serious? So suffocating? Sometimes I think about how easy it was to be carefree when we were younger, how our biggest worries revolved around snack time at school or what cartoons were on Saturday morning. I guess that's what we needed-we needed this chaos. Once Kevin had been thoroughly defeated-his protests fading into laughter-we all lay sprawled on the carpet, catching our breath, the warmth of friendship wrapping around us, keeping the winter cold at bay. It's moments like these that illuminate the joy in existence, the pieces that help patch together the more jagged parts of life. Who cares if the pizza was a little greasy, or the floor was an obstacle course strewn with board game pieces? We were living, breathing, young souls entangled in a fleeting moment, a small miracle of our own making. As the room settled and conversations flitted like butterflies, I stole a glance at the clock, realizing that soon enough, Christmas would be here. The excitement was absent, true, but there was a sense of peace, a calm certainty that what we had right then was enough. I turned to Meghan, who was smiling softly, and the moment lingered there, carried by the warmth of friendship and camaraderie. There's something undeniable about shared laughter; it's the thread that stitches us together. It's easy to forget, I thought, hard to see the beauty in the mundane moments, but if we just have each other-if we allow ourselves to be vulnerable and honest-maybe we can find that joy again, even amidst the chaos of unmet expectations and wants. So what if Christmas isn't hyped up? So what if gifts feel more like obligations? At least right now, we have this: a sanctuary of laughter, a story being told in the moments between breaths, and that's enough-more than enough.

And you know what? It works. I mean, it's not like they're trying to hide it. The game's director, Stig Asmussen, has straight-up said that they drew inspiration from those games. And I'm like, "Dude, you're not even trying to be subtle about it." But hey, if it ain't broke, right? So, Jedi Fallen Order is set between Episodes III and IV, and you play as Cal Kestis, a young Padawan who's trying to survive in a galaxy that's, you know, actively trying to kill him. The Empire's on the hunt for any remaining Jedi, and Cal's got a big ol' target on his back. The story's pretty standard Star Wars fare - there's some ancient artifacts, some mysterious MacGuffins, and a whole lot of running away from Stormtroopers. But the real star of the show is the combat. Oh man, the combat. It's like they took all the best parts of Dark Souls and Sekiro and mashed them together into this beautiful, brutal mess. You've got your standard lightsaber combos, but then you've also got these fancy Force abilities that let you slow down time, throw enemies around, and do all sorts of cool stuff. And the best part is, it's not just a button-masher - you actually have to think about what you're doing, use your abilities strategically, and time your attacks just right. And then there's the platforming. Oh boy, the platforming. It's like Uncharted, but with more jumping and less Nathan Drake. You've got these sprawling levels that are just begging to be explored, and Cal's got all sorts of abilities that let him climb walls, swing from vines, and do all sorts of crazy stuff. It's like a big ol' playground, and I am here for it. But, you know, it's not all sunshine and rainbows. The game's got some issues - the story's a little predictable, the graphics could be better, and there are some wonky camera angles that'll drive you nuts. But overall, I'd say Jedi Fallen Order is a solid addition to the Star Wars canon. It's not perfect, but it's a whole lot of fun, and that's what counts, right? And hey, speaking of fun, let's talk about our favorite Star Wars games. I mean, we've got the classics like Knights of the Old Republic and X-Wing, but what about some of the more... unusual ones? Like, has anyone played Star Wars: Demolition? That game was wild - it was like a vehicular combat game, but with Star Wars characters. I mean, who wouldn't want to play as a young Anakin Skywalker, driving around in a podracer and blowing stuff up? Or how about Star Wars: Masters of Teras Kasi? That game was like a fighting game, but with Force powers and lightsabers. I mean, it was basically just a Star Wars-themed Mortal Kombat, but it was still a lot of fun. And who can forget Star Wars: Yoda Stories? That game was like... well, I'm not really sure what it was like, but it was definitely something. Anyway, that's it for this week's episode of The Besties. Thanks for tuning in, and we'll catch you on the flip side. May the Force be with you, and all that jazz.

The integrity and control of the intestinal barrier is often attenuated by both nutritional and immunological challenges in the fish. Our knowledge of the fish immune system is advancing rapidly, with many of the cell types, humoral factors and regulatory molecules now identified (Collet, 2014; Castro and Tafalla, 2015) (Fig. 1). Within the intestine, immune activity is controlled by the gut associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) containing numerous immune cell types that are involved in both innate and adaptive responses (reviewed in Salinas and Parra, 2015). Of central importance is antigen sampling across the epithelial barrier, likely to involve antigen-sampling cells equivalent to mammalian microfold (M) cells and dendritic cells (DCs) (Fuglem et al., 2010). Although a specific DC subset has not yet been fully identified in fish, the presence of dendritic-like cells has been suggested in intestinal epithelium (Fuglem et al., 2010) and peripheral blood (Haugland et al., 2012) of Atlantic salmon as well as various non-intestinal tissues of rainbow trout (Johansson et al., 2012; Granja et al., 2015) and zebrafish (Lugo-Villarino et al., 2010). The intestinal dendritic-like cells are hypothesised to present luminal antigens to T and B cells ensuring the maintenance of the gut microbiome and identification of pathogens. B cells secrete different Ig molecules (Parra et al., 2013; Salinas, 2015) and are produced at high levels in the intestinal mucus to bind luminal antigens. The combination of B and T cells oversee the immune status of the intestine and ensure its correct functioning from early development. Specifically, Treg and Th17 cells in mammals maintain the intestinal balance between reacting in an inflammatory or non-inflammatory manner to sustain homeostasis, although the presence of these T cell subtypes in fish remains to be confirmed. Some aspects of the mucosal immunity are fish specific, such as immunoglobulin T (IgT), secreted from intraepithelial lymphocytes (Parra et al., 2013; Ballesteros et al., 2013). The intestinal immunity of fish is of special interest for the fish farming industry for a number of reasons. Firstly, farmed fish kept at high stocking densities are susceptible to intestinal infections, with the gut being an important entry point for pathogens (Salinas and Parra, 2015). Secondly, farmed fish are typically fed commercial pelleted feeds, which opens up avenues for manipulating fish health through the incorporation of various feed additives, drugs and vaccines into the feed (reviewed in Caipang and Lazado, 2015). Thirdly, the gut immune system of teleost fish allows microbial colonization by symbionts (Ringo et al., 2014), and this microbial community is a potential platform to modulate fish pathogens. Finally, gut microbiota in fish are likely to respond to dietary manipulations (Merrifield and Rodiles, 2015; Llewellyn et al., 2014; Rurangwa et al., 2015). Hence, a comprehensive understanding of the diet-gut interactions and immunoregulatory properties of intestinal epithelium in fish could aid in the development of new strategies to prevent and treat their multiple infectious and inflammatory diseases.

The battle was exceptionally well planned. American planners did a fine job of putting together a winning plan, yet due to logistical realities, almost from the beginning things went radically wrong for the Marines. On Tarawa, as in Iraq, the American forces adapted, and despite protests from the American press about casualties, continued the attack and prevailed against a determined and numerically superior force. The value of Betio, (Tarawa) was that we learned valuable lessons that served us well during the rest of the Pacific campaign. Yes, the casualties were high, but the hard-learned lessons of Tarawa actually helped reduce casualties in the future campaigns. Within hours of securing Tarawa, the island became a forward base of operation for air assaults on the Marshall Islands...and ultimately the attack on the Marshalls. From there, the Americans moved closer and closer to the island fortress of Japan, and ultimate victory in the Pacific. Iraq serves a similar purpose. We have suffered hard-learned lessons. However, a democracy in the Middle East, separate and apart from the blessings it brings the people of Iraq, serves a larger purpose, just like Tarawa. That is the true value of our painful lessons in Iraq. Syria, Iran and Saudi Arabia take note. As I watched the Iraqi soccer team at the Olympics I could not help but think how they would not be there except for our brave forces that liberated them and their country. Iraq was a brilliant military campaign, well executed despite difficulties. But Iraq was not Tarawa where the Press was concerned. The world press corps had a free hand to second-guess the American military high command and instantly call-up the bloody visage of Vietnam. Vietnam, the unexorcised ghost and ultimate "boogey man" of America's military past seems as powerful an image today as it was some 31 years ago. In point of fact, however, Iraq is not Vietnam, was not Vietnam, nor can it ever become Vietnam. Yet, it is most certainly "Vietnam" to those who are, once again, not familiar with America's history. This is all the more laughable when comparisons about Vietnam are made by people who are generations removed from having actually experienced it, and more importantly, having a full comprehension of what Vietnam was, and was not. As for John Kerry, his recollections of Vietnam are proving astonishingly inaccurate as of late.

Although it has long been known that poor nutrition can compromise immunity and resistance to infectious diseases in fish (Roberts, 1978), the underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. This review aims to summarize recent progress in understanding how different types of dietary deficiency affect immune responses in fish. ## Dietary deficiency and fish immunity ### Energy and macronutrient deficiency Energy deficiency is associated with decreased body weight, reduced muscle mass and fat stores, and impaired physical activity (Alvheim et al., 2013). In fish, inadequate energy intake reduces growth rate and feed conversion efficiency, while excessive energy intake increases the proportion of visceral fat and predisposes to obesity (Hendricks et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2016). Inadequate energy intake during critical developmental periods may also lead to irreversible stunting of growth (Wang et al., 2000; Alvarez et al., 2006). As energy deficiency affects all physiological processes in the body, its impacts on fish immunity are likely to be profound. One of the first indications of this came from a study in channel catfish ( Ictalurus punctatus ), where starvation was shown to reduce antibody titres and increase mortality following challenge with Edwardsiella tetaluri bacteria (Bly et al., 1986). A more recent investigation examined the effects of graded levels of energy restriction (30%, 40% and 50%) on immune parameters in juvenile rainbow trout ( Onchorynchus mykiss ) (Kakaei and Ebrahimi-Dorcheh, 2012). The experimental groups were fed a commercial trout pellet three times a day until satiation (control group) or restricted to 70%, 60% or 50% of the control ration. After four weeks, the fish were sampled and analysed for innate immune parameters. The results showed that all three levels of energy restriction significantly increased serum lysozyme activity, but had no effect on total complement activity or serum bactericidal activity. It remains unclear whether the observed changes represent an adaptive response to energy restriction or a sign of stress. In another study, juvenile rainbow trout were divided into three groups, which were fasted (no food provided) for one week before being fed either a low energy diet (LE) containing 11.22 MJ kg\({}^{-1}\) digestible energy or a high energy diet (HE) containing 17.23 MJ kg\({}^{-1}\) digestible energy (Alvheim et al., 2013). A third group of fish continued to be fasted throughout the experiment (FAS). At the end of the feeding trial (seven days post-fasting), the FAS group had lost 12.33 g of body weight (19.18%), while the LE and HE groups gained 24.75 g (49.41%) and 26.99 g (54.73%) of body weight respectively. The immune parameters measured included haematocrit, plasma cortisol, plasma glucose, white blood cell counts and differential leukocyte counts. No significant differences were observed among the treatment groups, although there was a trend towards lower haemoglobin concentration in the LE group compared to the other groups (\(P=0.06\)). Interestingly, the same study reported significantly lower expression of several genes related to inflammation and apoptosis in the liver of the HE group compared to the other groups. Taken together, these findings suggest that energy deficiency compromises some aspects of immune function in fish, although further research is required to elucidate the underlying mechanisms.

In these cases, it has been proposed that the observer simulates the observed action of the other person through mental imagery (Haggard, 2006). This simulation may involve a process of "mirror" activation of the motor system in which the observer imagines herself performing the observed action (Gallese, Keysers, & Rizzolatti, 2004; Kilner, Neal, Weiskopf, Friston, & Frith, 2009). Mirror neurons have been recorded in monkeys (Gallese et al., 2004) and are thought to play a key role in the perception-action link (Rizzolatti & Craighero, 2004), social cognition (Iacoboni, Molnar-Szakacs, Gallese, Buccino, Mazziotta, & Rizzolatti, 2005), and empathy (Keysers & Gazzola, 2009). Mirror activations in the observer have been reported in fMRI experiments involving observation of the actions of others (Carr, Iacoboni, Dubeau, Mazziotta, & Lenzi, 2003; Grezes, Costes, & Decety, 1998; Grezes, Costes, & Decety, 1999; Iacoboni et al., 2005; Koski, Wymbs, & Padoa-Schioppa, 2007; Uddin, Iacoboni, Lange, & Keenan, 2007) and in electroencephalographic (EEG) studies involving observation of whole-body movements (Oberman, Hubbard, McCleery, Altschuler, Ramachandran, & Pineda, 2006; Oberman, McClure, Altschuler, Pineda, & Ramachandran, 2007; Schutz-Bosbach & Prinz, 2007). In some of these studies, mirror activations were observed when participants viewed their own movements (Oberman et al., 2007; Oberman, Winkielman, & Ramachandran, 2008; Oberman, Winkielman, & Ramachandran, 2009). These findings suggest that observing oneself and others may trigger common mechanisms for representing bodily actions. To date, however, no study has investigated whether seeing the body of another person activates a shared representational format for the body of both the observer and the observed person. If such a shared representational format exists, we would expect to see enhanced tactile acuity when participants observe the body of another person. Here, we investigated the neural basis of VET using TMS and EEG. First, we used TMS to test the hypothesis that the hVIP mediates VET for the observed body. Second, we used EEG to investigate whether VET for the observed body involves a common representational format for the bodies of both the observer and the observed person.

As models to demonstrate this phenomenon, we selected three exogenous protein ligands that either do not traffic to lysosomes in their uncomplexed state (transferrin (Tf)) or do so minimally: the anti(MHC I) antibody W6/32 and the anti-Her2 antibody trastuzumab (TRz). The trafficking route of Tf has been extensively characterized: It first binds to the TfR, and both then internalize together via clathrin-mediated endocytosis,20 which requires the AP2-coat complex.21 Following release of bound iron, Tf:TfR is recycled to the plasma membrane, where the Tf is then released.22 The ability of Tf to recycle has been exploited for delivery of various therapeutics (drugs, genes, proteins) across biological barriers including the BBB.23,24 TfR-mediated transport across the BBB occurs via transcytosis, in which TfR:cargo complexes are endocytosed at the apical face of endothelial cells and subsequently recycled at the distal basolateral surface. In addition to Tf, antibodies that bind TfR have been investigated for their ability to cross this barrier, but these efforts have been hindered by trafficking of TfR to lysosomes.1,2,3 An understanding of TfR:cargo trafficking may therefore enable us to design improved vectors for delivery of therapeutics into the brain via a transcytosis route that avoids lysosomal delivery. Other work on TfR trafficking has shown that local clustering of TfR increases the rate of endocytosis25 and that lysosomal delivery can be induced using a monoclonal bivalent anti-TfR antibody.26 The W6/32 antibody targets the MHC class I complex, which localizes predominantly to the plasma membrane.27 In contrast to Tf, endocytosis of the anti(MHC I) antibody W6/32 is clathrin independent.28,29,30 A "quality control" mechanism is proposed to exist,31 in which loss of 2 microglobulin from the MHC class I complex results in clustering of the remaining MHC class I heavy chain (which contains the epitope for W6/32)32 and its subsequent delivery to lysosomes.33 It has further been shown that induced crosslinking of the MHC class I complex causes signaling,34,35,36,37 which may serve as an indicator for the integrity of the MHC class I complex. Determining the endocytic fate of complexed W6/32 is thus a crucial test of the MHC class I quality control hypothesis. TRz is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to Her2 and is used clinically either as an unconjugated antibody ("Herceptin")38 or as the ADC TRz-emtansine ("Kadcyla").39 Her2 is overexpressed in 15-20% of diagnosed breast cancers,40,41 where it forms oncogenic signaling dimers with other, ligand activated, receptors from the ErbB family.

However, a number of models use linear relationships between displacement and force because they are less computationally expensive to calculate thus allowing the simulation of larger systems using DEM. These include the recent models of Thakur et al. [17] and Pasha et al. [18], which also include adhesive forces, and the older Walton-Braun model [19], recently extended for cyclic loading [20]. Broadly speaking these models and the models of Luding [21] and Walton and Johnson [22] use linear springs, characterised by an appropriate stiffness, for each part of the force-displacement relationship. For the Thakur model stiffness values needed for a specific material are found by comparing the results of DEM simulations to experiment and calibrating the stiffnesses appropriately [23]. This requires experiments to be carried out for every material to be simulated. Similar procedures are required to find the stiffness values for the other models or alternatively the models can be fitted directly to experimental results [9,20]. The non-adhesive version of the Tomas model [27] is similar to the Thornton model. It uses the Hertz elastic model up to the same yield displacement. Above this displacement the loading relationship contains a parameter, the contact area coefficient, that represents the ratio of the plastically deformed area to the total deformed area. This parameter is 0 for perfectly elastic deformation and 1 for plastic deformation (at which point the loading relation is given by the same linear expression as in the Thornton model). Increasing this parameter with displacement allows the Tomas model to capture the non-linear nature of the force response in the intermediate elastic-plastic regime between pure elastic and pure plastic loading. In recent work [16,28] a fitting parameter is added to this loading relation in order to fit it to experimental results. The original Tomas model is used with a Hertzian model for unloading [27], similar to the Thornton model but with an unchanged radius of curvature, appropriate for 'healing' contacts [29]. It is also used with an adapted radius of curvature [28] based on the work of Stronge [30] with an additional adjustable parameter to allow fitting to experimental results. The Vu-Quoc and Zhang model [15] and the Li-Wu-Thornton (LWT) model [31] were developed using FEM simulations. They are both significantly more complex than the models previously considered and both models have to be solved numerically to obtain the force for a given displacement. This means that at every time-step numerous iterations have to be carried out for every collision in order to calculate the forces, making them computationally expensive. There are also a number of force-displacement models in the tribology literature [32-35]. These are designed for much larger relative displacements than typically seen in DEM in order to model high force impacts, often of a single spherical object onto a near-rigid flat. These models include the analytical Brake model [32] and the empirical Jackson and Green model [33].

I was drawn to the vibrancy of his vision and his ambitions for our people. But that glow has dimmed under the weight of his delusion. They are ambassadors of hope to many, not merely symbols of his nostalgic expectations. I cannot help but wonder if he even acknowledges the countless women who have fought and continue to fight for their place and rights amid the cacophony of cultures entwined in this land. To Kani, it's nothing short of a romantic tragedy when a woman does not conform to his ideal image. His disappointment is not just his; it has ramifications beyond his grasp. After sending my mother's email, I briefly toyed with the idea of penning my own diatribe to him, but what would be the point? Would he even listen? Perhaps the struggle lies not merely in correcting him but in attempting to reach him. Perhaps I'm guilty of selecting only my voice in this dialogue. And there it is again, that itch of urgency. Tomorrow is another day, and perhaps Kani will finally receive a wake-up call. Perhaps he'll begin to appreciate the incredible weight that words can carry, especially in the context of a people yearning for clarity and meaning in the chaos of the present day. Until then, I have my musings-a flurry of thoughts that may illuminate or further cloud the conversation yet to come. But I assure you, dear reader, I will no longer stand idly by while a man who should know better continues to reduce a vital movement to nothing more than his own sentimental ramblings. My resolve crystallizes like water turning to ice-ready to fight against the misunderstandings that hold us back. Perhaps that's a start.

The study of ice streams has been a crucial aspect of understanding the dynamics of Pleistocene ice sheets, particularly in the Northern Hemisphere. While significant progress has been made in identifying and mapping ice streams, there remains a lack of comprehensive reconstructions of their evolution during the deglaciation of the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS). The majority of research has focused on the largest ice streams, with many studies concentrating on the Hudson Strait Ice Stream and its role in the LIS's drainage network. However, a more nuanced understanding of ice streams is required to fully comprehend the complex interactions between ice streams, ice divides, domes, and catchment areas. The concept of ice streams as discrete, fast-flowing corridors of ice has been widely accepted, but the exact mechanisms governing their formation, evolution, and demise remain unclear. The lack of ice stream reconstructions in ice-sheet-wide models has hindered our ability to accurately simulate the LIS's response to climate change. Recent studies have made significant strides in improving our understanding of ice streams, particularly through the use of numerical modeling and paleo-ice stream reconstructions. For example, studies by Winsborrow et al. (2012) and Margold et al. (2015a, b) have highlighted the importance of ice streams in shaping the LIS's drainage network and have provided new insights into the evolution of ice streams during deglaciation. However, there is still a need for more comprehensive reconstructions that incorporate the interactions between ice streams, ice divides, and catchment areas. The study of ice streams in the LIS is particularly challenging due to the limited availability of data and the complexity of the ice sheet's dynamics. However, advances in remote sensing and geophysical techniques have provided new opportunities for investigating ice streams and their role in the LIS's evolution. For example, the use of satellite imagery and airborne radar data has enabled researchers to map the extent and morphology of ice streams, while seismic and gravity data have provided insights into the underlying bedrock topography. Despite these advances, there is still much to be learned about the dynamics of ice streams and their role in the LIS's evolution. Further research is needed to better understand the interactions between ice streams, ice divides, and catchment areas, as well as the mechanisms governing the formation and evolution of ice streams. This knowledge will be crucial for improving our ability to simulate the LIS's response to climate change and for understanding the impacts of future climate change on ice sheets. In conclusion, the study of ice streams is a critical component of understanding the dynamics of Pleistocene ice sheets, particularly in the Northern Hemisphere. While significant progress has been made in identifying and mapping ice streams, there is still a need for more comprehensive reconstructions that incorporate the interactions between ice streams, ice divides, and catchment areas. Further research is required to better understand the dynamics of ice streams and their role in the LIS's evolution, and to improve our ability to simulate the LIS's response to climate change.

Research into nanotechnology, for instance, holds particular promise, as it offers the potential to create nanoparticles that can encapsulate progesterone and facilitate sustained release while improving bioavailability (Rai et al., 2018). Such proposed systems can enhance targeting, ensuring that progesterone reaches its intended site of action more effectively and efficiently. Additionally, the development of biodegradable polymer matrices could offer a novel approach to managing the controlled release of progesterone. These systems, which degrade over time, provide a lasting therapeutic effect without requiring frequent administration, thereby addressing compliance issues often encountered with oral or parenteral formulations (Miller et al., 2019). This sustained release not only supports continuous delivery but also maintains progesterone levels within a therapeutic window, thereby maximizing its protective effects against preterm labour. Another consideration in formulation development may involve exploring combination therapies that include adjunctive agents to synergistically enhance the effects of progesterone. For instance, the incorporation of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or other tocolytic agents could potentially provide an additive benefit in managing uterine contractility and inflammation (Bo et al., 2018). The exploration of complementary mechanisms may pave the way for a multifaceted approach to preterm birth prevention, increasing the likelihood of maintaining gestational duration and promoting neonatal health. Moreover, it is important to underscore the significance of personalized medicine in this context. Individual variations in the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of progesterone due to genetic and environmental factors could profoundly impact treatment outcomes (Middeldorp et al., 2016). Investigating biomarkers and genetic predispositions among diverse populations may aid clinicians in identifying at-risk patients who would benefit most from progesterone therapy, thus fostering a targeted approach to intervention. Equally crucial is the establishment of an effective monitoring system, which can be implemented alongside any new formulation. The use of wearables or mobile health technologies may provide real-time monitoring of uterine activity and maternal vital signs, allowing for timely intervention and adjustments in therapy. Such innovations not only empower healthcare providers with data-driven insights but also encourage expectant mothers to participate actively in their care, enhancing the overall therapeutic alliance. In summary, addressing the challenge of preterm delivery necessitates a concerted effort to innovate and refine drug delivery systems for progesterone. Through the exploration of novel formulations-ranging from nanocarriers to biodegradable systems-and the integration of combination therapies and personalized medicine principles, there exists a genuine opportunity to significantly reduce preterm birth rates globally. Ongoing research and collaboration among clinicians, researchers, and pharmaceutical developers are critical in driving these advancements forward, ensuring that the next generation of strategies is both effective and accessible, particularly in the high-risk regions most affected by this pressing health issue. The journey toward mitigating the impact of preterm births is indeed complex, yet it is one laden with potential, promising substantial improvements in maternal and neonatal health outcomes worldwide.
