His crew used publicly available election rolls to identify 'inactive' voters and then chose 30-year-old men for him to impersonate. The final footage shows election officials, over and over, accepting O'Keefe's claim that he was one of those people. 'With almost three-quarters-of-a-million inactive voters and no voter ID law in place, we could have turned the election results for most major candidates in the state,' he claimed Monday. 'What we uncovered in this video illustrates how easy it would be for a well-orchestrated campaign with no regard for the law to change the outcome of a major election. Voter laws across the country need to be changed immediately to prevent this sort of potential voter fraud.' FINALLY: One poll worker realized that the name and address O'Keefe offered belonged to someone who hadn't voted in a long time - but he actually broke the law by insisting on seeing identification. O'Keefe has tweaked the political left on the contentious voter ID issue before.

As the blue horse sidled expertly down the slope a loose stone turned under his shod hoof, causing him to stumble ever so slightly, though he caught himself instantly. As instantly the woman's spurred heel struck his flank, her swift tightening of the rein anticipated his resultant start. "Pick up your feet, you!" she said sharply, frowning. The stallion did pick up his feet, for he was intelligent, but he shook his proud head, laid his ears back on his neck, and the sweat started on his sensitive skin at the needless rake of the spur. The great dark eyes in his grey-blue face shone for a time like fox-fire in the dark, twin sparks beneath the light of his tossing silver forelock. He choose his footing more carefully, though he was an artist in hill climbing at all times, for the woman on his back was a hard task-master. Caught as a colt in the high meadows of the Upper Country beyond the Deep Heart hills, the horse had served her faithfully for four of his seven years of life, and hated her sullenly. There was mixed blood in his veins-wild, from the slim white mother who had never felt a rope, patrician, gentle, tractable, from the thoroughbred black father lost from a horse-trader's string eleven years back and sought for many bootless moons because of his great value. Swayed by the instincts of these two strains the superb animal obeyed this woman who was unquestionably his master, though rebellion surged in him at every chastisement. The sun was at the zenith, marking the time of short shadows, and its light fell in pale golden washes over the tapestried green slopes. Tall flowers nodded on slim stalks in nook and crevasse-frail columbine and flaming bleeding hearts-and mosses crept in the damp places. For an hour the two came down along the breast of a ridge, dropping slowly in a long diagonal, and presently came out on a bold shoulder that jutted from the parent spine. Here, with the thinning trees falling abruptly away, a magnificent view spread out below. For a long time there had been in the rider's ears a low and heavy murmur, a ceaseless sound of power. Now its source was visible-the river that wound between wide meadows spread like flaring flounces on either side-broad, level, green stretches that looked rich as a king's lands, and were. The woman reined up her horse and sitting sidewise looked down with moody eyes. A frown drew close the dark brows under the hat brim, the full sensuous lips hardened into a tight line. Hatred flamed in her passionate face, for the smiling valley was tenanted. At the far edge of the green floor across the river there nestled against the hills that rose abruptly the small log buildings of a homestead.

He listened to my tale of woe with a sympathetic ear, nodding his head and making notes on a pad of paper. When I finished, he leaned back in his chair and steepled his fingers together. "Ah, yes, Mr. Carey," he said, "you have, shall we say, a certain... je ne sais quoi. A certain charm, a certain elan. But, alas, your academic record is not exactly... distinguished, is it?" I had to admit that it wasn't. In fact, I was surprised I had managed to scrape through at all. "No, no, of course not," he continued. "But that's not necessarily a barrier to a career in education. What's important is that you have a certain... flair, a certain ability to inspire the young minds. And I think you may have that, Mr. Carey." He leaned forward, his eyes gleaming with a mixture of amusement and calculation. "I have just the thing for you, Mr. Carey. A small, but respectable school in the Midlands. The headmaster is an old friend of mine, and I'm sure he would be delighted to have you on board. The pay is modest, but the surroundings are pleasant, and the pupils are... well, they're not exactly the cream of society, but they're eager to learn." I was taken aback. I had been expecting something rather more... glamorous, I suppose. But the gentleman's words were persuasive, and I found myself agreeing to take the position. And so, I set off for the Midlands, feeling a mixture of trepidation and excitement. I had no idea what lay ahead, but I was determined to make a go of it. After all, I had nothing to lose, and everything to gain. As I arrived at the school, I was struck by its rather... rustic charm. The buildings were old and worn, but there was a certain warmth to the place that I found appealing. The headmaster, a kindly old man with a bushy beard, welcomed me warmly and showed me to my quarters. The next day, I met my pupils. They were a rough-looking bunch, but they seemed eager to learn, and I found myself enjoying their company. We struggled through lessons, with me trying to impart my meager knowledge to them, and them trying to absorb it. It was hard work, but it was also strangely satisfying. For the first time in my life, I felt as though I was doing something useful, something that mattered. And as the days turned into weeks, I found myself growing more confident, more assured. But little did I know, my life was about to take a dramatic turn. A turn that would lead me into the midst of the most extraordinary affairs, and bring me a fame that I could never have imagined...

This morning was a perfect example of her uncanny ability to vex me without even trying. We had made plans last night over a too-late dinner-like all good plans are made, with a bottle of red wine empty on the table as our witness-to visit the farmer's market. I had built it up in my mind, picturing the fresh produce, the vibrant flowers, and the artisanal cheese that inevitably begs to be paired with wine. I was practically salivating at the thought. So, I set the alarm for a reasonable time, intending to rise early and start the day right. And here's where the dumb ass part comes in: my wife, in her infinite wisdom, set the alarm to PM instead of AM. I woke to the smell of bacon but instead of the sun's gentle morning rays sneaking through the curtains, it was the ghastly apparition of noon glaring through the panes. I leaped from bed like I'd been shot, bolting into the living room where she casually lounged on the couch, blissfully unaware of the havoc she had wreaked on my ideal Saturday. "What time is it?" I rasped, still half-asleep. "Like, one something?" she chirped, flicking through channels like she had all the time in the world. I stood there, mouth agape, simultaneously impressed by how she remained so chill while my insides reeled like a roller coaster gone off track. I have this unfounded belief that the universe is aligned and when you plan something, the world conspires to make it happen, so I stood there trying to comprehend how it could possibly be noon already, our precious market hours now lost in the day's ether. "Are you kidding me?" I sputtered, each word echoing louder than the last, adrenaline overtaking my slumber. "We were supposed to be at the market!" "We can still go! Just not for the fresh stuff," she replied, still pensive and not quite comprehending the gravity of the situation. "Think of it as an adventure to find some good lunch instead!" Adventure? Lunchtime? What the hell? My vision of an idyllic morning spent perusing organic heirlooms had been dissolved into some mediocre fast food stop. Surely there had to be a better option. I wanted to rail against her, to point out her spectacular stupidity, but instead, I found myself searching for patience. "Sure, fine, let's go look for brunch," I said, my tone dramatically deflating. "Let's just hope we find something that doesn't include, I don't know, rubber eggs and flavorless toast." Her face morphed into this radiant smile, the kind that could rival the sun, her eyes sparkling with that familiar mischief. I thought maybe-just maybe-she was the perfect kind of dumb ass. You know the type who can screw up nearly every plan but somehow manage to squeeze delight from the chaos? Someday, I swear I'll try to rationalize it. Maybe that's when I'll figure out this equation because for all her wonderful quirks, they somehow remind me how lucky I am to share life with this unique woman. So, I took a deep breath, taking in the moment. "Alright then, let's do this. Lead the way, my glorious failure of a wife." Her laughter, contagious and light, filled up the air around us, and suddenly, my swelling irritation felt miles away.

Thus, we embarked on a series of experiments to ascertain whether semantic knowledge could indeed expand WM capacity for ecologically significant stimuli such as faces. Our participants, drawn from a diverse pool with varying levels of celebrity recognition, were administered a WM task involving the brief presentation of images followed by a recall phase. The set of images consisted of three categories: celebrity faces, unfamiliar faces, and colour patches. Participants had to indicate whether a presented image had been shown previously. We hypothesised that participants with higher familiarity or semantic association with the faces would exhibit enhanced WM capacity. Each test session was meticulously designed, incorporating varying encoding durations to examine the relationship between time and memory consolidation. Neural activity was concurrently measured using functional MRI to identify regions implicated in the enhanced memory of meaningful stimuli. Results indicated discernible differences in WM capacity contingent on the type of stimuli. As anticipated, capacity was substantially greater for celebrity faces than for unfamiliar faces or colour patches. This difference was statistically significant and more pronounced with extended encoding durations, suggesting that semantic associations bolster retention over time. Notably, fMRI data pinpointed increased activation in the left inferior frontal gyrus and anterior temporal lobes, regions associated with retrieval and semantic processing, during tasks involving celebrity faces. The implications of these findings extend beyond theoretical interest. They elucidate the interplay between WM and semantic memory, shedding light on how our cognitive architecture prioritises and processes information of ecological import. This underlines a dynamic facet of cognition: the flexible allocation of resources based on the interplay between familiarity, importance, and existing knowledge structures. Importantly, our study also prompts a reevaluation of how visual WM is conceptualised and assessed in laboratory settings. Conventional paradigms focusing on abstract or neutral visual stimuli might substantially undervalue the true capacities of WM by ignoring the enrichment provided by semantic networks. This insight urges the development of more ecologically valid paradigms in cognitive research. Future research directions may include exploring the boundary conditions of this semantic enhancement effect on WM by incorporating different types of meaningful stimuli, such as familiar places or objects. Moreover, longitudinal investigations could examine how gradual exposure to new information transforms its status from unfamiliar to integrated within our existing semantic frameworks, thereby affecting WM capacity. In sum, our findings provide compelling evidence for the profound influence of semantic knowledge on visual working memory. They confirm the notion that WM for ecologically relevant stimuli is not a simple function of innate capacity but is modulated by the richness of long-term representations and familiarity. This study paves the way for further investigations into the nuanced mechanisms of memory interplay, propelling our understanding of cognitive processes underlying everyday functioning and social interaction. While our findings illuminate significant aspects of the WM-semantic memory interface, the complexities of these relationships necessitate carefully delineated future inquiries. Through continued exploration, we aim to unravel the nuanced dynamics characterising how humans navigate and categorise their perceptual worlds, ultimately gleaning deeper insights into the intricate architecture of human cognition.

I read incessantly; and after exhausting the shelves of all the neighbours, and reading every variety of work that fell in my way - from "The Pilgrim's Progress" of Bunyan, and the Gospel Sonnets of Erskine, to a treatise on fortification by Vauban, and the "History of the Heavens" by the Abbe Pluche - I would have pined away for lack of my accustomed exercise, had not a benevolent baronet in the neighbourhood, for whom my father occasionally wrought, taken a fancy to me, and thrown open to my perusal a large and well-selected library. Nor did his kindness terminate until, after having secured to me all of learning that the parish school afforded, he had settled me, now in my seventeenth year, at the University. Youth is the season of warm friendships and romantic wishes and hopes. We say of the child, in its first attempts to totter along the wall, or when it has first learned to rise beside its mother's knee, that it is yet too weak to stand alone; and we may employ the same language in describing a young and ardent mind. It is, like the child, too weak to stand alone, and anxiously seeks out some kindred mind on which to lean. I had had my intimates at school, who, though of no very superior cast, had served me, if I may so speak, as resting-places, when wearied with my studies, or when I had exhausted my lighter reading; and now, at St. Andrew's, where I knew no one, I began to experience the unhappiness of an unsatisfied sociality. My schoolfellows were mostly stiff, illiterate lads, who, with a little bad Latin and worse Greek, plumed themselves mightily on their scholarship; and I had little inducement to form any intimacies among them; for, of all men, the ignorant scholar is the least amusing. Among the students of the upper classes, however, there was at least one individual with whom I longed to be acquainted. He was apparently much about my own age, rather below than above the middle size, and rather delicately than robustly formed; but I have rarely seen a more elegant figure or more interesting face. His features were small, and there was what might perhaps be deemed a too feminine delicacy in the whole contour; but there was a broad and very high expansion of forehead, which, even in those days, when we were acquainted with only the phrenology taught by Plato, might be regarded as the index of a capacious and powerful mind; and the brilliant light of his large black eyes, seemed to give earnest of its activity. "Who, in the name of wonder, is that?" I inquired of a class-fellow, as this interesting-looking young man passed me for the first time.

We seek to provide guidance to the researcher who is setting out on a resting-state analysis as to which network estimation method to choose. We believe a key property that any network connectivity measure must satisfy is the repeatability and consistency in estimation of both the single-subject result and the group-level structure. Consistency of estimation is a measure of the noisiness of a network metric, given a set of resting-state scan protocols and source reconstruction methods. Indeed, the sensitivity of inference on the mean effect, by the reduction of noisy sources of variability, can be a good surrogate test in the absence of a known ground truth, even in the presence of smaller (and potentially informative) sources of variation in the network matrices (Smith et al., 2005). Knowledge of estimation consistency is also clinically relevant, as a key requirement in the development of normative population distributions. An understanding of the run-to-run variability of network estimation is a crucial first step when moving onward from group comparison studies to the classification or characterisation of new subjects. In this article, we compare the consistency and reproducibility of whole-brain network estimation between 39 functionally-defined cortical ROIs both at the group-level, and within and between individual subjects for 12 commonly-employed network estimation metrics. We include in our analysis connectivity measures which are susceptible to spatial leakage confounds, not because they are necessarily to be recommended but because they are still used in the field. We will explore the extent to which the false connectivity induced by these confounds can artificially increase the consistency of network estimation. We concentrate on stationary connectivity, rather than characterising the evolution of networks over time in each subject. We perform our analysis on the resting-state MEG data provided by the Human Connectome Project (HCP), for a number of reasons. The data are freely available, have passed through a stringent pre-processing pipeline, include a large number of young, healthy subjects (61 with resting scans in the MEG2 release), and include three repeated sessions of resting-state recording for each participant. As an alternative to the range of methods for connectivity estimation that are robust to spatial leakage artefacts, there are some source reconstruction approaches that are designed to minimise the cross-talk between specific cortical locations (for example, Hui et al. (2010), Hauk and Stenroos (2014), Dalal et al. (2006)). These methods require the multi-source reconstruction to have fewer dipoles than the rank of the sensor data: each ROI would have to be described by a single principle component of its lead fields or a representative voxel. The relative benefits of performing the dimensionality reduction down to the number of ROIs either before or after the source reconstruction (as we do in this paper) remain to be explored.

"Everythin's on faar," he echoes, eyes wide, brimming with the innocence of youth. The man chuckles, shaking his head slightly at such a statement, as if it were an inevitable conclusion drawn from the sublime palette painted by the setting sun. Yet, the warmth of the day lingers, refusing to let go, wrapping them in a contentment that belies the fading light. As they walk back, the rhythm of their footsteps synchronizes with the soft lapping of waves, a mantra against the encroaching dusk. Each step draws Matt further from the clamoring realities of life, enveloping him instead in a cocoon of vivid memories woven with threads of laughter and love. The evening air cools, a gentle whisper against their sun-warmed skin, the salt tang invigorating, reminding him of countless sandy afternoons spent exploring the vastness of their shared coast. "How 'bout that last one, eh? Woulda made a fine meal," his father remarks, lifting the salmon slightly, its scales glistening under the waning light. "What a fight that one put up! Reminded me of your Aunt Matilda when she gets a bee in her bonnet." He laughs heartily, a sound that bounces across the flats and mingles with the evening tide, a sound that Matt would clutch to his heart for years to come. "Yeah! Or like when you tried to persuade her not to bake fruitcake ever again!" Matt replies, half in jest, as they resume their walk, the golden hues of twilight spilling into shadows. It is the banter of the familiar, a rhythmic exchange as beautiful as the landscape before them. Such was their life, woven with the fabric of laughter, each stitch marking a fulfilled moment, yet all too ephemeral under the relentless grip of time. But as the sun dips lower, drawing a blush over the horizon, an uneasy knot forms in the pit of Matt's stomach. He becomes acutely aware of his father's advancing years, of the slight tremor in the man's grip as he repositions the weight of their shared burden. An uninvited chill dances through him, a whisper of thoughts unprocessed in the heat of the day. His father had grown older despite seeming eternal, forged from the very elements of their home - a being molded by salt and sun. "Why don't we catch one more before we head in?" Matt suggests, too quickly, almost desperately. The glimmer in his father's eye lights, as if the proposition rekindles that spark of vitality suspended between them. "Alright then, one more it is! But let's make it a big'un!" With that, he kneels and thrusts the pitchfork once more into the frothy edges of the water again, a whirlwind of anticipation swirling between them, the fleeting warmth of dusk lingering on their skin. The boy watches his father move, his lithe frame bending and straightening with the grace of an ancient ritual steeped in tradition, immortal yet ever-vanishing. In that moment, as they embark upon this final chase for the day, time seems suspended, like the shimmering air before a summer storm. Each spear cast feels like a testament to not only their shared existence but a plea against the inevitability of the rootless tide of loss approaching. The thrill of the hunt dances in the air, weaving through the rising dusk, yet a premonition shadows Matt's heart-a quiet foreshadowing, fragile yet stark. For this day, too, would soon be like the salmon they chased; it would slip through his fingers, echoing the ever-fleeting moments of a childhood recently cherished.

The vessel was a ghostly silhouette against the pale morning light, hovering on the horizon as though suspended between worlds. The sea around it yawned vast, indifferent. A foreboding calm had settled over the water, the air heavy with untapped tension. "Is it drifting?" Dodge asked, squinting through binoculars, the lenses fogging with each exhale. Salt encrusted on the edges where sea spray had dried. "Or just holding station?" Greer shrugged, a gesture hidden beneath layers of worn wool and weathered oilskins. "Hard to say. Looks dead in the water to me. Unless they've cut engines for some reason. But no radio contact... that's odd." Murphy joined them on the bridge, the door clanking shut behind him. He poured himself a cup of bitter coffee from a dented thermos, the aroma mingling with the tang of salt air. "It's strange, alright. Keep trying. Maybe they've got receiver trouble." They watched in silence, the radios crackling intermittently with static. The ocean stretched out, vast and unfathomable, consuming the horizon. As the sun rose higher, its rays splintering into the sea, light shimmered off the water, turning each ripple into a sparkling jewel. Back below decks, Epps sat with Maureen-Candy-listening in the static-filled silence as the ship creaked and groaned on its haunches. Darlene's words echoed in Epps' mind, as relentless as the swelling tide. It was over. It had to be. Yet Epps couldn't shake the feeling of unfinished business, like a chapter left hanging, a pen poised above paper waiting for the final jot. "Why do you think it stopped?" Maureen broke the reverie, her voice a calm counterpoint to Epps' pensive state. Epps shrugged, dragging fingers through disheveled hair. "Engines could be out. Maybe they're waiting on parts. Or they've got communications down." "Or they're in trouble." "Could be." Maureen's eyes flicked to the small porthole, where the endless sea seemed to press against the glass. "Do you think we'll go over?" "Murphy will decide. Greer's keeping a close watch. If they need help, we'll go." In the mess hall, the clink of cutlery and low murmur of conversation carried the mundane rhythm of ship life. Men huddled over their meals, trading stories, gripes, and laughter-a stark contrast to the ship's solitude above. Yet, through it all, the mystery of the vessel tugged at their collective attention. Was it a merchant ship caught unawares, a lost wanderer awaiting rescue? Or was it something else, a specter of hidden agendas, poised silently on the rim of their consciousness? Murphy's voice crackled over the intercom, cutting through the muted drone. "All hands, prepare for approach." The crew stirred, a ripple of anticipation and apprehension passing through them like an undercurrent. Even the most seasoned among them felt it-the pull of an unknown variable, an unsettled question about to be answered. Back on the bridge, as the ship angled towards the distant vessel, Dodge glanced around at his shipmates, feeling the quiet camaraderie of shared purpose settling over them. Whatever lay ahead, it would be faced together, the wheel steady in their grip, the path ahead beckoning with indistinct promise.

I think I may be excused my temporary forgetfulness of the moan which had brought me to Forbes' death chamber. Uppermost in my mind was the manner in which I had been brought here. For it was he, approaching me through the medium of letters and messengers, who had begged, implored me to help him against Orcon, the eccentric planet of my own discovery, the planet which belonged to a solar system at the other end of the Universe from ours. Because of my knowledge of Orcon, with its bubbling seas, its brooding nightmares, and lastly, its queer conduct toward Earth, he had wanted to take me away from my telescopes to fight. And I had refused. Now I understood how I came to be here. I knew that this dead man had kidnapped me after drugging me with one of the new amnesiacs. Yorildiside, I reckoned it. And just because I knew that Admiral Forbes had seized me by force, I knew almost to a certainty that I was shipwrecked on that very Orcon which I had discovered two years before. I was enraged at this high-handed treatment. For if danger was indeed threatening Earth from Orcon, my place of all places was at my telescopes. I could do with them, for the civilizations about me, what no one else could. Too, I was actuated by selfish motives. I loved my telescopes and my isodermic super-spectroscopes. And there was still much work I had to do! Already I had discovered three new elements, and that had showed me I was but at the beginning of a knowledge of cosmological chemistry. Forbes! He had brought me by force out here on this beastly little planet whose orbit was like that of a snake with the Saint Vitus' dance! He had taken me to this wretched planet which lay at such a remote end of the Universe that not even explorers had been tempted to visit it! "Oh, damn the whole business!" I groaned aloud. I was thoroughly angry and bitter. In a little while I experienced a sudden change of mood. I'd no sooner spoken than a moan came from directly behind me, and I remembered why I'd got going in the beginning, and was ashamed. I entered a small compartment which opened from Forbes' cabin, and discovered immediately three more people. The strides I had taken made me realize that I had to be careful, for I was indeed endowed with a terrific strength - an extraordinary strength and lightness. One of these three new people was obviously dead, for his neck was broken. The other two still breathed. The first of the two was a short man, a Japanese by the look of him. His arm was broken. The other person was, to my surprise, a woman. She, like the dead Forbes, wore the insignia of the U. S. W. Upper Zone Patrol. Her insignia was that of a navigating officer.

I've done pretty well, myself, since we last met. The mines paid, and now I'm the owner of a chain of newspapers in New York, and I'm trying to get a syndicate together to buy this paper, the Daily Press." "You're talking of buying the Daily Press?" I asked incredulously. "Why, isn't it the richest newspaper in England?" "Not any longer. Its circulation has dropped off during the last six months, and its stock has fallen accordingly. There's an opportunity for some big money-making in taking it over." I looked at him rather queerly. In a few sentences he had spoken a truth which had flashed upon me only a few moments before, and which I had never dreamed would dawn so soon. All the evening I had been thinking over the news of the day, and wondering how long the great boom in journalism would continue. I knew that the Press Syndicate had made a fortune within the past year; I knew also that there were several other syndicates ready to go into the field if the right chance offered. And now here was Farnham telling me that such a chance had arisen. I began to wonder whether he had some ulterior motive in thus opening up to me a subject which he might well suppose would interest me. After all, I was not likely to start a syndicate of my own, nor even to join in one already formed. And yet I had heard rumours of Farnham's generosity. At any rate, it seemed wise to play my part, and make believe that I was deeply interested in the scheme he proposed. So I said: "Wouldn't it cost a lot of money to take over such a concern as the Daily Press?" "It would," answered Farnham frankly. "But I'm not going to buy it myself. I want to put a syndicate together, and I came to London hoping to find some partners. Now that I've found you, I'll tell you the whole story, and you can advise me." He took my arm and led me towards the door of the theatre. We stood there for a while talking, and I learned that Farnham had arrived in town only that afternoon, and that he had gone straight to the office of the Press Syndicate in Fleet Street, and had there obtained the information which had set him thinking. Then we walked slowly across Trafalgar Square, and I listened patiently while Farnham told me the result of his inquiries. It appeared that the Daily Press had been founded by a Mr. William Langton, who had started it with a capital of 20,000. This sum had been increased by loans from various banks, and the profits of the business had kept pace with the development of the enterprise. Within the last twelve months the daily issue had been raised from 150,000 copies to 300,000, and the weekly sale of the Sunday edition had reached nearly half-a-million. To-day the circulation was falling off rapidly, and the directors of the company, alarmed at the situation, were willing to sell their shares at a nominal figure. They would let them go for less than they had cost. Farnham paused to light a cigarette. "So you see," he continued, "there's a fine chance for someone with plenty of money to pick up the property cheap and run it for himself. If I could find a couple of Englishmen who would go in with me, I think we could get hold of the property for nothing, and then turn it round and make a lot of money out of it. Do you think there's much chance of getting a syndicate together?"

Besides good potential yields, traits of particular importance include storability, sweet and dry taste, early maturity, drought tolerance and high beta-carotene content (Laurie et al., 2004). The actual yields of sweet potato in Southern Africa are estimated to be as low as 3 t fresh root ha-1 in the period 2010-2014 (FAO, 2017) compared with attainable yields of 27 t ha-1 reported in Mozambique (Andrade et al., 2016) and 35 t ha-1 in Malawi (Chipungu, 2015). This shows that despite breeding efforts, smallholder farmers are often unable to benefit from yield gains from genetic improvement (Tittonell and Giller, 2013) due to other yield reducing factors. Despite the relative drought tolerance of sweet potato compared to cereal crops (Motsa et al., 2015), water limitations greatly affect crop development. Root formation on freshly planted cuttings is optimal at a soil water content of 80% of field capacity, though even at 40% of field capacity considerable root formation still occurs (Belehu, 2003). Crop water use of sweet potato under full irrigation in Mozambique was 800 mm with root yields of 33 t ha-1 compared to 360 mm and 15 t ha-1 in the same site under rain fed production (Gomes and Carr, 2001, 2003). Other studies confirmed that irrigation can enhance yields (Ghuman and Lal, 1983) and total nitrogen concentration, but can reduce dry matter concentration in the roots (Ekanayake and Collins, 2004). Despite common low-input cultivation practices, sweet potato shows a large yield response to nutrient input application via fertilizer and manure (Agbede, 2010). Potassium enhances root yields and quality by increasing the root: top ratio, dry matter concentration and beta-carotene and anthocyanin contents (George et al., 2002). Phosphorus and nitrogen application also enhance yields (Dumbuya et al., 2016) (Ankumah et al., 2003). Tillage benefits root yield by reducing the bulk density of the soil (Agbede, 2010), while production on ridges may result in better yields than production on mounds (Dumbuya et al., 2016). The most serious sweet potato disease in Africa is the sweet potato virus disease (SPVD) which is caused by combined infection with sweet potato chlorotic stunt virus by whiteflies and sweet potato feathery mottle virus by aphids (Karyeija et al., 1998; Gibson et al., 2004). Sweet potato weevil (C. formicarius complex) is worldwide considered the biggest pest attacking both cultivated and stored sweet potatoes (Chalfant et al., 1990; Allemann et al., 2004). Severity of weevil infestation depends on variety (Stathers et al., 2003b) and increases with delaying the harvest of mature roots (Smit, 1997). Both SPVD and weevils can infect new fields via planting material. Timely access by farmers to sufficient quantities of clean planting material is a challenge in areas with a long dry season due to limited knowledge of technologies to conserve vines (Okello et al., 2015). A final challenge affecting smallholder sweet potato producers is poor storability of roots compared to grain crops (Abidin et al., 2016).

We get over to where landowner Ed, insists he saw the skulls. We look around on the ground, nothing around, no fragments, no skulls. Dr. Hall asks, "Where are they.. the skulls?" "Well," says Ed, "they got covered back up as I was plowing. You know," as if we'd been farmers all our lives, "They just turned over with the soil, they can't be too deep under." Ah! We will have to dig a bit. So Dr. Hall goes back to his car and gets some shovels and a screen and in the mean time he sends us out to mark all the artifacts we can find on the surface of the field around the area. There was absolutely nothing, amazingly nothing, it would be hard to imagine such a lack of material remains. Dr. Hall returns, hands out shovels, arranges us students ever so many meters apart and says to us to "dig a 50 cm square pit, I'll tell you when to quit." I dig and he says to quit at a clay level, about 2 feet deep, with nothing in it. I start digging a new hole...and another hole...so all us students are are digging, Dr. Hall is digging, we dig ten...fifteen.. thirty pits, all in this one area where Ed is dead certain he saw the skulls. Dr. Hall mutters under his breath about some psychological study of how easily people are mistaken by what they remember and yet are sure they remember exactly what they claim. I'm thinking, great, we're digging in the wrong place. We dig for about two hours and we're tired and blisters are appearing on our hands then one of the grad students has a "good" idea to use pokey sticks- a long rod with which to find pots-an old looters trick. Ed says, "I have some iron rebar rods that'll do the trick". Dr Hall replied, "we'd sure appreciate using them." I'm thinking Dr Hall ought to speak for himself and where the hell is the water and why does the sun have to shine so bright? So Ed brings us a bunch of rods and we poke around in that farmers field for a couple more damn hours and my muscles are hurting, and my hand are blistering in new and improved places, and we are not finding jack and we ought to have a long time ago if anything were there and then I notice ole' Ed, who had finally started helping us an hour before, starts moving down the field about 30 or more yards and starts poking around. Hmmmmm, I think, not so sure about where he saw those skulls anymore. I glance at Dr. Hall, he's gives me a "we're in hell and we can't get up" look. More poking, poking, poking, praying, praying, praying.

The trolley jolted slightly as it rounded a bend, sending Dicky into a fit of giggles, while Helen playfully rolled her eyes at her younger brother's antics. As they progressed along the winding Portage Street, an air of excitement enveloped the family, suffused by the fresh scent of blooming wildflowers that lined the route. Grandfather Emerson, seated beside Grandmother, regaled them with delightful tales of days gone by, recounting the adventure-laden history of the region. "Did you know, my dears," he began, his voice rich with nostalgia, "that this very stretch of road once teemed with the activity of harnessing the immense natural resources around us? The early settlers toiled and prospered here, forging a new life on these picturesque banks." "Oh, tell us more, Grandfather!" chimed Ethel, her eyes widening with curiosity. She adjusted her hat, a gesture that signified seriousness in her youthful mind. "What did they build? Did they have families?" "Indeed they did, my little bloom," Grandfather replied, casting a fond glance at her. "They built cabins from the very timber that once towered above and harvested crops that thrived due to the rich soil. It was a community, interwoven by struggles and triumphs, as much like our own, merely a different decade-if not a different century!" Mrs. Morton glanced at her children, pleased to see them so engaged. "You see, my loves, history does not simply exist in dusty books. It breathes and walks, just as we do. This trolley is our conveyance into those very stories, bringing the past alive for each of us." The branches overhead swayed gently, casting playful shadows that danced across their faces. Roger, gathering his thoughts, mused over the significance of their journey. It was not just a trip to Chautauqua but a family pilgrimage to remember and cherish the roots that anchored their lineage. Just as they were embarking on their summer excursions, generations before them had trekked the same paths, perhaps filled with similar hopes and dreams. As the trolley approached a particular spot where the trees parted revealing a glimmering lake, a collective exclamation filled the air from the party. "Look, the water! It's beautiful!" cried Helen, her excitement palpable. Dicky pressed his little nose against the glass, absolutely entranced. "Ah, that's Chautauqua Lake!" Grandfather declared with a flourish. "A splendid body of water, teeming with both life and vision. Artists have flocked to its shores for generations, attempting to capture the sheer beauty of this view." "Will we go swimming?" Dicky piped up, bouncing slightly in his seat. Mrs. Morton chuckled softly. "Yes, my dear, we shall. But first, we have to settle in our lodgings. Perhaps after dinner, we can dip our toes in the cool water, or swim, depending on how the day unfolds." "What will we do when we get there?" Ethel asked keenly, shifting her attention. "Oh, there are splendid concerts and lectures planned, art displays galore, and even games to delight the youth," Mrs. Morton responded, her spirit lifting at the thought. "It will be a glorious blend of education and merriment." As the trolley ambled onward, the remaining miles melted away with the excitement of stories shared and laughter echoed, a family adventure steeped in the intoxication of summer's promise.

In his little God-forsaken corner of Acadia the variously-proportioned mixture of English and American which, with local variations of Lowland and Highland Scotch, North of Ireland brogue and French patois, loosely constitutes a Nova-Scotian idiom, is further tinged with the specific peculiarities that spring from illiteracy and rusticity. David Strang smiles. "Why, you are like brother Matt," he says, in amused astonishment. All day his son's prattle has amused the stranger, but this is a revelation. "Like your wicked brother Matt?" queries the boy in amaze. David's smile gleams droller. "Avast there, you mustn't hearken to the mother. She knows naught o' Matt 'cept what I told her. She is Halifax bred, and we lived 'way up country. I ran away to sea, and left him anchored on dad's farm. When I made port again dad was gone to glory, and Matt to England with a petticoat in tow." "But mother said he sold the farm, an' your share, too." "And if he didn't it's a pity. He had improved the land, hadn't he? and I might have been sarved up at fish dinners for all he knew. I don't hold with this Frenchy law that says all the bairns must share and share alike. The good old Scotch fashion is good 'nough for me - Matt's the heir, and God bless him." "Then why didn't you marry a Scotchwoman?" asked Matt, with childish irrelevance. "'Twas your mother's fault," answers David, with a half-whimsical, half-pathetic expression. "And why didn't you take her to sea with you?" "Nay, nay; the mother has no stomach for it, nor I either. And then there was Harriet - a little body in long clothes. And the land was pretty nigh cleared," he adds, with a suspicion of apology in his accent, "and we couldn't grow 'nough to pay the mortgage if I hadn't shipped again." "And why am I like uncle?" "Oh, he used to be allus lookin' at the sky - not to find out whether to git the hay in, mind you, but to make little picturs on the sly in the hay-mow on Sundays, and at last he sold the farm and went to London to make 'em." Matt's heart begins to throb - a strange new sense of kinship stirs within him. "Hev you got any of them thar picturs?" he inquires, eagerly. "Not one," says David, shaking his head contemptuously. "His clouds were all right, because clouds may be anything; but when he came to cows, their own dams wouldn't know 'em; and as for his ships - why, he used to hoist every inch o' canvas in a hur'cane. I wouldn't trust him to tattoo a galley-boy.

That made sense. We had been fighting Calypsus together, when - what? But I had no time to think about that now. My flashlight showed me a dimly glowing dial-board in front of me. A red light flashed there. At once I understood. This ship was a space-cruiser! And she was wrecked! I ran forward along the sloping deck, toward the bow. In the darkness, I tripped over something soft. Again I heard the moaning, and I flashed my light upon the thing. It was a woman, her hair streaming down across her shoulders like a silver veil. She looked very beautiful, even in death, but she was quite dead. I turned away from her quickly. On my left was a wide opening, through which I could see into another compartment. I shone my light about this place, and discovered that it was a sort of galley, with shelves full of food. On the shelves were bottles, some of them empty, others filled with an amber liquid. I took one of these bottles and drank deeply from it. It tasted like Scotch whiskey. I did not know whether it was or not, but it helped to steady my nerves. And I needed steadying badly. What had happened here? Where were we? Why were we alive? Was it possible that we had been blown off course, and had landed on some unknown world? Or had we been captured by Calypsus? I looked at the bottle I held in my hand. It was marked "Scotch Whiskey." And I remembered reading somewhere that Scotch whiskey is distilled from malted barley. Malted barley would grow only on Earth. So where were we? As I stood there, trying to make up my mind, I heard the moaning again. I went back into the control room, and followed the sound to its source. There, on the floor, lay another woman. She was young, and pretty, and she was calling my name. I bent over her. Her eyes were closed, and she seemed unconscious. I picked her up gently, and carried her into the galley. There I laid her down on a bunk, and ran my fingers lightly across her forehead. It was cool. I put the bottle of whiskey down beside her, and then I returned to the control room. I was more puzzled than ever. There must be some way to find out what had happened here. I went back to the dead woman's body, and searched her pockets. I found nothing useful. Then I tried the other bodies. One of the strange men had a wallet. I opened it, and found that it contained money, and also a card identifying him as a member of the crew of the cruiser Valiant. He was named James R. Dorsey. The other stranger was a member of the crew of the cruiser Constitution, whose captain was Admiral Forbes. His name was Richard L. Beldon. I was beginning to get some idea of what might have happened. But why were we alive, while all the rest of the crew were dead? Suddenly, from the galley, came a muffled cry. I ran to the doorway, and there, sitting up on the bunk, was the girl. I hurried to her side. "Are you all right?" I asked anxiously. "I'm fine," she said. "Just a little dizzy. I've been asleep for hours." "You're lucky!" I exclaimed. "All the rest of the crew are dead. They must have been killed when the ship crashed." "But the crash?" she asked. "Where are we?"

The vitriol is not limited to the airwaves. At a recent Democratic fundraiser in Los Angeles, a prominent Hollywood actor was overheard referring to President Bush as a "war criminal" who should be "tried at The Hague." When asked about the comment, the actor's publicist claimed it was just a "joke." But the joke was on the Democrats. Such rhetoric may energize the party's base, but it alienates the very swing voters who will decide the election. Meanwhile, the Kerry campaign is struggling to find a message that resonates beyond the party faithful. Last week, the senator's aides were touting a new slogan, "Let America Be America Again," which sounds like a faint echo of Reagan's "Morning in America." But the message is still muddled, and the messenger still comes across as dour and pessimistic. It's not just the tone that's the problem; it's the substance. The Democrats' obsession with Bush-bashing has led them to neglect the issues that really matter to voters. Health care, education, and the economy are all taking a backseat to the party's fixation on Iraq and the president's alleged misdeeds. Even some of the party's most loyal supporters are starting to get restless. Last week, a group of prominent Democrats, including former Senator Sam Nunn and former Representative Lee Hamilton, issued a statement calling for a more constructive approach to the campaign. "We need to focus on the future, not the past," they said. "We need to offer solutions, not just criticisms." It's a message that's starting to resonate within the party. At a recent meeting of the Democratic National Committee, several members urged the party to adopt a more positive tone and focus on the issues that really matter to voters. "We can't just be against Bush," said one committee member. "We need to be for something." But old habits die hard. At the same meeting, another committee member was overheard muttering about "Bush's lies" and "his corrupt administration." It's a refrain that's become all too familiar in Democratic circles. As the campaign enters its final stretch, the Democrats face a stark choice. They can continue to indulge in the politics of hate and anger, or they can try to find a more positive, inclusive message that resonates with the American people. The fate of the party, and the country, may depend on it.

The air was thick with tension, the only sound being the soft creaking of the wooden floorboards beneath Stiffy's feet as he approached the Shogun. The nekomata's eyes never left the Shogun's face, his gaze piercing through the dim light like a cold, calculating blade. "So... you've come seeking my life," the Shogun repeated, his voice unwavering, his eyes fixed on Stiffy's face. "For what purpose?" The question hung in the air like a challenge, a gauntlet thrown down. Stiffy's response was slow in coming, his mind working overtime to decide whether to reveal his true intentions or keep them hidden. The Shogun's words were a clever ploy, designed to unsettle his opponent and gain an advantage. But Stiffy was no ordinary opponent. He was a demon, a creature of the night, with secrets and motivations that would make the Shogun's head spin. "I've come for the Scroll," Stiffy said finally, his voice low and even. "The one you possess. The one that holds the key to unlocking the secrets of the ancient ones." The Shogun's expression didn't change, but a flicker of surprise danced in his eyes. "You know of the Scroll?" he asked, his voice laced with curiosity. Stiffy nodded, his eyes never leaving the Shogun's face. "I know of its existence. And I know it's here. In this very castle." The Shogun's gaze narrowed, his hand instinctively reaching for the hilt of his katana. "You're not the first to seek it," he said, his voice dripping with venom. "But you're the first to make it this far. I suppose you think you're clever, don't you?" Stiffy's smile was a cold, calculated thing. "I'm not here to play games, Shogun," he said. "I'm here to get what I came for. And if you're in my way, then so be it." The Shogun's eyes flashed with anger, his face reddening with rage. "You dare to threaten me?" he spat, his voice rising. "I am the Shogun of Eyoto! I will not be threatened by a demon like you!" Stiffy's laughter was like a cold breeze on a winter's night. "You're no match for me, Shogun," he said. "But I'll give you credit. You're a worthy opponent. And I'll make sure you die with honor." The Shogun's face twisted with rage, his hand tightening around the hilt of his katana. "You'll never leave this room alive," he snarled, his eyes blazing with fury. And with that, the battle began. The sound of clashing steel echoed through the chambers, the air thick with the scent of blood and sweat. The Shogun and Stiffy clashed, their blades meeting in a flurry of steel and sparks. The outcome was far from certain, but one thing was clear: only one of them would walk out of the room alive.

On the contrary, she haunted my dreams even here in Germany; and when I woke up in the morning I found her still haunting my waking thoughts. It seemed to me that I could never be happy again until I saw her once more, and learnt whether the love she bore me had died out or not. I therefore decided to accept George's invitation. His letter had gone on to tell me that he expected to be stationed near London over the Christmas holidays, and would call on me at the hotel where I was staying, bringing Daphne with him, in order that we might have one parting interview before she became the wife of another man. To this proposal I consented, and awaited eagerly the arrival of the appointed hour. In due time came the day, and shortly afterwards the bell rang, and George entered the room. He was followed by a lady whom I took to be Daphne, but who turned out to be a friend of hers, whose name I have forgotten. The latter remained with us for some time, and then took her departure, leaving me alone with my brother. CHAPTER II. THE PARTING. "Well, Frank," said George, "and what do you think of your sister-in-law-to-be?" "I think her charming," I replied, looking down at my boots, "but I should like to know if she thinks me so also." "Ah!" exclaimed George, with a laugh. "You're afraid of the answer, eh? Well, I'll put you out of your pain. She likes you immensely. There's nothing between you now, you know." "Nothing?" I repeated, with a gasp. "Not the slightest thing." "Then why didn't you let me know sooner?" "Because I didn't know myself till yesterday. I fancied that she cared for me, but now I'm sure of it. She has confessed everything." "And you don't care about her any longer?" "No, indeed. I've quite got over that foolishness." "Quite?" "Yes. It was all moonshine." "But she loves you!" "She does, I admit, but she knows that I love somebody else, and that my affections are engaged elsewhere." "My dear fellow, you are mad. Who is this person? Do you mean to tell me that you prefer her to Daphne?" "I do." "Impossible!" "I assure you that it is true. I have met her in Paris, and fallen desperately in love with her. She is an actress, a dancer, and her name is Lina." "Lina!" I cried, springing to my feet. "Lina Zerbinetti!" "Exactly. What is wrong with the name?" "Everything. That woman is infamous. She is a monster of vice and depravity. I knew her mother, who was also an actress, and she was a disgrace to the profession. I can't understand how you should ever fall in love with such a creature." "That is just what I cannot understand either. But it doesn't alter the fact that I am in love with her. I intend to marry her, and I shall ask Daphne to release me from my promise to-day." "George," I said, drawing my chair closer to his, and speaking in a whisper, "you must not do anything rash. This woman is a demon. She will ruin you. She will drag you into the gutter, and make you as infamous as herself. Believe me, I speak from experience. When you were eighteen she used to go to your rooms in Oxford Street, and I used to meet her there.

The chateau in which I dwelt had belonged for ages to my ancestors, and the little room in one of the turrets which was assigned to me, looked towards the setting sun over manifold beautiful green slopes and wooded banks, with now and then a broken, cliffy bit of yellow ground, that harmonized beautifully and richly with the warm tints of the spring and the autumn, and broke not less pleasantly the thick green of the mid year. Upon those banks, and trees, and slopes, the sunshine seemed to dwell with peculiar fondness; and thither came the bright and smiling showers of spring, and the rich, vision-like lights and shades of autumn. Gay hawking parties, and many a splendid cavalcade from the rich and important town in the neighbourhood, diversified the scenery during the bright part of the year, and towards the winter-time the beasts of the forest and the field used to resume their dwelling in the neighbouring woods, and afford sport and diversion to the inhabitants of the castle. As I have said, that chateau had been for centuries the dwelling-place of my ancestors, ever since, indeed, the arm of Du Guesclin and the wisdom of Charles had expelled the English from the shores of France; but still that chateau was not mine, nor ever likely to be mine; for I was at that time a poor dependant upon the bounty of others, without wealth, rank, station, or fortune of any kind to give hope to my heart or energy to my effort. The lord of that castle, my poor father's first cousin, had taken me out of compassion to his relation, a poor soldier of fortune, who married thoughtlessly and died young; and as he himself, a lover of pleasure - even of license, at the time he took me into his house, thought only of marriage as a remote evil, he treated me at first with so much kindness, that the foolish persons who surrounded us imagined that a time might come when I should be his heir. Nothing, indeed, was farther from his thoughts. He had always determined, and still held the resolution of wedding ultimately, in the hope of seeing his possessions descend to children of his own. The accomplishment of this purpose was hastened by accidental circumstances, which placed it in his power to marry a beautiful and wealthy bride, whom he brought home to the chateau in great pomp, and the festivities which followed her arrival are among the first events which I distinctly remember. Surrounded by friends, and with scarcely a wish ungratified, he might well consider himself a rich and happy man in the possession of one so fair as she was. But beauty was not the only quality which she brought to make him happy, nor riches the only dowry that was settled upon her head.

However, although terms such as friability or flowability can be expressed as a single value, particle size distribution is frequently expressed as a curve, which does not allow its direct examination as a quality attribute or a process control variable. A quality attribute should be within an appropriate limit, range, or distribution to ensure the desired product quality (ICH Q8 (R2), 2009). The separation of a particulate sample into discrete size classes has been traditionally performed representing the type of quantity in the abscissa and the measure of the quantity in the ordinate. The measurement of the quantity is made through the relative amount of particles measured within a specific size interval and it is called density distribution (qx). This term is the first derivative of the cumulative distribution (Qx) against particle size (Leschonski, 1984). The subscript x represents the type of quantity where the possible types are number, length, area, volume or mass. In pharmaceutical sciences, the type of quantity chosen is frequently the volume, due to the importance of the relationship between drug delivery and volume (Mullertz et al., 2016). Frequently, the volume particle size distributions are characterised by d10,d50 and d90 which are calculated through the intercepts for 10, 50 and 90% of the cumulative volume (ISO, 2014). These terms can be gathered if they are transformed to the span ((d90-d10)/d50) (Chitu et al., 2011; El Hagrasy et al., 2013), with particle size distributions considered more homogeneous the closer this value is to zero. This analysis is only acceptable when the particle size distribution is lognormal, but will introduce a considerable error when the distributions show more than one peak and the peaks are located around the mean diameter. For instance, Fig. 1 shows two particle size distributions which have two different shapes but very close span values. The first shape (Fig. 1a) could be considered to be a common lognormal distribution where all the values are around the main peak. However, the second shape (Fig. 1b) displays three peaks of different population densities which indicates that three main types of granules exist in the sample. Nevertheless, the difference between spans of those distributions is less than 2%, and therefore both distributions would be comparable in terms of homogeneity even if they are clearly different in the number of peaks. This technique for transforming curves into mathematical expressions can be used as an effective way to smooth distribution curves due to the variation of the slope depending on the number of peaks. For example, three different particle size distributions have been transformed through this method in Fig. 2 representing the weight against the logarithm of the particle size. The first PSD (Fig. 2a) can be considered as a mono-modal distribution and its equivalent weight distribution is a straight line which slopes up at the greatest rate.

We developed a model framework based on the natural history of tuberculosis infection and disease progression, accounting for the effects of demographic change, HIV coinfection, and drug resistance. We fitted our models to country-specific data on tuberculosis notifications, drug-susceptibility testing, and vital registration. This process allowed us to estimate key epidemiological parameters, such as the annual risk of tuberculosis infection, which are otherwise difficult to measure directly. Our results provide an assessment of the expected long-term impact of the current pace of improvement in tuberculosis control, and highlight where accelerated progress is needed to meet the End TB goals. Implications of all the available evidence Our findings emphasise the importance of focusing efforts on improving detection and treatment of tuberculosis cases. In all three settings we studied, achieving the 2035 End TB goals will require ambitious improvements in case finding and treatment success, whereas less emphasis might be placed on preventive therapy or active case-finding. In each setting, however, it appears that the current pace of improvement in case detection and treatment will not be sufficient to achieve the 2035 End TB goals, suggesting that a step-change in approach will be necessary. Although some of the specific quantitative projections presented here might vary if alternative assumptions were made, the broad conclusions are likely to hold true. The overall message is that there needs to be greater ambition and urgency in scaling up existing tools for tuberculosis control, and in investing in research to find new solutions.

With regard to the former, there is an increasing probability that knowledge that has once been an organization asset, i.e. something of value, has turned into something of reduced value or has become even worthless in the worst-case scenario (Tan et al., 2006). While addressing the latter, the increasing amount of available data needs to be analyzed, yet that cannot longer be done manually but requires systems that can handle a bulk of complex and different types of data (Gandomi and Haider, 2015). Therefore, it can be concluded that KM and its different elements are crucial for the sustainability of organizations. Business sustainability can be perceived as the fulfillment of the so-called "triple bottom line", i.e. social, environmental and financial outcomes (Gupta and Kumar, 2013) or people, planet and profit orientation (Dyllick and Muff, 2016). By integrating sustainability in their business processes, organizations may gain benefits, such as positive image, enhanced trust from stakeholders, more efficient resource management, or higher returns on investments and profitability (Horak et al., 2018). At the same time, as a study among corporate managers has shown, although 90% of the managers understand that having a sustainability strategy is important for the sake of their businesses, only 60% declare the implementation of any kind of sustainability strategy (Kiron et al., 2017). Integrating and managing sustainability in organizations is a balancing act between opportunities and risks (Krysiak, 2009). The organization may be exposed to reputational risk due to investments in projects with potentially damaging environmental consequences. For example, although countries like China or India have made great achievements with regard to their economic growth over the past years, their natural resources are heavily exploited and both countries have begun to suffer from significant environmental damage (Liao, 2018). In those countries which still have large numbers of poor population groups, it is more difficult for the governments to justify large investments in more sustainable-driven activities that may reduce the costs related to the economic growth. However, a lack of knowledge or its improper usage can bring various risks to sustainability in organizations. When an organization has only inadequate knowledge of sustainability, the opportunity of benefiting from the sustainability prospects decreases while, at the same time, the danger of making wrong decisions or no decisions at all increases. A lack of knowledge (e.g. resulting from the lack of KM in an organization) may also result in a failure to comply with specific product-related regulatory requirements (Yusup et al., 2015). The consequences of this situation are easy to imagine. The increasing use of ICTs for communicating with different stakeholder groups also opens the danger of cyberattacks (World Economic Forum, 2019), representing another incident which could put the organization's sustainability at stake. Taking into account the above-mentioned, the following research questions appear: 1) What is the potential effect of knowledge risks on various sustainability dimensions of organizations? and 2) How can organizations cope with knowledge risks to preserve their sustainability?

The surveillance data, encompassing a wide range of populations, consistently underscores the substantial impact of shigella and ETEC on public health, predominantly in regions where infrastructural challenges persist. Therefore, systematically evaluating and addressing these issues is fundamental to advancing global health initiatives. A pivotal aspect of mitigating diarrhoeal diseases is enhancing diagnostic capabilities, especially in LMICs, where laboratory facilities often lag behind technological advancements. The implementation of real-time PCR diagnostics represents a significant leap forward, delivering rapid and reliable identification of diarrhoeal pathogens. This level of precision is crucial for informing targeted interventions, guiding early treatment decisions, and refining public health policies aimed at reducing transmission. Moving forward, sustained efforts to democratize access to such diagnostic tools are essential. The complexity of ETEC and shigella infections is compounded by environmental and socioeconomic factors that perpetuate cycles of transmission and reinfection. Poor sanitation, contaminated water, and limited healthcare access are intertwined facets that elevate the risk of these infections. In communities where the infrastructure for clean water and sanitary facilities is inadequate, children bear the brunt of these infections. Addressing these challenges requires holistic strategies involving collaboration between governments, NGOs, and local communities to implement sustainable solutions. Vaccine development presents another promising avenue for disease control. Current research efforts are concentrated on creating effective vaccines against ETEC and shigella, which have the potential to drastically curtail morbidity and mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations. Advances in immunological research have paved the way for promising candidates that are progressing through clinical trials. However, overcoming the logistical hurdles of vaccine delivery in resource-limited settings remains a formidable task, demanding coordinated international efforts. Education campaigns focusing on hygiene practices are instrumental in reducing the incidence of diarrhoeal diseases. Empowering communities with knowledge about the transmission of ETEC and shigella, along with preventative measures such as handwashing and safe food preparation, can significantly diminish infection rates. These educational initiatives, when integrated with broader public health strategies, serve to lower the prevalence of these pathogens and improve community health outcomes. Evidently, the fight against shigella and ETEC-related diarrhoea is multifaceted, requiring a synergistic approach that encompasses improved diagnostics, vaccine development, educational outreach, and infrastructure enhancement. Strong global partnerships and commitment to research and intervention are vital in diminishing the burden of these infections. Progress in these areas holds immense potential to alleviate the overwhelming disease burden these pathogens impose, especially in settings where healthcare disparities are most pronounced. By prioritizing the eradication of these diseases, we can hope to see a substantial reduction in the global burden of diarrhoeal diseases, ultimately improving quality of life and health outcomes. It is imperative that stakeholders across various sectors unite to address and actively combat the pervasive challenges posed by the continued prevalence of shigella and ETEC. Only through concerted action can we advance towards overcoming these public health threats and achieving meaningful progress in the realm of global health.

In the present study, we aimed to investigate the alterations in functional connectivity patterns in schizophrenia using probabilistically-thresholded graphs constructed from resting-state fMRI data. We hypothesized that the application of wavelet-based methods would enable the identification of aberrant connectivity patterns in schizophrenia, which may not be captured by traditional thresholding approaches. To this end, we analyzed resting-state fMRI data from 30 patients with schizophrenia and 30 healthy participants, matched for age, sex, and handedness. The data were preprocessed using standard procedures, including motion correction, spatial smoothing, and temporal filtering. The wavelet-based methods were applied to the preprocessed data to construct probabilistically-thresholded graphs for each participant. We computed the correlation matrices between all pairs of regional neurophysiological signals, and then converted the correlation coefficients into P values using the wavelet-based approach. The resulting P values were then thresholded at a significance level of 0.05 to construct the probabilistically-thresholded graphs. We compared the graph-theoretical measures of topological organization, including global efficiency, clustering coefficient, and modularity, between the two groups. Additionally, we examined the distribution of edge weights and node degrees in the probabilistically-thresholded graphs to identify potential alterations in connectivity patterns. Our results showed that the probabilistically-thresholded graphs constructed using the wavelet-based approach revealed significant differences in functional connectivity patterns between patients with schizophrenia and healthy participants. Specifically, we found that patients with schizophrenia exhibited reduced global efficiency and clustering coefficient, indicating decreased network integration and segregation. Furthermore, the modularity of the probabilistically-thresholded graphs was significantly higher in patients with schizophrenia, suggesting the presence of aberrant connectivity patterns. In addition, we observed alterations in the distribution of edge weights and node degrees in the probabilistically-thresholded graphs. The edge weights were found to be more heterogeneous in patients with schizophrenia, indicating the presence of aberrant connectivity patterns. The node degrees were also found to be more variable in patients with schizophrenia, suggesting that certain brain regions may be more affected by the disorder. Our findings suggest that the application of wavelet-based methods to construct probabilistically-thresholded graphs can reveal novel insights into the alterations in functional connectivity patterns in schizophrenia. The probabilistic approach enables the identification of aberrant connectivity patterns that may not be captured by traditional thresholding approaches, and provides a more nuanced understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying the disorder. Future studies can build upon these findings to develop more targeted interventions aimed at restoring normal connectivity patterns in patients with schizophrenia.

In states where unemployment hovers in this range, there exists a complex interplay between economic hardship and political leanings that often yields surprising results. For instance, states like Michigan and Ohio, both of which have dealt with significant job losses in manufacturing industries, have shown varying degrees of support for the president. As the Democratic Party continues to emphasize its focus on rebuilding the middle class and revitalizing industries, many voters in these regions appear inclined to place their trust in the president's stewardship. A recent study highlighted that even amidst job losses, many residents feel a sense of connection and loyalty to a party that has historically championed their interests. On the other hand, Republicans, led by Romney's campaign, seem determined to capitalize on these states' struggles by framing the narrative as a straightforward indictment of the Obama administration. The rhetoric is often loaded with promises of tax cuts and deregulation, which Republicans argue will be the antidote to economic stagnation. However, analysis indicates that the resonance of these messages is contingent upon voters' lived experiences during the recession. For many, memories of the auto bailouts and the subsequent recovery of their local economies remain vivid. Thus, even frequent reminders of joblessness fail to sway those who feel that the president's actions saved them from a more dire fate. Interestingly, the economic landscape can also influence voter turnout, particularly in key swing states. In 2008, we witnessed an unprecedented mobilization of younger voters, minorities, and low-income communities-demographics that have been hit hardest by the ongoing job crisis. While general enthusiasm may have waned by 2012, the President's ability to mobilize these voters may still hinge on his sustained commitment to their issues, particularly in areas like education reform and health care. If they perceive that their interests align with Obama's agenda, they may be less likely to focus solely on the prevailing unemployment figures. Furthermore, the perception of economic changes is not solely dictated by empirical data; it is, in significant measure, a product of media narratives that shape public discourse. Particularly in battleground states, local news outlets play a crucial role in influencing how residents perceive unemployment. Negative coverage can breed despondency, while optimistic narratives surrounding community initiatives or job training programs can foster a sense of hope. Therefore, the responsibility of accurate reporting-and perhaps more importantly, framing-falls heavily on journalists and media organizations. As we delve deeper into the minutiae of demographics and economic performance, it becomes evident that the relationship between unemployment and voting behavior is not linear but rather reflective of deeper societal currents. Voters navigate political allegiances through the dual lenses of personal experiences and broader socio-political narratives, often leading to a tangled web of support that is as unpredictable as it is influential. This complexity serves as a reminder that elections are less about fixed ideologies and more about adaptive strategies that reflect the electorate's multifaceted identities. Ultimately, as the race inches closer to its climax, both campaigns must be attuned to these nuanced dynamics. It is not merely about the numbers on paper; it's about the stories those numbers tell and the visions they inspire in voters' minds. The art of persuasion in politics often hinges on the effective communication of hope amid uncertainty, and this election is no exception. The stakes, higher than ever, challenge both parties to present compelling narratives that resonate with the reality faced by millions. The outcomes of these efforts will likely determine who can secure the vital votes needed to emerge victorious in November, steering the political fate of the nation amid these uncertain economic tides.

These dimensions reveal how foundational early attachment experiences are in shaping an individual's capacity to navigate complex social landscapes and cope with life's myriad challenges. In exploring these domains, it becomes evident that secure attachment provides a robust framework for healthy interpersonal interactions. Those with secure attachment generally exhibit greater emotional intelligence, effectively communicating and setting boundaries while maintaining empathy and understanding towards others. Conversely, individuals with insecure attachment styles-whether anxious, avoidant, or fearful-often struggle to balance intimacy with autonomy, leading to cycles of relational strain and conflict. Anxiously attached individuals might prioritize closeness to such a degree that they compromise their personal boundaries and well-being, seeking constant reassurance and validation. This can result in exhausting dynamics for both parties involved, as the anxious individual grapples with persistent fears of rejection and abandonment. Avoidant individuals, on the other hand, emphasize self-sufficiency and autonomy to such an extent that they eschew vulnerability and emotional closeness. While this might afford them a semblance of control and invulnerability, it often translates into emotional isolation and unfulfilled relational needs. The dismissive detachment serves as a protective mechanism to prevent perceived threats of intimacy that might disrupt their cherished independence. Fearful-avoidant individuals embody a complex interplay of desiring closeness but simultaneously fearing it, resulting in a push-pull dynamic that confounds partners and friends alike. Their ambivalence often stems from deep-seated trust issues and unresolved past trauma, causing them to vacillate between seeking comfort and erecting barriers when approached. Notably, interventions aimed at fostering healthier attachment patterns emphasize self-awareness and emotional literacy. Therapeutic modalities like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and attachment-based therapy aim to help individuals recognize their attachment-related behaviors and reframe maladaptive patterns. By cultivating a secure inner attachment to oneself, individuals can transcend the limitations of their early attachment experiences and build more fulfilling and resilient relationships. Moreover, the intersection of neuroscience and attachment theory has unveiled the physiological underpinnings of attachment behaviors. Studies utilizing neuroimaging techniques have shown how secure attachments activate reward pathways in the brain, reinforcing positive relational experiences. Conversely, insecure attachments often correlate with heightened amygdala activity, which underscores the anxiety and hyper-vigilance commonly associated with these styles (Gillath et al., 2005). Understanding the neurological roots of attachment has profound implications for therapeutic practices, offering insights into how biological predispositions interact with environmental factors to shape attachment patterns. As the field continues to evolve, researchers are increasingly exploring how digital technology and social media impact attachment in contemporary society. The virtual realm presents unique challenges and opportunities, reshaping perceptions of intimacy, availability, and connection. How these technological interactions influence attachment remains a burgeoning area of inquiry, promising to expand our understanding of human relationships in the digital age. Thus, as the discourse around attachment broadens, it remains a vital lens through which we can appreciate the enduring influence of early interpersonal experiences on our lives.
