The intricate web of obligation and expectation that accompanied my birthright tightened around me, entwining with my every thought and action. Indeed, I felt myself caught in a snare more insidious than the treacle-laden trunks I had so readily set for the moths. Unlike the bats who fluttered through the gathering darkness, I could not simply seize my prize and settle into the savage thrill of the night. I had responsibilities that shackled me to the earth, obligations I could neither evade nor ignore. The landscape around me transformed somewhat in my reverie, shaping itself into a reflection of my inner turmoil. Each crooked tree branching upwards spoke to a tangled inheritance of my own heritage, while the soft footfalls of creatures hidden in the underbrush echoed my anxiety about life's next course. I had returned to a place where flickering memories danced like the fireflies conspiring in the shadows, each one suggesting a different version of who I might be-a dutiful son, an ambitious heir, or a solitary wanderer keen on disappearing into obscurity. Far before I had been thrust into this uncertain role, childhood weekends were spent beneath the whispers of these same trees, trailing behind my father as he imparted gentle lessons on nature's fleeting beauty. They had lessons on resilience and the relentless passage of time, but they were spirited whispers lost in the wind of adolescence. The sanctity of those moments, so easily overlooked, now seemed to weigh heavier than the looming responsibility of the estate I could not yet claim. As twilight deepened into night, the eerie quietude of the wood enveloped me. I began to perceive the world of the unseen, those creatures who lived in constant murk and shadow, and I wondered unattainably if they, too, had stories crafted in similar strains of turmoil. Was there a bat, perhaps, dreaming in echoes of delight, as I ruminated on the chains that bound me to my station? Or did the moths, lured into complacency by the sticky allure of my devotion, lament the futility of their plight like me? With renewed vigor, I began to channel my discontent into another endeavor, the allure of the night now invigorating rather than oppressive. Existence can be far kinder to those who engage with it earnestly. The insects, flitting about their trivial lives, still held beauty-their exquisite patterns and delicate bodies painted the air with purpose. I would strive to preserve them, to illuminate even the smallest corners of existence with understanding and appreciation. In that moment of reawakening, I lifted my brush once more, ready to give my capture a worthy name in the annals of entomology. But not merely for the sake of cataloguing; no, it was now a testament-a reminder that within the clutches of fate, there lay the strength to forge a new path. As I tarried among the trees, my heart ignited with a sense of belonging that transcended the narrow drudgery assigned to me by society. Thus, I embraced the night with renewed clarity. Each moth that came to rest upon my briary trap transformed slowly from mere samples into kindred spirits, aligning my own struggles with theirs, bridging the distance between solitude and community, weaving myself into the larger tapestry of existence-one brushstroke at a time.

As we delve deeper into the essence of Tibetan Buddhism, we find that the concept of the Four Noble Truths is intricately linked with the understanding of the nature of reality. The Buddha's teachings emphasize the importance of recognizing the true nature of suffering, its causes, and the path to its cessation. This profound understanding is not limited to intellectual comprehension, but rather it is a direct experience that arises from a deep examination of one's own mind and heart. The first noble truth, the truth of suffering, is not a pessimistic view of life, but rather a realistic acknowledgment of the inherent dissatisfaction and impermanence that pervades all phenomena. This suffering is not limited to physical pain or discomfort, but also includes the subtle forms of dissatisfaction and discontent that arise from our unfulfilled desires and expectations. The Buddha's teaching on suffering is not meant to discourage or depress, but rather to awaken us to the reality of our existence and to inspire us to seek a path to liberation. The second noble truth, the truth of the origin of suffering, reveals the root cause of our suffering to be our own ignorance and delusion. Our ignorance of the true nature of reality leads us to grasp and cling to things that are impermanent and ephemeral, resulting in suffering. This ignorance is not a lack of knowledge, but rather a fundamental misunderstanding of the way things truly are. The Buddha's teaching on the origin of suffering is not meant to blame or condemn, but rather to empower us to take responsibility for our own liberation. The third noble truth, the truth of the cessation of suffering, offers us a profound hope and promise of liberation. The Buddha's teaching on the cessation of suffering is not a mere intellectual concept, but rather a direct experience that arises from the practice of the path. The cessation of suffering is not a state of mere absence of pain or discomfort, but rather a state of profound peace and freedom that arises from the understanding of the true nature of reality. The fourth noble truth, the truth of the path to the cessation of suffering, is the most precious gift that the Buddha offers to humanity. This path is not a set of dogmatic beliefs or rituals, but rather a practical and systematic approach to the transformation of our minds and hearts. The path is not a means to an end, but rather an end in itself, for it is the very practice of the path that brings about the transformation and liberation. In Tibetan Buddhism, the practice of the path is often referred to as the "Three Higher Trainings": the training in higher ethics, the training in higher concentration, and the training in higher wisdom. These trainings are not separate entities, but rather interconnected aspects of the path that mutually support and reinforce each other. The training in higher ethics provides the foundation for the development of concentration, which in turn provides the basis for the development of wisdom. The training in higher concentration, or meditation, is a crucial aspect of the Tibetan Buddhist path. Through the practice of meditation, we develop the ability to focus our minds and to cultivate a sense of inner peace and clarity. This concentration is not a means to achieve a trance-like state, but rather a means to develop a deeper understanding of the true nature of reality. The training in higher wisdom, or prajna, is the culmination of the path. It is the direct understanding of the true nature of reality, free from all conceptualizations and dualisms. This wisdom is not a mere intellectual understanding, but rather a direct experience that arises from the practice of the path. It is the wisdom that liberates us from the cycle of suffering and rebirth, and brings us to the state of enlightenment.

It's been a week since President Barack Obama won re-election, but there are still plenty of Americans who haven't accepted the results. For those who believe Obama stole the election, there's a petition for secession filed in each state except Vermont, according to data from the White House website. The petitions ask the Obama administration to "peacefully grant" these states withdrawal from the United States of America in order to "create its own new government." As of Saturday morning, residents of all but one state had filed petitions asking the administration to grant them permission to leave the country peacefully. Most of the petitions were created in recent days following the re-election of President Barack Obama. Texas' petition leads all others by a wide margin. If it reaches 25,000 signatures by December 9, the White House may respond. So far, the petition has garnered over 87,000 signatures. Many of the signers appear to be from outside Texas. Several other states with large numbers of signers include Louisiana (over 31,000), Florida (nearly 30,000) and Georgia (more than 26,000). The only state that hasn't filed a petition is Vermont. The same day, a drone strike in the eastern province of Marib killed four suspected militants, including another member of al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, the group's affiliate in Yemen. Last month, a senior al Qaeda operative accused of planning to bomb oil terminals and pipelines in Yemen died in a drone strike, Yemeni intelligence sources said. Also last month, a drone strike killed Said al Shihri, the No. 2 leader of AQAP. That strike came less than two weeks after a U.S.-backed offensive forced al Qaeda fighters from strongholds they'd held for more than a year in towns in southern Yemen. Al Qaeda-linked militants seized control of large swaths of land in southern Yemen last year amid political turmoil in the impoverished nation. But the Yemeni military, with U.S. assistance, launched a major offensive earlier this year to regain control of areas under militant control. In addition to the drone strikes, the United States has trained and equipped Yemeni counterterrorism forces and provided direct support to its military operations, Pentagon spokesman George Little said in September.

However, there is no systematic review available that summarizes and compares their performance across different agroecologies and seasons. Sweet potato yield gap analysis There are several ways to assess yield gaps: the difference between actual and potential yield; the difference between actual and best farmer's yield; and the difference between average and best farmer's yield (van Ittersum et al., 2013). In this study we used the latter method because of its simplicity and practicality. The objective was to analyze sweet potato yield gaps in Africa through a literature review and field survey. We hypothesized that sweet potato yields can be substantially improved by using improved varieties and agronomic practices. Furthermore, we assessed whether OFSP varieties performed equally well compared to white-fleshed varieties and if the magnitude of the yield gap differed according to agroecology and season. We conducted a comprehensive search in Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed articles published before January 31st, 2018, using various combinations of the following keywords: "sweet potato", "yield", "Africa", "tropical" and "trial". Only English language papers were included. In addition, relevant unpublished reports from NGOs, research institutes and universities were collected through internet searches and personal contacts. Studies that reported mean yields per treatment were selected and extracted. Yields were expressed in kg fresh weight/ha, unless otherwise stated. If necessary, yields were recalculated assuming a standard plot size of 100 m2 (10 x 10 m) and/or a plant density of 10,000 plants/ha. Yield data were categorized into three groups: best farmer's yield (BFY), average farmer's yield (AFY) and lowest farmer's yield (LFY). BFY refers to the highest yielding variety or practice tested in a trial, AFY is the mean yield of all treatments, while LFY is the lowest yielding variety or practice tested in a trial. For trials that did not report means, the highest and lowest yield values were taken. We assumed that these data represent the range of yields obtained by farmers in the area where the trial was conducted, including both high and low performing farms. The yield gap (YG) was calculated as the difference between the BFY and AFY. YG as percentage of BFY (YG%) was calculated as [(BFY - AFY)/BFY] * 100%. Yield data were grouped according to agroecological zone (AEZ), season and flesh color. AEZs were defined as arid, semi-arid, sub-humid and humid areas, based on long-term annual rainfall averages (FAO, 1996). Seasons were classified as wet, dry or rainy season, or as early or late season, depending on the local climatic conditions. Trials that were conducted during two consecutive seasons (e.g. rainy and dry season) were considered as multi-seasonal trials. Flesh color was either white/yellow or orange, the latter being rich in beta-carotene. Data were summarized and analyzed in Microsoft Excel 2010. Taylor et al. (2015) developed a heat vulnerability index for London using logistic regression to combine factors related to health, housing, age and ethnicity. They found that 85% of London's population are vulnerable to heat-health risks. In order to develop effective adaptation policies and measures, there is a need for better understanding of how the impacts of climate change on heat-risk vary across London. This study develops a framework for estimating the relative contribution of climate change and other drivers of heat-risk (e.g. population, demographics and urban form) in London. It uses this framework to estimate the impact of future climate change on heat-risk in London, while accounting for uncertainties in the relationship between climate change and heat-risk, as well as uncertainties in the magnitude of climate change. The first section of the paper describes the methodology used to assess the influence of climate change and other drivers of heat-risk in London. Section two presents the results from applying the methodology, showing the current heat-risk profile of London and its evolution under different scenarios of climate change. Finally, conclusions and recommendations are presented. In order to understand the role of climate change in driving heat-risk in London, we propose a framework that combines information about the influences of climate change and other drivers of heat-risk. Figure 1 shows the proposed framework where the relative importance of climate change is estimated by comparing the heat-risk projections under climate change and no-climate-change scenarios, while accounting for uncertainties in the relationship between climate change and heat-risk. The framework requires information on: (i) the baseline heat-risk profile of London; (ii) the future climate projection for London; (iii) the relationships between climate change and heat-risk; (iv) the sensitivity of heat-risk to changes in climate change, population, demographics and urban form; and (v) the scenarios of climate change and other drivers of heat-risk. Figure 1. Framework for assessing the relative importance of climate change in driving heat-risk in London. This paper focuses on the baseline heat-risk profile and the sensitivity of heat-risk to changes in climate change, population, demographics and urban form. We use the projections from the London Climate Change Partnership (LCCP) (Murphy et al., 2009) to estimate the future climate of London. These projections provide gridded data on daily temperature, precipitation and humidity at a resolution of 5 km * 5 km covering Greater London. The LCCP projections were produced using the Hadley Centre Regional Climate Model version 3 (HadRM3) driven by outputs from the Hadley Centre Global Coupled Atmosphere-Ocean General Circulation Model version 3 (HadCM3) for three greenhouse gas emission scenarios (SRES A1B, A2 and B1). The SRES A1B scenario represents a medium-emissions pathway with atmospheric concentrations stabilising at around 550 ppm CO2-eq by 2100. The SRES A2 scenario represents a high-emissions pathway with atmospheric concentrations reaching 850 ppm CO2-eq by 2100. The SRES B1 scenario represents a low-emissions pathway with atmospheric concentrations reaching 500 ppm CO2-eq by 2100. We select the SRES A1B scenario because it provides a good balance between the range of possible futures. For each scenario, the model output was bias-corrected using quantile mapping (Murphy et al., 2009). To estimate the baseline heat-risk profile of London, we combine information on: (i) population and demographics; (ii) urban form; (iii) heat-sensitive groups; and (iv) vulnerability to heat-health outcomes.

Smith and associates reported a case where 61% of the boys living in a Sudanese village with only 0.65 mg/L in drinking water developed dental fluorosis [18]. The not-so-direct relationship between dental fluorosis prevalence and F- content of drinking water as highlighted in the aforementioned studies may be explained by: (1) other sources of F- intake than drinking water might have contributed to the F- total daily intake; (2) other factors such as age, quality of nutrition, altitude and daily temperature influence the prevalence of fluorosis at any given level of F- intake. The role of these factors in fluorosis prevalence has been investigated and proved relevant [19,20]. Fluorosis is more prevalent in hotter regions, even when F- in drinking water is within the WHO acceptable levels. This is because hot conditions lead to higher consumption of water, hence higher F- intake [20]. The effect of altitude on the prevalence of fluorosis was found to be significant, with high fluorosis prevalence at higher altitude [15]. The reason for this observation is still unclear, but there appears to be high F- retention in body tissues at high altitude. On the basis of these findings, the WHO generally recommends that when setting the standards for a country or region, factors such as climatic conditions, volumes of water intake, and intake of F- from other sources be considered. AMMT is the Annual Mean Maximum Temperature over a 5-year period. Eq. (3) has been used to calculate optimum water F- levels in different countries [21-23] and for Uganda, the value was found to be about 0.67 mg/L [24]. The equation estimated the daily water intake under different temperature conditions in United States during the late 1950s, where children were presumed to take 44% of their total fluid intake as milk with negligible F- levels. Eq. (4) was used in this study to calculate the optimum F- in drinking water in Tororo. F- in groundwater comes mainly from leaching of fluoride-containing rocks. Phosphate minerals containing F-, such as fluorapatite (Ca10(PO4)6F2) and francolite (Ca10-x-yNaxMgy(PO4)6-z(CO3)zF0.4zF2) have been reported in Sukulu Hills in Tororo [26] and this coincides with several anecdotal reports of the high prevalence of fluorosis in the area. It has also been shown that F- accumulates in certain food crops grown in fluoride-rich soils [27], another route to the food chain. This route further increases the total daily intake of F- beyond recommended 0.7 mg per day from all sources for children of one to four years. The characteristics of groundwater are influenced by geochemical processes such as weathering of minerals, precipitation, dissolution, ion exchange, oxidation, reduction, and residence time (and flow rate) of groundwater [28]. F- levels in groundwater has been shown to be greater in dry seasons than wet seasons as a result of evaporative concentration of water [29].

We have developed a new X-ray CT system using a compact X-ray source and a flat-panel detector (FPD), which allows us to visualize the tree-ring pattern of wooden samples with a spatial resolution of approximately 50 1/2m without damaging the sample. In this paper, we introduce our system and present examples of applications to various types of wooden cultural properties. In order to realize the imaging of tree rings in wooden cultural properties using X-ray CT, it is necessary to achieve sufficient spatial resolution and reduce the radiation dose to prevent damage to the sample. In this section, we describe the development of a compact X-ray CT system with sufficient spatial resolution and minimum radiation exposure for the visualization of tree rings in wooden cultural properties. The schematic diagram of the compact X-ray CT system is shown in Fig. 1a. This system consists of a rotating sample holder (rotator), a compact X-ray tube, a flat-panel detector, and a computer. A collimator is placed between the X-ray tube and the sample rotator to irradiate the sample with parallel X-rays. The flat-panel detector is installed opposite to the X-ray tube and the sample to detect transmitted X-rays. The flat-panel detector is composed of a CsI scintillator, a TFT sensor array, and a readout circuit board. The size of the sensor array is 100 mm * 100 mm with a pixel pitch of 195 1/2m. The maximum frame rate of the detector is 15 frames per second, and the dynamic range is 16 bits. A computer controls the rotation angle of the sample rotator, acquires the images from the flat-panel detector, and reconstructs the three-dimensional images of the sample. In order to decrease the amount of radiation received by the sample, we used a micro-focus X-ray tube with a focal spot size of 40 1/2m. The structural similarity among these enzymes is thought to reflect their shared ability to recognize and process specific DNA structures, rather than a common catalytic mechanism. GEN1, on the other hand, has a distinct architecture, with a unique arrangement of its catalytic and DNA-binding domains. The crystal structure of GEN1 reveals a dimeric enzyme, with each monomer consisting of a catalytic core and a DNA-binding domain connected by a flexible linker (Rass et al., 2010). The catalytic core is composed of a nuclease domain and a helical domain, which together form a crescent-shaped active site. The DNA-binding domain, comprising a winged-helix motif, is responsible for recognizing and binding the four-way junction. The GEN1 dimer is thought to bind the four-way junction in a symmetrical manner, with each monomer interacting with two arms of the junction. This binding mode is supported by biochemical and structural data, which show that GEN1 binds specifically to four-way junctions and introduces symmetrical cleavages (Ip et al., 2008; Rass et al., 2010). The catalytic mechanism of GEN1 involves a two-metal ion-dependent phosphoryl transfer reaction, similar to that of other structure-selective nucleases (Grasby et al., 2012). However, the precise details of the GEN1 catalytic mechanism remain to be elucidated. In addition to its role in resolving four-way junctions, GEN1 has been implicated in the repair of other types of DNA lesions, including DNA interstrand crosslinks and DNA-protein crosslinks (Bailly et al., 2010; Munoz et al., 2009). The enzyme has also been shown to play a role in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, particularly in the context of meiosis (Lorenz et al., 2010; Matos et al., 2011). Furthermore, GEN1 has been linked to the maintenance of genomic stability, as its depletion leads to increased genomic instability and sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents (Garner et al., 2013). The SLX1-MUS81-EME1-SLX4 complex, on the other hand, is thought to play a more specialized role in the resolution of four-way junctions, particularly in the context of mitosis (Agostinho et al., 2013; Andersen et al., 2009; Fekairi et al., 2009; Munoz et al., 2009; Svendsen et al., 2009). The complex is composed of four subunits, each with distinct functions: SLX1 and MUS81 are responsible for recognizing and binding the four-way junction, while EME1 and SLX4 facilitate the cleavage reaction (Agostinho et al., 2013). The complex is thought to act in a coordinated manner, with each subunit playing a critical role in the resolution process. The regulation of GEN1 and SLX1-MUS81-EME1-SLX4 activities is still not fully understood, but it is clear that both pathways are tightly regulated to ensure proper DNA repair and maintenance of genomic stability. Dysregulation of these pathways has been implicated in various human diseases, including cancer and premature aging disorders (Garner et al., 2013). Further research is needed to fully elucidate the mechanisms of GEN1 and SLX1-MUS81-EME1-SLX4, and to explore their potential as therapeutic targets for the treatment of human diseases.

Bloom syndrome (BS) is caused by mutations in the BLM gene (Ellis et al., 1995). BLM encodes a DNA helicase that is 1,417 amino acids in length, with a predicted molecular mass of 159 kDa. BLM is called a caretaker tumor suppressor because almost all BS patients are prone to multiple types of cancers, ranging from solid tumors to lymphoma (Hickson, 2003). Because of the absence of BLM, BS patients accumulate wide range of DNA damage, including high rates of sister chromatid exchanges (SCEs) (McDaniel and Schultz, 1992). This is due to the effect of BLM in regulating multiple steps of the DNA repair machinery (Hickson and Mankouri, 2011; Tikoo and Sengupta, 2010). Although BLM was initially characterized as a DNA helicase, its unstructured N- and C-terminal extensions allowed it to make physical and functional interactions with multiple factors involved in the recognition of DNA damage, DNA repair, and maintenance of the genome (Bohm and Bernstein, 2014; Chu and Hickson, 2009; Tikoo and Sengupta, 2010). For example, BLM is recruited very early to the sites of stalled replication (Sengupta et al., 2004) and helps in enhancing the function of chromatin remodelers and histone chaperones (Jiao et al., 2004; Srivastava et al., 2009). BLM interacts functionally with multiple members of the DNA damage response pathways (such as ATM, MRN complex, BRCA1, p53, Chk1/Chk2, 53BP1), which recognize both stalled replication forks and DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Beamish et al., 2002; Kaur et al., 2010; Sengupta et al., 2003, 2004; Wang et al., 2000). BLM recruitment to the DSBs is independent of its own helicase function but depends on ATM, multiple members of the MRN complex, and its own uniquitylation by RNF8. Once recruited, BLM negatively regulates both HR and c-NHEJ in a cell cycle phase-specific manner (Tripathi et al., 2018). Although BLM interacts with Fbw7 in multiple phases of the cell cycle, it undergoes Fbw7 -mediated degradation only during mitosis (Kharat et al., 2016). This led to our hypothesis that during interphase, BLM may act as an adaptor for other Fbw7 substrates, thereby potentiating their degradation. Here, we have provided evidence that MIB1-ubiquitylated BLM (Ub-BLM) in G1 phase increased the binding between c-Jun and Fbw7, leading to enhanced Jun ubiquitylation (via K48/K63 linkage) and its subsequent degradation. BLM reactivates cancer-associated Fbw7 mutants, because of which these defective E3 ligases could promote c-Jun degradation. However, BLM mutants expressed in BS patients cannot enhance Fbw7 -dependent c-Jun ubiquitylation and degradation.

Deep eutectic solvents exhibit a range of favorable characteristics that can further enhance the green extraction of natural products. Their formation typically involves the combination of a hydrogen bond donor and a hydrogen bond acceptor, resulting in a significant reduction in melting point due to the strong intermolecular interactions. This unique property not only allows DES to remain in a liquid state at lower temperatures but also provides them with extraordinary solvation capabilities. Their tunable nature means that by varying the ratio of the cationic and anionic components, one can tailor the solvent properties to optimize solubility for specific bioactive compounds-all while working within an environmentally benign framework [13]. The versatility of deep eutectic solvents has been demonstrated across various extraction processes, including the efficient recovery of flavonoids, polyphenols, and essential oils from plant materials. Studies highlight the improved yields and purity levels achieved when using DES compared to traditional organic solvents, affirming their potential to revolutionize the extraction domain [14]. Furthermore, their biocompatibility positions them as appealing candidates in the pharmaceutical and food industries, where strict regulations regarding solvent residues are prevalent. Despite these advantages, challenges remain in the application of DES at an industrial scale. The production of deep eutectic solvents necessitates a careful consideration of cost-effectiveness and scalability, particularly as the concentration of components can influence not only the extraction efficacy but also subsequent separation and purification stages. Although DES can typically be synthesized from readily available, low-cost materials, achieving a consistent quality and purity during large-scale production is essential for regulatory compliance and commercial viability [15]. Moreover, while the benefits of using such solvents in extraction processes are clear, further research into their long-term environmental impact is inherently necessary. Investigations into biodegradability and potential toxicity are critical to ensure that the end products derived from plant extractions are indeed greener alternatives rather than contributing to new environmental challenges. Additionally, an exploration into the life cycle of DES-from production through usage to disposal-will provide comprehensive insight into their sustainability credentials. Moreover, the combination of DES with contemporary extraction technologies can yield synergistic effects. For instance, when employed alongside ultrasound-assisted extraction or microwave-assisted techniques, the efficacy of DES can be amplified, allowing for rapid extraction times and improved yields. Notably, the integration of these methodologies represents a compelling advancement in the quest for greener extraction protocols, leading to not only enhanced efficiency but also a reduced environmental footprint [16]. As lingering questions about the safety profiles of deep eutectic solvents continue to be addressed, the development of bio-based DES derived from renewable resources is becoming a focal point of investigation. Such advances could effectively mitigate concerns regarding sustainability, providing a reliable method to obtain solvents that contribute positively to the circular economy. Research into biodegradable and non-toxic DES formulations could ensure a significant stride towards more environmentally-friendly extraction processes [17]. In summary, deep eutectic solvents embody a promising avenue in the quest for greener and more efficient extraction methods for natural products. Their unique properties, tunability, and compatibility with other innovative extraction technologies mark their potential to surpass conventional methods. As research expands to explore their full capabilities and environmental implications, the adoption of DES could herald a new age of sustainability in the extraction of bioactive compounds. The future holds exciting possibilities for reimagining not only how we extract these valuable substances, but also how we ensure their sustainable usage in various applications, ultimately enhancing our quality of life while preserving nature.

John Brown," he said, "go and take your seat next to Elizabeth Bruce - but one above her." The new boy moved across the room, red-faced and clumsy in every movement. When he found himself in front of the class he grew still redder, and hung hesitatingly upon the step that led to the platform upon which the form was placed. Elizabeth looked at him disdainfully and drew her dress close around her. "Sit down, you silly," she said in a sharp whisper, and indicated with a little head toss the seat above her. John Brown slunk past her and dropped heavily into his seat. The master retired to his desk and made an entry or two in his long blue book while silence hung over the schoolroom. In Elizabeth's heart a flame of anger was spreading. That this boy, this new boy, should be placed above her, was in her eyes the greatest injustice. A small voice within told her that she had been punished sufficiently yesterday afternoon. Her head moved slightly in the direction of the new boy and her rosy lips opened. "You cheat!" she whispered. The boy sat motionless and the anger burned hotter in Elizabeth's heart. "Cheaty, cheaty; go home and tell your mother!" she said in a sing-song way. Still Brown did not move. Elizabeth slid her hand along the seat and gave him a sharp pinch, and he started uneasily. "Stand up the boy or girl who was speaking," ordered the master, without looking up. A small fair-haired fair-complexioned boy, two seats above Elizabeth, flushed. His name was Cyril Bruce and he was Elizabeth's twin brother - twelve years old. "I was only talking to myself - that's not speaking," he murmured. Elizabeth rose slowly to her feet and stood working a corner of her pinafore into a knot. The master looked around, and his brow grew dark when he saw the small offender. "Repeat aloud what you said, Elizabeth Bruce," he ordered. The little girl grew white, then red, then white again, and went on twisting her pinafore. "Do you hear me?" shouted the master. "Stand upon the form and repeat your words." Once again Elizabeth clambered into a higher position. "I said - I said, 'Cheaty, cheaty; go home and tell your mother,'" she said in a clear voice that sounded all over the room. A shocked expression passed over the face of the class. "To whom were you addressing yourself?" asked the master. "The new boy," said the little girl. "Sit down, and stay in the dinner-hour and write out the sentence fifty times." Elizabeth sat down, and again her anger against the new boy blazed high. She put out her foot and kicked the heel of his boot, but this time she eschewed words, for the face of the master was towards her, and an expectant silence hung over the schoolroom.

However, Isotope Dilution (ID) assays provide a more robust mechanistic description of the size of the reactive pool of metals, as they measure the pool of metal that is in equilibrium in the soil-pore water system, but until now, its use has been relatively limited in flooded soil. Early work by Tiller et al. (1972) examined the use of Zn isotopes in determining E and L-values in paddy field soils. More recent examples include those by Stroud et al. (2011) who assessed changes in As lability in soils from Bangladesh, but reducing conditions such as those occurring in paddy fields were not successfully achieved. The use of multi-element ID assays, in particular, has the potential to add new insights into the complex interactions that affect the reactivity of different metals simultaneously in submerged soils. Recently, Marzouk (2012) used multi-element isotopic dilution to assess changes in the E-value of Fe, Cd, Zn and Pb in mine spoil-rich soils from the UK subjected to alternate aerobic/anaerobic 15-day long cycles. As a result of the large variation in geochemical conditions produced when a soil undergoes submergence, methodological considerations need to be considered with respect to the fundamental rules of ID assays; these being (i) that the background electrolyte should not mobilise non-labile metal, (ii) that the metal-complexes in the solution phase remain labile so that complete isotope equilibrium may occur and (iii) that the isotope spike does not precipitate. For example, recent work by Izquierdo et al. (2016) demonstrated the fixation of the Zn isotope spike within 5 days leading to overestimates of the E-value. Thus to fully utilise ID assays in examining the behaviour of trace elements in submerged soils a greater understanding of how different redox conditions affect the assay is required. Two major influences that may affect the efficacy of the ID assay are (i) the nature of the carbon substrate that the microbial biomass use and the metabolites produced and released into solution and (ii) the submergence time. These parameters could affect the isotopic exchangeability in solution or cause tracer removal before the exchange with the native isotope occurs, thus compromising the results. Bell (1969) demonstrated that changes in Eh, pH and gas evolution varied between different carbon sources. For example, whilst reducing conditions can result in the release of dissolved organic carbon (Buettner et al., 2014), volatile fatty acids (VFA) such as acetate, propionate and butyrate can be formed during fermentation reactions when sugars are decomposed (Krylova et al., 1997; Chidthaisong et al., 1999). Fermentation by-products such as acetate have different binding properties for trace metals than humic (HA) and fulvic acids (FA) and the potential for violating one of the fundamental ID principals exists; the formation of non-labile complexes in the solution phase. However, the fermentation phase is one where the use of E-values could be of great value because of the associated rapid pH and Eh changes.

In neocortex, LTP is normal but paired-pulse facilitation is increased (Cramer et al., 2015). However, in other brain regions, LTP is impaired. For example, LTP is impaired in the hippocampus (Fernandez et al., 2014), medial prefrontal cortex (Gao et al., 2014), amygdala (Sekino et al., 2017) and nucleus accumbens (NAC) (Kishi et al., 2016). The NAC is a major centre for reward and motivation and it contains two types of medium spiny projection neuron, which are distinguished by the expression of the dopamine D1 receptor (Drd1+ MSNs) or the dopamine D2 receptor (Drd2+ MSNs) (Alcantara et al., 1993; Surmeier et al., 1996). Drd1+ and Drd2+ MSNs are involved in distinct aspects of motivated behaviour (Morris et al., 2014; Soria-Gomez et al., 2014). Drd1+ MSNs are activated by psychostimulants such as cocaine and amphetamine (Kalivas and Duffy, 1988; Kalivas and Stewart, 1991) and their activation by drugs of abuse promotes drug-seeking behaviours (McFarland and Kalivas, 2001; McFarland et al., 2004). Drd2+ MSNs are activated by opiates, nicotine and alcohol (Beckstead et al., 2009; Kourrich et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2005) and their activation by drugs of abuse suppresses drug-seeking behaviours (Carelli et al., 2003; Cunningham et al., 2011; O'Dell et al., 2000). Drd1+ and Drd2+ MSNs are important for learning and memory because they can undergo LTP (Calabresi et al., 1992; Koos and Tepper, 1999; Shen et al., 2008; Tang et al., 2016; Yung et al., 1995). LTP at Drd1+ MSN synapses is important for associative learning (Chen et al., 2016; Morikawa et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2010). Moreover, LTP in Drd1+ MSNs is necessary for the development of behavioural sensitisation to psychostimulant drugs (Chen et al., 2016; Morikawa et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2010). In contrast, LTP at Drd2+ MSN synapses is important for habit formation (Yin et al., 2008). These findings highlight how synaptic plasticity in Drd1+ and Drd2+ MSNs contributes to motivated behaviours. Previous work has shown that synaptic transmission and plasticity are altered in Drd1+ MSNs in Tc1 mice (Kishi et al., 2016). Here we investigate whether synaptic transmission and plasticity are altered in Drd2+ MSNs in Tc1 mice. We find that baseline synaptic transmission at Drd2+ MSN synapses is normal but LTP is impaired. The impairment in LTP is due to a deficit in Ca\({}^{2+}\)/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII)-dependent long-lasting LTP. This study highlights how synaptic plasticity is disrupted in the NAC in a mouse model of DS.

The ride was actually quite pleasant, and when we landed the torrential downpours that had just started when we got to Dulles had abated. Once we got out of the main terminal at Newark, we were corralled by a limo driver, who quoted a pretty fair price and headed out to Soho, where Ellen was waiting for us. Her loft is the first I've ever been in - it is peppered with folk art: an old flag with 36 stars; an ancient shell quilt; a tree that's been painted over texture; old wire patterns for men's suits; an ancient folding ladder; her dining room chairs are s&m black leather complete with threaded tie lacing up the back of the seats; her bathtubs have clawed feet; and there's daylight everywhere. When we came in we were introduced to Steve, the camera man who worked for Michael Moore during his TV Nation days; Melissa, her dearest friend and camera woman, who has schlepped with Ellen from Kentucky to St. Louis, to DC., to Naples, Florence, basically all around the world for this project; Karen, the still photographer; and Jim, the boom man (now I know what that means, he's the one who swings the mike back and forth!). There was also a guy putting the finishing touches on a mannequin's head - the look of which was definitely Holofernes. So I knew we were going to be involved with Judith somehow. Then we met the other ladies who had come to participate: Stephanie, from Florence via Chicago, most recently in Burma, Nepal, and other Asian countries, who had met Ellen at Michelangelo Buonnaroti's house, admiring the Gentileschi contributions to a ceiling; Joan, recently retired from Wellesley College's interactive culture program, and now living in Florence, who had met Ellen at the Urbino Gallery; Susan, a shy baroque painter from Bucks County, Pennsylvania, who had also met Ellen at the Met; and finally, Catherine, an amazing artist from Providence, who had met Ellen in Naples. We started chatting, asking each other questions, mainly what the heck got us to this loft, and were filmed by Melissa right away. It wasn't as difficult as I thought it would be to ignore the camera, but I attribute that to the stories I was hearing from these women. Joan is definitely an ultra feminist, but she's probably the oldest of our bunch, and remembers having to fight her way in her business, in her art, in life en toto. Stephanie is such a determined soul, determined to see the world, determined to exert her independence, and determined to participate in whatever comes her way. For example, she started taking pictures when she was in Burma and Nepal and the results are stunning. Susan quietly asserts her vision - we experienced this more than once when we were reenacting the paintings. It was her eye that guided us to the right movements, lighting, and props.

Throughout the second half of the twentieth century, the bulk of world trade was taking place between similar countries. Likewise, economic unions initially included countries with comparable levels of income and factor endowments. A key feature of this type of economic integration is that it does not imply the reallocation of resources predicted by conventional models of trade driven by differences in factor endowments. Accordingly, one of the original motivations for developing models of trade in differentiated varieties was the need to account for episodes such as the creation of the European Economic Community, in which trade liberalization had faced little political opposition because it had led to rises in real income for owners of all factors in all member states (Helpman and Krugman, 1985). Yet, the enlargements of the European Union to the East, trade liberalization in developing countries and the rise of China in global markets have brought distributional considerations to the forefront. As a result, many now fear that the negative consequences of import competition can overshadow the benefits of market size. To shed light on these phenomena, in this paper we develop a theoretical framework to study the effects on trade, income distribution and welfare of economic unions that differ in size and scope. We then apply our model to interpret the process of European integration. Section 2 presents the basic setup of our theory. It considers a multi-country, multi-industry and multi-factor framework that combines the Krugman model of trade and monopolistic competition with the Ricardo-Viner model of specific factors. In particular, countries produce differentiated varieties in a continuum of industries employing sector-specific human capital. They differ both in size and in the distribution of their factor endowments across sectors. These differences entail potential gains from both intra-industry and inter-industry trade. In Section 3, we add to our framework a theory of border costs. We assume that in some industries trade is possible only in the presence of union policies that overcome non-tariff barriers. For instance, common regulations or standards are often needed for firms to sell their products in foreign markets, especially in certain sectors such as financial services. We explicitly recognize that all economic unions are not the same. In particular, unions vary in their depth, i.e., the measure of industries covered by union policies; and their breadth, i.e., the set of countries included in the union. We study how these aspects of the union determine its impact on the world distribution of income and welfare. In Section 4, we determine the sources of political support for specific economic unions and derive predictions on how this political support varies across countries, and how it reacts to changes in the depth and breadth of the union. We find that some of the effects of union policies are homogeneous within each country because they reflect changes in prices that accrue entirely to consumers.

I thought maybe she didn't want me touching her. I turned to look at her and she was staring at me. I tried to ignore her but I couldn't. I looked away and pretended to read my notes. I heard her whispering something under her breath. I don't know what she was talking about but I knew she wasn't talking to me. I continued reading until the bell rang. When I looked up again Alisha was gone. I was puzzled and I wondered what was wrong. After school I decided to walk home with Kylie and Petronella. They lived right across the street from each other. I looked at Kylie and then at Petronella. They both shrugged their shoulders and we walked over to where Alisha was sitting. I asked her what was wrong. She didn't respond. I took a step forward and touched her arm gently. She jumped up and glared at me. She backed away from me and yelled, Why are you always trying to touch me? I just stood there dumbfounded. I didn't know what was going on with Alisha. I hoped everything would be okay. Later that night after dinner I went upstairs to my room. I opened my laptop and logged onto Facebook. I saw that Alisha hadn't posted anything new. She usually posts something every few hours.

As I delved deeper into the essay, I was struck by the parallels between the sentiments expressed then and the current state of affairs. The French perception of American cultural imperialism, for instance, remains a contentious issue. The notion that the United States is exporting its values, often at the expense of local traditions, continues to be a point of contention. This is evident in the French resistance to globalization, which is often seen as a euphemism for Americanization. Furthermore, the French concerns about the erosion of their cultural identity are not unfounded. The proliferation of American fast food chains, the dominance of Hollywood in the global film industry, and the widespread adoption of American English in international communication all contribute to a sense of cultural homogenization. The French, with their rich cultural heritage, are particularly sensitive to these developments, and it is understandable that they would want to preserve their unique identity. On the political front, the relationship between the two nations remains complex. The Iraq War, which France opposed, created a rift in Franco-American relations that has yet to be fully bridged. The subsequent diplomatic efforts to repair the damage have been hindered by disagreements over issues such as trade, climate change, and Middle Eastern policy. The election of Donald Trump as President of the United States has only added to the uncertainty, with his administration's "America First" approach being seen as a threat to French interests and values. Despite these challenges, there are still areas where cooperation between the two nations is thriving. In the realm of science and technology, for example, French and American researchers are working together on cutting-edge projects such as the ITER fusion reactor and the Square Kilometre Array telescope. These collaborations are a testament to the enduring spirit of scientific cooperation that has characterized Franco-American relations since the days of Benjamin Franklin and the Enlightenment. In conclusion, as I reflect on my essay from two years ago, I am struck by the prescience of my observations. The issues that I identified then - cultural differences, political tensions, and the complexities of globalization - remain relevant today. However, I am also heartened by the resilience of Franco-American relations, which have endured despite the challenges. As we move forward, it is essential that both nations continue to engage in open and honest dialogue, recognizing their differences while celebrating their shared values and interests. Only through such cooperation can we build a stronger, more prosperous relationship that benefits both nations and the world at large.

However, the literature on interoception in autism is mixed; while Garfinkel, Tiley et al. (2016) found that adults with autism demonstrated worse performance on the Heartbeat Counting Task (HCT; Dale & Anderson, 1978; Schandry, 1981), a commonly-used measure in which participants are required to count their heartbeats over a specified interval and their count is compared to an objective measure, they were unimpaired on another measure of cardiac interoceptive sensitivity (the heartbeat discrimination task, in which participants are required to judge whether auditory or visual signals are synchronous with their heartbeat). In addition, Schauder, Mash, Bryant, and Cascio (2015) examined HCT performance in autistic1 children and found them to be unimpaired. In fact, autistic children performed better on the task than typical children over longer durations. Noel, Lytle, Cascio, and Wallace (2018) also found that a small sample of adults with autism performed at a level similar to typical individuals on the HCT. Brewer, Happe, Cook, and Bird (2015) have argued that the pattern of deficits predicted by Quattrocki and Friston's interoceptive model does not characterise autism, but that some of the deficits instead characterise alexithymia (a sub-clinical condition in which individuals are poor at identifying and describing their emotions, and have an externally-oriented thinking style (Bagby, Parker, & Taylor, 1994). The possibility of a link between alexithymia and interoceptive sensitivity was supported by the results of an initial study, which found that increased levels of alexithymia were associated with worse performance on the HCT (Herbert, Herbert, & Pollatos, 2011). As approximately 50-60% of individuals with autism also have alexithymia (e.g., Berthoz & Hill, 2005), it is possible that sampling variance with respect to alexithymia within the autistic population explains the inconsistent findings concerning autism and interoception. It may be the case that when samples of autistic individuals are largely comprised of alexithymic individuals, group level deficits are observed, but when the autism sample has a smaller proportion of alexithymic individuals, the autistic group perform as well as a group of typical individuals. This hypothesis was supported in a study in which the impact of autistic and alexithymic traits on the HCT were contrasted. Across two experiments, alexithymia, rather than autism, predicted lower sensitivity to cardiac signals as measured using the HCT (Shah, Hall, Catmur, & Bird, 2016). While the relationship between alexithymia and HCT performance replicated across both experiments, samples were relatively small (N < 50), likely providing an imprecise measure of the true effect size. Indeed, the magnitude of the correlation between alexithymia and performance on the HCT varied considerably across experiments (-0.36 and -0.64). It is notable, therefore, that the one previous study to examine the relationship between alexithymia and performance on the HCT in a larger (N = 155) non-clinical sample found a correlation of -0.37 (Herbert et al., 2011).

It was the only explanation. The dreamlike trance came over him once more. He tried to fight it, but it was useless. His eyes closed slowly. With a sigh, I walked out the door, letting it slam behind me. The afternoon sun was relentless, casting sharp shadows across the cracked pavement. I kicked a loose stone, watching it bounce until it disappeared into the weeds along the road. Beaufort was like that, a mix of beauty and rough edges, a place where dreams could sprout up as easily as dandelions in the cracks. Marvin's Auto Shop was a few blocks down, nestled between the old diner and a boarded-up grocery store. The sign was missing a couple of letters, so it read "Marvin's Aut Shp," as if the town had given up fixing anything that wasn't absolutely necessary. The bell above the door jingled as I entered, and a familiar smell of grease and gasoline welcomed me. Marvin looked up from behind the counter, his expression settling somewhere between surprise and skepticism. "Didn't expect to see you here," he said, wiping his hands on a rag that was more oil than cloth. "Mom said you might have a job for me," I replied, shoving my hands into my pockets. He grunted, a sound that could mean anything from 'hello' to 'I've seen better days.' "Assistant manager," he said, not looking up from his workbench. "Basically means you do whatever I say. You think you can handle that?" I shrugged. "I wasn't planning on staying forever." "Just remember," he said, finally meeting my eyes, "even dreams need a little grease to run." I nodded, unsure of what he meant, but knowing that Marvin had been around long enough to have earned the wisdom etched in the lines on his face. He gestured to a car in the bay, its hood popped open like a yawning mouth. "Start with that one." I spent the afternoon under the hood, the radio playing softly in the background and drowning out the silence of my thoughts. Working with my hands had a way of quieting the questions swirling in my head, the 'what ifs' and 'what nexts' that haunted me since the principal's office. As the sun dipped below the horizon, washing the town in hues of gold and purple, Marvin appeared at my side, inspecting my work. "Not bad," he said gruffly. "But you've got to tighten this here," he pointed, and I nodded, adjusting the wrench. When I finally stepped outside, the evening was cool against my sweaty skin, the scent of pine and sea salt riding the breeze. A familiar sound caught my ear-laughter spilling from a nearby porch, a clinking of glasses, the kind of music that only small towns know. With one more glance back at Marvin's, I started walking down the street, my steps leading nowhere in particular. Maybe tomorrow I'd figure out what to do next. Maybe I'd stay a while, just to see if this town still had any surprises for me. Or perhaps, like the tides that kissed the shores of Beaufort, I'd come and go, leaving traces of myself in the sand, wondering if anyone would notice. But for now, I walked, blending in with the shadows, the distant roar of the ocean my only companion, carrying echoes of a life not yet lived.

Participants kept a button pressed, and therefore the corresponding muscles flexed and motor cortex activated, while they were presented with an arm- or leg-related word. This allowed us to study the spatio-temporal brain dynamics during processing of different types of action-words while different parts of motor cortex were pre-activated. Furthermore, participants had to perform lexical and semantic Go/NoGo decisions at the end of each trial by releasing the button, thus offering the possibility to detect behavioral movement priming effects. With respect to point 1) above, the high temporal resolution of EEG/MEG allows monitoring brain activity at latencies that have been associated with earliest stages of semantic information retrieval, e.g., around 150 msec after word presentation (Amsel, Urbach, & Kutas, 2013; Hauk, Coutout, Holden, & Chen, 2012; Moseley, Pulvermuller, & Shtyrov, 2013; Pulvermuller, Shtyrov, & Hauk, 2009). The exact time course of semantic processing is still debated, and the boundary between early lexico-semantic processing and later imagery or mental simulation processes may be fuzzy (Barsalou, 2009), but effects at such early latencies would rule out a "post-translational" explanation. Furthermore, state-of-the-art source estimation of combined EEG/MEG data - although not as precise as fMRI localization - allows the dissociation of effects in different language-related brain areas, such as inferior frontal lobe ("Broca's area"), anterior temporal lobe (ATL), and posterior superior temporal lobe (pSTL, "Wernicke's area"). With respect to point 2), we propose to study effects of pre-activation of a specific effector or movement type (e.g., left/right finger/foot) on word processing. Thus, rather than showing that word processing activates motor areas, we can potentially reveal whether the activation state of the motor system affects language processing. Similar paradigms have already been used in behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) research (Boulenger et al., 2006; Dalla Volta, Gianelli, Campione, & Gentilucci, 2009; Glenberg et al., 2010; Helbig, Steinwender, Graf, & Kiefer, 2010; Liepelt, Stenzel, & Lappe, 2012; Sato, Mengarelli, Riggio, Gallese, & Buccino, 2008; Shebani & Pulvermuller, 2013; Van Elk, van Schie, & Bekkering, 2008; Van Elk, van Schie, & Bekkering, 2010). In our approach, we can study the effect of motor priming on both behavior and spatio-temporal brain dynamics. In principle, this paradigm could also be applied to other stimulus modalities, e.g., using color priming of color words. The motor system is of particular interest, since it allows precise hypotheses about somatotopic activation patterns, and because motor cortex is relatively easy to study using different types of neuroimaging methods such as fMRI, electro- and magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG), and TMS. fMRI studies have reported that stimuli referring to actions performed with different body parts elicit a somatotopic activation pattern within motor and premotor areas (e.g., "kick" or "pick" in leg- and hand-motor cortex, respectively) (Aziz-Zadeh, Koski, Zaidel, Mazziotta, & Iacoboni, 2006; Boulenger, Hauk, & Pulvermuller, 2009; Buccino et al., 2001; Hauk, Johnsrude, & Pulvermuller, 2004; Kemmerer, Castillo, Talavage, Patterson, & Wiley, 2008; Raposo, Moss, Stamatakis, & Tyler, 2009; Tettamanti et al., 2005; Willems, Hagoort, & Casasanto, 2010).

Such was Lord Guloseton. To my surprise no other guest but myself appeared. "A new friend," said he, as we descended into the dining-room, "is like a new dish - one must have him all to oneself, thoroughly to enjoy and rightly to understand him." "A noble precept," said I, with enthusiasm. "Of all vices, indiscriminate hospitality is the most pernicious. It allows us neither conversation nor dinner, and realizing the mythological fable of Tantalus, gives us starvation in the midst of plenty." "You are right," said Guloseton, solemnly; "I never ask above six persons to dinner, and I never dine out; for a bad dinner, Mr. Pelham, a bad dinner is a most serious - I may add, the most serious calamity." "Yes," I replied, "for it carries with it no consolation: a buried friend may be replaced - a lost mistress renewed - a slandered character be recovered - even a broken constitution restored; but a dinner, once lost, is irremediable; that day is for ever departed; an appetite once thrown away can never, till the cruel prolixity of the gastric agents is over, be regained. 'Il y a tant de maitresses, (says the admirable Corneille), 'il n'y a qu'un diner.'" "You speak like an oracle - like the Cook's Oracle, Mr. Pelham: may I send you some soup, it is a la Carmelite? But what are you about to do with that case?" "It contains" (said I) "my spoon, my knife, and my fork. Nature afflicted me with a propensity, which through these machines I have endeavoured to remedy by art. I eat with too great a rapidity. It is a most unhappy failing, for one often hurries over in one minute, what ought to have afforded the fullest delight for the period of five. It is, indeed, a vice which deadens enjoyment, as well as abbreviates it; it is a shameful waste of the gifts, and a melancholy perversion of the bounty of Providence: my conscience tormented me; but the habit, fatally indulged in early childhood, was not easy to overcome.

As the sun dipped below the horizon, casting a warm orange glow over the rolling hills and the thatched roofs of the surrounding cottages, the Ragnor family gathered around the fire in the great hall of their estate. The fire crackled and spat, sending sparks flying up the chimney as Conall Ragnor, the patriarch of the family, regaled them with tales of his adventures on the high seas. His wife, Rahal, sat beside him, her eyes shining with a quiet intelligence as she listened to her husband's stories of bravery and cunning. Their children, Magnus and Elspeth, sat on the floor, their eyes wide with excitement as they listened to their father's tales of battles fought and won, of treasure discovered and of the great deeds of the Viking heroes of old. The firelight danced across their faces, casting flickering shadows on the stone walls as they laughed and cheered at their father's jokes and exploits. Outside, the garden was bathed in the soft light of the moon, the flowers and shrubs silhouetted against the dark sky like a canvas of black and silver. The air was filled with the sweet scent of blooming roses and the distant sound of the sea, a constant reminder of the vast expanse of water that lay beyond the shores of the island. As the night wore on, the family retired to their quarters, the fire burning low in the great hall. Conall Ragnor sat alone for a moment, his eyes lost in thought as he gazed into the flames. He was a man of great physical and mental vigor, but he was also a man of strong convictions, and he knew that the world was changing fast. The winds of change were blowing across the land, and he knew that the old ways were slowly being swept away. In bacteria, SMC loading, translocation, and DNA entrapment is less well known but likely involves the ParA-ParB-parS system (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Lin and Grossman, 1998; Minnen et al., 2011). ParB is a DNA-binding protein that nucleates on a centromere-like parS sequence (Mohl and Gober, 1997) and then spreads non-specifically along the DNA, likely forming a large nucleoprotein complex (Breier and Grossman, 2007; Graham et al., 2014). ParA, a Walker-box ATPase, interacts with ParB and is required for the segregation of replicated chromosomes to daughter cells (Figge et al., 2003). In B. subtilis, ParB loads SMC onto the chromosome mainly at the ori-proximal parS sites (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Marbouty et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015). Loaded SMC then translocates from parS to distal parts of the chromosome in an ATP hydrolysis-dependent manner (Minnen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017). This action is thought to individualize the origins of replicated chromosomes, thereby helping to segregate replicated chromosomes. It has been proposed that B. subtilis SMC loaded at parS translocates the full length of the chromosome to ter to promote chromosome arm alignment (Gruber and Errington, 2009; Minnen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017). However, chromatin immunoprecipitation with deep sequencing (ChIP-seq) studies indicate that B. subtilis SMC is most enriched near ori, so whether SMC directly promotes arm alignment uniformly across the genome is unclear (Minnen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017). Caulobacter harbors both a canonical SMC-ScpA-ScpB complex as well as a ParA-ParB-parS system. The ParA-ParB-parS complex is essential (Mohl and Gober, 1997). In contrast, Caulobacter SMC is not required for survival in laboratory conditions (Le et al., 2013). Caulobacter cells lacking SMC grow slightly slower but are not temperature sensitive or prone to accumulating suppressor mutations as originally suggested (Jensen and Shapiro, 1999). Nevertheless, ectopic overexpression of an ATPase-defective smc mutant shows a severe defect in sister chromosome segregation in this bacterium, consistent with Caulobacter SMC playing a role in chromosome segregation (Schwartz and Shapiro, 2011). How SMC influences other cellular processes, like transcription, and is, in turn, influenced by these processes is not well understood. In yeast, cohesin is pushed along the chromosome in the same direction as transcription, without dissociating (Ocampo-Hafalla et al., 2016). Similarly, in budding yeast, RNA polymerase can drive the short-range relocation of condensin (D'Ambrosio et al., 2008; Johzuka and Horiuchi, 2007). Whether bacterial RNA polymerase affects SMC has not been systematically investigated. Notably, in almost all bacteria, most genes, especially highly expressed genes, are transcribed from ori to ter (reviewed in Rocha, 2008). This co-orientation of genes could help push SMC toward ter; alternatively, or in addition, genes transcribed in a head-on orientation could antagonize the translocation of SMC.

Piper betle's significance extends beyond the realms of mere culinary delight, manifesting prominently within the holistic practices of Ayurvedic, Unani, and traditional Chinese medicine. Its leaves harbor an array of bioactive compounds that contribute to its therapeutic properties, including phenols, tannins, and saponins, which collectively endow the plant with antimicrobial, antifungal, and anti-inflammatory properties (Guha, 2006; Kumari and Babu Rao, 2014). Within Ayurveda, P. betle is esteemed for its role in balancing the kapha and vata doshas, often being prescribed to alleviate respiratory ailments, enhance digestion, and even as a remedy for bad breath due to its aromatic prowess (Pradhan et al., 2013). The heritage of P. betle within the medicinal domain did not remain confined to the ancient sages and healers of the East. Modern pharmacological investigations have unveiled its potential benefits in preventing oxidative stress and offering cardio-protective effects, further consolidating its status as a plant of immense medicinal promise (Khan et al., 2013). Additionally, its efficacy in wound healing and its antiseptic nature has garnered attention, leading contemporary scientists to delve deeper into unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying its therapeutic effects. The role of P. betle transcends the boundaries of medical utility and ventures into the social and ritualistic fabric of life in the regions where it is cultivated. In many Southeast Asian weddings, the betel leaf serves as a symbol of love and prosperity, often part of ceremonial exchanges between families (Guha, 2006). Its omnipresence in rituals and social gatherings underlines its cultural potency, where it sustains not only traditions but also communal relationships, acting as a conduit of social lubrication. In contemporary settings, efforts to conserve P. betle and other traditionally significant plants are on the rise, as they face threats from urbanization, agricultural shifts, and climate change. The onus is on researchers and conservationists to document traditional knowledge and integrate it with modern scientific perspectives to ensure the perpetuation of these ancient practices (Pradhan et al., 2013). This synthesis of tradition and modernity holds promise for innovative health solutions, revealing that age-old wisdom has much to offer modern science. Furthermore, the commercial potential of P. betle cannot be overlooked. With increasing interest in natural and organic products, P. betle's extract manifests as a key ingredient in numerous health and wellness products, ranging from toothpaste to cosmetics, highlighting its multifaceted utility (Khan et al., 2013; Kumari and Babu Rao, 2014). By investing in sustainable cultivation practices and ensuring fair trade, stakeholders can secure both the plant's future and the cultural heritage it supports. P. betle, in its myriad dimensions, stands as a testament to the profound interconnectedness of nature, culture, and health. Its journey from the wild vines of Malaysia to the bustling markets of Kathmandu and vibrant streets of Kolkata embodies a bridge between the past and future, a living tribute to the enduring dialogue between humanity and the natural world. As we continue to explore and document such remarkable plants, the intrinsic wisdom encapsulated within their leaves and roots offers hope for holistic and harmonious advancements in human well-being, promising a greener and more informed approach to health and vitality.

The "true path" is the one path by which we arrive at true cessation. Hinayana To attain nirvana, we must follow a prescribed path: the true path, or the Four Noble Truths. Hinayana and Mahayana represent two schools of thought by which we discern this path. According to Hinayana, the so-called Smaller vehicle, whose practitioners seek nirvana for their own sake, the mind should be trained to exercise a will strong enough to renounce samsara. The practitioner should pursue religious ethics and simultaneously practice meditative absorption and insight so that delusion and its seeds may be purged, ultimately, never to grow again. Thus, we attain nirvana. The paths to be followed are the Paths of Preparation, Application, Seeing, Practice, and Fulfillment. Mahayana Followers of Mahayana, the so-called Greater Vehicle, aim at attaining the highest stage o f nirvana-buddhahood. They do this not only for themselves but also for all sentient beings. Motivated by the aspiration of Enlightenment and by compassion for all sentient beings, Mahayanists follow almost the same path as Hinayanists, but they also practice other expedient means such as the Six Perfections. By these methods, they seek to rid themselves of delusion as well as the defilement of karmic imprints, thereby working to attain buddhahood. Although the five paths are the same for both vehicles-Preparation, Application, seeing, Practice, and Fulfillment - a qualitative difference is that Mahayana emphasizes the motivation to benefit all beings. It is said that Hinayanists who have achieved nirvana will eventually adopt methods to attain buddhahood. Tantrayana The paths I have mentioned are doctrinal paths that aspirants must follow to provide a sound foundation before practicing Tantrayana, the way of yogic methods. The Tibetan School took great care before introducing any tantric doctrine. Spiritual teachers always investigated whether the doctrine was among those the Buddha preached. Competent pandits submitted it to logical analysis, and tested it in the light of experience, before confirming its authenticity and adopting it. This process was necessary because there were many non-Buddhist tantric doctrines that were apt to be confused with those of Buddhism because of their superficial resemblance. Tantrayana falls into four classes and includes a vast number of treatises that cannot be enumerated here. In the simplest terms, according to this system as already explained, negative karma is considered the cause of the various kinds of misery we suffer. Negative karma results from delusion, which is essentially the product of an undisciplined mind. Therefore, the mind needs to be disciplined and controlled by exercises that stop the flow of harmful and negative thoughts. This flow can be stopped and the wandering or projecting mind brought to rest by concentration on the makeup of one's mind. One can also focus one's mind on external objects to diminish negative thoughts. For this practice, one needs strong contemplative powers. The figures of deities have been found to be the most suitable objects, thus resulting in many images of deities in Tantrayana.

Although solid progress has been made in understanding humoral immune responses to EBOV in humans, less is known about the mechanisms underlying cellular immunity. It has been clearly demonstrated that CD8+ cytotoxic T cells (CTLs) are required for survival in macaques and that depletion of this subset in vaccinated animals results in complete abrogation of protection in lethal challenge models (Sullivan et al., 2011; Ruibal et al., 2016; Theaker et al., 2016; Simmons et al., 2004; Dikhit et al., 2015; Sundar et al., 2007; Yasmin and Nabi, 2016; Herrera et al., 2018; Sakabe et al., 2018). T cell epitopes in the EBOV nucleoprotein (NP) have been identified in immunized mice, and several computational studies have predicted further epitopes in both NP and GP. In humans, T cell responses to NP, GP, and VP40 determined by interferon-gamma ELISPOT have been described in both survivors and seropositive asymptomatic individuals. Although CD8+ T cell epitopes in the EBOV NP have been characterized in studies of Ebola survivors, to date no minimal epitopes have been characterized in the GP (Sakabe et al., 2018). This is despite the potent immunogenicity of the GP both in the context of natural infection (McElroy et al., 2015; Dahlke et al., 2017b) and in vaccines expressing GP as the target antigen (Dahlke et al., 2017a; Milligan et al., 2016; Ewer et al., 2016; Venkatraman et al., 2019). Identification of immunogenic epitopes in pathogen genomes has been used as a tool to generate novel vaccine candidates and identify potentially protective targets for CTL (Sanchez-Trincado et al., 2017). A number of in silico bioinformatics tools are available for prediction of epitopes and associated HLA-restriction elements (Soria-Guerra et al., 2015; Hoof et al., 2009). This information can be used to design so-called "mosaic" antigens; an approach that has been widely used for the development of novel HIV vaccines (Azizi et al., 2008; Fischer et al., 2007; Ondondo et al., 2016), particularly where broad coverage of conserved proteins is required. Characterization of protective or dominant HLA-restricted CD8+ T cell epitopes has been undertaken for a range of diseases, including influenza A, cytomegalovirus (CMV), HIV, and tuberculosis (TB) (McMichael et al., 1983; Wu et al., 2011; Borthwick et al., 2017; Lehmann et al., 2019; Lewinsohn et al., 2013). This information can be used to study mechanisms of immunity to inform rational vaccine design (Gras et al., 2010). Heterologous prime-boost vaccination with viral vectors elicits strong antibody and CTL responses, making them ideal candidates for immunization against EBOV. We have previously reported a clinical trial in which volunteers were primed with a monovalent chimpanzee adenovirus encoding the EBOV GP gene (Ewer et al., 2016). One to 10 weeks later, individuals were boosted with the multivalent MVA-BN-Filo vaccine, which encodes the EBOV, SUDV, and Marburgvirus GP and TAFV NP genes. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from these individuals were used to identify thirteen highly reactive nonamers.
