However, illumination of endothelial cell lining of the arteries that have possibly taken up PS can lead to atherosclerotic plaque rupture (Demidova and Hamblin, 2004), which should by all means be avoided. Therefore, selectively targeting the neo-vessels inside the plaques and/or the macrophages located in the plaques is highly desired. Importantly, most effective PS have low water solubility, therefore a simple intravenous injection is complicated and a safe solubilizing excipient or carrier system is necessary. If one aims for PDT to become the future treatment of atherosclerosis, the problems stated above have to be overcome (Mulder et al., 2014). A method to circumvent these problems is by encapsulating the hydrophobic PS in nanoparticles. Besides enabling intravenous injection, nanoparticles are also known for enhancing therapeutic efficacy and safety of encapsulated drugs by improving solubility, ability of combining multiple drugs, protecting against metabolism, and controlling release (Mulder et al., 2014; Szelenyi, 2012). Furthermore, the formation of leaky vessels from the vasa vasorum in atherosclerotic plaques allows for accumulation of nanoparticles by the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect inside the plaque and avoids uptake by the endothelium layer (Fang et al., 2011). Current research in atherosclerosis and nanoparticles primarily focuses on the targeted delivery of anti-inflammatory drugs (Lobatto et al., 2015; Sanchez-Gaytan et al., 2015; van der Valk et al., 2015), however such drugs usually only delay progression of atherosclerosis (Berman et al., 2013) thereby becoming a reoccurring medication during the lifetime of patients. In the present study we therefore combine the advantages of PDT and nanomedicine to develop a curative treatment for atherosclerosis. Meta-tetra(hydroxyphenyl)chlorine (mTHPC) is a photosensitizer currently used in the PDT treatment of squamous-cell carcinoma (Lorenz and Maier, 2008) and available in a variety of commercial and EMA approved formulations including liposomes (Foscan(R), FosLip(R), FosPEG(R)). Previous research in our group showed that benzyl-functionalized micelles based on poly( mu -caprolactone)-b-methoxy poly(ethylene glycol) (Ben-PCL-mPEG) block copolymers can encapsulate mTHPC with very high loadings and remarkable stability (Carstens et al., 2007, 2008; Hofman et al., 2008). Most interestingly, it was shown that the release and subsequent photocytotoxic activity of mTHPC are controlled by lipase induced enzymatic degradation of the micelles (Hofman et al., 2008). This can be advantageous since it is known that macrophages present in the plaque synthesize lipoprotein lipase (LPL) (O'Brien et al., 1992), and therefore we hypothesized that it could thus potentially promote local release and activation of the photosensitizer once the loaded micelles are delivered to and internalized by the macrophages. In this paper, mTHPC-loaded micelles were conveniently prepared by a film hydration method. We investigated if the LPL produced in macrophages can provide some cell specificity as compared to endothelial cells due to the enzymatic degradation of the micelles. The small size of the micelles might be advantageous for plaque penetration by the EPR effect.

Our results show sustained improvement during the preschool period as a result of early responsive stimulation (with or without enhanced nutrition) on child IQ, executive functions, pre-academic skills, and pro-social behaviours, while children who received early enhanced nutrition sustained significant benefits to motor development. Our study also contributes to the evidence by investigating sustained benefits to caregiving. Mothers who were exposed to early responsive stimulation (with or without enhanced nutrition) showed significant continued improvement in responsive caregiving behaviours and in the quality of the caregiving environment, while the enhanced nutrition exposure showed significant continued benefit to the quality of the caregiving environment. This longitudinal follow-up demonstrated that responsive stimulation delivered in a programme setting in a rural highly disadvantaged low-income and middle-income population can sustain benefits on children's development 2 years after the end of intervention. However, compared with the short-term effects at the end of the original intervention, the effect sizes are reduced. Implications of all the available evidence More studies are needed to investigate the independent and combined effects of early stimulation and nutrition interventions. These studies should be designed not only to provide insights into the effectiveness of these interventions, but also how to optimise integrated implementation. Further, in contexts such as Pakistan, in which access, retention, and attainment in future primary education remains extremely poor, the extent of development protection that early responsive stimulation might provide in the long term is likely to be small. Risks that threaten children's development will continue to accumulate; therefore strategies to bolster development along the life course should be explored. Evidence of the enduring effects of interventions that promote early child development on later life outcomes and the potential cost-benefits to society from low-income and middle-income countries is scarce.2,3 Only four cohorts (from Colombia and Jamaica) have been followed up after the original stimulation interventions were implemented between 1978 and 2004.6-10 The Jamaica cohort is the most prominent example of a cohort tracked into adulthood following exposure to early stimulation and nutrition interventions.6 In the efficacy randomised controlled trial, undernourished infants from poor neighbourhoods of Kingston, Jamaica, were randomly assigned into four groups to receive stimulation, nutritional supplementation, combined interventions, or control (standard health care). After 24 months of intervention exposure, both interventions had independent and additive benefits on child development and the nutrition intervention improved early growth. The effects of the stimulation intervention on cognitive capacity and behaviour were sustained into adulthood, whereas the nutrition intervention sustained small cognitive benefits only up to 7 years of age.

But as fate would have it, I found myself gravitating back to my true passion for vehicles, particularly in the realm of gaming. It was an odd juxtaposition, really; transported from sketches of everyday cars to the intricate designs of futuristic spacecraft. My leap into that universe ignited a spark I hadn't anticipated. Did you ever find yourself overwhelmed by the scope of where you could take your art? Absolutely. I mean, one minute, you're doodling cars in school notebooks, and the next, you're sketching out intergalactic vehicles that exist in entirely different realms. The initial challenge was absorbing all that information, you know? The technology, the physics-all of that plays a crucial role. But the cool thing is, when you design a vehicle, it's not just about the aesthetics. There's a story embedded in how that vehicle operates, who it belongs to, and what its purpose is. That narrative aspect is what excites me as much as the art itself. So, would you say that storytelling is a critical element in your design process? Without a doubt! Every line, every angle, even the color palette is a deliberate choice aimed at enhancing the narrative. When I start a project, I typically begin with brainstorming ideas related to the world surrounding the vehicle. Is it a post-apocalyptic world, a utopian future, or perhaps an alien planet? Each environment opens a myriad of possibilities for design. It frames the context in which this vehicle will not only exist but thrive. That's fascinating. Now, when you mention a vehicles' purpose-let's backtrack a bit. Can you talk about your transition from conceptual work to modeling? Oh, for sure! Once the concepts are fleshed out, the translation into 3D modeling is where the magic really happens. It's like taking a dream and materializing it into something tangible. At that point, every detail must be considered meticulously; things like construction materials, aerodynamics, and even usability. There's an intrinsic satisfaction in seeing a flat concept evolve into this robust 3D form that players can actually interact with. It adds a whole other layer of validation to the artistic journey, you know? Definitely, I can imagine! Speaking of materials and usability, what sorts of tools do you find help you the most in your workflow? I've found that tools like Blender for modeling, Substance Painter for texturing, and of course, Unreal Engine for implementation are invaluable. Each tool has its strengths, and I often find myself switching between them throughout a single project. A great piece of advice I'd give to anyone is to familiarize themselves with a mix of software-it really broadens your creative horizons. Now, transitioning back to your artistic beginnings, was there a defining moment or a particular artist who inspired you early on? Absolutely! I can't discount the impact of artists like Syd Mead and his work on films like Blade Runner. The way he intertwined form and function makes you rethink the relationship between art and storytelling. I remember seeing his designs for the first time and feeling like a door had opened, leading me into a world of endless possibilities. It sparked something deep within me-a desire to create worlds that provoke thought and emotion. His artistic philosophy deeply resonates with your own journey in vehicle design, it seems. What a compelling connection! Thank you! It's nice to see how our inspirations shape our paths, isn't it? By the way, I'm curious, have you ever collaborated with other artists on larger projects? How has that influenced your approach?

Her mother's determination and selflessness had inspired Lucy to take on her own role in the war effort, even if it meant leaving behind the comforts of home and family. She felt a pang of guilt for the ease with which she had settled into life at Highland House, surrounded by her cousins and their warm hospitality. Lucy smiled, remembering the afternoon she had spent helping the children with their gardening lesson. It had been a chaotic but joyful experience, with the children's giggles and shouts mingling with the sweet scent of the earth and the warm sunshine. As she lay there, Lucy's thoughts turned to Bob's letter, which she had read earlier that morning. His words had been full of humor and bravado, but she had detected a hint of longing beneath the surface. Do you want to feel worthy? Guess what? Lose some weight. It's the mantra we've all heard echoing in our heads, isn't it? This pervasive notion that a slimmer silhouette equates to a better life, a life filled with joy, fulfillment, and validation. And let me just pause for a moment to say-what a load of nonsense! Seriously, who came up with this? We've been sold this idea that if we just fit into that "ideal" mold, then we can unlock happiness, contentment, and all those magical rewards we've been dreaming of. But the truth is, my sweet friends, this narrative can lead us down a spiral of obsession, guilt, and misalignment with our true selves. Let's unpack this for a moment-not just over coffee, but deep into the realm of self-discovery and acceptance. Isn't it ironic that in our pursuit of weight loss, we often lose sight of the very thing we are trying to gain? Health? Confidence? Joy? Here's the kicker: when we focus too much on weight, we often neglect the incredible nuances of our bodies and minds that deserve appreciation. By perceiving weight loss as a "cure-all," we can easily slip into self-judgment and harsh comparisons, robbing ourselves of the true pleasures and experiences life has to offer. Let me share a personal anecdote, just to keep things relatable. A while back, I found myself trapped in that all-too-familiar cycle. I was convinced that losing those pesky pounds would make me happier, more social, and somehow more valid. But as I stood in front of my closet, starved of options and stuffed with body image insecurities, it dawned on me-what if I turned that energy toward gratitude for what my body can do rather than what it looks like? What if, instead of figuring out how to shrink myself, I focused on growing my sense of self-worth and exploration? So, here's my challenge for you, dear listeners. Instead of fixating on numbers that flicker on the scale or the reflection in the mirror, why not devote some time to your passions? Engage in activities that light you up! Dance like nobody's watching, paint that masterpiece (or, ya know, stick figures work too), or take that epic hike you've been dreaming about. Truly living, in all its messy, beautiful glory, doesn't require a certain body type. It requires a heart ready to embrace the moment. And here's where the plot thickens further. The relationships we cultivate with ourselves are perhaps the most essential of all. Instead of striving to alter how we look, how about we pivot to celebrating who we are, both within and outside? Let's replace the weight-loss dialogue with conversations around self-love, nourishment, joy, and acceptance. Because guess what? You do not need to shrink to fit into this world. You are inherently worthy, just as you are in this very moment, imperfections and all. So as we journey together through this wild world swirling with diet culture narratives, remember this: your value is not tethered to a number. Your essence is rooted in authenticity, in kindness toward yourself, and in unapologetic love for the body that carries you through life. Now go forth, my beautiful friends, and choose a path of empowerment over restriction!

The northwest European continental shelf, as part of the northeast Atlantic, is not only susceptible to the global climate's variability and long-term anthropogenic change but also faces direct anthropogenic pressures from its proximity to the industrialized regions of northern Europe. The combination of these factors has a profound impact on the shelf sea ecosystem, with far-reaching consequences for the environment and human communities that depend on it. The direct anthropogenic pressures on the northwest European continental shelf are numerous and varied. Fishing activity, such as demersal trawling, not only disturbs the seabed but also induces mortality in benthic fauna, leading to disruptions in food webs and biogeochemical cycles in the vicinity of the disturbance (Kaiser et al., 2006). The impact of fishing activity is exacerbated by the fact that many species of fish and invertebrates are already vulnerable to climate-related changes, such as shifts in distribution and abundance (Holt et al., 2012). In addition to fishing, riverine nutrient input to the ocean is another significant source of anthropogenic pressure. High nutrient loads or imbalances in the ratio of nutrients can lead to deleterious eutrophication impacts, such as high biomass, toxic algal blooms, and near-bed hypoxia (Cadee and Hegeman, 2002; Anderson et al., 2002; Dethlefsen and Von Westernhagen, 1983). These impacts can have far-reaching consequences for the entire ecosystem, from the base of the food web to the top predators. The policy driver behind this work is the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD: Directive 2008/56/EC) of the European Commission, which requires member states to develop strategies to achieve a healthy marine environment and make ecosystems more resilient to climate change in all European marine waters by 2020 at the latest. To achieve this goal, it is essential to understand the complex interactions between climate change, anthropogenic pressures, and ecosystem responses. The northwest European continental shelf is a critical region for understanding these interactions, as it is characterized by a unique combination of oceanographic and ecological features. The shelf's proximity to the open ocean and its connection to the North Sea and the Atlantic Ocean create a complex circulation pattern, which influences the distribution of heat, nutrients, and marine life. The region's coastal ecosystems are also highly productive, with many areas of high biodiversity and ecological importance. To address the challenges posed by climate change and anthropogenic pressures, it is essential to develop a comprehensive understanding of the northwest European continental shelf's ecosystem dynamics. This requires a multidisciplinary approach that integrates knowledge from oceanography, ecology, biology, and policy. By combining these disciplines, scientists and policymakers can develop effective strategies to mitigate the impacts of climate change and anthropogenic pressures, and to achieve a healthy and resilient marine environment for future generations.

"I knew him in the 1990s, I admired him, I admired what he stood for, and I hope now a thorough investigation will determine who is responsible for this outrage." The opposition politician was shot Friday night as he walked across a bridge about 100 meters (330 feet) from the Kremlin with his girlfriend, Ukrainian model Anna Duritskaya, 23. Duritskaya - the only known witness to the shooting - left Moscow for Kiev late on Monday. She had been staying at the apartment of an aide to Nemtsov under constant police guard. Her mother, Inna Duritskaya, told CNN on Monday that her daughter faces constant psychological pressure from Moscow authorities and fears she will be implicated in his death. The Moscow Investigative Committee said Duritskaya was not detained while in Moscow and that she was offered witness protection, which she turned down. Duritskaya was free to leave at any point but wanted to give her testimony and contribute to the investigation process, "understanding the important of it for the investigation," the statement said. "It is needless to state how important her testimony is." Edward Lucas, a senior editor for The Economist and a senior vice president at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told CNN that the manner of Nemtsov's death was highly suspicious. "The circumstances of his shooting point very much to official involvement," he said. "If it was some random, ragtag extremist militia from eastern Ukraine killing him, I doubt they would've been able to do it with such precision in the heart of Moscow." Lucas also said that the recent history of politically motivated killings in Russia suggested that the investigation would come to little. "One of the signal things that they all have in common is that they are not cleared up. We have a lot of bluster at the time of the death, promises of investigation, but either the culprits are never found or the culprits who are found are very unconvincing ones and the people who gave the orders are never identified." Meanwhile, he said, the Kremlin continues to pump out propaganda which suggests opposition activists or those critical of Russia's involvement in Ukraine are traitors to their country. Some of Nemtsov's supporters accuse the Kremlin, if not of direct involvement, of creating an atmosphere of hatred which fostered the killing. Not everyone who hoped to attend Nemtsov's funeral has been able to do so. Latvia's former foreign minister and European Parliament member Sandra Kalniete said she was denied entry to Russia on Monday night on spurious grounds.

Tucker leaned back in his chair, a smug grin plastered across his face, reveling in the disbelief of his audience. "Yep," Tucker replied, drawing out the word for maximum effect. "Remember last summer when I took that solo trip down the coast? Met her at a friend's party. Didn't even realize she was deaf until we were midway through a conversation." Jeff shook his head, still not convinced. "You mean she didn't say anything?" "Well, she did," Tucker replied with a chuckle, "but it's the way she was speaking. It wasn't until she whipped out her phone and started typing, 'I can't hear you!' that it all clicked. Kind of refreshing not having to shout over club music, you know?" This revelation drew a murmur of amusement from the group, a mix of admiration and envy. One of them cocked his head, curiosity piqued. "So, what? There's like, a special language or something?" Tucker nodded, leaning forward to share his wisdom. "Yeah, it's called sign language. Took me a bit to get the hang of it, but it's fascinating once you dive in. We had our little communication system worked out. Pretty cool, actually." "You learn how to say 'I love you' or something?" another friend teased, jabbing Tucker playfully. "Something like that," Tucker returned, unfazed. "It's amazing what you can say without words." Jeff shook his head, absorbing it all while offering a rueful grin. "Man, you do manage to find the weirdest adventures." "Not weird," Tucker corrected with a wag of his finger, "just different. Makes life interesting." "Alright, alright, Mr. Interesting Life," Jeff conceded, rolling his eyes. "So what was her name?" Tucker tapped a finger to his chin momentarily, pretending to ponder before breaking into laughter. "No idea. Didn't think to ask, really. Too busy having my mind blown." This confession elicited an uproar of laughter from the table, shaking heads and shared looks of disbelief marking the collective reaction. Amid the banter, Tucker's buoyant attitude was infectious, drawing everyone more deeply into his orbit. Jeff chuckled, shaking his head once more. "You're something else, man. Your future wife better be ready for all this craziness." Tucker shrugged nonchalantly. "Can't help it if I keep life interesting." The rest of the group slowly dispersed, the library resuming its usual studious ambiance. Jeff lingered for a moment, eyeing Tucker. "Thanks, man," Jeff said finally, sincerity lining his words. "Needed the laugh today." "Anytime," Tucker replied with a grin, patting Jeff on the shoulder as they both stood up to leave. "Just wait until the bachelor party." "Do I even want to know?" Tucker merely winked, gesturing with a finger to his lips. "Trust me, you'll love it." Walking out of the library together, their voices faded among the steady hum of activity. As they disappeared into the corridor, one couldn't help but wonder where life would take them next, especially with Tucker's penchant for surprises waiting just around the corner.

Mary's thoughts drifted to their inevitable talk with Zoey, mentally rehearsing words she worried might only widen the gap already forming between them. James would be bustling back through the door soon, with his professional charm worn thin by the day's dealings. He would take over preparations, check and double-check every system as the aria of tension built slowly around their home-a silent crescendo leading to the inevitable chime of the first sirens at dusk. Grasping her resolve, Mary eased off the sofa to climb the staircase leading to Zoey's door. There, she hesitated briefly, hand poised to knock, mind braced for a conversation fraught with love and conflict, as the first tinges of deepening shadow crept beneath the thickening clouds of night.

The cathode electrode can be limiting for MFC operation, which is why many groups still rely on platinum and other catalysts. However, there has been significant progress in recent years in developing materials comparable to platinum - in the short term - or even preferable to platinum in the long term (Cheng and Wu, 2013). The competitive advantage of these materials, compared to platinum, is the lower cost. One other component that requires attention is the ion exchange membrane (IEM). MFCs use liquid feedstock in the anode, which in itself can carry charged ions such as protons, and so the IEM is not an essential requirement (Logan, 2008), provided that there is physical or electrochemical separation between the anode and cathode electrodes. One strategy is therefore simply to remove the membrane altogether from the design and membrane-less MFCs have been described in the literature (Liu and Logan, 2004). Whilst this design reduces the cost of the reactor, it also has the disadvantage of oxygen diffusion towards the anode electrode and the requirement to keep the electrodes a certain distance apart. Furthermore, the chassis of membrane-less reactors still needs to be built from rigid materials and often these are plastic-based. An ideal scenario then, would be an inexpensive material that doubles as both the chassis and the medium for proton exchange. This would also enable electrodes to be in close proximity to each other whilst preventing a high flux of oxygen to the anode. A number of porous materials have been reported including microporous filtration membranes (Zuo et al., 2007), canvas (Zhuang et al., 2009), nylon infused membrane (Hernandez-Fernandez et al., 2015) and paper (Winfield et al., 2015). Furthermore, there have been some thorough investigations comparing a number of these low cost separators in terms of enhancing power generation and allowing field application (Kondaveeti et al., 2014). Perhaps the most exciting of the porous materials to be used in MFCs is ceramic. MFCs are operated in less extreme environments than the SOFCs because the mesophilic bacteria thrive in much lower, ambient temperatures. It's a chaotic ecosystem, really. Each day unfolds like a poorly scripted teen drama, complete with plot twists that only serve to amplify the confusion. The cafeteria, or as I like to call it, the social battleground, is where alliances are formed and rivalries are ignited. You can almost hear the whispers cloaked in the scent of overcooked pasta and suspiciously soggy fries, the kind of whispers that float through the air like a couple of gossipy vultures circling fresh roadkill. The infamous Tuna Meltdown Tuesdays are particularly noteworthy, as the smell alone can send even the most loyal seniors fleeing to the nearest port of call for a semblance of culinary deliverance. Outside the cafeteria, the hallways pulsate with a frenetic energy. The air is thick with secrets and stolen glances. The hall monitors-only slightly more authoritative than the kids themselves-fail to notice some of the more clandestine exchanges, like that time I accidentally walked in on a secret meeting of the chess club turned underground rave on the upper deck. They thought they were "cultured," bonded over energy drinks and mismatched socks until they realized that their meeting spot doubled as the deck where the crew was supposed to offload supplies. Oops. But hey, who needs rules when you have the thrill of a stolen midnight encounter? Then, of course, there are the captains of this ship-shaped soap opera. Some of the officers strut around like they own the place, looking down their noses at everyone, particularly the 'shoppies', whom they perceive as little more than floating distractions. It's an interesting kind of power dynamic, ripe for those fleeting moments of drama that our lives lack at home. You'd think they were the kings of some grand castle, but at the end of the day, they, too, are just another notch in this high school hierarchy. Let me not forget the awkward crushes bubbling just beneath the surface. In a space this confined, feelings are magnified and spread like wildfire. One moment, a casual locker-room banter; the next, you've got someone serenading another in the corner, saying sweet nothings to the tune of a local sea shanty. It's beyond cringeworthy, yet somehow endearingly innocent too. And that-perhaps-serves as the true essence of this floating institution: a collage of youth, folly, and the faintest hope for something more. And when night falls, the ship takes on a different personality altogether. Suddenly, we're not bound by the cliques of the day. The ship transforms, lit by the soft glow of party lights, and we tumble into a world where everyone forgets they're just characters in a drama. Here, we might all become the stars of our own feature-length film, trading in our uniforms for silly outfits and merging our personal dramas into one chaotic narrative of laughter and liberating chaos. But as dawn breaks and reality sets back in, we don our uniforms anew, chuckling softly at last night's outrageousness, securing the fresh memories deep in the vault of "Did that really happen?" Perhaps this is what keeps us afloat in this unpredictable high school of the seas, the promise of unpredictable experiences and a laughter that echoes against the endless, lapping waves.

A more recent approach to code optimality is an 'engineering approach', which uses a genetic algorithm (GA) to search for the best and the worst code for a property following a chosen evolutionary hypothesis. The GA starts with a random code, which is run through multiple cycles of variation and selection in order to find the extreme values. Since GAs can be stuck in local extrema, the GA is run with different random starting codes. Finding the best and worst codes allows calculation of the distances of the SGC to these codes (Blazj et al., 2018) and also allows inferring the scale of optimization and how difficult it is to evolve the code. But it is not possible to determine whether the SGC has been optimized at all in this approach. If the set of possible codes is not distributed symmetrically around some mean value, it could be that the worst code is much further away from most codes than the best code is. So, even if the distance of the SGC to the best code is much smaller than to the worst code it does not necessarily mean that the SGC has been optimized. Also it is not clear what level of optimization for a given property we should expect under a hypothesis of selection. Assuming the SGC has evolved through selection, the SGC could have evolved to a local or even global fitness peak, but the fitness of the SGC may not only be determined by a single property but simultaneously by many. Most studies only consider a single property as it is not clear how to weight different properties and combine them into a fitness function. Studying only a single property might create lower values of optimality. It is also not clear how far the SGC has been optimized. The process could have been stopped before a maximum was reached. One possible cause is Crick's concept of the 'frozen accident' (Crick, 1968), namely that the organism carrying the SGC was complex enough such that a change in the SGC would be more deleterious than beneficial. Another possible scenario is fixation of the code following the evolution of horizontal gene transfer (HGT). In order for HGT to be efficient all organisms need to have the same genetic code, which has been shown to lead to stable convergence to a single code (Aggarwal et al., 2016). An objection to the optimization hypothesis is that it appears that many steps are needed on average to create a code as optimal as the SGC (Massey, 2010). However this does not make the optimization hypothesis hugely more unlikely than any alternatives, as the evolution of the SGC was noted as a 'notoriously difficult problem' from the beginning (Crick et al., 1976), before the optimization was recognised, and remains so today (Kun and Radvanyi, 2018). In this study we are interested in determining whether the genetic code shows evidence of having been optimized or not, thus we use the 'statistical approach'.

In particular, the literature shows that transfers do not result in unwanted impacts such as increased spending on alcohol or tobacco (Evans & Popova, 2017) and reduced labor supply (Izmalkov, 2004), and that cash transfers have positive impacts on a wide variety of welfare indicators, such as consumption, assets and educational status. The literature has firmly established that cash transfers have significant benefits and limited costs (Bastagli et al., 2016), partially legitimizing the poor but efficient hypothesis. In addition, though Schultz's hypothesis was highly influential (Nerlove, 1999, Abler & Sukhatme, 2006), some researchers contend that empirical data is inconsistent with efficient allocation of resources by agricultural households, or holds only for specific forms of efficiency (Ball & Pounder, 1996; Shapiro, 1983; Nyariki, 2011; Umar, 2014). Finally, the application of behavioral economics to development has suggested that behavioral biases may lead to irrational decision making, and perhaps an inefficient allocation of resources. The view put forth is not that the poor are intrinsically less rational than the rich, but that they are equally irrational, and that the condition of poverty may augment the negative effects of irrational decisions (Bertrand, Mullainathan, & Shafir, 2004; Bernheim, Ray, & Yeltekin, 2015; Mani, Mullainathan, Shafir, & Zhao, 2013). The behavioral economics view has spawned a new class of behaviorally informed development interventions (e.g., Ashraf, Karlan, & Yin, 2006; Duflo, Kremer, & Robinson, 2011; Duflo & Hanna, 2005). In light of this research, the behavioralist view of aid suggests that interventions should be designed to shape the decisions of aid recipients to generate optimal long-term outcomes, and cash transfers fully at the disposal of recipients may not generate these optimal outcomes. While behavioral interventions in development have become more common, and though traditional commodity based assistance continues, the enthusiasm of the aid industry for cash transfers appears to have grown in recent years. The mutual existence of these approaches to aid creates a tension between the behavioralist and Schultzian view: are development outcomes best achieved by enabling aid recipients to optimize according to their unique information and constraints? Or is it better for the aid industry to implicitly or explicitly influence the decisions of recipients and the use of aid resources? This study addresses this question empirically by assessing whether individuals who express a high valuation for a particular assistance program benefit more from that program than similar individuals who receive an equally valuable resource. Through a randomized controlled trial, low-income Kenyans were selected to receive either a particular non-cash development program (agricultural extension, agricultural inputs, poultry transfers) or an amount of cash equal to the cost of the program. Prior to receiving any intervention, we elicited respondents' indifference point between cash and the program in question. Subsequently, we randomly assigned individuals to receive a program or a cash transfer equal to its cost.

The roses, with their heady aroma wafting through the rooms, transform the atmosphere into something almost ethereal, like stepping through a portal where time briefly stands still. Each bloom carries with it a sense of history, a lineage that speaks of countless summers past. They are the whispers of a garden alive with the songs of bees and the floating thrum of dragonfly wings. As I fill my home with these storied petals, the vibrant color palette-from the softest blush to the deepest scarlet-mirrors the dawn sky, holding within them the echoes of classical poets and mystics. The rose's lineage is long, its ancestry often discussed in hushed tones by those who understand its storied past. In each petal lies an elegy penned by time itself, a reminder of the beauty that binds generations across the ages. In Victorian times, floriography-the language of flowers-granted roses a spoken voice. Red spoke of passionate love, white of purity and innocence, while the yellow rose cheerfully connoted friendship. Today, though fewer may read the language of petals, their meanings persist in the collective consciousness, their symbolism ingrained as deeply as the scent within their folds. A walk through the garden offers more than just visual pleasure; it's a tapestry alive with memory and potential. Every bush is richly threaded with stories, a living chronicle of care, compost, and seasonal nurture. A careful pruning here, a watchful eye against the unwanted explorers of aphid and fungal disease there, all bear testament to the gardener's ongoing devotion. They tell of the hands that coaxed them from mere cuttings into full, mature blooms, and the many seasons spent folded against the frost, waiting patiently to unfurl once more. There's an inherent democracy in a garden rose-available to all who care to cultivate them. Their stately poise does not require a king's ransom but the humble outlay of earth, water, and time. Those new to gardening can find camaraderie with seasoned cultivators, both drawn by an inexplicable magnetism to this royal bloom. And what of the serendipitous beauty of nature's arrangement? These blooms, set against an informal cottage backdrop, assume an unparalleled charm, tumbling effervescently over pathways, pruned hedges demurely supporting their careless overflow. Here, nature overrides artifice; a capricious breeze will play with heavy-head sways, and petals will eventually scatter, each drift across the flagstone like the falling notes of an orchestral symphony. The roses, as twilight descends, dare us to imagine more. Each night, as shadows lengthen, they inhale the day's warmth, exhaling it as fragrance into the cool evening air-a bewitching, lingering caress. It's in these quiet moments, perhaps, that the rose is most profound. Unseen by the busy eyes of daylight, their true spirit emerges, whispering secrets to the moon and stars, and to anyone who takes the time to pause and listen. To walk among them is to brush up against the fabric of both past and present; a gentle reminder of timeless beauty that holds the power to soften hearts, to pause thoughts, and to inspire stories anew.

Now that he stood before him in his torn coat he looked the very image of a beggar. He was one of those poor ordinary clerks, nicknamed in Russia "inky souls," "pettifoggers." Hard were his wrinkles as though fossilized, hard the cold look in the small dim eyes, hard his neglected grizzled beard, his face colourless and dull as the papers which he had been copying and had pored over may be for thirty years in his office. He had accepted bribes from agents "in all fairness"; he may have even been guilty of roguery, and this was the conclusion he had suddenly arrived at: Antichrist is coming! "Is he not simply an impostor?" surmised the Tsarevitch, looking steadily at him. There was nothing deceitful or sly in this face, but rather something artless and helpless, sombre and stubborn, as with people who are possessed by an idee fixe. "There was yet another reason for my coming here," added the old man, and then stopped short, unable to continue; the idee fixe was slowly working its way through his hard features. He cast down his eyes, fumbled with one hand in his breast pocket, pulled out some papers, which had apparently slipped into the lining through the pocket-hole, and gave them to the Tsarevitch. They consisted of two thin, greasy, quarto booklets, filled with the large legible handwriting of a clerk. Alexis began to read them carelessly, but gradually became more and more absorbed. At the beginning came passages from the Holy Fathers, the prophets, and the Apocalypse, with reference to Antichrist and the end of the world. Then followed an appeal to the chief clergy of great Russia, and of the world, together with a prayer that they would forgive him, Dokoukin, his impudence and rudeness for thus writing this without their fatherly blessing, prompted as he had been solely by much suffering, sorrow and zeal for the Church, and with a further prayer that they would also intercede on his behalf with the Tsar and entreat him to show mercy unto himself, and vouchsafe him a hearing. Then followed what was evidently Dokoukin's main idea, "God has ordained man to be master of himself (to exercise self-will, to be autonomous,)" and at the end came an accusation against the Tsar Peter: "Nowadays we are cut off from this divine gift-life absolute and free; as well as deprived of houses, markets, agriculture, handicrafts and all the old established trades and laws, and, what is worse still, of Christian religion. We are hunted from house to house, from place to place, from town to town; we are insulted and outraged.

It is a multi-period, spatially-resolved multi-echelon model considering the production of hydrogen, for fuel cell vehicles, from natural gas, electricity, biomass and coal. The model represents GB spatially using 34 square cells and considers the transition from 2015 to 2044 using 6 five-year periods. The focus of the model is on the hydrogen network alone: it determines the location of the hydrogen-production technologies and the transport of hydrogen between the cells but the raw materials cannot be transported. The operation of the network is based on a user-specified daily demand for hydrogen in each cell and each period that represents the average demand over a five-year period. While others have used variants of this model in a number of studies, e.g. Refs. [8-18], they have similarly focused on a long-term horizon and not considered any finer time resolution. As the model was designed only to consider these five-year periods, it is not suitable for the problem described above, where it is necessary to account for hour-by-hour operation of the network including a proper inventory balance for storage. The model is also unable to convert hydrogen back to electricity, due to its multi-echelon nature, and is therefore not sufficiently flexible to cover all possible routes from wind power to hydrogen-powered transport. Conversely, there are models that focus on the operation of the network for a pre-determined design (the locations and size of the technologies are fixed), an example of which is that of Chaudry and co-workers [19,20]. The original model [19] was developed to optimise the operation of gas-electricity networks over 30 one-day intervals. It has recently been extended to include wind generation and hydrogen injection into the natural gas grid and the operation of the network was optimised over 24 one-hour intervals [20]. Finally, the last group of models can determine the design and/or operation of stand-alone renewable energy networks but because there are no spatial representation in these models, the transport of energy between technologies installed at different locations cannot be modelled. Examples of such models include [21-27]. In the context of modelling and optimising integrated energy networks that include intermittent renewables with a detailed representation of storage, which will almost certainly be needed to increase the contribution of renewables on the grid, the models described above lack one or more of the elements required. Although the hydrogen supply chain model of Almansoori and Shah [7] was not designed for the short time scales required to model intermittent renewables and does not include an inventory balance for energy storage, it is also not sufficiently flexible to allow all possible pathways to be modelled, especially circular ones (e.g. conversion of electricity to hydrogen and back again).

Although it is not currently possible to detect cytoarchitectonic boundaries within the cingulate cortex using fMRI alone, it is possible to partition the cingulate cortex into sub-regions with unique connectivity fingerprints (Beckmann et al., 2009; Neubert et al., 2015). This makes the cingulate cortex an excellent model to establish our data-driven parcellation approach. As well as being an excellent model for investigating connectivity-based parcellation, the cingulate cortex is also one of the most reported structures implicated in ASD (Cauda et al., 2011). There is a large body of literature highlighting that individuals with ASD have differences in cingulate anatomy and cytoarchitecture, cingulate connectivity as measured by RS-fMRI and DTI, and cingulate function. Post mortem studies of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) have shown that Area 32 in individuals with ASD has decreased long range fibres but increased short-range connections (Zikopoulos and Barbas, 2010), whilst Area 24b showed significantly decreased neuron size and area in ASD, and Area 24c shows decreased neuron density in layer VVI in ASD (Simms et al., 2009). Simms et al. (2009) also investigated the presence of Von Economo Neurons (VENs), and found that three of the nine cases presented with a significant increase in VENs whilst the remaining six presented with a significant decrease in VENs. The heterogeneity present in these post-mortem analyses is also present in-vivo structural analyses such as voxel based morphology (VBM), as well as cortical thickness and surface area. In a meta-analysis of VBM studies by Cauda et al. (2011) they found that individuals with ASD showed a significant increase in subgenual ACC grey matter volume (putatively Area 33). However, two other meta-analyses conducted by Nickl-Jockschat et al. (2012) and Via et al. (2011) did not find any differences in cingulate cortex grey matter (GM) volume in ASD. It is possible that this variability is due to differences in the developmental trajectory of individuals with ASD, and depending on the age of acquisition you may or may not find group differences (Uddin et al., 2013). Indeed, Duerden et al. (2011) found that children and adolescents with ASD were more likely to show a difference in cortical thickness in the ACC compared to adults with ASD. Greimel et al. (2013) also showed different developmental trajectories in GM volume in the middle cingulate cortex (MCC), although similar studies by Foster et al. (2015) and Zielinski et al. (2014) did not find Group * Age interactions in the cingulate cortex. There is also a large body of literature using fMRI and functional connectivity (RS-fMRI) to investigate the cingulate cortex in ASD. However, the majority of these studies have investigated the default mode network (DMN) in ASD rather than the cingulate cortex specifically. Like the cingulate cortex, the DMN has been linked to social cognition and theory of mind processes (Buckner et al., 2008), making the DMN a target for investigation in ASD.

The fact that univariate models work better than multivariate ones is puzzling, because economic theory would suggest that fiscal variables should be tightly intertwined, and therefore, in theory, models based on a system of macroeconomic variables, such as VARs, should produce better forecasts than simple univariate specifications. Favero and Marcellino (2005) suggest that these results are due mostly to the short sample available with respect to the number of coefficients to be estimated (overparameterization), the robustness of simple methods to structural breaks, and the difficulty of modelling the joint behaviors of several variables in a period of substantial institutional and economic change. In this paper, we consider using econometric models that can deal with these problems efficiently. The models that we consider allow the information contained in a large data set to be used without incurring the overparameterization problem, and can allow for time variation in the coefficients and the volatilities, a characteristic which makes them robust to structural changes, regardless of whether such changes happen smoothly or abruptly (breaks). We show that once overparameterization and structural change have been dealt with appropriately, multivariate models do provide a better description of the macroeconomy than univariate specifications, and the use of a large panel of macroeconomic data does provide improvements in terms of forecast accuracy. A key aspect in the forecasting of macroeconomic variables is the assessment of the overall uncertainty that exists around point forecasts. This aspect seems particularly relevant for fiscal variables, as assessments of fiscal stability and of the overall credit and default risk of a country should typically be based on the specification of a complete probability distribution for the future state of the economy. Accordingly, the second contribution of this paper is to focus on forecasting the whole predictive distribution of fiscal variables, rather than limiting the interest to point forecasts only. Our empirical results show that the use of models that allow for drifting coefficients and volatility does provide a better characterization of the uncertainty in the economy, which translates into substantial gains in density forecasts with respect to simpler specifications with constant coefficients and volatilities. To deal with the problem of overparameterization, we consider the use of Bayesian Vector Autoregressions (BVARs). BVARs have a long history in forecasting, stimulated by their effectiveness, as documented in the seminal studies of Doan, Litterman, and Sims (1984) and Litterman (1986). In recent years, these models seem to have been being used even more systematically for policy analysis and the forecasting of macroeconomic variables. Starting from the paper of Banbura, Giannone, and Reichlin (2010), the benefits of using BVARs for macroeconomic forecasting using large data-sets have been documented in several recent papers (e.g., Carriero, Clark, & Marcellino, 2013a; Carriero, Kapetanios, & Marcellino, 2011; Koop, 2013).

The moon, now higher in the sky, cast a silver glow over the scene, illuminating the tender expression on Imelda's face. Norman's eyes, still filled with surprise and longing, searched hers for an explanation. "Keep your lover?" he repeated, his voice low and husky. "What do you mean by that, Imelda? Do you mean to say that you love me, but you are already bound to another?" The words hung in the air like a challenge, and Imelda's face grew pale beneath the moon's gentle light. Norman's grip on her hand tightened, his fingers digging into her skin as if trying to hold onto her words. "Tell me, Imelda, is it true? Are you already promised to another?" The words were torn from him, and Imelda's eyes seemed to cloud over as she struggled to find the right words. The silence that followed was oppressive, heavy with unspoken secrets and unrequited love. The sound of crickets and the distant hum of a night bird broke the stillness, and Norman's eyes never left Imelda's face. He felt his heart racing, his mind reeling with the possibilities. Could it be true? Was she already promised to another? The thought was like a knife twisting in his chest, and he felt his breath catch in his throat. Imelda's eyes, still clouded, seemed to bore into his very soul. He could feel her turmoil, her uncertainty, and his own emotions swirled in a maelstrom of confusion. The world around them melted away, leaving only the two of them, suspended in a sea of uncertainty. And then, as if a dam had burst, Imelda's words poured forth in a torrent. "Norman, I do not know what to do. I love you, I do, but I am bound to another by a promise made long ago. A promise I made in innocence, in ignorance of the feelings that have grown within me for you." Her voice was barely above a whisper, and Norman's heart went out to her, his love for her deepening with every word. The moon continued its steady course across the sky, casting its silvery light over the couple, as they stood there, lost in a world of their own making. The air was heavy with the scent of roses and new-mown hay, and the sound of crickets provided a soothing background hum, a reminder of the beauty and wonder of the world around them.

As the digital camera market continues to evolve, camera manufacturers are forced to think outside the box to stand out from the crowd. With the economy in a state of flux, consumers are becoming increasingly discerning about their purchases, and premium features are no longer enough to guarantee success. Instead, camera makers are turning to innovative technologies and unique selling points to differentiate themselves from the competition. One such innovation is the built-in GPS support found in Nikon's latest cameras. This feature allows photographers to record the exact location where a photo was taken, making it easier to organize and geotag images. While it may seem like a niche feature, it's precisely this kind of attention to detail that sets Nikon apart from its competitors. Another area where camera makers are pushing the boundaries is in high-speed video capabilities. Casio's EX-F1, for example, can shoot 16 frames per second in high-definition, making it ideal for capturing fast-moving subjects like sports and wildlife. This kind of feature is sure to appeal to enthusiasts and professionals alike, and could be a major selling point for Casio in a crowded market. The Micro Four Thirds camera system, developed jointly by Panasonic and Olympus, is another example of innovation in the digital camera space. This system offers a more compact and lightweight alternative to traditional DSLRs, making it perfect for travel and everyday shooting. With its interchangeable lenses and advanced image stabilization, the Micro Four Thirds system is a major player in the market, and its popularity shows no signs of waning. Despite the challenges facing the digital camera market, there are still opportunities for growth and innovation. As the market consolidates, smaller players may struggle to stay afloat, but those with the resources and vision to invest in premium features and innovative technologies will be well-positioned for success. For Canon, the challenge is to maintain its dominance in the compact camera market while also staying competitive in the SLR space. The company's G series has long been a favorite among enthusiasts, but with the rise of low-end DSLRs and high-end point-and-shoot cameras, Canon must continue to innovate to stay ahead of the curve. The company's latest G10 model offers impressive features like 14.7 megapixels of resolution and full manual controls, but it will need to continue to push the boundaries of what's possible in order to stay relevant. In the end, the digital camera market is a complex and ever-changing landscape, and only those companies that are willing to take risks and invest in innovation will be able to thrive. As the market continues to evolve, one thing is clear: the days of simply adding a few more megapixels to a camera and calling it a day are behind us. The future of digital photography belongs to those who are willing to think outside the box and push the boundaries of what's possible.

Glistening under the playful dance of sunlight, the water spread itself as a liquid tapestry, weaving stories beneath the shadows of elder and willow. Here, at the bridge, was a cherished vantage point, a perch where one could observe the lively art of trout in their native ballet. The trout, mischief gleaming in their eyes, dashed with swift elegance, teasing a child's imagination with their elusive nature. My fantasies, much like the waters themselves, would cascade and eddy, swirling with dreams of adventure and discovery. This river was a school of patience and wonder, with each ripple and shimmer bearing silent lessons. As the daylight lounged and the shadows lengthened, the river whispered ancient lullabies, recounting tales of seasons past. The banks were resplendent with the rustic attire of the countryside, decked in shades of emerald and umber, stroked lovingly by the gentle hand of spring breezes. Here, in this pastoral idyll, was a sanctuary, a place where the burdens of the outside world seemed to float away like an errant leaf upon the current. The melody of water and earth, intertwined so seamlessly, was a song that played upon the heartstrings, striking chords of nostalgia that lingered long after the sun had bid adieu to the day. The mischievous songbirds, heralds of joy and heralds of change, would flit from branch to branch, their notes intertwining with the river's symphony. These feathered minstrels contributed to the ever-changing chorus that was the valley's life. It was as if nature herself conducted an orchestra, with every whispering breeze and buzzing bee contributing to the grand opus. Amidst the verdant theatre stood the faithful watcher, the heron, poised with majestic patience, as though time itself dared not intrude upon its vigil. Nature's theatre had countless stories to tell, of foxes darting through the dusk and hares pausing in the moonlight's embrace. In the quiet solitude, lovers of tranquil beauty often found themselves entranced, swept away in reverie. As the river journeyed through its realm, it bore witness to the clandestine meetings of otters and the secret roundelays of dragonflies. Each creature, in its modest way, played its part in the great cycle of life that revolved ceaselessly around the water's edge. Yet, even in this bucolic joy, change loomed on the horizon. Rumors of iron and steam disturbed these gentle waters, threatening to carve new routes through ancient paths. What might once have seemed immutable now stood in the shadows of inevitability. The gentle heart of the river, accustomed to whispers and the soft padding of paws, would soon face the roar and clatter of human ambition. Even so, I held hope that this spirit would endure, flowing beneath the surface like the timeless undercurrent that had always been its secret strength. For in the end, the river would remain, its voice eternal, singing its song to those willing to pause, listen, and perhaps-just perhaps-understand its timeless tale. As day turned to night, and the stars cautiously peeked behind indigo curtains, the Culm, with grace and dignity, continued its dance toward destiny, assuring all who loved its flow that some dreams never cease.

To get back to the rising cost of unleaded, one would think, judging by the squeals from the American consumer, that the world was coming to an end. You would get the idea that there is a passage in the Bill of Rights guaranteeing that Americans will pay the same price for gasoline as their grandfathers. I'm not going to suggest that extra quarter or half buck a gallon isn't a hardship for some folks. But not for most. We have a country filled with people who will spend over a hundred dollars to buy brand-name sneakers for their kids, blow ten bucks on a lousy movie and another few dollars for seven cents worth of popcorn, squander a fortune on play stations a and, most telling of all, forty grand on an SUV that gets about four blocks to the gallon! When I point out that gas wasn't free before this, and that people managed to survive, I've had friends say that the problem isn't just at the pump, but the additional costs added on to everything we buy because of the added costs of shipping them. To them, I point out that, inevitably, the price of gas will go down, but the added-on costs of all those other items won't a but nobody will raise a stink about it, just as nobody will say anything nice about the falling price of petrol. Speaking of SUVs, how is it that everyone who interviews Arianna Huffington, archenemy of those over-priced, over-sized vehicles, never nails the lady for her blatant hypocrisy? Let's face it: The only reason anybody has even heard of her is because she once married a wealthy bisexual and then derived untold millions from dumping the shmoe. With all that money, she has been able to set up shop as the reigning doyen for L.A.'s limousine liberals. None of which, I hasten to point out, makes her a hypocrite. No, what makes her an Olympic-caliber phony is the fact that this single lady lives alone in a Brentwood mansion with her two tots, and I am willing to make a good-sized wager that it requires a lot more energy to heat and cool the Huffington homestead than a squad of soccer moms consume driving to and from the playground. There are those who suggest I count sheep as a cure for my sleeplessness, but it becomes increasingly difficult to focus on four-legged sheep when there's such an abundance of the two-legged variety making me crazy. For instance, it strikes me that there is no lie, no matter how obviously false, that won't be taken up by those on the left and repeated ad nauseam. Both Joseph Stalin and George Orwell pointed out the effectiveness of the oft-repeated lie, but even they would be astonished at how gullible Americans have become.

Furthermore, the use of binary responses may not capture the full range of cognitive processes involved in WM, as they do not allow for the assessment of confidence or uncertainty associated with recall. Moreover, the reliance on accuracy as the primary outcome measure may mask potential effects of tDCS on other aspects of WM, such as reaction time or response bias. To overcome these limitations, more nuanced and sensitive measures of WM performance are needed. One approach is to use continuous report paradigms, which allow observers to provide a graded response indicating their level of confidence or certainty about the recalled information (Zhang and Luck, 2008). This type of paradigm has been shown to provide a more detailed understanding of WM processes, as it can reveal subtle effects of experimental manipulations on WM performance that may not be captured by binary responses (Kornell et al., 2007). In addition, the use of computational models of WM can provide a more mechanistic understanding of how tDCS affects WM processes. For example, models such as the Slot-Resource model (Ma et al., 2014) or the Binding of Features model (Vogel et al., 2001) can be used to quantify the effects of tDCS on specific components of WM, such as the capacity to store information or the ability to bind features together. By combining these models with continuous report paradigms, researchers can gain a more detailed understanding of how tDCS affects the underlying mechanisms of WM. Another important consideration is the individual differences in WM performance and how they may interact with the effects of tDCS. Previous studies have shown that individuals with lower WM capacity may be more susceptible to the effects of tDCS (Tseng et al., 2012), but the underlying mechanisms of this interaction are not well understood. By examining the effects of tDCS on WM performance in individuals with varying levels of WM capacity, researchers can gain a better understanding of how tDCS affects WM and how it may be used as a therapeutic tool to enhance cognitive performance. In conclusion, while the effects of tDCS on WM are still not fully understood, the use of more nuanced and sensitive measures of WM performance, combined with computational models and individual differences approaches, can provide a more detailed understanding of how tDCS affects the underlying mechanisms of WM. By using these approaches, researchers can gain a better understanding of how tDCS can be used to enhance cognitive performance and develop more effective therapeutic protocols.

The cardinals and bishops, typically known for their warm smiles and gentle nods, sat with their faces stern and unyielding. The air was thick with tension, as if the very fabric of the Curia was being ripped apart. The Pope's words had struck a chord, and it seemed that some of those present were not pleased with the harsh reality he had revealed. The 15 "Ailments of the Curia" had been a long time coming, and Francis' speech had been a culmination of his frustration with the bureaucratic inefficiencies and power struggles that had plagued the Holy See for decades. He had spoken of the "terrorism of gossip," which could "kill the reputation of our colleagues and brothers in cold blood." He had mentioned the cliques that could "enslave their members and become a cancer that threatens the harmony of the body," and the "friendly fire" that could destroy even the most well-intentioned efforts. The Pope's words were not just a critique of the Curia, but a call to action. He urged the cardinals and bishops to "always improve themselves and grow in communion, holiness and knowledge to fulfill their mission." As the Pope finished speaking, the room remained silent, the only sound the soft rustling of papers and the quiet murmur of whispers. It was as if the very foundations of the Curia were being shaken, and the cardinals and bishops were struggling to come to terms with the harsh realities that Francis had revealed. In the days that followed, the Pope's words would be met with a mix of reactions. Some would praise his courage and honesty, while others would criticize his harsh tone and perceived lack of tact. But one thing was certain: the Pope had struck a chord, and the Curia would never be the same again. The 15 "Ailments of the Curia" would serve as a wake-up call, a reminder that even the most powerful and esteemed institutions can fall prey to the same human frailties and weaknesses that plague us all.

The lack of understanding of EV-mediated drug delivery kinetics is further complicated by the complexity of EV-cell interactions, which involve multiple steps, including EV uptake, trafficking, and cargo release. To date, most studies have focused on the biochemical analysis of EVs, neglecting their dynamic behavior and kinetic properties. The development of novel methodologies to investigate EV kinetics is essential to overcome these limitations. One promising approach is the use of single-particle tracking (SPT) techniques, which enable the real-time monitoring of individual EVs in live cells. SPT has been successfully applied to study the dynamics of various cellular processes, including vesicle trafficking, membrane protein diffusion, and virus entry. However, its application to EV research is still in its infancy. Recent advances in SPT have enabled the development of high-speed, high-resolution imaging techniques, such as single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (STORM). These techniques offer unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution, allowing for the tracking of individual EVs with nanometer precision and millisecond temporal resolution. Furthermore, the development of novel fluorescent probes and labeling strategies has enabled the specific labeling of EVs, allowing for their selective tracking in live cells. The application of SPT to EV research has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of EV-mediated drug delivery. By tracking individual EVs in real-time, researchers can gain insights into their uptake kinetics, trafficking pathways, and cargo release mechanisms. This information can be used to optimize EV-based drug delivery systems, improving their efficacy and reducing their toxicity. Moreover, SPT can be used to investigate the effects of EV surface modification on their kinetic properties, providing valuable information for the design of targeted EV-based therapeutics. In addition to SPT, other novel methodologies, such as super-resolution microscopy and correlative light-electron microscopy (CLEM), can be used to investigate EV kinetics. Super-resolution microscopy techniques, such as stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy and structured illumination microscopy (SIM), offer higher spatial resolution than conventional fluorescence microscopy, enabling the imaging of EVs with nanometer precision. CLEM, on the other hand, allows for the correlative imaging of EVs using both light and electron microscopy, providing valuable information on their ultrastructure and dynamics. The development of novel methodologies to investigate EV kinetics is crucial for the advancement of EV-based drug delivery. By gaining insights into the dynamic behavior of EVs, researchers can optimize their design and functionality, improving their therapeutic potential. Furthermore, these methodologies can be used to investigate the role of EVs in various diseases, including cancer, inflammation, and infectious diseases, providing valuable information for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

In pored MPs made of an anionic copolymer (Eudragit(R) S100, abbreviated as S100), the presence of surface pores is responsible for the direct and solvent-free encapsulation, thus avoiding destabilization of the drugs during the loading process [29]. MPs with macropore exhibited a wide range of advantages originating from their unique architecture, such as the easy loading of drugs and pH-modulated pore opening-closing behavior. Although the few micron-sized MPs developed by Kumar et al. had the capability for the encapsulation of large-size ingredients (i.e. 100 nm drug), bigger MPs with micron-scale pores promise for the encapsulation and delivery of even larger-sized biopharmaceuticals, such as viruses and bacteria and offer an excellent platform for the administration of large doses of drugs. Nevertheless, increasing the size of the droplets in the emulsion drastically decreases the Laplace pressure inside the particles prepared through the emulsion solvent evaporation/extraction techniques, leading to the destabilization of the emulsion droplets [39]. Therefore, the development of a new process to fabricate large MPs with pH-responsive macropores is recognized as another critical challenge for the successful implementation of the oral drug delivery systems. This research aims to develop an innovative solvent evaporation method for fabricating MPs with pH-responsive macropores that can be used for the small intestine-targeted delivery of oral drugs to the small intestine. Here, we report a facile technique to manufacture MPs with macropores by utilizing the Eudragit(R) L100-55 polymer (hereafter referred to as L100). This is based on our observation that the L100 polymer powder consists of MPs with a few micron-sized surface pores. The size of these MPs ranges from a few to tens of micrometers. Hence, our approach was to devise a facile method that can modify the original powder to have macroscopic pores, and use them as an oral drug delivery system. As a biocompatible FDA approved enteric formulation, L100 is an anionic environmental-sensitive copolymer with pKa around 5.5, which is not metabolized in the body, remains stable at the gastric environment, and responds to intestinal pH. The original polymer powder, which consists of anionic MPs, was incubated in a single organic phase, dichloromethane (DCM). The reasons for selecting DCM include: 1) the insolubility of the polymer in DCM, 2) the small size of the solvent molecule, which facilitates its diffusion through the polymer matrix, and 3) its low boiling point (39.6 C), which is much lower than the glass transition temperature (Tg) of the polymer. The suspension went through the solvent evaporation step to form and enlarge the interior void space and the surface pores present in the original polymer particles. This approach incorporates the critical parameters previously investigated in the solvent evaporation method for the creation of surface pores in the MPs [29,40]. As such, the effects of solvent evaporation temperature and the incubation time were evaluated to test the pore size controllability in the MP system.

I reflected, as I picked up my coat and walked toward the house, that if any one but Paul Stoddard had sent me such a message I should most certainly have ignored it; but I knew him as a man who did not make demands or impose obligations lightly. As the founder and superior of the Protestant religious Order of the Brothers of Bethlehem he was, I knew, an exceedingly busy man. His religious house was in the Virginia mountains; but he spent much time in quiet, humble service in city slums, in lumber-camps, in the mines of Pennsylvania; and occasionally he appeared like a prophet from the wilderness in some great church of New York, and preached with a marvelous eloquence to wondering throngs. The trap swung into the arched driveway and I bade the coachman make haste to the Annandale station. The handsome bays were soon trotting swiftly toward the village, while I drew on my gloves and considered the situation. A certain Miss Holbrook, of whose existence I had been utterly ignorant an hour before, was about to arrive at Annandale. A clergyman, whom I had not seen for two years, had telegraphed me from a town in Connecticut to meet this person, conduct her to St. Agatha's School - just closed for the summer, as I knew - and to volunteer my services in difficulties that were darkly indicated in a telegram of forty-five words. The sender of the message I knew to be a serious character, and a gentleman of distinguished social connections. The name of the lady signified nothing except that she was unmarried; and as Stoddard's acquaintance was among all sorts and conditions of men I could assume nothing more than that the unknown had appealed to him as a priest and that he had sent her to Lake Annandale to shake off the burdens of the world in the conventual air of St. Agatha's. High-born Italian ladies, I knew, often retired to remote convents in the Italian hills for meditation or penance. Miss Holbrook's age I placed conservatively at twenty-nine; for no better reason, perhaps, than that I am thirty-two. The blue arch of June does not encourage difficulties, doubts or presentiments; and with the wild rose abloom along the fences and with robins tossing their song across the highway I ceased to growl and found curiosity getting the better of my temper. Expectancy, after all, is the cheerfullest tonic of life, and when the time comes when I can see the whole of a day's programme from my breakfast-table I shall be ready for man's last adventure. I smoothed my gloves and fumbled my tie as the bays trotted briskly along the lake shore. The Chicago express whistled for Annandale just as we gained the edge of the village. It paused a grudging moment and was gone before we reached the station.

Furthermore, these systems often fail to capture the nuanced and multifaceted nature of student learning and engagement, which transcends mere interaction with digital platforms. As educators seek to better grasp and predict student success, there is an emerging recognition that an integration of comprehensive data sources is necessary. Beyond digital footprints, real-time data gathered from in-class participation, peer collaboration, and feedback loops paints a richer picture of a student's academic journey. To advance the scope and efficacy of predictive models, institutions must consider a hybrid approach that captures both cognitive and non-cognitive factors affecting student performance. Cognitive factors, such as academic abilities and prior knowledge, are undoubtedly significant. However, non-cognitive factors like motivation, self-regulation, and socio-emotional skills also play critical roles in influencing academic resilience (Zimmerman, 2008; Duckworth & Seligman, 2005). These attributes, often overshadowed by conventional metrics, could provide pivotal insights into students' potential success trajectories. Building upon this framework, a promising avenue is the incorporation of qualitative data into predictive models. Collecting thoughtful qualitative feedback from students and educators alike could align prediction tools more closely with classroom realities. This requires collaborative engagement between faculty, students, and institutional technologists to architect systems that are as adaptable as they are predictive. Moreover, investing in faculty development to boost instructors' competencies in utilizing data-driven insights cannot be overlooked. As instructors become adept at interpreting predictive analytics, they can differentiate instructional strategies and offer tailored support, ultimately fostering an environment that is responsive to student needs and conducive to personal growth. Such professional development initiatives could bridge the gap between raw data interpretation and pedagogical application. Complementing this premise, a shift in institutional culture toward data ethics must occur. Protecting students' privacy while collecting and analyzing data is paramount, necessitating robust protocols and transparency in how data is leveraged to support academic success. Institutions should uphold stringent data governance and provide students with clear communication about data use, ensuring trust and ethical stewardship. To embolden predictive modeling and support systems, leveraging emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and machine learning can further enhance model precision. These technologies can identify complex patterns across diverse datasets, offering refined insights into student engagement and learning dispositions. However, they must be deployed thoughtfully, ensuring that technology augments rather than overshadows the human element of education.
