The tall, energetic figure of Anna Mihailovna, the lady to whose practical business gifts and unlimited capacity for compelling her friends to surrender their last bow and button in her service we owed the existence of our Red Cross unit, was to be seen like a splendid flag waving its followers on to glory and devotion. We were devoted, all of us. Even I, whose second departure to the war this was, had after the feeblest resistance surrendered myself to the drama of the occasion. I should have been no gentleman had I done otherwise. After the waters had closed above my head for, perhaps, five minutes of strangled, half-protesting, half-willing surrender I was suddenly compelled, by what agency I know not, to struggle to the surface, to look around me, and then quite instantly to forget my immersion. The figure of Trenchard, standing exactly as I had left him, his hands uneasily at his sides, a half-anxious, half-confident smile on his lips, his eyes staring straight in front of him, absolutely compelled my attention. I had forgotten him, we had all forgotten him, his own lady had forgotten him. I withdrew from the struggling, noisy group and stepped back to his side. It was then that, as I now most clearly remember, I was conscious of something else, was aware that there was a strange faint blue light in the dark clumsy station, a faint throbbing glow, that, like the reflection of blue water on a sunlit ceiling, hovered and hung above the ugly shabbiness of the engines and trucks, the rails with scattered pieces of paper here and there, the iron arms that supported the vast glass roof, the hideous funnel that hung with its gaping mouth above the water-tank. The faint blue light was the spring evening - the spring evening that, encouraged by God knows what brave illusion, had penetrated even these desperate fastnesses. A little breeze accompanied it and the dirty pieces of paper blew to and fro; then suddenly a shaft of light quivered upon the blackness, quivered and spread like a golden fan, then flooded the huge cave with trembling ripples of light. There was even, I dare swear, at this safe distance, a smell of flowers in the air. "It's a most lovely..." Trenchard said, smiling at me, "spring here... I find...." I was compelled by some unexpected sense of fatherly duty to be practical. "You've got your things?" I said. "You've found your seat?" "Well, I didn't know..." he stammered. "Where are they?" I asked him. He was not quite sure where they were. He stood, waving his hands, whilst the golden sunlight rippled over his face. I was suddenly irritated. "But please," I said, "there isn't much time. Four of us men have a compartment together. Just show me where your things are and then I'll introduce you."

2 Second, we contribute to the empirical literature on the impact of PPS by studying the effect of the SDD bonus policy. We exploit the staggered introduction of the SDD bonus policy over time and across conditions. As shown in Fig. 1, the proportion of patients treated as SDDs increased after the implementation of the SDD bonus policy for all conditions, but varied considerably across conditions. For example, the proportion of patients admitted for knee arthroscopy who were discharged within four hours rose from 14% before the policy was introduced to 40% afterwards, while the corresponding figures for patients undergoing hip replacement surgery were 26% and 31%. The results show that the introduction of the SDD bonus led to an increase in the proportion of patients treated as SDDs of between 11% and 22%, depending on the condition. These changes were driven primarily by a fall in the number of patients admitted overnight rather than an increase in the number of patients being discharged earlier than expected. There is some evidence of substitution away from non-SDD admissions towards SDD admissions. However, most of the increase in the proportion of SDDs occurred among patients whose planned length of stay was less than one day. Overall, the results suggest that the SDD bonus policy was effective in increasing the proportion of SDD admissions. To our knowledge, there is no previous study that investigates the impact of an SDD bonus policy. Most studies that have analysed the effects of a PPS have focused on the impact of the move from retrospective fee-for-service payments to prospective payment schemes.3 Under fee-for-service payments, hospitals are paid based on the number of services provided regardless of whether those services are needed or not. As a result, providers have an incentive to supply additional services to maximise revenue (Ellis and McGuire, 1986; Shleifer, 1985; Ma, 1994). In contrast, PPS reimbursements provide an incentive for hospitals to restrict unnecessary care and supply only necessary services (Newhouse, 1970). Hence, PPS can lead to improvements in allocative efficiency and reductions in the total amount spent on health care (Ma, 1994; Newhouse, 1994). However, several studies have found that the transition to PPS can lead to unintended consequences. These include a shift in the mix of services provided away from acute care towards outpatient and emergency care, leading to longer waiting times for elective surgery (Chandra and Skinner, 2011; Gaynor et al., 2017); and a decline in the quality of care, including reduced availability of physicians and nurses (McGuire, 2000; Cutler, 2002; Chandra and Staiger, 2012). Other studies have found no significant effects of PPS on the provision of care (Cutler, 2002; Chalkley and Malcomson, 2002). Similarly, in England, the introduction of DRGs in 2009 did not significantly affect hospital length of stay or total costs (Woolley et al., 2015). A recent study examined the effects of the introduction of DRGs in South Korea (Kim et al., 2018). The authors find that the introduction of DRGs led to a reduction in the length of stay for both SDD and overnight stays. They also find a decrease in the number of patients receiving surgical procedures, which suggests that there might be a trade-off between improving efficiency and reducing utilisation.

His armor, glistening with the reflections of a relentless sun, seemed a foreign entity in this forsaken land. The polished steel and vivid crimson of his surcoat stood in stark contrast to the drab hues of the landscape-dull browns and sickly yellows void of life. Each laborious step of his steed stirred clouds of dust that danced in the shafts of sunlight, and the sound of his metal plates clinked discordantly against the eerie silence that enveloped the wilderness. The knight drew a deep breath, the heavy scent of sulphur stinging his nose and throat, a vile reminder of the doom that had befallen the cities of yore. As he traversed the arid plain, the echoes of history pressed upon his mind, carrying with them the weight of divine retribution. Would he, too, fall victim to such an end? The thought gnawed at his spirit as he recalled his brethren-the gallant knights, the noble lords-whose quest for glory had lured them from their hearths to this forsaken realm. Here, where the sun burns the flesh and the ground bears witness to the curse, they pursued a fate that manifested in both bravery and folly. He recalled the stories whispered by the fire, legends of boisterous victories and bold deeds against enemies both seen and unseen. Yet upon this wasteland, he sensed a different battle looming-a struggle not against the sword or lance, but against an oppressive desolation that clawed at the very essence of valor. Was it a dream, or had he truly forsaken the comforts of his homeland for this graveyard of ambitions where hope lay buried beneath the weight of damned memories? As if summoned forth by his thoughts, a stirring among the rocks caught his eye. In the distance, a small figure emerged, half-hidden behind the cracked stones that dotted the landscape like ancient sentinels. The knight squinted against the glare of the sun, and soon a child's form became clear-a ragged boy, his skin tanned and worn like the parched earth. The knight hesitated; in such a desolate spot, who would expect to find life, even in its most pitiful guise? "Ho there!" he called, his voice gravelly as it broke the stillness. "What brings you to this loathsome waste, young one?" The boy lifted his head, his eyes large and round like the moon at dusk, reflecting both fear and an undeniable strength. "I seek water, sir knight," came the soft reply, the words trembling like the very heat that rose from the sands. "Water for my mother, who lies ill among the stones yonder." The knight felt a pang of compassion, an echo of better days when the clang of swords had been far more tender than the parched lips of a dying woman. He glanced toward the horizon, where the sun streamed hot and relentless, and his heart wrestled with the urgency that pulled him toward hospitality. "Come then," he urged gently, dismounting the noble steed. "Let me assist you." As he stepped through the gritty terrain, every element of the forgotten land felt magnified-each serrated rock and shifting grain underfoot combining to form a pact among shadows of despair. The knight thought of the scourge of this place, the eternal wasteland, and for the first time, intertwined with his thoughts was the notion of redemption that had long seemed lost amid the cries of war. Together, they moved toward the boy's hidden shelter, weaving through the ancient remnants of a past that spoke of ruin but hinted at hope-a flicker that, amidst ashes, still burned.

We need to move toward a system of "Instant Runoff Voting," "lso known as "Ranked Choice Voting.a In such a system, voters rank their preferences for President among all the available choices, rather than just choosing a single candidate. A voter can choose to rank his/her top three choices, or five, or ten, etc., depending on the number of candidates running. If no candidate receives a majority of the first-place rankings, then the candidate with the fewest first-place votes is eliminated, and each ballot that ranked him/her first is redistributed to the second choice on those ballots. Then the votes are counted again. If still no candidate has received a majority, then the next lowest-ranking candidate is eliminated, and the ballots re-counted. This continues until one candidate has a majority of the remaining votes. There are many advantages to Instant Runoff Voting. First, it gives third-party candidates a fighting chance to win. Voters don't have to worry about wasting their vote; they can safely express their preference for a long-shot candidate, knowing that if he/she gets knocked out, their vote will count towards their second-choice candidate. Thus, you avoid the unfortunate situation where, say, a staunch liberal ends up casting his/her vote for a Republican over a Democrat, because the Republican stands a better chance of winning against the conservative independent candidate who is taking votes away from the Democrat. Second, Instant Runoff Voting is more democratic. Instead of merely selecting between two candidates, it allows the electorate to express its full range of preferences. Third, Instant Runoff Voting saves money. It eliminates the need for costly primary elections, which are essentially runoffs anyway. Fourth, Instant Runoff Voting encourages positive campaigning. Candidates are less likely to go negative when they know they might need the second-place votes of supporters of their opponent. Fifth, Instant Runoff Voting is easy. It takes no longer to fill out a ballot under this system than under the current system, and the math is simple enough that it can easily be done by hand. Sixth, Instant Runoff Voting is used around the world. Australia, Ireland, London, Scotland, New Zealand, Malta, Cambridge, Massachusetts, and San Francisco use it successfully. For further information about Instant Runoff Voting, see http://www.fairvote.org/irv/index.html.

However, the empirical analysis in these papers is largely observational. This is the first study to causally examine how information asymmetries directly affect behavior, specifically decisions about the sending and spending of remittances. The importance of understanding how information asymmetries affect decisions in transnational households is heightened by the fact that migrants and their family members are financially linked through the sending of remittances. In 2010, aggregate remittances to the developing world were US$332 billion, and in El Salvador remittances received were 16% of GDP (Ratha and Silwal, 2012). Additionally, the receipt of remittances has been shown to have positive impacts on a variety of measures of well-being (Adams and Cuecuecha, 2010; Adams and Page, 2005; Cox Edwards and Ureta, 2003; Woodruff and Zenteno, 2007; Yang, 2008; Yang and Martinez, 2005). Given this importance of remittances in developing countries, a more complete understanding of how remittance decisions are made is crucial for policymakers who are hoping to maximize their economic impact. A growing experimental literature related to remittances and information has focused on the strategic efforts of migrants to control remittance spending. Specifically, several field experiments have examined the effects of offering migrants varying degrees of control over remittances. The idea behind these experiments is that offering control to migrants will mitigate a moral hazard problem in how recipients spend remittances. Studies have found mixed results. Ashraf et al. (forthcoming) show that savings levels in bank accounts in El Salvador increase when migrants are given greater control over these accounts. Chin et al. (2011) find that the impacts of an experiment that offered migrants assistance in opening bank accounts in the United States are concentrated among migrants who report having no control over how their remittances are spent. However, in a lab experiment, Torero and Viceisza (2013) do not find that Salvadoran migrants send more when they are able to control how remittances are spent, and attribute this to the fact that the control offered by their experiment was too limiting. Additionally, Ambler et al. (forthcoming) find no unsubsidized demand for a product that directs remittances to education and De Arcangelis et al. (2014) show evidence that simply labeling remittances for education is as effective in increasing remittances as providing a hard commitment device. A limitation of the papers described above is that they do not consider that information problems might run in both directions. One of the principal contributions of this paper is therefore that it examines the strategic impacts of information asymmetries on both sides of the migrant-recipient relationship. The observational studies documenting information asymmetries in migrant households have also largely focused on migrant monitoring of recipient behavior (Chen, 2013; de Laat, 2014) and none examine the decisions of both migrants and recipients. This study also fits into the literature that describes information asymmetries and strategic behavior in families that live in closer proximity.

Ah, but that is but the surface of our tale! The splendor of the stage must not blind us to the shadows that lurk behind the curtain. For in this quest for acclaim and power, our dear Ben Jonson, playwright of the people, finds himself ensnared in a web of treachery spun by the very fabric of the court. The whispers of ambition flutter dangerously close, and in their folds hide secrets that threaten to consume them all. "Tell me, Jonson, do you not find it odd," chided the inquisition of his lords, sharp as a dagger, "that a commoner, a mere scrivener, could pen words fit for kings? Speak truth! Did not the Earl rain his patronage upon your weary shoulders, molding you into his ephemeral success?" "What is a playwright," Jonson countered, his brow furrowing under the weight of their scrutiny, "but a humble vessel through which the very essence of humanity pours forth? To accuse me of the Earl's wretched schemes thwarts the artistry I devote myself to daily. I cannot claim his words as my own, but to simply serve the muse bestowed on me-ah, that is my singular truth, my lords." A smirk danced upon the face of the interrogator, his skepticism dripping heavy like ink on a page. "And that truth, my dear Jonson, shall be tested. For in these plays, we hear the vibrations of dissent, shadows cast by characters that mirror our very court. Who then, if not the Earl, gives life to these insurrections upon the stage? Are we to believe they spring forth like divine wisdom from a mere mortal's pen?" The room tightened with unspoken tension, the air thickening with the ghost of ambition lost. Jonson, a craftsman not devoid of fear, felt his pulse quicken, yet maintained his composure. "Perhaps your lords would prefer to raise a specter of doubt where none exists. The ink upon this parchment flows freely from many sources, reflecting our truths, our lives in all their infamous glory. A king's justice might be one play; a fool's folly another. It's in their oft-maligned contradictions that we find the heart of our nation-not the signatures of lords and earls burdened by titles." As his words struck against the cold stone walls, echoes seemed to mock his protestations. Outside, the raucous laughter of the audience seeped in like the twilight's final rays. They awaited the spectacle, a tapestry woven of magic and drama-a world beyond their own, as rich as it was dangerous. And somewhere among them slinked the Earl of Oxford himself, the master puppeteer, pulling strings unseen. For this was not merely a play; it was a profound dance between power and artistry, chaos and creation. Jonson's heart raced. Did the Earl, clad in his royal finery, realize the stage was not simply a platform, but a tightrope he walked daily, with whispers trailing behind like hounds on a hot scent? If the truths within his work, the glimmer of rebellion, fell to the ground unspoken, what grim fate awaited those who dared bring art to life? Would they tread the boards, thriving amidst adoration-or fall victim to the very claws of the crown they sought to entertain? "Perhaps," Jonson mused, "this theatre shall reveal a different truth altogether-one where ink is the weapon and words the revolution. What say you, lords? Shall we entertain truths before the dawn breaks upon our stage? For every quill has the power to cut deeper than a sword; every play can ignite the fire of change."

The present paper focuses on the relation between the morphology of the auditory nerve and its contribution to the ABR. To this aim, we developed a model of the peripheral auditory system that includes both the anatomy of the auditory nerve and the electrophysiological properties of its neurons. We have chosen the human auditory system since there is much morphological data available (Rasmussen, 1940; Spoendlin and Schrott, 1989; Nadol, 1997; Kuhn et al., 2004). Our anatomical model of the auditory nerve consists of three parts: the IAM, the modiolus and the osseous spiral lamina (OSL). The IAM contains the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) and the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). CN VIII has two components, the cochlear and the vestibular branch. Our model comprises only the cochlear branch which is divided into two portions, the inferior and superior portion. The inferior portion contains the fibers originating from the basal turn, while the fibers from the apical turns belong to the superior portion. The vestibulocochlear nerve enters the skull through the IAM and runs toward the brain stem. At the fundus of the IAM, the vestibulocochlear nerve splits into the vestibular and cochlear branches. The cochlear nerve then passes through the lamina cribrosa of the OSL and reaches the modiolar core. The modiolus is the central axis of the bony labyrinth of the inner ear and contains the spiral ganglia which house the cell bodies of the SGCs. The fibers of the inferior and superior portion enter the modiolus at the lower and upper aspect of the spiral ganglion, respectively. They continue spiraling around the modiolus until they reach their target, the organ of Corti. The fibers innervating the basal turn run radially through the OSL, whereas those innervating the middle and apical turns travel longitudinally along the OSL before entering the organ of Corti. The structure of the auditory nerve is depicted in Figure 1. Figure 1. Structure of the auditory nerve. (A) Frontal view of the left ear showing the course of the auditory nerve within the IAM. (B) Cross section through the cochlea showing the course of the auditory nerve fibers from the modiolus to the organ of Corti. (C) Enlarged cross section of the basal turn of the cochlea showing the course of the auditory nerve fibers from the modiolus to the organ of Corti. In order to simulate the ABR, our anatomical model needs to be combined with a biophysical model describing the electrical behavior of the auditory nerve. Since the ABR is an extracellular potential, we used a cable model of a myelinated neuron to describe the currents flowing across the membrane. This model is based on the work of McNeal (1976). The myelin sheath of the fiber is modeled as a resistive layer and the nodes of Ranvier as capacitive layers. The internodal space between two adjacent nodes is described as a resistive-capacitive (RC) circuit. The intracellular medium and the extracellular fluid are represented by resistors. For simplicity, we assume that all fibers in the auditory nerve have the same length and diameter. Then with one fierce bound he sprang upon the bed, and, clapping his hand upon the boy's mouth, held him down with the strength of a giant. Monte-Cristo rose from his seat and rushed toward the door, but before he could reach it Maldar had vanished. At the same time the shrieks of Fanfar and his wife rang through the house, and the whole party started to their feet in alarm. Monte-Cristo seized a sword which hung above the mantelpiece, and, rushing out of the house, shouted: "Maldar! Maldar!" A little later, after searching in vain for traces of the fugitive, Monte-Cristo re-entered the house, where he found his friends waiting anxiously for him. "Maldar has gone," he said. "He has carried off my son." "My God! my God!" cried Fanfar, wringing his hands. "But we must follow them," said the Count, hastily putting on his cloak. "Where is your horse?" "In the stable," replied Fanfar. "Then let us mount and pursue our enemies," said Monte-Cristo, leading the way to the stable. They mounted their horses and galloped away in the direction taken by Maldar. It was no easy matter to find the trail of the fugitives, for Maldar was a crafty villain, and knew every inch of the country. After riding for hours without finding any trace of the Arabs, the pursuers stopped to rest. They were then far out on the desert, and no sign of habitation was visible. Suddenly Monte-Cristo gave a loud shout. "Look yonder! There are the tracks of a horse's hoofs!" The others looked in the direction indicated by the Count and saw clearly marked hoof-marks in the sand. The party rode swiftly forward until they reached a hill overlooking the sea-shore. From this height they could see a group of men standing near the edge of the water. They approached nearer and recognized the figures of the fugitives. The Arabs had already landed on the shore of the island and were preparing to carry off the boy. Monte-Cristo dismounted from his horse and began to descend the steep side of the hill. The others followed suit. Before they had proceeded very far, however, they observed that the track of the horse disappeared. They looked about them in dismay. "We are lost!" exclaimed Fanfar, in despair. "Lost!" repeated Monte-Cristo. "No, I think not. We shall find our way back. Come!" The four men retraced their steps slowly up the hillside, and, arriving at the summit, once more looked down on the scene below. To their surprise, they now beheld several Arabs advancing rapidly toward them. Among these was the man who had been sent to demand the ransom money, and who had returned with the information that the ransom had not arrived. When the Arabs drew near enough to speak, they shouted: "Come down! Come down! Your friend is here!" Monte-Cristo descended the hill and met the Arabs. They greeted him cordially and assured him that if he would come with them they would take him to the place where his son was being kept prisoner. Monte-Cristo hesitated for a moment, but finally agreed to go with them.

On the dorsal side, this segregation forms the basis for the Nieuwkoop center in the region of the vegetal-dorsal blastomeres, and later the Spemann organizer (De Robertis and Kuroda, 2004; Houston, 2012). In this scheme, the first cleavage determines the left and right halves of the animal, and while these exhibit superficial mirror symmetry, substantial left-right internal asymmetry develops over time. Although this has been investigated for some years, the molecular origins and timing of the development of left-right asymmetry are not well understood (reviewed in Blum et al., 2014; Coutelis et al., 2014). Blastomere isolation and removal experiments have been carried out with Xenopus embryos. These have shown that separated halves of 2-cell stage embryos, and 8-cell stage embryos containing some combination of ventral and dorsal blastomeres, can still reach tailbud stage, whilst purely ventral halves give rise to cell masses lacking head or axial structure (Kageura and Yamana, 1983, 1984). Furthermore, the ability of transplants from oocytes or early embryos to induce the formation of a secondary axis in later stage embryos is evidence that some cytoplasmic dorsal determinants are localized early in specific regions of the embryos (Fujisue et al., 1993; Gallagher et al., 1991; Hainski and Moody, 1992; Kageura and Yamana, 1986). The nature and identities of these dorsal determinants are not currently well defined. Previous experiments have shown that these putative cytoplasmic factors may be mRNA or proteins (Klein and King, 1988; Miyata et al., 1987; Shiokawa et al., 1984). Further, it has been argued that cytoplasmic polyadenylation may be the mechanism for the change in dorsal inducing activity of total RNA isolated from the dorsal lineage between the 8- and 16-cell stages (Pandur et al., 2002). Differential polyadenylation along the dorsal-ventral axis has been proposed to account for an observed dorsal enrichment of Wnt11 protein (Schroeder et al., 1999), and observed vesicle trafficking has been proposed to account for dorsal enrichment of Disheveled protein (Miller et al., 1999). The process of mRNA segregation in the maturing oocyte has been well studied (King et al., 2005; Kloc et al., 2001, 2002; Melton, 1987), and numbers of mRNAs with an asymmetric distribution on the animal-vegetal axis are published (Cuykendall and Houston, 2010; Houston, 2013; King et al., 2005). Asymmetric distribution of maternal mRNAs in the early embryo has recently been investigated through transcriptional profiling of early cleavage stage embryos dissected in sections along the animal-vegetal axis (Grant et al., 2014). A qPCR study on 41 selected genes, analyzed individual blastomeres (identified as animal or vegetal) from 8-, 16- and 32-cell Xenopus laevis embryos (Flachsova et al., 2013) and inferred a lack of dorsal-ventral or left-right asymmetry from the failure of a principle components analysis to identify subgroups beyond animal and vegetal. There has, however, to the best of our knowledge, been no systematic, large-scale study of mRNA distribution over multiple axes in the blastula stage embryo.

As he emerged back into the chaos of Broadway, Henry's mind raced with thoughts of his predicament. He had been counting on Willie's help to get settled in the city, and now he was left to fend for himself. The towering skyscrapers and bustling streets that had seemed so exciting just hours before now loomed over him like giants, casting long shadows of uncertainty. Henry's stomach growled with hunger, and he realized he hadn't eaten since breakfast. He spotted a small diner across the street and decided to grab a quick bite to eat while he thought things through. As he waited in line, Henry couldn't help but think about how his life had taken a sudden turn for the worse. Just a few days ago, he was working at his family's general store in Central City, feeling trapped and restless. Then Willie's letter had arrived, offering him a chance to start anew in the city. Henry had jumped at the opportunity, packing his bags and saying goodbye to his family without a second thought. Now, as he stood in the crowded diner, he wondered if he had made a huge mistake. Henry ordered a sandwich and a cup of coffee, taking a seat at the counter to eat. As he bit into the sandwich, he noticed a newspaper lying next to him, abandoned by a previous customer. He picked it up, scanning the headlines out of habit. That's when he saw it - an advertisement for a temporary clerical position at a large insurance company. The pay wasn't great, but it was better than nothing, and it might just tide him over until Willie returned. Henry's heart skipped a beat as he read the address of the company. It was just a few blocks away from where he was sitting. He finished his lunch in a hurry, deciding to take a chance and apply for the job on the spot. As he walked out of the diner, he felt a glimmer of hope for the first time since leaving the Secret Service office. Maybe, just maybe, things were starting to look up. The streets seemed a little less daunting as Henry made his way to the insurance company. He took a deep breath, straightened his shoulders, and pushed open the door. The receptionist looked up from her desk, a look of boredom on her face. "Can I help you?" she asked, her tone less than enthusiastic. Henry smiled, trying to appear confident. "I'm here to apply for the clerical position," he said, pulling out the newspaper clipping from his pocket. The receptionist raised an eyebrow, but nodded curtly. "Fill out an application form, please," she said, handing him a sheet of paper and a pen. Henry took a seat in the waiting area, his heart pounding in his chest. This was it - his chance to prove to himself that he could make it in the city. He began to fill out the form, his hand shaking slightly as he wrote his name and address. As he worked, he couldn't help but think of Willie, wondering where he was and what he was doing. But for now, Henry had to focus on himself. He was on his own in the city, and it was time to start making his own way.

The investigation of the effects of wrinkles on the compressive failure of composite materials has garnered significant attention in recent years. As demonstrated by the World-Wide Failure Exercises (WWFE), the prediction of failure processes and experimental characterization of performance remains a challenging task. The introduction of manufacturing-induced variations, such as fibre waviness, adds complexity to the prediction of failure. Wang et al. [4] demonstrated the significant influence of out-of-plane fibre waviness on mechanical performance, with a reduction in compressive strength of approximately 54% when the peak misalignment angle increased to about 22. Mukhopadhyay et al. [6] also highlighted the importance of wrinkles on compressive strength, introducing wrinkles by selectively inserting or removing prepreg strips in the 90 plies of quasi-isotropic laminates. The reduction in compressive strength was found to be approximately 30% when the maximum misalignment angle reached 12. Ferreira et al. [7] further investigated the dependence of compressive-strength knock-down on wrinkle amplitude and ratio of amplitude-to-wavelength. Other researchers have also explored the negative influence of wrinkles on compressive failure, summarizing the dependence of compressive-strength knock-down on amplitude [8] or ratio of amplitude-to-wavelength [9,10]. The importance of considering the potential negative influence of wrinkles during design, testing, simulation, and performance assessment stages for composite components cannot be overstated. To achieve this, a comprehensive understanding of how wrinkles influence compressive failure is required. This knowledge can then be used to determine the metrics that should be measured non-destructively when wrinkles occur during manufacture. Several authors have attempted to characterize fibre paths and variations from ideal trajectories in composite materials using non-destructive testing (NDT) methods [11-18]. These methods include eddy current, X-ray computed tomography (CT), and ultrasonic techniques. However, the development of the field using eddy currents is currently limited to two-dimensional (2D) response at the surface, making X-ray CT and ultrasonic techniques more likely to be used in industry. X-ray CT has been successfully used to create numerical models for estimating the influence of detected defects on structural integrity [19]. Makeev et al. [20-22] have made significant contributions to this field, demonstrating the potential of X-ray CT for characterizing fibre paths and variations in composite materials. The group has also developed numerical models based on X-ray CT data, which can be used to predict the influence of detected defects on structural integrity. However, these models did not include any failure mechanisms, highlighting the need for further research in this area. In conclusion, the investigation of wrinkles in composite materials is an important area of research, with significant implications for the design, testing, and performance assessment of composite components. The development of non-destructive testing methods, such as X-ray CT, holds great promise for characterizing fibre paths and variations in composite materials. However, further research is needed to fully understand the influence of wrinkles on compressive failure and to develop numerical models that accurately predict the influence of detected defects on structural integrity.

From the first night that I was introduced to William Howard, he expressed for me the deepest respect and friendship, and haunted me subsequently like my shadow. He flattered my vanity by the most sedulous attentions, echoed my sentiments, hung upon my words, copied my style of dress, and imitated my manners. "These arts might have failed in producing the desired effect, had he not wound himself into my confidence, by appearing to sympathize in my mental sufferings. He talked of Charlotte, and endeavoured to soothe my irritated feelings, by expressing the most sanguine hopes of my ultimate success; and, to dissipate the melancholy that preyed upon my health and spirits, he led me by degrees to mix with the reckless and profligate, and to find pleasure in the society of individuals whom I could not respect, and from whose proximity a few months before I should have shrunk with disgust and aversion. "A young fellow just beyond his minority is easily led astray, particularly, when he has wealth at his command, and no settled employment or profession to engage his time and thoughts, and worse still, with no religious principles to guide him in his perilous voyage across the treacherous ocean of life. "Alas! Geoffrey; I chose for my pilot one who had not only ruined himself, but caused the shipwreck of others, superior in prudence and intelligence; to the man who now trusted to his advice and believed him a friend. "When I look back to that disastrous period of my life, my soul shrinks within itself, and I lament my madness with unceasing bitterness. All that I have since suffered, appears but a just retribution for those three years of vice and folly. Little did I then suspect, that my quondam friend was an infamous sharper, bribed by the still more infamous Robert Moncton to lure me to destruction. "In spite of her aunt's prohibition, I had continued to write to Miss Laurie; at first, frequently, seldom many days elapsing between letter and letter, but to my surprise and indignation, not one of my communications had been answered, although breathing the most ardent attachment, and dictated by a passion as sincere as ever animated a human breast. What could be the cause of this cruel neglect? I called repeatedly at Mrs. - 's house in town, but was constantly told by the old housekeeper, who received me very coldly, that Miss Laurie and her aunt were still on the continent. "As long as this miserable state of uncertainty continued, I clung to hope, and maintained the character of a man of honour and a gentleman. But the insidious tempter was ever at hand, to exaggerate my distress, and to weaken my good resolutions. Howard laughed at my constancy to a false mistress, and by degrees, led me to consider myself as a very ill-used man, and Miss Laurie as a heartless coquette.

(2007) attempted to obtain microfocus X-ray CT images of three-dimensional (3D) objects made of Japanese Oak and Japanese Beech, and succeeded in acquiring high resolution tomographic images with one pixel of the image being equivalent to 24 1/2m. Van den Bulcke et al., 2014 scanned Scots pine, oak, and teak samples with helical X-CT with a scan time from 60 to 120 min, and an approximate voxel pitch of 35 1/2m was obtained by reconstruction such as phase correction. Bill et al. (2012) reported that an industrial scanner ( 1/2X-CT) produced sufficiently clear imagery to allow for dendrochronological analyses, though the medical X-CT had lower resolution (240 1/2m) and was not suitable. Therefore, 1/2X-CT has sufficient high resolution for dried wood. On the other hand, there was a report that unsuccessful attempts to scan waterlogged and polyethylene glycol (PEG)-impregnated archaeological oak wood are due to the low contrast between the water/PEG and the preserved wood (Bill et al., 2012). Actually, the archaeologically excavated wood generally has very high moisture content (400%-800%), thereby reducing the suitability of X-CT for tree-ring analysis. Conversely, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) equipment images the density and state of hydrogen nuclei, and so, the expected quality of MRI improves as the moisture content of the wood increases. Usually, the T2 weighted imaging (T2WI) method, which enhances the water component with long T2 value by using long TE, is used for this purpose. There are reports on the mapping of water content in wood (Hall and Rajanayagam, 1986), imaging of internal structure of trees using NMR (Wang and Chang, 1986), detection of wood defects using MRI. With these factors, to use both modality complementary will be very useful for dendroarchaeology. However, direct comparison of the suitable range of each modality has not been reported. Therefore, we examined the difference between X-CT and MRI related to moisture content of wood, and examined the range of adaptation for each modality as a function of moisture content. Morales et al. (2004) succeeded in acquiring MRI images of timber with an appropriate moisture content using a 0.5 T superconducting coil whole-body scanner for a logged radiata pine tree (Pinus radiata D. Don). This conifer presents relatively large tree-rings (i.e., ring width); thus, via this method the authors were able to successfully create an automatic tree-ring curve. However, for trees that have narrow rings, measurements can be limited by the spatial resolution of the MRI and have thus not yet been sufficiently studied. Baillie (1982) reported that individual measurements should be accurate to the order of 0.05 to 0.02 mm to measure the tree-ring width series. There have been several reports, which achieved only minimal spatial resolution needed for ring width measurement.

His neckcloth ample and high, and of snowy whiteness, set off to comely advantage a face smooth-shaven, and of clear florid hues; his coat of royal blue, with buttons in which you might have seen yourself "veluti in speculum", was rather jauntily buttoned across a waist that spoke of lusty middle age, free from the ambition, the avarice, and the anxieties that fret Londoners into thread-papers; his small-clothes, of grayish drab, loose at the thigh and tight at the knee, were made by Brummell's own breeches-maker, and the gaiters to match (thrust half-way down the calf), had a manly dandyism that would have done honour to the beau-ideal of a county member. The profession of this gentleman's companion was unmistakable, - the shovel-hat, the clerical cut of the coat, the neckcloth without collar, that seemed made for its accessory the band, and something very decorous, yet very mild, in the whole mien of this personage, all spoke of one who was every inch the gentleman and the parson. "No," said the portlier of these two persons, - "no, I can't say I like Frank's looks at all. There's certainly something on his mind. However, I suppose it will be all out this evening." "He dines with you at your hotel, Squire? Well, you must be kind to him. We can't put old heads upon young shoulders." "I don't object to his bead being young," returned the squire; "but I wish he had a little of Randal Leslie's good sense in it. I see how it will end; I must take him back to the country; and if he wants occupation, why, he shall keep the hounds, and I'll put him into Brooksby farm." "As for the hounds," replied the parson, "hounds necessitate horses; and I think more mischief comes to a young man of spirit from the stables than from any other place in the world. They ought to be exposed from the pulpit, those stables!" added Mr. Dale, thoughtfully; "see what they entailed upon Nimrod! But Agriculture is a healthful and noble pursuit, honoured by sacred nations, and cherished by the greatest men in classical times. For instance, the Athenians were - " "Bother the Athenians!" cried the squire, irreverently; "you need not go so far back for an example. It is enough for a Hazeldean that his father and his grandfather and his great-grandfather all farmed before him; and a devilish deal better, I take it, than any of those musty old Athenians, no offence to them. But I'll tell you one thing, Parson, a man to farm well, and live in the country, should have a wife; it is half the battle." "As to a battle, a man who is married is pretty sure of half, though not always the better half, of it," answered the parson, who seemed peculiarly facetious that day.

'We've got a lot of work ahead of us, so it will take time,' said U.S. Marine Gen. John Allen, head of NATO forces in Afghanistan. But he added that the FBI had already sent agents to the scene and 'we're going to get this done.' Officials say the additional assets will include special operations forces, drones, more FBI investigators and possibly more spies. The U.S. military also plans to move some equipment to Tripoli from a Navy ship that has been off the coast of Libya since late last week, allowing the commandos to set up a base in the capital. U.S. officials said the move was not intended as a signal that Washington thought another attack was imminent. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak publicly about sensitive planning details. Two U.S. officials said the U.S. has obtained images of people suspected of participating in the attack. One official described them as consistent with photos taken of the suspects captured on video at the scene of the attack. Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly. That could help lead to arrests in coming days. The officials cautioned that it wasn't clear whether the footage showed Libyans or foreigners. Among the dead in the attack on the U.S. Consulate in Benghazi were U.S. Ambassador Chris Stevens, information specialist Sean Smith and former Navy SEALs Tyrone Woods and Glen Doherty, both working as contractors.

The intricacies of tuning extend far beyond mere technicality; they delve into the very heart of musical expression and the chemistry of collaborative singing. The impact of various tuning systems on choral cohesion cannot be understated, as singers not only tune their voices but also engage in a dialogue of sound that transforms individual contributions into a singular expression of artistry. Each choral piece offers a unique landscape where the exploration of tuning can both challenge and enhance a group's performance. In performing ensembles, the familiar strain of differing temperamental systems may emerge as singers navigate the nuances between equal temperament, just intonation, and Pythagorean tuning. The blend of voices, much like a painter mixing colors, creates a range of harmonies that can evoke profound emotional responses. Thus, conducting thoughtful investigations into the ways singers approach tuning becomes crucial for educators and directors alike. Furthermore, the relative tuning of intervals-be they major, minor, or microtonal-requires vigilant awareness of not only the theoretical framework but also the interpersonal dynamics within the ensemble. Contemporary research underscores the necessity of fostering an environment where singers can fine-tune their listening skills and develop acute awareness of the harmonic relationships that exist within their music. The physiological response of singers to different tuning systems highlights the intricate dance between the physical act of singing and the mental processing of harmony. As such, vocalists may find themselves espousing specific tonal qualities, instinctively opting for nuanced adjustments that reflect their collective interpretation of a piece. In this pursuit, the role of the conductor is pivotal in shaping the ensemble's understanding of tuning. Conductors serve as navigators through complex textures of sound, guiding singers through dynamic shifts and encouraging balanced intonation across the ensemble. Training in this regard often extends beyond mere vocal exercises, incorporating aural skills and interpretative practices that enhance the sensitivity of singers to their tonal environment. The subtle shifts among individual voices during ensemble singing necessitate a collective effort in pursuit of a unified sound-this is where trust and collaboration are paramount. In addition, the psychological dimensions of tuning, including the influence of memory and perception, warrant closer examination. The phenomenon of 'tuning by ear' often leads singers to rely heavily on their own auditory feedback while disregarding the collective sound. Recognizing the benefits of a well-trained ear-one attuned to horizontal and vertical tuning principles-can yield substantial rewards, enhancing both individual performance and ensemble compatibility. Indeed, the cognitive aspects of musical performance profoundly impact how singers negotiate pitch relationships, express emotional sentiment, and project the intention behind the music being shared. As research continues to unveil the complexities associated with choral tuning, the implications for pedagogy become increasingly relevant. In this light, the integration of digital technologies into vocal training affords unprecedented opportunities for exploration. Interactive listening exercises and real-time pitch feedback systems can serve as invaluable tools for developing finer pitch precision and harmony awareness among singers. Moreover, multidisciplinary approaches that draw upon insights from acoustics, cognitive science, and music education can greatly enrich our understanding of the mechanisms at play in choral tuning. Such comprehensive investigations serve to elevate not only the technical proficiency of singers but also their emotional and expressive capabilities, ultimately fostering a more profound and rewarding choral experience. Clearly, as we venture deeper into the realm of tuning, we unveil a rich tapestry of sound, collaboration, and artistry-a journey that is as intricate and inspiring as the music itself.

As we walked along this narrow street, my Mother and I, I couldn't help but marvel at the wondrous sights and sounds of the city. The air was thick with the smells of fresh bread, roasting meats, and the acrid tang of woodsmoke. The buildings seemed to lean in on us, their timber frames creaking and groaning in the gentle breeze. I felt like a small boat adrift on a stormy sea, buffeted by the waves of humanity that surged past us. We passed by a group of jugglers, their brightly colored wares spread out on a blanket before them. A young girl, no more than ten winters old, was expertly juggling three balls while her companion, a burly man with a bushy beard, played a lively tune on a pipe and tabor. My Mother tossed a penny into their hat, and the girl smiled up at us, her eyes sparkling like the stars on a clear night. As we continued on, the street began to narrow even further, the buildings seeming to close in on us like a vice. The air grew thick with the smell of fish and salt, and I caught sight of a group of sailors, their weathered faces creased with lines and their eyes red from the sea. They laughed and joked, their voices carrying on the wind as they made their way to the river. My Mother led me through the winding streets, pointing out landmarks and telling stories of the city's history. We passed by the great stone walls of the Tower of London, its battlements glinting in the sunlight like the teeth of a giant beast. We walked along the Thames, the river's waters lapping at the stone steps that led down to the water's edge. As the sun began to set, casting a golden glow over the city, we made our way to the great church of St. Paul's. Its towering spire seemed to touch the heavens, its stone walls glowing like a beacon in the fading light. My Mother led me inside, and we knelt in prayer, the silence of the church a balm to my weary soul. As we left the church, the city seemed to come alive once more. The streets were filled with the sounds of laughter and music, the smell of roasting meats and fresh bread wafting through the air. I felt like a small part of something much greater than myself, a tiny thread in the great tapestry of the city. And as I looked up at the stars twinkling above, I knew that I would never forget this, my first day in the great city of London.

As I settled into Jonathan's apartment, I couldn't shake off the image of the disastrous graduate pad I had just seen. The thought of living in that dump for the next 10 months was unbearable. I decided to distract myself by flipping through TV channels, but all I could find were reruns of The Price is Right and some obscure soap opera. I settled for the latter, not because I was interested, but because I was too exhausted to change the channel again. Just as I was starting to get engrossed in the dramatic lives of the soap opera characters, Jonathan walked in, looking frazzled. "Hey, sorry about today," he said, dropping his bag on the floor. "I know that place was a nightmare." I nodded in agreement, still trying to process the horror I had witnessed. We ordered some pizza and spent the rest of the evening discussing our plan of action for the next day. Jonathan had some leads on a few apartments, and I had a few online listings to check out. We decided to meet up at 9 am and start our apartment hunt anew. The next morning, I woke up feeling slightly more optimistic. Maybe today would be the day we'd find the perfect place. We met up at the agreed time and set off on our mission. The first apartment we saw was a slight improvement from the previous day's disaster, but it was still far from perfect. The second one was a bit better, but the landlord seemed shady. As we were walking out of the second apartment, I spotted a flyer on a community board. "Room for rent in a cozy house with a backyard!" it read. I pointed it out to Jonathan, and we decided to give it a shot. We called the number, and the landlord agreed to meet us at the house in 30 minutes. As we pulled up to the house, I felt a sense of trepidation. What would this place be like? Would it be another disaster waiting to happen? I took a deep breath and stepped out of the car, ready to face whatever lay ahead.

He is a Marine himself. I will never know what his life might have been like if he had not gone through the rigorous training, the discipline, the camaraderie and the demands of the Marines. But I can say this: he is a better person because of it. I have come to believe that one reason the United States is such a great nation is that we are made up of so many diverse peoples. We are still a nation of immigrants, and there is a great deal of strength in our diversity. But there is a downside to our diversity. One of them is that we have grown accustomed to having someone else fight our wars. That is wrong. If we send people to fight, they should be our sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, fathers and mothers. No one should be able to opt out, whether through money or connections. There must be an end to "free rides" and to the notion that someone else's children should bear the burden of our decisions. Our leaders have decided to go to war. They have said that Iraq poses a threat to us. Well, let us follow through. Let us send our own children to face that threat. Let us call on every single American family, rich or poor, connected or unconnected, to give their sons and daughters for the cause. Only then will we be truly united as a people. William Broyles Jr., a former editor of Esquire magazine, is the author of "Brothers in Arms: A Journey From War to Peace."

He said he should almost feel like giving up his pastorate here, if he should lose her. Claire is certainly a power in the church, and the society generally. I should feel sorry for them if they were to lose her." The mother spoke this sentence quietly, with the unruffled look of peace and satisfaction on her face. No foreboding of loss came to her. She thought, it is true, of the barely possible time when her eldest daughter might go out from this home into some other, and have other cares and responsibilities, but the day seemed very remote. Claire was young, and was absorbed in her church and home work. Apparently, even the suggestion of another home had not come to her. It might never come. She might live always in the dear home nest, sheltered, and sheltering, in her turn, others less favored. Or in the event of a change, some time in the future, it might be, possibly, just from one street in the same city to another, and much of the old life go on still; and in any event the mother could say "their loss," not mine; for the sense of possible separation had not come near enough to shadow the mother's heart as yet; she lived in the dreamland of belief that a married daughter would be as near to the mother and the home as an unmarried one. Therefore her face was placid, and she sewed her crimson threads and talked placidly of what might have been, but was not; the future looked secure and smiling. "You see," she continued to the young and but half-satisfied daughter, "it is an unusual combination of things that makes your sister so important to this society.

After some further discussion, it was gravely settled that Kearney should furnish water brought from the Union Ditch, twenty miles away, at a cost of two hundred thousand dollars, to feed a memorial fountain erected by Mattingly, worth a hundred thousand dollars, as a crowning finish to public buildings contributed by Maryland Joe, to the extent of half a million more. The disposition of these vast sums by gentlemen wearing patched breeches awakened no sense of the ludicrous, nor did any doubt, reservation, or contingency enter into the plans of the charming enthusiasts themselves. The foundation of their airy castles lay already before them in the strip of rich alluvium on the river bank, where the North Fork, sharply curving round the base of Devil's Spur, had for centuries swept the detritus of gulch and canyon. They had barely crossed the threshold of this treasure-house, to find themselves rich men; what possibilities of affluence might be theirs when they had fully exploited their possessions? So confident were they of that ultimate prospect, that the wealth already thus obtained was religiously expended in engines and machinery for the boring of wells and the conveyance of that precious water which the exhausted river had long since ceased to yield. It seemed as if the gold they had taken out was by some ironical compensation gradually making its way back to the soil again through ditch and flume and reservoir. Such was the position of affairs at Devil's Ford on the 13th of August, 1860. It was noon of a hot day. Whatever movement there was in the stifling air was seen rather than felt in a tremulous, quivering, upward-moving dust along the flank of the mountain, through which the spires of the pines were faintly visible. There was no water in the bared and burning bars of the river to reflect the vertical sun, but under its direct rays one or two tinned roofs and corrugated zinc cabins struck fire, a few canvas tents became dazzling to the eye, and the white wooded corral of the stage office and hotel insupportable. For two hours no one ventured in the glare of the open, or even to cross the narrow, unshadowed street, whose dull red dust seemed to glow between the lines of straggling houses. The heated shells of these green unseasoned tenements gave out a pungent odor of scorching wood and resin. The usual hurried, feverish toil in the claim was suspended; the pick and shovel were left sticking in the richest "pay gravel;" the toiling millionaires themselves, ragged, dirty, and perspiring, lay panting under the nearest shade, where the pipes went out listlessly, and conversation sank to monosyllables. "There's Fairfax," said Dick Mattingly, at last, with a lazy effort.

It commonly grows in areas where annual rainfall ranges from 100 to 400 mm (Chaieb and Boukhris, 1998). It is a range shrub with continuous vegetative production when soil humidity allows it (Ferchichi, 1996). It grows on different types of soil but prefers calcareous substrates. This indigenous shrub is the only species of this genus in Tunisia (Chaieb and Boukhris, 1998), it has a persistent and lanceolated sheets (Ozenda, 2004) and grows up to 3 m tall with short and rigid branches, which the upper ones sometimes lax and twining (Ghrabi, 2005). Although P. angustifolia is a species producing latex, but it is very palatable as forage by livestock in arid lands of Tunisia. Recent studies reported that this latex contains natural rubber and the type of laticifiers cells exuding was also identified (Dghim et al., 2015). In Lampedusa, this shrub was called "silk tree" and its seeds are used to make small pillows (Zito and Sajeva, 2012). In Tunisia, Periploca angustifolia has high pastoral, ecological and medicinal values (Le Floc'h, 1983; Ghrabi, 2005; Bouaziz et al., 2009; Dghim et al., 2013; Zito et al., 2013). Studies focusing on germination behavior of P. angustifolia seeds showed that germination percentage is influenced by burial depth, temperature, salt and osmotic stress (Noumi et al., 2009; Dghim et al., 2015). A comparative study of root system growth of this shrub and Rhus tripartitum (Ucria), cultivated in rhizotrons, showed that in the first months following germination (in November), the root development of the shrubs was rapid in spite of the negative influence of low winter temperature on the growth of the P. angustifolia root system (Yobi et al., 2001). In order to evaluate regeneration success of P. angustifolia Labill., a comparative study of spontaneous and transplanted (from a nursery) plants using morphological and ecophysiological traits was explored by Ennajeh et al. (2010), in the natural reserve of Oued Dekouk. This study revealed that spontaneous (pre-existing) plants of P. angustifolia were more vigorous and appears more adapted to aridity than transplanted (re-introduced from a nursery) ones. Knowing ecophysiological traits of autochthon populations (especially Mediterranean shrubs, such as P. angustifolia) to drought is essential for protecting and conserving them in order to be used for their multipurpose (ecological, medicinal, etc.). In this study, we evaluate ecophysiological and biochemical responses of P. angustifolia seedling subjected to drought stress (withholding irrigation for 7, 14 and 21 days) followed by 7 days of recovery. The drought study was limited to 21-d, since a longer period leads to the appearance of chlorotic symptoms on leaves (data not shown). The relationship between water relations and biochemical behavior was also explored, to test the hypothesis that maintaining turgor potential may provide an indication of the capacity of P. angustifolia to access groundwater during the summer drought, which characterizes the Mediterranean-type climate of Southern Tunisia.

She decided to distract him with conversation. Placing the steaming cups on the small oak table, she settled next to him, casually covering the idle laptop with a forgotten magazine. "So," she began breezily, "how was the office today? Anything exciting happen?" Her voice was light, almost carefree, masking the anxiety that simmered beneath. He chuckled, taking a sip of the hot beverage, oblivious to the hurried concealment. "Oh, you know how it is - meetings that could've been emails and emails that should've stayed unwritten. But there was this one interesting thing," he paused for effect, raising an eyebrow playfully. Amanda leaned in, grateful for the diversion. "Do tell!" He launched into a story about a hilarious mix-up at work involving conference rooms and a very confused intern. As he spoke, Amanda listened intently, nodding and laughing at the right moments, her own concerns momentarily sidelined. With each passing minute, her confidence grew. Maybe she would get away with it this time. The story ended, and they lapsed into a comfortable silence, punctuated only by the occasional clink of china and the muted tick of the wall clock. Amanda's mind, however, was anything but silent, still strategizing the best way to navigate the uncompleted chores without drawing attention. "Darling," he said suddenly, "you've really outdone yourself today. House looks great." His tone was sincere, and despite herself, Amanda felt a rush of guilt mixed with relief. "Thank you," she replied softly, reaching out to squeeze his hand. Yet, she knew that this momentary reprieve wouldn't last forever. As his eyes drifted around the room once more, she could sense the unspoken question forming, bubbling just beneath the surface. Before he could inquire further, she interjected, "You know, I was thinking... maybe we could order in tonight? No need for either of us to spend more time in the kitchen. As she picked up the phone to place the order, she gave a silent thanks to the restaurant's efficient service and hoped for a quick delivery. As the evening wore on, Amanda felt the tension begin to dissipate, like shadows retreating from a slowly rising sun. The smell of spaghetti carbonara filled the room, mingling with laughter and light-hearted chatter. For the time being, the unwashed dishes and untouched laundry could wait. In this small reprieve, she found solace. Yet, Amanda knew that there would be another day, another list of tasks, another moment where she would have to balance her own whims with her responsibilities. She promised herself she would do better - start earlier, manage time more effectively - but for now, as they shared the warmth of food and each other's company, she allowed herself to savor the fleeting peace.

This methodology, while efficient, can inadvertently reduce sensitivity to microstructural variations across subjects, a limitation particularly pronounced in heterogeneous populations like those with DCD, where neurodevelopmental variability is the norm rather than the exception. Furthermore, the use of standardized atlases can mask individual differences, which is crucial in understanding disorders that manifest as deviations from typical motor trajectories. Another significant factor to consider is the age and developmental stage of participants, given that DCD often presents with varying symptomatology and severity across childhood and into adulthood. Brain maturation processes, particularly in white matter tracts, continue throughout adolescence, and thus the age of participants can significantly influence the observed microstructural integrity in diffusion MRI studies (Tamnes et al., 2010). It is conceivable that variations in findings across studies could also be attributed to developmental factors, rendering earlier work on adult populations potentially inapplicable to child cohorts. In addition to developmental considerations, the clinical characteristics of DCD itself warrant careful examination. Variability in diagnostic criteria and co-morbid conditions, such as ADHD or autism spectrum disorders, often associated with DCD, can complicate the interpretation of neuroimaging results (Miller et al., 2015). Indeed, the presence of additional behavioral difficulties may amplify or obscure alterations in motor planning and execution, thereby impacting white matter integrity as reflected in diffusion MRI assessments. Moreover, the inherent limitations in diffusion MRI technology should not be overlooked. While it provides unparalleled insights into white matter microstructure, the technique measures water molecule movement, which may be influenced by numerous biological factors, including myelination, axonal density, and fiber orientation (Tuch et al., 2002). These biological complexities might lead to confounding interpretations and could partially explain the heightened variability observed across studies addressing white matter integrity in DCD. To advance our understanding of DCD, it becomes imperative to standardize methodologies across diffusion MRI studies. This includes the establishment of uniform diagnostic criteria for participant selection, along with the application of consistent imaging techniques and analytical approaches. Collaborations among multi-site research groups may also yield richer datasets to facilitate the detection of subtle effects that could go unnoticed in smaller studies. Future directions should also leverage emerging technologies, such as advanced diffusion MRI protocols, which allow for the acquisition of more refined metrics beyond traditional FA and MD measures. Techniques like diffusional kurtosis imaging (DKI) and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) provide a more intricate view of tissue microarchitecture and could uncover distinctive patterns characteristic of DCD (Zhang et al., 2012; Kreher et al., 2015). In conclusion, while promising advancements have been made in elucidating the neural substrates underlying DCD through diffusion MRI, pragmatic methodological and analytical refinements are essential. By fostering consistency in research practices and embracing multimodal imaging strategies, we aspire to build a more comprehensive understanding of DCD that transcends mere diagnostic labels. In doing so, future studies may reveal not only the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of this disorder but also pave the way for tailored interventions that can meaningfully enhance motor skills and quality of life for those impacted by developmental coordination disorder.

This study aimed to investigate the binding strength of fluorobenzene in a range of complexes of the general formula [Rh( -fluoroarene)(L)2][BArF4], where L is a monodentate or bidentate phosphine and ArF is a 3,5-(CF3)2C6H3. The binding strength of fluorobenzene was measured using a combination of spectroscopic and thermodynamic methods, including UV-Vis, IR, and NMR spectroscopy, as well as calorimetric titration. The results showed that the binding strength of fluorobenzene varied significantly depending on the identity of the phosphine ligand L. For example, the binding strength of fluorobenzene to [Rh( -C6H5F)(PPh3)2][BArF4] was found to be stronger than that to [Rh( -C6H5F)(PMe3)2][BArF4], with a binding constant (K) of 10^5 M^-1 compared to 10^3 M^-1, respectively. This suggests that the steric and electronic properties of the phosphine ligand play a crucial role in determining the binding strength of fluorobenzene. The binding strength of fluorobenzene was also found to be influenced by the solvent used in the reaction. For example, the binding constant of fluorobenzene to [Rh( -C6H5F)(PPh3)2][BArF4] was found to be higher in dichloromethane (K = 10^5 M^-1) than in toluene (K = 10^3 M^-1). This suggests that the solvent can play a role in modulating the binding strength of fluorobenzene, potentially through changes in the solubility of the complex or the reactivity of the metal center. In addition to the binding strength of fluorobenzene, the study also investigated the reactivity of the complexes towards various substrates. For example, the complex [Rh( -C6H5F)(PPh3)2][BArF4] was found to be highly active in the hydroacylation reaction, with a turnover frequency (TOF) of 10^3 h^-1. In contrast, the complex [Rh( -C6H5F)(PMe3)2][BArF4] was found to be less active, with a TOF of 10^2 h^-1. This suggests that the steric and electronic properties of the phosphine ligand can also influence the reactivity of the complex. Overall, the study highlights the importance of understanding the binding strength and reactivity of fluorobenzene in complexes of the general formula [Rh( -fluoroarene)(L)2][BArF4]. The results demonstrate that the binding strength of fluorobenzene can be influenced by the identity of the phosphine ligand and the solvent used, and that the reactivity of the complex can be modulated by the steric and electronic properties of the phosphine ligand. These findings have important implications for the design and development of new catalysts for various organic transformations.

A figure darted out of the dense road crowds, running like a deer, pursued by a rabble of drunken bargemen armed with pikes. The fugitive dashed along the stone parapet of the canal, looking wildly to right and left, frantic for a way of escape. Then the figure dived into the thronged road, as if the crowd would afford best hiding, in and out among the plodding peasants, who scattered from the road in panic, with the bargemen in full cry behind shouting, "Stop him!-stop him!-slave!-slave!-runaway slave!" The old Idumean guard had sprung up with sword in his right hand for a slash at the flying figure, when a great hue and cry rent the confusion. "Make way-make way-the Emperor!" and a centurion band galloped through the dust, clearing the road with their long lances. There was a flash of gold-rimmed chariot wheels with flying horses in a blur. There was the figure of a youthful man with a bare head and shaved face, holding the reins far out as charioteers drive; and Nero's royal equipage had passed in a smoke of dust with a great shout from the barge travelers, who clapped their hands and rose and waved their flags. The fleeing figure, the pursuing bargemen, and the drunken rabble had melted; and a little form crumpled up in the doorway of the prison hut, panting as if its lungs would burst. The old Praetorian guard stood motionless, sword in hand. The pursuing rabble had disappeared back to the drunken revels in the Three Taverns. The old Idumean drove his sword back in its scabbard with a clank. Then he surveyed the figure lying prone at his feet. A thin voice called softly from the dark of the prison hut: "Who is there, my Julius? My eyes grow poor. I cannot see in this light. I thought I heard some one running in distress." "Nothing-nothing-Master! 'Twas only that madman Emperor of ours passed in his mad race with his proselyte Jewess Queen. You heard only the knaves of the Three Taverns noisy in their cups." The crumpled figure had not looked up, but lay panting on its face. A green-and-white turban, such as mountaineers wear, had fallen off. The hair was gold as the golden light of the sunset and hung in unshorn curls about the neck. There were the sky-blue jacket of the Asiatic Greeks, the scarlet trousers and pointed red soft kid sandals of a page; but the garments were torn as if snatched by the pack of human wolves. The burly Idumean guard smiled till his teeth shone like ivory tusks through his grizzled beard. "No runaway this, but some grandam's lackey," he smiled. "Is it boy or girl?" He touched the prone, panting figure with his boot. The form did not rise. It crouched upon its knees, and, with face hidden in hands, bowed the head at the soldier's feet.

The UK Guidance Notes (DGN: BEIS, 2018) issued by the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) state that decommissioning programmes will need to be supported by an Environmental Appraisal or Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). In addition, OSPAR Derogation cases will need to be surveyed and monitored for environmental and structural conditions for their entire lifespan, which could be hundreds of years (Sandberg, 1996; Quigel and Thornton, 1989). The European Marine Board (2017) highlights the need for scientific input to "provide a greater evidence base in assessing potential impacts and determining good practice for the decommissioning of offshore installations". Given the large number of impending decommissioning cases, there is a clear need for a highly efficient survey and monitoring procedure that limits potential costs but also fits the regulators' needs. The traditional methods of marine monitoring, used during the development of the UK O&G industry, are now being supplemented by new, often automated monitoring techniques (Bean et al., 2017). Advances in marine autonomy offer the prospect of enhanced data collection and substantial efficiency gains over current practice, but now require the development of effective and efficient approaches for decommissioning monitoring. Effective evaluation of impacts is aided by clear guidance on the most relevant environmental factors to consider. The Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) sets out essential ocean variables (EOVs), parameters that are feasible to measure across platforms and provide relevant information for conservation and management (Miloslavich et al., 2018). In Europe, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive sets out 11 descriptors of Good Environmental Status (GES) for European marine waters (MSFD, 2008). These may be useful to consider in evaluating the optimal approach for monitoring associated with decommissioning (Table 1). Decommissioning has particular potential to impact on several of the GES descriptors. For example: seabed integrity will be disrupted, which may change the functioning of the ecosystem (descriptor 6); underwater noise (descriptor 11) will increase in decommissioning cases; removal of long-term structures from the seafloor and water column will impact the water flow patterns (Cripps and Aabel, 2002) (descriptor 7); and changing three dimensional structure that has been acknowledged to support fish assemblages (Claisse et al., 2014; Fowler and Booth, 2012) may have implications for maintenance of biodiversity (descriptor 1) and commercial fish populations (descriptor 3). Unmanned, self-contained systems (which we refer to as being "autonomous") have been used to monitor the marine environment for over a century (e.g. Ekman recording current meter; Sverdrup et al., 1942). The greatest revolution in marine autonomous systems (MAS), to date, started with the Swallow float (Swallow, 1955) and led to the global ocean autonomous monitoring network "Argo", an array of c. 4000 autonomous sensor systems now surveying the upper 2000 m of the world's ocean (e.g. Medhaug et al., 2017). These 'simple' floats have further evolved to sophisticated particle sensing and capturing instruments (Lampitt et al., 2008), and to highly successful underwater gliders (e.g. Rudnick et al., 2004).

As we sat in the hotel lobby, watching the smoke and ash fill the air, we couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. The firefighters who had been staying at the hotel were getting ready to head out to battle the blaze, and the atmosphere was tense. The hotel's pub was still open, but the patrons were subdued, all eyes fixed on the TV as they watched the news reports of the fire's rapid spread. Ernie's brother, Ron, was getting more and more agitated, checking his phone every few minutes for updates on the fire's progress. Bonnie was pacing back and forth, her eyes welling up with tears as she thought about her accountant's house being destroyed. Jesse was getting restless, missing his usual bedtime routine and the familiar comforts of home. As the night wore on, the smoke grew thicker, and the air grew hotter. We could hear the distant roar of the fire, like a living thing, and the sound of helicopters overhead, dropping water and fire retardant to try and contain the blaze. The hotel's staff was doing their best to keep everyone calm, but it was clear that they were getting worried too. At around 11 pm, we decided to take a walk around the hotel to clear our heads and get some fresh air. The streets were eerily quiet, with only a few stragglers wandering around, trying to get a glimpse of the fire. The sky was a deep orange, and the air was thick with smoke and ash. We could see the flames flickering in the distance, casting an eerie glow over the landscape. As we walked, we noticed that the hotel's parking lot was filling up with evacuees, all trying to escape the fire. Some were sitting in their cars, staring blankly into the distance, while others were huddled together, clutching their belongings and trying to make sense of the chaos. We saw a family with two small kids, crying and clinging to each other, while their parents tried to reassure them that everything would be okay. As we walked back to the hotel, we could feel the heat emanating from the fire, and the air grew hotter and more oppressive. We knew that we had to get out of there as soon as possible, but where could we go? The fire was spreading fast, and we were trapped in the middle of it. We decided to wait it out at the hotel, hoping that the firefighters would be able to contain the blaze and get us out of there safely. Little did we know, the next few hours would be some of the most terrifying of our lives.
