It was on a quiet summer's evening in July that Mary Stansfield was walking leisurely homeward along the highroad which passed through the Riverton estate and skirted the park. Miss Stansfield was the orphan child of an officer who had perished, with his wife and other children, in the Indian Mutiny. She had been left behind in England, in the family of a maiden aunt, her father's sister, who lived on her own property, which was situated between the Riverton estate and the town of Franchope. She had inherited from her father a small independence, and from both parents the priceless legacy of a truly Christian example, and the grace that rests on the child in answer to the prayers of faith and love. The world considered her position a highly-favoured one, for her aunt would no doubt leave her her fortune and estate when she died; for she had already as good as adopted her niece, from whom she received all the attention and watchful tenderness which she needed continually, by reason of age and manifold infirmities. But while our life has its outer convex side, which magnifies its advantages before the world, it has its inner concave side also, which reduces the outer circumstances of prosperity into littleness, when "the heart knoweth its own bitterness, and a stranger doth not intermeddle with its joy." So it was with Mary Stansfield. She had a refined and luxurious home, and all her wants supplied. She was practically mistress of the household, and had many friends and acquaintances in the families of the neighbouring gentry, several of whom had country seats within easy walk or drive of her home. Yet there was a heavy cross in her lot, and its edges were very sharp. In her aged aunt, with whom she lived, there were a harshness of character, and an inability to appreciate or sympathise with her niece, which would have made Mary Stansfield's life a burden to her had it not been for her high sense of duty, her patient charity, and God's abiding-grace in her heart. Misunderstood, thwarted at every turn, her attentions misinterpreted, her gentle forbearance made the object of keen and relentless sarcasm or lofty reproof, her supposed failings and shortcomings exposed and commented upon with ruthless bitterness, while yet the tongue which wounded never transgressed the bounds imposed by politeness, but rather chose the blandest terms wherewith to stab the deepest, - hers was indeed a life whose daily strain taxed the unostentatious grace of patience to the utmost, and made her heart often waver, while yet the settled will never lost its foothold.

Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus (hRSV) is an enveloped virus of the Orthopneumovirus genus within the newly created Pneumoviridae family [1] which also includes bovine RSV (bRSV) and pneumonia virus of mice (PVM). hRSV strains are classified into two main antigenic groups - hRSV A and hRSV B- which cause seasonal epidemics in winter months and circulate worldwide. For each group a number of clades have been identified (currently 16 for hRSV A and 22 for hRSV B) [2]. hRSV has a negative stranded RNA genome which is approximately 15 kb long with 10 gene transcripts encoding 11 proteins [3], two of them being the major surface glycoproteins, namely the attachment or G glycoprotein and the fusion (F) glycoprotein. In 2015, it was estimated that infection with hRSV resulted in 33.1 million episodes of lower respiratory infection (bronchiolitis and pneumonia) leading to 3.2 million hospitalisations and around 120,000 deaths worldwide in children younger than five years [4]. In addition, hRSV is an important cause of respiratory disease in the elderly and in immunocompromised adults, contributing to a substantial disease burden in these populations [5]. Despite such a high disease burden, no licensed hRSV vaccine is yet available. Initial attempts to create an hRSV vaccine in the 1960s were unsuccessful: a heat and formalin inactivated whole virus vaccine administered to young children did not only fail to prevent infection in the subsequent season, but led to more severe infection (enhanced disease) upon natural infection in a high percent of vaccinees and two deaths [6]. However, almost twenty prophylactic vaccine candidates and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are now in clinical trials, progressing from Phase I to III [7]. If, when available, they achieve widespread use, these vaccines could have a substantial effect on hRSV disease morbidity and mortality. This new impetus in the search for a much needed hRSV vaccine originates mainly from the realisation that protection against virus infection correlates with high levels of neutralising antibodies [8,9] which are mostly directed against one of the hRSV glycoproteins: the F glycoprotein. This glycoprotein mediates fusion of the viral and cell membranes, allowing entry of the viral ribonucleoprotein into the cell cytoplasm and thus initiation of a new infectious cycle [10].

Why is it that lounging at a perfectly manicured resort on a pristine beach could be considered detrimental? The crux of the issue lies in the fact that all-inclusive resorts, more often than not, are owned by foreign corporations. This means that the bulk of the profits generated from tourism flow right back out of the host country, contributing little to the local economy. Instead of benefiting local businesses, artisans, and communities, the money lines the pockets of distant shareholders. Furthermore, these resorts often consume considerable local resources like water and electricity, straining an infrastructure that could otherwise be used to serve native populations better. Picture this: pristine beaches littered with waste once all the sunbathers pack up and leave for the day. It's a grim reality that sees coastal ecosystems damaged, wildlife disturbed, and communities dependent on the natural environment struggling to maintain their way of life. The social impact is equally damaging. The all-inclusive model facilitates a bubble-like experience where tourists are insulated from the local culture, traditions, and daily struggles of the residents. This lack of interaction prevents the kind of cultural exchange that enriches both traveler and host-an element essential to the transformative power of travel. The commodification of culture in resort settings often reduces rich, vibrant histories to mere performances, sterilizing traditions that deserve respect and understanding. So, Andrew, if your aim is to seek out new experiences, culture, and adventure, there are innumerable alternatives to consider. Eco-friendly lodges and community-based tourism initiatives are sprouting up all over the globe. These options allow travelers to more responsibly engage with the local communities, whether that means participating in a family-run homestay in a rural village or hiking through a nature reserve guided by someone who calls that environment home. Experiences like these align more closely with the ideals of sustainable tourism, ensuring that your presence as a visitor leaves a positive footprint rather than a negative one. Of course, it isn't just about what happens abroad; it's about the mindset you carry with you everywhere. Choosing accommodations and activities that respect and uplift the host country takes a conscious decision. It also means looking beyond the typical, carefully curated travel brochures that promise a worry-free paradise, and asking questions about where your money goes, who benefits from your visit, and how your actions might affect the place long after you've departed. The point is to realize the profound influence travel can carry-for better or worse. It's not about sacrificing comfort or forfeiting fun; rather, it's about maximizing the positives for everyone involved, travelers and hosts alike. Travel is too important a gift, bridging worlds and understanding, to be squandered on superficial experiences that leave no lasting impact on the good, but a heavy toll in the wrong corners. In conclusion, it comes down to personal choice-a choice to opt for travel experiences that align with what Andrew and those like him truly seek. Maybe it's time to step outside the confined walls of all-inclusive resorts and into a larger world of meaningful, reciprocal travel adventures. As you pack your bags, remember, how you choose to explore the world tells your story just as much as the tales you bring home. Let it be a story worth telling.

Moreover, ice formation also leads to increased load on the blades and on the tower structure, causing high amplitude vibrations, resonance, and mass imbalance between blades [10], [11], and [12]. This might result in the reduction of the turbine's lifetime due to fatigue damage or in turbine shutdown when such loads go beyond a structural integrity safety threshold, thus decreasing the electricity generation and the overall profitability of the wind park. A viable solution to this problem might be the adoption of alternative operating strategies adapted to the environmental conditions. In this way, when conditions favourable to ice accretion occur, the operational strategy can switch from a "clean-blade" to an "iced-blade" mode, thus mitigating the performance degradation of the turbine. Few studies are available in this direction; in particular Homola et al. [13] suggest not to operate the turbine according to a controller torque-speed map under icing conditions, but instead to force the rotor to keep a constant TSR equal to a clean-blade optimal value. A different solution, as suggested in Ref. [14], can be decreasing the rotational speed of the turbine during the early phase of ice formation in order to decrease the water capture and thus the amount of ice accreted on the blade. However, these alternatives have been assessed for an icing event lasting for a relatively short duration, i.e. approximately 1 h [13,14], and neglected the interaction between ice-shape accretion and wind turbine performance during the event. This assumption is reasonable for small variations of wind turbine performance, and thus for short icing events only. Longer events with higher detrimental effects on turbine performance require the ability of the numerical model to account for the interaction between ice-shape accretion and wind turbine aerodynamics. The objective of this paper is address this gap, providing the scientific community with the results of a numerical approach capable of simulating the ice accretion transient phenomenon by dynamically coupling three different numerical codes, namely a blade momentum code, a computational fluid dynamics solver, and an ice accretion code. As test case the 5 MW NREL wind turbine blade is adopted [15] and submitted to both rime and glaze icing conditions. The icing event is assumed to last for approximately 8 h and the turbine is operated with the reference NRWT operational strategy as baseline and with the two aforementioned alternative strategies from Refs. [13] and [14], evaluating its wind energy conversion performance during and after the icing event. Section 2 provides the reader with an overview of the numerical workflow and of the numerical setup and its validation. Section 3 provides a quick overview of the environmental conditions and operational strategies tested; it then focuses on the ice accretion and wind energy conversion results. Section 4 summarises the results achieved in the present work and highlights the potential of the numerical workflow presented.

On another table, which stood near the window, was spread a cold supper - cold beef, ham, and chicken, with a bottle of old port wine, and a plate of fine biscuits. Annie Lane was the daughter of a younger brother of the Laird's wife, who had died many years ago, leaving his daughter, then quite a baby, entirely dependent upon the charity of her aunt and uncle. This had never failed, however. From the very first they had treated her as one of themselves, and she had grown up into a beautiful girl, who, although she knew nothing of her father's history, nor where he had lived or died, loved both aunt and uncle as dearly as if they had been her own parents. They did not live altogether alone. In addition to the servants there was old Mr. Scrymgeour, a retired merchant, who spent most of his time in a library, which was fitted up with shelves from floor to ceiling, and contained thousands of books of all kinds. He was a good-natured, kind-hearted old gentleman, but terribly deaf, and so absent-minded that he seldom spoke to anyone, unless it was to Annie. Sometimes he would sit for hours gazing vacantly out of the window. When asked what he saw, he replied, "The past, my dear, the past!" At other times he would leave the room hurriedly, and return with some book under his arm, which he would proceed to pore over. As we have said, he was very deaf, but that didn't prevent his being an excellent judge of music. He would listen intently to the songs sung by Annie, and sometimes shake his head approvingly, and utter the word "Good!" If she sang badly, however, he would shake his head, and mutter "No, no!" in a tone of disapproval. He was a very learned old gentleman, and was fond of talking about the stars and planets, and geography, and chemistry, and natural philosophy, and the wonders of electricity. Indeed, there seemed scarcely anything he didn't know something about. He was also exceedingly fond of Annie, and often told her she would make some happy fellow a splendid wife. "And you'll marry soon, my dear," he added. "You're too pretty to remain single. I hope your husband will be a noble young fellow, like yourself, and love God above everything else in the world." "I don't want to get married yet, Mr. Scrymgeour," Annie would reply. "I am sure I shall never meet with a better home than this." "Nevertheless, my dear, you'll marry some day, and I hope it will be happily." Annie laughed merrily. "We'll see about that, Mr. Scrymgeour. The expansion of oilseed rape cultivation in Europe has significant implications for N2O emissions, particularly in Germany, where the crop is widely grown. As mentioned earlier, N2O emissions from agricultural soils are closely tied to N fertilization, and oilseed rape is a crop that requires substantial N inputs to achieve optimal yields. In fact, a study by Sieling et al. (2013) found that N2O emissions from oilseed rape fields in Germany ranged from 0.5 to 3.5 kg N2O-N ha-1, with an average emission factor of 1.3 kg N2O-N ha-1. This is comparable to other studies that have reported N2O emission factors for oilseed rape ranging from 0.6 to 2.5 kg N2O-N ha-1 (e.g., Velthof et al., 2011; Choudhary et al., 2012). The high N2O emissions from oilseed rape fields can be attributed to the crop's high N demand, which is typically met through the application of synthetic N fertilizers. In Germany, for example, the recommended N fertilizer application rate for oilseed rape is around 150-200 kg N ha-1 (KTBL, 2016), which is significantly higher than the recommended rates for other crops such as wheat or barley. Furthermore, oilseed rape is often grown in rotation with other crops that also require high N inputs, such as potatoes or sugar beets, which can lead to a buildup of soil N surpluses and increased N2O emissions. In addition to N fertilization, other factors such as soil type, climate, and management practices can also influence N2O emissions from oilseed rape fields. For example, studies have shown that N2O emissions tend to be higher in soils with high organic matter content, such as those found in regions with high rainfall or poor drainage (e.g., Clough et al., 2013). Similarly, management practices such as tillage and irrigation can also impact N2O emissions, with reduced tillage and irrigation systems often resulting in lower emissions (e.g., Kallenbach et al., 2010). Given the significant contribution of oilseed rape to N2O emissions, it is essential to develop strategies to mitigate these emissions while maintaining crop yields and profitability. One approach is to optimize N fertilizer application rates and timing to minimize N surpluses and reduce N2O emissions. This can be achieved through the use of precision agriculture techniques, such as soil sensors and crop monitoring systems, which can help farmers tailor N applications to crop needs. Additionally, the use of cover crops and crop rotations that include legumes or other N-fixing species can help reduce N fertilizer inputs and promote soil health. Ultimately, a combination of these approaches will be necessary to minimize the environmental impacts of oilseed rape production while meeting the growing demand for biofuels and other products.

He had chosen this hazardous mode of conveyance at night, as the coach crept by his place of concealment in the wayside brush, to elude the sheriff of Monterey County and his posse, who were after him. He had not made himself known to his fellow-passengers, as they already knew him as a gambler, an outlaw, and a desperado; he deemed it unwise to present himself in his newer reputation of a man who had just slain a brother gambler in a quarrel, and for whom a reward was offered. He slipped from the axle as the stage-coach swirled past the brushing branches of fir, and for an instant lay unnoticed, a scarcely distinguishable mound of dust in the broken furrows of the road. Then, more like a beast than a man, he crept on his hands and knees into the steaming underbrush. Here he lay still until the clatter of harness and the sound of voices faded in the distance. Had he been followed, it would have been difficult to detect in that inert mass of rags any semblance to a known form or figure. A hideous, reddish mask of dust and clay obliterated his face; his hands were shapeless stumps exaggerated in his trailing sleeves. And when he rose, staggering like a drunken man, and plunged wildly into the recesses of the wood, a cloud of dust followed him, and pieces and patches of his frayed and rotten garments clung to the impeding branches. Twice he fell, but, maddened and upheld by the smarting spices and stimulating aroma of the air, he kept on his course. Gradually the heat became less oppressive; once, when he stopped and leaned exhaustedly against a sapling, he fancied he saw the zephyr he could not yet feel in the glittering and trembling of leaves in the distance before him. Again the deep stillness was moved with a faint sighing rustle, and he knew he must be nearing the edge of the thicket. The spell of silence thus broken was followed by a fainter, more musical interruption - the glassy tinkle of water! A step further his foot trembled on the verge of a slight ravine, still closely canopied by the interlacing boughs overhead. A tiny stream that he could have dammed with his hand yet lingered in this parched red gash in the hillside and trickled into a deep, irregular, well-like cavity, that again overflowed and sent its slight surplus on. It had been the luxurious retreat of many a spotted trout; it was to be the bath of Lance Harriott. Without a moment's hesitation, without removing a single garment, he slipped cautiously into it, as if fearful of losing a single drop. His head disappeared from the level of the bank; the solitude was again unbroken. Only two objects remained upon the edge of the ravine, - his revolver and tobacco pouch. A few minutes elapsed.

Justice Harry Blackmun wrote for the majority that a woman's liberty to choose to terminate her pregnancy before viability outweighed the state's interests in protecting the potential life of the fetus. He noted that the Constitution does not explicitly mention abortion, but that the right to privacy protects certain personal decisions, including those regarding marriage, procreation and contraception. In addition, he said, the government cannot deny benefits to married couples because they use contraceptives, nor can it restrict access to contraceptives. "If this suggestion of constitutionality be sound, no judicial argument can prevent this Court's adoption of it," Blackmun wrote. The decision immediately sparked criticism. At the time, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the ruling, saying it "legalizes the taking of human life in defense of convenience." In the years following the Roe decision, there were numerous attempts to overturn it. President Ronald Reagan, who opposed abortion rights, appointed two justices to the court, Sandra Day O'Connor and Antonin Scalia. But neither voted to overturn Roe. In 1989, however, Chief Justice William Rehnquist and Justices Byron White, Anthony Kennedy, Scalia and O'Connor joined in a 5-4 decision, Webster v. Reproductive Health Services, which upheld Missouri's ban on using public facilities for abortions and allowing doctors to refuse to perform abortions if they had moral objections. That decision was followed by Planned Parenthood v. Casey, a 1992 case that affirmed the basic principles of Roe, but gave states greater latitude to regulate abortion. Then-President George H.W. Bush called it "a great victory for the unborn." "It is not a good day for America," said President Bill Clinton, who took office shortly thereafter. In 2007, Congress passed the federal Partial Birth Abortion Ban Act, prohibiting a specific type of late-term abortion procedure. While the act had been struck down by lower courts, the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in Gonzales v. Carhart that the procedure was not necessary to preserve the health of the mother and therefore unconstitutional. On the other side, opponents of abortion have long complained that the decision effectively legalized abortion on demand through all nine months of pregnancy. They argue that the definition of viability is too subjective and that the standard allows for elective abortions even after 24 weeks of gestation. According to Guttmacher research, 91 percent of abortions occur within the first trimester. A 2008 study by researchers at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, found that abortions performed later in pregnancy were generally safer than earlier ones, and that the risk of complications increased with advancing age of the pregnant woman. In recent years, the abortion debate has focused on new legislation in several states requiring women to undergo ultrasounds prior to having an abortion, and to view the image of the fetus. Some states have banned abortions based on gender selection. Other measures require parental notification before minors can obtain abortions, and prohibit state funding for abortion services. Critics call these regulations unnecessary infringements on women's rights. Supporters say the laws provide information to help women make informed choices, and keep minors safe from abuse. After the November elections, Republican lawmakers in a number of states introduced bills that would impose strict limits on abortions. A handful of states considered banning abortion altogether. None succeeded, but advocates for both sides predict further battles ahead.

It was a comical sight, indeed, this regal raccoon, clad in his luxurious coat of gray, all bushy and fluffy, mesmerized by the gleam of the kettle perched so high and mighty above the crackling flames. The distinguished raccoon felt ill at ease, as if the very heat of the fire had whispered secrets too grand for his ears. His eyes widened, reflecting the flicker of both flame and copper, an eager curiosity shaded by caution. From his corner of the hearth, the kettle seized the opportunity to showcase its splendor. "Ah, dear friend," it chimed, "fear not my steaming ascendance. I am but a humble kettle, devoted wholly to the delightful task of brewing warmth and joy! Join me in my merry sing-song! Let us not dawdle in this quiet gloom." With that proclamation, the kettle broke into a bright trilling melody that rose and fell with infectious cheer. "Come now, dear raccoon! You needn't fear the heat, for it is we who make the warmth welcome! What would you prefer, a hearty cup of tea to wrap your paws around or shall we consider bubbling delights from the pot?" The kettle's glimmer danced in the warm glow, while the raccoon leaned ever closer, intrigued despite his reticence. At this moment, the kettle's black companion, full of good spirit and bounteous wisdom, interjected, "Ah, lovely kettle, let us not forget the joys of a bubbling feast!" It brimmed with rich broth, a concoction of roots and herbs, which had been simmering with gentle patience, drawing forth the very essence of flavor from each ingredient. "We gather herbs, we gather laughter! In this cozy kitchen, let all take note!" The raccoon's nose twitched, drawn by the fragrant wafts escaping the pot - a most divine blend that could make even the most cautious hearts leap with anticipation. He moved a touch closer, his initial apprehension ebbing softly into warm intrigue as curiosity took the helm. "Why, listen!" he exclaimed, finding his voice. "What delectable treasures cross your lips, mighty kettle? What boons have you to offer this frosty eve?" The flames flickered, mirrors of his growing wonder, and they danced with delight as the kettle bestowed a knowing gurgle in return. "Gather 'round, little wanderer!" proclaimed the kettle heartily, "For an elixir is brewing, a sumptuous melange that banishes the bitter bite of winter. Just a taste will bring cheer to the dreariest of chills!" The great black pot shared tales of yore, of distant lands where spices grew lush and flavors sang among the rivulets of sunlit meadows. Drawn in by such storytelling, the raccoon felt his trepidation dissipate completely, as the wonders of the kettle wrapped around him like a warm blanket. And so commenced an evening of camaraderie; it was then that the snowflakes outside seemed to pause in their dance, yearning to draw nearer, to inch closer to the warmth that flickered and whispered within. In the glow of the firelight, secrets were shared: tales of long whiles spent in kitchens, of flavors conjured into existence - all coming together in a jubilation that turned the winter evening into a tapestry of warmth and friendship. The kettle and the pot sang harmoniously, a duet that hid in their murmurs a promise of feasting and fellowship. The raccoon, at first a mere observer, was transformed into a participant, his heart swelling as he pondered the sweet magic of the night - an evening layered with laughter, narrative, and the sweet aroma of soup that assured warmth would never leave. And so, each tick of the clock turned minutes into memories, simmering in that kitchen retreat, while outside, the world unfurled in a quiet white hush.

I've always been drawn to the arts-whether it's the sweeping grandeur of a masterful painting or the intricate melodies of a timeless symphony. I adore wandering through art galleries, losing myself in canvases filled with color and life. There's a kind of magic there, a suspended reality where anything is possible and the world outside fades away. It's something I need more of in my life-a retreat from the chaos and complication. Speaking of complications, my wardrobe is a constant battle between wanting to dress in beautifully tailored clothes and the reality of my budget. I dream of closets filled with cashmere and silk, of structured blazers and soft cotton tees that are both stylish and comfortable. I'm a sucker for a good sale and find myself hunting down bargains more often than I'd care to admit. And shoes! I can't resist a beautiful pair of shoes, even though my budget often calls for practical flat loafers over the tantalizingly impractical stilettos I occasionally covet. Books are another passion of mine. There's nothing quite like the feeling of cracking open a new novel and inhaling the scent of fresh ink on paper. I could spend hours browsing through bookstores, searching for hidden gems and getting lost in the worlds between their pages. Cooking is an activity I engage with as if it were an art form. There's a rhythm to it, a melody in the sizzle of onions in a pan, a harmony in the blending of flavors and scents. They've been subjected to enough of my "experimental" dinners-some magnificent, others best left unmentioned-that they now approach invitations to dine with wary excitement. I find joy in the small things: the first sip of morning coffee, an unexpected breeze on a hot day, the familiar comfort of an old movie. I like the idea of having routines; they give me a structure upon which to build the chaos of everyday life. The constant ebb and flow between the routine and the unexpected, between the structured and the spontaneous, is perhaps what keeps me grounded. Life is, after all, an intricate dance between the things we can control and those we cannot, and learning that dance is what makes every day a new opportunity for discovery and growth. For all my likes and dislikes, my passions and pet peeves, the world continues to turn, offering endless possibilities.

They have been used for a variety of endpoints related to drug safety, including several assays present in the ICH S2 battery such as the bacterial mutagenicity, mouse lymphoma assay, the in vitro chromosome aberration assay and the in vivo micronucleus assay (Hsu et al., 2018; Kruhlak et al., 2012; Matthews et al., 2006b). In a regulatory environment, (Q)SAR models can contribute to the weight of evidence for decision-making by predicting toxicological endpoints for chemicals with limited or no experimental data (Kruhlak et al., 2012; Rouse et al., 2018). While (Q)SAR models have historically been used for predicting the toxicological profiles of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), models have more recently found mainstream use for predicting the mutagenic potential of drug impurities. Under the ICH M7(R1) guideline, drug impurities and degradants can be assessed for bacterial mutagenicity using two complementary computational methodologies, statistical-based (QSAR) and expert rule-based (SAR) (ICH, 2017). Statistical-based models offer the benefit of being rapid to construct from extremely large and chemically diverse datasets, while expert-rule based models provide greater interpretability capturing human derived and often mechanistically defined structural alerts that contribute to biological activity. If, following expert review, an impurity is predicted to have mutagenic properties by either methodology and the carcinogenic potential is unknown, the ICH M7 guideline recommends that the compound be controlled to a level at or below the threshold of toxicological concern (TTC) (ICH M7, 2017; Muller et al., 2006). Under the ICH M7 guideline, (Q)SAR data may be submitted by pharmaceutical applicants in place of conventional in vitro bacterial mutagenicity assay data for drug impurities up to 1 mg (ICH, 2017). Over the past several decades, numerous bacterial mutagenicity (Q)SAR models have been constructed using a variety of (Q)SAR modeling methodologies and data sets (Cariello et al., 2002; Chakravarti and Saiakhov, 2018; Chakravarti et al., 2012; Contrera et al., 2005; Hanser et al., 2014; Jolly et al., 2015; Marchant et al., 2008; Matthews et al., 2006b; Saiakhov et al., 2013; Stavitskaya et al., 2013a, 2013b; Valerio and Cross, 2012; Votano et al., 2004; Williams et al., 2016; Zeiger et al., 1996). In one of the earlier studies, Zeiger et al. (1996) described the development of Salmonella mutagenicity (Q)SAR models using CASE and TOPKAT, as well as an SAR model based on structural alerts extracted from the published literature (Ashby, 1985; Ashby and Tennant, 1988, 1991). Two versions of the CASE models were constructed: (1) CASE/n contained 820 NTP chemicals and (2) CASE/e contained 808 EPA GENE-TOX chemicals. The external validation performance statistics of these models ranged from 67% to 78% in sensitivity and 66%-84% in specificity. Similarly, the TOPKAT model was also constructed using data primarily derived from the EPA GENE-TOX database. External validation was performed using a set of less than 100 chemicals (45% positive) and performance statistics for these models showed 71% in sensitivity and 76% in specificity (Zeiger et al., 1996).

The calotype process used a paper coated with silver chloride to produce a negative image, which could then be used to create multiple positive prints. This was a significant breakthrough, as it allowed for the mass production of photographs. The 1840s and 1850s saw a rapid expansion of photography, with the establishment of photographic studios and the development of new techniques and technologies. The wet collodion process, introduced in the 1850s, involved coating a glass plate with a light-sensitive solution called collodion, which allowed for faster exposure times and more detailed images. This process became the standard for photography for many years, and it was used to capture some of the most iconic images of the 19th century. In the late 19th century, photography continued to evolve, with the introduction of new technologies and techniques. The introduction of roll film in the 1880s allowed photographers to take multiple exposures without needing to reload a new plate each time. As the 20th century dawned, photography continued to play an increasingly important role in society. It was used to document historical events, such as World War I and the Great Depression, and it became a powerful tool for social commentary and activism. Photographers such as Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans used their cameras to capture the struggles of everyday people, and their work helped to raise awareness about social and economic issues. Today, photography is more widespread than ever, with millions of people around the world capturing and sharing images every day. The advent of digital technology has made photography more accessible and convenient, and it has opened up new possibilities for creative expression. As we look back on the history of photography, we are reminded of the power of this medium to capture and preserve our experiences, and to shape our understanding of the world around us.

The Officer leaned forward, eyes narrowing as he deliberated his words. "It's about the latest reports from the outposts-the disappearances. I've assigned you a task, Grey. We need someone to investigate-dig deeper." The young constable swallowed, stifling the instinctual fear that crept into his mind. "What's the lead? Do we have any suspects?" The Commanding Officer paused, a troubled frown forming. "Some folk speak of strange lights in the sky-others whisper of wolves roaming too close to town. But all we know for sure is that three men have disappeared without a trace, and it's sending ripples of anxiety through the community. We can't afford to reflect weakness." "Understood." Grey felt the familiar stirrings of resolve buoying him. This was no time for hesitation. The people depended on the Order, their safety riding on the unwavering courage of its men. "I'll gather a team. We'll comb the last-known locations-interview those who remain." The Officer nodded appreciatively, a flicker of hope igniting in his weary eyes. "You have our support, Grey. Be vigilant; remember that fear can distort - what appears to be mystery may well hide a far more treacherous truth." With that, he dismissed Grey, who turned on his heel, a curious mix of trepidation and determination thrumming in his chest. As he emerged into the night air, an invigorating cold settled on his skin, sharpening his senses. The weight of the task ahead pressed firmly upon him, but within it lay the pulse of life in the Yukon, a call he could not ignore. With each step back to the Canteen, he felt the camaraderie of the men awaiting him, their shared purpose knitting together their resolve against the shadows that threatened to engulf them all.

In the spirit of experimentation, I find myself lost in thought about the nature of podcasts and their place in our ever-evolving world. They're more than just conversations; they're a portal to endless ideas, a treasure chest filled with the jewels of human experience. Each episode is like a rabbit hole waiting to be explored, offering insights that can shift our perceptions and broaden our horizons. There's something hypnotic about listening to someone articulate the intricacies of their thoughts-it's as if you're sharing a secret with the universe, a connection made through mere words spoken over a mic. Now, as I sit here in this quiet little corner of Marshfield, the soft glow of the Christmas lights dances across the room and I can hear the faint sound of holiday cheer drifting through the walls. It's a reminder that this time of year is all about reflection and gratitude. It makes me think about the shared experiences we often discuss on the podcast, the human condition, our struggles, triumphs, and the absurdity of it all. It's wild to ponder that people from all walks of life can come together over a shared sense of understanding, even when we stand on opposite sides of the spectrum. Imagine a world where every story, every experience, and every thought could be packed into an audio file and released into the ether, just waiting for someone to tune in. There's a magic in that-each podcast episode is reminiscent of a fireside chat, where thoughts flow like a warm drink on a cold winter night. You can almost visualize the coziness, the laughter, the empathy exchanged with each narrative shared. We've all been there, those moments when you feel utterly alone, and then suddenly, you hear someone articulating exactly what you thought, what you felt, and for a second, it feels as if you're not alone anymore. And let's not forget about the accessibility of it all. With platforms like Anchor, creating and sharing your own podcast is as easy as pie. You don't need to have a fancy studio or a degree in broadcasting; all you need is a voice and a story. It's beautifully egalitarian. It's a proverbial megaphone for the collective consciousness-a space where anyone can step up and share their truth, no matter how unconventional or mundane. In a world overflowing with curated content and heavily edited videos, there's something refreshingly raw about podcasting. It's candid, often unscripted, and deeply authentic. You can hear the sincerity in someone's voice when they talk about their passion, their fears, and their lessons learned. It's an unfiltered glimpse into their reality, one that invites listeners to ponder their own lives through a different lens, perhaps inspiring action or simply comforting them in their solitude. So here we are, with Christmas just a breath away, I find myself contemplating what we can learn from these conversations. In a way, every podcast is an invitation to a dialogue, a discussion that we are all part of, whether we choose to actively engage or simply listen from the sidelines. What better time to reflect on that than during the holidays, when connection becomes paramount? I don't know what the future holds for my own podcasting journey, but the mere act of speaking into this microphone feels liberating. As I dive into various topics, I expect nothing and everything at the same time. Maybe, just maybe, by sharing my musings, I can contribute to that beautiful tapestry of thoughts and ideas that binds us all. I raise my glass now, in anticipation of the stories yet to be spun, and the connections yet to be made. Cheers to our adventures beneath the nebulous stars that guide us on this remarkable journey!

The fluid moisturizes the inner surfaces after filling the cracks with the help of the gradient, pressure and concentration (diffusion theory), thus increasing the stiffness and strength of the two pieces and ultimately restoring the cracks [3]. Self-healing speed, quantity, quality and other properties or phenomena are influenced by a number of factors. Researchers have investigated some of the most important factors, including temperature, bitumen characteristics, asphalt mix, rest periods, crack width, additive modification, humidity, and loading conditions. Obviously, these factors sometimes interact with one another and their effects may differ [1]. The self-healing capability of bitumen, mastic and asphalt has also been evaluated in the laboratory and more recently in the field. For this purpose, a range of methods of examining bitumen and asphalt self-healing molds have been described experimentally. There are generally three types of fatigue-based tests, including rupture-based and non-destructive tests. In fatigue-based tests, samples are placed for a given period of time under abrupt and repetitive loading conditions (e.g. in a normal fatigue test). Loading is carried out through a two-point bending test, a four-point bending test (4PB), or sometimes an inertial tensile test to evaluate the repair ability of asphalt mixtures [1]. According to Bazin and colleagues' laboratory research on the fatigue of asphalt mixtures, resting periods had a beneficial effect on bitumen, which was fatigued and even ruptured. Moreover, the tested specimens exhibited superior healing capability, especially at relatively high temperatures. The researchers pointed out that several other parameters may nonetheless affect this phenomenon [5]. Temperature is deemed the most significant external factor affecting repair ability. A suitable temperature to trigger the restoration process depends on the bitumen number from 30 to 70 C. In this temperature range, bitumen acts as a Newtonian fluid, thus facilitating the recovery process. The chemical properties of bitumen also significantly influence healing capability. Besides, various molecules in bitumen, including asphaltenes, resins, aromatics and saturated colorless fluids that are found in chains, rings and other forms, vary with each type of bitumen, giving bitumen diverse properties [6]. Quan Lv (2016) carried out BBS and CT-Scan experiments to investigate the factors affecting bitumen repair ability. They found that with increasing temperature the bitumen healing capability increased, while temperature was much more effective than restoration time [7]. The properties of bitumen are highly effective on the repair ability of asphalt mixtures, which is why many researchers have investigated the asphalt healing capability of bitumen. Bitumen is a viscoelastic material, whereby at high temperatures it acts as a Newtonian fluid and penetrates cracks through its fluidity (including capillary and flow properties), resulting in asphalt restoration [8]. Fiber asphalt has also been studied by many researchers investigating the effect of fiber on repair ability, heat absorption, energy, and other factors associated with healing. Some researchers added wool fiber to asphalt mixtures and examined their impact on the mechanical and physical properties of asphalt mixtures.

Football clubs are experts when it comes to keeping a player in peak physical condition, but Pericard is convinced the game has room for improvement when it comes to addressing issues of mental well-being. "A player spends 80% of his time outside of the club's supervision and only 20% inside of the club," continued the Frenchman. "It is one thing to look at how a player is physically, but the mental well being of a player is just as important. It can be the difference between teams going up, getting relegated or reaching the Champions League. "The mind plays a massive part in a player's development and performance and this is something clubs need to tap into if they want to increase their chances of winning." The view that talent alone is not enough is one which is widely supported by sports psychologists. That is an approach not lost on five-time European champions Liverpool. "It is absolutely vital that young players are given support right from the start," said Rebecca Symes, Sport Psychologist from British organization Sporting Success, who argues the amount of psychological support available to footballers decreases as they progress into the first team. The Professional Footballers' Association (PFA), a body which represents the interests of soccer players in England and Wales, was not available for comment when contacted by CNN. "The transition from an academy into a senior squad is a really significant time," continued Symes. "I don't think enough emphasis is put on providing support to players during this transition and then throughout their professional career. It is remarkable how the administration clings to its narrative, seemingly impervious to the reality that continues to unfold around it. This week, in a newly published study, experts echoed what many Americans have already felt: the promise of economic prosperity is as elusive as ever. What stands as more troubling is the growing disconnect between the White House's proclamations and the lived experiences of countless citizens who face rising costs and stagnant wages. The numbers released don't lie, they paint a portrait of a nation where the gap between the haves and the have-nots is not merely widening; it is gaping. Yet, in their incandescent certainty, the Bush administration has resolutely painted a rosy picture of the economy, issuing press releases celebrating job growth and low unemployment rates while ducking the hard truths of underemployment and the struggling American family. It seems the administration's approach is built on a foundation of selective data and optimistic spin, rather than addressing the acute economic anxieties that plague so many households. Critics have noted the unsettling trend: millions of working families are caught in a cycle of working harder yet falling further behind, an economic paradox that reeks of neglect. In the realm of healthcare, the statistics are similarly grim. Prescription drug prices soar while access to care grows more tenuous. Each day, people grapple with the agonizing choice of foregoing medication or depleting what little savings they have left. Meanwhile, the government's strategy appears fixated on touting its Medicare reforms as a panacea, all the while sidelining the pressing need for comprehensive healthcare that is accessible to all. It's a classic example of how the administration spins its initiatives without confronting their true implications for the average American. Let's also not overlook the middle class, traditionally viewed as the backbone of the American economy, which now finds itself precariously perched on the edge of collapse. The American Dream feels increasingly out of reach for many, as they question whether hard work still guarantees a stable future. The hollow platitudes from the administration, assuring us that "the economy is strong," do nothing to assuage the fears of those barely scraping by, who wonder how long they can afford to stay afloat in such turbulent waters. Moreover, in conversations about national security, the administration continues to divert attention to the specter of terrorism, using fear as a tool to justify its ongoing agenda. The specter of Iraq looms large, but underlying that narrative is a silence regarding the emerging dynamics of global alliances and the far-reaching consequences of unilateral military action. The very fabric of our foreign policy seems frayed, leaving many to ponder: when will the administration admit to its missteps? When will accountability be demanded? As the months stretch into years, an increasing chorus of voices rises, demanding answers and transparency. The complexities of governance are manifold, yes, but when faced with constant inconsistencies and miscalculations, it becomes clear that the need for genuine engagement with the populace has never been more urgent. In an age where truth seems malleable, it is incumbent upon our leaders to rise above partisanship and embrace the reality that affects us all. As we move forward, one must ask: will we cling to illusions of grandeur, or will we commit to confronting the profound challenges that lie ahead? In an era defined by rapid change and uncertainty, we owe it to ourselves-and future generations-to forge a path grounded in honesty, integrity, and a shared commitment to the truth. The American people deserve nothing less.

Linus entered the store and looked around. There were many computers lying around. A big signboard read "386s $1000". Linus stared at it. His eyes widened. That was almost half of his college fees. He couldn't afford to buy one. But then, he saw a guy with long hair wearing a black t-shirt, carrying a 386. Linus followed him outside and asked him what he did with it. The guy replied, "I sold my soul to the devil for it." Linus quickly ran inside and purchased the 386. He walked back home to his dormitory. When he opened the door, he found Tove waiting for him. She smiled and said "Hello, Linus. You're finally here.". He blushed and said, "Tove, I'm sorry I came so late. I had some work to do." She replied, "That's okay. We'll go out tonight and celebrate your arrival." She kissed him on the cheek and left. Linus sat down on his bed and stared at the 386. "This is great", he thought. Then he remembered the letter from Prof. Tannenbaum. It said, "You must write me a monolithic operating system within 6 months. If you fail to do so, you will be expelled from the university." Linus had never written anything before. He wondered if he could manage it. He took out a pen and paper and started writing. He wrote, "Linux is a monolithic operating system". He laughed. He decided to write a program that would tell him whether Linux was a monolithic OS. He started typing on the keyboard, "Linux is a monolithic OS". Then he tried to compile it. But there was no compiler. He searched through his bookshelf and found a copy of K&R. He started reading it. After several hours of reading, he understood the basics of C programming. He started writing the program again. This time he wrote, "int main() { printf("Linux is a monolithic OS"); }". He compiled it and got an error saying, "syntax error: missing semicolon at line 3". He scratched his head. What the hell was a semicolon? He checked the book and discovered that he needed to put a semicolon at the end of every statement. He added the semicolons and tried compiling again. This time he got another error. He checked the book again and found out that he had forgotten to declare the function 'printf'. He declared it as follows, "extern int printf();". He recompiled and this time he got a warning message saying "warning: unused variable 'printf' defined at line 4". He checked the book again and found out that he had forgotten to call the function 'printf'. He changed the code as follows, "int main() { printf("Linux is a monolithic OS"); return(0); }". He compiled it and got the following output, "Linux is a monolithic OS" Linus grinned. He had done it. He had written his first program. He was a programmer. He was going to change the world. He was going to write the greatest operating system ever. He was going to rule the computing world. He was going to become rich and famous. He was going to marry Tove. He was going to live happily ever after. He fell asleep. Next morning, he woke up to the sound of a knock on the door. He opened the door and found Tove standing there. She smiled and said, "Good morning, Linus. Are you ready to go out?".

Amaryllis did not stay to think of the century, but ran round the corner of the house, and came face to face with the east wind, which took her with such force as to momentarily stay her progress. Her skirts were blown out horizontally, her ankles were exposed, and the front line of her shape (beginning to bud like spring) was sketched against the red brick wall. She laughed, but the strong gale filled her throat as if a hand had been thrust down it; the wind got its edge like a knife under her eyelids, between them and the eyeballs, and seemed as if it would scoop them out; her eyes were wet with involuntary tears; her lips dried up and parched in a moment. The wind went through her thick stockings as if the wool was nothing. She lifted her hand to defend her eyes, and the skin of her arm became "goosey" directly. Had she worn hat or bonnet it would have flown. Stooping forwards, she pushed step by step, and gradually reached the shelter of the high garden wall; there she could stand upright, and breathe again. Her lips, which had been whitened by the keen blast, as if a storm of ice particles had been driven against them, now resumed their scarlet, but her ears were full of dust and reddened, and her curly dark hair was dry and rough and without gloss. Each separate hair separated itself from the next, and would not lie smooth - the natural unctuous essence which usually caused them to adhere was dried up. The wind had blown thus round that corner every March for a century, and in no degree abated its bitter force because a beautiful human child, full of the happiness of a flower, came carelessly into its power. Nothing ever shows the least consideration for human creatures. The moss on the ridge of the wall under which she stood to breathe looked shrivelled and thin, the green tint dried out of it. A sparrow with a straw tried hard to reach the eaves of the house to put it in his nest, but the depending straw was caught by the breeze as a sail, and carried him past. Under the wall was a large patch recently dug, beside the patch a grass path, and on the path a wheelbarrow. A man was busy putting in potatoes; he wore the raggedest coat ever seen on a respectable back. As the wind lifted the tails it was apparent that the lining was loose and only hung by threads, the cuffs were worn through, there was a hole beneath each arm, and on each shoulder the nap of the cloth was gone; the colour, which had once been grey, was now a mixture of several soils and numerous kinds of grit. The hat he had on was no better; it might have been made of some hard pasteboard, it was so bare.

He had brought me up in solitude, and I was old for my age, learned in some things far beyond my years, and ignorant of others I should have known. I loved the man passionately. In the long winter evenings, when the howl of wolves and "painters" rose as the wind lulled, he taught me to read from the Bible and the "Pilgrim's Progress." I can see his long, slim fingers on the page. They seemed but ill fitted for the life he led. The love of rhythmic language was somehow born into me, and many's the time I have held watch in the cabin day and night while my father was away on his hunts, spelling out the verses that have since become part of my life. As I grew older I went with him into the mountains, often on his back; and spent the nights in open camp with my little moccasins drying at the blaze. So I learned to skin a bear, and fleece off the fat for oil with my hunting knife; and cure a deerskin and follow a trail. At seven I even shot the long rifle, with a rest. I learned to endure cold and hunger and fatigue and to walk in silence over the mountains, my father never saying a word for days at a spell. And often, when he opened his mouth, it would be to recite a verse of Pope's in a way that moved me strangely. For a poem is not a poem unless it be well spoken. In the hot days of summer, over against the dark forest the bright green of our little patch of Indian corn rippled in the wind. And towards night I would often sit watching the deep blue of the mountain wall and dream of the mysteries of the land that lay beyond. And by chance, one evening as I sat thus, my father reading in the twilight, a man stood before us. So silently had he come up the path leading from the brook that we had not heard him. Presently my father looked up from his book, but did not rise. As for me, I had been staring for some time in astonishment, for he was a better-looking man than I had ever seen. He wore a deerskin hunting shirt dyed black, but, in place of a coonskin cap with the tail hanging down, a hat. His long rifle rested on the ground, and he held a roan horse by the bridle. "Howdy, neighbor?" said he. I recall a fear that my father would not fancy him. In such cases he would give a stranger food, and leave him to himself. My father's whims were past understanding. But he got up. "Good evening," said he. The visitor looked a little surprised, as I had seen many do, at my father's accent. "Neighbor," said he, "kin you keep me over night?" "Come in," said my father.

Or was it something darker something more sinister lurking inside of them waiting for the right moment to strike. When we last left off Evelyn Walsh McLean the newspaper heiress who purchased the diamond in 1912 was facing her worst nightmare. Her son Vincent was dead after crashing his car into a tree while driving under the influence of alcohol. He was only nine years old. His death devastated Evelyn and she fell into a state of depression. She locked herself away in her bedroom refusing to eat or talk to anyone. Her husband Ned attempted to console her, but he was still reeling from his own tragedy. Just two months before Vincent's accident. Their daughter Marjorie died of typhoid fever. It was too much for Ned. He started drinking heavily and spending time with other women. He would disappear for days without telling Evelyn where he was going. One day he came back home to find that Evelyn had changed all the locks. She refused to speak to him ever again. She banished him from their house and he moved into a hotel room. A few weeks later Evelyn received a phone call from Ned's lawyer. He told her that Ned was being committed to a mental hospital. He had been diagnosed with severe dementia and needed professional care. Evelyn did not visit Ned in the hospital. She had grown tired of his infidelity and drunken behavior. She believed that his illness was punishment for his sins. In reality Ned had fallen victim to syphilis a sexually transmitted disease that causes insanity. It was incurable at the time and would eventually kill him. But Evelyn never knew that because she cut off contact with him completely. She was determined to move forward with her life and put the past behind her. She began traveling across Europe. She visited France Italy Spain Morocco and Egypt. She would go on extravagant shopping trips buying expensive clothes jewelry and furniture. She spent millions of dollars a year living lavishly and giving money to charities. She even bought a private island in Florida called Mystery Island where she built a mansion and entertained famous guests such as Charlie Chaplin and Winston Churchill. On the surface it appeared that Evelyn had recovered from her grief. But underneath she was still struggling. She continued to wear the Hope Diamond around her neck despite warnings from friends and family that it was bad luck. She believed that the diamond could protect her from harm. But little did she know that the diamond was slowly destroying her from within. In 1946 Evelyn was diagnosed with breast cancer. She underwent surgery to remove one of her breasts. But the cancer spread to her lymph nodes. Doctors gave her six months to live. But Evelyn refused to give up hope. She traveled to Lourdes France a town known for its healing waters. She drank the water and prayed to Saint Bernadette. But her health continued to decline. She lost weight became weak and bedridden. She was forced to sell most of her possessions including Mystery Island to pay for medical bills. In May of 1951 Evelyn passed away at the age of 60. She was buried wearing the Hope Diamond. According to legend whoever wears the diamond will die a violent death. But Evelyn's death was peaceful compared to those of her predecessors. Maybe the curse had finally run its course. Or maybe it was just getting started. After Evelyn's death the Hope Diamond was inherited by her grandchildren. They decided to donate it to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington DC. They hoped that by giving it away they would break the curse once and for all. The Hope Diamond arrived at the Smithsonian on November 10th 1958.

Other forms of parasomnia include sleep-eating; sleep sex, in which sexual acts are carried out by a person who's asleep; and somniloquy, when someone talks aloud while sleeping, even making long speeches. Some disorders, like Jodie's hallucinatory somnambulism (sleepwalking), are associated with partial waking up - and many are thought to have a genetic component to them. Indeed, Jodie's mother and aunt suffer from the condition, too. Jodie was four when she first remembers it happening. 'I had tonsillitis and a fever. I woke up and saw yogurt pots and spoons marching around my bedroom,' she says. 'I screamed out to my mother and she soothed me back to sleep. She told me it was just a bad dream.' All children suffer nightmares, of course, and some experience night terrors with a sleepwalking element to them, particularly when they're feverish. But Jodie's parasomniac episodes didn't stop there. They increased in frequency and intensity, until, by the time she reached her 20s, she was suffering night-time hallucinations many times each night. If it happened when she was alone, she would barely remember it the next day. But when friends came to stay, they were in for an eerie shock. 'I once had some girlfriends over, and got up in the night believing they were trapped in nets or plastic bags,' she says. 'I ran over to them, screaming, trying to "free" them from suffocation.' Jodie took to warning boyfriends of her 'dark side'. 'At night, I'd see all sorts of things - burglars, people standing in the room, floating objects, police coming to arrest us. Some boyfriends would be understanding. Some not so much.' By the age of 24, she was at her wits' end, and at last went to her GP, who prescribed sleeping pills. 'I tried one brand and it did diminish the hallucinations a little,' she says. 'But I'd wake up so groggy and exhausted, it was counter-productive. I was as tired as if I'd been up six times as usual.' Over the years, Jodie has tried various pills but none stopped the disorder completely. Often she'd be so exhausted she couldn't focus at work. In her late 20s, she was referred to a sleep clinic, but to her disappointment, found no answers there either. Jodie (pictured aged 2) remembers her first experience of the condition aged four. 'I hoped they'd analyse my sleep patterns but they didn't,' she says. 'The consultant simply told me I would "grow out of it", which I found strange as I was already an adult.' Children do grow out of some disorders associated with the hypnagogic state. The form of sensory distortion known as Alice In Wonderland Syndrome, for example - where people feel as though parts of their body shrink or grow - is thought to affect far more children than adults. Yet other parasomnias affect those of any age.

The remaining 14 councils said they planned to start using the cameras before the law changed. Of these, three said they would wait until March 31, when the government's consultation period ended, while 11 said they would begin immediately. They include Leeds City Council, Newcastle City Council, Hull City Council, Wakefield Metropolitan District Council, Wigan Metropolitan Borough Council, Cheshire West and Chester Council, Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council, Blackpool Council, Oldham Council, South Tyneside Council and Brighton & Hove City Council. Two other local authorities, Doncaster Metropolitan Borough Council and Bournemouth Borough Council, said they intended to buy CCTV cars but had not done so yet because of delays caused by the government's decision to consult on banning them. These two authorities said they wanted to see the outcome of the consultation before deciding whether to proceed. Meanwhile, 17 councils said they currently had no plans to launch CCTV cars but had discussed the issue during the past year. Many of those said they had received calls from members of the public asking if they could bring in the technology. Among them were some of the largest councils in the country, including Birmingham City Council, Coventry City Council, Nottinghamshire County Council, Cornwall Council and Bristol City Council. Others that said they had considered the idea included Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council, Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council, Trafford Metropolitan Borough Council, Wirral Metropolitan Borough Council and Sunderland City Council. At least 39 councils said they had not considered bringing in the technology. A further 21 refused to say anything about it. Among those refusing to comment were London councils Islington, Camden, Hackney, Tower Hamlets, Lambeth, Lewisham, Newham, Redbridge and Croydon. They all claimed they were covered by the Official Secrets Act and therefore unable to respond. The data suggests that councils in the north east, north west and Yorkshire are most likely to use CCTV cars. In total, 36 per cent of councils in the north east and 35 per cent of councils in the north west have bought or plan to buy the technology. By contrast, only 13 per cent of councils in the south west have taken this step. Mr Pickles first spoke out against the use of CCTV cars in July 2012, saying they were 'not acceptable'. He said the practice undermined natural justice and meant drivers were forced to pay without knowing what offence they had committed. He said he had seen evidence of CCTV cars being used to catch drivers who did not know where they were supposed to park. The use of the technology was also criticised by the Police Federation, which called for a crackdown on the 'cash cow' industry. And the AA issued a warning over councils using CCTV to target drivers on yellow lines, which are supposed to be enforced only when signs tell motorists they are in operation.

In the same study conducted by J. Brame et al. [25], significant inhibitory effect of NOM on the degradation of pharmaceuticals in UV/H2O2 process was reported. Viewing the aforementioned facts, recently studies have been carried out to investigate the efficacy of employing photosensitization induced by visible light and solid photosensitizers for organic chemical removal in various water matrices [12,26,27], where singlet oxygen (1O2) was considered to be the primary oxidant. 1O2 is an energetically rich form of molecular oxygen, which has about 1 eV higher energy and is more reactive than ground state oxygen [28]. As an oxidant which has a higher oxidizing potential (about 1 V higher [28]) than ground state oxygen, its application in organic pollutant elimination has been investigated [29-32]. However, involvement of solid photosensitizers is still a drawback. Because 1O2 has a very short life time, the presence of 1O2 is limited to a thin layer close to the solid phase; only adsorbed pollutants can be well degraded [33]. Moreover, inorganic ions and NOMs in water matrices can still reduce the process efficiency by blocking the active site of solid sensitizers. In this manner, homogeneous singlet oxygen mediated processes can be an alternative, because the aforementioned problems associated with heterogeneous system can be avoided. Methylene blue (MB) has great potential to be utilized as homogeneous photosensitizer for such purpose. It has strong light absorption in visible range which can avoid the inner filter effect of NOMs in complex water matrices, has a relatively high quantum yield of singlet oxygen formation [34], and has a long history of safe use in human treatment without major side effect. The red light induced MB photosensitization process for singlet oxygen formation is reported to have a broad application field including disinfection in not only wastewater treatment but also blood products [35-40], where singlet oxygen was generated to kill pathogens, as well as medical therapy, where red light induced MB photosensitized singlet oxygen was directed to selectively kill tumour cells for cancer therapy [38]. Nevertheless, no attempt has been made to employ MB as homogeneous photosensitizer for pharmaceuticals removal. Light source is another important factor for photon-involved processes, because it imposes great influence on the operational and maintenance costs. Conventional light sources include mercury lamps (for UV involved systems), fluorescent lamps and Xe-arc lamps (for visible light involved systems), etc. Recently, light emitting diodes (LED) are gaining increasing interests in view of their advantages: short warm-up time, no hazardous materials disposal, long life time, compatibility, narrow light emission spectra, etc [20,41]. Attempt has been made to utilize LED as light sources in photo-oxidation processes very recently [41-43]. However, to the best of the authors' knowledge, no studies have been conducted to investigate the use of red light LED for photodegradation of pharmaceuticals.

Often based on spectral density mapping (20,21), most of these approaches rely on the model-free formalism, with residue-specific correlation times (22,23) (i.e., without an overall diffusion tensor), a distribution of picosecond and nanosecond correlation times (24,25), or a statistical analysis of extended model-free parameters (26). An analysis based on a distribution of correlation times necessarily introduces a physical bias, since one must choose a mathematical function to describe the distribution. In the case of the model-independent correlation (MIC) time distribution (26), the statistical independence of three types of motions is not required, since the extended model-free results are considered as a simplified representation of a continuous distribution of correlation times. However, the significance of such a statistical treatment is necessarily limited, since it provides little information about the number of modes of the actual distribution of correlation times. Neither approach seems suited to describe a distribution of correlation times that is a priori unknown. However, simply increasing the number of correlation times or distributions in either approach would be questionable, since the empirical information available from nuclear spin relaxation is limited. Here, we introduce an approach we call interpretation of motions by a projection onto an array of correlation times (IMPACT) to analyze multiple-field relaxation data in disordered proteins. This method relies as little as possible on any particular physical model of protein motions but constitutes a mathematical reconstruction of the distribution of correlation times. We define an array of n correlation times, i (or, equivalently, of reciprocal frequencies, i = 1/ i) in a range that is effectively sampled by nitrogen-15 relaxation. The experimental spectral density function is then reproduced by a sum of n Lorentzian functions, Ji( ), one for each correlation time i. The result of this process, similar to a projection onto a basis of Lorentzian functions, is a discrete distribution of correlation times spanning a range that is relevant to rationalize relaxation. This approach is analogous to the discretization step encountered in regularization methods (27,28), but the volume of experimental data exploited in this study is too limited to use a full regularization approach. Nevertheless, the multimodal character of the distribution of correlation times can be nicely revealed, and the most relevant correlation times for backbone motions can clearly be identified. IMPACT was originally conceived for a set of relaxation rates obtained at five magnetic fields ranging from 9.4 to 23.5 T (i.e., with proton Larmor frequencies of 400, 500, 600, 800, and 1000 MHz) and later applied to a more limited set recorded at 500, 600, and 800 MHz. Relaxation rates were recorded for a uniformly nitrogen-15-labeled sample of the protein Engrailed 2. Engrailed 2 is a transcription factor that possesses a well-folded DNA-binding homeodomain and a long, 200-residue, mostly disordered N-terminal region.

The ecophysiological role of this red pigment has been investigated in a number of instances, and, in many - but not all - cases, anthocyanins have been ascribed a photoprotective role in the ecophysiology of the plant (Neill and Gould, 2003). This red pigment is usually found in the exposed leaf epidermis and, as a consequence, the anthocyanin absorbs photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), thereby shading the chlorophyll deeper in the leaf (Gould et al., 2002a, 2002b; Hatier and Gould, 2007). This shading is thought to protect the chlorophyll and, hence, leaf from photodamage of the photosynthetic apparatus (Neill and Gould, 2003; Liakopoulos et al., 2006; Manetas, 2006; Hughes and Smith, 2007; Shao et al., 2008; Fondom et al., 2009). Although Kyparissis et al. (2007) found that anthocyanin shaded the underlying chlorophyllous tissues in Prunus cerasifera, and they reported that these leaves indeed exhibited no evidence of photoinhibition, yet neither did leaves of a related Prunus species lacking anthocyanin. Similar findings were reported for Cornus stolonifera by Field et al. (2001). Furthermore, Kytridis et al. (2008) found less photoprotection in red, anthocyanic leaves of Cistus creticus, relative to green leaves that lacked anthocyanin. Li et al. (2009) reported that the degree of photoprotection provided by anthocyanin depended on the spectral quality of the incident radiation in Berberis thunbergii, while Karageorgou and Manetas (2006) found that the degree of photoprotection provided by anthocyanin depended on the concentration of chlorophyll present in the leaves of the oak Quercus coccifera. Clearly, based on all these studies, the role of anthocyanins in protecting leaves from photoinhibition is difficult to generalize. In most plants investigated thus far, the majority of anthocyanin is found in the epidermis or mesophyll only of the exposed surface of the leaf (Hart, 1988), which fits well with a photoprotective role. In contrast, the leaves of the South African succulent A. rufescens are purple on both adaxial and abaxial surfaces (Fig. 1), typically appearing more so on the abaxial surface. Such plants often grow in arid regions of South Africa in shallow soil or in cracks on large rocks that are light-colored (light gray or tan), which would expose both sides of the leaves of this succulent to a high radiant energy load, i.e., direct sunlight from above and reflected sunlight from below. As a result, it is reasonable to predict that the pigment anthocyanin might play a crucial role in photoprotection and survival of this species in its arid, high-insolation environment. It was the goal of this study to determine if this prediction is accurate. A precedent for this study exists in Hughes and Smith (2007), who reported that "doubly" anthocyanic leaves - with anthocyanin layers on both the adaxial and abaxial surfaces - of the forest understory herb Galax urceolata maintained greater photosynthetic efficiency than did green leaves.

On the other hand, Choi et al. [12] investigated experimentally flow distribution in a parallel plate microchannel heat sink using water as working fluid. The microchannel consisted of nine identical square channels having 500 1/2m width and height. The microchannel was made from a copper block. The experiments showed that there was a difference between the mass flow rate entering each channel and this difference was attributed to the fabrication error during the manufacturing process. This indicates that it is difficult to produce a perfect geometry without any defect. Also, the authors found that the pressure drop across the microchannel was larger than expected and they attributed this to the presence of bubbles inside the microchannels. In addition, the measured Nusselt number was much smaller than the one predicted by the conventional theory, which may be due to the fact that the microchannel used in this study was too long and this led to the development of fully developed flow. Furthermore, Wong et al. [13] performed CFD simulations for two different geometries of a microchannel heat sink using air as a test fluid. The first geometry had a serpentine configuration where the fluid flowed through the channels vertically and then horizontally. While the second geometry had a parallel configuration where the fluid flowed horizontally. The results showed that both geometries gave almost similar thermal performance in terms of the maximum temperature reached by the microchannel. However, the pressure drop was higher in the case of the serpentine geometry compared to the parallel one. Additionally, the authors mentioned that the entrance region was long enough to allow the flow to become fully developed before reaching the end of the microchannel. Therefore, the heat transfer coefficient calculated based on the entire length of the microchannel should be reduced accordingly to account for the developing flow. The same conclusion was drawn by Wu and Cheng [14] who performed CFD simulations for a multi-channel micro heat sink. Their results showed that the maximum temperature reached by the micro heat sink was lower when the inlet flow velocity was increased. Moreover, the results also showed that the maximum temperature was lower for the serpentine micro heat sink than for the parallel one. This is because the former has more surface area available for heat dissipation than the latter. The authors pointed out that the entrance region was long enough to allow the flow to reach a fully developed state along the micro heat sink. Thus, the heat transfer coefficient calculated based on the entire length of the micro heat sink should be reduced accordingly to account for the developing flow. On the other hand, Koo and Kleinstreuer [15] performed CFD simulations for four different configurations of a parallel plate microchannel heat sink using water as a test fluid. The four configurations differed in the inlet/outlet location of the microchannel with respect to the finned surfaces. It was found that the configuration with the inlet located near the top edge of the microchannel gave the best performance in terms of heat transfer and pressure loss. The authors stated that the reason behind this result was that the flow was less likely to enter the fins directly since the flow was directed into the microchannel first. Therefore, the flow would be disturbed less by the fins and thus could transport more heat away from the heated surface. Another important parameter affecting the performance of micro heat sinks is the Reynolds number. Koo and Kleinstreuer [16] investigated experimentally and numerically the effect of Reynolds number on the thermal performance of a microchannel heat sink. The experimental results showed that the average temperature decreased linearly with increasing Reynolds number. Also, the results showed that the temperature difference between the center and edge of the heat sink increased as the Reynolds number decreased.
