Major 6ths were found to be consistently tuned to equal temperament. The interval of a third has received particular scrutiny in research from a performance and perception perspective due to the large discrepancies between tuning systems (particularly equal temperament and just tuning) for these intervals, with a general understanding amongst trained a cappella ensembles to narrow major thirds and widen minor thirds to be more in keeping with just intonation (Potter9 p. 160). Mayer10 in describing how choirs can aspire to just tuning asserts that it is "certainly the most difficult of all intervals to sing in tune" (p. 110). Focusing on the tuning of thirds but from the perspective of the listener, Ternstrom and Nordmark11 conducted a study on tuning perception whereby expert listeners (mainly choral musicians but some orchestral) tuned synthesized dyads into major thirds. The mean results were closer to equal temperament than just intonation; however, the spread of results within subjects suggested no preference to a particular tuning system. Listeners distinguished between equal temperament and just intonation in another perceptual study, which used synthesized sounds to consider pitch drift in short chord progressions, however preference to tuning system was found to be individual.12 The results emerging from empirical research which reveal ambiguous perception preferences towards specific tuning systems/temperaments are also reflected in literature discussing best practice, in which the issue of tuning and temperament in a cappella singing continues to be highly topical and often contentious. In "A Performer's Guide to Renaissance Music" Planchart13 asserts that, "Given the tenacity of the resistance of modern singers to just intonation," singers will find it difficult to deviate from equal temperament but "directors should ultimately neither give up or let up" (p. 38). In the same book, Blachly,14 also extolling the importance of just intonation as producing "a more satisfying in-tune result," acknowledges that "training a small choir or vocal ensemble to sing in tune can be the most difficult challenge facing the director of the early music ensemble" (p. 25). The application of just intonation as common practice has been an area of dispute for some time, although it is often purported to be the ideal practice for a cappella singing ensembles, especially when performing early music. Barbour15 insists that "there is no system of tuning that has the virtues popularly ascribed to just intonation. Neither singers nor violinists use just intonation" (p. 48) whilst Timm16 comments that "A Cappella choirs and string quartets [...] often boast of the use of just, or true, intonation instead of the tempered scale" (p. 19). More recently, it has become commonly reported as a trait of "good ensemble singing" for professional groups to employ just tuning: "Performances by vocal groups such as The Hilliard Ensemble, The Tallis Scholars, and Gothic Voices have made it apparent that approaching perfection in tuning is not an impossible dream" (Duffin,17 p. 287).

From Portsmouth the elated Sea Scouts crossed by steamer to Ryde, their one disappointment being that they were unable to have a glimpse of Nelson's Victory, but the staunch old three-decker was in dry dock, undergoing a thorough overhauling to repair the ravages of Father Time. At Ryde they commenced their four-mile tramp to Wootton Bridge, their gear being piled upon a trek-cart lent them by some obliging brother-Scouts. It was late in the afternoon when the Sea Scouts had their first view of Wootton Creek, and rather unfortunately it was nearly low water. From the top of the hill they could see a very narrow stream meandering between banks of mud. On either side the ground rose steeply, the left bank being thickly wooded. Away to their right the Sea Scouts could discern the creek winding towards the open waters of Spithead, while in the distance the flat coast of Hampshire cut the skyline. "Where's the guardship, sir?" asked Hayes. "There she is, unless I'm greatly mistaken," replied the Scoutmaster, pointing to a long, low, black hull with a white superstructure. "She's not very big," remarked Ted Coles, the greenhorn, dubiously. "And the creek's little larger than a ditch." "Don't look a gift-horse in the mouth," said Desmond. "Wait till we're aboard. Things look a bit deceptive from a height. Come on, you fellows, it's down hill all the rest of the way." At length the Sea Scouts and their trek-cart came to a halt outside an old mill. Here the main road from Ryde to Newport, the "capital" of the Isle of Wight, crosses the creek by means of a brick bridge. Close to it is the village that takes its name from the bridge. "Now to find out Mr. Johnson who has the key of the guardship," announced the Scoutmaster; but, before he could take further steps in the matter, an old, grey-bearded man, wearing a blue reefer suit and a peaked cap, came out of a cottage near by. "You'rn the gen'l'man what's a friend to Mr. Tweedie's, I take it, sir?" he inquired. "Johnson's my name, master mariner for nigh on thirty-five year. I've got the keys, sir. Here they be, an' a list of where everything be to. If you'rn wantin' any help, come to Cap'n Albert Johnson, being me." "Thanks awfully, Captain," replied the Scoutmaster. "I suppose there's a dinghy to get off to the guardship with?" "Ay, ay, there's a nice li'l boat belonging to our Sea Scouts. She'm alongside yon steps, but there ain't enough water just now, seein' as 'ow the tide's out." "In that case we must wait," rejoined Mr. Graham. "How long will it be before the dinghy is afloat?" Captain Johnson gave a glance at the mud-banks. "Matter of an hour, mebbe an hour an' a half," he replied.

I don't know that I feel as sympathetic as you have a right to expect, but, at any rate, I shall be able to do something for you, and if you could contrive to make over a little of what is really inconveniencing you, I have not the slightest objection to be troubled with it. Where is your mistress?" As he spoke he turned towards the door and went in. The house seemed to have fallen by accident among all the great buildings of Florence: it had no porter, no staircase with flats going on and on; it had been built or altered by some Englishman, who had a fancy for a home that should be like England, although the beautiful Italian skies were overhead; and Jack Ibbetson, when he came out with his aunt, Miss Cartwright, to look for a house, fell upon this place, and did not rest until he got hold of it for her. Inside the door there were flowers; a few steps led into a passage which turned off at right angles, and then Ibbetson opened the door of a small salon, and walked through it towards the window, while his eye took in certain evidences that Cartouche had been holding high revel there to the detriment of cushions and covers. "So you still go on the rampage, old fellow?" he said to the dog, who kept close to his heels in a state of suppressed excitement. "If I were you I would leave off this style of thing, I really would. It is nothing short of tyranny on your part. Hallo! what's up now?" For with a wild swoop Cartouche pounced into a corner, dragged out a basket, rushed to the window, and in a moment more was careering round and round the little garden in which the proprietor had indulged his English tastes. It was an odd little garden, with a wall round it, and a poor pretence at English grass, but the wall had capers and pretty hanging things growing out of it, and lizards darting up and down; and the beauty of the garden lay in its great flowering shrubs, in the magnolias, just beginning to show scarlet flames of seed among their glossy leaves, in the bright green of an orange tree and the broad ribbed foliage of Japanese medlars. That some one was sitting there became evident in another moment, when there were uttered a series of appeals in a feminine voice - "Cartouche, Cartouche! Oh, Cartouche, how can you! Come here, you naughty, naughty dog! I shall be obliged to beat you, you know I shall! Come, now, like a good dog. Cartouche, Cartouche, come here!"

All behind is green, from the meadows that mark the southern edge of the bay to the swelling uplands that stretch away and away far in the distance, till the blue mist of the mountains at Braemar sets a kind of barrier. In the centre of the bay the highest point of the land that runs downward to the sea looks like a miniature hill known as the Hawklaw; from this point onward to the extreme south, the land runs high with a gentle trend downwards. Cruden sands are wide and firm and the sea runs out a considerable distance. When there is a storm with the wind on shore the whole bay is a mass of leaping waves and broken water that threatens every instant to annihilate the stake-nets which stretch out here and there along the shore. More than a few vessels have been lost on these wide stretching sands, and it was perhaps the roaring of the shallow seas and the terror which they inspired which sent the crews to the spirit room and the bodies of those of them which came to shore later on, to the churchyard on the hill. If Cruden Bay is to be taken figuratively as a mouth, with the sand hills for soft palate, and the green Hawklaw as the tongue, the rocks which work the extremities are its teeth. To the north the rocks of red granite rise jagged and broken. To the south, a mile and a half away as the crow flies, Nature seems to have manifested its wildest forces. It is here, where the little promontory called Whinnyfold juts out, that the two great geological features of the Aberdeen coast meet. The red sienite of the north joins the black gneiss of the south. That union must have been originally a wild one; there are evidences of an upheaval which must have shaken the earth to its centre. Here and there are great masses of either species of rock hurled upwards in every conceivable variety of form, sometimes fused or pressed together so that it is impossible to say exactly where gneiss ends or sienite begins; but broadly speaking here is an irregular line of separation. This line runs seawards to the east and its strength is shown in its outcrop. For half a mile or more the rocks rise through the sea singly or in broken masses ending in a dangerous cluster known as "The Skares" and which has had for centuries its full toll of wreck and disaster. Did the sea hold its dead where they fell, its floor around the Skares would be whitened with their bones, and new islands could build themselves with the piling wreckage. At times one may see here the ocean in her fiercest mood; for it is when the tempest drives from the south-east that the sea is fretted amongst the rugged rocks and sends its spume landwards.

Up the shallow, wide, old-fashioned staircase, past the wainscoted walls, dark and shining like a mirror, down a long narrow passage with many doors, which but for their gleaming brass handles one would not have known were there, the oldest of the three old servants led little Griselda, so tired and sleepy that her supper had been left almost untasted, to the room prepared for her. It was a queer room, for everything in the house was queer; but in the dancing light of the fire burning brightly in the tiled grate, it looked cheerful enough. "I am glad there's a fire," said the child. "Will it keep alight till the morning, do you think?" The old servant shook her head. "'Twould not be safe to leave it so that it would burn till morning," she said. "When you are in bed and asleep, little missie, you won't want the fire. Bed's the warmest place." "It isn't for that I want it," said Griselda; "it's for the light I like it. This house all looks so dark to me, and yet there seem to be lights hidden in the walls too, they shine so." The old servant smiled. "It will all seem strange to you, no doubt," she said; "but you'll get to like it, missie. 'Tis a good old house, and those that know best love it well." "Whom do you mean?" said Griselda. "Do you mean my great-aunts?" "Ah, yes, and others beside," replied the old woman. "The rooks love it well, and others beside. Did you ever hear tell of the 'good people,' missie, over the sea where you come from?" "Fairies, do you mean?" cried Griselda, her eyes sparkling. "Of course I've heard of them, but I never saw any. Did you ever?" "I couldn't say," answered the old woman. "My mind is not young like yours, missie, and there are times when strange memories come back to me as of sights and sounds in a dream. I am too old to see and hear as I once could. We are all old here, missie. 'Twas time something young came to the old house again." "How strange and queer everything seems!" thought Griselda, as she got into bed. "I don't feel as if I belonged to it a bit. And they are all so old; perhaps they won't like having a child among them?" The very same thought that had occurred to the rooks! They could not decide as to the fors and againsts at all, so they settled to put it to the vote the next morning, and in the meantime they and Griselda all went to sleep. I never heard if they slept well that night; after such unusual excitement it was hardly to be expected they would.

Granny's voice was full of disappointment. With anyone but Mona she would have been very cross indeed, but she was rarely cross with her. "I daresay it'll catch up again quickly with a few sticks," she added patiently. Mona, really ashamed of herself, ran out to the little wood-rick which stood always in the back-yard. "Stupid old fire," she muttered impatiently, "of course it must go out, just to spite me because I wanted to have a little read," and she jerked out the sticks with such force that a whole pile of faggots came tumbling down to the ground. She did not stay, though, to pick them up again, for she really was sorry for her carelessness, and wanted to try and catch up the fire as quickly as possible. She had fully meant to have a nice fire, and the tea laid, and the kettle on the point of boiling, and everything as nice as could be by the time her grandmother got back from the town. But one never got any credit for what one meant to do, thought Mona with a feeling of self-pity. By the time she got back to the kitchen her grandmother had taken off her bonnet and shawl and was putting on her apron. "My feet do ache," she sighed. "The roads are so rough, and it's a good step to Milbrook and back - leastways it seems so when you're past sixty." Mona felt another pang of shame, for it was she who should have gone to the town to do the shopping; but she had not wanted to, and had complained of being tired, and so granny had gone herself, and Mona had let her. "Let me unlace your boots, granny, and get your slippers for you." She thought she would feel less guilty if she did something to make her grandmother more comfortable. "You sit down in your chair, I'll do all that's got to be done." Mrs. Barnes leaned back with a sigh of relief. "Bless the dear child," she thought affectionately, "how she does think for her old granny!" She had already forgotten that Mona had let the fire go out, and neglected to make any preparations for her home-coming; and Mona, who could be very thoughtful and kind if she chose, knelt down and unlaced the heavy boots, and slipped the warm, comfortable slippers on to the tired old feet, laughing and chattering cheerfully the while. "Now you are to sit there, gran, and not to dare to move to do one single thing. I'm going to talk to that fire, and you'll see how I'll coax him up in no time, and if that kettle doesn't sing in five minutes I'll take the poker to him."

The Hinomaru flag has also become a symbol of Japanese militarism (which is driven by Japanese Shinto belief). HISTORY OF PERSECUTION - RELATED TO POWER AND JAPANESE NATIONALISM The first known Christian missionary to Japan was Francis Xavier who arrived in 1549. Christian activity was concentrated around Nagasaki. At this time, Japan was ruled by "shoguns", or military dictators, who monopolised power whilst maintaining a facade of obedience to the emperor. Aiming to stop the spread of Christianity, Shogun Toyotomi Hideyoshi had 26 foreign and Japanese national Christians crucified in Nagasaki on 5 February 1597. Shogun Tokugasa Ieyasu ruled Japan from 1600. Through the 1600-1700s there was severe persecution of Christians - primarily for political and power reasons - after an edict was declared to crush Christianity. "The Kirishitan (Christian) band have come to Japan, not only sending their merchant vessels to exchange commodities, but also longing to disseminate an evil law, to overthrow true doctrine, so that they may change the government of the country and obtain possession of this land. This is the germ of great disaster, and must be crushed." (1603 edict: footnote 1) In 1622, 51 Christians were executed at Nagasaki, and two years later 50 were burned alive in Edo (Tokyo). In 1633 some 30 missionaries were executed. During these years many Christians recanted to escape persecution while some 3,000 were executed and others died in prisons or in exile. In 1865, communities that together totalled some 60,000 Kakure Kirishitan ("hidden Christians") were discovered in the Nagasaki area. These Christian communities had perpetuated the faith in hiding for two centuries. PERSECUTION AND AGGRESSIVE EXPANSION - RELATED TO SHINTO NATIONALISM In 1853, Japan opened its doors to Western trade. Then in 1868, after a brief civil war and palace coup, the shogunate was overthrown and the power of the emperor was restored. This incident is known historically as the "Meiji Restoration". Emperor Meiji instigated revolutionary changes that ushered in sweeping industrialisation, a restoration of Shinto nationalism, and Japanese expansionism, which was fuelled by the belief that Japan was endowed with a unique and divine ruler. Emperor Meiji founded Japan's Yasukuni Shrine in 1869, which was dedicated to the "souls" of all the Japanese soldiers who would fall in conquest. Japan went to war against China in 1894 (with victory in nine months), against Russia in 1904 (with victory in 1905), and against Korea in 1907 (annexing Korea in 1910).

Such a paradigm allows us to investigate not merely whether sensorimotor areas activate in response to linguistic stimuli but whether these activations in turn influence linguistic comprehension and semantic retrieval. By analyzing event-related potentials (ERPs) elicited by word presentations subsequent to the motor actions, we aspire to capture the immediacy of semantic processing in relation to preceding sensorimotor engagement. Engagement of the motor systems at the onset of a word presentation enables us to assess how pre-activated sensorimotor representations correlate with behavioral outcomes on language processing tasks. This methodology not only emphasizes the temporal resolution offered by EEG/MEG but also supports the hypothesis that our understanding of language is fundamentally intertwined with our sensory and motor experiences. In advancing the exploration of the embodied cognition hypothesis, it is essential to delineate the specific ways in which the activation of these sensorimotor systems may coalesce with canonical linguistic networks in the brain. Moreover, we will delve into nuances of semantic categorization as influenced by motor activation. For instance, action verbs that align closely with the type of motion undertaken during the priming phase (e.g., pressing a button with a finger) may elicit distinct ERP patterns when compared to words that are semantically distant from the invoked motor movement. This may offer insights into the specificity of the embodied effects, suggesting that not all sensorimotor activations yield uniform enhancements in semantic processing. Critically, we will also incorporate measures of individual differences, such as motor proficiency, which may elucidate varied extents to which individuals draw upon sensorimotor representations in semantic processing. The integration of these factors shall enrich our understanding of the embodied semantics framework further, providing a nuanced portrayal of how both innate and experiences shape one's engagement with language. Furthermore, the results of such an investigation could have significant implications for broader theories of language acquisition and comprehension. By establishing clearer connections between the physicality of actions and the cognitive processing of language, we may begin to reframe principles of language learning, highlighting the role of embodied experiences as adjunctive to formal linguistic instruction. Additionally, the findings could inform therapeutic approaches for individuals with language impairments, suggesting that reintegrating motor tasks alongside language exercises may foster improvements in communication capabilities. In a similar vein, this investigation should encourage interdisciplinary dialogues between cognitive neuroscience, linguistics, and rehabilitation disciplines, aiming for a more integrated understanding of the cognitive mechanisms underpinning language. Through meticulous analysis and interpretation of the resultant data, we will aim to clarify the interplay between embodied experiences and semantic processing-critically expanding upon the current landscape of embodied cognition theories. As we embark upon this research endeavor, we remain mindful of the complexity and multiplicity of factors that influence language processing, as well as the ever-evolving nature of our understanding within this intriguing field. Our methodological approach underscores a commitment to advancing empirical evidence towards a more comprehensive model of language, one that acknowledges the profound impact of bodily interaction with the world, while simultaneously striving to reconcile it with traditional cognitive frameworks.

She was tall and slender, yet well developed, full of grace without affectation, elegant without effort or constraint. Her arms, uncovered by any sleeve, save that of the jacket, were round and plump, and her hands small and white, though somewhat roughened by housework. The face was oval shaped, with large, almond-shaped eyes, whose color it would be difficult to describe, since they changed according to the varying emotions that stirred her soul, passing from a dark brown to greenish tints; eyes that were soft and languishing, and yet flashed forth lightnings when the spirit within grew angry or indignant. The eyebrows were thin and delicately penciled, the nose straight, and the mouth rather large, with lips that were fresh and ruddy. Her hair, which was abundant, wavy, and of a chestnut hue, was dressed with charming simplicity, and crowned with a wreath of orange blossoms. She was dressed entirely in gray, wearing over her jacket a mantilla of the same color, fastened on the head by means of a tortoise-shell comb, and falling down behind in graceful folds. The train of the bridegroom was composed principally of men, who formed a compact group near him, leaving him exposed, as it were, to the gaze of all beholders, just as the bride stood out in relief against the background of the female crowd. These men, with few exceptions, were of the class which forms the lowest stratum of the middle class, and which in Spain goes by the name of gente decente. This appellation may seem strange, considering the great variety of persons whom it includes. It embraces not only those who are really decent, but also those who, without being so, consider themselves entitled to the epithet because they wear shoes and stockings, and are not obliged to work with their hands. The genuine representatives of this class, however, are the petty officials, clerks, shopkeepers, and tradesmen, who live in modest comfort, and who, while they do not feel called upon to imitate the manners of the aristocracy, yet contrive to preserve intact certain traditions of dignity and decorum inherited from their ancestors. The appearance of these men was perfectly in harmony with their condition. Some of them were attired in frock coats and top hats, others in the ordinary dress coat. Hank's hand clapped him on the shoulder, bringing him back to the urgency of the chase. The boat glided nearer, each stroke an echo of those who had come before, in search of knowledge, in pursuit of a dream, under skies boundless and blue. While many assumed their influence had waned irreparably post-Gingrich, they stealthily regrouped, redefined their strategies, and bided their time, lurking patiently in the shadows of the political landscape. Their quiet persistence has manifested ominously under the umbrella of the Bush administration, creeping back into the limelight not through overt declarations, but through calculated endorsements and policymaking that undermine the very fabric of inclusivity this country attempts to champion. The administration's covert pandering to their ideals is a troubling echo of past challenges. By cloaking discriminatory policies in the veneer of religious freedom and traditional family values, they provide a perfect masque for latent intolerance to manifest under the guise of a moral crusade. This deception is more perilous than outright bias, as it gains legitimacy in the subtlety of its delivery, seeping slowly into the psyche of the public and sowing division under the pretense of unification. President Bush, with his strategically ambiguous vocabulary, avoids addressing these divisive concerns head-on, leaving ample interpretative leeway to those who wish to harness his leadership for their own ideological battles. His reluctance to explicitly champion the rights of the LGBTQ+ community serves as tacit approval for those who feel emboldened by religious rhetoric against them. With this administration, the Religious Right sees a fertile ground for the reintroduction of their once-overthrown dogmas. They trade the firebrand confrontations of the past for quieter, bureaucratic battles; their strategy honed in the miserable lessons from their historical defeats. As they insinuate themselves into the political machinery, they become a voice in shaping policies, appointing judges, and influencing the platforms which will dictate societal norms for generations to come. And therein lies my trepidation-this repackaged agenda is insidiously meticulous. It insulates itself against counterarguments through the manipulation of deeply held beliefs, by pushing the narrative of being under ideological persecution while simultaneously leading the charge in persecuting those who cannot fight back on equal ground. This presidency offers them a mechanism not of explosive revolution, but of slow erosion, enabling them to subtly, yet indelibly, reshape America's moral landscape to mirror their long-standing theological vision. Awakening to this reality has been disconcerting. How often have we believed naively in the ebb and flow of political power, thinking that the pendulum would swing to bring us back from the brink? Yet, here is a stark challenge: the cost of complacency is too high. To abstain from voting or to lend support inadvertently by sheer oversight would be an indictment of our own moral duty. With Bush at the helm, the rise of this clandestine yet determined force imposes upon us a clarion call to vigilance-to not only reject complicit assent but to actively dismantle the ideological structures that seek to define this country's conscience along fractured lines. It is not simply a matter of who is in office, but of what we allow our nation to become. As citizens, our decision must reflect not just a repudiation of discriminatory practices but a heartfelt endorsement of the diverse fabric of humanity-we must choose leaders who mirror these ideals unequivocally.

The limitations of numerical methods have led to the development of analytical and predictive approaches, which can better capture the complexities of occupant behavior and building operation. Analytical methods, such as regression analysis and sensitivity analysis, are often used to identify key factors influencing energy consumption and to optimize building performance. However, these methods rely on simplifying assumptions and may not accurately capture the nonlinear relationships between building parameters and energy consumption. Predictive methods, on the other hand, have shown great promise in building energy forecasting. Artificial neural networks (ANNs), for instance, have been widely used to predict building energy consumption due to their ability to learn complex patterns from historical data. ANNs can be trained using various inputs, such as weather data, building characteristics, and occupancy patterns, to predict energy consumption with high accuracy. Other predictive methods, such as decision trees and support vector machines, have also been applied to building energy forecasting with promising results. Despite the advancements in building energy forecasting, there are still several challenges that need to be addressed. One of the main challenges is the lack of high-quality data, which is essential for training accurate predictive models. In many cases, building energy data is incomplete, inconsistent, or missing, which can lead to inaccurate predictions. Additionally, the complexity of building systems and occupant behavior can make it difficult to identify the most relevant inputs for predictive models. Another challenge is the need for more advanced data analytics and visualization tools to facilitate the interpretation of building energy data. Currently, many building energy management systems (BEMS) provide basic data visualization capabilities, but they often lack advanced analytics and machine learning capabilities. The development of more advanced data analytics tools can help building energy managers and facility managers to better understand building energy consumption patterns and identify opportunities for energy savings. Furthermore, the integration of building energy forecasting with other building systems, such as HVAC and lighting systems, is crucial for optimal building operation. Real-time energy forecasting can be used to optimize HVAC and lighting systems, reducing energy consumption and improving indoor air quality. Additionally, the integration of building energy forecasting with smart grid systems can enable real-time pricing and demand response, which can help to reduce peak demand and improve grid stability. In conclusion, building energy forecasting is a critical component of decarbonizing the global building stock. The development of advanced predictive models, data analytics, and visualization tools can help to improve the accuracy and reliability of building energy forecasts. However, more research is needed to address the challenges associated with building energy forecasting, including the lack of high-quality data, the complexity of building systems and occupant behavior, and the need for more advanced data analytics and visualization tools. By addressing these challenges, we can unlock the full potential of building energy forecasting and accelerate the transition to a low-carbon built environment.

Declan was diagnosed with congenital heart disease - a defect in the structure of his heart - soon after his birth in May 2001. His lips had turned blue and he was transferred to the paediatric unit at Leeds General. Infirmary. Scans showed that the blood vessels in his heart were in the wrong place, while a blockage was obstructing blood flow to his lungs. The wall dividing the left and right lower chambers of his heart was also faulty. As a result blood was not being pumped properly around his body, causing cyanosis - where the skin turns blue because of poor circulation - and fatigue. Doctors warned Kevin and Paula that, as Declan grew up, he would need operations to improve the efficacy of his heart. If these were successful, his life expectancy could still be normal. In the meantime he would need to take aspirin every day to thin his blood so that it could circulate better. Kevin, from Wakefield, Yorkshire, says: 'We clung to the hope that Declan could still lead a normal life - especially as he developed healthily as a baby.' In fact, at six months Declan was deemed robust enough to endure a nine-hour operation to have a shunt - a 3cm tube - fitted in his heart to create a detour from the heart to the lungs, so blood picks up more oxygen and circulation is improved. The operation was a success and Declan blossomed. 'He occasionally grew tired if he over-exerted himself, but refused to let it hold him back,' says Kevin. 'He took his first steps at a year and thrived at school.' (Although Kevin and Paula separated when Declan was 12 months old, they remained friends and shared custody of their son). But in 2008 Declan, then seven, fell and cut his arm. Although only a small 2cm graze, within days he developed flu-like symptoms, caused by an infection in his blood that travelled to his heart. The following month he was diagnosed with endocarditis - a potentially fatal heart infection. Declan spent three months in hospital on an intravenous antibiotic drip. Though the infection cleared up, his heart had become weaker. Paula says: 'His condition could have deteriorated anyway. We'll never know if the cut was the cause.' There, too, was the terrible red man, who, though he built not his wigwam in these wilds, made it his frequent custom of resorting thither, sometimes to follow the chase, but oftener to war with the whites, who lived in great terror of him the whole year round. The Christian name of our hero's father, whom he called "Pap," was Jervis; the Christian name of his mother, whom he called "Mam," was Elster, and the surname was Whitney. They dwelt in a roomy cabin, rudely built of logs and boards, with a clay-topped chimney at each end, and a porch or shed on each side. Under the front porch Jervis hung his saddle, fishing tackle, beaver traps and the like. Under the back porch Elster kept her spinning wheel, crockeryware, garden seed, a big cedar water bucket, with its crooked-handle gourd, and the like; while in there, on the earthen floor of the kitchen, stood her huge, unwieldly loom. The cabin was situated in the midst of a small patch of cultivated ground, hemmed in on every side by dense and lofty woods, which spread their waving shadows for miles and miles away to the north and south, to the east and west, with only here and there, at wide intervals, a similar clearing, or a natural glade to speck the boundless green. Now Sprigg, you must know, happened to be an only child - a most uncommon circumstance in backwoods life - your backwoodsman, like your poor woodcutter, who makes such a figure in old-time story-books, rarely stopped short of a baker's dozen, as a replenisher of the earth. Such being the case, "Pap" and "Mam" must need, of course, do their very utmost to make their one chub as troublesome as six, in order to realize, so it would seem, how much kind Providence had done for them; i. e., by overdoing the thing to make him happy; underdoing the thing to make him good enough to be what they most desired. These innovative methodologies aim not only to enhance the uniformity of the ADC product but to also bolster the therapeutic potential of these conjugates against diverse malignancies. By leveraging advancements in biotechnology, researchers are exploring the use of engineered antibodies designed for optimal binding affinity and specificity towards tumor-associated antigens, thus revolutionizing the ADC landscape [18]. As the understanding of tumor biology evolves, the selection of antigens that are both overexpressed in tumor cells and minimally present in normal tissues has become increasingly essential. This precision in target selection is paramount in mitigating risks of off-target effects, which have been a prominent concern in prior ADC designs. Each step along the ADC development pathway necessitates rigorous validation processes, including thorough preclinical studies to assess both the efficacy and safety of these constructs. In vitro and in vivo models serve as critical platforms for evaluating how ADCs behave in biological systems, guiding optimizations before clinical trials are initiated. Moreover, particular attention is given to the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of each candidate, as these properties directly influence the therapeutic index of the ADC, a crucial factor in the transition from bench to bedside [19]. Beyond mere efficacy, safety profiles of ADCs stand to benefit from emerging conjugation techniques that minimize non-specific binding, a common pitfall of traditional therapeutic methods. Through strategic design, such as utilizing cleavable linkers that release the cytotoxic agent preferentially within the tumor microenvironment, researchers are striving to confine the harmful effects of the cytotoxic drugs to the intended targets [20]. This specificity reduces systemic exposure and the potential for dose-limiting side effects that accompany conventional chemotherapeutics. The landscape of ADC development is further enriched by the integration of personalized medicine principles. Customization of therapies based on individual patient tumor profiles allows for greater therapeutic efficacy and reduced adverse effects [21]. As genomic and proteomic technologies advance, the potential to tailor ADCs to the specific characteristics of a patient's tumor becomes increasingly feasible, facilitating treatments that are as unique as the patients themselves. Moreover, combination therapies involving ADCs are garnering attention. When paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors or other modalities, ADCs can elicit robust anti-tumor immune responses, broadening the scope of therapeutic strategies available for patients with resistant tumors [22]. Synergy from such combinations may lead to improved outcomes, particularly in the treatment of hematologic malignancies and solid tumors notorious for their heterogeneity and complexity. As more ADCs progress through clinical trials, a wealth of clinical data will emerge, informing best practices and optimizing future designs. The ongoing investigation into bispecific ADCs, which can simultaneously target two different antigens, holds promise for tackling tumors that exhibit resistance by evading single-target therapeutics [23]. Such innovations exemplify the relentless quest for improved cancer therapies in the face of daunting challenges posed by tumor diversity, resistance mechanisms, and the intricate tumor microenvironment. In summary, the landscape of antibody drug conjugates is rapidly evolving, characterized by ongoing research and development efforts aimed at overcoming historical limitations. With advancements in technology and a deeper understanding of cancer biology, ADCs represent the forefront of targeted therapies, offering renewed hope in the fight against cancer while consistently striving to optimize safety, efficacy, and personalization.

I had a great affection for the man, and had become so used to his ways and unwearying service that I had not the courage to refuse his prayers to go with me to America. I had not a farthing of my own - he would serve me for nothing - nay, work for me. "Sure," he said, taking off my coat and bringing me my gown, - "Sure, your honour was not made to work." To cheer me he went on with some foolish footman's gossip that there lacked not ladies with jointures who would marry me, and be thankful. I smiled sadly. "That was when I was Mr. Carvel's heir, Banks." "And your face and figure, sir, and masterful ways! Faith, and what more would a lady want!" Banks's notions of morality were vague enough, and he would have had me sink what I had left at hazard at Almack's. He had lived in this atmosphere. Alas! there was little chance of my ever regaining the position I had held but yesterday. I thought of the sponging-house, and my brow was moist. England was no place, in those days, for fallen gentlemen. With us in the Colonies the law offered itself. Mr. Swain, and other barristers of Annapolis, came to my mind, for God had given me courage. I would try the law. For I had small hopes of defeating my Uncle Grafton. The Sunday morning dawned brightly, and the church bells ringing brought me to my feet, and out into Piccadilly, in the forlorn hope that I might see my lady on her way to morning service, - see her for the last time in life, perhaps. Her locket I wore over my heart. It had lain upon hers. To see her was the most exquisite agony in the world. But not to see her, and to feel that she was scarce quarter of a mile away, was beyond endurance. I stood beside an area at the entrance to Arlington Street, and waited for an hour, quite in vain; watching every face that passed, townsmen in their ill-fitting Sunday clothes, and fine ladies with the footmen carrying velvet prayerbooks. And some that I knew only stared, and others gave me distant bows from their coach windows. For those that fall from fashion are dead to fashion. Dorothy did not go to church that day. It is a pleasure, my dears, when writing of that hour of bitterness, to record the moments of sweetness which lightened it. As I climbed up to my rooms in Dover Street, I heard merry sounds above, and a cloud of smoke blew out of the door when I opened it. "Here he is," cried Mr. Fox. "You see, Richard, we have not deserted you when we can win no more of your money." "Why, egad! the man looks as if he had had a calamity," said Mr. Fitzpatrick. "And there is not a Jew here," Fox continued.

For Yemen's civilians, getting to a medical facility equipped to cope with severe trauma can be hellishly difficult. It can involve an hours-long journey by car, fraught with danger from flying bullets and falling missiles. On Thursday, a young pregnant woman arrived at Al-Jumhori with 60% of her body burned. Like so many who come through the hospital's doors, her home had been hit by an air strike, this one in the heavily-targeted Razeh district of Saada province, close to the border with Saudi Arabia. With travel too risky, the woman was forced to wait for a week before her family could take her to a nearby clinic. From there she was moved by ambulance to the Al-Jumhori, a five-hour journey. "I could not imagine how much pain she was in," said Dr Carrara. "By the time she reached us she was septic and had severe organ failure. We did what we could but there was no hope." The woman died 16 hours later. She was in her 20s. If she had made it to Saada city within eight hours, she and her child could almost certainly have been saved. Patients arriving at MSF facilities in Yemen are immediately graded with one of four colours: green denotes that they are walking wounded; yellow that they must be seen within an hour; red that they need immediate resuscitation; black that they are already dead, or have no hope. "We grade a lot of people black and red," said Dr Carrara. "Most of them are young. They have crash injuries, vascular injuries, fractures, open fractures on the legs and arms, head trauma, penetrating head trauma, abdominal trauma, chest trauma, open chest trauma, blunt trauma. "Air strikes cause multiple, severe injuries. They put people in critical condition." The first day we spoke, a family of seven was rushed in to Dr Carrara's A&E. Five - the mother, father, and three children - were immediately graded black. Two boys were alive. The older of the two, aged 20, was graded green - he would survive. The younger boy, aged just eight, was graded red. He had a penetrating head trauma and was in a coma. When we spoke again the following day, the boy's condition had deteriorated. He will probably die. Emergencies are not the difficult part of treating the war-wounded, said Dr Carrara. The difficulty comes later, as she follows them through their recovery - "sometimes 10 days, sometimes a month, sometimes more". "That is when you hear their stories, what happened to them, who they lost. That's when I wonder how they can continue. And that's when it gets difficult." At what point does it become too much? "It doesn't," she said. "You do what you have to. You do the work, that gets you through." An average day for an MSF doctor in Yemen would be too much for most.

The consumption of seal meat and organs is a significant part of Inuit culture and tradition in Arctic and subarctic Canada and Greenland. In addition to subsistence harvests, some seal species are also harvested commercially in a government-regulated sustainable manner in eastern Canada. Seal meat is available at retail in this region and is often served as rare seal steak or seal tartare in restaurants in metropolitan areas such as Toronto, Montreal, and Quebec City. Seven pinniped species are hunted in Canada, including walrus, bearded seals, ringed seals, harbour seals, hooded seals, harp seals, and grey seals. Most of these species are hunted for subsistence purposes by Inuit and others, but the latter three species are commercially hunted, with meat and by-products being sold to restaurants and exported. Ringed seals have a northern circumpolar distribution and are widespread in Arctic and subarctic Canada, with an estimated 100,000 being harvested annually for subsistence. Harp seals are separated into three populations based on specific pupping sites, with the Northwest Atlantic population being commercially harvested in Atlantic Canada. Hooded seals are also separated into two breeding herds based on specific pupping sites, with the Northwest Atlantic population having subsistence and commercial harvests in Atlantic Canada. Grey seals are found on both sides of the North Atlantic and are distributed in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and coastal Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. There is a small commercial hunt in the Magdalen Islands and eastern shore of Nova Scotia of less than 1700 animals in 2016. Despite the importance of seal meat in Inuit culture and tradition, little is known about the risk to humans from the consumption of seal meat containing zoonotic pathogens and parasites that they may carry. However, various studies have identified pathogens and parasites in marine mammals of concern to human health.

Further, Sri Lankan paratransit drivers have also organized unique groups, called "societies," which offer several welfare services to member drivers. Societies are being established in all surveyed cities in Sri Lanka. The 3W drivers are strengthening their relationships with other individuals, groups, and organizations to establish the means to facilitate their 3W operation. In emergency situations, such as traffic accidents, they can expect assistance from other members of their societies or groups, which secures their lives. On the contrary, if 3W drivers do not trust their government, they feel uncomfortable, which may have a negative impact on their lives. Therefore, enriching their relationships with other objects can be considered likely to improve their lives; this corresponds to the creation of social capital networks, which are networks with shared norms, values, and understanding that facilitate relationships within or among groups (Portes, 1998; Putnam et al., 1994). Further, social capital networks can exist among friends, family members, former colleagues, and so on (Portes, 1998). In line with its general definition, social capital is defined in this study as the richness of the relationships among the stakeholders in the 3W industry (e.g., the relationship between drivers and local governments and that between drivers and their societies). According to Currie and Stanley (2008), social capital describes the advantage held by individuals and communities in gaining the benefits of social participation, mutual assistance, and trust. In this context, social capital possibly ensures 3W drivers' well-being and their existence in the society. Hence, if we can identify the social capital related to the 3W industry as an important factor affecting the life satisfaction of 3W drivers, we can improve the drivers' life satisfaction by enriching the social capital. This is particularly relevant in Kandy, where the relationship between the 3W industry and the local government is currently worsening (Kumarage, 2014). Considering the above information, the objectives of this study are to clarify the actual condition of the industry and to identify the social capital related factors that affect the life satisfaction of 3W drivers in the three cities of Colombo, Moratuwa, and Kandy in Sri Lanka. Few previous studies have examined Sri Lankan 3Ws, particularly in relation to supply-side issues (i.e., drivers and governments). Kumarage et al. (2010) analyzed fundamental information regarding 3W drivers in Moratuwa, including their education level and salary. Meanwhile, Somasundaraswaran et al. (2006) analyzed the personal characteristics of 3W drivers, such as their age and family size, while Kirkorowicz (2012) examined the health problems experienced by 3W drivers in Galle City. However, these studies performed only fundamental analyses and mainly addressed the attributes of 3W drivers in Sri Lanka and, to date, no study has examined the 3W industry's operation system or specifically conducted social capital based transportation research.

Neuroimaging studies have demonstrated that the presence of the APOE mu 4 allele is associated with notable changes in brain morphology and function, highlighting the profound implications of this genotype beyond cognitive performance alone. For instance, research utilizing neuroimaging techniques, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET), has revealed that mu 4 carriers show accelerated rates of atrophy in critical regions associated with memory, like the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, even in the absence of clinical symptoms of Alzheimer's disease (Snyder et al., 2016). This neuropathological progression hints at an underlying vulnerability within the neural circuitry that could be exacerbated by the effects of other risk factors, including vascular health, lifestyle choices, and comorbidities. Moreover, functional imaging methods, including task-based fMRI, have shown aberrant activation patterns in regions responsible for memory encoding and retrieval. For example, mu 4 carriers often exhibit heightened activation in the prefrontal cortex during working memory tasks, suggesting that they may be recruiting additional neural resources to compensate for their deficits (Elliott et al., 2016). Interestingly, this compensatory mechanism may reflect an early adaptation process, yet as neurodegeneration advances, the ability to maintain such compensatory strategies may diminish, leading to a marked decline in cognitive performance. The interplay of genetic risk factors and environmental influences also underscores the complexity of Alzheimer's disease pathology. Emerging evidence suggests that lifestyle interventions, such as physical exercise, cognitive training, and diet, may mitigate the cognitive decline associated with APOE mu 4 (Johnson et al., 2016; Mowrey et al., 2018). Particularly, engaging in regular physical activity has been shown to bolster neurogenesis and maintain synaptic plasticity, potentially counteracting the adverse effects elicited by the mu 4 allele. This resilience emphasizes the importance of considering modifiable factors when assessing risk and devising preventive strategies. Furthermore, the heterogeneity in cognitive trajectories among mu 4 carriers presents an intriguing paradox. While some individuals may succumb to neurodegeneration within a relatively short time frame, others maintain cognitive function well into advanced age, suggesting that the relationship between the APOE mu 4 genotype and cognitive decline is not deterministic (Cruchaga et al., 2013). Factors such as education, social engagement, and psychological well-being appear to modulate the impact of genetic predispositions, leading to differential outcomes in cognitive aging. As research continues to advance in elucidating the nuances of APOE's role in Alzheimer's disease, it becomes increasingly clear that early detection and intervention remain paramount. Identifying at-risk populations, particularly those with mu 4 alleles, and employing sensitive neuropsychological tests to capture subtle cognitive changes could empower healthcare providers to initiate preventive measures before significant impairment occurs. Such approaches could encompass cognitive enhancement interventions, psychosocial support frameworks, and strategies that promote overall brain health. In conclusion, the fusion of genetic, cognitive, and environmental factors creates a complex tapestry that shapes the clinical narrative of Alzheimer's disease. The intricate relationship between the APOE mu 4 allele and cognitive function prompts a shift in perspectives: from a mere focus on genetic determinism to a more integrative understanding that encompasses both biological and experiential dimensions of aging. Consequently, ongoing longitudinal studies exploring these multifaceted interactions will be crucial as we endeavor to unravel the mysteries of Alzheimer's disease and optimize the care and prevention strategies for those at risk. Invoking a multidimensional approach will not only enhance our comprehension of Alzheimer's pathology but also guide therapeutic advancements.

A third network termed the "frontoparietal control network" (fPCN) includes anterior insula/frontal operculum, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and inferior parietal lobule (Dosenbach et al., 2007; Vincent et al., 2008). The fPCN appears to be involved in cognitive control (Cole and Schneider, 2007; Dosenbach et al., 2008; Vincent et al., 2008). A fourth network, the cingulo-opercular network (CON), includes dorsal anterior cingulate/medial superior frontal cortex, anterior prefrontal cortex, and lateral fronto-insular cortex (Dosenbach et al., 2007). It is thought to monitor behavior and signal the need for control processes (Dosenbach et al., 2008). Finally, a fifth network, the ventral attention network (vATN), is comprised of ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and temporoparietal junction (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Vincent et al., 2008). The vATN is recruited during stimulus-driven reorienting of attention (Fox et al., 2006; Corbetta et al., 2008). This brief review of the organization of cortical networks illustrates two key points: First, several distinct networks exist and are spatially distributed across association cortex. Second, each of these networks contains nodes that span the temporal, parietal, and frontal lobes. This raises an interesting question: Do these networks share common principles? In particular, do they comprise a set of parallel distributed networks, each with its own specific computational properties? Or does each network perform a different operation on a similar type of input, leading to a shared architecture? Answering these questions requires data that provide sufficient detail to compare and contrast the structure of the networks. A fundamental challenge in comparing the structure of networks is defining their boundaries. At present, network boundaries are often defined using seed-based correlation approaches (e.g., Biswal et al., 1995; Raichle et al., 2001; Greicius et al., 2003). However, these methods rely on assumptions about the location of seed regions and the presence of strong correlations. Moreover, they do not permit straightforward comparison of the relative strength of connections among the various networks. To address this issue, we used an approach called gradient-weighted Markov random field modeling (gwMRF; Robinson et al., 2015) to estimate the probability of transitions between all pairs of voxels in the brain, given a whole-brain map of resting-state FC (RSFC) data. This method allows us to make probabilistic statements about the likelihood of observing a transition from one voxel to another without making any assumptions about the underlying network structure. We used gwMRF to examine the structure of three networks: the DN, the dATN, and the vATN. All three networks are distributed across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortices. Moreover, they exhibit topographic gradients along the rostral-caudal axis, with more caudally located subregions showing greater engagement in external stimuli (Hasson et al., 2008; Vaziri-Pashkam et al., 2017; Baldassano et al., 2018; Braga and Buckner, 2017; DiNicola et al., 2020).

For some reason or other he had long shown a desire to obtain possession of this box, but the owner could not be induced to part with it. Before he could express his thanks for the gift Tom was half-way across the street on his way home. "This is just the thing I wanted," said Guy joyfully, as he and George Wolcom resumed their walk. "I shall think of Tom every time I look at this box when I am out on the prairie." "When you are out on the prairie?" echoed George. "What do you mean by that?" "Oh, it is my secret. You may know it some day, but not now. What do you suppose is the reason why I want a cross-gun?" "Why, to kill birds with." "No, sir; I want to practice shooting at a mark. I shall have use for a rifle every hour in the day before I am many months older." "You will? Where are you going?" "You needn't ask questions, for I sha'n't answer them," said Guy, shutting the box with a click, and making a motion to put it into his pocket. "Wait a second," exclaimed George suddenly. "I know why Tom Proctor was generous enough to give you that box. It will be of no use to you for the spring is broken." "It isn't either," replied Guy. "Yes it is; I saw it. Hand it out here and I will show you." Without hesitation Guy passed the box over to his companion, who, after opening and shutting it a few times, and making a pretense of examining the spring, coolly put it into his own pocket. Guy looked at him in great surprise, but George walked on without noticing him. "Now that's the biggest piece of impudence I ever witnessed," said Guy at length. "I'd like to know what you mean by it." "Didn't I tell you that I always get even with a fellow who does me a mean trick?" asked George, in reply. "I'll keep this box as part payment for the cross-gun I made you." "Do you call this thing a cross-gun?" demanded Guy, once more holding up the stick he carried in his hand; "I don't, and I sha'n't pay you a cent for it either. Give me that box." "Give me that half-dollar you owe me." "I don't owe you any half-dollar. Here, take your old cross-gun and give me my box." "It isn't my gun-it is yours; and you can't have your box till I get my just dues. You may depend upon that." A long and spirited debate followed this reply, and would most likely have ended in blows had the two boys been of equal age and size, for Guy was a spirited fellow, and always ready to stand up for his rights.

9. The BrainGate System. Neural signals from the motor cortex of the brain are amplified and fed into a computer which translates them into commands for moving a cursor on a screen. This enables paralyzed people to control computers and eventually wheelchairs, robotic arms, etc. 10. Gene therapy. The basic idea behind gene therapy is to insert healthy genes into diseased cells, but researchers haven't yet found a safe and effective delivery mechanism. Now they're trying to use viruses stripped of their infectious components. 11. X-ray vision. By combining data from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and ultrasound waves, doctors can see inside the human body without cutting it open. 12. The artificial pancreas. Insulin pumps deliver insulin in response to changing glucose levels monitored by implanted glucose sensors. This eliminates the need for injections several times a day. 13. Cloned organs. By cloning organs from embryonic stem cells, scientists will eliminate the need for donated organs and the problems associated with rejection. 14. The new pill. By coating a pill with a polymer that dissolves only in the intestine, scientists can prevent the pill from being destroyed by stomach acids. This makes it possible to take oral doses of many medications previously available only by injection. 15. Super antibodies. Antibodies are proteins made by white blood cells to fight off invaders like bacteria and viruses. Genetically engineered antibodies have already been approved to treat certain types of lymphoma, and soon may be used against rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, psoriasis, multiple sclerosis, and other autoimmune disorders. 16. Botox therapy. Botulism toxin causes paralysis, but in tiny doses it can relieve pain caused by muscle spasms. It's been approved for treating eye-muscle problems and is being tested on cerebral palsy victims. 17. DNA chips. DNA microarrays are tiny glass slides containing thousands of snippets of DNA. When a sample of tissue or blood is applied, they indicate whether specific genes are active. This will allow doctors to tailor treatments to individual patients. 18. New cholesterol drugs. Cholesterol-lowering statins have proven to be highly effective, but new drugs target HDL (good) cholesterol rather than LDL (bad) cholesterol. 19. Organ regeneration. Research shows that the liver can regenerate itself if damaged. Doctors are looking for ways to stimulate this regenerative capacity in other organs, such as the kidney. 20. Ultrasound surgery. Focused sound waves can destroy tissues deep within the body without damaging surrounding areas. Currently used to treat prostate cancer and uterine fibroids, it may also prove effective against ovarian cancer and other tumors. 21. Cancer vaccines. Vaccines are currently in development which will train the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. The first thing we notice about this list is that it includes many items which would clearly fall into the category of aealth care.a None of us are likely to object to the notion of finding cures for various diseases. But even here there are moral issues which must be addressed. For example, what is the cost of developing these new technologies? Will the poor have access to them? Is it appropriate to spend vast sums of money on health care when so many people lack food, clothing, shelter, education, and other necessities? We don't know the answers to these questions, but they should not be ignored. One question which comes immediately to mind is whether any of these advances involves experimentation on human embryos. If so, then there is a serious ethical question involved. There is also the question of how to allocate scarce resourcesae.g., how do you decide who gets a new organ transplant?

This theory posits that autism results from a disruption in the predictive coding hierarchy of the brain. Predictive coding is a framework describing how the brain uses prior knowledge to predict sensory input, then compares predictions to actual sensory inputs in order to adjust its predictions accordingly (Friston, 2009). According to Quattrocki and Friston (2014), autism results from a failure in this process, specifically a failure of interoceptive predictions being generated from the posterior insula (PI). The PI receives sensory information from the body, processes it according to past experience, and generates an expectation about incoming sensations (Quattrocki & Friston, 2014). These expectations are then used to guide behaviour, and to generate predictions about future sensory events. In autism, Quattrocki and Friston propose that a failure to use interoceptive prediction signals leads to a lack of integration between internal bodily states and conscious experience. The authors suggest that this inability to integrate interoceptive information leads to difficulties in social interaction, communication and repetitive behaviours. The interoceptive abilities of autistic adults have been investigated using a range of tasks. Several studies have reported reduced interoceptive accuracy in autistic individuals compared to neurotypical controls (Cohen, Minshew, & Klin, 1998; Ginty et al., 2013; Happe & Frith, 2014; Kleinhans et al., 2005; Mobbs et al., 2007; Mobbs et al., 2009; Schuwerk, Hecht, Brieber, Friederici, & Paulus, 2014; Tavassoli, Tsakiris, & Haggard, 2011; Weissman et al., 2014), however, several studies have found no differences between autistic and neurotypical groups in terms of interoceptive accuracy (Dziobek, Fleck, Kalbe, Rogers, Hassenstab, Brand, Steininger, Bulut, Polzer, Roessner, & Convit, 2006; Mostofsky et al., 2006; Schuwerk, Hecht, Brieber, Friederici, & Paulus, 2014; Van der Burgh, Smeets, & Jansen, 2017). It should be noted that these studies varied in terms of their assessment methods, with some studies assessing interoceptive accuracy via heartbeat estimation tasks, and others via tasks involving detection of passive mechanical stimulation applied to the skin. Studies investigating interoceptive sensitivity have also yielded mixed findings. Some studies report lower interoceptive sensitivity in autistic participants than control groups (Ginty et al., 2013; Schuwerk, Hecht, Brieber, Friederici, & Paulus, 2014), whilst others find no significant difference between groups (Mobbs et al., 2009; Tavassoli, Tsakiris, & Haggard, 2011; Van der Burgh, Smeets, & Jansen, 2017). Research examining interoceptive sensibility has largely focused on interoceptive awareness. A recent review of research into interoceptive sensibility in autism concluded that there were no differences between autistic and neurotypical groups in terms of interoceptive awareness (Van der Burgh, Smeets, & Jansen, 2017). However, it should be noted that all studies included in this review were cross-sectional in design, and therefore did not allow conclusions regarding developmental changes in interoceptive sensibility to be drawn.

The ejection sequence begins, and the canopy blows off with a deafening roar. Hawk and Frank are slammed back into their seats as the rocket-assisted ejection seats blast them clear of the stricken aircraft. The G-forces are intense, and the pilots' vision grays out for an instant. When their sight returns, they're staring up at the curved horizon, the stars twinkling like diamonds against the blackness. Hawk's voice crackles over the radio, laced with a hint of panic. "Mayday, Mayday, this is Falcon! We've suffered engine failure and are ejecting at 112,000 feet! Requesting assistance, over!" Frank's response is laced with a mix of fear and anger. "Roger, Daedalus, this is Falcon-2. We're going down, and we need a recovery team ASAP. We're not going to make it back to the base, over." The silence that follows is oppressive, punctuated only by the sound of their own heavy breathing and the distant rumble of the stricken aircraft plummeting towards the earth. As they drift downwards, Hawk's gaze is fixed on the altimeter unwinding on his wristwatch. 100,000 feet... 90,000... 80,000... The numbers blur together as the air thickens, and the wind buffets them about like rag dolls. Frank's voice is laced with a growing sense of desperation. "Hawk, we need to deploy the chutes! Now!" Hawk's response is calm, almost detached. "Not yet, Frank. We're still too high. We need to get below 50,000 before we deploy." The silence that follows is oppressive, punctuated only by the sound of their own ragged breathing. The stars above seem to be growing larger, more menacing, as if they're being pulled towards some celestial abyss. Suddenly, a burst of static crackles over the radio, followed by a voice laced with a hint of urgency. "Falcon, this is Daedalus. We have you on radar. Hang in there, boys. Recovery team is en route. Just hang in there..." Hawk's response is laced with a mix of relief and skepticism. "Roger, Daedalus. We're doing our best to hang in there. But we're running out of time, over." The altimeter continues to unwind, the numbers ticking away with maddening slowness. 40,000 feet... 30,000... 20,000... The air is growing thick and heavy, the wind buffeting them about like rag dolls. Frank's voice is laced with a growing sense of panic. "Hawk, we need to deploy the chutes! Now, Hawk, now!" Hawk's response is calm, almost detached. "Not yet, Frank. Just a little longer..." And then, in an instant, the world goes silent. The wind dies, the stars fade, and the only sound is the soft rustle of the parachute deploying above them.

Their model optimises the configuration of a hydrogen supply chain with various options for production, storage and delivery to refuelling stations, while considering uncertain demand. Another recent example from the second category is given by Sabio et al. [8], who developed an MILP model that optimised the daily operation of a system consisting of a wind farm, electrolyser, compressor and storage tank. They did not consider transport of energy, since they assumed that all these facilities were located at the same site. To the authors' knowledge, no previous work exists that considers both the optimal design and operation of hydrogen networks. This paper presents a novel mixed integer linear programming (MILP) model for the strategic planning of hydrogen infrastructure. The model minimises the annual cost of supplying hydrogen to a set of geographically-distributed refuelling stations under uncertainty in future vehicle uptake. The cost includes investment and operating costs of hydrogen production plants, compressors, fuel cells, storage tanks and pipelines, as well as the cost of buying electricity from the grid. The model determines the number, capacity and location of all components in the network, including the pipeline routes. The objective function is subject to mass balance constraints, technical and operational constraints, and logical constraints. The resulting model is a large-scale MILP problem that is solved using CPLEX 12.1. The approach described here represents a significant step forward over existing methods.

Mine was filled with a new emotion. I do not mean to say that I had never loved before. I had been in love many times, and once had felt sure that I had found the woman whom I wanted to marry. That affair had ended unhappily, and the scar still remained. Indeed, I had come to Chicago hoping to forget her and to find consolation in the excitement of the convention. But what was the convention to me now? I was not thinking about it. I was not thinking about anything. I was feeling, and that was sufficient. In the dim light of the art-gallery, I sat and let the soft music of my emotion play upon my senses. Its charm lay in its novelty. It was unlike anything I had ever known. If you have been in love you know how little resemblance there is between the love of eighteen and the love of thirty-five. This love was like neither of those. It was altogether different. I cannot describe it better than by saying that it was a sort of celestial intoxication. It seemed to lift me up and bear me along, and filled me with a sense of power and happiness. How it came about I did not understand. I had seen her only once, and then for but a few minutes. Yet the result was already complete. I was hers. She was mine. And yet she knew nothing about it! That was part of the joy of it. I thought of her with a sort of rapture, and the very name of love seemed too coarse to apply to the passion with which I was inspired. I would not have dared to speak to her of love. I hardly ventured to think of it. She was so far above me that I should have shrunk from presuming to offer her my hand, if I had not been intoxicated by the strange certainty that she belonged to me. How can I express it? I was hers by right of conquest. I had taken her captive without knowing it, and now I held her fast within my breast. My happiness consisted in contemplating her image. I did not want to see her again. I feared lest her presence might dispel the enchantment. I dreaded the possibility of disillusion. I was afraid that if I saw her again, I might lose her. I had no desire to speak to her. I did not care to make her acquaintance. I wished simply to sit and look at her. I wanted to dream of her. I was satisfied to worship her unseen. And this was why I sought the quiet of the art-gallery. I wanted to be alone with her. I did not wish to talk politics. I desired to commune with the divinity who possessed my soul. It may seem absurd to you, but I assure you that I was perfectly sincere. I was really in love. I had a genuine case of it. I was in earnest. I meant business. I was dead in love with a girl whom I had seen but once, and that for a moment only, and who had said but a word to me. What would you expect under such circumstances? Would you not suppose that I was prepared to make any sacrifice for her sake? Well, that is just what happened. I gave up my ambition. I resigned my hopes. I abandoned my career. You will remember that I was a delegate to the national convention. I intended to be nominated for Governor when I returned home. I expected to be elected. I hoped to go to the United States Senate eventually. But now I surrendered all these ambitions. I was willing to give them up. I was ready to renounce everything for her sake. And I did. I forgot my duty. I neglected my friends.

The quest for standardization in EEG/MEG data preprocessing and analysis is a crucial step towards facilitating mega-analysis and unlocking the full potential of these modalities. While fMRI has benefited from the development of standardized methods and tools, such as the BrainMap project and the BIDS specification, EEG/MEG data preprocessing has lagged behind. The lack of standardization has led to a proliferation of ad-hoc methods, which can result in inconsistent and potentially biased results. To address this issue, several guidelines for best practices in EEG/MEG data acquisition and preprocessing have been proposed (Gross et al., 2013; Keil et al., 2014; Pernet et al., 2018). However, these guidelines are not yet widely adopted, and the preprocessing of EEG/MEG data remains a highly variable and subjective process. The recent development of BIDS extensions for MEG and EEG imaging (Niso et al., 2018) provides a promising framework for standardizing EEG/MEG data sharing and analysis. However, the lack of standardized preprocessing methods and benchmarks hinders the development of mega-analysis pipelines for EEG/MEG data. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to normalizing EEG data across studies by leveraging the spatial, temporal, and spectral properties of channel-level and source-level signals. We analyze a dataset comprising 18 studies performed at six different experimental sites, and provide preliminary guidance on the optimal normalization strategies for EEG data. Our results demonstrate that a combination of spatial and temporal normalization techniques can significantly improve the comparability of EEG signals across studies. The development of standardized preprocessing methods and benchmarks is essential for facilitating mega-analysis and unlocking the full potential of EEG/MEG data. We propose a comprehensive framework for standardizing EEG/MEG preprocessing, which includes the following components: 1. A standardized set of preprocessing pipelines for EEG/MEG data, including filtering, artifact removal, and data cleaning. 2. A set of benchmarks for evaluating the performance of different preprocessing pipelines and algorithms. 3. A data sharing platform for sharing raw and processed EEG/MEG data, along with associated metadata and preprocessing scripts. By providing a standardized framework for preprocessing and analyzing EEG/MEG data, we can facilitate the development of mega-analysis pipelines and accelerate the discovery of new insights into brain function and dysfunction.

However, that was a matter for the future. At the moment the four Sea Scouts who had come by train were anxious to meet their colleagues, and the latter, with one exception, were equally eager to see them again. And this meeting-place was to be none other than the guardship of the Wootton Bridge Sea Scouts, a vessel that had seen many years of service in the Royal Navy, and which now formed an integral part of the Southsea Marine Museum. She was moored alongside the pier-head at Portsmouth Harbour Station, and the party came aboard her without difficulty. Once inside, the sight that met their eyes was most pleasing to the eye. There were the familiar faces of Mr. Tweedie, the Scoutmaster of the 6th Wootton Bridge Sea Scouts; Dick, the Assistant Scoutmaster; and the six boys of the troop. The latter were seated round a table, lunching off cold meat, bread and cheese, pickles, biscuits, jam, and cake. They were also drinking tea. In a few minutes the newcomers joined them. A little later, when the meal was finished, Mr. Graham and his party were given a guided tour of the guardship. This particular craft was a small gunboat, built during the early 'nineties of last century, and had served throughout the Boer War. She was armed with a single quick-firer mounted amidships, and carried a crew of twenty men. Her engine-room and boiler-room were below decks forward, while the galley was aft, between the engine-room bulkhead and the mainmast. On either side of the poop deck, where she was tied up alongside the pier-head, were the bunks allotted to the boys. The cabins occupied by Mr. Tweedie and Dick were further aft, towards the stern. Moreover, we propose a novel imitating attack detection mechanism based on Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to identify and mitigate the impact of malicious users. The GCNs are trained on a graph constructed from the user-web content interaction data, where nodes represent users and Web pages, and edges represent the ratings and reviews provided by users. Our proposed system, named WebCred, is designed to address the two challenges mentioned earlier. Firstly, WebCred integrates a recommendation model to attract users to rate more Web pages, thereby increasing the coverage of the system. The recommendation model is based on a hybrid approach that combines Matrix Factorization (MF) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to learn users' interests in Web content. Specifically, each Web content is represented as a "bag-of-words" and the recommendation model predicts the probability of a user rating a particular Web page based on their past behavior and preferences. Secondly, WebCred incorporates a novel imitating attack detection mechanism based on GCNs to identify and mitigate the impact of malicious users. The GCNs are trained on a graph constructed from the user-web content interaction data, where nodes represent users and Web pages, and edges represent the ratings and reviews provided by users. The GCNs learn to identify patterns in the graph that are indicative of imitating attacks, such as consistent ratings and reviews from a single user. To evaluate the effectiveness of WebCred, we conducted experiments on a large-scale dataset of Web pages and user interactions. Specifically, WebCred achieves a coverage rate of 80% compared to 42.67% of MyWOT, and detects imitating attacks with an accuracy of 95% compared to 60% of the state-of-the-art approach.
