There is a fierce loyalty among them, forged in both fire and frost. They scorn the waves as a gnat scorns a summer's breeze, knowing that the roar of the water is but a call to battle, a siren's song urging them into the dance of violence. The men are long-haired and bearded, with gaudy shields that catch the light like the scales of a dragon; each bears the mark of their lord, a token of honor that inspires their every stroke. The shipmaster chuckled to himself, shaking his head at the tall warrior's fervor. "You sing sweetly of your foes, yet tell me how many of these gilded creatures will stand firm when the winds turn wild, and the claws of the waves reach out for their very souls?" But the Frankish lord remained undeterred, his eyes narrowed, focused beyond the mist and the morning gloom. "It is not the storm that defines a man, but the mettle within him, Frisian. Trust in steel and courage; that is what prevails upon the open water. And yet you, a mariner of these treacherous tides, prefer to scorn while you lay your wealth upon their backs!" A squall swept across the river at that moment, sending ripples and shivers through the vessel. The ship creaked in response, as if awakening from its slumber, echoing the warrior's fervid resolve. The shipmaster, resisting the urge to fret, drew his weathered hands about the helm, steadying their path against the suddenly flaring gusts. As the fog began to part, revealing fragments of the river bordered by darkened trees and thickened brush, the crew stirred, blinking against the dim light like sprites drawn from slumber. "Look there!" The warrior pointed ahead with a sinewy arm, gesturing toward a distant silhouette rising above the fog, shrouded in mystique and whispered legends: a fragment of the ancient fort of Lutetia, the city's heart still beating strong even in the shadows cast by the burgeoning dawn. "Such places welcome both friend and foe. The tales only hint of the riches that lie within, lord Frisian." The shipmaster's brow furrowed, caught amidst the anticipations of adventure tinged with trepidation. "Aye, the city we may find, but what of its defenders? The fringes of our knowledge are overgrown with thorny truths, and tales smothered in opulence may bear venomous fangs. A reckless heart and empty purse may lead even the mightiest of men into snares of their own making." The Frank sighed, the weight of responsibility settling upon him like a heavy cloak. "Perhaps caution must guide our course, but the lure of treasure remains. We are but fleeting figures upon this grand tapestry of fate, drawn together by invisible threads nuancing both fortune and folly." With that declaration, the crew roused themselves further, rolling their shoulders and wiping sleep from their eyes, purpose rekindled in their chests. The shipmaster barked orders about the sails, readiness blooming like spring after the long winter's cold. The thrumming heart of the vessel echoed the pulses of their growing ambition, and they made for the embrace of the distance, hands steady on ropes and wood. The cool briskness of the day welcomed them forth, the scents of adventure and ephemeral gilded promises beckoning like a haunting melody carried upon glimmering waves. And as they neared the shrouded silhouette of Lutetia-a blend of hope and shadow-their fate swayed just as the oaken prow upon the roiling tide.

Several ethnopharmacological surveys have revealed that betel leaf juice is taken as a sex stimulant, applied on wounds to stop bleeding, and taken orally with a mixture of seed powder of Tamarindus indica and Piper nigrum together with salt at a dose of 3 teaspoons twice daily for the treatment of fever until alleviation of symptoms (Rahmatullah et al., 2011; Uddin et al., 2013). Further therapeutic use of P. betle includes the treatment of urinary complicacy, sore throat, cough, pulmonary infection, boils, constipation, and during breastfeeding as lactogogues (Mula et al., 2008; Satyal and Setzer, 2011; Pradhan et al., 2013; Dwivedi and Tripathi, 2014). Scientific evaluation has further confirmed the biological activities of P. betle ascribed to its reservoir of panoply of phytochemicals (Satyal and Setzer, 2011). The leaves of P. betle have been shown to possess significant free radicals scavenging power mainly due to the presence of cathecol and allylpyrocathecol (Parillon and Edward, 2006; Pradhan et al., 2013). The essential oil of P. betle has also been demonstrated to exhibit larvicidal, insecticidal, and anti-filarial activities (Singh et al., 2009; Nagori et al., 2011; Rekha et al., 2014). Moreover, it has been shown that P. betle exhibits anti-allergic (Wirotesangthong et al., 2008), anti-cancer (Banerjee and Shah, 2014), anti-hypercholesterolemic (Rekha et al., 2014), anti-diabetic (Arefin et al., 2012), anti-platelet (Nagori et al., 2011), and anti-nociceptive (Arefin et al., 2012) effects. Additionally, P. betle has been demonstrated in vitro to have significant antimicrobial potential against a broad spectrum of microorganisms including bacteria and fungi and has been further described as an effective alternative to reduce biofilm formation in membrane bioreactors caused by both Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Candida albicans (Ali et al., 2010; Siddiqui et al., 2012; Pradhan et al., 2013; Rekha et al., 2014). The antimicrobial potential is most likely due to hydroxichavicol, stearic acid, and palmitic acid. The antimicrobial activity explains the use of P. betle as an oral care agent in Asian countries (Ramji et al., 2002; Rekha et al., 2014). P. betle has also displayed the greatest potential value, among 12 Philippine medicinal plants, against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive multidrug-resistant bacteria (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, extended spectrum -lactamase-producing, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, and metallo- -lactamase-producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii) which are responsible for nosocomial infections (Valle et al., 2015). Nosocomial infections represent one of the main causes of premature deaths worldwide (Davies, 1994; Robin et al., 1998; Udgirkar et al., 2012). Previously, antibiotics represented a major option for treating bacterial infections. However, it was soon discovered that bacteria eventually adapted themselves to become resistant to these antimicrobial drugs, leading to complications in managing infections. Therefore, there is a critical need to investigate alternative options, namely, products from plant origin in combination with conventional antimicrobial drugs, to tackle the emerging issue of multi-drug-resistant pathogens.

On one side of the room stood a number of large glass cases filled with salt-water, and containing specimens of sea-life, such as crabs, lobsters, shell-fish, and other creatures, whose existence in the ocean depths would otherwise have remained unknown. These cases had been gathered together by Baldwin during his long experience of diving, and he was justly proud of them, especially of those which contained rare and beautiful examples of the coralline polypus and the zoophyte, which grow only in great depths, and are seldom brought up by fishermen or dredgers. In another corner of the room there was a small but well-stocked aquarium, wherein were kept fish of various kinds, and one or two starfishes, which were fed every day with morsels of food placed on the surface of the water. Near this tank was a small shelf with a few books on it, among which were several works relating to marine zoology, and a copy of the Diving Manual, printed by order of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty. A couple of old-fashioned chairs, an oil-cloth-covered table, and a couple of deal benches completed the furniture of the place, which looked like a rough-and-ready office rather than a workshop. "Very well, sir," said Baldwin, after a moment's reflection, "we'll begin tomorrow morning early, when the tide is low enough for us to get down to the bottom easily. But mind, sir, you must be punctual to time, as we shall have a good deal to do." "Oh, I won't fail you, Baldwin," said Edgar, emphatically. "Now, where shall we meet? At the top of the new pier, I suppose?" "No, sir, we must keep clear of the pier altogether. It may be finished in a month or two, but I want to teach you how to dive without having any one to bother us, as we shall probably have to do some work for ourselves, and I don't want to risk being interfered with." "What! Do you intend to take me down to the bottom of the harbour?" asked Edgar, with a smile. "Yes, sir, if you're game," replied the diver. "We shall have plenty of time to go down as far as you like, and I shan't force you to go below sixty fathoms. If you're not afraid, however, we might try to reach the bottom of the harbour, which is between seventy and eighty fathoms. There's a lot of things down there, sir, worth seeing. You wouldn't believe what beauties lie hidden beneath the waves. Why, sir, there's a whole forest of kelp growing on the bottom of the harbour, and scores of fish shoals. The thing that interests me most, though, is the coral. You remember the great bunch of it we found last year, sir, when we went down to the wreck of the Clio?" "I should think I did!" exclaimed Edgar. "It was a splendid specimen, and I still have it in the aquarium. How did you manage to find it?" "Well, sir, I knew that the Clio lay somewhere near the mouth of the harbour, so I took a sounding-line with me and dropped it until I touched the bottom. Then I followed the line down with the helmet on, and soon came to the ship. She's lying on her beam-ends, and has been there since 1865, when she was lost on the rocks.

The murderer afterwards acknowledged that it was Grey's coolness, and the terrible gleam of determination in his eyes which unnerved him and made his hand shake as if he had the palsy." Grey in the meantime had crossed the Barracks Square, and was admitted by a quiet, passionless-eyed Jap into the presence of his Commanding Officer. Giving the customary salute he stood at attention, and awaited orders. Major Sterling was sitting at his desk when Grey entered, with his eyes fixed upon a map lying before him. Pacing up and down the room was a small, middle-aged man whose agony of face and excited manner plainly bespoke the agitated state of his mind. "Major, find my boy," he was saying. "Spare no pains or money in your efforts to run those villains down. They hate me, and have sworn to have revenge. They demand twenty thousand dollars. Think of it, twenty thousand dollars! The population has shrunk over the years. Shops have closed down and the once-bustling shopping district, which used to include Woolworths, Marks & Spencer and Littlewoods, among others, has become a ghost town. The once-thriving Ritz cinema has long since closed its doors, and the town's historic Plaza Theatre is now home to a bingo hall. The death knell for the works has been ringing for a few decades now. But this latest blow will surely sound its last call. My father, now approaching retirement age, is one of the lucky ones. Having worked there for 36 years, he is entitled to a decent pension, unlike many of his younger colleagues who face unemployment. In 1962, the year he was born, the works employed around 20,000 people. Today, that number stands at less than 5,000. In two generations, the workforce has diminished by more than half. There are few families in Port Talbot without at least one member working for the company, whether past or present. Even my wife's father, a man originally from north Wales, moved to Port Talbot after serving in the Royal Navy to find work. He found it in the steel works. And even though the works may seem like a monster to outsiders, it has provided employment and security for generations of workers. So much so that, despite the dwindling numbers, there remains a loyalty and pride among those who continue to work there. While I cannot speak for everyone in Port Talbot, the loss of the works will leave a gaping hole in the community, and not just financially. For many, it is all they know. Like it was for many who grew up in the town of Port Talbot, the dystopian mesh of pipes, turrets, chimneys and constant smoke was considered a viable career prospect and, for some, a certainty - a safe bet. I was the first in my family to go to university, an opportunity afforded to me by the hard work of my parents.

We tested this hypothesis using an event-related fMRI design in which participants had to judge whether the first and second half of a visually presented stimulus were identical (word completion task) or not (word detection task) (see Figure 1A). In the word completion task, participants had to decide if the first and second part of the stimulus formed a meaningful word (e.g., "the" + "house"). If yes, they pressed one button ("yes") otherwise another ("no"). In the word detection task, participants had to decide if the first and second part of the stimulus formed a word (regardless of meaning) (e.g., "ther" + "ouse"). If yes, they pressed one button ("yes"), otherwise another ("no"). The stimuli consisted of 96 high-frequency words, 48 low-frequency words, 24 high-frequency pseudowords, 24 low-frequency pseudowords, and 96 nonwords. All items were matched on word length, number of syllables, number of bigrams, and number of tri-/tetragrams (see Table S1). The results showed that both tasks resulted in significant activation in the left vOT. Critically, however, the magnitude of activation was significantly higher in the word completion task compared to the word detection task, indicating that the region hosted more robust representations of words than of pseudowords. More recently, we replicated these findings using a different experimental paradigm (Kronbichler et al., 2010). Participants performed a lexical decision task in which they had to decide whether the center stimulus was a real word or a non-word. In each trial, the center stimulus was preceded by a prime word (which was either semantically related or unrelated to the target word) that was presented in a different font type (e.g., Times New Roman or Arial) and color (green or red). This allowed us to test the influence of semantic priming and font and color primes on left vOT activation. As in our previous study, we observed stronger activation in response to words compared to pseudowords (and non-words). Importantly, this effect was independent of semantic priming and font/color manipulation. Together, these data indicate that the left vOT encodes not just sublexical information but also whole words. Interestingly, we did not observe any effect of font or color manipulations, suggesting that the left vOT does not encode arbitrary graphemic information such as font type and color. Figure 1. Illustration of the experimental paradigms used in Kronbichler et al. (2004) and Kronbichler et al. (2010). (A) Stimuli used in the word completion task (left) and the word detection task (right). Each trial started with the presentation of a fixation cross followed by the presentation of the complete stimulus (1500 ms). After a blank interval of 1000 ms, the first half of the stimulus was displayed until the participant responded. Note that in the word completion task, the stimuli consisted of two halves that together formed a meaningful word (e.g., "the" + "house"; "the house"). In the word detection task, the stimuli consisted of two halves that together formed a pronounceable but meaningless word (e.g., "ther" + "ouse"; "ther house"). (B) Illustration of the experimental procedure used in Kronbichler et al. (2010). Each trial started with the presentation of a fixation cross (500 ms) followed by a prime word (300 ms) and a blank screen (800 ms).

Far and away the two largest quarter-to-quarter price increases in the OPEC era were $21.41 between 1973:IV and 1974:I and $22.04 between 2008:I and 2008:II. There was a slowdown in the world economy in 1974:II, a recession beginning in 1974:III, and a recession beginning in 2008:III. The third largest increase in price during the OPEC era of $12.63 occurred between 2007:III and 2007:IV. The large shock in 1973 preceded a long term slowdown in world economic growth, and the 2008 recession has been termed "Great". Over two quarters, from 1978:III to 1980:I, price increased $39.51. GDP declined at an annual rate of more than 8% from 1980:I to 1980:II and 0.7% the following quarter. The price of oil may change in response to a macroeconomic shock or to a shock to production of oil. One might argue that instability in price occurs because OPEC is not consistently effective at counteracting the impacts of such shocks on price. OPEC has been described as "clumsy",4 but I argue that 1) asymmetric effects of price on GDP incent OPEC to allow shocks to cause price to fluctuate more than it would with symmetry, and I observe that 2) the asymmetry causes fluctuations in price to reduce GDP over time, a bad combination for the world economy. In the dataset used here, the impact of changes in the price of crude oil on the macroeconomy is negative, but the correlation between price and world GDP is positive (0.24), and is significant at the 99% level. Variation in price originates more in shocks to GDP than in shocks to production of oil. Variation in price originating in shocks to production of oil is countercyclic, destabilizes the consumption (of all goods) of consumers (excepting those with countercyclic incomes), and makes the incomes of producers of oil, including OPEC, less procyclic. Variation in price originating in shocks to GDP is procyclic, smooths the consumption of most consumers, and makes the incomes of producers more procyclic. Since variation in price originates mainly in variation in GDP, unstable oil prices overall tend to smooth the consumption of consumers and make the incomes of producers of oil more procyclic. However, if OPEC production changes, as when war or civil conflict causes production in an OPEC country to fall, the resulting "oil price shock" will slow the macroeconomy, covariation will be inverse, and profits to OPEC, and other sellers of oil, will be countercyclic. OPEC can use such countercyclic profits to hedge the systematic risk to world GDP caused by the shock to price. In Section 4.4.3, I estimate demand to be inelastic in the short term, so, assuming increasing marginal cost, an increase (decrease) in price will raise (lower) revenue, lower (raise) cost, and lower (raise) world GDP.

As she slowly got out of bed, Jazz couldn't help but think about the procedure. She had been through it five times before, and each time it had ended in disappointment. But this time was different. This time, she had a feeling that it would work. She brushed off the thought, not wanting to get her hopes up. She knew that hope was a cruel mistress, and she didn't want to get hurt again. She walked into the kitchen, where Cooper was already making dinner. The smell of his famous chicken wafted through the air, and her stomach growled in anticipation. She hated that she had gone behind his back, but she knew he would understand. He loved her, and he wanted a child just as much as she did. "Hey, baby, where are you?" he yelled, looking up from the stove. Jazz smiled, feeling a pang of guilt. She should have been at the door, waiting for him like she always was. But she just couldn't bring herself to face him right now. Not yet. "I'm in the bedroom," she called back, trying to sound casual. Cooper nodded, his eyes narrowing slightly. He knew something was up, but he didn't press the issue. He set the table, and Jazz joined him a few minutes later, trying to push aside her doubts and fears. As they ate, the tension between them was palpable. Jazz knew that Cooper was waiting for her to tell him about the procedure, and she knew she couldn't put it off any longer. She took a deep breath, trying to steel herself for the conversation that was about to ensue. "Coop, can we talk?" she asked, her voice barely above a whisper. Cooper looked up, his eyes locking onto hers. "What's wrong, Jazz?" he asked, his voice laced with concern. Jazz took another deep breath, trying to find the right words. "I went to see Doc Riley today," she said, her voice trembling. Cooper's eyes narrowed, and he set his fork down. "What did he do?" he asked, his voice cold. Jazz hesitated, feeling a lump form in her throat. "I had the procedure," she said, her voice barely above a whisper. Cooper's face fell, and he looked like he had been punched in the gut. "Jazz, why didn't you tell me?" he asked, his voice filled with anger and hurt. Jazz felt tears pricking at the corners of her eyes. She knew she had made a mistake, but she had done it for them. She had done it for their future. "I'm sorry, Coop," she said, her voice cracking. "I just couldn't help it. I had to try one more time." Cooper's face twisted in pain, and he pushed his chair back. "You lied to me," he said, his voice shaking with rage. "You lied to me again."

Ever since he came on leave the weather had been abominable: high wind, incessant rain, all the elements conspiring to prevent the enjoyment of his hobby. Rodier had suggested that he should apply for an extension of leave, but Smith, though he did not lack courage, could not screw it to this pitch. He remembered too vividly his interview with the captain when coming off ship. "Don't smash yourself up," said the captain, "and don't run things too fine. You're always late in getting back from leave. Last time you only got in by the skin of your teeth, when we were off shooting, too. If you overstep the mark again you'll find yourself brought up with a round turn, you may take my word for it." "I couldn't beg off after that," he said to Rodier. "Anyway, it's rotten bad luck." "Precisement ca!" said Rodier sympathetically. For some little time they sailed slowly on, seeking in vain for a rift in the blanket of mist: then Rodier cried suddenly - "Better take a drop, mister. In three minutes all the petrol is gone, and then - " "I'm afraid you're right, Roddy, but goodness knows what we shall fall on. We must take our chance, I suppose." He adjusted the planes, so as to make a gradual descent while the engine still enabled him to keep way on the machine, and it sank into the mist. Both men kept a sharp look-out, knowing well that to encounter a branch of a tree or a chimney-stack might at any moment bring the voyage, the aeroplane, and themselves to an untimely end. All at once, without warning, a large dark shape loomed out of the mist. Smith instantly warped his planes, and the machine dived so precipitately as almost to throw him from his seat. Next moment there was a shock; he was flung headlong forward, and found himself sprawling half suffocated on a damp yielding mass, which, when he had recovered his wits, he knew to be the unthatched top of a hayrick. His first thought was for the aeroplane. Raising himself, and dashing the clinging hay wisps from his face, he shouted - "Is she smashed, Roddy?" "Ah, no, mister," came the answering cry. "She stick fast, and me also." Smith crawled to the edge of the rick and dropped to the ground. Two or three dogs were barking furiously somewhere in the neighbourhood. A few steps brought him to the aeroplane, lying in a slanting position between the hayrick and a fence, over which it projected. Rodier had clung to his seat, and had suffered nothing worse than a jolting. "This is a pretty mess," said Smith despairingly, "one end stuck fast in the hayrick, the other sticking over the fence: they'll have to pull it down before we can get her out. Get off, you brute!" he exclaimed, as a dog came yapping at his legs.

It is perhaps inevitable that in the vast ocean of literature, certain titles shimmer brighter than others, anchoring themselves not only in our imaginations but also in the lexicon of our cultural dialogues. These tomes - whether they parade under the banners of fantasy, romance, or dread realism - serve as vessels that carry us across uncharted waters, allowing the ordinary reader to traverse realms of contemplation, emotion, and revelation. As such, the act of assembling a list of revered narratives encapsulates a dual essence: an acknowledgment of personal affinity and a courageous engagement with the literary canon. Take, for instance, the ethereal realms of Tolkien's Middle-Earth, where every leaf echoes with ancient lore and every shadow conceals the epic potential of courage woven through fellowship. Such immersion is not merely escapism; it acts as a beacon of the human spirit, inviting us to confront our own trials while standing beside hobbits and elves locked in their grand narrative. Likewise, the sharp wit of Austen dances through centuries, imparting lessons of social minutiae wrapped in the exquisite art of courtship and character exploration. Through Elizabeth Bennet's critical gaze, we are challenged to reflect on the systems of our own societies, evaluating both personal and societal expectations. The beauty of such narratives is that they resonate anew with each generation, offering layers of meaning that shift and evolve as we do. In the clutches of dystopia, Orwell's 1984 invokes the specter of surveillance and autonomy, prodding at our notions of freedom and truth. This timeless dissection of power dynamics encourages readers to linger in a state of ceaseless questioning, igniting a flame of resistance against complacency. And amid these serious undertones, the fanciful glee embodied by the whimsical narratives of Dahl and Milne offers a contrasting reprieve - a childlike wonder that weaves innocence with introspection, inviting us to smile knowingly at both the absurd and the profound. As I survey this vast landscape of literature, I cannot gaze without gratitude toward those who have shaped and colored my reading journey. Each title on the list serves not merely as a marker of consumption, but rather as a waypoint in my personal growth - moments where I've traversed together with characters who embodied fragments of my own philosophy or experience. In continuation, I yearn to delve into the uncharted territory of titles yet unread; the anticipation of discovery hangs thick in the air, tantalizing with the promise of unwrapped stories waiting to imprint upon my consciousness. Who knows what further revelations lie in the pages of each new adventure? Each book, each author, becomes not just a name etched in the annals of my literary history, but also a partner in the ongoing exploration of humanity in all its shades - light and dark alike.

As the darkness enveloped Yeoman, he felt a sense of desperation wash over him. He pounded on the stone walls, screaming for someone to hear him, but his cries were met with silence. The dust and mortar he had disturbed while trying to dig his way out only made it harder for him to breathe. He coughed and hacked, his lungs burning from the particles he had inhaled. As he slumped against the wall, his mind began to wander back to the events that had led him to this predicament. He had been a monk, after all, and his faith had always been a source of comfort and strength. But now, as he faced the possibility of being trapped forever in this tiny, windowless room, he felt a creeping sense of doubt. Was this the end? Was this the fate that awaited him for his meddling in the affairs of the nobles? He thought of his flock, his people, and the lives they had built together. Would they ever know what had become of him? As he struggled to clear his mind, Yeoman heard a faint noise. It was soft at first, but grew louder with each passing moment. He cocked his head to the side, trying to pinpoint the source of the sound. It was a scraping, a scratching, a gentle but insistent noise. His heart racing, Yeoman slowly made his way to the wall, his hands outstretched in front of him. He felt the stone beneath his fingertips, searching for any hint of a hidden door or latch. And then, suddenly, he felt it. A slight give, a tiny movement in the stone. With renewed hope, Yeoman pressed harder, and the wall began to slide open, revealing a narrow passageway. He stumbled forward, his eyes adjusting to the dim light that filtered through the passage. As he made his way deeper into the darkness, he realized that he was not alone. The sound of footsteps echoed through the passageway, growing louder with each step. Yeoman's heart pounded in his chest, his breath coming in ragged gasps. Who was coming for him? Would it be his salvation, or his downfall? As he turned a corner, he saw a figure emerging from the shadows. It was a woman, her face pale and gaunt, her eyes sunken with a deep sadness. She reached out a bony hand, and Yeoman felt a chill run down his spine. "Welcome, Yeoman," she whispered, her voice like a sigh on the wind. "I have been waiting for you."

Don Luiz returns the nod with a slight, almost imperceptible tilt of his head, conveying a silent understanding. The sun casts long shadows now, dramatizing every corner of the town square. The tension is palpable, and the crowd, sensing an impending climax, falls into an expectant hush. Meanwhile, Alejandro and Joaquin continue their stealthy navigation through the throng. Heads down, hearts racing, they dart from one concealed spot to another, their small forms unnoticed amid the charged atmosphere. Joaquin's grip on Alejandro's hand tightens, a silent vow of protection. They reach the edge of the square, where a low wall provides a temporary refuge. "I'm telling you, it's him!" Alejandro's voice is just a breath in Joaquin's ear. His eyes, wide with a mixture of excitement and fear, scan the scene for any sign of the elusive figure they've come to admire. "Where? I can't see him!" Joaquin replies, his frustration evident. His attention is divided between keeping a lookout for soldiers and searching for their hero. Just then, a flicker of movement catches Alejandro's eye. The figure, known only by his shadow and legend, emerges momentarily from the alley beside the Viceroy's Building. Clad in black, face obscured, he is a wraith of justice. "There!" Alejandro whispers urgently, pointing furtively. Joaquin's eyes follow his brother's finger, his breath catching as he spots their hero, the man known as Zorro. The masked vigilante moves with the grace of a panther, each step deliberate and assured as he slips into the crowd like a shadow. Suddenly, a murmur rolls through the assemblage, building into a crest as the crowd pivots towards the same figure Joaquin and Alejandro have been watching so intently. It seems the legend's presence has been detected, and the square comes alive with whispers, exclamations, and gasps. From their position, the boys can now see the soldiers shifting uneasily, their disciplined facade beginning to crumble under the gaze of the man who embodies defiance. The Shipmaster glances towards the firing squad leader again, a silent directive passing between them. Even as the soldiers rally to confront him, Zorro turns with a flourish of his cape, the very embodiment of cool disdain. He stands, center stage, in a moment that feels suspended in time. Then, with a deftness that defies belief, he leaps onto the nearby cart, drawing the saber from his side in a single, fluid motion. The crowd erupts, its silence shattered by a cacophony of cheers and cries. The soldiers, bewildered yet resolute, raise their muskets, training their sights on the singular target. Joaquin and Alejandro, hearts hammering in their chests, exchange a glance. The moment is electrifying, a rush of danger and exhilaration binding them in their shared secret. Zorro lifts his sword, its blade glinting sharply in the sun as if to challenge the very heavens. For the boys, it is a moment of titanic import. Reverence, adventure, and a spark of rebellion-everything the figure of Zorro represents-ignite within them. Then, Zorro moves, a whirlwind of black and silver, weaving through the line of garrisoned soldiers like a breeze through the reeds. His laugh-a deep, resonant sound-echoes through the square, a promise of victory. Their fates take root in this place of destiny, under the gaze of a legend who is everything they aspire to be.

Conversely, taxonomic relations elicit stronger recruitment of visual regions, potentially reflecting the visual similarity of objects within categories (Kalenine et al., 2009; Kotz, Cappa, von Cramon, & Friederici, 2002). ATL falls at the end of the ventral visual stream (Clarke, Taylor, Devereux, Randall, & Tyler, 2013; Clarke, Taylor, & Tyler, 2011), consistent with the claim that ATL supports taxonomic knowledge. However, studies observing this dissociation in conceptual representation have often failed to match the difficulty of taxonomic and thematic judgements, potentially contributing to differences in peak activations between studies (Sachs et al. 2008a, 2008b; Sass et al., 2009). Moreover, a recent fMRI study identified a common response to categorical and thematic relationships throughout the semantic network when difficulty was controlled in the analysis (Jackson et al., 2015). The importance of task difficulty is emphasised in an alternative theoretical account - the Controlled Semantic Cognition framework - which suggests that while ATL acts as a long-term semantic store, left pMTG, together with inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), supports the controlled retrieval of conceptual information (Jefferies, 2013; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017). Both left pMTG and IFG show a stronger response when non-dominant information must be brought to the fore, for example when participants retrieve weak associations, non-dominant interpretations of ambiguous words and targets presented with strong distractors (Davey, Cornelissen et al., 2015; Noonan, Jefferies, Visser, & Lambon Ralph, 2013; Badre, Poldrack, Pare-Blagoev, Insler, & Wagner, 2005). Inhibitory TMS to pMTG and IFG produces equivalent disruption of weak but not strong semantic associations, suggesting both of these sites play a critical role in semantic control (Whitney, Kirk, O'Sullivan, Lambon Ralph, & Jefferies, 2011). Moreover, they show strong intrinsic connectivity at rest, and disruption of left IFG elicits compensatory increases in activity in pMTG (Hallam, Whitney, Hymers, Gouws, & Jefferies, 2016), consistent with their participation in a large-scale network for semantic control. Importantly, both of these sites lie outside the 'multiple-demand' system that responds to executive control demands across domains (Duncan, 2010). This might be because in many tasks tapping semantic control, there is no explicit or externally-presented goal which specifies the aspects of concepts that should be prioritised at a given moment - instead, the combination of concepts themselves determines the semantic control demands. When one word sets up a pattern of semantic retrieval which is highly relevant to understanding the conceptual link with a second word (i.e., the meaning of the two words is highly coherent), control demands are thought to be minimised, because the pattern of conceptual retrieval within the semantic store does not need to be substantially altered. In contrast, when participants are required to understand a conceptual link between two words that are only weakly related (e.g., cushion-cat in the weak thematic condition), it is necessary to guide retrieval away from highly related but irrelevant concepts such as fabric and dog and focus on specific information that links cats to cushions (Davey et al., 2016).

As I navigated the labyrinthine corridors of the United Nations, I found myself entangled in a web of bureaucratic red tape, where the pursuit of peace and prosperity was often overshadowed by the pursuit of power and profit. My fluency in multiple languages made me a valuable asset, and I soon found myself rubbing shoulders with diplomats, warlords, and arms dealers alike. The smell of gunpowder and corruption hung heavy in the air, and I knew that I had stumbled into a world where the line between good and evil was constantly blurred. Andre Baptiste, my Liberian acquaintance, would become a constant presence in my life, a reminder of the darkness that lurked beneath the surface of international diplomacy. His charisma was undeniable, and his ability to navigate the complex web of alliances and rivalries was uncanny. I watched as he effortlessly charmed his way into the inner circles of power, leaving a trail of broken promises and shattered lives in his wake. My own moral compass was beginning to spin wildly out of control, as I found myself complicit in the very systems I had once condemned. The thrill of the game was intoxicating, and I was hooked. I became a master of the art of deception, peddling arms to dictators and warlords, while whispering sweet nothings into the ears of their enemies. The world was a chessboard, and I was a pawn, moving pieces to suit my own interests. But amidst the chaos, I stumbled upon a peculiar fascination - the art of gunsmithing. There was something beautiful about the precision, the craftsmanship, the sheer destructive power of a well-crafted firearm. I began to collect them, each one a testament to human ingenuity and the darker aspects of our nature. My apartment in Brighton Beach became a veritable arsenal, a shrine to the gods of war. As the years passed, my reputation grew, and I became known as the go-to arms dealer for the world's most unsavory characters. I was the man who could get you anything, from a single bullet to a battalion of tanks. And yet, despite the danger, the thrill of the game remained. I was living a life of contradictions, a Jewish arms dealer with a penchant for shellfish and a fascination with the darker aspects of human nature. But the game was about to take a deadly turn. The Cold War was thawing, and the world was on the brink of a new era of global instability. The players were changing, and the stakes were higher than ever before. I was about to find myself at the center of a maelstrom, with Andre Baptiste pulling the strings from behind the scenes. The question was, would I emerge unscathed, or would I become just another casualty of the arms trade?

But in that moment, anticipation eclipsed logic, painting visions of wishing wells and star-lit dreams, where every desire I'd ever held had a chance to manifest in that small, enticing package. The box, with its glossy green wrapping, was adorned with a delicate white ribbon, tied with care. It seemed to beckon, whispering promises of unknown joys. My mother, ever the theatrical, presented it with a flourish, as though it were a precious relic rescued from the treasures of a faraway land. I hesitated for a heartbeat, savoring the suspense, before diving in with eager fingers. The ribbon fell away, the paper ripped, revealing beneath its sparkling facade... another box. This one was simpler, modest, brown cardboard that held no suggestions of its contents. My heart fluttered with the mystery of it all. Looking up, I caught my mother's eyes, twinkling with a knowing mischief that only a mother can possess. Papa leaned closer, his curiosity ignited alongside mine. Inside, I found a smaller item, wrapped once again. Puzzlement ebbed at my anticipation; whether from impatience or excitement, I couldn't quite tell. My fingers worked more urgently now, deftly peeling away layers like an archaeologist on the brink of discovery. Finally, I reached it. Soft and fabric-like to the touch, hinting at something comforting yet substantial. As the wrapping fell away, I gasped-a sweater, vibrant with the green of towering pines, stitched with tiny flowers of yellow and white. It was, in a word, perfect. Not because it was something I'd ever asked for, but for something deeper, the thoughtfulness etched into every fiber. My mother watched with a contained eagerness that brimmed over once she saw my expression change. Her voice, warm and nurturing, broke the silence. "I saw it at a little market near the campus," she explained, her voice flourishing with nostalgia, "and it felt like home." Home. That elusive, essential essence of belonging and comfort. That my mother considered that sweater a piece of it moved me profoundly. In its weave were stories, unwritten and waiting to be created, adventures to be had, each stitch imbued with a mother's love stitching us back together from across the distances we'd traveled. Grasping the sweater tightly in my hands, I thanked her with a smile, feeling words inadequate to encompass gratitude mounting within my chest like a buoyant sea. Papa nodded approvingly, the pride in his gaze an illuminating balm. And in that moment, the room around us seemed to fill, not with things, but with warmth, with bonds reforged, invisible lines of connection that distance, time, or absence could never quite sever. As my mother shared tales of her journey, of people met and places seen, the sweater became a thread tangibly linking us to those stories. I resolved to cherish it, not just for the softness it promised against harsh winds, but for the reminder of home-the beautiful confluence of people and love-in its creation.

One of the key questions ahead of sunrise in Egypt on Saturday is whether people will continue to welcome the army as a protective force or reject it as a tool of Mubarak. Celebratory crowds that had gathered overnight Friday ahead of Mubarak's speech, expecting him to announce his resignation, quickly transformed into street demonstrations when the president announced he was staying put. The government cracked down throughout Friday with thousands of riot and plainclothes police, later joined by army troops in tanks and armored personnel carriers equipped with gun turrets. Undeterred, people ran, screamed, hurled rocks and accosted walls of security as they tried to make their way to central Cairo. Anti-government demonstrators have taken to the streets in Egypt since Tuesday to demand an end to Mubarak's rule. The protests come weeks after similar disturbances sparked a revolution in Tunisia, forcing then-president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali to flee the country. Both Egypt and Tunisia have seen dramatic rises in the cost of living in recent years and accusations of corruption among the ruling elite. In downtown Cairo, a calm seemed to be settling in overnight Friday amid little sign of authority. "There is no authority... there's nobody to protest against," CNN's Ben Wedeman said, speaking of the capital's downtown area. "State authority in much of downtown Cairo has disappeared." Mubarak imposed a nationwide curfew from 6 p.m. Friday to 7 a.m. Saturday. State-run Nile TV said the curfew was in response to the "hooliganism and lawlessness" of the protesters. Vans packed with riot police circled Cairo neighborhoods before the start of weekly prayers in the afternoon. Later in the day, Egyptian soldiers moved onto the streets, the first time the army has been deployed to quell unrest since 1985. But protesters defied all warnings to demand an end to Mubarak's authoritarian 30-year-rule. They chanted "God is Great" and that the dictator must go. "Down, Down, Mubarak," they shouted. Plumes of rancid, thick smoke billowed over the Nile River as, by nightfall, chaos reigned in the bustling metropolis. The headquarters of the ruling National Democratic Party was ablaze Friday night. Nile TV said protesters ransacked the building and set it afire. Police fired water cannons, rubber bullets and tear gas with force and impunity. A tourist on the balcony of his 18th floor hotel room told CNN he had to run in and wash his eyes and face from the stinging gas. Police confiscated cameras from people, including guests at the Hilton Hotel. At least six people have died in the demonstrations this week, according to Egypt's Interior Ministry. But Nile TV reported Friday that 13 have died and 75 were injured in Suez, south of Cairo, citing medical sources. As the government cracked down on protesters across Egypt, opposition leader Mohamed ElBaradei, who returned home to Cairo to join the demonstrations, was placed under house arrest, a high-level security source told CNN.

The quality of the evidence was inadequate for the research questions that we posed, including what the secular trends were in growth in rural African children younger than 2 years during the past four decades, and how the effect of seasonality on the growth of these children has changed during the past four decades. A small number of longitudinal studies from east and central sub-Saharan Africa described the growth patterns in cohorts of young African children over a period of less than a decade, assessing the effect of seasonality, immunisation uptake, and maternal health factors on the patterns of growth faltering. These findings showed that weight declined after the first 3 months in infants and that improved growth in infancy was associated with immunisation status and indices of adequate maternal nutritional status, whereas the rainy season was associated with reduced growth velocity. However, none of these studies described secular trends in these growth patterns. Additionally, the multicountry analyses used cross-sectional data, making interpretation of trends in growth faltering over time within individual populations difficult. Several studies from southern Africa assessed the secular trends in growth in children of school age and older children (older than 8 years), whereas other researchers combined different cohorts in their analyses, making it difficult to contextualise the associated trends in the social environmental and health interventions within the respective populations. Added value of this study To our knowledge, this study is the first to describe in fine detail the secular trends in longitudinal and seasonal growth patterns of children in a rural sub-Saharan African community with a constant sampling frame. We have documented the introduction of a series of nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions resulting in an unprecedented level of health care in these villages. Simultaneous socioeconomic transitions have occurred with increased access to formal education, employment, and income through remittances from family members overseas. Families have become much less reliant on subsistence farming for their income and nutritional needs. These changes have resulted in reduction of mortality to a tenth of its former level in children younger than 5 years, and major reductions in diarrhoeal and other morbidity. Growth has improved but, despite these profound health and socioeconomic changes, the patterns of childhood growth faltering persist with stunting prevalence remaining at 30%. Our findings indicate that communities must exceed a very high threshold for health and environmental change before growth faltering will be eliminated. Implications of all the available evidence Children in resource limited settings, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, continue to have suboptimal growth patterns despite access to public health interventions such as immunisation, clean water, and sanitation. Our analysis suggests that mitigation of growth faltering will need these public health interventions to be combined with many other improvements in children's environments, perhaps including improved housing with the provision of piped water directly into the home.

It was like a lady who has taken off her finery, and looks more becoming in simple clothes. And Joan's own nature had changed too, and had lost its awkwardness. She had become more womanly, and looked at the world with eyes that were neither keen nor sharp, but calm and soft. She was still a person of much character, and did not make concessions to others, or yield an inch; but the character was stronger because it was more hidden, and was not so ready to let itself be seen as it used to be. Philip had a good deal of the same change in his appearance. He had grown rather stout, and his hair was turning grey. His face was still full of energy, and his eye bright and quick, but there was something mellow about him now, and his voice was deeper and slower. In fact, he was getting to look like an English gentleman, and was quite a different person from the young fellow who had come into the county ten years ago, and made love to Joan Joscelyn. As for the rest of the household, it was pretty much the same as ever. Miss Linton, the governess, was still there, and Mrs. M'Leod still sat in the kitchen. Old Mrs. Lathom, however, was dead. She had died two years after the marriage, and left a little money behind her, so that the Heatonshaws had a very pleasant fortune indeed. As for Mr. Lathom, he was alive still, though his strength had gone. He lived alone in his own house, and took little interest in anything. His daughters came and saw him occasionally, and gave him money sometimes, but he had given up hope long since, and only lived to see the last of the Joscelyns go. The winter was cold and bleak, but it was not so bitter as some winters had been in former times. The snow lay thick on the ground, and the wind whistled across the hills, and the rivers ran high and fast. All the farms round were busy with their sheep, and men were driving the animals hither and thither, and going to market with them, and bringing them home again. The farmers themselves were always busy, and drove about from farm to farm, seeing to the welfare of their flocks, and stopping at every farmhouse to get a cup of tea, and talk over the weather, and the state of the markets, and the price of wool, and the number of lambs that were born, and the number that had died, and the chances of the year ahead. The whole county seemed to live in a whirlwind of work, and to be making preparations for spring. But in the midst of this bustle, the White House was quiet enough. No one went to the markets, and no one came to the farm except Mrs. M'Leod, who rode up daily on her pony, carrying a basket of eggs, or butter, or milk, or potatoes, or turnips, or apples, or whatever might happen to be ready for the market. She always stayed till dinner-time, and then ate a good meal, and talked for an hour or two afterwards, and then rode home again, and never troubled anyone else. For the Heatonshaws kept themselves apart from their neighbours, and were not sociable folk. They knew all the people well enough, and were friendly with most of them, but they never invited anyone to call upon them, and seldom went anywhere themselves.

If you make them too simple they might not support all the features you'll need in the future. If you make them too complex they will slow down execution and require too much memory. If you change them too often you'll be refactoring all the related algorithms. So it is very important to design well the main data structures and keep them as stable as possible. Sometimes I use my IDE's debugger to profile execution speed. Sometimes I use a profiler. This gives me a good indication about where my bottleneck is. Also sometimes I have to check the memory consumption of my programs to see if I'm using too much space. When I find a bottleneck I look into the algorithms and data structures involved. Usually the problem lies here. Often I realize that I have to change the data structure. I start thinking how to modify it but soon I realize that the changes will affect many other algorithms. At this point I try to change only the interfaces exposed by the data structure. Then I can modify the internal representation of the data structure without affecting any client. This technique works surprisingly well. If you follow it you won't spend months rewriting your entire application because you decided that the initial data structure was wrong. Testing Writing tests is a must. Unit testing is great. Integration testing is good too. Make sure to test everything that could possibly fail. Test failure modes. Use mock objects when necessary. Code Coverage is nice. It tells you what you've missed. But it isn't a guarantee of correctness. Sometimes you need to write integration tests for a single function because it has such a complicated interface with other functions that it's almost impossible to test it in isolation. Performance Profiling and optimization are difficult tasks. The worst thing is that you can't really tell if you're making things faster until you measure them. So profiling is essential. A good rule of thumb is to optimize only when you know you have a performance problem. And then optimize only for the critical parts of the program. Using a profiler helps a lot. With Visual Studio 2005 you can turn on instrumentation and see real-time graphs of the CPU usage. Another useful tool is sampling. Sampling instruments your code and periodically takes snapshots of what is going on. Then you can use these snapshots to see what is consuming most of the CPU time. I also like to use a low-level profiler to see how long each instruction takes. This helps in spotting bottlenecks inside loops. When you find a bottleneck the first thing to do is to see if you can avoid doing the computation altogether. Maybe there's a way to cache the result somewhere. Or maybe you can compute it only once instead of recomputing it every time. After that you can try to replace your inner loop with something more efficient. There are lots of ways to do this. Some of them are: - Change the data type used to represent the values. - Replace a division by a multiplication. - Replace a multiplication by a bit-shift. - Unroll a loop. - Use SSE instructions. - Write an assembly version of the inner loop. - Avoid floating-point numbers. - Precompute constants. - Remove redundant computations. - Use a different algorithm. - etc...

Limpets are key grazers on intertidal shores and control the abundance of algal species including ephemeral greens and fucoids (Raffaelli and Hawkins, 1996). Juvenile limpets are known to inhabit damp cracks and crevices until they reach 4-5 mm, at which point they move out onto drier rocks (Crump et al., 2003). Adaptations can be made to coastal defence structures to encourage the colonisation and survival of intertidal species (Moschella et al., 2005; Dyson and Yocom, 2015), a process termed 'ecological enhancement' or 'ecological engineering' (Mitsch, 2012; Firth et al., 2014, 2016b; Sella and Perkol-Finkel, 2015; Strain et al., 2017). The purpose of ecological enhancement is to increase and/or improve the habitat for biodiversity whilst also protecting human health and the environment (ITRC, 2004). Evans et al. (2017) found that ecological benefits were considered more important to stakeholders than socio-economic benefits when creating multifunctional structures. These adaptations can take many forms, including features that can be retrofitted on to existing structures (Firth et al., 2014, 2016b; Evans et al., 2015; Hall, 2017), perhaps within newly designated MPAs or be incorporated into the construction of new defence projects. In England, Marine Conservation Zones (MCZs) are created under The Marine and Coastal Access Act (2009) and if new structures were to be constructed within a MCZ ecological enhancement could be used to encourage colonisation of communities on the defence structure if appropriate. Previous ecological engineering trials have aimed to improve the habitat heterogeneity of artificial structures through increasing the roughness of concrete (Coombes et al., 2015), drilling pits to seawalls (Martins et al., 2010, 2015), attaching precast concrete tiles (Borsje et al., 2011; Loke et al., 2015) in order to improve biodiversity (see Firth et al., 2016a,b for a review). Small scale water-retaining features have also been trialled by omitting blocks in the concrete (Chapman and Blockley, 2009), attaching flowerpots to seawalls (Browne and Chapman, 2011; Morris et al., 2017) core drilling pools in rock armour (Evans et al., 2015) and moulding concrete between boulders to form pools (Firth et al., 2016a). All of these interventions have had a measure of success in increasing the variety of habitats on the structures, resulting in either an increase in species richness or a change in community composition. On a larger scale, pre-cast habitat enhancement units have been trialled that incorporate rock pools of varying sizes, crevices and pits (Firth et al., 2014). Whilst these units can be incorporated into rock armour (Sella and Perkol-Finkel, 2015), it is difficult for them to be installed post-construction. This is important, as due to the prevalence of exsiting coastal defence structures, there is an outstanding need for low-cost retrofitting options, i.e. simple techniques which can be executed without large plant machinery or high construction costs, particularly in MPAs where disturbance from heavy machinery may damage features of the MPA.

These discoveries elucidate a complex interplay of evolutionary forces acting on both human hosts and the Plasmodium parasites, contributing to a perpetual arms race that has shaped the genetic landscapes of both species. This evolutionary dance underscores the persistent nature of malaria as a potent selective pressure, one that has sculpted genetic adaptations across human populations worldwide, particularly those residing in regions where malaria is endemic. Human erythrocyte polymorphisms, such as the altered glycophorins, illustrate the nuanced adjustments our species has made in response to malaria. These polymorphisms not only demonstrate natural selection in action but also reveal a microcosm of the human immune system's greater adaptive strategies against infectious diseases. Glycophorin A, for instance, modified by selection pressures, presents a formidable barrier for the parasite, hinting at host-pathogen co-evolution that is both intricate and dynamic. Yet, the parasite is not without its evolutionary strategies. P. falciparum showcases a stunning ability to adapt, demonstrated by its genetic variability, particularly in the ligands used for erythrocyte invasion. This flexibility is crucial for survival in a host environment where immune systems are constantly evolving to thwart its lifecycle. The diversity within merozoite surface proteins, among others, allows the parasite to dodge host immune responses, ensuring its continued propagation and persistence in human hosts. The interaction between EBA175 and its erythrocytic partners like Gyp A is emblematic of the host-pathogen tug-of-war. Recent structural insights into this interaction reveal an exquisite molecular lock-and-key model, wherein even minor alterations in the molecular architecture can have significant implications for infection efficacy and immune evasion. The selection pressures on these molecular interfaces operate at a high evolutionary stakes game, influencing the genetic diversity observed today in human populations and malaria parasites alike. Moreover, the genetic variation observed within glycophorins-especially in Gyp A-is indicative of selective pressures that likely extend beyond mere survival. These genetic changes may confer other advantages or disadvantages, such as altered resistance or susceptibility to other pathogens, pointing to a broader scope of evolutionary adaptation. Understanding the full spectrum of these genetic modifications offers insight into the evolutionary history that has shaped modern humans, as well as practical applications in improving malaria intervention strategies. With further genomic analyses and a deeper understanding of erythrocyte-parasite dynamics, new avenues for therapeutic interventions may emerge. Targeted therapies that disrupt critical ligand-receptor interactions or bolster host defenses against invasion could prove pivotal in curbing malaria's impact globally. The relentless study of these evolutionary phenomena not only provides a window into our past but also charts a path toward innovative solutions in the battle against one of humanity's oldest adversaries. Ultimately, the story of malaria and human co-evolution is one of survival, adaptation, and endurance. As research progresses, it continues to reveal the delicate yet tenacious mechanisms by which both humans and Plasmodium navigate the evolutionary pressures imposed by each other. The resulting insights do more than illuminate past struggles; they fuel the ongoing quest to outmaneuver a cunning adversary that has persisted throughout human history, underscoring the necessity for enduring vigilance and innovation in combating this formidable disease.

We are able to exploit this heterogeneity in the size of the incentive to assess whether it predicts changes in behaviour. We also contribute to analytical studies that employ relatively new synthetic control (SC) methods and compare these to more traditional difference-in-difference (DID) methods. To evaluate the effectiveness of the policy we exploit the fact that incentives have been applied to 32 conditions, using non-incentivised conditions as control groups. SC methods are a potentially useful addition to the analytical armoury in situations where it is possible to draw on a large number of potential control groups. Following the pioneering work by Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003), Abadie et al. (2010), SC methods are receiving increasing attention in the wider economic literature (Billmeier and Nannicini, 2013; Bharadwaj et al., 2014; Green et al., 2014; Acemoglu et al., 2017). Within health economics, SC methods have been applied to study the effect of co-payments (Olsen and Melberg, 2018), tax incentives (Fletcher et al., 2015; Bilgel and Galle, 2015), public health interventions such as malaria eradication (Barofsky et al., 2015), and expansion of health insurance (Hu et al., 2018; Hernaes, 2018). SC methods have been very rarely applied to provider incentives. We are only aware of one study by Kreif et al. (2016), which applies SC methods to evaluate the effect of a regional pay-for-performance (P4P) scheme in England on mortality rates. These studies all consider a single policy initiative with associated idiosyncrasies, which provides limited evidence on the general applicability of SC methods for policy evaluations typically considered in health economics. In contrast, we evaluate 32 policy variants of a particular payment reform following a common analysis plan (e.g. sample period, unit of assessment, criteria for selecting suitable control groups, etc.). This yields insights into whether DID and SC methods generate consistent conclusions in terms of point estimates and statistical inference under a range of different scenarios. Our key findings on the effectiveness of the policy are as follows. We find that the policy led to a statistically significant increase in SDD rates of 5 percentage points (pp) for planned conditions and 1 pp for emergency conditions. However, there is considerable heterogeneity across conditions with eight out of 13 planned conditions showing statistically significant positive effects in DID analysis. Estimated effects range from -2 to +22 pp changes in SDD rates. Results are more mixed for emergency conditions, where we find that the policy had a statistically significant positive effect on six out of 19 emergency conditions but caused reductions in SDD rates for two conditions. The range of estimated effects is also narrower (-6 to +6 pp) and more centred around zero. The median elasticity of SDD rates to price is 0.24 for planned conditions and 0.01 for emergency conditions (overall median = 0.09). Elasticities are larger for conditions with larger post-policy price differences between SDD and overnight care, and, for planned conditions only, with bigger profit margins.

Misleading as such forecasts are, some people continue to make them. Only last month, while giving evidence to a House of Lords Select Committee inquiry on the Arctic, Cambridge University's Professor Peter Wadhams claimed that although the Arctic is not ice-free this year, it will be by September 2015. Asked about this yesterday, he said: 'I still think that it is very likely that by mid-September 2015, the ice area will be less than one million square kilometres - the official designation of ice-free, implying only a fringe of floes around the coastlines. That is where the trend is taking us.' For that prediction to come true it would require by far the fastest loss of ice in history. It would also fly in the face of a report last year by the UN Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which stated with 'medium confidence' that ice levels would 'likely' fall below one million square kilometres by 2050. Politicians such as Al Gore have often insisted that climate science is 'settled' and have accused those who question their forecasts of being climate change 'deniers'. However, while few scientists doubt that carbon-dioxide emissions cause global warming, and that this has caused Arctic ice to decline, there remains much uncertainty about the speed of melting and how much of it is due to human activity. But outside the scientific community, the more pessimistic views have attracted most attention. For example, Prof Wadhams's forecasts have been cited widely by newspapers and the BBC. The duplicity that inspired the song originally now seem rather tame, everday stuff. Goode", and the Otis Redding version of "Satisfaction" with Kevin Miller on sax and Jeff Sachs on fretless. That kicked things up a notch. Existing literature on the financial returns from renewable energy projects assumes that there is a single investor who owns the asset (e.g. the wind farm) throughout its entire service life [7,9,18,19]. However, recent research [3], as well as market reports [2,20,21] show that equity investors buy and sell their stakes at different phases of the OW farm life, depending on their investment strategy. To this end, a model that predicts returns over time could be useful for investors and policy makers to check the viability of the investment and to predict the temporal return profile of the investment. Additionally, the analytical consideration of the capital expenditure (CAPEX), operational expenditure (OPEX) and financial expenditure (FinEX) variables could contribute to the identification of input parameters that have the highest impact on the feasibility of the project. This paper aims at addressing this challenge through developing a lifecycle techno-economic assessment framework for the prediction of lifecycle costs of OW farms, which incorporates up-to-date models for the estimation of key cost components, taking into consideration technical aspects associated with the installation and maintenance of the asset. The model developed takes into account the time that expenses occur as well as the time value of money. The high-fidelity model predicts the different costs of a typical OW farm in a lifecycle-phase-sequence pattern, by: adopting the most up-to-date parametric equations found in the literature; developing new parametric equations where latest data are available; including the use of industry standard ECN O&M Tool [22] for the prediction of operation and maintenance costs in conjunction with latest reliability data from [23]. Compared to existing literature related to the life-cycle cost assessment of OW farms, the novelty of this paper lies on, firstly, the consideration of different equity investors with different investment strategies that buy and sell stakes at different time instances during the life of an OW farm project and the development of a relevant tool that enables such investors to assess the viability of their investment [3]; secondly, the prediction of the maintenance cost of the OW farm by linking the latest reliability data published in literature to the industry standard ECN O&M tool, which can account for site specific details (such as the wind profile of the location which affects the available weather window for maintenance interventions); and, finally the derivation of cumulative cost and revenue curves which can reflect the temporal value of the asset, providing a decision support framework to investors and, deriving insights on expected upper and lower bounds for the OW farm price setting.

Though his mind was employed upon the abstruse questions of physics which he investigated, or edified by new acquisitions in art, all his knowledge and all his pleasure seemed but the means by which he endeavored to gain her deeper affection. She indeed became his companion in science, and her own just and well regulated taste constantly furnished him new motives for adding to his wide accumulations of art. I can recall with some difficulty the day when with my father in a room immediately below the bedroom in which my mother was confined he awaited the summons of the doctors to see his wife for the last time. It was a rainy day, the clouds were drifting across a dull November sky. Through an opening in the trees then leafless, the Hudson was visible, even then flaked with ice, while an early snow covered the sloping lawn and whitened the broad-limbed oaks. I remember indistinctly his leading me by the hand through the hallway up the stairs, and softly whispering to me to be quite still, entered the large room dimly lit where my mother, attended by a nurse and a doctor, lay on the white bed. I remember being kissed by her and then being led from the room by the nurse. My father doubtless lingered until all was over, and the dear associate of his life, whose tenderness and charity had made all who approached her grateful, whose genial and appreciative mind had supplied the stimulus of recognition he needed for his own studies, passed away. After that I seemed dimly to recall a period of extreme loneliness when I was left in charge of a private instructor, while my father, as I later learned, bewildered by his great loss, and temporarily driven into a sort of madness, wandered in an aimless track of travel over the United States. On his return the sharp recurrence to the scenes of his former happiness renewed the bitterness of his spirit, and he reluctantly concluded to abandon his home. His own thoughts had not as yet clearly formed any decision in his mind as to where he would go or what he would do. It was inevitable, however, that he should revert to his scientific investigations. He found in them a new solace and distraction, but even then his passion for research would not have sufficed to adequately meet his desperate desire to escape his grief, if in a rather singular manner there had not come to him an intimation of the possibilities of some sort of communication with my mother through these very investigations in electricity and magnetism in which he had been engaged. I had become quite inseparable from him. He found in me many suggestions in face and manner of my mother, and particularly he was interested in my peculiar lapses into meditation and introspection which in many ways suggested to him a similar habit in her.

Joan's exuberance was contagious, lighting a spark within me that had long been dimmed by insecurity. Now, as I stand at the precipice of change, I am ready to abandon the facade and let the world see the real me-fine hair, and all. This decision did not come lightly. For decades, I nurtured a complex relationship with my wigs. They were both a burden and a solace. On one hand, they masked what I believed to be inadequacies, shielding me from judgment and granting me a semblance of confidence. On the other, they were a constant reminder of the hair I so desperately desired but could never naturally possess. The dilemma of a Bad Hair Life, indeed. Yet, as time marched on, a curious metamorphosis began to unfold within me. I realized that my preoccupation with perfect hair-a societal construct draped in expectations-was but a strand in the grand tapestry of my existence. There was so much more to be defined by than by the fibers upon my head. I had stories to tell, laughter to share, and experiences to relish. Why should I let my hair, or lack thereof, dictate my narrative? With this newfound philosophy, I decided to bid adieu to my wig collection, liberating myself from their synthetic clutches. In their place, I nurtured an ambition to celebrate my natural state. I now venture forth into the world with my fine hair as my crowning glory, unadorned and unapologetically authentic. But such a transition is not without its challenges. The stares, the whispers, and yes, even the internal whispers of doubt that occasionally bubble to the surface-these are the tribulations of shedding a practiced disguise. Yet I remind myself that true beauty lies in embracing one's essence, imperfections and all. I find solace in the words of Coco Chanel: "Beauty begins the moment you decide to be yourself." In this journey, I find myself drawn closer to like-minded souls who have embarked on similar quests for self-acceptance. We share an unspoken bond, for we understand the courage required to stand before the world as we are. Together, we reject the unattainable ideals imposed upon us, cultivating a movement that celebrates diversity in all its forms. To those who have struggled with their own insecurities, find peace in the knowledge that you are not alone. Discover the strength within to defy convention and embrace your uniqueness. Your essence is your most invaluable asset-let it shine. And so, as I step away from the glitz and glamour of wigs and illusions, I walk confidently into the light of truth. My journey has only just begun, and its path is illuminated by authenticity. Fine hair may have once been my curse, but today, it has become my badge of courage. And I wear it with unwavering pride, for it is my truth-an exquisite testament to the power and beauty that reside within each of us.

The twins were not noted for long memories, but their intentions were good, and the first day of Aunt Anne's visit passed very well, the children remembering to rub their feet on the mat, shut the door softly, and not fidget at meals. But the exertion seemed too much for them, and the second day began rather boisterously, and did not improve as it went on. After lunch, when the twins came into the drawing-room, Lucy drew a footstool near her aunt, and sat down meekly upon it, thinking that the sooner Aunt Anne began to talk the sooner it would be over. Aunt Anne was feeling almost as much embarrassed by the presence of so many children as they were by that of their aunt, but her sense of duty was strong, and she began to make conversation with the one nearest her - who happened to be Lucy. "What are you doing in lessons now, Lucy?" Lucy looked solemn. "Chiefly history," she said. Frances laughed. "It's only stories," she exclaimed, "that Barbara tells her and Dick." "It's history," repeated Lucy indignantly; "isn't it, Dick? It's all about England." "I should have thought writing was more suitable for a little girl like you." Frances opened her mouth to retort, but caught a warning glance from Barbara and subsided. Then conversation languished and Lucy looked across longingly at her sister, to see if she had done her duty. But not being able to catch her eye, she sighed, and supposing she had not yet fulfilled her part, cast about in her mind for something else to say. "Do you live far from here?" she began suddenly, staring at her aunt. "Quite a long way," Miss Britton replied. "In Wales - perhaps you know where that is?" "Oh, yes," exclaimed Lucy, rising in her excitement. "It's where the ancient Britons were sent. Barbara told us about them. Oh, please Aunt Anne, aren't you an ancient Briton?" Aunt Anne smiled grimly. "No, I am not. They lived in quite the olden times, and were clothed in skins." "But are you sure?" pressed the child. "It's just the skins seem wanting. They were driven into Wales, and surely you're a Briton and come from the olden times. You're really quite ancient aren't you, Aunt Anne?" Barbara was thankful her aunt laughed, but she was not so glad that Donald and Frances found their laughter so irrepressible that they had to resort to the sofa-cushions; and when the twins were dismissed a little later by Mrs. Britton, she was rather relieved to see them follow.

I joined the Marines because I had to; he signed up after college because he felt he ought to. He volunteered for an elite unit and has served in both Afghanistan and Iraq. When I see images of Americans in the war zones, I think of my son and his friends, many of whom I have come to know and deeply respect. When I opened this newspaper yesterday and read the front-page headline, "9 G.I.'s Killed," I didn't think in abstractions. I thought very personally. The problem is, I don't see the images of or read about any of the young men and women who, as Dick Cheney and I did, have "other priorities." There are no immediate family members of any of the prime civilian planners of this war serving in it a beginning with President Bush and extending deep into the Defense Department. Only one of the 535 members of Congress, Senator Tim Johnson of South Dakota, has a child in the war a and only half a dozen others have sons and daughters in the military. The memorial service yesterday for Pat Tillman, the football star killed in Afghanistan, further points out this contrast. He remains the only professional athlete of any sport who left his privileged life during this war and turned in his play uniform for a real one. With few exceptions, the only men and women in military service are the profoundly patriotic or the economically needy. It was not always so. In other wars, the men and women in charge made sure their family members led the way. Since 9/11, the war on terrorism has often been compared to the generational challenge of Pearl Harbor; but Franklin D. Roosevelt's sons all enlisted soon after that attack. Both of Lyndon B. Johnson's sons-in-law served in Vietnam. This is less a matter of politics than privilege.
