My dear Aunt Caroline was one who never failed me. She came to me that night, after a dinner at which I had sat silent and morose, and when she saw my grief she wept also. In her woman's way she sought to find excuses for Dolly. I listened to her, but was unconvinced. "She loved me, aunt," I said. "How can she marry another?" Mrs. Murray shook her head sadly. "The world, dear Richard, is full of girls who love, and yet marry others than their loves," she answered. "If only they might have their own way! But they are the playthings of fortune, and must suffer accordingly." Dix came duly with the papers, which I signed. It was a heavy burden for me to assume, - thirty thousand pounds at five per cent. I had no means of paying the interest save from my income, and that was already pledged to pay for the house in Dover Street. But I set my teeth grimly, and resolved to get rid of the encumbrances as soon as possible. I did not see how this was to be accomplished, but I trusted blindly to Providence. The next day I dined at Carlton House with the Prince of Wales, who had sent me an invitation the week before. His Royal Highness was in high spirits over his marriage, and made us all laugh with his sallies about the Princess. I kept my trouble locked within my breast, and tried to appear gay. There were some dozen of us present, including the Duke of York and Mr. Sheridan, and I remember that there was much talk of the American war, which had just ended disastrously for England. Mr. Sheridan was very witty, and held forth eloquently against the ministry and Lord North. It appeared that the King had been driven into a corner, and was compelled to dismiss his ministers.

She busied herself with her usual tasks, finding some comfort in the familiar routine of tidying shelves and ensuring everything was in its rightful place. The clatter of Ann Packet in the kitchen, preparing breakfast, was a soothing background melody to her thoughts. Despite the tension with Mr. Wesden, the shop retained its rhythm, like a heartbeat that wouldn't be stilled by passing storms. As she dusted the wooden counter meticulously, her mind wandered back to Sidney Hinchford. His departure had left a void-not solely in the shop's operation, but in her heart as well. Sidney's laughter, his buoyant spirit, had been a balm to the atmosphere. Without him, everything seemed slightly out of tune, a song missing its chorus. The bell above the door chimed merrily, announcing the entrance of a customer. Mattie straightened up, forcing a smile. It was Mrs. Crumple, a regular, her gray curls escaping from beneath a wide-brimmed hat. "Morning, dear," the older woman said, peering over her spectacles. "Looks like rain again." "Good morning, Mrs. Crumple. Yes, the sky did look a bit foreboding," Mattie replied, taking the woman's list and beginning to gather her usual purchases. "How is Mr. Crumple feeling this week?" "Ah, no better, poor thing. The doctor says we must expect it with age," Mrs. Crumple sighed, watching Mattie efficiently select the best produce. "And you, my dear? You seem a bit... weighed down." "I've been better," Mattie admitted, appreciating the concern. "Just a bit of trouble at work. Nothing that won't pass." Mrs. Crumple patted her arm kindly. "These things have a way of working themselves out. You just keep doing your best, and the rest will follow." As Mattie wrapped up the shopping and bade the woman farewell, she pondered those words. Everything did have a way of shaking into place eventually-perhaps she just needed to be patient and let things unfold on their own. The day wore on slowly, each tick of the clock resonating in the shop's hush. Customers came and went, each bringing a brief distraction, a flurry of greetings and goodbyes, leaving Mattie again with her thoughts and the faint hope of redemption in Mr. Wesden's eyes. In the quiet moments, her resolve strengthened. She would find a way to repair what little damage had been done, to restore her standing in the eyes of Mr. Wesden and regain the shine of her own self-worth. The secret, she mused, must lie in perseverance-not backing away in the face of failure but meeting it and rising above. By the day's end, with shutters drawn and the till reconciled, Mattie felt a strange peace settle over her. She knew not what the morrow would bring, nor how she might mend the rift that had formed. But she believed fervently in the strength of her heart and in the kindness of those around her. As the moon rose over Great Suffolk Street, casting long shadows and gentle light, Mattie allowed herself one final hope-that the coming days would grant her the chance to prove herself anew. Tomorrow was another day-a fresh start waiting just around the corner.

For example, we have recently reported the strength of binding of fluorobenzene, relative to an alternative solvent complex, can be modified as a function of the bite angle [27,28] of the supporting chelating phosphine ligand in [Rh( -C6H5F)(L)2][BArF4] complexes where L = chelating ligand, in which wider bite angle ligands promote equilibria that favour the solvent-species, [Rh(L)2(acetone)2][BArF4] [4]. As fluoroarenes are usually installed on metal centers to either stabilize a low-coordinate metal center or act as a masking ligand to reveal such a reactive center, a straightforward measure of the relative binding strengths of different fluoroarenes with the same metal fragment, or different metal fragments with the same fluoroarene, would be useful. Of course, equilibrium studies in solution can provide such information, however we were interested in developing other techniques that might complement such methods, and turned to ESI-MS to do this. Fluorobenzene is quite polar enough to permit the acquisition of high quality ESI mass spectra [29]. Mass spectrometry techniques have been previously used to study the binding affinities of fluorobenzenes with metal cations. Klippenstein, Dunbar and co-workers reported the coordination of fluorobenzenes with Cr+ ions probed by radiative association kinetics in the gas-phase using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry [30]. The energetics of the arene binding in the [Cr(fluorobenzene)]+ fragment were determined and showed that increasing fluorination results in weaker binding affinity. Previous studies have suggested that coordination to the system of arenes by transition metals has a significant electrostatic component [31,32], and that additional fluorine substituents reduce the negative charge located across the region so that in the extreme case of hexafluorobenzene the region has a partial positive charge. Other, more accessible for the synthetic chemist, mass spectrometric techniques can be used for determining relative binding strengths, for example tandem electrospray ionization mass spectrometers (ESI-MS/MS) have the capability to selectively fragment ions in a collision cell and determine the energetics of their dissociation [33,34]. More generally, ESI-MS is a useful technique for characterizing charged complexes in polar solvents, as it is a "soft" ionization technique and allows the parent ion to be observed with little or no fragmentation [35]. This property is particularly useful for studying weakly-bound, or transient, organometallic complexes [36,37] and can be coupled with inert atmosphere glove-box techniques in order to study air-sensitive complexes [38]. In this contribution we utilize Collision Induced Dissociation (CID) techniques to establish comparative binding affinities of various fluorobenzene ligands in a range of complexes [Rh( -C6H6-xFx)(L)2]+ where the chelating phosphine (L) is also varied. We also correlate these results from ESI-MS with both ESI-MS/MS and solution-based equilibrium studies. In doing this we present ESI-MS as a simple and straightforward methodology for determining qualitative information on the relative binding strengths of the arenes.

One framework in particular distinguishes between task-informative and task-uninformative neurons in the stimulated cortex at baseline (Bienenstock, Cooper, & Munro, 1982; Cattaneo, Rota, Vecchi, & Silvanto, 2008; Cattaneo, Sandrini, & Schwarzbach, 2010; Silvanto, Muggleton, Cowey, & Walsh, 2007; Silvanto, Muggleton, & Walsh, 2008), or the related concepts of signal and noise (Abrahamyan, Clifford, Arabzadeh, & Harris, 2011; Miniussi et al., 2010; 2013; Ruzzoli et al., 2010; Schwarzkopf, Silvanto, & Rees, 2011), and highlights that it is the relative activity of task-informative versus uninformative neurons (or signal-to-noise ratio) at baseline that will shape NIBS-induced perceptual/behavioural effects (for examples see Silvanto et al., 2007; or Abrahamyan et al., 2011). Accordingly, it is of interest to test measures that index the balance between these types of neuronal activities at baseline as to their explanatory potential for tDCS outcome, alongside other potentially determining factors (e.g., tDCS-intensity). One such measure is the slope of the psychometric function (PF). In PFs derived from two-alternative forced choice (2-AFC) tasks, changes in slope have been linked to changes in intrinsic uncertainty, or the ability to distinguish information from task-relevant and task-irrelevant "channels", in guiding perceptual decisions (Gold & Ding, 2013; Kontsevich & Tyler, 1999; Pelli, 1985, 1987; Tyler & Chen, 2000) (see also Aihara, Kitajo, Nozaki, & Yamamoto, 2008; 2010 for use of the slope/width of the PF as a measure of internal noise). This intrinsic uncertainty reflected in the slope has been proposed to arise at a late readout stage of sensory information processing, and Gold, Law, Connolly, and Bennur (2010) have identified selective neuronal pooling mechanisms in the parietal cortex that may reduce this intrinsic uncertainty and hence increase the PF slope. Based on this interpretation of the slope of the PF and the NIBS/tDCS-literature reviewed above, we predicted that tDCS effects may differ depending on the administered current intensity and the psychophysical measure of intrinsic task uncertainty at baseline, and tested for the first time for an interaction between the two. To this end, we applied tDCS at 1 mA and 2 mA (between participants) and split our participant into groups according to the slope of the fitted PF (discrimination sensitivity). We tested this within the cognitive domain of visuospatial attention, known to be governed by a bilateral frontoparietal network (Benwell, Harvey, & Thut, 2014; Blankenburg et al., 2010; Kinsbourne, 1977; Szczepanski & Kastner, 2013). Stimulation of this network by tDCS has been shown to influence both spatial (Giglia et al., 2011; Loftus & Nicholls, 2012; Sparing et al., 2009; Wright & Krekelberg, 2014) and non-spatial aspects of visual attention in healthy participants (Ball, Lane, Smith, & Ellison, 2013; Bolognini, Fregni, Casati, Olgiati, & Vallar, 2010; Bolognini, Olgiati, Rossetti, & Maravita, 2010; Jacobson, Goren, Lavidor, & Levy, 2012; Moos, Vossel, Weidner, Sparing, & Fink, 2012), although with more consistent results across studies for the spatial aspects of performance.

He did not approve of young ladies running away to become cowboys. He said he would rather see them dead, and Teddie believed him. So she returned home, crestfallen, and was punished by being denied the pleasure of going to a children's party given by one of her schoolmates. The party consisted of a series of games, and the last game of the afternoon was to have been a treasure-hunt. There is nothing more tantalizing than to be debarred from a treasure-hunt; it haunts your dreams like a lost opportunity. So Teddie decided that she must make up for it. That night she crept down-stairs and buried her gold watch under the roots of a tree in the garden. Then she drew a map of the grounds, showing the exact location of the watch, and hid it in a book in the library. Then she climbed back into bed, and fell asleep, dreaming that she had found the watch. When morning came, however, she remembered what she had done, and tried to dig up the watch again. But she couldn't find it. She hadn't marked the spot carefully enough. So she had to spend most of her time digging for it, instead of playing with her dolls. The days grew into months, and the months into years, and still Teddie kept on looking for the watch. Sometimes she thought that perhaps she ought to give up looking for it; but whenever she came near making this decision something seemed to tell her that she would be sorry if she stopped searching now. So she continued digging, and wondering why the watch eluded her. Once she heard some one say that perhaps the watch wasn't there any longer. This frightened her, because she knew how important the watch was. It was the symbol of her freedom, the key to the door of the cage. If she could only get hold of it, she would be able to unlock the gate and go free. She felt sure of this, and yet she couldn't find it. One day she told her mother about it. Her mother listened patiently, and then asked: "What makes you think you'll be happier outside?" "Because I shall!" cried Teddie. "I'm sure of it." "How can you be sure?" asked her mother. "You've always lived inside here. How do you know what it's like out there? Perhaps you wouldn't like it." "But I've read books about it," protested Teddie. "And the people in the books are happy outside. Why shouldn't I be?" "Perhaps they aren't really happy," suggested her mother. "Perhaps they're only pretending to be happy." "But they look happy," insisted Teddie. "They laugh and sing and dance, and they don't seem to mind being shut up in cages." "Yes, but suppose they do mind?" said her mother. "Suppose they're only laughing and singing and dancing because they're afraid to show their real feelings? Suppose they're really miserable underneath?" Teddie considered this possibility for a moment. Then she shook her head decisively. "No," she declared, "I don't believe it. They're too happy to be miserable." Her mother sighed. "Well, my dear," she said resignedly, "if you feel that way about it, I suppose there's nothing more to be said. You must follow your own conscience." "Thank you, Mother," said Teddie gratefully. She kissed her mother good-bye and started off toward the door of the cage. But just as she reached it, her father appeared in the doorway. "Where do you think you're going?"

We stopped here for about half an hour, having a dip in the stream, and a little bit of lunch a bread. The next bit of the hike was 4 miles again, and described by all books as the most difficult. In all honesty, it was exhausting, but I don't know if I thought it was the toughest part. The worst thing about it was having shoes that didn't fit so well and numerous blisters starting, and when I say blisters, it was like someone cut off the back part of my heel, pretty rough. There was one set of switchbacks all going up hill, probably 3 miles into that portion where I thought it might never end. It was really strenuous for about 30 minutes, it seemed like a lot more, but was probably a lot less, but was richly rewarded with a brilliant view of the coast at the top. These 4 miles were really cool though, most of it was out in the open on the side of the mountain, sometimes we had to grip the wall and go sideways the path got so narrow and the drop offs were so high, but the views were indescribable, just absolutely breathtaking. This part of the trail was also quite dry, but the ocean was a perfect aquamarine, blueish, can't even describe it, the pictures won't do it enough justice, you have to see it to believe it. Eventually we got to the 10 mile marker, which for us had been 15 miles and we ended at Kalalau stream. The last mile or so we had some naked people hiking behind us, and we saw loads of goats. At the end there were goats everywhere! I also saw my first centipede, maybe a millipede on the hike. At the stream, we took another hike 2 miles in to this big pool located in the stream. It was cool, but as exhausted as I was and as late in the day as it was, it wasn't worth it for 4 miles round trip. The last mile to the beach was absolutely mad. It was all down hill on slippery gravel and odd shaped ground, plenty of place to lose your footing and screw up your feet, which I did. You could see the beach the whole way down, but I swear it wasn't getting any closer. Eventually I got there and it was spectacular. The beach was almost completely isolated, there were people camping there but I didn't see many. Maybe 5 or 6 couples, 20 people total? The sand was so powdery I would sink down when I stepped in it, there was a waterfall at one end of the beach where fresh water was available. The water was crystal blue and sandy on the bottom. I caught sunset that day too which was a gorgeous redish pink that filled all the clouds with all sorts of shades and made the beach almost glow.

Confidently, he balanced on the bricks like a tightrope walker, and Polly leaned toward him curiously. "I'm Digory," he announced with the air of a young magician about to reveal something fantastical. "We just moved here yesterday. Polly asked eagerly, the notion of befriending this adventurous boy thrilling her like the first sip of lemonade on a summer's day. It was, after all, quite rare to stumble upon another child with the same flair for curiosity and imagination. Digory's eyes widened, alight with a shared spark of mischief. "Absolutely! Inconsistency Detection in Flexible Models Kapitsaki G.;Kolovos D. S.;Perry P.;Zdravkovic J. Conventional Domain-Specific Languages (DSL) definition processes start with the creation of a metamodel which is then used to instantiate models and guide the development of editors and other artefacts such as model-to-model and model-to-text transformations. Such a process implies expertise in metamodelling, and in relevant technologies. While this may be an easy or at least understandable process for MDE experts, this is not always the case with domain experts [1] who are more familiar with tools like simple drawing editors [2]. However, the involvement of domain experts is important in the definition of high quality and well-defined DSLs that cover all the needed aspects of a domain. To address the aforementioned issue, flexible modelling approaches have been proposed in the literature (e.g. [3-5,1]). Such approaches are based on sketching tools and do not require the definition of a metamodel during the initial phases of language engineering. More specifically, in flexible (or bottom-up) MDE, the process starts with the definition of example models [1,6,7]. These example models help language engineers to better understand the concepts of the envisioned DSL and can be used to infer draft metamodels manually or (semi-)automatically which eventually lead in the definition of the final metamodel. In this fashion, a richer understanding of the domain can be developed incrementally, while concrete insights (e.g. type information) pertaining to the envisioned metamodel are discovered. Fig. 1 depicts the stages taking place in a typical flexible MDE process as this is interpreted by studying different flexible MDE approaches in the literature (e.g. [1,2,8]). The sketching tools used in such processes allow the quick definition of exemplar models sacrificing the formality that model editors, which are based on a rigorously-defined metamodels, offer. In addition, drawing tools do not require MDE-specific expertise. The elements (nodes and edges) of these flexible example models can have type annotations assigned to them to describe the domain concept they represent and can also be amenable to programmatic model management using MDE suites like Epsilon [9]. On the other hand, since sketching tools cannot enforce syntactic and semantic correctness rules, flexible models are prone to various types of errors [10]: User input errors: Elements that should share the same type have different types assigned to them by mistake or as a result of a typo (e.g. Animal vs. Anmal). Changes due to evolution: Elements representing concepts that have evolved during the domain exploration process do not have their types updated (e.g. Animal vs. Herbivores and Carnivores). Inconsistencies due to collaboration: When multiple domain experts collaborate in the definition of the models, multiple types representing the same concept can be used (e.g. Doctor vs. Veterinarian). Omissions: Elements can be left untyped especially when models become large as it is easier to overlook some of the elements. To address the aforementioned issues, we propose an approach that uses machine learning techniques to automatically detect inconsistencies in flexible models defined using sketching tools.

It is one of the most widely grown vegetable crops globally and is susceptible to several viruses including begomoviruses (Mansoor et al., 2003; Morales and Jones, 2004). Several tomato varieties were previously tested for their suitability as hosts for Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) and Tomato yellow leaf curl Sardinia virus (TYLCSV) (Pico et al., 1999). A comparison of five tomato varieties revealed differences in susceptibility to TYLCV infection but none of the varieties could be considered completely resistant (Ji et al., 2007). Here we report on the evaluation of six tomato varieties for their suitability as hosts for geminivirus research. Six commercially available tomato varieties were selected for this study based on their growth characteristics (Table 1). Seeds were sown into 96-cell trays containing composted pine bark growing medium (Kulnura, Somersby, NSW Australia) supplemented with Osmocote Exact Standard 16-8-12 + TE (ICL Specialty Fertilizers, Durbanville, South Africa). Plants were maintained under glasshouse conditions with temperatures ranging from 18 C to 25 C and a photoperiod of 14 h light:10 h dark. Seedlings were transplanted into pots after four weeks and watered daily with fertilizer solution (Nutrifeed 2-3-2, Nutri-Tech Solutions Pty Ltd, Yandina, Queensland, Australia). The viruses used in this study included three mastreviruses, Maize streak virus strain A (MSV-A), Tobacco yellow dwarf virus (TbYDV) and Chickpea chlorotic dwarf virus (CpCDV); and five begomoviruses, African cassava mosaic virus (ACMV), East African cassava mosaic virus (EACMV), Pepper huasteco yellow vein virus (PHYVV), Tomato golden mosaic virus (TGMV) and Tomato leaf curl New Delhi virus (ToLCNDV) (Table 2). All of these viruses were infectious clones except for MSV-A, which was purified from maize leaves displaying characteristic streak symptoms collected in Zimbabwe (Ndunguru et al., 2005). Seeds were surface sterilized by soaking them in 70% ethanol for 30 sec followed by 0.5% sodium hypochlorite for 15 min. They were then rinsed five times with sterile distilled water before being placed onto half-strength Murashige and Skoog (MS) media plates containing 100 mg/l kanamycin (Sigma Aldrich, St Louis, MO USA). Plates were kept in a growth chamber at 24 C with a 13 h light/11 h dark cycle. After two days, seeds were transferred onto fresh plates without antibiotics and incubated for another week. The cotyledons of the seedlings were excised and placed onto full strength MS media plates for callus induction. Calli were subcultured every two weeks until sufficient amounts were produced for biolistic inoculation. For each of the viruses, Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain GV3101 carrying the appropriate binary plasmids were cultured overnight in LB broth with appropriate antibiotics. Cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 4000 rpm for 20 minutes at room temperature and resuspended in infiltration buffer (10 mM MgCl2, 150 mu M acetosyringone, 10 mM MES pH 5.7) to give an OD600 of 0.5. The bacterial suspension was left at room temperature for 2 hours prior to use.

The sun beat down upon the sandy dunes, relentless in its intensity. I trudged through the endless expanse, my eyes scanning the horizon for any sign of life. The desert was unforgiving, a merciless expanse of sand and rock that seemed to stretch on forever. I had been walking for hours, with no respite, no shade, and no water. My canteen was almost empty, and my throat was parched and dry. As I walked, I couldn't help but think of Anck-su-namun. She was the love of my life, the reason I had risked everything to defy the gods and bring her back from the dead. But now, she was gone, lost to me once again. I had failed her, and I knew it. I thought of the Book of the Dead, hidden away in the statue of Anubis, and the incantations that could bring her back to life. I had tried to use them, but they were no match for the power of the gods. I had been cursed, doomed to roam the earth for eternity, a monster, a creature of the night. I stumbled upon a small oasis, a cluster of palm trees and a spring of fresh water. I collapsed to the ground, my body aching with thirst and exhaustion. As I drank from the spring, I noticed a figure watching me from the shadows. It was a woman, her eyes piercing and cold. "You're a long way from home, aren't you?" she said, her voice low and husky. I nodded, my throat still dry from the sand and dust. "I'm searching for something," I said, my voice barely above a whisper. The woman stepped forward, her eyes never leaving mine. "What are you searching for?" she asked. I hesitated, unsure of how much to reveal. But something about her seemed different, something that made me trust her. "I'm searching for a way to bring back the one I love," I said, my voice cracking with emotion. The woman nodded, her eyes never leaving mine. "I know the way," she said. "But it's not going to be easy. Are you prepared to pay the price?" I nodded, my heart pounding in my chest. "I'll do whatever it takes," I said. The woman smiled, her eyes glinting with a cold light. "Then let's get started," she said.

To achieve this optimisation, a multidisciplinary approach is essential, integrating advancements in materials science, engineering, and information technology. Innovations such as bifacial solar panels, which can harvest sunlight from both sides, and concentrator photovoltaic systems, which utilise lenses and mirrors to focus sunlight onto small, high-efficiency solar cells, are at the forefront of this evolution. These technologies not only enhance the energy output per square meter but also contribute to reducing the overall cost of solar installations. Furthermore, enhancing the efficiency of solar panels through the application of nanotechnology and better semiconductor materials has shown promising results, pushing the boundaries of what is currently achievable in terms of energy conversion rates [11]. In addition to improving the technology itself, there is a pressing need for comprehensive energy storage solutions. The intermittent nature of solar energy generation necessitates that excess energy produced during peak sunlight hours can be effectively stored and utilised during times of low production. Energy storage systems, including advanced battery technologies and pumped hydro storage, play a crucial role in this context. For instance, lithium-ion batteries have become synonymous with modern energy storage, yet ongoing research aims to develop even more efficient and sustainable alternatives, such as solid-state and flow batteries [12]. These advancements will facilitate not only a more robust grid but also the integration of solar energy into existing energy systems without risking reliability. Public policy and regulatory frameworks must also adapt to this emerging energy landscape. To catalyse the widespread adoption of solar energy, governments should focus on creating favourable conditions that encourage investments and innovation. This could involve enhancing feed-in tariffs, establishing renewable portfolio standards, and providing tax incentives for solar installations. Furthermore, engaging communities through outreach programs can raise awareness about the benefits of solar energy, thus fostering a culture of sustainability and conservation. As the transition towards cleaner energy sources continues, it is imperative to ensure that such approaches remain inclusive-allowing not only large corporations but also individual homeowners and small businesses to contribute to and benefit from the solar revolution. Collaboration is another cornerstone of an effective solar energy strategy. Partnerships among stakeholders, including governments, academic institutions, and private enterprises, can drive research and development efforts that enhance the solar energy landscape. Such alliances can also pave the way for improved supply chains, ensuring that materials needed for solar technologies are sourced sustainably and ethically. By sharing knowledge, resources, and best practices, these stakeholders can foster an ecosystem that is conducive to innovation, resilience, and scalability in solar energy projects. As we look ahead to the next decade and beyond, the imperative for action cannot be overstated. The transition to solar energy, while promising, is fraught with challenges that necessitate a concerted effort across multiple domains. For solar energy to escape the confines of its current niche status, it must transform into a cornerstone of global energy policy. This evolution will rest on the foundation of technological innovation, supportive regulations, community engagement, and collaboration. If realised, such a transition can lead to a renewable energy landscape that is not only sustainable but also equitable, prosperous, and resilient against the backdrop of a changing climate. Indeed, the transformation of the energy sector has the potential to define the socio-economic fabric of the future, marking an era defined not by scarcity, but by abundance and accessibility in the realm of energy.

The "troubles" have been a centuries-old dispute between England and Ireland over who controls Northern Ireland. In 1609 British colonial settlers confiscated native-owned land in Northern Ireland and settled in Ulster with mainly Protestant British planters. There was conflict between the planters and the native Irish. The planters won the bloody ethno-religious conflicts that followed and cracked down on the political and religious freedoms of the indigenous Irish. In the 1700s groups formed (including the Ulster Orangemen that continue to this day) and antagonisms between the two communities became entrenched. Ireland was incorporated into the UK in 1801 and reformers such as Daniel O'Connell called for the repeal of the union as well as the end of discrimination of Catholics (around 75 percent of the population). The agitation of the Irish Parliamentary Party, who sometimes held the balance of power in Westminster, led to the unionists further entrenching their position for British rule. In 1920 guerilla warfare between what became known as the IRA and Unionists led to the partitioning of southern Ireland and Northern Ireland. Nationalists in Northern Ireland, who numbered around 35 per cent of the population, did not accept legitimacy of the new partition. Between 1970 and 1972 tensions that had been brewing erupted into violence with almost 500 people killed in Northern Ireland. One explanation for this was the formation of the real IRA, which embraced "armed struggle" against British rule. Another was the introduction of internment without trial (the vast majority of those imprisoned were Catholic) which succeed in politicizing many into the nationalist cause. Bloody Sunday - a January 1972 shooting in Derry of 14 unarmed nationalist civil rights activists by the British Army - was a flashpoint in the conflict. In 1972 the retaliation of the Provos came at a massive cost - more than 100 soldiers were killed, 500 were wounded and there were 1300 bombings. Yet the nationalists vowed to continue their campaign until there was a united Ireland. Successive British governments failed to solve the "Irish question" so the participants settled in for what the IRA called the Long War, which involved sustained, low-level violence, hunger strikes and protests. It is like a guiding light, which for me, was very much needed when everything seemed to be going sideways. Hebrews 7 introduces us to Melchizedek, a figure symbolizing eternal priesthood, laying a foundation of strength and perpetuity. It's in times like these, when life is unpredictable and overwhelming, that I find comfort in knowing there is a grander design at work. Much like the eternal priesthood, our challenges are fleeting compared to the everlasting growth and happiness that will, indeed, come. Despite the turbulence of my current reality-my children's job changes, our travel plans going awry, and the impending holiday stress-there's solace in understanding that these are just temporary trials. Progressing to Hebrews 8, we see the promise of a new covenant, written in our hearts rather than on tablets of stone. This metaphor echoes in my personal journey, urging me to internalize these experiences, learn from them, and carry those lessons forward. Instead of seeing this week as a series of unfortunate events, I choose to see them as opportunities to grow closer to my faith and family. This perspective couldn't be more timely. When my son chose to leave his job for the sake of his well-being, it illustrated an act of prioritizing, purifying the clutter for what truly matters. Initially, it felt like another thing falling apart. But upon reflection, it became a moment of clarity-allowing him to focus on his education and mental health is a powerful service to himself and, eventually, to others. Then, we reach Hebrews 11, often dubbed the "Faith Hall of Fame," celebrating the faithful who trusted divine promises through adversity. This chapter is particularly uplifting-it narrates how faith served as a compass, guiding individuals like Noah, Abraham, and Moses through their trials. It inspired me to re-frame our family's narrative this week into one of a journey where, despite setbacks, we continue to persevere with faith as our anchor. Lastly, I found great encouragement in Hebrews 12 and 13, which speak to endurance in our race of faith and remind us that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Just as these scriptures impart courage and reassurance, they implore me to remain steadfast and hopeful amid these trials. With holiday preparation looming, rather than dreading the bustle, I'm committed to embracing it as an opportunity to weave meaningful memories and lasting traditions. So, as I navigated through the lesson, though it began with a sense of confusion mirroring my week's chaos, it blossomed into clarity. The scriptures offered a reminder of strength and continuity, underscoring the promise of good things to come. Looking back over the week's events, amidst the disarray, I find hope and resilience-gifts that are indeed pretty good things.

The investigation of size structure changes in benthic species in the northern Adriatic Sea is crucial to understanding the ecological responses to the aforementioned disturbances and stressors. In the Gulf of Trieste, sediment cores have been used to reconstruct the history of benthic communities, providing valuable insights into the temporal shifts in species composition and abundance (Gallmetzer et al., 2017; Tomasovych et al., 2018a). However, the focus on species composition and abundance has neglected the crucial aspect of body size, which is a critical component of ecosystem functioning and resilience. Studies have shown that body size can be a sensitive indicator of environmental changes, as it responds to shifts in bottom-water oxygen concentrations, temperature, and food supply (Angilletta Jr. et al., 2004; Wall et al., 2011; Beukema et al., 2014; Moss et al., 2016). For instance, increases in body size have been linked to improved food availability and reduced predation pressure, while decreases in body size have been associated with reduced food availability and increased predation pressure (Beukema et al., 2014; Moss et al., 2016). In the context of the northern Adriatic Sea, the replacement of T. communis by C. gibba in low-energy muddy habitats below the summer thermocline during the 20th century (Gallmetzer et al., 2017; Tomasovych et al., 2018a) may have been accompanied by changes in body size. For instance, C. gibba is generally larger than T. communis, and its increased abundance may have been driven by improved food availability and reduced predation pressure. Conversely, the decline of T. communis may have been linked to reduced food availability and increased predation pressure. To investigate the temporal shifts in size structure of benthic species in the northern Adriatic Sea, we analyzed a dataset of benthic invertebrate specimens collected from the Gulf of Trieste and the Po prodelta during the 20th century. Our results show that the mean body size of benthic invertebrates increased significantly over the 20th century, with the largest increases observed in species such as C. gibba and Amphiura filiformis. Conversely, the mean body size of T. communis and other species that dominated the early 20th-century communities decreased significantly over the same period. These findings suggest that the changes in body size of benthic species in the northern Adriatic Sea were driven by shifts in environmental conditions, including changes in bottom-water oxygen concentrations, temperature, and food supply. The increase in body size of C. gibba and A. filiformis may have been driven by improved food availability and reduced predation pressure, while the decline of T. communis may have been linked to reduced food availability and increased predation pressure. Our results highlight the importance of considering body size as a critical component of ecosystem functioning and resilience, and underscore the need for further research into the ecological responses of benthic species to environmental changes in the northern Adriatic Sea.

Thus, for example, ICT services can allow travellers to continue working while en route, to maintain contact with family and friends via text, voice, video or social media, or simply to relax by reading or listening to music. The third factor has been the recognition that many aspects of travel time use are not well captured by conventional measures of utility (Lyons et al., 2014). There is also increasing awareness of the potential importance of the quality of in-travel time use as a component of overall trip satisfaction (Ettema et al., 2012; Olsson et al., 2013). Fourthly, there is an emerging realisation that the way in which travel time is used may have significant implications for transport planning and policy, especially in relation to the valuation of travel time savings (Borjesson and Eliasson, 2014; Borjesson et al., 2012; Hensher, 1977; Hjorthol, 2013; Jain and Lyons, 2008; Ory and Mokhtarian, 2005; Tseng and Verhoef, 2008). For instance, if it is assumed that travellers value the opportunity to undertake productive activities during their journey, then they would prefer modes of transport which enable them to do so (e.g. rail over car driving). Furthermore, as suggested by Borjesson and Eliasson (2014), the fact that productivity gains from better ICT connectivity could increase the willingness-to-pay for faster travel speeds suggests that these gains should be considered when evaluating infrastructure investments. Finally, the increasing prevalence of shared mobility services provides new opportunities for individuals to engage in multi-activity behaviour, and to transform previously unproductive travel time into more productive activity.

Moreover, recent investigations have ventured beyond traditional proxies of Cognitive Reserve (CR) to explore the multifaceted interplay of lifestyle factors that might confer resilience against cognitive decline. For instance, social engagement, defined as the breadth and depth of interpersonal interactions, has garnered attention as a potential modifier of cognitive outcomes. The premise here is straightforward: individuals who actively cultivate social networks and partake in communal activities may benefit cognitively, as these engagements stimulate neural pathways and reinforce cognitive functioning (e.g., Zunzunegui et al., 2003; Ybarra et al., 2008; Seeman, 2000). Participation in group activities, such as clubs, volunteer organizations, or team sports, not only promotes social interaction but may also enhance mood and emotional well-being, factors that are inherently linked to cognitive health (e.g., Cattan et al., 2005). Research has shown that older adults who maintain a rich social life exhibit better cognitive performance, reinforcing the notion that social cohesion is a critical component of CR (e.g., Fratiglioni et al., 2000). Indeed, it appears that cognitive stimulation arising from social contexts may be as significant as structured educational pursuits in fostering resilience against cognitive decline. In addition to social variables, emerging findings have also emphasized the role of physical lifestyle habits, particularly regular physical activity, as a potent contributor to CR. Engaging in aerobic exercises, for instance, has been associated with increased cerebral blood flow, neurogenesis, and even the promotion of certain neurotrophic factors like BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor), all of which sustain cognitive health (e.g., Ratey and Loehr, 2011; Hillman et al., 2008; Erickson et al., 2011). Such exercise-induced neuroplasticity not only enhances memory and learning but may also serve as a critical buffer against age-related structural brain changes (e.g., Colcombe and Kramer, 2003). Moreover, dietary patterns, too, have emerged as influential players. The Mediterranean diet, characterized by high intake of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, fish, and healthy fats, has been linked to lower incidences of dementia and cognitive decline (e.g., Martinez-Lapiscina et al., 2013; Scarmeas et al., 2006). With emerging studies suggesting protective benefits of specific nutrients, such as omega-3 fatty acids and antioxidants, it is clear that nutritional choices may substantively impact cognitive functioning. In light of these findings, it becomes increasingly evident that Cognitive Reserve is not a monolithic construct confined to education and intellectual engagement. Rather, it is a dynamic mosaic woven together by diverse experiential threads-social interactions, physical activity, and nutritional habits-all contributing to the solidification of cognitive fortitude. The implications of these insights for therapeutic interventions and public health initiatives are profound. Individuals and communities can cultivate Cognitive Reserve through a holistic approach encompassing formal education, lifelong learning, vigorous social networks, regular exercise, and sound dietary practices. These factors not only have the potential to buffer against cognitive decline but may also enhance quality of life, instilling a sense of agency and control during the aging process (e.g., Rowe and Kahn, 1997). Consequently, the quest for understanding and leveraging Cognitive Reserve necessitates an ongoing dialogue that encompasses both scientific inquiry and practical application, acknowledging its multifactorial nature. As research continues to unravel the complexities of CR, the prioritization of a multifaceted life course approach can pave the way for preventative strategies that empower individuals to thrive cognitively, regardless of their genetic predispositions or health adversities.

Changing the data structure later means changing all the algorithms already implemented. So do this design in the begining and do it right. Most of the features you will implement will require the design of at least one algorithm. It might be trivial (more often than not) or it could be a really smart one. In whatever category it is pay close attention to its complexity. Then plug in some numbers and see which choice is acceptable in terms of space and time and also easiest to implement and maintain. Choose that one! If profiling shows you are wrong, and the program is to slow (or too memory hungry) then your algorithm inventory will help you choose a better one. Does it pay to optimize away constant factors? Usually not! But never be rigid; take rules of thumbs (like the ones presented here) with a grain of salt. Sometimes you DO need to optimize for constant factors. But this is a rare situation. Test Suites After you decide what is the next feature, even before you choose the algorithm (but usually after you have the data structures) you should generate a test suite for that feature. Even mathematicians do work by trial and error. There is nothing wrong in using a limited set of tests that could never proove your implementation correct (Dijkstra said the last part). What is important is that very often just trying things out is a revealing experience. It shows bugs and stimulates intuition. Rigouros reasoning should temper this process. So, even if you create tests before implementing any new feature, don't be sure your code is 100% correct. Knowing this makes you smarter, not the other way around. ("People ask me very often how can I live without knowing. I don't know what they mean. It's simple, I do it all the time." Feynman.) Specification and Design Documentation Ok. So now you know what the next feature will be and how it fits in the overall picture. You also know what data structures and algorithms you'll use. Write it down! Make a specification. But don't stop here. Describe also the structure of the code that you WILL write. Often you'll use diagrams to do it. For object-oriented design there is a well developed graphical language: UML. When you write this document you'll often notice little things that you missed. Go back and revise your attack plan. Repeat. When you feel comfortable with the document you just wrote, and only after that, it's time to go hit the keyboard. Logging Before discussing about code I shall make a short detour. There is a feature that is special. It is special because it helps the development process itself. This is a good enough reason to include this feature into the big picture and also to make it one of the first on your chronological feature implementation list. It is logging.

The moon was broad, like one of the shields in the great hall, whither I went often when the great Duke was not at home, and when old Hanne would be busy cleaning the pavement and scrubbing viciously at the armor of the iron knights who stood on pedestals round about. "One day I shall be a man-at-arms, too," I said once to Hanne, "and ride a-foraying with Duke Ironteeth." But old Hanne only shook her head and answered: "Ill foraying shalt thou make, little shrimp. Such work as thine is not done on horseback - keep wide from me, toadchen, touch me not!" For even old Hanne flouted me and would not let me approach her too closely, all because once I had asked her what my father did to witches, and if she were a witch that she crossed herself and trembled whenever she passed him in the court-yard. Now, having little else to do, I loved to look down from the top of the tower at all times. But never more so than when there was snow on the ground, for then the City of Thorn lay apparent beneath me, all spread out like a painted picture, with its white and red roofs and white houses bright in the moonlight - so near that it seemed as though I could pat every child lying asleep in its little bed, and scrape away the snow with my fingers from every red tile off which the house-fires had not already melted it. The town of Thorn was the chief place of arms, and high capital city of all the Wolfmark. It was a thriving place, too, humming with burghers and trades and guilds, when our great Duke Casimir would let them alone; perilous, often also, with pikes and discontents when he swooped from the tall over-frowning Castle of the Wolfsberg upon their booths and guilderies - "to scotch the pride of rascaldom," as he told them when they complained. In these days my father was little at home, his business keeping him abroad all the day about the castle-yard, at secret examinations in the Hall of Judgment, or in mysterious vaults in the deepest parts of the castle, where the walls are eighteen feet thick, and from which not a groan can penetrate to the outside while the Duke Casimir's judgment was being done upon the poor bodies and souls of men and women his prisoners. In the court-yard, too, the dogs, fierce russet-tan blood-hounds, ravined for their fearsome food. And in these days there was plenty of it, too, so that they were yelling and clamoring all day, and most of the night, for that which it made me sweat to think of.

Although, the description of the technical solution is out of the scope of this paper, it is important to mention that it presents challenges for tenant participation: standardization of design and home systems will create a technically and financially feasible design, but raises the question about the choices tenants would have for their specific building. Pre- and post- renovation monitoring campaigns are intended to assess and improve the performance of the buildings. The renovation performance target has been defined as 'zero on the meter' (NOM). In the Netherlands, the concept of zero on the meter (nul-op-de-meter) is defined as a building (usually social housing renovation projects) in which the yearly building-and user-related energy consumption equals the generated renewable energy in the building and surrounding area, for example with Photo Voltaic panels on the roof [2]. The concept is based on residential buildings with 'standard' occupancy defined in Dutch norms [2]. However, actual occupancy patterns and their effect on energy consumption are currently not reflected in the 'standard' occupancy patterns defined in norms and simulation tools. Therefore, the achievement of energy targets defined by the concept (NOM) is uncertain. In addition, there is still uncertainty about the causes of rebound effects [7]. The acceptability process consists in the early involvement of the tenants in the renovation process so that they can give an input that can render the project acceptable to them. In other words, this is a participation process. Part of acceptability is that the process serves to enable tenants to understand and consider the new systems and solutions in their homes. In the Netherlands, 70% of the tenants in a building must agree on the renovation process, for it to be performed. This is not always achieved [8]. Additionally, if a renovation does go through, rebound effects often occur afterwards, meaning that the actual energy consumption is higher than predicted in calculations [13]. The reasons are still unclear, but are presumed to lie in residents' post-renovation behaviour and interaction with their home systems [14]. The current literature on good communication processes with tenants presents well-developed processes emphasizing open and timely communication, financial security, and a reliably scheduled and brief renovation process [15]. Breukers et al. [15] concur that a careful process of resident participation ahead of renovation would improve acceptability. However, the current literature on processes lacks a focus on daily living practices of tenants, both pre- and post-renovation, although these may affect energy use (pre-bound and re-bound). The acceptability research therefore adds this element by starting from the meanings that people attach to their home [15], to enable residents to find their own motivation for the renovation and to be open to the new experiences it brings. A new business model is required for this renovation concept in order to implement and upscale the solution. Housing associations have only a limited budget to invest on their portfolio, and so, for a deep renovation, extra investments are needed.

She wishes she could go back in time, to when Emma was younger, to when she was still her little girl. She feels a pang of nostalgia, of longing, of regret. She wishes she could turn back the clock, to when life was simpler, to when her children were younger, to when she was still in control. But time keeps moving forward, and all she can do is try to keep up.

I think now that if I had had some guiding will stronger than my own, I might never have done what I did, and I might now be a highly respectable citizen, respected by those who knew me, and with a life of easy contentment spreading itself fairly about my feet. Instead of which - I had made up my mind to be an artist; to that direction all my thoughts and dreams and ideas tended. I would paint great pictures; I would wander through the cities of the world, and see the pictures other men had painted; I would live a life that had in it nothing of commercialism, and nothing of the sordid. I did not know then how circumstances mould a life and change it; how rough-fingered Fate can step in, and tear asunder in a moment the fair threads we have woven, and twist and tangle them, and ruin the fabric. Like many another poor fool before me, I told myself that I could do what I liked with my life, and shape it in what fashion I would. Up to this time - that is, the time when I began to think for myself, and to take my life into my own hands - I had not met my guardian. I had had one or two curt and business-like notes from him during my schooldays; and when I went to London I found that he had taken a lodging for me, and had made various arrangements for my future. He was a little contemptuous as to the profession I had adopted; but shrugged his shoulders, and suggested that it was no real concern of his. I met him first, on my coming to London, at his office in the City - an office in a narrow dingy court, where he was in a position of some authority as manager to a big firm. I know nothing of business, and knew nothing then; I only know that he received me in a private room, and that I had a dim understanding that in another room still more private was one greater than himself, to whom he looked for instructions, just as all those below him looked to him. Jervis Fanshawe, with half a dozen little white stops let into the edge of the big desk at which he sat, to enable him to communicate with his subordinates, was evidently a power to be reckoned with. One such factor that has garnered attention in recent years is the role of dietary habits and the nutritional landscape during these formative years. Evidence suggests that the quality and type of food consumed can have pronounced effects on neurodevelopment. High intake of refined sugars and saturated fats has been linked to cognitive impairments and increased emotional dysregulation, potentially exacerbating the effects of obesity on brain structure and function (Gomez-Pinilla, 2008; Hsu et al., 2016). Indeed, a diet lacking in essential nutrients-such as omega-3 fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals-can detrimentally influence neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity, critical processes that underpin learning and memory (Benton, 2008; McNamara et al., 2010). Conversely, nutritious diets rich in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins have been associated with enhanced cognitive outcomes, emphasizing the importance of early dietary interventions (Hannum et al., 1999; O'Neil et al., 2014). In this respect, understanding the intricate relationship between dietary intake and adiposity becomes imperative, particularly when considering the alarming trends of obesity in youth. The window of adolescence represents a pivotal opportunity for interventions aimed at transforming unhealthy eating patterns, which could simultaneously provide benefits for body composition and cognitive health. Moreover, the psychosocial environment surrounding young individuals cannot be overstated. The influences of familial support, peer relationships, and socioeconomic status play a significant role in shaping not only dietary choices but also lifestyle behaviors that contribute to obesity (Benson et al., 2013). For instance, children and adolescents who face social stigma and bullying due to their weight may engage in emotional eating or withdrawal from physical activity, thereby perpetuating a cycle of weight gain and negative mental health outcomes (Braun et al., 2017). Furthermore, exploring the neurobiological underpinnings of these psychosocial stressors may elucidate the pathways through which obesity exerts its deleterious effects on the developing brain. Physical activity, another crucial variable, warrants attention in this discourse. Regular engagement in exercise has been shown to provide neuroprotective benefits, enhancing cognitive function and supporting neuroplasticity (Ratey and Loehr, 2011). Conversely, sedentary behaviour has emerged as a distinct risk factor for both obesity and cognitive decline, highlighting the need to promote active lifestyles among adolescents. Importantly, how physical activity interacts with dietary habits and their collective impact on brain structure and function during adolescence constitutes an area rich for exploration. To comprehensively assess the implications of these multifactorial influences on adolescent obesity and brain development, longitudinal studies employing advanced neuroimaging and neuropsychological methodologies are essential (O'Reilly et al., 2020). Such investigations could unveil critical periods for intervention, shedding light on how early lifestyle and environmental factors might mitigate, or exacerbate, the risk of obesity and its associated neurodevelopmental challenges. In conclusion, as we strive to unravel the complex construct of obesity, it is imperative to acknowledge its far-reaching consequences on neurodevelopment during adolescence. Addressing obesity through a multi-layered approach that integrates dietary, psychosocial, and behavioural perspectives will not only help to mitigate its prevalence but also safeguard the cognitive and emotional well-being of future generations. This synthesis of knowledge serves as a cornerstone for public health strategies aimed at promoting lifelong well-being, underscoring the urgent need for collaborative efforts across communities, policymakers, and health professionals dedicated to forging healthier futures for young people.

He ran off, and I sat down on a pile of old oars, still fuming as I thought over Stoddard's insolence. "Who is Miss Patricia Holbrook?" I asked myself. Who indeed? What business has Stoddard sending her to me, and what right has he to send anybody to me anywhere? I had been Stoddard's friend ever since we were boys together in college, but I was no longer a mere boy, nor had I any intention of becoming a mere tool of his. We had drifted apart. I had been teaching in Boston for ten years, and I had just published a book on Russian literature. The success of the book had given me the courage to ask Stoddard for a loan of two thousand dollars to enable me to go to Europe for a year and study the subject first-hand. His reply had been prompt and courteous, and I had received the money a few days before sailing for England. I had written him that I would return to America in time to spend the following winter in New York, and had hoped that we might renew our friendship. When I landed in London I found a letter waiting me from Stoddard, saying that he had been unable to attend the wedding of his sister to a millionaire brewer in Cincinnati, but that he was going to Turkey to teach the Sultan how to build bridges. He added that he wished to visit the principal European universities and museums during the coming autumn, and suggested that I accompany him. "My dear fellow," he wrote, "you can't find out more about Russia than I can about Greece, and together we can learn a great deal." This proposal appealed to me, for I was anxious to see some of the world's famous places before settling down again in New York. So I replied that I would be glad to join Stoddard in Paris. In fact, I wrote him that I should arrive in Paris at noon on the twenty-fourth of August. Then I packed my bag and started out to see the sights of London. Stoddard's letter had also said that he would write me in detail regarding hotels and routes, and that he would leave all arrangements to my taste. I had no idea that he was such a busy man that he could not attend his own sister's wedding, and, as I walked through Piccadilly, I wondered why he had not answered my letter. The next morning I took the train for Dover, and then, for three weeks, I traveled everywhere, stopping only long enough in each place to take notes. When I reached Paris I went directly to the Hotel de la Paix, but there was no letter for me. On the second day, however, I received one from Stoddard, asking me to come at once to the Grand Hotel des Terres Noires, Rue d'Antin. I went at once. Stoddard was standing in the middle of the room, looking very serious. As I entered he held out both hands to me. "You are a week late!" he exclaimed. "What does it mean? Where have you been? Have you seen my letters?" "No, I haven't," I said, puzzled. "There must be some mistake. I arrived in Paris on the twenty-fifth." "The twenty-fifth!" he repeated. "Why, I left for Athens on the twenty-third!" I stared at him. "But you told me to come here on the twenty-fourth," I protested. "So I did," he admitted. "It's a mistake. You're a week late. I've looked all over town for you.

In practical engineering applications, the unstructured grid model has distinct advantages in dealing with complicated domain and local refinement around rapidly varying bathymetry, for instance around structures, that are not easily achievable in a structured grid (Wang and Shen, 2011). With the potential of dynamic mesh adaptation using an unstructured grid, the model is also able to deal with simulations involving strong spatial and temporal variations, as shown in Huang et al. (2008). In addition, the proper description of the turbulence characteristics is also often crucial for the simulation of WEC due to wave breaking as demonstrated by many existing studies. However, most of the former studies are based on models such as k- mu, k-kl that are calibrated for an equilibrium turbulence production and dissipation state, which are strictly speaking not applicable for the simulation of the wave breaking process (Burchard, 2001; Umlauf and Burchard, 2003). The K-profile parameterization (KPP) is also found difficult to represent accurately the mixing in the bottom boundary layer and in nearshore regions (Durski et al., 2004). Partly, this is due to the fact that to develop and verify a turbulence scheme's suitability in modeling wave breaking, much detailed measurements in laboratory controlled conditions in both flow hydrodynamics and turbulence characteristics, as well as free surface variations are required. But such comprehensive datasets are still scarce in the literature. With few most recent experimental studies, e.g. van der A et al. (2017) and van der Zanden et al. (2016), it is possible to implement practical turbulence closure coupling with the WEC processes for better model accuracy in simulating wave breaking and wave-current interactions. The above considerations motivated the development of a new three-dimensional coastal hydrodynamic model system with fully coupled 3D wave-current interactions on an unstructured grid, which can be used as a basis for an effective morphodynamic model system. This is achieved by coupling the unstructured version of the third generation wind wave model, Simulating WAves Nearshore (hereinafter Un-SWAN, Booij et al., 1999; Zijlema, 2010), as wave module to the unstructured-grid, three-dimensional oceanic circulation model, Finite Volume Coastal Ocean Model (FVCOM, Chen et al., 2003). A new wave-current interaction scheme based on a VF approach (MRL04, U10) is implemented into FVCOM to account for wave effects on currents (WEC). The Generic Length Scale (GLS; Umlauf and Burchard, 2003) scheme is incorporated and modified to better account for the wave-enhanced turbulence generation, dissipation and vertical mixing in breaking-wave conditions. A wave roller transport model is implemented in this modeling system to account for wave breaking under influence of the surface wave roller, which is absent in original FVCOM code. In addition, a new coupling module is also developed to facilitate the communication between Un-SWAN and FVCOM, and realize the model coupling procedure.

But here's the thing. In the quest to shield our children from any pain or discomfort, we inadvertently rob them of the opportunity to develop resilience. When every fall is cushioned, every failure dismissed as unimportant, we are crafting a narrative for them that discomfort is foreign, even wrong. This perpetual comfort bubble is detrimental in the long run. Now, let's dive deeper into the realm of discomfort. Discomfort, my friends, is not the enemy. It is merely a signal, a guidepost directing our journey toward growth. When we lean into discomfort, we allow ourselves to stretch beyond the safe parameters of our understanding and capabilities. We evolve. We build resilience. So, how can we, as parents, guardians, or mentors, shift this paradigm? How do we prepare our young ones for a world that won't always offer a soft landing? Firstly, let's introduce challenges, calibrating them according to age and ability. Start small - perhaps a puzzle slightly above their level, an athletic challenge, or a creative project that pushes their boundaries. This makes them understand that it's okay to struggle, even to falter, and that getting back up is where the true strength lies. Next comes the art of modeling. As adults, we sometimes stumble as well; it's only natural. Sharing our own challenges and missteps openly with our children provides them with a true-to-life perspective. "Hey, I tried to do this today and it didn't work out as planned. But that's alright, here's what I learned." These conversations teach kids that it's normal not to have all the answers, and perseverance is key. Moreover, let's teach the value of failure not as a dark cloud hovering over success but as a stepping stone. Failure is not final; it's feedback. It tells us what didn't work so we can approach a problem differently next time. Celebrate attempts, no matter the outcome, and encourage analysis: What worked? What didn't? How can we approach this differently next time? Instill the capacity to delay gratification. In a world of instant likes and immediate responses, patience has become a rare commodity. Encourage activities that require waiting, like gardening or cooking, to demonstrate that the best things in life often take time and effort. Lastly, and perhaps most importantly, weave a fabric of support. Let children know that while they navigate the choppy waters of growth and exploration, they can always count on us to be in their corner - not with ready-made solutions, but with a listening ear and an encouraging nudge in the direction of figuring things out. So, as we continue raising the next generation, let's choose to gift them not with perpetual safety nets, but with the tools to build their own. Let's foster an environment where challenges are met with courage, and failures with introspection. For it's through these experiences, these moments of discomfort and stretching, that true character is born. And with it, the capacity to forge paths we never dreamed possible, chasing after dreams and goals with fervor, resilience, and a heart full of unyielding hope. Here's to crafting a future defined not by pre-determined greatness but by the achievements carved out through perseverance and grit.

Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and linoleic acid (LA), from the omega-3 and omega 6 families respectively, are described as essential FAs because the body lacks the enzymes to synthesise them and so both must be obtained through diet. Due to the inefficient conversion of ALA to the longer chain omega-3 FAs, such as DHA, an adequate supply of dietary omega-3 FAs is important, however the modern Western diet tends to consist predominantly of omega-6 FAs. DHA and arachidonic acid (AA), an omega-6 FA, are known to be vital during pregnancy for foetal brain development, as well as during lactation and throughout the life cycle (Simopoulos, 2009). During the last trimester, the foetal brain undergoes rapid growth and requires increased levels of DHA. As such, maternal FA status is likely to deteriorate while the foetal demand for DHA is high (Steer et al., 2012; Hornstra, 2000; Kendall-Tackett, 2010). Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) is a precursor to DHA, and beneficial effects in several conditions, such as schizophrenia and depression, have been linked to this FA (Emsley et al., 2002; Marshall and Rathbone, 2011). In studies investigating the association of omega-3 FAs and depression, randomised controlled trials have tended to focus on supplementation with EPA, or EPA administered in parallel with DHA (Appleton et al., 2010), making it difficult to tease apart the effect of either FA. Arguments in support of both EPA and DHA as the more beneficial FA have been put forward, with a meta-analysis by Martins (2009) concluding that EPA has a greater effect in alleviating depression. However, other studies have focused on DHA, given its role as the major FA constituent of brain phospholipids, and the fact that it is the predominant omega-3 FA obtained through fish consumption (Sinn et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2013). In this study we investigate the association between antenatal FA levels and perinatal depression using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) cohort. ALSPAC is uniquely placed to investigate the causality of any association with data collected on both FA levels throughout pregnancy and depressive symptoms at several time points during pregnancy and the postnatal period. In this study, we use a Mendelian Randomisation (MR) approach within the analysis to investigate whether there is a causal link between levels of two omega-3 FAs (DHA and EPA) and perinatal depression. MR is a method of assessing causality from observational data through the use of instrumental variables. Captain Iles leaned back in his chair, his eyes narrowing as he studied Haven's face. "I'm afraid it's become a necessity, Mr. Haven. The gold rush has brought a lot of... unsavory characters to this territory. We've had several stages hijacked, and the miners are getting restless. They're demanding more protection, and I don't have the men to spare." Haven's gaze drifted around the room, taking in the worn furniture and the faint scent of cigar smoke. "I see. And what makes you think these murders are more than just ordinary hijackings?" Captain Iles' expression turned grim. "The way they were killed, Mr. Haven. It was... brutal. And there was no attempt to take the gold. Whoever did it wanted to send a message." Haven's eyes snapped back to the Captain's, his interest piqued. "What kind of message?" The Captain hesitated, glancing at Mrs. Caslon before continuing. "I think it's best if you see the bodies for yourself, Mr. Haven. The local sheriff has them stored in the icehouse on the edge of town. You can draw your own conclusions." Haven nodded, his mind already racing with possibilities. "I'll take a look. What's the situation with the Indians?" Captain Iles sighed, rubbing his temples. "The usual, Mr. Haven. Raids, skirmishes... they're getting bolder. We've had reports of a new leader, someone who's been stirring them up. I've got a feeling it's all connected, but I don't have the proof." Haven's gaze locked onto the Captain's, his eyes cold and calculating. "I'll find the proof, Captain. And I'll find the person responsible for those murders." Mrs. Caslon's voice cut in, smooth as silk. "I'm sure you will, Mr. Haven. And perhaps, while you're at it, you can also find out who's been spreading rumors about the Army's involvement in the gold trade." Haven's eyes flicked to hers, a hint of amusement dancing in their depths. "Rumors, Mrs. Caslon? I hadn't heard anything about that." Captain Iles cleared his throat, his face reddening. "Just small-town gossip, Mr. Haven. Nothing to concern yourself with." Haven's smile was a thin, cold thing. "Oh, I think I'll concern myself with it, Captain. After all, I'm here to uncover secrets, aren't I?"

As I grew older, I began to sense the whispers and murmurs that followed my father wherever he went. The men of the Cross-Roads would gather 'round, their faces creased with concern, and speak in hushed tones of the "strange" ways of Alec Trimble. My mother, God rest her soul, would try to reassure me, but even she seemed wary, her eyes darting nervously towards the door as if she feared the very mention of my father's name would conjure him into the room. I didn't understand what all the fuss was about, but I knew it had something to do with my father's books. Yes, books! He had a small collection of them, bound in worn leather and filled with strange symbols and words that meant nothing to me. He would spend hours poring over them, muttering to himself, and occasionally exclaiming over some particularly fascinating passage. The men of the Cross-Roads would snicker and shake their heads, saying, "Alec Trimble's got a storehouse of knowledge, but it's all Greek to him." But I knew better. I knew that my father's books held secrets, secrets that only he could decipher. As I grew older, I began to notice that my father's lapses, as I called them, became less frequent. He seemed to be drinking less, and his talk became more measured, more deliberate. He would sit for hours, staring into the fire, his eyes lost in thought. I would creep up beside him, and he would absently stroke my hair, his fingers tracing the contours of my face as if trying to commit me to memory. I loved those moments, those stolen glances into the depths of his soul. And I began to sense that he was hiding something, hiding a truth that he knew I wasn't ready to hear. One night, as the fire crackled and spat, my father turned to me with an intensity in his eyes that made my heart skip a beat. "Thomas," he said, his voice low and urgent. "I have something to tell you. Something that will change everything." I felt a shiver run down my spine as he reached for a book, his fingers tracing the worn cover as if searching for a particular passage. And then, with a slow, deliberate movement, he opened the book, revealing pages filled with strange symbols and diagrams. "This," he said, his voice barely above a whisper, "is the key to our world. The key to understanding the mysteries of the universe." I felt a thrill of excitement mixed with fear as I gazed upon the pages, my mind reeling with the implications. And in that moment, I knew that my father's secrets were not just about books, but about the very fabric of reality itself.

Balaji and Lakshminarayanan [12] modelled a two-dimensional microchannel plate to study the effect of number and location of the inlet and outlet ports on flow distribution along the channels of micro heat exchangers. The dimensions of the microchannel plate were 8.6 * 7 mm and the width and length of the microchannel were 0.2 and 4 mm, respectively. The depth of the channel was not reported. The flow entered and leaved the micro heat exchanger vertically from the top surface. It was found that uniform flow distribution can be achieved using either an aligned single inlet and single outlet ports or single inlet port located at the centre line of the micro heat exchanger with two outlet ports located at each corner of the micro heat exchanger. Pan et al. [13] investigated numerically the effects of geometrical parameters such as length, width, manifold area and inlet/outlet port positions on flow uniformity in microchannels plate consisting of ten channels. The inlet/outlet manifold geometry was rectangular. The length and width of the channels were varied from 10 to 50 mm and 0.1 to 0.7 mm, respectively. It was found that the longer microchannel with smaller width resulted in better flow uniformity. Moreover, a relatively uniform velocity could be reached with a large area inlet/outlet manifold and also, when the direction of inlet/outlet ports was perpendicular to the microchannel plane. Therefore, the design of manifolds and microchannels is of considerable importance in micro heat exchanger design. Most researchers, however, only focused on the optimal design and neglected the effect of axial conduction that leads to non-uniform heat flux in microchannel flow. This is evidenced in the work of Huang et al. [14] who conducted an experimental study to investigate the effect of axial heat conduction on heat transfer analysis. The parallel microchannel design contained seven microchannels, 40 mm in length, 0.5 mm wide, 0.057 mm deep and a hydraulic diameter of 0.102 mm. The temperature in the axial direction measured at the centre line inside the channel was found to be non-linear for a certain range of Re numbers. Furthermore, the Nusselt number obtained from experimental data varied between 2.55 and 2.58, which is smaller than that predicted by the theoretical model with a constant heat flux boundary condition. These deviations were attributed to axial heat conduction in the experiment.

While all around there was confusion, whispers of rebellion simmered beneath the surface. Men and women rallied, drawn by differing ideologies, yet united by a palpable desire for change. In dimly lit taverns, clandestine meetings bustled with revolutionary fervor, stirring up a storm potent enough to rattle the very foundations of this young Republic. Amid this tumult, whispers spoke of a new leader-a figure who would champion not just unity but impose order upon chaos in ways the current administration purportedly could not. Yet, who was this person? The townsfolk offered differing descriptions: a fiery orator, an intrepid soldier, or perhaps an innovator from the bustling streets of the capital. And while the legitimacy of these claims remained uncertain, the shadow of discontent only grew as uncertainty mixed with hope, leading to an outcome no one could predict but which, at once, everyone could feel drawing near. Caught in this swirl of tumult, President Whittingham watched. Observing the rising tide, he realized that the very dreams which once ignited the spirit of Aureataland hung by a thread, teetering precariously on the edge of collapse. Stroll along the levee to watch the Mississippi roll by on the way to your private, century-old cottage, where you can prearrange to have champagne, chocolate-covered strawberries or souvenir waffle robes waiting.
