Nortan et al. [8] developed and tested a micro catalytic burner for power generation using thermoelectrics having a thermal output of 150 W and 0.5 W electrical power generation. A catalytic combustion based thermoelectric power generator is reported by Xiao et al. [9], the thermal output of the burner was around 500 W and generated 1/28 W of electrical power using eight thermoelectric modules. A catalytic propane burner is developed by Merotto et al. [10] for integration with commercially available thermoelectric modules. The combustion efficiency is reported to be 96% and the electrical power generation 9.86 W using two TEG modules [11]. Mustafa et al. [12] developed and investigated a hexagonal shaped porous gas (butane) burner, thermal output of 1/21.6 kW, for power generation using six thermoelectric modules. The maximum power output reported is 1.05 W. In another research, Mustafa et al. [13] used liquid fuel, kerosene-vegetable cooking oil, in a porous catalytic burner which had 10 TEG modules attached to it. The power generation was in a range of 4-21.9 W, depending upon the operating parameters. Mueller et al. [14] conducted a research on employing super-adiabatic porous catalytic burner in thermoelectric generators. The maximum power was recorded to be around 0.3 W after 5 h of operation using one TEG. An example of integration of thermoelectric to a comparatively larger scale of combustion (thermal output of up to 150 kW) can be seen in the work of Aranguren et al. [15] where they attached 48 TEG modules to the chimney of a combustion chamber. The electrical power generated is reported to be 21.56 W. In order to achieve high power densities, new thermoelectric modules were developed by Zhang et al. which consisted of nanostructured bulk half-Heusler alloys [16]. They have reported a power output of 94.5 W using 8 TEG modules integrated into a residential boiler. A thermoelectric generator hybrid system consisting of direct-carbon-fuel-cell is reported by Zhao et al. [17]. Hasani and Rahbar [18] reported a waste heat recovery system using thermoelectrics from a 1/25 kW PEM (proton exchange membrane) fuel cell, employing four TEG modules, they were able to produce 0.5 W of electrical power at a temperature difference of 20 K. Some recent experimental work carried out in recovering waste heat from combustion appliances, such as stoves, using TEG modules can be found in the study of Montecucco et al. [19] and O'Shaughnessy et al. [20]. The former reported 27 W electrical power output using four TEG modules at a temperature difference of 250 K; and the later around 5 W using one TEG. The scale of the burner presented in this study has been classified based on the previous work done by various authors in small scale combustion.

"Are you quite ready for breakfast, daughter? if so, suppose we go down together. You will want to help mamma and Elsie get the little ones fed and dressed, and perhaps I can give some assistance, too, since the storm prevents me from taking my accustomed walk in the grounds." "I should like to do all I could for them, papa, but I don't want to rob you of any of my company," she replied, looking lovingly into his face. "You never do that, daughter," he answered with a gratified look, and drawing her closer to him. "Nor do I ever mean to, papa dear," she responded, putting an arm round his neck and laying her cheek to his. "No, I know better than to expect anything so unnatural from my eldest daughter," he said with a smile. "So come along, for I am beginning to feel hungry." "I am glad to hear that, papa," she said gaily. "Oh, how nice it is to see you looking so well again!" "Yes, I seem to have fully recovered my health and strength," he remarked in a tone of satisfaction. "Mamma says it is all owing to our delightful summer at Viamede and fall and winter at Woodburn," she said with a look of affectionate gratitude directed toward her mother, whom they met just leaving her dressing-room. They exchanged greetings, Mrs. Dinsmore saying: "Good-morning, papa and daughter. I am very glad to find you both looking so bright and well." Then Violet came tripping in to join them, followed by Harold and Herbert, who had been waiting in the hall till their father and sisters were ready to accompany them downstairs. "We will all go down together," Mr. Dinsmore said, leading the way. "Come, Harold and Herbert, take hold of my hands and I will carry you down." "Thank you, papa, I'd rather walk," returned Harold, stepping briskly along by his side. "And so would I, papa," echoed Herbert, keeping close beside his brother. "Well, my manliness, I am pleased with you both," their father said, giving a hand to each. "There is nothing like having the use of one's own limbs, is there, boys?" "No, sir; 'twouldn't be nice to be lame or sick," replied Harold. "Not at all," said Herbert. "How good God is to let us be well and strong." "Yes," responded Harold thoughtfully; "it makes me love Him more every time I think of it." "That is right, sonny boy; and I hope you will try hard to live so that everybody who sees you will take knowledge of you that you have been with Jesus, and learned of Him to be meek and lowly in heart." "I'm trying, papa," replied the little fellow, looking lovingly up into his father's face. "Am I doing pretty well?" "Pretty well, yes, my son; but don't you think you sometimes speak a trifle impatiently to your little brothers and sisters - Dorothy and Donald especially?" "I 'spect I do, papa; but I'll try to stop it," Harold answered humbly, adding, "Please tell me whenever I do, so I can ask God to help me to keep from doing it any more." "That is right, sonny; and I will gladly do as you request." On reaching the dining-room they found the others already seated at the table, and took their places among them.

Interesting thing B The human brain uses a whopping 50% of its energy processing vision. The eyes are the only organs in the body that have direct contact with the brain. They are connected by the optic nerve, which is actually an extention of the brain. Not just any old nerve. If you look at the front of someone's head and imagine where their eyes would be if they were closed, you're looking directly at the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe controls logic and reasoning, creativity, abstract thinking, planning, and motivation. It's the center of personality. It's also the area that develops latest, and doesn't finish until the early twenties. Some interesting facts about it. It's the most sensitive to alcohol, and the most easily damaged. It's why people act differently when drunk, and why people with frontal lobe damage are often unemotional and have no sense of humor. Interesting thing C The brain is divided into four sections. Frontal Lobe Temporal Lobe Parietal Lobe Occipital Lobe Each section has specific functions. The temporal lobes are responsible for memory, hearing, language, and emotion. The parietal lobes deal with movement, orientation, recognition, perception of stimuli. The occipital lobes process visual data. Interesting thing D The brain is made up of two hemispheres, left and right. They are each further divided into sections, and perform different functions. The left side deals with logical and analytical thought, while the right side deals with creative and artistic thought. The corpus callosum connects the two halves together. It allows communication between the sides. Without it, you'd have two brains working seperately in your skull. You can read about split-brain patients online. They are fascinating. Interesting thing E The brain has an amazing ability to compensate for damage. After a stroke, new pathways develop to bypass the damaged area. The brain can reorganize itself to function without certain parts. It's called neuroplasticity. This is why physical therapy works. By repeating movements, you encourage the brain to form new connections and find alternate routes. It takes time and effort, but it's possible. Interesting thing F The brain is constantly changing. Every experience creates new synapses and strengthens existing ones. The more you practice something, the easier it becomes. This is because the neural pathways become more efficient. They fire faster and require less energy. It's why experts seem to do things effortlessly. Their brains have optimized themselves for those tasks. If the tree grew there, then there too stood the Roussillon house with its cosy log rooms, its clay-daubed chimneys and its grapevine-mantled verandas, while some distance away and nearer the river the rude fort with its huddled officers' quarters seemed to fling out over the wild landscape, through its squinting and lopsided port-holes, a gaze of stubborn defiance. Not far off was the little log church, where one good Father Beret, or as named by the Indians, who all loved him, Father Blackrobe, performed the services of his sacred calling; and scattered all around were the cabins of traders, soldiers and woodsmen forming a queer little town, the like of which cannot now be seen anywhere on the earth. It is not known just when Vincennes was first founded; but most historians make the probable date very early in the eighteenth century, somewhere between 1710 and 1730. In 1810 the Roussillon cherry tree was thought by a distinguished botanical letter-writer to be at least fifty years old, which would make the date of its planting about 1760. Certainly as shown by the time-stained family records upon which this story of ours is based, it was a flourishing and wide-topped tree in early summer of 1778, its branches loaded to drooping with luscious fruit. So low did the dark red clusters hang at one point that a tall young girl standing on the ground easily reached the best ones and made her lips purple with their juice while she ate them. That was long ago, measured by what has come to pass on the gentle swell of rich country from which Vincennes overlooks the Wabash. The new town flourishes notably and its appearance marks the latest limit of progress. Electric cars in its streets, electric lights in its beautiful homes, the roar of railway trains coming and going in all directions, bicycles whirling hither and thither, the most fashionable styles of equipages, from brougham to pony-phaeton, make the days of flint-lock guns and buckskin trousers seem ages down the past; and yet we are looking back over but a little more than a hundred and twenty years to see Alice Roussillon standing under the cherry tree and holding high a tempting cluster of fruit, while a very short, hump-backed youth looks up with longing eyes and vainly reaches for it. The tableau is not merely rustic, it is primitive. "Jump!" the girl is saying in French, "jump, Jean; jump high!" Yes, that was very long ago, in the days when women lightly braved what the strongest men would shrink from now. Alice Roussillon was tall, lithe, strongly knit, with an almost perfect figure, judging by what the master sculptors carved for the form of Venus, and her face was comely and winning, if not absolutely beautiful; but the time and the place were vigorously indicated by her dress, which was of coarse stuff and simply designed.

A comprehensive review of the application of Richards equations for soil water flow simulation was published by Kool et al. (2014). This project will focus on a quantitative assessment of the effect of climate change on the hydrology of small catchments. For this purpose, a combination of remote sensing and field measurements will be used. Remote sensing provides data at high spatial and temporal resolutions which allow to study the interactions between soil moisture, evapotranspiration, vegetation cover and groundwater recharge. The aim is to improve our understanding of the mechanisms behind water storage, water movement, and water losses from the unsaturated zone to the atmosphere and from there to the saturated zone. The main goal of this research project is to develop and validate a new method for estimating the hydraulic conductivity of soils using information derived from satellite observations. This method will then be tested against existing methods and compared to field observations of hydraulic conductivity. In this PhD project, we aim to develop a new model structure for the description of the coupled dynamics of soil organic matter and nitrogen. In particular, we want to include microbial processes and quantify their contribution to N {2} O emissions. We also aim to couple the newly developed model to existing models of soil biogeochemistry. This project focuses on the development of a physically based model for soil water retention curves. In particular, we aim to include the effects of swelling clays, macropores and cracks into the model formulation. This project focuses on the characterization of soil physical properties, including soil texture, bulk density, porosity, air content, and water retention characteristics. These properties play an essential role in many physical processes in the unsaturated zone. However, they vary strongly both spatially and temporally. Our aim is to develop improved methods for the estimation of these properties based on field measurements, remote sensing, and laboratory experiments. This project focuses on the development of novel statistical models for the prediction of soil physical properties. In particular, we aim to develop Bayesian models for the prediction of soil texture and hydraulic properties.

In these days of wonderful hopes and fears there was, in Maiden Lane, a very handsome residence - an old house even in the days of Washington, for Peter Van Clyffe had built it early in the century as a bridal present to his daughter when she married Philip Moran, a lawyer who grew to eminence among colonial judges. The great linden trees which shaded the garden had been planted by Van Clyffe; so also had the high hedges of cut boxwood, and the wonderful sweet briar, which covered the porch and framed all the windows filling the open rooms in summer time with the airs of Paradise. On all these lovely things the old Dutchman had stamped his memory, so that, even to the third generation, he was remembered with an affection, that every springtime renewed. One afternoon in April, 1791, two men were standing talking opposite to the entrance gates of this pleasant place. They were Captain Joris Van Heemskirk, a member of the Congress then sitting in Federal Hall, Broad Street, and Jacobus Van Ariens, a wealthy citizen, and a deacon in the Dutch Church. Van Heemskirk had helped to free his own country and was now eager to force the centuries and abolish all monarchies. Consequently, he believed in France; the tragedies she had been enacting in the holy name of Liberty, though they had saddened, had, hitherto, not discouraged him. He only pitied the more men who were trying to work out their social salvation, without faith in either God or man. But the news received that morning had almost killed his hopes for the spread of republican ideas in Europe. "Van Ariens," he said warmly, "this treatment of King Louis and his family is hardly to be believed. It is too much, and too far. If King George had been our prisoner we should have behaved towards him with humanity. After this, no one can foresee what may happen in France." "That is the truth, my friend," answered Van Ariens. "The good Domine thinks that any one who can do so might also understand the Revelations. The French have gone mad. They are tigers, sir, and I care not whether tigers walk on four feet or on two. WE won our freedom without massacres." "WE had Washington and Franklin, and other good and wise leaders who feared God and loved men." "So I said to the Count de Moustier but one hour ago. But I did not speak to him of the Almighty, because he is an atheist. Yet if we were prudent and merciful it was because we are religious. When men are irreligious, the Lord forsakes them; and if bloodshed and bankruptcy follow it is not to be wondered at." "That is true, Van Ariens; and it is also the policy of England to let France destroy herself." "Well, then, if France likes the policy of England, it is her own affair.

On Amy's porch four necks craned, the better to view his advance, and four pairs of eyes were expectant. "If there's anything for me," observed Peggy hopefully, "mother'll wave, I know." But Mrs. Raymond, who sat sewing on her own porch, opened the solitary letter the postman handed her, and proceeded to acquaint herself with its contents in full view of the watchers on the other side of the street. "This must be Mother's Day," Amy exclaimed disapprovingly, when, a moment later, she accepted from the letter-carrier's hand a fat blue envelope directed to Mrs. Gibson Lassell. But, in spite of her rather resentful tone, she scrambled to her feet, and carried the letter through to the shaded back room where her mother lay on the couch, with a glass of ice-tea beside her, devoting herself to the business of keeping cool. Some time passed before Amy's return. Priscilla's hammock barely stirred and the rhythmic creak of Ruth's rocking-chair grew gradually less frequent. Peggy, cuddling down among the cushions, let her thoughts stray again to the joys of being without sidewalks, and all that was implied in such a lack. The porch with the silent trio would not have seemed out of place in that enchanted country where the sleeping princess and her subjects dreamed away a hundred years. All at once there was a rush, a slam, a series of little rapturous squeals. The Amy who had carried the blue envelope indoors, had been mysteriously replaced by a young person so bubbling over with animation as to be unable, apparently, to express herself, except by ecstatic gurgles and a mad capering about the porch. Had a crisp October breeze all at once dissipated the languors of the June day, the effect on the occupants of the porch could hardly have been more immediate. Priscilla came out of the hammock with a bound. Peggy's cushions rolled to the bottom of the steps, as Peggy leaped to her feet. And so precipitately did Ruth arise, that her rocking-chair went over backward, and narrowly escaped breaking a front window. "Amy Lassell!" Peggy seized her friend by the shoulders and gave her a vigorous shake. "Stop acting this crazy way, and tell us what's happened." "Talk of fairy godmothers!" gasped Amy, coherent at last. "Talk of dreams coming true! Oh, girls!" "What is it?" Three exasperated voices screamed the question, and even Amy began to realize that her explanation had lacked lucidity. She tried again. "That letter, you know. It's the strangest coincidence I ever heard of. But haven't you noticed lots of times - " "Oh, Amy," Ruth implored, "do let that part wait, and get to the point." "Why, this is the point. That letter was from an old friend of mother's, Mrs. Leighton.

Monseigneur had been overgracious, and two hundred thousand francs was after all only a small sum to come out of Rose Marie's ample marriage portion. M. Legros now walked with a brisk step along the right bank of the Seine, then crossing the Pont Neuf he found himself near the Chatelet prison, and thence by narrow by-paths at his own front door in the Rue de l'Ancienne Comedie. Here he gave a sharp rap with the polished brass knocker, and within a very few seconds the door was opened and an anxious feminine voice hailed him from out the darkness of the narrow passage. "Eh bien? - Monseigneur? - What did he say?" M. Legros closed the door behind him with great deliberation, then he turned, stretched out both arms and, catching the speaker round the shoulders, imprinted two well-sounding kisses on a pair of fresh young cheeks. "He says," said the worthy bonhomme gaily, "that Rose Marie, the fairest maid in France, shall be called Countess of Stowmaries before the year is out, for right and justice and indissoluble marriage vows are all on her side." A little gasp - which sounded almost like a hysterical sob - broke from the woman's throat. It seemed as if the news - evidently very anxiously expected - was overwhelmingly good. There was silence in the little passage for a moment, then the fresh voice, now quite cheerful and steady, said lightly: "Let us go and tell maman!" Together father and daughter went up the steep, slightly-winding stair which led to an upper story. Rose Marie, silent once more, felt as if her young heart would presently burst through her corselet, so rapidly did it beat with excitement and anticipation. She followed her father into the large, cheerful-looking room which gave on the first landing. Here a bright fire blazed in an open hearth; blue cotton curtains hung on each side of the single, narrow window, through which the last rays of this October day struggled faintly. A large iron stewpot, from which escaped a jet of savoury-smelling steam, stood invitingly upon the hob, and beside the hearth, wooden spoon in hand, her ample proportions carefully draped in a thick brown linen apron, stood Mme. Legros herself, the wife of one of the wealthiest men in the whole of Paris. "Eh bien! Legros, 'tis good news then?" she asked with cheerful optimism, whilst a benevolent smile shone all over her round face, red as an Eydam cheese and quite as shiny and greasy, for Madame had been cooking and she was mightily hot. "The best, Maman," came in hilarious accents from her husband; "our daughter shall be installed in her English castle before many moons are over. The Holy Father himself will interfere, and this - this - milor Stowmaries will have to obey at once - failing which 'twill be excommunication and nothing less than that."

Many studies have shown that natural source HOCs (humic/fulvic acid, hydrophobic organic matter from algae and plant leaves, etc) are potent precursor for the formation of toxic DBPs, such as trihalomethane, haloacetic acids, haloketone and haloacetinitriles (Reckhow et al., 1990; Nikolaou et al., 2004; Abouleish and Wells, 2015; Sun et al., 2018). Our previous study also showed hydrophobic algal protein served as potent precursors of genotoxicants during chlorination (Lui et al., 2011). In contrast, information on chlorination of anthropogenic HOCs is very limited. Only a few studies showed that PAHs could be transformed into chlorinated PAHs (Cl-PAHs) upon chlorination, and some of which are more genotoxic than the parent PAHs (Xu et al., 2018; Chao et al., 2018). Richardson et al. reviewed that although chemical analysis has identified about 600 DBPs, the amount of uncharacterized organics suggests that >50% of the total organic halide remaining to be identified (Hockaday et al., 2009; Richardson et al., 2007; Liviac et al., 2011). Therefore, one focus of this study was to identify formation patterns of DBPs and genotoxicity after chlorination of HOCs extracted from local drinking water reservoirs, due to the fact that HOCs in local drinking water reservoirs contained PAHs (Liang et al., 2008a, 2008b), and effect of chlorination as well as the associated toxicities have remained unknown. Following an understanding of DBPs genotoxicity derived from chlorinating HOCs, the other focus of this study was to investigate effects of dietary antioxidants against DBPs genotoxicity. It was hoped that consumption of antioxidant-containing foods or drinks might help protecting human cells from exposure to DBPs. In fact catalase has been shown to be effective in reducing DNA damage induced by iodoacetic acid (Cemeli et al., 2006), but effect of dietary antioxidants (e.g. vitamin C (VC) and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG)) against DBPs toxicity have remained unknown. For example, VC is one of the most studied and powerful dietary antioxidant, in directly scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and donating electrons in various enzymatic and non-enzymatic reactions, and therefore can reduce ROS induced toxicity (Noctor and Foyer, 2002). VC can also reduce amount of aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) in inducing CYP1A1 gene, so that genotoxic metabolites could be reduced (Chang et al., 2009). In particular, VC was found to inhibit tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) induced Ecto-ATPase activity, which is required for AhR translocation to the nucleus (Chang et al., 2009). EGCG performs its function similar to VC, particularly that low-dose of H2O2 in cells could be generated upon exposure to these antioxidants and thus served as pro-oxidant to increase cell resistance against high-dose oxidative stress in short period of incubation (Elbling et al., 2010). Therefore, it was expected that VC and EGCG might exert protective effects if DBPs caused oxidative DNA damage or AhR-mediated genotoxicity in cells.

On its turn, parental behavioral traits seem to also being propagated across generations via non-genetic (epigenetic) mechanisms (Mitchell et al., 2016; Sigal et al., 1988; Toth, 2015), clearly indicating the overall complexity of the underlying factors involved in stress-vulnerability. Especially early life adversity is the leading non-genetic risk factor for the development of stress-related psychopathologies later in life (Huh et al., 2017; Teicher et al., 2016; Vrijsen et al., 2017) and, importantly, not all individuals are equally affected by early life adversity. There are excellent examples of the moderate impact of specific genes, particularly from the monoaminergic system and the HPA axis, in defining subsequent behavioral adaptations (Nugent et al., 2011; Scheuer et al., 2016; Zannas and Binder, 2014). However, the field is still exploring the relevance of sensitive periods and the suitability of different theoretical models (e.g., diathesis-stress; differential susceptibility) to guide studies on the role of gene-environment interactions (GxE) in explaining vulnerability to psychopathology (Leighton et al., 2017). Notably, personality traits have been shown to explain a significant share of the variance observed in both individuals' responsiveness to stress and susceptibility to develop stress-induced psychopathologies (DiGangi et al., 2013; Duggan et al., 2003; Tosevski et al., 2010), particularly depression (Bagby et al., 1995; Enns and Cox, 1997; Kendler et al., 1993). Personality traits are defined as behavioral predispositions that reflect a reliable behavioral responsiveness of a given individual across time and circumstances. Their predicting value in this context might be to some extent due to their polygenic character (Noblett and Coccaro, 2005). Human personality is typically considered to comprise five major factors: "openness" (person's degree of intellectual curiosity, creativity, and preference for novelty and variety), "conscientiousness" (tendency to show self-discipline, act dutifully, and aim for achievement), "extraversion" (describes energy, positive emotions, assertiveness, sociability, talkativeness, and the tendency to seek stimulation in the company of others), "agreeableness" (tendency to be compassionate and cooperative towards others rather than suspicious and antagonistic) and "neuroticism" (vulnerability to unpleasant emotions like anger, anxiety, depression, or vulnerability); each of these factors comprising different traits (Digman, 1990; Goldberg, 1993; McCrae and John, 1992). Notably, many studies examining the link between personality and stress-related psychopathologies have highlighted the factor neuroticism as the personality factor that captures the largest proportion of genetic risk for depression (Barlow et al., 2014; Brown and Rosellini, 2011; Kendler and Myers, 2010; Ormel et al., 2013). Here, we argue that high anxiety trait is relevant to define vulnerability to develop stress-induced depression. To this end, we provide an overview about the literature presenting evidence that high anxiety trait is an important vulnerability factor for stress-induced psychopathology. Then, we summarize work dealing with molecular alterations in individuals with high anxiety trait, including neurotransmitters, neuroendocrine factors and mitochondrial function, and their potential role in mediating stress-vulnerability.

As I sit here, surrounded by the cacophony of the cafe, I'm reminded of the impermanence of silence. It's a fleeting concept, a brief respite from the constant din of the world. Even in the quiet moments, there's always some residual hum, some echo of the sounds that came before. It's as if silence is merely a temporary reprieve, a brief pause in the never-ending symphony of noise. I think about the Iraqis, and how their lives are forever changed by the constant din of war. The sounds of gunfire, the wail of sirens, the screams of the innocent. It's a constant reminder that silence is a luxury, a rare and precious commodity in a world that's increasingly loud and chaotic. And yet, even in the midst of all this noise, I find myself craving silence. I crave the stillness of a quiet morning, the peacefulness of a forest glade, the hush of a moonlit night. It's as if I'm searching for a refuge from the constant barrage of stimuli that assails me from all sides. But perhaps that's the problem. Perhaps I'm expecting silence to be a destination, a place I can arrive at and stay. But silence is not a place, it's a state of mind. It's a choice, a decision to tune out the noise and tune in to the present moment. As I sit here, surrounded by the din of the cafe, I make a conscious decision to focus on the silence. I tune out the music, the TV, the chatter of the patrons. I tune in to the sound of my own breath, the beating of my heart. I become aware of the silence that lies beneath the noise, the stillness that lies beneath the chaos. And in that silence, I find a sense of peace. I find a sense of clarity. I find a sense of connection to the world around me, to the people and the things that truly matter. It's as if the noise has receded, and I'm left with the quiet truth of the present moment. It's a fleeting feeling, to be sure. The noise will come back, the distractions will return. But for now, in this moment, I'm grateful for the silence. I'm grateful for the reminder that it's always there, waiting for me to tune in.

Throughout the history of video games, people have always raised concerns about the potential for addiction. From the early days of Pong to the modern era of virtual reality, the debate has been ongoing. Some argue that video games are inherently addictive, while others claim that the issue is overstated. As a society, we've made significant progress in understanding the psychological mechanisms underlying addiction, and it's time to take a closer look at the tactics used by game developers to keep players hooked. One of the most common arguments against the idea that video games are addictive is that they're simply a form of entertainment, and people choose to play them voluntarily. This perspective is oversimplified, as it ignores the complex psychological dynamics at play. Research has shown that the brain's reward system is wired to respond to novelty, excitement, and social interaction, all of which are present in many modern video games. Game developers have taken note of these psychological triggers and have designed their games accordingly. For example, the use of variable rewards, such as loot boxes or daily challenges, is a common tactic used to keep players engaged. These rewards activate the brain's reward centers, releasing dopamine and creating a feeling of pleasure. This can lead to a psychological dependence on the game, making it difficult for players to stop playing. Another tactic used by game developers is the use of social pressure. Multiplayer games, in particular, rely heavily on social interaction and competition to keep players engaged. This can lead to a sense of FOMO (fear of missing out) and a desire to stay connected with friends and peers. The fear of being left behind or missing out on important events can be a powerful motivator, keeping players coming back for more. The use of artificial intelligence is another area where game developers have made significant strides in recent years. AI-powered chatbots and NPCs (non-player characters) can create a sense of immersion and realism, making the game feel more lifelike and engaging. This can lead to a sense of emotional investment in the game, making it harder for players to stop playing. As we move forward, it's clear that the gaming industry will continue to evolve and adapt to the changing needs and desires of players. The rise of free-to-play mobile gaming has led to a new era of monetization strategies, with games designed to extract as much money as possible from players. This has raised concerns about the ethics of game development and the impact on player behavior. In the next segment of this episode, we'll be joined by a special guest who has overcome gaming addiction and is now working to help others do the same. We'll also be discussing the future of the gaming industry and what needs to be done to address the issues surrounding addiction and player well-being. Stay tuned for more on that and much more on this episode of Gaming the System.

Underwhelmingly unoccupied, but back then it was the place to be if you wanted to see a ghost girl with long, stringy black hair. Before we dive too deep, though, let's give you a bit of a breakdown on what made this supposed horror film more of a confusing echo of silent screams and awkward eye rolls. I mean, come on, folks. The plot decided to take frequent nap intervals, leaving us all scratching our heads like we had stepped into a chipotle line without a practiced pitch in mind. Now, don't get me wrong, I adore a good horror flick as much as the next jaded podcast host looking for entertainment that isn't another rerun of Midwest Housing Adventures. But what's up with the scare tactics here, huh? Was it just Sarah Michelle's perpetually confused expression, or was there more lurking beneath that surface confusion? Honestly, the film's misadventures boiled down to as thrilling as trying to spot Waldo in a featureless desert. This was not, I repeat, not a spellbinding affair, nor was it the least bit engaging-unless you count the times the theater's AC kicked on and brought more chills than the movie itself. So, why in the world did we brave this straight face of nonsensical hauntings? You got me, but hey, Big Bloated Calf and I are nothing if not committed to furnishing our listeners with the blow-by-blow of movies we affectionately-or not-deem as cinematic train wrecks. Now, let's take a stroll back to those ten-minute increments where anything actually happened. Picture this: forlorn suburban homes with moans drifting through walls, ghostly apparitions flipping their hair like they're auditioning for a Rogue Pantene commercial. Yeah, it's that type of showstopper. Then there's the proverbial trips up and down stairs that somehow echo Jane Austen adaptations more than any self-respecting horror sequence should. That being said, if you enjoy characters making life decisions as poor as subprime mortgage investments, then this film's decision-making process will undoubtedly resonate with you. It's a complete sandbox of calamities-each one more head-scratchingly dismal than the last. Quite the feat, if you ask me. And trust me, Tad Nico is usually eternally optimistic, so take my disappointment with the gravitas it deserves. And here's the kicker, the cornucopia of anticlimactic climaxes that manifest throughout. Oh yes, the film possesses an almost mystical power to build tension and suspense and then yawn through the punchline like a weary dad joke. So, we got a curse that clings tighter than those Christmas sweaters your mom always insists on buying, and let's not forget the repetitively cyclical nature of the plot-that's the sorta charm we're talking about here. In conclusion, folks, if you've made it this far into our diatribe and are somehow still curious about The Grudge, pop it on when you've exhausted your chia pet collection or need background noise for a mundane game of Solitaire. The movie might boast a sprig or two of hair-raising moments, but at its core, it's just a go-anywhere GPS set eternally to "meh." To summarize, there's a grudge, there's a movie, and there's us-two brave souls who faced the cinematic frights so you didn't have to. You're welcome-times three, for emphasis.

However, in the quest for broader adoption, one cannot overlook the intrinsic trade-offs these organic photovoltaic (OPV) systems present. Although OPV devices have demonstrated promise through their lightweight nature and flexibility, making them ideal for applications where traditional solar panels prove cumbersome, their commercial viability hinges upon overcoming certain technical challenges. Chief among these challenges is the inherently low efficiency of OPV cells, which continues to lag behind that of established crystalline silicon (c-Si) counterparts [35]. Yet, it's imperative to acknowledge that efficiency is not the sole determinant of a technology's potential; aspects such as ease of production, integration capabilities, and unique application setups afford OPV technologies a competitive edge. Moreover, research into the longevity and environmental impact of OPV systems is critical. Unlike silicon-based solar cells, OPV devices often grapple with degradation issues, primarily due to the organic compounds' sensitivity to factors such as moisture, oxygen, and UV radiation [36]. Addressing these vulnerabilities necessitates innovative protective encapsulation strategies alongside advanced material development to enhance lifespan and operational stability. This aspect of research not only improves device durability but also mitigates potential environmental impacts, a crucial step since the materials used in OPV devices may include elements that pose disposal challenges [37,38]. Significant strides have been made in enhancing OPV efficiency through the synthesis of novel semiconductor polymers and small molecules [39,40]. These materials are engineered to optimize light absorption, charge transportation, and energy conversion efficiencies. For instance, advancements in non-fullerene acceptors have led to notable performance gains, allowing OPV cells to reach efficiencies surpassing 15% in laboratory settings [41,42]. Equally, tandem configurations, which stack multiple layers to capture a broader spectrum of sunlight, offer promising avenues for efficiency improvements [43,44]. Such innovations not only close the efficiency gap with more traditional technologies but also reinforce the notion that OPV devices, with their tunable properties, are well-suited for custom applications ranging from wearable technology to building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV). The growing synergy between industry and academia fosters a dynamic environment for accelerating OPV research and development. Collaborative efforts have seen the successful translation of laboratory-scale innovations into pilot projects and practical prototypes, thereby pushing OPV closer to widespread commercial deployment [45]. Initiatives such as joint ventures, government incentives, and cross-disciplinary research programs are essential to sustain this momentum, paving the way for a future where OPV plays a significant role in the global energy landscape. In summary, while OPV technologies may not currently rival the efficiency of crystalline silicon, their unique properties and the intense research focus present compelling prospects for future growth. A comprehensive strategy addressing efficiency, durability, and environmental sustainability will be pivotal in overcoming existing barriers. By harnessing these elements, OPV can carve out a substantial niche in the photovoltaic marketplace, contributing to the diversification and resilience of global energy sources. Thus, continued investment in OPV research holds the promise of a greener, more adaptable energy solution that aligns with the goals of a sustainable and energy-secure future.

We savored the simple yet delicious fare, letting the conversations flow as naturally as the breeze that rustled the leaves overhead. There's something special about sharing a meal with someone you love - it's like weaving threads of intimacy with every bite and every shared glance. I know he feels it too, even if he doesn't say it out loud. It's in the way his eyes soften when he looks at me, the way his hand finds mine across the table. Later, as we wandered back home under the canopy of a starlit sky, the conversation turned to music. He put on "Ocean Gypsy" and we danced slowly in the driveway, the world around us fading into a blur. There, beneath the watchful gaze of the moon, we moved in a rhythm dictated by our shared hopes and dreams. Sunday morning arrived lazily, embraced in warm sheets and half-whispered promises. We made blueberry pancakes, and he gallantly attempted to juggle ingredients with an amusing lack of coordination that had us both in stitches. Breakfast was accompanied by tales of childhood escapades - stories of treehouses and scraped knees, of dreams that seemed so far away then but feel so close now. The hours slipped by, inevitable as the tide, and soon it was time for him to leave. We stood by the door, locked in a prolonged embrace, reluctant to let go even as reality nudged us apart. He kissed me softly, a promise of return, and with a final wave, drove away, leaving me with the echo of laughter and the warmth of fleeting moments on my skin. And now, here I am, recounting all of this, trying to encapsulate a weekend of wonder into mere words. The house feels a little emptier without him here, but my heart feels full, buoyed by the memories and the promise of August 30th. It isn't loneliness, not really. It's the space between reunions, the anticipation, the build-up to more moments like those just passed. There's something beautiful in the waiting, in the knowledge that there's someone out there waiting for you too, under the same sky. And so, with each day that passes, with every star that twinkles in the night, I find myself a little less lonely and a lot more hopeful. Soon, I tell myself. Soon, these days apart will be just another chapter in our story, each one filled with promise and possibility. Soon, we'll be together again, and these moments of solitude will only amplify the joy of togetherness. Until then, I hold tight to my dreams and to the love that never truly leaves my side.

All around stood the new recruits, watching the musician. Bartek gazed too, but did not understand why they admired the fellow so much. The integration of omics data with other types of data, such as phenotypic and environmental data, has also been facilitated by the development of new computational tools and frameworks. One of the major challenges in the analysis of omics data is the need for standardization and harmonization of data formats and annotation standards. The development of community-driven standards, such as the Minimum Information About a Plant Experiment (MIAPPE) checklist, has helped to address this issue (Taylor et al., 2018). The use of standardized vocabularies and ontologies, such as the Plant Ontology (PO) and the Gene Ontology (GO), has also facilitated the integration of omics data across different species and experiments. For example, the use of chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) data has enabled the identification of transcription factor binding sites and the elucidation of gene regulatory networks (Ezer et al., 2017). The integration of omics data with genomic data has also enabled the identification of novel genetic variants associated with complex traits, such as crop yield and disease resistance (Ferrari et al., 2018). She was probably about nine years old, and in every respect a perfect contrast to her companion, her senior by several summers, for the latter was strongly built, and from beneath his beautiful fair locks a pair of big blue eyes flashed defiance at the world, while Ruth was a delicate little creature, with slender limbs, pale cheeks, and coal-black hair. The little girl wore a fashionably-made, though shabby dress, shoes and stockings - the boy was barefoot, and his grey doublet looked scarcely less worn than the short leather breeches, which hardly reached his knees; yet he must have had some regard for his outer man, for a red knot of real silk was fastened on his shoulder. He could scarcely be the child of a peasant or woodland laborer - the brow was too high, the nose and red lips were too delicately moulded, the bearing was too proud and free. Ruth's last words had given him food for thought, but he left them unanswered until the last bundle of sticks was tied up. Then he said hesitatingly: "My mother - you know.... I dare not speak of her before father, he goes into such a rage; my mother is said to be very wicked - but she never was so to me, and I long for her day after day, very, very much, as I long for nothing else. When I was so high, my mother told me a great many things, such queer things! About a man, who wanted treasures, and before whom mountains opened at a word he knew. Of course it's for such a word your father is seeking." "I don't know," replied the little girl. "But the word out of which God made the whole earth and sky and all the stars must have been a very great one." Ulrich nodded, then raising his eyes boldly, exclaimed: "Ah, if he should find it, and would not keep it to himself, but let you tell me! I should know what I wanted." Ruth looked at him enquiringly, but he cried laughingly: "I shan't tell. But what would you ask?" "I? I should ask to have my mother able to speak again like other people. But you would wish...." "You can't know what I would wish." "Yes, yes. You would bring your mother back home again." "No, I wasn't thinking of that," replied Ulrich, flushing scarlet and fixing his eyes on the ground. "What, then? Tell me; I won't repeat it." "I should like to be one of the count's squires, and always ride with him when he goes hunting." "Oh!" cried Ruth. "That would be the very thing, if I were a boy like you. A squire! But if the word can do everything, it will make you lord of the castle and a powerful count. You can have real velvet clothes, with gay slashes, and a silk bed."

White noise or noise adjusted to the time-varying frequency of the TMS "click" can be administered via sound-proof in-ear headphones to prevent the TMS sound to be singled out by the brain (Massimini et al., 2005). Noise masking can substantially reduce auditory evoked components in the TEPs, but often no complete suppression can be achieved at sound levels bearable for the participants, and a low frequency component can still be perceivable via bone conduction (Tchumatchenko and Reichenbach, 2014; ter Braack et al., 2015). A foam layer underneath the coil can dampen bone conduction and attenuate scalp sensations caused by mechanical coil vibration. However, the effectiveness of this method varies across participants (ter Braack et al., 2015). At physiologically effective stimulus intensities, TMS will always cause significant peripheral co-stimulation, producing spatiotemporally complex cortical responses that do not result from direct transcranial cortical activation. The quantity and quality of somatosensory and auditory co-activation varies from site to site and depends on stimulation intensity and coil design. Since indirect multisensory (non-transcranial) and direct transcranial brain stimulation occur simultaneously, their evoked EEG responses are superimposed and hard to disentangle. Consequently, sham conditions have been used to characterize the non-transcranial multisensory contribution to the TEP. Sham stimulation is often achieved by the TMS coil being physically distanced from the scalp or tilted (Du et al., 2017; Fuggetta et al., 2008), thereby reducing the induced electric field in the cortex to a magnitude below stimulation threshold. The physical separation of the coil from the scalp preserves the airborne "click" sound but allows for little or no bone conduction and completely lacks somatosensory co-stimulation (Nikouline et al., 1999; ter Braack et al., 2015). The mere control by median nerve stimulation-evoked somatosensory potentials (Paus et al., 2001; Rosanova et al., 2009) not only lacks auditory stimulation but the evoked potentials may also not resemble those evoked by stimulating the scalp (Hashimoto, 1988). Sham TMS coils, generating only a very small electric field in the cortex, provide simultaneous somatosensory and auditory stimulation (Bonato et al., 2006; Opitz et al., 2014), but the area of stimulation is broader (Opitz et al., 2014) and somatosensory stimulation may be markedly reduced compared to real TMS (Bonato et al., 2006; Opitz et al., 2014). On the other hand, even when the transducing coil is placed on another body part such as the shoulder blade, stimulation still produced late evoked components reminiscent of those commonly seen in TEPs caused by real TMS (Herring et al., 2015). This study systematically examines the contribution of multisensory co-stimulation to the TEP. We stimulated two different locations (frontal and parietal cortex) with two different coil orientations (orthogonal and parallel to the target sulcus/gyrus) and included a realistic sham condition for each location. The sham stimulation matched somatosensory and auditory co-stimulation of real TMS as closely as possible, while inducing only a subthreshold electric field in the brain.

The Gingrich campaign believes those and other May contests such as Arkansas, Kentucky and Texas will be fertile ground for delegates as well. The 152 delegates at stake in Texas could be a boon for all the candidates. Gingrich has the endorsement of Gov. Rick Perry, who unsuccessfully sought the GOP presidential nomination. Expect Gingrich to lean on Perry when the primary turns to Texas. "With 4 candidates remaining, the GOP nomination now moves into unchartered waters with history in the making," wrote Randy Evans, senior adviser, and Martin Baker, political director to Gingrich, in a recent campaign memo. "The sequencing and pace of the second half favors Newt." For Gingrich and Paul, the numbers are more difficult. They need 78% and 83% of the remaining delegates, respectively, to earn the nomination. Paul's plan: unpledged delegates. Delegates: Pledged, unplugged and the power to switch. Not all delegates are the same. "Pledged" delegates are required to vote for the candidate based on the results of their state's contests. "Unpledged" delegates are allowed to vote for any candidate they choose, regardless of the results in their state. For Paul, this could mean picking up delegates in states that have already held their first round of voting. In many caucus states, the first round usually has a nonbinding presidential straw poll and an election of delegates to another local convention. These delegates then go to a county, congressional district or state convention. At this second-stage convention, which could occur months after the initial vote, the actual delegates for Tampa are selected. The process varies from state to state. In some states such as Iowa, delegate selections are done at different events. Congressional district delegates are elected at the district conventions, while at-large delegates are elected at the state convention. This is where the Paul campaign sees an opening. The congressman is counting on his strong grass-roots organization to help him pick up delegates at these local conventions. "Our campaign has continued to follow up and work the delegate selection processes in the states where contests have already been held, and we plan to work hard to collect delegates in upcoming states where the awarding of delegates is proportional," Gary Howard, Paul's national press secretary, said in a statement. "No one can afford to think too far ahead right now, it is still a wide open race so our campaign will continue to hunt for as many delegates as we can gain up until the convention." Most of the delegate-selecting conventions in caucus states have yet to take place. In Wyoming, Paul did see a loss of a couple of delegates between the first straw poll and the county conventions. His supporters will have to rally stronger to make sure he maintains - if not picks up - delegates. Unpledged delegates can also change their minds and vote for a different candidate.

I would sooner have faced a dozen ghosts than a somnambulist. I had no doubt in my mind that the Dux's empty bed was to be accounted for in this uncanny manner, and that the shot and yell were intimately connected with his mysterious disappearance. Now I thought of it, he had not been himself for some time. For a whole week he had not licked me. Ever since he had got his entrance scholarship at Low Heath he had been queerer than ever. He had not broken any rule of importance; he had been on almost friendly terms with Faulkner; he had even ceased to plot the assassination of Plummer. He was evidently in a low state, and suffering from unusual nervous excitement, thus violently to interrupt the usual tenor of his way; and, as I knew, such a state lends itself readily to the grisly practice of somnambulism. What was to be done? Yell? I couldn't do it for the life of me. Get up and look for him? Wild horses could not have dragged a toe of me out of bed. Stay where I was till the unearthly truant returned? No, thank you. At the bare notion my rigid muscles relaxed, my erect hair lay down, and I collapsed, a limp heap, on to the pillow, with every available sheet and blanket drawn over my tightly closed eyes. And yet, in my unimpassioned moments, I do not think I was a notorious coward. I had stood up to Faulkner's round-arms without pads, and actually blocked one of them once, and that was more than some of the fellows could say, I could take my header into the pool from the same step as Parkin. And once I had not run away from Hector when he broke loose from his kennel. Even now, but for the dim recollection of that awful automatic machine, I might have pulled myself together sufficiently to strike a light and jog my next-bed neighbour into wakefulness. But somehow my nerves had suffered a shock, and since there was no one near to witness my poltroonery, and as, moreover, the night was chilly enough to warrant reasonable precautions against cold, I preferred on the whole to keep my head under the clothes, and drop for a season, so to speak, below the surface of human affairs. But existence below the sheets, when prolonged for several minutes, is apt to pall upon a body, and in due time I had to face the problem whether, after all, the vague terrors without were not preferable to the certain asphyxia within. I had put my nose cautiously outside for the purpose of considering the point, when my eyes, thus uncovered, chanced to fasten on the door. As they did so paralysis once more seized my frame; for, at that precise moment, the door softly opened, and a figure, tall, pale, and familiar, glided noiselessly into the dormitory. It was Tempest.

In light of the growing significance of drought as a perilous environmental challenge, research has increasingly sought to refine methodologies for effective assessments and interventions. Understanding the multifaceted relationship between drought, agricultural productivity, and the broader ecosystem is critical not only for immediate responses but also for long-term sustainability. The application of various drought indices, including the VTCI, sheds light on the intricate dynamics of regional climate variability and its impacts on vegetation health. As drought continues to escalate in frequency and intensity due to climate change, the need for timely and accurate monitoring systems becomes paramount in mitigating adverse effects on food security and thus, livelihoods. The potential of remote sensing technologies to revolutionize drought assessment cannot be overstated. By providing spatially explicit data that can be analyzed over time, remote sensing enables researchers and policymakers to discern patterns and make informed decisions. The integration of satellite-derived indices with ground-based observations enhances the reliability of drought monitoring efforts, thereby allowing for more nuanced understanding of local climate impacts. For instance, studies have demonstrated how combining the VTCI with meteorological data such as rainfall and temperature can improve the predictive capabilities of drought forecasts (Gao et al., 2017b). This synergistic approach promises better preparedness for agricultural stakeholders, empowering them to implement adaptive strategies in a timely manner. Moreover, the implications of drought extend beyond crop yields to encompass broader socio-economic dimensions. Regions heavily reliant on agriculture are particularly vulnerable; thus, a comprehensive examination of drought impacts includes socio-economic assessments to gauge the socio-political ramifications of crop failures. The 2012 United States drought, for example, resulted in staggering losses not only in projected agricultural output but also in job security and community stability, underscoring the interconnectedness of environmental conditions and human welfare (Zhang et al., 2019). Therefore, interdisciplinary efforts combining environmental science with economics and sociology will be essential for addressing the complexity of drought impacts and fostering sustainable development. As drought resilience strategies evolve, they will need to encapsulate both technological advancements and community-centered practices. Engagement with local farmers can enhance the effectiveness of drought mitigation measures, ensuring that solutions are rooted in real-world applicability. Programs aimed at education and the dissemination of best practices can facilitate the adoption of drought-resistant crops and improved irrigation techniques, which in turn can bolster community resilience. Furthermore, investments in infrastructure, such as water harvesting systems and improved logistics for water distribution during droughts, represent vital initiatives to enhance adaptive capacities (Khan et al., 2018). In summary, the multidimensional nature of drought highlights the urgency for both ongoing research and proactive measures. As we stand at the crossroads of climate science and agricultural sustainability, the integration of remote sensing data with ground-level practices remains imperative. Through continuous dialogue between researchers, policymakers, and farming communities, a more integrated and holistic response to drought can be developed, potentially leading to new paradigms in environmental management that prioritize not only economic considerations but also social equity and environmental stewardship. With global temperatures rising and drought events becoming more common, the time to rethink our approach to these natural disasters is now, fostering resilience strategies that respect both ecological limits and community needs.

Subsequently, the development of objective criteria for palaeo-ice stream identification (Stokes and Clark, 1999, 2001), their application to the research of the LIS (see e.g., Clark and Stokes, 2001; De Angelis and Kleman, 2005; Kehew et al., 2005; Ross et al., 2006; Shaw et al., 2006), together with updated LGM ice extents on the continental shelf (England, 1999; Dyke et al., 2003; Dyke, 2004; England et al., 2006; Shaw et al., 2006), has resulted in a rapid increase in the number of ice streams that have been recognised (e.g., 1/210 in Stokes and Clark, 2001; 1/250 in Winsborrow et al., 2004; 1/2120 in Margold et al., 2015a, b). Nevertheless, detailed reconstructions of ice streaming through time have thus far only been carried out for some specific sectors of the LIS, namely the south-western part of the CAA, Foxe Basin, the Hudson Strait region (De Angelis, 2007b; De Angelis and Kleman, 2007; Stokes et al., 2009) and the Atlantic seaboard south of Newfoundland (Shaw et al., 2006). Elsewhere, such as on the southern Interior Plains, ice streams have been studied but their evolution at the regional scale has not yet been fully constrained with the available chronological data (Evans et al., 1999; Evans et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2009; O Cofaigh et al., 2010; Evans et al., 2012, 2014). Furthermore, some regions of the LIS have largely escaped attention from an ice dynamical point of view; namely the central Interior Plains, the north-eastern coast of Labrador, and large parts of the LIS interior on the Canadian Shield (Margold et al., 2015a). The modelling of ice streams in the LIS has also seen some important advances (e.g. Sugden, 1977; MacAyeal, 1993; Marshall et al., 1996; Marshall and Clarke, 1997a; b; Kaplan et al., 2001; Calov et al., 2002; Stokes and Tarasov, 2010; Robel and Tziperman, 2016), but few studies have investigated the behaviour of ice streams throughout deglaciation. In addition to the complexity of the physics involved, a key limitation has been a lack of information on the location and timing of ice streams within the ice sheet that could either be compiled into an empirical reconstruction of ice streaming activity or used to test numerical modelling results (Stokes et al., 2015). Here we build on and extend recent work on LIS ice streams. Margold et al. (2015b) produced an updated inventory of Laurentide ice streams based on a review of the literature and new mapping from across the ice sheet bed (reviewed in Margold et al., 2015a, Fig. 1). Using this inventory and the ice margin chronology of Dyke et al. (2003), Stokes et al. (2016a) recently bracketed the duration of each ice stream and calculated their likely discharge during deglaciation, guided by empirical data from modern ice streams.

Her wild spirit and unyielding resolve continue to inspire generations, inviting us to confront our own narratives amid the colors of life.

Furthermore, the precipitation of lithium carbonate from the raffinate is also a critical step that affects the overall Li recovery efficiency. The conventional method of adding sodium carbonate to the raffinate to precipitate lithium carbonate can lead to the formation of impurities, such as lithium sodium carbonate, which reduces the purity of the final product [19]. Moreover, the precipitation process is often carried out at high temperatures, which can result in the loss of lithium through evaporation [20]. To address these issues, researchers have explored alternative methods, such as the use of organic solvents [21] or ionic liquids [22] to extract lithium from the raffinate, but these approaches are still in their infancy and require further optimization. In addition to the technical challenges, the economic viability of Li recycling from spent LIBs is also a significant concern. The current market price of lithium is relatively low, making it difficult for recycling companies to operate profitably [23]. Moreover, the recycling process itself is energy-intensive, which adds to the overall cost [24]. Therefore, there is a need to develop more efficient and cost-effective recycling technologies that can recover lithium and other valuable metals from spent LIBs. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of closed-loop recycling systems for LIBs, where the recycled materials are reused to manufacture new batteries [25]. This approach not only reduces the demand for primary lithium but also decreases the environmental impacts associated with mining and processing of lithium ores [26]. However, the development of closed-loop recycling systems requires significant advances in recycling technologies, as well as changes in the design and manufacturing of LIBs to facilitate recycling [27]. In conclusion, the recycling of lithium from spent LIBs is a complex and challenging task that requires significant advances in technology, economics, and policy. While there have been some promising developments in recent years, much work remains to be done to achieve the goal of 90% Li recycling from spent LIBs. Further research is needed to develop more efficient and cost-effective recycling technologies, as well as to address the economic and environmental challenges associated with Li recycling. Numerical methods, such as those based on Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations, can be used nowadays to calculate the hydrodynamic performance of a stepped hull with good accuracy. In the last few years, several studies investigated this research field. Garland and Maki [6] conducted a numerical study on a 2D stepped planing surface. Their results showed that the lift-to-frictional-drag ratio varies very little with respect to the step location. Makasyeyev [7] developed a solution method for the 2D mathematical problem of planing of the stepped air cavity hulls. Matveev [8] applied hydrodynamic discrete sources for 2D modeling of stepped planing surfaces, calculating the water surface deformations, wetted hull lengths, and pressure distribution at given hull attitude and Froude number (Fr). Matveev, in another study [9], presented the steady hydrodynamic modeling of semi-planing hulls with pressurized and open air cavities. This method is based on a linearized potential-flow theory for surface flows. Brizzolara and Federici [10] developed an integrated semi-theoretical/numerical (CFD) method for the design of V-shaped stepped planing hulls that presented a considerable resistance reductions with respect to conventional hull forms. Lotfi [11] used an unsteady RANS solver (ANSYS-CFX) based on a Volume of Fluid (VoF) approach for examining the characteristics and performance of a planing hull having one transverse step. Similar research was conducted by Bakhtiari [12]. Moreover, an extended overview of the state of art of the simulations in the air layer drag reduction is reported in Stern et al. [13]. It is clear, nowadays, that CFD is becoming a fundamental support for hydrodynamic investigations in order to perform detailed analysis and to reduce the number of more expensive towing tank tests. EFD however, are always necessary alongside validation of numerical results. In this work, an integrated approach between EFD and CFD tests has been applied with the aim to investigate the quite complex hydrodynamic field generated by the stepped hull. All experimental and numerical tests were performed for a stepped hull in calm water. Several simulations were carried out with different meshing techniques in order to achieve good numerical convergence and to capture the vortical structures observed in towing tank tests. The physics of the hydrodynamic field generated by the stepped hull are quite complex, more than planing craft. For this reason, particular attention has been paid in the unsteady RANS simulations of the resistance tests. Hence, more than one mesh approach has been used for the body motion simulation, such as the overset/chimera grid and morphing mesh technique [14]. In fact, planing/stepped hull performance is very sensitive to hull position (sinkage and trim) [15] as opposed to the displacement hull. For this reason, accurate simulations of the hull motion are necessary. Therefore, non-conventional approaches (i.e.: overset mesh and morphing grid) for the simulation of the hull motion are required, as indicated in [16]. Overset/chimera meshing allows bodies to move freely throughout the computational domain without being artificially constrained by the mesh.

My frustration seems to accumulate like relentless rain clouds, filling to bursting, yet holding back the downpour. It's not just about the money or the crabcakes or the fact that my brother-in-law and his wife live what feels to me like a paradoxical lifestyle. They-masters of the occasional splurge at WholeFoods and connoisseurs of artisan footwear-yet, suddenly, their fiscal daring seems sacrificed at the altar of artistic pursuits and part-time labor. It's baffling to me how they balance or justify their ledger, dipping into luxury while claiming the struggle, though it's more than financial; it's an emotional equation that refuses to balance. In these moments, steeped in what feels like justified vexation, I find myself circling back to the small, silent guy in the background-my husband. The one who maneuvers through the familial minefield with a nonchalance that sometimes borders on the miraculous and sometimes maddening. He bears it all with a shrug, a zen-like demeanor that's both infuriating and admirable. As he defuses my outbursts, like ones over the crabcakes, there's a brief flutter of resentment in my chest. I wish for his unyielding calm, an immunization against the pettier demons that plague my peace. Meanwhile, the therapist's office-the supposed haven of clarity and understanding-feels like it's closing in. The air is thick with my confessions and his probing nods. He asks if maybe, just maybe, I resented my husband's generosity because it made me feel ungenerous by contrast. A question almost maddening in its suggestion but one that lodges in my thoughts as I mull over its uncomfortable possibility. When my brother-in-law's kid comes to our house that weekend, a toddler tornado with sticky fingers and astonishing energy, I watch my husband play the role of doting uncle. I'm struck by a pang of something I can't name, something raw that challenges my earlier frustration. It's not pity for my in-laws or even annoyance anymore, but a grudging admiration for my husband's quiet commitment to family-a value that dissolves the rigid walls my judgment constructs. Still, there remains the unresolved issue of travel. My therapist suggests-though the word "suggest" feels too gentle-an adventure on my own terms. A suggestion that trickles into my consciousness like water finding the smallest crack in a wall. Maybe a solo trip, his voice echoes in my memory, a retreat far enough to face and quell my fears, bringing back stories untamed by the propellers or specter of return. Not to Utah, where the ghosts of insomnia and anxiety linger, but somewhere vibrant yet solitary-a place where the air is untainted by what-ifs, where I craft new endings and beginnings uninterrupted by the ticking clock or familial obligations. The thought hangs in the air, between therapy sessions and family dynamics, brimming with the possibilities of courage and the unwritten chapters of my journey. Suddenly, there's a flicker-a dim light of hope-that the new me who sleeps and flows could be a step closer, a self unmoored and free, adept at both forgiving and embracing the messiness of unplanned detours as parts of the fabric of my life's tapestry.

Endeavors to scale these technologies to directly measure liquid distribution patterns in full-scale industrial column internals have led to the exploration of non-invasive, non-radiation-based technologies. Techniques such as electrical capacitance tomography (ECT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are being investigated for their potential to provide comparable levels of detail without the complications inherent in radiation-based approaches. Early studies suggest that ECT can yield valuable insights into phase distribution with significantly reduced safety risks, albeit with some trade-offs in resolution and accuracy when compared to X-ray tomography. Meanwhile, MRI, traditionally used in medical applications, offers a radiation-free alternative with detailed imaging capabilities, though its adaptation to industrial settings requires overcoming significant technical hurdles such as size constraints and the development of industrial-scale apparatus [17,18]. In tandem with technological advancements, efforts are focused on the development of refined mechanistic and mathematical models that capitalize on the data afforded by these new visualization techniques. Enhanced computational models leveraging the high fidelity data derived from lab-scale experiments hold promise for reliably predicting the hydrodynamics of large-scale systems. These models are pivotal in aiding the design and optimization of structured packing systems, ultimately enhancing the efficacy and efficiency of separation processes like those involved in post-combustion CO2 capture. Another frontier being explored involves the utilization of machine learning and artificial intelligence to process and interpret the vast datasets gleaned from advanced characterization techniques. Pattern recognition algorithms and predictive models trained on experimental data and historical operational data from industrial processes can reveal subtle hydrodynamic behaviors and guide design improvements. This approach not only bolsters the predictive power of simulation tools but also provides a means to optimize operations in real-time, assuring adaptability and resilience to process variations [19,20]. In summary, while radiation-based tomography has significantly advanced our understanding of liquid distribution in structured packings, alternative non-invasive techniques are being developed to overcome their limitations for industrial applications. Combining these emerging technologies with robust computational models and the power of artificial intelligence may ultimately provide a comprehensive solution to the challenges of modern separation process design. The goal remains to achieve an optimal balance between detailed hydrodynamic characterization, practical industrial applicability, and safety considerations. As research progresses, the synergy between innovative technologies and sophisticated computational approaches is likely to drive continuous improvements in the efficiency and sustainability of separation processes, contributing to broader efforts in addressing climate change through effective carbon capture solutions and other industrial applications. Pioneers in the field continue to collaborate across disciplines, pushing the boundaries of what is possible in liquid distribution characterization, aiming for breakthroughs that can seamlessly integrate into the commercial landscape, thereby enriching the realm of industrial process optimization with advanced technological ingenuity.

Ned had many a time asserted, with truth, that although he might go upon the river every day for fifty years, each time his mother would be worried about him until he came home again. A mother's heart is a very anxious heart. Ned and Hal hastened down the street. Ahead of them they could see the river sparkling under the rays of the sun. Ordinarily it was not visible from this distance; but at present, far out of its bed, it was right on a level with the railroad skirting it. "My! She's on a tear, isn't she!" said Hal, enthusiastically. "If ever she gets over the tracks she'll come whooping, my father says," responded Ned. "She's higher than the street, now!" Without question the river was, to use Hal's expression, "on a tear." People along the Mississippi expect, as a matter of course, high water in the spring and early summer. Moderate high water is welcomed. It enables the logging companies to float their stranded logs; it washes clean the banks and the lowlands, carrying away tons of stuff that otherwise might breed illness; it is one of nature's thorough purifiers. But here was a "June rise" with a vengeance. Up in the northern pineries the heavy snows of the past winter were melting all at once beneath long-continued rains. Every stream was a torrent, pouring its swollen tide into the Mississippi. As a consequence of this hearty diet, the old Father of Waters had increased his girth enormously. Never was a prize grunter fattened so rapidly. His bulk began to take up more room than was comfortable for his neighbors. Some persons were forced to flee for their lives; others were prepared to leave their homes at a moment's notice. Whole towns were in danger of being flooded. At Beaufort the sewers were being filled and the water, creeping through them, flowed out far inland. Cellars were being invaded; and seeping up, the crafty flood inundated great tracts of street and yard in the lower-lying resident portions of the town. When, after school on the previous afternoon, Ned had gone down to look at the river, there had been hardly any water inside the tracks at the foot of Maple Street. But this morning the boys found quite a pond had gathered during the night. In places the board walks on either hand were afloat, and children were running back and forth over them, shouting with delight as the water spurted up between the cracks. "She's soaking through," commented Hal. Ned nodded, and saying, "Come on," deliberately continued on the route, over the wavy, unsteady walk. Hal followed. Both boys disdained to hurry their pace one bit, even to avoid wet feet. They deemed that a show of dignity was necessary, to impress the scampering, screaming youngsters who were spectators.

With regard to imaging studies there are two types of radiographs that should be ordered in order to make a diagnosis of hip osteonecrosis. These are anteroposterior pelvis views and frog leg lateral views. Early on these radiographs show no changes in bone density. But later they will show subchondral sclerosis and collapse of the articular surface. Bone scans are useful early on because they show increased uptake in the affected area. But they cannot differentiate between active ischemia and revascularization. Mri is the gold standard for diagnosing hip osteonecrosis and can detect the presence of osteonecrosis in its earliest stages. It can show areas of decreased signal intensity in the femoral head due to fat accumulation in the marrow space. And it can also show areas of increased signal intensity in the femoral head due to edema in the marrow space. However, MRI findings do not correlate well with clinical outcome. CT scans can show the extent of the lesion in the femoral head. And can show changes in the trabecular architecture. But it is not as sensitive as MRI for detecting the presence of osteonecrosis. Ultrasound is sometimes used to diagnose hip osteonecrosis, but it is not as accurate as MRI. The treatment of hip osteonecrosis depends on several factors including the size and location of the lesion, the stage of the disease, the age of the patient, and the activity level of the patient. Nonoperative treatment options include core decompression, which involves drilling a hole through the necrotic region of the femoral head to relieve pressure and increase blood flow to the area. Joint preserving procedures such as osteotomy and resurfacing are also nonoperative treatments. They involve realigning the joint or resurfacing the femoral head respectively. Total hip replacement is considered a last resort when all other treatments fail.
