Two natty officers stepped to the prow of a Russian gunboat, that was white and trim as a bride, and fixed their glasses keenly on the caique. "Curse you!" growled the captain, involuntarily opening his hand, the Greek sign of an imprecation. "St. Nicholas strike you blind! Look all you will, and again I'll cheat you." But the time had come to tack, and he shouted the order to the sailors. The convenient canvas was shifted, the helm was put over, and the caique bore straight for the narrow mouth of the harbor. A great sail was thrown out on either side like a pair of wings. The vessel turned its beak to the south and swooped down the wind like a hawk. The three young men stood with their feet apart now, their legs of equal length. "By Jove, that's glorious!" shouted one of them, his accent betraying the American - probably the Bostonian. The sun stood on the tiptop of Salamis, saying good-night to the world. Athens was a pillar of purple dust, shot through and through with lances of flame. The stately columns of the Parthenon were of liquid amber. The church on the summit of Mount Lycabettus caught fire and blazed. The mountain itself was hidden in a column of dust and the church floated in mid-air. Then suddenly, as if by a stroke of some grand, celestial magic, the glow died from everything as the blood fades from a frightened face. The Parthenon was a pale, stately white, the ghost of the temple of a moment ago; the church on the hill had turned gray - ashes in place of fire. The sun had dropped behind Salamis. But now came a greater wonder: Hymettus and all the hills that surround the lovely plain of Attica took on a deep, quivering, unearthly tint of violet. This light was delicate, fluffy, spiritual. You fancied it was fragrant; you imagined that all the fresh spring violets of a hundred worlds had been plucked and poured sea deep over the hills. A sudden lurch of the ship threw the American against the man at his side. "I beg your pardon," he said, "or perhaps you do not speak English?" "O, yes," replied the person addressed; "not perfectly, but sufficiently to make myself understood. Permit me to introduce myself." Producing a large leathern pocketbook, he extracted from its recesses a card. The hand that presented the bit of pasteboard was large, pink and well groomed. The American read: Peter Lindbohm, Lieutenant de Cavalerie. Lieutenant Lindbohm read on the card which he received in return, Mr. John Curtis. "I am happy to meet you, Mr. Curtis," said the Lieutenant, politely lifting his straw hat and then drawing it down over his ears with both hands. The hat was secured to the button-hole by means of a shoe string, and had a startling habit of leaping to the end of its tether every few moments.

Typically for Murthy, he had a dream and no money.

Seeing an opportunity to make more money, Riggs challenged both Court and King, claiming that even in middle age - he was 55 - he could beat the top women players. King ignored him at first, but Court took up the challenge and played him in a match in California on May 13, 1973. King had realized the significance of the occasion and had done her best to encourage the Australian to take it seriously. "I said, 'Margaret it's not a tennis match, it's about social change, it's about social justice, it's about all the things we're working for,' and she goes, 'I don't'. She wasn't politically orientated! Riggs match. "So Margaret played him Mother's Day in 1973 and lost (6-1 6-2). it's called the Mother's Day massacre and I just thought, 'Oh no!' " King needed no second bidding, and the famous "Battle of the Sexes" match came to fruition on September 20 in the Houston Astrodome. "I thought it would set us back 50 years if I didn't win that match," said King. "It would ruin the women's tour and affect the self esteem of all women." The entrances - King on a gold litter in the style of Cleopatra, Riggs on a rickshaw pulled by women models in skimpy outfits - added to the theater. Once the match started, King, at 29 and the peak of her powers, made her opponent eat his earlier words and boasts. With a winner-take-all $100,000 check riding on the outcome, Riggs lost his nerve and was beaten 6-4 6-3 6-3. Iconic moment. "The drop shot and volley heard around the world," said Britain's Times newspaper as an estimated global TV audience of 50 million watched the rout. King and Riggs embraced at the end, and became friends off the court until his death in 1995 of prostate cancer. Prior to the WTA's formation, King had realized the significance of legislation passed through the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives and signed into law by President Richard Nixon in June 1972. Title IX made it a requirement under law for male and female students to be afforded equal federal funding in their high school and college studies. "Before that, young women were not getting anything, there was gender quotas - like 5% in the medical school at Harvard - there were really terrible gender quotas and also women could not get an athletic scholarship in the States," said King. "Now because of Title IX, women from all over the world can go to our American colleges on a scholarship and get grants. It's very powerful because it's about equality in education and activities, and sports comes under activities." Quantum leap. According to 18-time grand slam singles winner Navratilova, King took advantage of the mood of the moment to push through changes which were ahead of their time.

But how often do we truly understand the deep connection between love and prayer? Much like a seed planted in the fertile soil of faith, prayer allows love to grow and manifest in myriad ways. It is not merely about asking for blessings or material needs but about cultivating a relationship with the divine. Prayer is an expression of the soul's deepest yearnings-a heartfelt conversation with God. Without this communication, much like an unfed flame, love can dwindle. Reflecting upon the analogy of my college days, I realize that just as education required active engagement and respect to truly transform my understanding, so does spirituality. Without the effort of prayer, our spiritual lives risk becoming stagnant; blessings, like the unappreciated sessionals of my past, could be received without reverence or gratitude. Just as the mentor's guidance transformed my approach to studies, prayer transforms our spirit, aligning our desires with divine will and elevating our understanding beyond the mundane. Through prayer, we express humility, acknowledging that despite our efforts and strengths, there is always a higher power guiding us. This humility does not diminish our capabilities; rather, it enriches them, showing us the paths we might never have considered, just as my studies found new depth and direction under the guidance of an inspiring teacher. Each prayer, be it a whisper of sorrow or a shout of joy, connects us deeper to love-to Jesus-and through him, to a boundless reservoir of grace and compassion. Moreover, prayer is not limited to supplication. It's an invitation to pause, reflect, and listen. In the cacophony of daily life, how often do we silence our minds to truly hear-to understand what is being whispered from the eternal? Just as reading with respect opened new worlds within textbooks, listening with attentiveness during prayer helps us to discern the gentle nudges, the divine counsel we might otherwise overlook. In those days, the court was a microcosm of Europe's grand stage, a sphere where diplomacy wove complex tapestries and whispers of intrigue navigated shadowy corners. Tutored by my associations and influences, I grew in understanding, wielding the subtle art of conversation with as much dexterity as I would handle a blade. Mary, too, was a student of the court's nuanced choreography. Though young, she was astute, with a perceptive grasp of politics that belied her years. At twenty-six, the games of state intensified. Mary, adorned with her own vision of the world, turned her gaze toward Scotland, the land of her birthright. I found myself torn, an unwilling traveler between the familiar climes of France and the looming prospect of a perilous journey north. And in the midst of impending strife stood our queen, her eyes alight with determination and dreams of unifying a divided land. My role beside Mary demanded vigilance and counsel. It required every ounce of my training, for Scotland's courts harbored dangers unknown even to France. The whispers of suspicion, the unyielding stares of the lairds, and the summons of dark ambition curled pernicious fingers around the corridors of power, threatening the vision Mary sought to embody. Thus, amid the mists and murmurings, my resolve crystallized. The virtues I had known-the loyalty and love encoded into my very being-mounted like a bulwark against doubt. Methods that rely on terrain analysis include network approaches, like the application of graph theory on sediment cascades in alpine catchments (Heckmann and Schwanghart, 2013), the network definitions by Czuba and Foufoula-Georgiou (2014) and Phillips et al. (2011) and the measurements by Masselink et al. (2016). Many topographic indexes describing hydrological and sediment connectivity are based on the wetness index by Beven and Kirkby (1979). Examples include the rainfall-runoff-phosphorus model by Lazzarotto et al. (2006) and the Network Index as defined by Lane et al. (2004) and as applied for the identification of sediment source areas by Reid et al., 2007, Reaney et al., 2011 and Shore et al., 2013. Borselli et al., 2008 propose a spatial index that combines a characterisation of the contributing area of a location with that of the flow path down to a sink. Vigiak et al. (2012) showed that this Index of Connectivity (IC) is a scale independent terrain index that improved the estimation of specific sediment yields for a large catchment (3300 km2) in Australia. Ortiz-Rodriguez et al. (2017) carried out a connectivity analysis in an actively evolving volcanic landscape to map sediment source areas. Wohl et al. (2017) use reach gradient as an input for connectivity classification in the analysis of a stream network. An example of the successful integration of a spatially distributed connectivity index in a sediment delivery model is given by Hamel et al. (2017). In contrast to these findings, Grauso et al. (2018) report that a connectivity index was less suitable than other terrain metrics to estimate specific sediment yields. In this study the hypothesis is tested that IC can be scaled and used as a multiplier to derive specific sediment yields from soil erosion risk rates at point or field level. Jamshidi et al., 2014, Vigiak et al., 2016 assumed a sigmoid function to characterise the relationship between IC values and the sediment delivery ratios of sub-catchments in an Australian river basin. The specific sediment yield of an area in a catchment will, besides depending on topography and weather conditions, be a function of vegetative cover. Vigiak et al. (ibid.) used a crop factor to calculate connectivity as a function of land use. Foerster et al. (2014) derived time-variable IC factors for two upland catchments in the Pyrenees, dominated by natural vegetation and meadows. No other studies were found where vegetation-variable connectivity was differentiated over time. When connectivity is defined as a function of vegetative cover, it can be expected to show a seasonal trend, especially so in catchments dominated by agriculture. Understanding of the temporal aspect of sediment yields is therefore of great relevance for the identification of CSAs, but also for the ex-ante evaluation of soil conservation measures like reduced tillage.

Recent research into the neural underpinnings of interoceptive processes has further underscored the role of the insula and its connectivity with other brain regions. This intriguing development invites a closer examination of how these circuits may deviate in autism, potentially illuminating the complexities of interoceptive dysfunction in this condition. The role of the anterior insula, for instance, in integrating sensory and cognitive-affective information, has been robustly implicated (Uddin, Nomi, Hebert-Seropian, Ghaziri, & Boucher, 2017). Its hypo-activation in autism adds a compelling layer to our understanding of the neurobiology underlying this multifaceted disorder. Moreover, investigations examining functional connectivity highlight potential disruptions in the salience network, which includes the insula and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) (Menon, 2011). This network is critical for detecting and filtering salient stimuli and might explain the atypical sensory behaviors observed in autism. Given the intricate relationship between interoceptive processing and the salience network, it becomes clear that disruptions in this network may contribute to the disparities in interoceptive accuracy and awareness in autism. Observations of diminished connectivity between the insula and the ACC in autistic individuals suggest deficits in effectively integrating interoceptive information with emotional and cognitive processes (Di Martino et al., 2009). These neural discrepancies cascade into behavioral outcomes, manifesting in altered emotion recognition and empathy, hallmark challenges in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The connection between interoceptive processing and empathetic capacity is particularly evocative. Recent studies propose that interoceptive accuracy mediates the relationship between emotional awareness and empathy, thereby highlighting its role as a fundamental process underpinning effective social interaction (Fukushima et al., 2011). Therefore, examining interoceptive processes could provide crucial insights into interventions aimed at enhancing empathetic skills in individuals with ASD. Furthermore, the developmental trajectory of interoceptive faculties in autism deserves attention, particularly the dichotomous findings regarding interoceptive accuracy in children. The atypical growth patterns suggest that age-related changes in interoceptive processing, coupled with cognitive development variances, might uniquely shape sensory perception in autistic children (Mash et al., 2017). This underscores the importance of longitudinal studies to unravel how early interoceptive experiences might shape later social and emotional competencies. Interoception's relevance extends beyond social cognition, with implications for emotion regulation and mental health-a domain where autistic individuals often face challenges. The anxiety and stress prevalent in ASD might reflect, at least in part, an interoceptive processing imbalance, exacerbating their emotional dysregulation. The intricate ballet between body and brain in processing physiological signals can fuel or quell the emotional storms experienced by those on the spectrum. In sum, integrating interoceptive science with autism research broadens our understanding of the sensory and emotional facets of ASD. Future research directions should hone in on the interplay between neural circuitry, interoceptive perception, and behavioral outcomes, potentially guiding new therapeutic avenues. By elucidating how interoceptive dysfunction interacts with broader cognitive and emotional processes, researchers can better address the layered complexities of autism, paving the way for more nuanced, effective interventions tailored to individual sensory profiles. As we untangle the threads of interoception and autism, a clearer picture of these intertwined systems continues to emerge, holding promise for transformative impacts on autism care and support.

The study of GM alterations in overweight youth has largely been limited to group comparisons of GM volume, with few studies examining CT. In the cortex, increased childhood BMI percentile has been related to GMV reductions in frontal and limbic regions (Alosco et al., 2014). Similar results were reported in obese adolescents, where pathological eating behaviour correlated with reduced orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) volume (Maayan et al., 2011). Overweight adolescents with (Yau et al., 2012) and without (Moreno-Lopez et al., 2012) metabolic syndrome have shown reduced hippocampal volume relative to controls. However, examinations of CT have reported diffuse increases in thickness amongst adolescents with an elevated visceral fat ratio (Saute et al., 2016). Furthermore, a large, longitudinal study reported no impact of body mass on CT in typically developing children (Sharkey et al., 2015). Studies of GM variation in adult overweight and obesity, while more numerous, have produced similarly inconsistent findings (e.g., Willette and Kapogiannis, 2015). Elevated BMI (Ho et al., 2010; Raji et al., 2010) and obesity (Gunstad et al., 2009; Yokum et al., 2012) have been associated with reduced total GMV; however, body mass has been consistently unrelated to global mean CT. Local GMV reductions have been observed in the OFC and the anterior cingulate cortex with increasing BMI (Raji et al., 2010), and decreased posterior parietal and temporal volumes have been reported in overweight adults (Gunstad et al., 2009; Walther et al., 2009). Meta-analytic findings have related obesity measures (e.g., BMI, waist circumference) to reduced GMV in the medial prefrontal cortex, bilateral cerebellum and left temporal pole (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2019). Studies examining local CT have primarily shown BMI-related reductions in left inferior parietal cortex, inferior temporal and insular cortex (Hassenstab et al., 2012; Veit et al., 2014), and prefrontal cortex, including ventromedial (Medic et al., 2016), superior frontal and orbitofrontal (Marques-Iturria et al., 2013) thickness. Although the structural correlates of neurocognitive phenotypes in obesity remain poorly characterised, reduced thickness in the superior frontal gyrus has been related to poorer performance on an inhibitory control task and higher BMI (Lavagnino et al., 2016). Taken together, despite emerging evidence of GM reductions with increasing body mass, the association between adiposity and age-related CT alterations has not been directly examined. We therefore aimed to quantify associations between CT, age and adiposity in otherwise healthy adolescent and adult cohorts. We predicted that age-related CT reductions would be increased, both globally and locally, in those with greater adiposity, with local effects found in the frontal lobes of the adolescent group and in bilateral temporal, parietal and ventral frontal lobe regions in adults. In another analysis, we examined the functional correlates of adiposity-related alterations by assessing whether adiposity and delay discounting, taken as a measure of impulsivity, related to CT of the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), a brain region strongly linked to impulse control (Aron et al., 2014).

The advancements in anode and cathode materials have led to significant improvements in the performance of BESs, enabling them to efficiently treat a wide range of wastewater types and produce valuable products. For instance, researchers have developed novel anode materials with enhanced electron transfer capabilities, such as graphene-based materials and nanostructured electrodes, which have shown improved power output and stability [39-41]. Additionally, the development of advanced cathode materials, such as platinum-free catalysts and air-breathing cathodes, has enabled the production of high-quality electricity and valuable products [42-44]. The integration of BESs with other technologies has also been explored to further enhance their performance and scalability. For example, the combination of BESs with membrane bioreactors (MBRs) has been shown to be effective in treating complex wastewater streams and producing high-quality effluent [45-47]. Similarly, the integration of BESs with solar power systems has been investigated as a means of harnessing renewable energy and reducing the carbon footprint of wastewater treatment [48-50]. Despite the progress made in BES technology, there are still several challenges that need to be addressed before they can be widely adopted. For instance, the scaling up of BESs to large-scale commercial applications remains a significant challenge, as it requires the development of cost-effective and efficient materials and systems [51-53]. Additionally, the optimization of BESs for specific wastewater streams and applications is still an area of ongoing research, as the performance of BESs can be highly dependent on the type and concentration of pollutants present in the wastewater [54-56]. In conclusion, BESs have shown great promise as a sustainable and efficient technology for wastewater treatment and energy production. While there are still challenges to be addressed, the advancements made in anode and cathode materials, as well as the integration of BESs with other technologies, have the potential to overcome these challenges and enable the widespread adoption of BESs. As the demand for sustainable and renewable energy solutions continues to grow, BESs are likely to play an increasingly important role in the quest for a more sustainable future.

Despite the difference between spontaneous alternations in bistable perception and updating based on actual, albeit subtle, changes - a similar mechanism may be involved. In both cases the transition from the old to the new interpretation is determined internally by the participant rather than being determined by events in the environment. A second way to explain our prior results is via perceptual uncertainty: While all picture sets were based on the prerequisite that they were perceived categorically in our normative study (Stottinger et al., 2016), we cannot fully rule out that decisions were accompanied by a certain degree of perceptual uncertainty. This would fit with research showing that a network including the anterior insula is engaged when belief updating is based on relative uncertainty in a gradually changing, noisy, uncertain, or perceptually degraded environment (Ploran et al., 2007; Heekeren et al., 2008 for review). Similarly, activation in the insula is modulated by the ambiguity of sensory information (Lamichhane et al., 2016; Sterzer and Kleinschmidt, 2010 for a review). A third potential explanation of our results would suggest that activations reflected a more general network always active whenever we update mental representations. This is in line with research on surprise-based updating which assigns a central role to the anterior insula and ACC. When observations in our environment saliently deviate from expectations, the right anterior insula initiates attentional control by activating the central executive network and deactivating the default mode network. As a consequence, cognitive resources are assigned to facilitate processing of the surprising, salient stimulus. The co-activation with the ACC allows rapid access to the motor system (Craig, 2009; Menon and Uddin, 2010; Uddin, 2015 for a review). The network found in our study might therefore be best understood more generally as a network for updating mental representations, signaled either by bottom-up salience, or internal signals. The aim of this research was to evaluate each of these three explanations. That is, which brain areas are active regardless of the mechanism involved (proactive decision vs. perceptual uncertainty) and which brain areas are specific to each process. We presented participants with three different conditions: (1) gradual-naive condition: In 10 separate sets pictures morphed gradually from one object to a second - replicating our initial study (Stottinger et al., 2015). (2) A gradual-repeat condition: where all gradually morphing sets were presented twice thus diminishing perceptual uncertainty. For both series continuous changes result in the proactive decision to update a perceptual model due to the gradual accumulation of evidence. In the gradual-naive condition the decision is accompanied by a greater degree of uncertainty, given the participant does not know what the second object will be. This uncertainty is reduced when the participant is exposed to this same set a second time (the gradual-repeat condition).

He also questioned whether the election should be held now, given the current violence in eastern Ukraine. According to Russian state media, Deputy Foreign Minister Alexei Meshkov said Friday that Russia would decide whether or not to recognize the Ukraine vote only after it takes place. "Let's wait for the elections first. Naturally, when Russia considers this issue (on legitimacy) we will take into account all factors," the official ITAR-Tass news agency quoted Meshkov as saying. The latest violence extended increased unrest in recent weeks in eastern Ukraine, which includes areas with ethnic Russian populations loyal to Moscow instead of the Ukrainian government in Kiev. After the Russian takeover of Crimea, Putin massed an estimated 40,000 or more Russian troops near the border with eastern Ukraine. This week, he said those forces were starting to withdraw, as called for by Obama and NATO allies. On Friday, Pentagon spokesman Rear Adm. John Kirby said the United States has seen small numbers of Russian troops withdrawing back to their garrisons or home bases from the border region. Kirby described those numbers as "not great" and said tens of thousands of Russian troops remained near the border. According to Kirby, it was "too soon for us to say this is the wholesale withdrawal" of troops that Putin indicated he had ordered. Donetsk violence. Four of the pro-Ukrainian militia fighters got trapped in a cafe and were presumed by pro-Ukrainian militias to be dead or captured, he said. As the Academy of Plato continued to flourish, a young student named Aristotle (384-322 BC) emerged as a brilliant and inquisitive thinker. Aristotle was deeply influenced by Plato's ideas, but he also had significant reservations about the notion of a world of forms. He believed that Plato's concept was too abstract and did not provide a sufficient explanation for the natural world. Aristotle sought to develop a more empirical and observation-based approach to understanding the world. Aristotle's philosophical system was based on the concept of hylomorphism, which posits that reality consists of matter (hyle) and form (morphe). He believed that the world is composed of individual substances, each with its own unique form, which is the essence or nature of that substance. For example, the form of a human being is what makes it a human being, and the form of a chair is what makes it a chair. Aristotle's concept of causality was also crucial to his philosophical system. He identified four causes or explanations for why things exist: material, formal, efficient, and final. The material cause is the substance or matter that something is made of, the formal cause is the form or essence of the thing, the efficient cause is the agent that brings the thing into being, and the final cause is the purpose or end for which the thing exists. Aristotle's philosophy had a profound impact on the development of Western thought, and his ideas continued to influence scientists and philosophers for centuries. His emphasis on observation, experimentation, and empirical evidence laid the foundation for the scientific method, and his concept of causality remains a fundamental aspect of scientific inquiry. In the realm of biology, Aristotle's work on the natural world and the classification of living organisms was particularly influential. He recognized that living things share certain characteristics, such as growth, reproduction, and nutrition, and he developed a system of classification based on these characteristics. His work in this area laid the groundwork for the development of modern taxonomy and the classification of living organisms. Aristotle's philosophical system also had a significant impact on the development of ethics and politics. He believed that humans have a natural tendency towards social organization and that the state is a natural consequence of human nature. He argued that the state is a necessary institution for the protection of individuals and the promotion of the common good. In conclusion, Aristotle's philosophical system was a significant development in the history of Western thought. His emphasis on observation, experimentation, and empirical evidence laid the foundation for the scientific method, and his concept of causality remains a fundamental aspect of scientific inquiry. His work in biology, ethics, and politics also had a profound impact on the development of Western thought, and his ideas continue to influence philosophers and scientists to this day.

The 10-20 procedure (or extension thereof) can also be applied to computer models of the scalp to determine electrode positions on a volume conduction model of the head (Jurcak et al., 2007), but this does not take the limited accuracy of the anatomical landmarks into account: especially the inion is not always easy to identify in an anatomical MRI. Another problem in the (extended) 10-20 electrode placement procedure is that many researchers use caps from a flexible fabric with electrodes mounted at fixed locations, where the cap manufacturer has placed the electrodes approximately at the locations of the 10-20 system. Although these caps exist for different head circumferences (usually in steps of 2 cm, i.e. 54, 56, 58, and 60 cm) and have some flexibility, the expected average difference between a subject's head circumference and the best fitting cap is still 0.5 cm. Furthermore, caps are designed and manufactured to fit a typical head, whereas individuals' head shapes differ. Consequently, when EEG caps are used to position electrodes on the scalp of an individual, the position of the electrodes can deviate from the ideal position according to the 10-20 system. As the practical application of the 10-20 procedure using a measuring tape has limited accuracy, researchers have been developing and implementing different solutions for more accurate placement of the electrodes. For example, in 1981 Ary et al. (1981) used a Plexiglas helmet to capture the conformation of the head. To create this helmet, they placed a swimming cap on the subject and pushed a bowl of fast setting gel around the head while the subject's head was upside down. After some further processing, this resulted in a hard Plexiglas helmet that fits the subject's head. As the last step, they used a rotating protractor device to draw contours on the helmet that were used to reproducibly locate electrode positions on the helmet. A method using more recent technology is described by Song et al. (2018), who demonstrate how augmented reality can be used to improve placement and replacement of EEG electrodes. Although the consistent placement of electrodes over subjects is relevant for group studies and meta-analysis of scalp-level EEG results, the holy grail of EEG consists of source reconstruction and interpreting results at the level of the cortical activity. For this, it is not a necessity to have electrodes placed according to some pre-specified scheme, only that electrode positions are correctly modeled. Hence, rather than placing the electrodes on the scalp as accurately as possible according to the 10-20 scheme, researchers have developed methods to measure the actual position of the electrodes after placement. In 1991 De Munck et al. (1991) described the use of a caliper to manually measure the relative distances between the electrodes and to use these distances to fit electrode positions to a spherical model.

The guilt was eating away at me, just like the hunger that seemed to never subside. I tried to distract myself with video games, but even the virtual worlds couldn't escape the thoughts of Tara's escape. I'd pause the game, staring blankly at the screen, wondering what I could've done differently. The what-ifs haunted me: what if I had put the tag on her the night before? What if I had checked on her earlier that morning? What if I had been a better owner? The peanut butter jar seemed to be calling my name, a constant reminder of my failures. I'd open it, scoop out a spoonful, and devour it in one swift motion. The creamy texture and nutty flavor were a temporary escape, but the guilt would always come flooding back. I started to avoid my friends and family, not wanting to face their questions about Tara. I didn't want to relive the pain and guilt of losing her again. Additionally, the concentration of HA varies from 65 to 400 mu g/mL in adult human, 50-570 mu g/mL in bovine vitreous and 160 mu g/mL in porcine vitreous Reardon et al. (1998). This large variation could be related to the heterogeneous distribution of vitreous components throughout the bulk hydrogel (Balazs et al., 1959), as well as age-related changes in its composition (Denlinger et al., 1980). Furthermore, it has been reported that the micro-rheology of the bovine vitreous humour undergoes a length scale dependent transition; changing from a viscous liquid state to an elastic solid profile (Xu et al., 2013). Overall, this gelatinous structure does not have a homogenous density and appears denser adjacent to the vitreous cortex and more at the ora serrata (Green and Sebag, 2006). The network of collagen fibrils has been recognised to serve the load-bearing function because the vitreous does not collapse during enzymatic removal of hyaluronan but dissolves completely after digestion with collagenase, converting the vitreous into a viscous liquid (Bishop, 2000; Pirie et al., 1948). Previously, it has been shown that in human vitreous, collagen fibrils are presented in loose and roughly parallel bundles with a considerable gap from their adjacent bundles and with some at right angles to the others (Fig. 1). Such pattern of parallel collagen fibrils tied together by proteoglycan bridges is similar to the pattern seen in cornea where parallel collagen fibrils are also bridged by proteoglycans (Scott, 1992). In addition, it was suggested that swollen and charged polysaccharide chains of hyaluronan simply hydrate the vitreous network and help to prevent aggregation by filling the space between the fibrils (Nickerson et al., 2008). Another important characteristic of the CGN is its porous structure which changes throughout the eye with a change in the CGN density. For instance, in the central vitreous with a low CGN density, pore size can vary from 500 nm to over 1 1/2m (Xu et al., 2013). Such properties of the vitreous are essential to provide structural support for the growth of the eye, to maintain a clear path to the retina, and to support the various ocular tissues during physical activity (Sebag and Balazs, 1989). To date, a significant amount of work has been dedicated to the study of the anatomical and physiological structure of the vitreous. Amongst which, there have been few studies that have investigated diffusion through the vitreous humours, typically using ex vivo animal vitreous. For instance, Kasdorf et al. (2015) have studied FITC-dextran and peptide penetration into the ovine vitreous humour. Ohtori and Tojo measured the diffusion coefficient of dexamethasone sodium m-sulfobenzoate in rabbit vitreous by designing a glass ring diffusion apparatus (Ohtori and Tojo, 1994). A study by Gisladottir et al. (2009) used a diffusion cell with a middle chamber to study diffusion of dexamethasone through saline solution with different concentrations of hyaluronan as well as porcine vitreous humour.

"Let go of that bridle!" Ben exclaimed, his voice rising with a mix of frustration and sarcastic bravado. He leaned forward, as if to lean his weight against the horse, whose eyes darted nervously, sensing the rising tension. John, however, stood resolute, his grip tightening. "You can't just take what doesn't belong to you, Ben. Not without a fight," he declared, his tone taking on a determined edge that belied his relatively smaller stature. The sun began to dip low on the horizon, casting long shadows across the grassy knoll where they stood. A breeze picked up, rustling the leaves above and echoing the turmoil of the moment. It felt as though the entire world was holding its breath, waiting to see what would happen next. "Fight? Is that what you want? Because I see nothing but cowardice in your eyes." Ben's lips curled into a smirk, his confidence shining through his earlier frustration. He seemed to relish the opportunity to goad John, while the horse whinnied in protest, its muscles taut beneath the leather saddle. "You're all talk and no action, Brayton," John shot back, his heart pounding not just from anger, but from a swiftly kindling sense of defiance. "You've been handed everything, riding on the coattails of your mother's marriage to my father. Do you even know what it feels like to earn something for yourself?" Ben's face fell momentarily-anger flashed in his chocolate-brown eyes, a reflection of the sibling rivalry that had been ignited since the day the papers had been signed and the family arrangements had changed. "Earning? What, like you think your dad's legacy is somehow yours by right? Newsflash, John: it ain't! My mother's here now, and she's the one who keeps a roof over your head." With a swift motion, John yanked the bridle again, pulling it toward him, causing Ben to lose his balance slightly. "Maybe it's time for you to learn that just because they married, it doesn't make you the rightful owner of everything in this house. And as for that horse, I'll be damned if I let you prance around on it like a king on his throne." The horse shifted nervously, sensing the rising tempers of its riders. It stomped a hoof, but the boys were too engrossed in their quarrel to pay much heed. A precious moment slipped by, and John felt a wave of determination wash over him. "I challenge you, Ben. A race. If you win, you keep the horse; if I win, it's mine." Ben's smirk returned, as bright as ever. "You think you can outrun me? That's rich! But sure, I'll take you up on that. It'll be the easiest race of my life." "So, we race to the old sycamore and back. Winner takes the horse," John declared, releasing his hold on the bridle, allowing Ben to regain his position. "Agreed," Ben shot back, his voice showing no signs of wavering. They exchanged a tense glance, the air thickening with unspoken truths and masked emotions, before both boys turned, striding away to prepare for the race that could change everything. As they approached the starting line, a soft rustle whispered through the tall grass, and the distant sound of a bird took flight, cutting through the tension like a knife. The world around them faded into the backdrop, leaving only their rivalry and the fate of a horse hanging in precarious balance.

The results of surveys of attitudes and perceptions have indicated the implications for local communities that live adjacent to protected areas, and which factors influenced their attitudes towards protection and support for such protection. Such knowledge is important to ensure that efficient protection policy measures are taken (Kaltenborn et al., 2006), such that both protection goals and local demands for ecosystem services are fulfilled (Hartter et al., 2012). In recent years, there has been an increase in the number of studies of perceptions and attitudes among local communities living adjacent to protected areas in developing countries. Some studies have dealt specifically with local people's perceptions of forest conditions, ecosystem services and protected areas (e.g., Adhikari et al., 2014; Amin et al., 2015; Dolisca et al., 2007; Ezebilo and Mattsson, 2010; MacKenzie et al., 2017; Min et al., 2018; Muhamad et al., 2014; Paudyal et al., 2018; Permadi et al., 2018; Shahbaz et al., 2011; Stickler et al., 2017; Sullivan et al., 2017; Vodouhe et al., 2010; Yaoitcha et al., 2015), while others have examined local communities' attitudes towards conservation and management of protected areas (e.g., Allendorf, 2007; Allendorf et al., 2006; Badola et al., 2012; Chuang and Yen, 2017; Dewu and Roskaft, 2018; Grilli et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2014; Infield and Namara, 2001; Kaeser and Willcox, 2018; Kideghesho et al., 2007; Rahman et al., 2017; Tomicevic et al., 2010). Some researchers have analyzed the interests, influence and power of different actors involved in the management of protected areas and community forestry (e.g., Nurrochmat et al., 2017; Schusser et al., 2015), and have reported that the perceptions and attitudes of local communities toward conservation issues and protected areas are strongly influenced by their "intrinsic" or true interests, although they are often hidden (Nurrochmat et al., 2017). By contrast, few studies have assessed local communities' perceptions and attitudes towards conservation issues and protected areas (e.g., Htun et al., 2012; Hussain et al., 2016; Nurrochmat et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2006). These include a number of studies conducted specifically to examine local communities' perceptions and attitudes towards conservation and protection issues in Ethiopia (Bessie et al., 2014; Birhane et al., 2017; Mekuria, 2013; Moges and Taye, 2017; Tadesse and Teketay, 2017; Tesfaye et al., 2012; Tessema et al., 2010). The diversity of factors determining local communities' perceptions of protected areas and their attitudes towards such areas has made it necessary to develop a theoretical framework. Only few of the studies of local perceptions of and attitudes towards protected areas are based on or concerned with theory (Chuang and Yen, 2017; Kaeser and Willcox, 2018; Nurrochmat et al., 2017; Tesfaye et al., 2012). The use of social exchange theory (Turner and Turner, 1978) in the present paper is an attempt to address the shortcoming by providing a theoretical orientation. Homans (1958) developed social exchange theory to understand human behavior and explain human interactions.

Evidenced by their elevated three-dimensional shape, coral mounds reveal higher average aggradation/sedimentation rates compared to the adjacent sea floor, even though their temporal development is often discontinuous and marked by unconformities (e.g., Eisele et al., 2008; Matos et al., 2017; Raddatz et al., 2014; Ruggeberg et al., 2007; Thierens et al., 2010; Victorero et al., 2016; Wienberg et al., 2018). Nevertheless, coral mounds represent unique sedimentary archives as they particularly aggrade under high energetic conditions, and hence, preserve sedimentary successions, which are often lacking in the surrounding area where non-deposition or erosion prevail (Thierens et al., 2013; Titschack et al., 2009). The current knowledge about coral mounds largely originates from examples that have today an elevated and exposed position at the seabed surface. However, coral mounds also occur as buried structures beneath the seafloor. Due to their highly heterogeneous composition (coral skeletons, other shells, fine hemipelagic sediments), the internal structure of coral mounds appears acoustically transparent and can be detected by seismic mapping (e.g., Huvenne et al., 2003). Such "buried mounds" have so far been discovered along the Irish, Moroccan and Mauritanian margins and in the Mediterranean Sea (Colman et al., 2005; Foubert et al., 2008; Huvenne et al., 2007; Lo Iacono et al., 2014), where they root either on one single horizon (Henriet et al., 1998; Huvenne et al., 2007) or originated from multiple horizons (Vandorpe et al., 2017; Lo Iacono et al., 2014). Mound deposits comprise a substantial content of carbonate that is mainly produced by the cold-water corals and to a minor degree by their associated fauna. This carbonate (defined as "mound-derived carbonate" according to Titschack et al., 2015) can contribute up to 50 wt% to the total mound sediments (Dorschel et al., 2007a; Ruggeberg et al., 2007; Titschack et al., 2009). A first study by Lindberg and Mienert (2005) pointed out that the amount of carbonate deposited within coral mounds might play a significant role in global carbonate budgets. However, these potentially important carbonate factories are still largely neglected in any calculations (for an example see Smith and Mackenzie, 2016). This is partly ascribed to the low number of existing and locally restricted studies estimating carbonate accumulation rates for individual coral mounds (along the Irish margin; Dorschel et al., 2007a; Ruggeberg et al., 2007; Titschack et al., 2009) or for specific regions (Mediterranean Sea, Norwegian shelf; Titschack et al., 2015, 2016). The limited amount of studies quantifying the contribution of coral mounds to the ocean carbon cycle is even more related to the facts that we are still facing an incomplete picture (i) about the worldwide distribution of coral mounds, particularly due to the rather limited availability of high-resolution bathymetric data to map exposed coral mounds and also of seismic data to detect buried mounds, and (ii) about their temporal development.

That name meant a good deal to Hiram Dobbs, and a great deal more to Dave Dashaway. It marked the starting point in the aviation career of the latter, and that in its turn had meant a first step up the ladder for his faithful comrade, Hiram. In the first volume of this series, entitled: "Dave Dashaway, the Young Aviator; Or, In the Clouds for Fame and Fortune," the career of Dave Dashaway has been told. The father of the young airman had been a noted balloonist, and when he died a mean old skinflint named Silas Warner had been appointed Dave's guardian. Warner had acted the tyrant and hard taskmaster for the youth. A natural love for aeronautics had been born in Dave. He had made an airship model which his guardian had maliciously destroyed. Warner had also appropriated a package dropped accidentally by a famous aviator, named Robert King, from a monoplane. Dave had found this package, containing money, a watch and a medal greatly prized by Mr. King. Dave resolved that this property should be restored to the airman. He got hold of the lost articles, which his guardian had secreted, and ran away from home. After various adventures, during which he was robbed of the airman's property, Dave managed to reach the aero meet at Fairfield. He found Robert King and described to him the boy thief. That thought floated across his mind with others, and was of the same cynical complexion. It was very well for the sun to shine, making the glistening poplars and plane-trees glow, and warming all the mellow redness of the old houses, but what did he mean by it? No warmth to speak of, only a fictitious gleam - a thing got up for effect. And so was the affectionateness of woman - meaning nothing, only an effect of warmth and geniality, nothing beyond that. As a matter of fact, he reminded himself after a while that he had never wanted anything beyond, neither asked for it, nor wished it. He had no desire to change the conditions of his life: women never rested till they had done so, manufacturing a new event, whatever it might be, pleased even when they were not pleased, to have a novelty to announce. That, no doubt, was the state of mind in which the lady who called herself his aunt was: pleased to have something to tell him, to fire off her big guns in his face, even though she was not at all pleased with the event itself. But John Tatham, on the other hand, had desired nothing to happen; things were very well as they were. He liked to have a place where he could run down from Saturday to Monday whenever he pleased, and where his visit was always a cheerful event for the womankind. He had liked to take them all the news, to carry the picture-papers, quite a load; to take down a new book for Elinor; to taste doubtfully his aunt's wine, and tell her she had better let him choose it for her.

In reflecting on Seacole's life, one must grapple with the intricate interplay between history and memory, between fact and idealization. Even as discussions about her worthiness swirl, the statue of Mary Seacole stands resolutely at the edge of St Thomas's Hospital, a testament to her enduring impact on the cultural memory of Britain. For many, it symbolizes a victory over historical amnesia, capturing the essence of an individual who looked beyond race and bureaucracy to serve those in desperate need. For others, it ignites an ongoing deliberation about historical integrity. In grappling with Mary Seacole's legacy, the lessons extend beyond the specifics of her life. As we look toward the future, Seacole's story invites both admiration and inquiry, urging society to remember, reflect, and refine the stories it chooses to celebrate.

The reason most of us love roses is the combination of the delicacy of the scent and the incredible voluptuousness of the flowers, ranging from an almost wistful delicacy in a rose such as Alba Semiplena to the impossibly full convolutions of a centifolia such as Juno or Fantin Latour. Rose scent rarely wafts on the air; you have to nuzzle up to them and intimately smell their fragrance as you might savour the bouquet of a fine wine. I grow centifolias, damasks, albas, gallicas, bourbons, hybrid perpetuals, moss roses and rugosas. All have superb scents, but my favourites are the albas, which somehow manage to be both delicate and lingering in the nose. Appeal: The reason most of us love roses is the combination of the delicacy of the scent and the incredible voluptuousness of the flowers. This scent of fresh roses has an active ingredient called phenylethylamine (also contained, intriguingly, in chocolate) which contains an amino acid known to slow the breakdown of the endorphin hormone. So a bunch of roses and a box of chocolates is more than just a romantic gesture. They actually induce a chemical enhancement of wellbeing and romance. Certainly, a garden with several shrub and climbing roses, burdened with flowers in midsummer, is as near to a romantic heaven as we are likely to find on this earth. In Greek mythology, Aphrodite was not only the goddess of love but also the goddess of gardens and fruitfulness, and the rose was sacred to her. The blood-pure flower, so universally accepted as a definition of loveliness, was adopted by early Christians as the symbol of the Virgin Mary, the five petals representing the five senses, and the thorns the tribulations of life that have to be braved to reach the flower. I grow a lot of roses in my garden and have ramblers scrambling up apple trees, climbers on my walls and scores of shrub varieties in my borders. Although I love the richness of red roses such as Tuscany or the rich burgundy of Souvenir du Dr Jamain - one of the few roses that is better grown in shade - no colour becomes a rose better than pink. My favourite of all is a full, many-petalled flower that is a delicate, almost shy pink called Cuisse de Nymphe, which literally means 'thigh of a nymph' - the mythological beautiful girls that were spirits of Nature - but which was translated by the rather shocked Victorians as 'Great Maiden's Blush'. By any name, it is a seductive rose. Aphrodite: In Greek mythology she was not only the goddess of love but also the goddess of gardens and fruitfulness. We think of roses being a very English flower but, although we have 14 native wild roses, the multi-petalled roses that we all recognise and love originate from the Middle East and were bought to this country by Crusaders when they returned home.

"Hey, I'm just saying, it's a cold world out there, and you're playing dice with snowflakes." They continued on, their breath mingling with the icy air. Kit trailed a half-step behind, her body trembling as much from the chill as from something deeper. "Viv," she said, her voice wavering. "It won't be long until we're safe. Just a little more. I promise." There was a desperation in her tone that felt like a flimsy lifeline. Vivian could hear the unspoken plea hanging in the air. They'd promised each other once-that they wouldn't let the streets swallow them whole. The streetlights flickered above, casting pale pools of light onto the pavement where shadows danced like lost souls. Ahead, a quartet of men loitered, their laughter echoing into the night as if taunting the cold. Vivian squared her shoulders, focusing on the task at hand. "Let's stick to the corners. Night's still young." "Yeah," Kit replied softly, her voice fading, hardly carried by the wind. The chill sharp against her skin, Kit rubbed her hands together, wishing for warmth that evaded her. The conversations around her blurred into a muffled hum, each laugh a jarring reminder of what lay just out of reach. In another life, she could have been anything but this. A teacher, perhaps, or a barista with a smile that lit up the room. But here she was, reduced to fleeting moments, fragments of whispers shared with strangers in dark alleys. "Vivi," Kit finally spoke, breaking through the haze as they approached a corner just outside a diner. "What if we just... what if we just left? Like, really left. Here's a thought-what if we just hopped a bus to somewhere warm?" The flicker of a dream brightened Vivian's eyes for a fraction of a second-a getaway from this frozen hell. "Dreaming, huh? We can't even afford the fare, let alone a ticket out of this mess." "Maybe we could work something out," Kit insisted, a hint of hope creeping into her tone. "Like we could save up, just a little. You know, for a real chance." Vivian rolled her eyes, stepping slightly away from her friend as a group of young men approached. They weren't the type that would buy a pretty face-they were all bravado, aiming for scores and cheap thrills. "Yeah? And what, you think the universe is just going to hand us a bus ticket? You think it's that easy?" Her voice was harsher than she planned, but the edge was necessary. Kit felt the weight of Vivian's words settle over her like a damp blanket. "No, I know it's not easy. But what if it could be?" Vivian shook her head, glancing at the men with an icy detachment. "What if the sky turned green and the stars fell down, too?" It was harsh, but it was the truth they both lived in. "Just give me a chance," Kit pleaded again, desperation tingeing her words as they approached the group, her voice quivering just below the threshold of hope. The men smirked, eyeing both women hungrily, lost in their own world, unaware of the fire flickering gently inside Kit's brave heart. "Well, lookie what we got here," one of the men leered, his eyes roving hungrily. Vivian forced a smile, an armor of bravado cloaked over her heart. She would protect Kit, keeping those dangerous dreams alive within. If only for tonight.

You need n't hurry back, because I reckon Margar't won't be buried until tomorrow." Mrs. Warren paused for a moment, and then replied, "No, I suppose not. Good-bye," and went out, closing the door after her. Mrs. Austin turned around and looked at the corpse. Margaret Hays lay upon the bed, clad in a plain cotton night-dress. Her long black hair, falling free over her shoulders, made a sombre background for her pale face, and served only to accentuate the pallor of her skin. Her large brown eyes were open, and stared blankly upward. Her lips were parted, and showed between them her white teeth. She was lying on her back, and her hands were folded across her breast. "Poor Margar't! Poor Margar't!" " murmured Mrs. Austin. "She 's better off where she 's gone to. She never had much of anything in this world, and I guess she did n't expect to have." She sat down on the edge of the bed, and began to cry quietly. The tears rolled slowly down her thin cheeks and dropped upon the hands of the dead girl. There was nothing in the room save the bed, two chairs, a wash-stand, and a stove. The floor was bare and dirty. The window-sash was broken, and stuffed with rags to keep out the draughts. The walls were covered with cheap paper, half torn away. It was a miserable room. One who knew nothing whatever of Margaret Hays might have told something of her story simply by looking at the room in which she lived. After a few moments Mrs. Austin dried her eyes, rose, and looked around the room. Then she walked over to the closet and opened the door. There were a couple of calico dresses hanging against the wall. Mrs. Austin took them down, and folding them carefully, placed them on a chair near the head of the bed. Next she picked up a pair of coarse shoes, and set them beside the dresses. Then she went over to the bureau and opened the drawers. There were two or three pieces of underwear and a few odds and ends of clothing. These she placed upon another chair. She went back to the closet again and took out a faded shawl and bonnet. They were both worn and frayed, but they were the best ones that Margaret possessed. Mrs. Austin held them up and looked at them for a moment. Then she sighed and muttered to herself, "She always thought so much of these clothes." She placed them also upon the first chair. Then she turned to the body of the dead girl. She felt very awkward.

The mining camp at the mouth of the great canyon had been worked out, so far as the placer mines went, and these few broken men who remained, as a rule, were turning their attention to other things. Here one had planted a little garden on the hillside, on a spot that had once been a graveyard. There, an old lawyer had grown grape-vines all over and about the door and chimney of his cabin, till men said it looked like a spider-web. But old Forty-nine only bored deeper and deeper into the spur of the mountain, and paid but little attention to any of the changes that went on around him. He had been working in that tunnel alone for nearly twenty-five years. He was a man with a history - men said a murderer. He shunned men, and men shunned him. Was he rich? He professed to be very poor; men said he must be worth a million. Would a man work on twenty-five years in one tunnel, and all alone, for nothing? But if rich, why did he remain? Still further down, and quite on the edge of the valley, stood another cabin. And this was quite overgrown with vines, and was quite hidden away in a growth of pines that gathered over it. Then there was an undergrowth of fruit trees that grew inside the fence and about the lonely porch. On this porch had sat, for years and years, a tawny, silent old woman. She was sickly - had neither wealth, wit nor beauty - and so, so far as the world went, was left quite alone. But there was another and an all-sufficient reason why neither man or woman came that way. She was an Indian. Do not imagine this a wild Indian woman. Indian she was; but remember, the Catholics had more than half civilized nearly all the native Californians long before we undertook to kill them. This Indian woman would have been called by strangers a Mexican woman. She was very religious, and had imbued her boy with all her beautiful faith and simple piety. I know that the spectacle of an old Indian woman and her "half-breed" son, represented as the morality and religion of a camp made up of "civilized" Saxons, will seem somewhat novel to you. But I knew this Indian boy and his mother well, and know every foot of the ground I intend to go over, and every fact I propose to narrate. And if you are not prepared to receive this as truth, I prefer you to close this page right here. To make a moment's digression, with your permission, let me state briefly and frankly, once for all, that the only really religious, unquestioning and absolutely devout Christians I ever met in America are the Indians. I know of no other people so faithful and so blindly true to their belief, outside of the peasantry of Italy.

Here, again, laterality preference was not explicitly addressed. As described above, two attachment dimensions (anxiety and avoidance) could change one's preferred physical distance to the attachment figure. Tucker and Anders (1999) observed nonverbal behaviors of romantic couples and found that insecure subjects typically do not feel comfortable with physical closeness. Oxytocin is a peptide hormone, which increases a level of subjects' trust to others (Kosfeld et al., 2005), producing a mental closeness and affiliative behaviors. The number of oxytocin receptors is different among attachment styles (Bradley et al., 2011). Oxytocin is released by physical touch (e.g., holding hands, hugging) (Light et al., 2005). The frequency and quality of physical proximity from a caregiver in childhood is different among attachment styles, possibly providing one of the reasons why the sensitivity of physical touch depends on attachment styles. Thus, physical proximity plays a part in adult attachment, where the IWM might serve as a mental base for it. In addition to parameters such as physical distance, lateral preference is likely to play an important role in physical proximity: a subject may prefer to be on the left or right side when in physical proximity. Handedness (Oldfield, 1971) is one factor which is likely to affect lateral preference significantly. Genetic factors might affect the nature of lateral preferences that an individual develops (Fagard, 2013). There might be a kind of cognitive spontaneous symmetry breaking (Arodz et al., 2012), where a subject, who originally did not have any specific laterality preference, might acquire a weak initial preference, which becomes stronger as the preference is reinforced and consolidated. In addition, there could be some cultural influences, e.g. on which side of the road a pedestrian is expected to walk. Furthermore, many studies reported the physical laterality of interaction with an attachment figure in childhood. A mother carrying a baby in her arm tends to put the baby on her left side with the right side of the infant's body touching its mother (Rheingold and Keene, 1965; Richards and Finger, 1975) in many cultures investigated (Julius Harris et al., 2007). The left cradling bias was not attributed to handedness (Saling and Bonert, 1983; Harris et al., 2001). One of the reasons behind such laterality preference might be so that mother's heartbeat could give babies a sense of security through laying their ears against her left chest (Salk, 1973). Alternatively, mothers might cradle on her left side, bringing their infant into her left view, so as to be able to interpret the infant's emotions and respond to his or her needs employing the right hemisphere of the cortex (Huggenberger et al., 2009). It is important to build attachment so that mother could respond to infants' signals appropriately (Seifer et al., 1996). Indeed, right-cradling mothers are less sensitive to the signals from infants and likely to have more anxiety (Chateau and Andersson, 1976).

The sound startled the boys, and they exchanged glances filled with intrigue and a hint of apprehension. Grimshaw strode to the door, the light from inside spilling out into the ominous evening murk. He swung the door open to find a drenched figure, soaked to the skin but brimming with energy, his face obscured by a cap pulled low. "Dave! Theo!" Dave's heart raced; the unexpected twist sent adrenaline coursing through his veins. "What?! The urge to fly surged within Dave, the horizon beckoning him closer, promising a rendezvous with fate.

I tried to distract myself by exploring my hometown, visiting old haunts, and catching up with acquaintances. But my mind kept wandering back to Cat. I couldn't shake off the feeling that I was so close to finding her, yet so far. And then, on the fifth day, my phone rang. I hesitated for a moment, my heart skipping a beat. I picked up, and a voice on the other end said, "Hello?" It was her. It was Cat. My Cat. We talked for hours, reminiscing about our time in the children's home, sharing stories about our lives since then, and laughing together like we used to. It was as if no time had passed at all. The connection was still there, strong and palpable. We made plans to meet in person, and I couldn't sleep that night, my excitement and nervousness getting the better of me. What would she look like now? Would she still have that mischievous glint in her eye? Would we still have that spark? The day of our meeting arrived, and I arrived at the designated spot, my heart pounding in my chest. And then, I saw her. She walked towards me, her smile illuminating the entire room. We embraced, holding each other tightly, tears of joy streaming down our faces. It was like coming home, like finding a piece of myself that I thought I had lost forever. We spent the rest of the day together, rekindling our love, and making new memories. We talked about our past, our present, and our future. We laughed, we cried, and we loved. As the sun began to set, we sat on a bench, holding hands, and looking out at the world around us. We knew that we still had a long way to go, that life would throw its challenges our way. It means we're doing something right! I.F.: How many songs do you estimate you have in your library? Donovan: We have around 8,500 songs available for airplay, all ripped from original vinyl. We try to stay away from CD compilations because they tend to be too polished. We like the scratches and pops that come along with the old LPs and 45s. I.F.: Have you ever tried to figure out the total amount of hours you spend searching for these songs? Donovan: If I were to add up all the hours spent in thrift shops, record shows, garage sales, etc., looking for these gems, it would probably be close to 2,000 hours. And that doesn't include the countless hours spent ripping the tracks onto MP3s and organizing them into playlists. I.F.: You guys have an interesting dynamic on the show. One minute you're dead serious about a song or artist and the next you're cracking jokes. Is this planned or spontaneous? Donovan: It's definitely spontaneous. We don't plan any of the banter between us. When we go live, we just wing it. I think that's part of the charm of the show. Sometimes we get carried away and go off on tangents that last longer than expected. We just feed off each other. I.F.: Who is your favorite character on the show? Donovan: That's a tough one... I'd have to say that I like the Colonel Sanders character the most. He was created after we got the idea to buy a Colonel Sanders mask off of ebay. Once we got the mask, we decided to incorporate him into the show. We just thought it would be funny to see a guy in a chicken suit who talks like an old man. He's been a hit with the listeners. I.F.: Do you have a particular audience in mind when you produce the show? Donovan: Not really. I mean, we try to appeal to anyone who likes oldies. Most of the listeners seem to be people in their late thirties and forties who remember hearing some of the songs on the AM radio growing up. We also have a younger crowd who listen to the show because they're interested in the history of pop music. I.F.: Are there certain artists you won't touch? Donovan: Well, we don't play anything by Elvis Presley or The Beatles. Those two artists are way too overplayed on the radio already. We prefer to dig deeper and find the forgotten gems. I.F.: Where do you see yourself going with the show? Donovan: We'd like to keep expanding our audience and eventually turn it into a full-time job. Right now, we're just having fun with it and seeing where it takes us. I.F.: Now, let's move on to your film career. Your first feature length film, The Fearless Freaks, was released last year. Tell me about it. Donovan: It's basically a documentary about the band The Flaming Lips. We followed them around for a few years, filming their concerts and interviewing them backstage. It's a very intimate look at the band and their creative process. I.F.: What made you decide to make a documentary about them? Donovan: We've been big fans of The Flaming Lips for a long time. We saw them perform at a small club in Salt Lake City back in 1999 and we were blown away. We knew right then and there that we wanted to make a film about them. I.F.: How did you manage to get access to the band? Donovan: We contacted their management and pitched the idea to them.

The cravat, once a triumph of silks and artistry, now hung about his neck in a fashion both earnest and antiquated, as if echoing the whispers of a past grandeur unacknowledged by this modern throng. A waistcoat, still bright with once-vibrant colors dulled by years, clung to his sturdy frame like an indolent reminder of lost elegance. Ever so often, he adjusted his cuffs, the gold of the buttons glinting faintly against the burgeoning tumult of contemporary fashion that he so resolutely ignored. It was not that he despised the present; rather, he seemed to touch it gently, with the reverence due to an estranged child. His companion, on the other hand, carried an air of frivolity tempered by a knowing wisdom. A lighter fellow, possessing a smirk that seemed too perfectly honed for the social intrigues of yore, he sauntered beside the burly gentleman, one eye ever alert for the glimmering edges of the past that might still flicker in the midst of the tawdry present. Sporting a hat that perched precariously atop his head, he was the very embodiment of misplaced confidence, as if he, too, belonged to an epoch when men took pride not only in fashion but in the art of entertaining discourse. Together, the two men navigated the hodgepodge of modernity, a pair of old stones amidst a river of flowing change. As they ambled forth, such discomforting thoughts of bygone days swelled within them, for they too carried their ghosts, and the ghosts were both companions and adversaries. The murmur of the morning air buzzed with the hustle of life, the carriage wheels clattered on the cobbled stones below, and not a soul paused to grant them acknowledgment. They conversed in hushed tones, words wrought with nostalgia, tales of the dapper fellows of their youth exchanging pleasantries in parlors where society still favored class and charm over the raucous jabber of trade and industry. "Ah, my dear fellow!" exclaimed the burlier of the two, gesturing with his gloved hand. "Do you recall that charming soiree at Lady Harrington's? An exquisite evening! We had but to produce the slightest jest, and her napkin would flutter with laughter, as if each quip were a feather tickling her fabled wit." His eyes gleamed a little with the memory, but a weight of loss clung to his voice. "Indeed! And the dancing! How we glided!" His more flamboyant companion responded, a grin sprawling across his features, though tinged by the bittersweet edge of time. "Such merriment cannot be recalled outside of dreams, yet here we are, mere shadows passing between the living." He swept his gaze across the street crowded with shopping ladies and earnest gentlemen at work. "Do you see what this place has become? See how these wretches scurry forth, mere cogs in society's machine! Where is the genteel sloth of a true Lounge?" A silence clothed them, thick and contemplative, as they resumed their stroll. They were suddenly aware that their place-Bond Street-echoed still, but the melody was transformed. The familiar notes were lost amidst the cacophony of trade, their symphony obscured by the raucous shout of economy. Each step felt heavier, burdened with the weight of history eroding away like so much sand on the shore. Yet within them simmered a belief, a fading hope that perhaps a remnant of their age might be glimpsed still-if not in the flesh, then at least in the spirit of casual camaraderie they had long cherished under the gossamer glow of gaslights and genteel laughter.

He liked to see her working for him like this. He was a rich man, but a woman ought to work with her hands for her husband, whether he was rich or poor. It was her wifely duty, and incidentally it kept her out of mischief. Mrs. Clinton, at the age of fifty-four, with her smooth yellow-grey hair and her quiet and composed face, did not look as if she would be up to serious mischief, even if this and other restrictions were removed from her. She looked up when her husband addressed her, and marked the furrow between his heavy eyebrows. Then she looked down again at her work and waited for him to unbosom himself further. "How old is Dick?" asked the Squire, leaning forward to put a spoonful of yolk of egg into his mouth with one hand, while he shielded his grey beard with the other. She knew then the subject upon which he had expressed himself as infernally worried, for he was not accustomed to keep the first stirrings of discontent to himself. "He was thirty-four last April," she said. "Thirty-four," he repeated. "Yes; and I was twenty-four when I married you. That's early. I shouldn't advise any young man to marry at that age, unless, perhaps, he was the only one to keep a name going - as I was, of course - at least in my immediate family. But thirty-four! It's really time Dick thought about it. He's the eldest son. It's his duty. And as far as I can see he never gives the matter a thought. Eh?" "As far as I can see he is not thinking about it," said Mrs. Clinton. "Well, if I couldn't see you couldn't see. I say it is time that he did begin thinking about it. I'm getting on now - good for another twenty years, I should hope, but I want to see the succession assured. Walter is the only one of the boys that's married, and he's only got two girls. Of course, he may have a son - they're coming pretty quick - but I've never got over that doctoring business. I shouldn't like the heir of Kencote to be brought up in a place like Melbury Park, and I say so freely - to you." This was the echo of an old disturbance. The Squire's third son had refused to take Orders, with a view of occupying the family living, but had studied medicine, and was now practising in a suburb of London, and not one of the most genteel suburbs either. That furrow always appeared faintly in the Squire's brow when he was forced to mention the distasteful words Melbury Park. "I think it would be a good thing if Dick were to marry," said Mrs. Clinton. "Good thing? Of course it would be a good thing. That's just what I'm saying.
