There's a certain charm to these small towns, where every street corner is adorned with stories, whispered secrets, and shared dreams. In Ephraim, life is measured not by the ticking of clocks but by the laughter of children and the gentle rustle of the aspen leaves. As the Emmits guided Mrs. Catt along the weathered Main Street, they passed quaint little shops, their wooden signs creaking softly in the breeze, announcing the wares within-handcrafted pottery, freshly baked bread, and even the occasional pie cooling on a windowsill, its scent sweet and inviting. "Now, don't be fooled by our simple exterior," Mr. Emmit continued, leaning slightly closer to Mrs. Catt as if sharing a grand secret. "Underneath this humble facade lies a spirit that's both fierce and warm-hearted." He gestured toward a neighboring home, where an elderly couple sat on their porch, engaging in jovial debate over the best way to tend a garden. "Why, if you stop by old Mr. Harris's place, you'll find the best tomatoes outside of Salt Lake, I promise you that." Mrs. Catt nodded, eyes twinkling with the energy of someone eager to immerse herself in the local culture. The sun hung low in the late afternoon sky, casting a golden hue over the charming homes, and it wasn't long before their footsteps led them to the Emmit's porch, where a crocheted sign swung lazily, proclaiming "Welcome" to all who approached. As they settled into the cozy living room adorned with family photos and handmade quilts-the love-laden handiwork of the matriarch, of course-Ephraim's essence seemed to seep into the very air they breathed. "You see, Mrs. Catt," Mrs. Emmit began, her hands clasped in her lap, "we hold onto our traditions tightly, yet we're not unkind to change. We love a good story, and even more, we love sharing those tales with visitors." Betty, now feeling emboldened by the warmth of the conversation, chimed in. "And I can tell you a story! I have a pet rabbit-I named him Cottontail. He's the fastest in all of Ephraim!" Betty's exuberance drew laughter from her parents and a genuine smile from Mrs. Catt. "Oh, I'd love to meet him! And perhaps we can arrange a race one of these days?" she replied, now fully engaged in the charming world that Ephraim had to offer. It was the type of place where the lines between newcomers and residents began to blur almost immediately, with an unspoken understanding that differences would gently fade into the backdrop of shared experiences. Conversations flowed easily as the sun dipped lower, giving way to the gentle glow of the porch light, where shadows danced softly against the walls, whispering tales of those who had come before. "Perhaps you'll learn something from us too, Mrs. Catt," Mr. Emmit said, a knowing smile playing at the corners of his mouth. "After all, there's strength to be found in community, and sometimes it's not just about teaching but listening as well." The New-Yorker nodded, acknowledging the humility in his statement, for it struck a chord deep within her. Here, in this small town that greeted her with open arms, she found a life unraveling-rich in connection and vibrant with its tapestry of existence. And as the night settled in, the prospect of new friendships bloomed like the wild violets on the side of the road, promising adventure just beyond the horizon.

It's the kind of night that begins with whispers of irony and culminates in unforeseen revelations. Those of us crammed into the bus - all hopeful commuters turned reluctant adventurers - were now woven into the fabric of an unfolding urban odyssey. As the bus crawled forward at a snail's pace, the driver, scratching her head in confusion, attempted to decipher the ambiguous signals of the traffic. The faces around me varied from exasperation to amusement, each person reacting differently to this strange confluence of events. I noticed a young man in a corner seat, animatedly gesticulating as he chronicled his own Black Thursday, illuminating his story through vibrant gestures that managed to grab hold of our collective attention. He spoke of him and his buddies gathering in a park, blissfully convinced that the mere absence of power would not diminish their spirits. "We lit some candles, brought out a guitar, and made the best of it," he proclaimed, his enthusiasm infectious. "You haven't truly lived until you've strummed 'Wonderwall' by candlelight!" Giggles punctuated the bus's interior-a shared moment of irreverence that simmered just beneath the surface of the chaos outside. Another passenger, a middle-aged woman with a penchant for dramatic storytelling, chimed in with her own account. "You know, my dear husband was in the middle of grilling when the lights went out!" She threw her head back in exasperation, her animated recounting making it appear as if she were on a stage, putting on an improvisational performance for an eagerly waiting audience. "Fish sticks, you know! He was frying up fish sticks! And the power goes out! Can you believe that? I just stood there, holding a plate of cold fish sticks, waiting for our dinner to vanish into thin air along with the electricity!" As the bus stopped for what teased to be another interminable red light, we caught glimpses of the city's landscape altered by gloom. Unlit storefronts on the sidewalk looked like sleeping giants, their presence muted by the darkness encroaching on the boulevard. Flickering candlelight from a few windows vibrated against the night air like a wink from some unseen friend, a whisper that all was well in the midst of chaos. There was unity in our shared plight-a synchronicity that bore witness to a peculiar form of camaraderie bonding complete strangers in the dimness of an urban grid. And then a sound echoed through the air-a cacophony that would have seemed ordinary on any other day but now resonated differently. The indistinct hum of a generator droned in the distance, the last gasp of civilization attempting to cling to its mechanized visage. "There's life after darkness!" declared a man seated closer to the front. "Did you see that gas station back there? They're still pumping gas like it's just another Thursday!" The absurdity of the moment intensified the laughter that rolled through the bus, illuminating our faces with glimmers of both hope and humor. "Let's just be grateful for this little adventure!" A woman called from the back, and her sentiment swept through us, enhancing the vibrant tapestry of our moments-an impromptu gathering of souls sailing through the waves of unanticipated circumstance. We were all tethered by threads of stories shared, illuminating the shadowy corridors of uncertainty that this Black Thursday had laid before us.

However, despite these advances, no vaccine candidate has yet been approved for use in humans. In light of this, there remains an urgent need to identify additional immunological correlates of protection that could be incorporated into future vaccines. Previous studies using animal models have shown that T cells play a role in controlling filovirus infection (Hensley et al., 2002; Sullivan et al., 2009). For example, depletion of CD8+ T cells during challenge with EBOV in mice resulted in increased virus titers, decreased survival, and enhanced pathology (Sullivan et al., 2009). In contrast, depletion of B cells had no effect on survival, although some animals did succumb to disease. Similarly, treatment of guinea pigs with anti-CD4 antibodies resulted in higher peak viremia, increased weight loss, and reduced survival following EBOV challenge compared to control animals (Daly et al., 2014). These results suggest that T cell responses may provide protection against filoviral infection, although the contribution of specific T cell subsets and epitopes remain unclear. As such, we sought to characterize the breadth and magnitude of the EBOV-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in a cohort of Ebola survivors who were admitted to the United States military hospital in Liberia between May and July 2015. We enrolled 14 Liberian patients hospitalized at the US Naval Medical Research Unit No. 3 (NAMRU-3) during the West African EBOV outbreak. All subjects were seropositive for IgG against EBOV GP by ELISA (Figure 1A). All patients presented with symptoms of fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and/or cough. Eleven patients presented with bleeding manifestations including mucosal hemorrhage, epistaxis, hemoptysis, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, vaginal bleeding, or petechiae (Table 1). Laboratory tests revealed thrombocytopenia in 12/13 patients tested, leukopenia in 10/13 patients, elevated liver enzymes in 11/13 patients, and elevated creatinine in 7/13 patients (Table 1). Chest X-rays performed upon admission showed pneumonia in four patients and pulmonary edema in three patients. At the time of enrollment, most patients reported having experienced severe symptoms during their illness (Table 1). Fourteen days after symptom onset, all patients had resolved symptoms except for one patient who remained febrile. Twelve of the 14 patients received intravenous fluids, antipyretics, antibiotics, and electrolyte replacement therapy. Two patients were treated with intravenous ribavirin. One patient was treated with convalescent plasma, and one patient was treated with both convalescent plasma and intravenous ribavirin. All patients survived their acute infection and none required intensive care unit admission. (A) Anti-EBOV IgG ELISAs were performed on serum samples collected from 14 Liberian Ebola survivors at the time of enrollment (May-July 2015) and again 6 months later (January 2016). Data points represent individual patient responses. (B) Representative flow cytometry plots showing detection of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from blood collected at the time of enrollment from a representative survivor. Cells were gated based on forward and side scatter properties and then analyzed for expression of CD4 or CD8, respectively. (C) The percentage of total CD4+ T cells expressing each indicated activation marker was calculated for each subject at the time of enrollment and plotted as a box-and-whisker plot.

The truth loomed always, like a shadow over his consciousness. It clawed at the edges of his awareness, a persistent whisper at the back of his mind, relentless and inescapable. For all his outward composure, his internal world was one of crumbling fortifications, as if some vital structure deep within his psyche had been irrevocably compromised, leaving him vulnerable to the smallest tremors of unease that life inevitably delivered. Peter knew the catalyst for his slow descent lay not in some obscure physical ailment but in a more insidious adversary - the silent crippling of his spirit by the machinery of civilization, by the invisible gears of obligation and disappointment that ground against the fiber of his being day by day. He perceived life as a theater of perpetual expectation, each aspect of it demanding more than he felt equipped to offer. The promise held by his earlier years, brimming with optimism and an unyielding faith in a noble cause, had gradually been sapped by the weight of pragmatism, by the necessity of fitting into shapes predetermined by those whose confidence in the structures of the past continued to set the molds for the future. And while his peers engaged energetically in the drama of life, alert to its cues and promptings, Peter found himself increasingly an observer - a spectator to his own diminishing fortunes. How acutely dominant his resignation had become, that final capitulation to disenchantment, he could hardly articulate even to himself. It was one thing to formulate and embrace the idea of failure's inevitability but quite another to reconcile it with the flickers of ambition and desire that still, against all odds, ignited within him from time to time. On occasion, some ghost of inspiration would alight upon his consciousness, rekindling an imaginative vigor he thought long extinguished. These ephemeral visits invigorated him temporarily, only to dissolve into dust as the reality of his situation reasserted its cold dominion. Peter knew that life had not singled him out for any undue hardship nor conspiratorial malice - his was a discomfort existing ubiquitously, clothed in different guises, familiar to many though unanalyzed by most. He reflected on his contemporaries, secure and thriving, appearing masterful navigators of existence, and wondered at the gulf between perception and actuality - how many shared his plight, veiled behind brave facades? His thoughts cycled back to Doctor Dempsy, to the understanding shade of blue in the physician's kind eyes - eyes that often seemed to speak of recognition, perhaps even of shared confidences, as if to indicate a knowledge held in common but unspoken. Peter valued that more than any prognosis or platitude - a kinship not founded on health or illness but on some deeper, unspoken acknowledgment of human frailty and the profound complexity of truly understanding oneself amid the ceaseless demands of existence. Thus, Peter resolved - not with optimism, but neither with utter despair - to continue his search for meaning within the ordered chaos of the world. If nothing else, he held onto the belief that in the endeavor itself lay something worth pursuing, some filament of hope stretched thin but never wholly absent. In moments of lucidity, this search presented itself as its own reward, an unwavering endeavor to construct meaning amid life's ceaseless cascade, and perhaps therein lay the truest measure of success.

It was there, amid the austere stone walls and whispered prayers, that he found his calling, though the price was steep. The spiritual journey of Padre Pio was fraught with trials, and yet, through his deep faith and resilience, he emerged not only as a conduit of grace but also as a beacon of hope for countless souls seeking solace. As news of the miraculous encounter traveled through both local communities and on social media platforms, debates erupted amongst skeptics and believers alike. Some dismissed the claims as mere folklore, while others hung on to every word as if it were scripture. Witnesses stood by their testimonies, recounting the scene with unmistakable conviction. I thought we might perhaps put up a deer, antelope, buck, or something." "Venison roast, hot, juicy! Oh Drew, old man, don't; pray don't! You gave me such an awful pang. Oh dear! oh dear!" "Pst! I thought we might get wounded, or have a touch of fever, but I never expected that we should run the risk of being starved to death." "Then give us a chance of escaping that fate by keeping your tongue quiet. If we don't get a shot at something down there, we may still hit upon a bag of fish." "Forward!" whispered the young officer, and together the pair approached the wooded gully and cautiously began to descend it to reach the river; but all proved to be silent, and in spite of their caution not a bush rustled, and their patient movements were in vain. "I did expect a shot at something," said the elder officer in a disappointed tone. "Venison was too much," said Bobby. "I expected it would be a sneaking leopard, or one of those doggy-looking monkeys." "The baboons? Oh no; they'd be among the rocky hills. "Fishermen have bad luck enough always, without your prophesying ill before we begin." "One can't help it out here. Hang it all! we've had nothing but misfortunes ever since we came. Could Jules, the quintessential Berliner with his monocle poised ever-so-snugly over his right eye, truly pass for anything other than German? Yet, in the company of Henri, even Jules wore an air of British nonchalance, as though their outward appearance might shield them from the looming shadow of suspicion that was casting a pall over the city. With his bowler hat tipped at a jaunty angle and a Chesterfield coat draped over his arm, Jules exuded a practiced ease. Still, beneath his composed exterior, a faint tension flickered in his gaze-a furtive recognition of the precarious position they both occupied. Their conversation, as they ambled through the hustle and bustle of Berlin's Unter den Linden, was peppered with hurried undertones of apprehension and fleeting glances that betrayed an underlying anxiety. For the reality of their circumstance, under the pale wash of the Berlin sun, was that their presence here was becoming increasingly perilous; the churning mechanisms of war had been set into irreversible motion. In such tumultuous times, every shared word and exchanged glance seemed urgent, imbued with the gravity of imminent change. "We'll need a story, should someone press us about our roots," Jules mused thoughtfully, adjusting his monocle with a swift flick of his wrist. "A story indeed," Henri agreed, nodding almost imperceptibly, his thoughts retracing the steps of their shared history-old anecdotes and half-remembered tales spun on cold Parisian nights. "We are unaware, as yet untouched by any great patriotism; we are mere civilians, business partners even, caught quite unawares." The rhythm of their feet echoed their collective determination, a steady beat against the cobblestones that marked their path. They had little with them-some hastily packed luggage, a few cherished letters concealed discreetly within coat pockets. What they carried most, however, was the burden of identities borrowed in desperation, a cloak of Britishness stretched thin over the undeniable truth of their French heritage. It was an oddly jarring juxtaposition to see the duo navigating amid Berliners, whose spirited discussions and emphatic gestures were punctuated by the crisp click-clack of boot heels and the clatter of trams busily dissecting the metropolis. Yet they managed to weave seamlessly through pedestrian streams, the artifice of belonging elegantly worn as if it were their natural guise. A passing German officer cast them an indifferent glance. Jules, ever the actor in their shared charade, responded with a cordial tip of his bowler, disguising any trace of hesitation with perfected ease. Henri mirrored the act, their mutual resolve unspoken yet unwavering. "Let's depart at dawn," Henri suggested with a feigned air of casualness, though his heart beat a disordered rhythm. "Trains to Holland are still running without scrutiny, from what I understand." Jules nodded, his gaze momentarily distant, caught in the tide of thought but anchored by friendship. A brief, shared silence, then: "Agreed. Dawn it is. And, Henri-if we are parted by fate, remember to whistle Debussy. I'll understand." "Of course," Henri replied, the gravity of the undertone suffusing their pact. They continued down the avenue, past the tumbled faces and fervent gazes of strangers unaware of their silent pact, two Frenchmen cloaked in British finery, bound by duty and an unspoken promise of reunion.

He had never said as much before, and I must admit that his words gave me keen pleasure, for I had often been piqued by his indifference to my admiration and to the attempts which I had made to give publicity to his methods. I was proud, too, to think that I had so far mastered his system as to apply it in a way which earned his approval. He now took the stick from my hands and examined it for a few minutes with his naked eyes. Then with an expression of interest he laid down his cigarette, and carrying the cane to the window, he looked over it again with a convex lens. "Interesting, though elementary," said he as he returned to his favourite corner of the settee. "There are certainly one or two indications upon the stick. It gives us the basis for several deductions." "Has anything escaped me?" I asked with some self-importance. "I trust that there is nothing of consequence which I have overlooked?" "I am afraid, my dear Watson, that most of your conclusions were erroneous. When I said that you stimulated me I meant, to be frank, that in noting your fallacies I was occasionally guided towards the truth. Not that you are entirely wrong in this instance. The man is certainly a country practitioner. And he walks a good deal." "Then I was right." "To that extent." "But that was all." "No, no, my dear Watson, not all - by no means all. I would suggest, for example, that a presentation to a doctor is more likely to come from a hospital than from a hunt, and that when the initials 'C.C.' are placed before that hospital the words 'Charing Cross' very naturally suggest themselves." "You may be right." "The probability lies in that direction. And if we take this as a working hypothesis we have a fresh basis from which to start our construction of this unknown visitor." "Well, then, supposing that 'C.C.H.' does stand for 'Charing Cross Hospital,' what further inferences may we draw?" "Do none suggest themselves? You know my methods. Apply them!" "I can only think of the obvious conclusion that the man has practised in town before going to the country." "I think that we might venture a little farther than this. Look at it in this light. On what occasion would it be most probable that such a presentation would be made? When would his friends unite to give him a pledge of their good will? Obviously at the moment when Dr. Mortimer withdrew from the service of the hospital in order to start in practice for himself. We know there has been a presentation. We believe there has been a change from a town hospital to a country practice. Is it, then, stretching our inference too far to say that the presentation was on the occasion of the change?" "It certainly seems probable."

This is kind of charming, isn't it? Snowflakes whirl through the air, softening the world into something pleasingly surreal. Billie tries to catch one on her tongue, but misses, laughing lightly. That kind of infectious laughter you hear on holiday trips-freezing cold, warmed by the brief moment of joy. Meanwhile, Pete, ever the instigator, begins to gather a handful of snow, shaping it into something that might resemble a ball, his determination writ large on his face. You can see the gears in his mind working; he craves a snowball fight, much like he catnip-craved a challenge. "Okay, boys-who's ready?" He holds up his creation with a theatrical flourish, like a magician revealing their best trick. The boys' eyes sparkle, their competitive spirits igniting, even as they try to suppress their giggles. "Dad, you're not gonna hit us! That's illegal!" Max, with his unmistakable bravado, shoots back, eyes wide with mock horror. "Illegal? In Austria?" Pete roars with laughter, "We don't do law here-this is the land of apres-ski, my friend!" He throws the snowball, but it's just a poor aim, disintegrating harmlessly against a tree. The boys erupt in a chorus of fake gasps, eyes sparkling with delight. "Do it again, but actually try this time!" Oliver yells, the fire of challenge in his voice. It feels like the thrill of the mountains has seeped into their veins. When did snow become this sacred arena? Billie's smile widens as she admires her family, proud yet slightly amused at their antics. They are in their element-joy unrestrained, just like kids in a candy store, which is almost poetic here among the snowy firs. She thinks back to how they all jammed into the rented car earlier, a flurry of jackets and laughter, a cacophony of voices harmonizing into a delightful disarray. It's a stark contrast to the surface-level calm of the picturesque Austrian Alps. "Alright! One for the money!" Pete is suddenly serious again, his mock-serious expression almost comical as he readies another snowball. The boys huddle together, arms cocked, imitating their father's fervor. It feels surreal as the laughter rings into the mountains, punctuated by the crunch of snow beneath their winter boots. Billie feels something shift in the air, a hint of nostalgia mixed with happiness, memories spooling out like twinkling lights. It's warmth amidst the frost, family entangled with the mountain backdrop-a tableau just begging to be painted. "Three... two... one!" Pete counts down, racing his boys against unspoken rules, creating layers in his fabric of parenting that seem delicate yet strong. They scatter across the snow, flinging snow toward one another with abandon-a symphonic engagement that could only happen here. "Keep moving, don't let him get you!" Billie encourages, her voice a cheerful song. She's on the outside looking in, and for a moment, she contemplates joining, chucking her own snowball into the fray, letting her childhood rush back as adrenaline coursed through her veins. But instead, she plants her feet firmly, undeterred by the playful skirmish unfolding in front of her. It's fun to watch; it's enough. Just in this moment, she's content to be the observer of their joy, forever etched into her memory-a frame encapsulated, the perfect family outing under the sun-kissed pyrotechnic skies of a winter wonderland. She can drift there forever if she lets her thoughts keep wandering, but life has a way of calling you back, demanding you step into the frame, to join the beautiful chaos. And the mountain waits, beckoning her with the promise of sublime freedom, inviting her to trade laughter for the rush of the slopes, the unknown just a breath away.

At that exact moment, up-stairs, in a private laboratory in the house, sat a young man at a desk - a handsome, strong-faced, clean-cut chap. All about him were the scientific instruments which he used to test inventions offered to Brent. A look of intent eagerness passed over his face. For Quentin Locke was not testing any of Brent's patents just now. Over his head he had the receivers of a dictagraph. It was a strange act for one so recently employed as manager of Brent's private laboratory. Yet such a man must have had his reasons. One who was interested might have followed the wire from the dictagraph-box in the top drawer of the desk down the leg of the desk, through the very walls to the huge chandelier in the library below, where, in the ornamented brass-work, reposed a small black disk about the size of a watch. It was the receiving-end of the dictagraph. Suddenly the young man's face broke out into a smile and without thinking he stopped writing what the little mechanical eavesdropper was conveying him from below. He listened intently as he heard a silvery laugh over the wire. "Oh, I didn't know you were busy. I thought these flowers - Well, never mind. I'll leave them, anyway." It was Eva Brent, daughter of the head of the firm, who had danced in from the conservatory like a June zephyr in December. "My dear," Locke could hear the patent magnate welcome, "it is all right. Stay a moment and talk to this gentleman while I go down to the museum." Locke listened eagerly, glancing now and then at a photograph of Eva Brent on his own desk, while she chatted gaily with the inventor. It was evident that Eva had not the faintest idea of the hard nature of the business of her father. Meanwhile, Brent himself had left the library and passed through the portiered door into the hall. He did not turn up the grand staircase in the center of the wide hall, but hurried, preoccupied, to a door under the stairs that opened down to the cellar. He started to open it to pass down. As he did so he did not hear a light footstep on the stairs as his secretary, Zita Dane, came down. But he did not escape her watchful eye. "Mr. Brent," she called, "is there anything I can do?" Brent paused. "Wait a moment for me in the library," he directed, as he turned again to enter the cellar. He closed the door and Zita watched him with an almost uncanny interest, then turned to the library to join Eva and the new-comer. Down the cellar steps Brent made his way, and across the cellar floor, pausing at the rocky wall of the foundation of the house blasted and hewn out of the cliff on which it towered above the river.

Tomorrow, we would not just admire greatness but seek to embody it-interpret it through our lens, becoming part of a story that began centuries ago.

He was the son of an eccentric, flamboyant and rebellious high society mother from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, Serrill Headley; and a strict, formal Pakistani diplomat father, Sayed Salim Gilani. The couple met at the Pakistani Embassy in Washington but moved to Lahore, Pakistan, when their son was very young. "He was the first baby I had anything to do with," his uncle William Headley said. "He was the first baby I ever touched or held or anything like that. And somewhere I have a photograph of me in my pajamas holding little Daood.... He was a nice-looking little baby." Fractious union of East and West. After only a few years, Daood's parents split up, an early sign of the fractious union of East and West. The separation left Daood straddled between his traditional Muslim father and his very Western, very American mother. For a time, his mother remained in Pakistan, but she eventually returned to Philadelphia, where she opened a popular bar called the Khyber Pass. The Khyber Pass is the name of the main passage between Pakistan and Afghanistan. Daood remained in Pakistan throughout much of his childhood, and as a teenager he was enrolled for several years at a prestigious and regimented Pakistani military academy, the Hasan Abdal Cadet College. But then his mother pulled him out of the school and brought him back to Philadelphia. There, the teen moved into his mother's apartment above the bar. In 2006, Daood Gilani changed his name to David Coleman Headley, borrowing the family's American name, and even the middle name of William Headley's father, Coleman. The change was made, U.S. officials believe, to help Headley escape detection and travel more easily between the United States, India and Pakistan. In an exclusive television interview with CNN in January, Headley's uncle described his disbelief in learning that his own nephew was connected in any way to the massacre in Mumbai - disbelief that lingered until he began receiving letters from his nephew in his jail cell. "To find an insider in my own family involved [in terrorism] - you're not responsible for what your family does and yet you have such a close association with it, it's your blood." Headley wrote to his uncle from jail, saying that despite his heritage, he was now 100 percent Muslim. Headley's life has been full of twists and turns, from his dual heritage childhood - being equally comfortable in Pakistan's Muslim circles and in Philadelphia's social scene - to his marriage to a blond American beauty and subsequent divorce, after which he took a traditional Muslim wife. Drug trafficking snare. In the 1990s, Headley became a major drug dealer and turned informant for the Drug Enforcement Administration after being caught, according to his family. His involvement with the DEA may have been one of the factors that pushed him toward Islamic extremism. In 1997, he was running a video shop in New York.

JOHN F. KENNEDY, 25th anniversary, 1969. In his statement, Kennedy noted that the D-Day invasion represented 'the turning point' of World War II. He also declared that 'our victory in the West would never have been won without the courage and sacrifice of those who fought and died in Europe.' RICHARD NIXON, 30th anniversary, 1974. Nixon delivered a speech at the White House on the eve of the anniversary and met with veterans and family members of fallen soldiers. JIMMY CARTER, 35th anniversary, 1979. Carter issued a statement saying: 'The valor of those who fought on D-Day helped save Western civilization. Their heroism will be remembered long after the last of them has passed away.' GEORGE BUSH, 40th anniversary, 1984. Bush did not attend the ceremonies. His father, former President George H.W. Bush, attended in his stead. RONALD REAGAN, 40th anniversary, 1984. Reagan attended the ceremonies and delivered an address that remains one of the most memorable speeches of his presidency. 'Today is the day we remember the souls, and it is fitting we do so where the brave young men met their fate,' he said. 'Here, high upon these cliffs, their young hearts burning with faith and pride, they came like adventurers to a new world, a stranger land. Here the Americas began. Here the crusade that carried democracy to half the people in the world was launched.' BILL CLINTON, 50th anniversary, 1994. Clinton participated in ceremonies at Omaha Beach. In a speech there, he praised the sacrifices of the soldiers, saying: 'They came ashore knowing they might die. They came because they knew freedom was worth dying for.' CLINTON, 55th anniversary, 1999. Clinton returned to Normandy and spoke at the cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer. He called the D-Day invasion 'a shining moment in the history of mankind.' GEORGE W. BUSH, 60th anniversary, 2004. Bush visited the Normandy beaches, then attended the commemorative ceremonies in Portsmouth, England, and later at Arlington National Cemetery. He told the crowd at the cemetery that the soldiers 'gave everything they had for the sake of liberty and justice and peace."

He was standing at the very margin of the brook, hemmed in by cliffs, and was bending down to it, but before he had moistened his lips he drew back: just because he was so thirsty he resolved to deny himself drink. Hastily, almost vehemently, he turned his back on the spring, and after this little victory over himself, his storm-tossed heart seemed a little calmer. Far, far from hence and from the wilderness and from the Sacred Mountain he felt impelled to fly, and he would gladly have fled then and there to a distance. Whither should he flee? It was all the same, for he was in search of suffering, and suffering, like weeds, grows on every road. And from whom? This question repeated itself again and again as if he had shouted it in the very home of echo, and the answer was not hard to find: "It is from yourself that you would flee. It is your own inmost self that is your enemy; bury yourself in what desert you will, it will pursue you, and it would be easier for you to cut off your shadow than to leave that behind?" His whole consciousness was absorbed by this sense of impotency, and now, after the stormy excitement of the last few hours, the deepest depression took possession of his mind. Exhausted, unstrung, full of loathing of himself and life, he sank down on a stone, and thought over the occurrences of the last few days with perfect impartiality. "Of all the fools that ever I met," thought he, "I have gone farthest in folly, and have thereby led things into a state of confusion which I myself could not make straight again, even if I were a sage - which I certainly never shall be any more than a tortoise or a phoenix. I once heard tell of a hermit who, because it is written that we ought to bury the dead, and because he had no corpse, slew a traveller that he might fulfil the commandment: I have acted in exactly the same way, for, in order to spare another man suffering and to bear the sins of another, I have plunged an innocent woman into misery, and made myself indeed a sinner. As soon as it is light I will go down to the oasis and confess to Petrus and Dorothea what I have done. They will punish me, and I will honestly help them, so that nothing of the penance that they may lay upon me may be remitted. The less mercy I show to myself, the more will the Eternal judge show to me."

The initial phases of pre-processing include the reconstruction of interaction cross sections with resonances to interpolated data points on a fine energy grid. The differential and double differential cross sections2 undergo a different type of processing. NJOY allows two different ways of dealing with these distributions; a legacy method that is fast to sample as part of the Monte Carlo (MC) approach and minimises data requirements, or a newer method that tends to better represent the data in comparison [3], though this has never strictly been quantified. The cost of this is a longer sampling time and larger data file. A major consideration when running MC simulations of ITER scale is computational efficiency. Not only are huge numbers of individual histories required to achieve the necessary statistical convergence, but all material data required for the simulation is loaded into physical memory. From here the data are accessed, so the amount of available memory is an additional limiting factor for these simulations. For this reason we will be looking at the applicability of the legacy method of data processing to fusion data, to determine if the loss in data accuracy outweighs the need for computational efficiency. When the MC method is applied to neutron transport, many histories are run and these each undergo a series of interactions to simulate the average behaviour of neutrons within the system. Examples of how this average behaviour is used are: to determine the energy dependent neutron flux incident on a breeder blanket, which in turn leads to calculations for tritium self-sufficiency; to check if any streaming occurs from the vacuum vessel and hence determine shielding requirements in these areas; to calculate the corresponding activation calculation of materials post irradiation. Each interaction within the history is determined by the random sampling of the nuclear data. Of particular interest here is the sampling of the differential and double differential cross section distributions to determine the exit energy and angles of radiative particles after each interaction. The MC process used by MCNP is described by the block diagram in Fig. 2, with each sampling stage indicated. The original method for processing the differential and double differential cross section distributions is to represent them with 32 equal probability channels. This particular format is specific to the ACE files used in MCNP, though many other codes use an equal probability structure in a similar fashion with differing numbers of channels. The downfall of using this representation is the loss of features or information within the range of the reaction distribution. For fission relevant reactions, this loss of information is less noticeable as these reactions tend to be more isotropic than those expected for fusion reactors. One example of this can be seen in Fig. 3. The reaction channels shown here are for angular distributions of elastically scattered neutrons from natC at 2.0 MeV, i.e. a fission relevant reaction channel, and from 56Fe at 14.1 MeV, a fusion relevant reaction channel.

The detrimental effects of atrazine on non-target species have sparked intense scientific scrutiny, with studies highlighting its potential to alter the ecological balance and biodiversity of ecosystems. For instance, research has shown that atrazine can affect the development and behavior of aquatic organisms, such as frogs and fish, even at concentrations considered safe for human consumption (Hayes et al., 2011). Moreover, the herbicide has been linked to the decline of amphibian populations, with some species experiencing significant declines in population sizes and altered sex ratios (Kohler and Triebskorn, 2013). The widespread use of atrazine has also raised concerns about its impact on human health, particularly in rural communities where exposure to the herbicide is more likely. Epidemiological studies have suggested a link between atrazine exposure and an increased risk of certain cancers, such as non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, as well as reproductive problems and birth defects (Victor-Costa et al., 2010). Furthermore, atrazine has been detected in drinking water sources, posing a potential risk to human health, especially for vulnerable populations such as pregnant women and children. The development of portable biosensors for the detection of atrazine and other triazine herbicides is therefore crucial for monitoring and mitigating the environmental and health impacts of these chemicals. Such devices could enable real-time monitoring of water and soil samples, allowing for swift identification of contaminated areas and implementation of remediation strategies. Moreover, biosensors could provide a cost-effective and convenient means of monitoring atrazine levels in agricultural settings, enabling farmers to make informed decisions about pesticide use and minimizing the risk of environmental contamination. One potential approach to developing atrazine-specific biosensors is to utilize biological components that interact with the herbicide, such as enzymes or antibodies, and combine them with transduction elements that can detect changes in the biological component upon atrazine binding. For example, researchers have explored the use of tyrosinase, an enzyme that can oxidize atrazine, as a biological component in biosensors (Wang et al., 2012). The oxidation of atrazine by tyrosinase can be detected using electrochemical or optical methods, providing a sensitive and selective means of detecting the herbicide. Another approach is to utilize whole-cell biosensors, which involve genetically engineered microorganisms that respond to atrazine exposure by producing a detectable signal, such as bioluminescence or fluorescence (Tecon and van der Meer, 2008). These whole-cell biosensors can provide a highly sensitive and specific means of detecting atrazine, and can be easily adapted for use in portable devices. The development of portable biosensors for atrazine detection is a critical step towards mitigating the environmental and health impacts of this herbicide. By providing a convenient and cost-effective means of monitoring atrazine levels, these devices can help to reduce the risk of environmental contamination and protect human health. Furthermore, the development of biosensors for atrazine and other pesticides can pave the way for the creation of a new generation of monitoring tools that can help to ensure the sustainable use of agricultural chemicals.

The old sailor, with his weather-beaten face and grizzled beard, leaned against the rail, his single eye glinting with the sharpness of distant seas and his stories beloved like tales from ancient mariners. With the younger men gathered about him like eager fledglings waiting at the nest, he cleared his throat, preparing to weave the fabric of another spellbinding narrative. "All right, lads," he began in his raspy voice, seasoned by years of salt and wind. "Here's a yarn from when I sailed upon the Pegasian Queen, far from the comforts of the known shipping lanes, into those remote whispers of the Indian Ocean." Instantly, the young men leaned closer, the anticipation a palpable thing in the evening air, laden with the scent of salt and adventure. The horizon stretched endlessly before them, much like the nights when the old sailor's stories seemed to fold time back upon itself, transporting them to other decks and distant shores. "Now," said the sailor, his eye squinting as though peering again into the sun of that old voyage, "there was this evening, calm as a pond, with the skies as clear as a newly-polished sextant. We were becalmed, you see, our sails hanging loose and the sea swelling beneath us like the lung of some great sleeping beast." The old man's voice carried the crew outward, each wave of his words matching the rise and fall of the ocean beneath their own ship. He paused for a moment, allowing the image to take hold in the imagination of his audience. "And just then, from the fo'c'sle, came a shout that was half surprise, half terror. There appeared, not fifty yards from us, a behemoth unlike anything recorded in the annals of our sailing lore. A leviathan, they called it, with eyes the size of saucers and scales that caught the dying light as though fashioned of smelted gold." A murmur ran through his audience, the air thickening with a mixture of skepticism and hope. After all, on nights such as these, the boundary between possibility and reality blurred like a haze along the horizon. "But mark me words," he went on with pride, "it was no mere figment, no conjured phantom of an idle mind. We watched it navigate the deep, its enormity rendering our ship no more than a speck upon the vast stretch of aquamarine blue. Ships in tales be capsized by their fortunes, but we, ah, we claimed a rare boon in the winning of those waters." The old man's voice dropped to a conspiratorial whisper, compelling every soul to lean just a little closer. "For one of us," he pointed a bony finger skyward, "climbed atop the mainmast and swore he saw, within the beast's unblinking gaze, reflections of lands uncharted and riches unseen by any man of Europe." The others envied the audacious thrill of such claims, their minds alight with the tempting dreams of the voyages yet to come. Here were stories to be taken with realms of salt, but gossamer threads of enchantment woven deftly into the heart of each listener. "And so," concluded the old sailor, with a knowing nod, "we sailed forth anew, bearing not just cargo and men, but the very spirit of longing that ever seeks the unseen, that ever breathes life into yarns spun beneath the stars."

In this context, the role of alloying elements, particularly titanium, has emerged as a focal point of ongoing research. Beyond their contribution to the formation of finer dispersoids, titanium and its interactions with other alloying elements can facilitate the development of a complex microstructure that encompasses a variety of phases. The interplay between these phases can modulate the material's response to neutron irradiation, adding an additional layer of sophistication to the design of ODS steels. Notably, the incorporation of elements such as molybdenum or tungsten alongside titanium has demonstrated potential benefits in enhancing thermal stability, thereby augmenting the operational capabilities of the alloys at elevated temperatures-an essential requirement for reactor materials that must withstand not only significant radiation damage but also prolonged thermal loads. Beyond compositional adjustments, the optimization of processing conditions has been identified as a crucial factor influencing the eventual performance of ODS ferritic steels. Innovations such as advanced mechanical alloying techniques allow for greater control over particle size distribution and morphology, directly impacting the subsequent sintering and consolidation stages. By meticulously adjusting the milling duration and the intensity of mechanical energy applied, researchers have noted improvements in atomic homogeneity and dispersoid uniformity, translating into enhanced mechanical resilience. Furthermore, the integration of novel consolidation techniques, including innovative additive manufacturing solutions, presents a paradigm shift in the fabrication of complex geometries that are not only lightweight but highly resilient. The potential dual-use of research aimed at nuclear applications also opens the door to exciting developments in material science beyond the confines of energy generation. The principles guiding the design and optimisation of ODS steels may find cross-disciplinary applications in sectors such as aerospace, where materials must withstand extreme conditions coupled with stringent safety and performance requirements. As the pursuit of knowledge becomes increasingly interdisciplinary, the dialogue among technologists, physicists, and materials scientists will be pivotal in addressing the multifaceted challenges posed by next-generation engineering applications. The urgency to develop sustainable energy solutions whilst ensuring safety and efficiency has engendered a renewed focus on nuclear technologies. With ODS ferritic steels at the forefront, the path towards realising their full potential remains laden with opportunities for innovation and discovery. Understanding the microstructural intricacies and utilizing advanced techniques in processing will ultimately propel this research from theoretical frameworks into tangible, real-world applications that can satisfy the burgeoning energy demands of tomorrow's society. As research continues, collaboration among institutions and industries alike will be essential in driving such advancements forward, ensuring that the outcomes of these developments resonate not only within the nuclear sector but across a broader spectrum of technological domains. In conclusion, the exploration of ODS steels represents a convergence of scientific inquiry and practical necessity, fostering synergies that are poised to enhance nuclear energy generation and accelerate the transition towards a sustainable energy future. Through ongoing diligence and innovation, the path ahead looks promising, heralding a new era of nuclear engineering steeped in efficiency and safety.

In areas where the F- levels exceed the recommended guidelines, the condition can lead to severe health problems, including skeletal fluorosis, dental fluorosis, and other systemic effects. The World Health Organization (WHO) has set a guideline value of F- in drinking water of 1.5 mg/L, while the United States Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) recommends a concentration between 0.6 and 0.9 mg/L. However, the actual levels of F- in drinking water can vary significantly depending on the location and geological composition of the area. In Africa, fluorosis is a major public health concern, particularly in countries such as India, China, and parts of the Rift Valley region. In Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania, fluorosis is prevalent in areas where the F- levels in groundwater exceed 1.5 mg/L. In Uganda, the prevalence of dental fluorosis has been reported to be as high as 45% in some districts, with average F- levels in water ranging from 0.5 to 1.5 mg/L. The high prevalence of fluorosis in these regions can be attributed to a combination of factors, including inadequate treatment of drinking water, lack of awareness about the risks associated with excessive F- intake, and limited access to alternative sources of clean drinking water. In some cases, the F- levels in drinking water may be naturally high due to geological factors, such as the presence of fluoride-rich rocks or minerals in the area. To address the issue of fluorosis, it is essential to implement effective strategies for monitoring and controlling F- levels in drinking water. This can be achieved through the installation of treatment systems that can remove excess F- from water, as well as public education campaigns to raise awareness about the risks associated with excessive F- intake. Additionally, governments and international organizations can work together to develop and implement policies that promote the use of alternative sources of clean drinking water, such as rainwater harvesting and borehole drilling. In conclusion, fluorosis is a significant public health concern in many parts of the world, particularly in regions where groundwater is the primary source of drinking water. The condition can lead to a range of health problems, including skeletal fluorosis, dental fluorosis, and other systemic effects. To address this issue, it is essential to implement effective strategies for monitoring and controlling F- levels in drinking water, as well as promoting public awareness about the risks associated with excessive F- intake.

Ben Brayton struck the horse sharply, hoping that John would be frightened and let go; but our hero clung to the bridle, and the horse began to back. "Let go, I tell you!" exclaimed Ben. "I won't!" said John, sturdily. The horse continued to back, until Ben, who was a coward at heart, becoming alarmed, slid off from his back. "That's right," said John, coolly. "Another time you'd better not meddle with my horse." "I'll meddle with you, and teach you better manners!" exclaimed Ben, a red spot glowing in each of his pale cheeks. As he spoke, he struck John smartly over the shoulders with the small riding-whip he carried. John was not quarrelsome. I am glad to bear this testimony to his character, for I have a very poor opinion of quarrelsome boys; but he had a spirit of his own, and was not disposed to submit tamely to a blow. He turned upon Ben instantly, and, snatching the whip from his hand, struck him two blows in return for the one he had received. "I generally pay my debts with interest, Ben Brayton," he said, coolly. "You ought to have thought of that before you struck me." A look of fierce vindictiveness swept over the olive face of his adversary as he advanced for another contest. "Stand back there!" exclaimed John, flourishing the whip in a threatening manner. "I've paid you up, and I don't want to strike you again." "I'll make you smart for your impudence!" fumed Ben, trying to get near enough to seize the whip from his hands. "I didn't strike first," said John, "and I shan't strike again, unless I am obliged to in self-defence." "Give me that whip!" screamed Ben, livid with passion. "You can't have it." "I'll tell my mother." "Go and do it if you like," said John, a little contemptuously. "Let go that horse." "It's my own, and I mean to keep it." "It is not yours. My mother gave it to me." "It wasn't hers to give." John still retained his hold of the saddle, and kept Ben at bay with one hand. He watched his opportunity until Ben had retreated sufficiently far to make it practicable, then, placing his foot in the stirrup, lightly vaulted upon the horse, and, touching him with the whip, he dashed out of the yard. Ben sprang forward to stop him; but he was too late. "Get off that horse!" he screamed. "I will when I've had my ride," said John, turning back in his saddle. "Now, Prince, do your best." This last remark was of course addressed to the horse, who galloped up the street, John sitting on his back, with easy grace, as firmly as if rooted to the saddle; for John was an admirable horseman, having been in the habit of riding ever since he was ten years old.

However, the limitations of DEM simulations have also been recognized, and there is a growing need for more sophisticated models that can capture the complex behaviors of real-world granular materials. The development of new models and the improvement of existing ones will require a deeper understanding of the underlying physics of granular materials and the development of more advanced numerical methods.

The mines brought him in gold, and in his later years he purchased this estate, pulled down the house that was upon it - a high, narrow, old thing, looking like a crazy tower or a capacious belfry - and had erected this one, calling it "Verner's Pride." An appropriate name. For if ever poor human man was proud of a house he has built, old Mr. Verner was proud of that - proud to folly. He laid out money on it in plenty; he made the grounds belonging to it beautiful and seductive as a fabled scene from fairyland; and he wound up by leaving it to the younger of his two sons. These two sons constituted all his family. The elder of them had gone into the army early, and left for India; the younger had remained always with his father, the helper of his money-making, the sharer of the planning out and building of Verner's Pride, the joint resident there after it was built. The elder son - Captain Verner then - paid one visit only to England, during which visit he married, and took his wife out with him when he went back. These long-continued separations, however much we may feel inclined to gloss over the fact, do play strange havoc with home affections, wearing them away inch by inch. The years went on and on. Captain Verner became Colonel Sir Lionel Verner, and a boy of his had been sent home in due course, and was at Eton. Old Mr. Verner grew near to death. News went out to India that his days were numbered, and Sir Lionel Verner was instructed to get leave of absence, if possible, and start for home without a day's loss, if he would see his father alive. "If possible," you observe, they put to the request; for the Sikhs were at that time giving trouble in our Indian possessions, and Colonel Verner was one of the experienced officers least likely to be spared. But there is a mandate that must be obeyed whenever it comes - grim, imperative death. At the very hour when Mr. Verner was summoning his son to his death-bed, at the precise time that military authority in India would have said, if asked, that Colonel Sir Lionel Verner could not be spared, death had marked out that brave officer for his own especial prey. He fell in one of the skirmishes that took place near Moultan, and the two letters - one going to Europe with tidings of his death, the other going to India with news of his father's illness - crossed each other on the route. "Steevy," said old Mr. Verner to his younger son, after giving a passing lament to Sir Lionel, "I shall leave Verner's Pride to you." "Ought it not to go to the lad at Eton, father?" was the reply of Stephen Verner. "What's the lad at Eton to me?" cried the old man.

The once-thriving frozen food aisles are now a ghost town, with sales plummeting to unprecedented lows. The 43 per cent decline in frozen burger sales and 13 per cent drop in frozen ready meals are stark reminders of the power of consumer trust. Despite the overwhelming evidence of contamination, a glimmer of hope emerges. Surveys reveal that a significant number of consumers would be willing to eat horse meat, provided it is labelled correctly and deemed safe. This willingness to consider alternative protein sources may be a silver lining in an otherwise dark cloud. The recent revelations about Ikea's meatballs and Tesco's Everyday Value range frozen bolognese have left consumers reeling. It will take more than just recalls and apologies to restore consumer confidence. Companies must be willing to make fundamental changes to their practices and prioritize transparency, accountability, and consumer trust. As the dust settles, one thing is clear: the horse meat scandal has changed the way consumers think about food. The days of blind trust are over, and shoppers are demanding more from the companies they buy from. The industry must adapt to this new reality, or risk losing customers forever. This suggests that structural factors aside from regional water policy could have played a significant role in Las Vegas' water conservation, and further demonstrates the importance of understanding changes in the entire urban water consumption portfolio, rather than evaluating the effects of policies in isolation. We overcome these challenges by taking a synthetic approach to examining multiple simultaneous drivers of water use. We pair a traditional regression analysis with two decomposition strategies: 1) the Gelbach decomposition (Gelbach, 2016), which uses the omitted variables bias formula for linear regression to estimate the relative importance of multiple drivers of change in water consumption; and 2) retrospective counterfactual scenarios, predictions for water consumption if important drivers had remained at their 1996 levels rather than evolving according to their historical trajectories. By comparing these scenarios to actual water consumption trends, we can infer how individual factors (and combinations thereof) contributed to Las Vegas' impressive reductions in per-household water use. This synthetic approach is novel because it explicitly addresses the city's dynamic consumption portfolio, and so provides a robust estimate of the water consumption context that conservation programs have operated within. Our Las Vegas case study provides an excellent demonstration of these methods for two reasons, their population growth and the breadth of conservation policy that was tried there. First, for much of the 1990s and 2000s Las Vegas was the paragon of "Sun Belt" urban growth. The MSA population increased by 800,000 between 1996 and 2007 (an average of 5.7% per year). The overwhelming majority of this growth occurred outside existing "core" areas (shown in Fig. 1) rather than as infill development - expanding residential land area in the Las Vegas MSA area from 175 km2 to 320 km2 and more than doubling the number of single-family residential structures. We define the city core as census tracts in which there were fewer than 200 new residential structures built between 1996 and 2007. Other approaches of classifying the core and periphery show similar patterns and generate similar results. The share of LVVWD households in areas outside the established core rose from 20% of the population in 1996 to 60% in 2007 (Fig. 2). This expansion provided policymakers with an opportunity to shape the water intensity of the city's infrastructure, but it also brought with it a rapid rebalancing of the vintage of household infrastructure that may have generated per-capita water savings even in the absence of strong regional policy. New homes bring with them changes in appliances like washing machines, plumbing fixtures, and irrigation systems that govern patterns of indoor and outdoor consumption and tend to change slowly once the house has been constructed. This rapid and geographically concentrated population growth allows us to compare the effects of different policies in established versus newly developed neighborhoods, which also allows comparison of the effects of different kinds and vintages of infrastructure.

It was a clever little gambit, a strategic retreat from the battlefield of my mother's indifference. I wore my guilt like a shroud, but oh, how I relished that sweetness of softly spoken disappointment over the blaring sirens of confrontation. My new strategy worked, at least for a while. I found ways to glide under her radar, making myself as unobtrusive as possible. The exchanges between us became mere artifacts of obligation, like post-it notes stuck to a fridge, reminders of tasks long past and seemingly forgotten. As I honed my survival skills in the emotional terrain of our home, I watched others. Friends at school-bright-eyed with laughter, coming from houses resonant with love, joy, and snapshots of family vacations-made my own home life feel increasingly like the shadow of a sitcom in perpetual rerun. Their mothers cracking jokes, their fathers wrestling them playfully until they giggled, their dinner tables cluttered with affection. I realized, painfully, that their realities were papered in bright, cheerful colors, while mine was a muted sepia, a faded image of what should have been. But then, didn't we all wear our scars? Didn't every child come with their own deconstructed family narratives? The stories unfolded in fragmented memories, twisting into something astonishing throughout the years. In my mind, they morphed with the slightest provocation, reminding me of that one time my friend told me about the year her father inexplicably left for a job in another state and didn't come back. Or the pall of sadness hanging over the boy who found solace in comic books because his parents were forever wrapped in a blanket of hostility. So yes, I sat there one night in my jumbled state, sipping cheap red wine and ruminating like an unhinged philosopher, when Zippy's story danced in my subconscious. Her laughter, her misadventures, sparked a certain domestic envy that was terrifying yet liberating. The sun-drenched scenes of her childhood felt oddly contagious. I began to stir from my self-imposed stupor, tentatively swimming into the ocean of nostalgia. I decided that those stories-other people's, even if just flickering shadows-held more weight than I initially understood. My counter-narrative became one of resilience. I imagined the lone flower sprouting from a concrete crevice, defiantly flourishing amidst the grit. I thought of my dad again, how he poured his love into our little garden, fighting oblivion with petunias and marigolds. No matter how tumultuous the storm raged in the house, there was always a corner of that backyard filled with sunshine, an echo of laughter-our escape. So that's what I clung to. I would tell the tales, re-tell my father's love, and I would sift through the ash of my mother's chaos, seeking the gems hidden there. Yes, I was shaped into this being crafted from pain and miscommunication, but also something else; something wild, unpredictable, and hopeful-all at once. A little girl longing to be a bear, cuddled by her father, riding the waves of both light and dark. When I pour my soul into the blank canvas of paper and ink, I remember that little girl who slipped seamlessly into her father's arms, giggling in the shadow of a lion's roar. And that, my friends, is a story worth telling.

I paid him a guinea, I think it was, and he then took down my qualifications. When I mentioned my "Blue" with pride, he shook his head. "My dear sir, 'Blues' are now a drug in the market," he said. "Surely you read the daily papers, especially the Daily Wire"? "No," I replied, "I am no bookworm." He coughed rather nastily and I began to get irritated with the fellow. "Then I must explain," he continued, "that there has been a great outcry against over-athleticism in the public schools, in all schools, in fact, and I fear your 'Blue' is not worth..." "Quite so," I broke in; "'not worth a damn,' you were going to say." "I was going to say no such thing, Mr. Carey," he replied stiffly. "At any rate, we will do our best for you. You cannot hope for more than a private school at first, and your success in the profession you have - er - chosen, will depend entirely upon your success in a comparatively humble sphere." A week afterwards, I received two or three little forms telling me to apply to various headmasters. Prospects were not cheering, and the salaries offered would about have kept me in cigarettes at Oxford. To cut a long story short, I eventually became third master - there were only three of us - in Morstone House School in Norfolk, at a salary of eighty pounds a year and all found - except washing. Morstone House School was a sort of discreet modern edition of Dotheboys Hall. I do not mean to say, of course, in these enlightened days, that the boys were starved or ill-treated. But everything was cut down to the very margin - to the margarine, as my colleague Lockhart, who was a cripple, and a wit - the Head got him cheap for that - would occasionally remark. For two years I remained at Morstone, a miserable enough life for an ex-blood, you will say - only there were consolations. One of them, and to me it was a very great one indeed, was that Morstone was situated in a remote village on the east coast, on the edge of vast saltings or sea marshes intersected by great creeks of sullen, tidal water. It was five miles to the nearest little town, Blankington-on-Sea, and as lonely a place as well could be conceived. Nevertheless, these vast marshes stretching for many miles on either side formed one of the finest wild-fowl districts in the whole of England. I was, and always had been, passionately fond of shooting. I had saved my guns from the wreck, and the whole of my leisure time in winter was taken up with perhaps the most fascinating of all sports. The wild geese would fly at night over the lonely mud-flats with a noise like a pack of hounds in the sky. Duck of all sorts abounded, teal, widgeon, mallard, and the rarer pintail and even the crested grebe.

Potential adaptation to chronic metal exposure has been reported in various wild fish populations. For example, brown trout (Salmo trutta) from the River Hayle in Cornwall, UK, have shown tolerance of high concentrations of a mixture of metals that are lethal to naive trout. These trout displayed relatively little evidence of overt toxicity, despite accumulating high tissue concentrations of metals, and showed evidence of several mechanisms of metal tolerance including up-regulation of metal-handing pathways and ion homeostasis (Uren Webster et al., 2013). Genetic analysis revealed differences between populations, both within this river and compared to clean rivers nearby, which were predicted to coincide with increases in local mining activity, suggesting that local adaption to metal contamination had contributed to a reduction in gene flow between these populations (Paris et al., 2015). Studies on yellow perch (Perca flavescens) populations inhabiting lakes in North America contaminated through industrial and mining activity have shown tolerance of high concentrations of metals including copper and cadmium, and the potential mechanisms of tolerance were reported to include elevated metallothionein and oxidative stress responses (Defo et al., 2015; Giguere et al., 2005; Pierron et al., 2009). There is also some evidence of selection in these perch populations driven by metal contamination (Belanger-Deschenes et al., 2013; Bourret et al., 2008). Evidence of considerable toxicity was also found in yellow perch chronically exposed to metals, including impaired metabolism and poor condition (Couture and Kumar, 2003; Levesque et al., 2003; Pierron et al., 2009; Rajotte and Couture, 2002), compared to less obvious signs of toxicity in the Hayle brown trout (Uren Webster et al., 2013). This may reflect a greater adaptive change in the trout following longer historical contamination in the river Hayle ( 1/21000 years) compared to the 1/2100 years of contamination experienced by fish in the North American lakes. A genetic contribution to metal tolerance in fish therefore seems likely, but the precise mechanisms of this adaptive change and the potential relative contributions of phenotypic plasticity or other mechanisms are yet to be established. In addition, little is known about the response of depurated individuals to metal exposure or whether metal tolerance is inherited in F1 or subsequent generations raised in clean environments. Three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) inhabit many water systems worldwide, are relatively tolerant of stressors and can undergo rapid speciation in response to environmental change (McKinnon and Rundle, 2002). We have previously used global transcript profiling to establish the transcriptional signatures of response to copper and 17alpha-ethinylestradiol (EE2) in stickleback originating from a reference site (Houghton Springs, Dorset, UK), receiving borehole water with no known history of metal or oestrogenic contamination (Katsiadaki et al., 2010; Santos et al., 2010). Here, we examined the hypothesis that historical exposure to these classes of pollutants modifies the tolerance of exposed populations, altering their response to further exposure.
