The beauty of The Imitation of Christ lies in its timeless relevance-though it was written in the 15th century, its spiritual insights ring just as true today. Thomas Kempen, or Thomas a Kempis, gives us a mirror to examine our own lives, challenging us to rise above the mundane and seek a higher, more purposeful existence. In today's excerpt, we're diving into "The Interior Life," a chapter that calls us to focus on our inward spiritual journey. In our busy, often chaotic world, it is easy to lose ourselves in the endless demands and distractions. But Thomas reminds us of the necessity to pause, reflect, and cultivate a sense of inner stillness. He invites us to understand that peace doesn't come from external sources but from the quiet confidence within, born out of faith and devotion. As I read through this passage, I'm struck by how relevant this call to introspection is in our current age. With social media, 24-hour news cycles, and constant connectivity, finding time for reflection has never seemed more elusive. Yet, it is precisely this retreat into our inner sanctuaries that can refresh and renew us, allowing us to engage more fully and authentically with the world around us. This idea of retreating inward to find strength and guidance is not an escape but a preparation for life's battles. Thomas uses beautiful, simple language to invite us into a deeper relationship with God. It is not about performing great deeds or achieving worldly success, but about cultivating humility and sincerity. I love this approach because it shifts the focus from achieving to being. It asks us to consider-not what we can do for God, but what we can be in God. This transformation of being speaks to the heart of Christian spirituality, and it's a reminder that the journey is as important as the destination. One of the passages that resonates deeply is where Thomas discusses the notion of humility. He writes that true peace and happiness are found not in being exalted or praised but in submitting oneself to the will of God. Humility is portrayed not as weakness but as a profound strength. In a culture that often equates success with power and prestige, this is a radical, counter-cultural notion. Humility is about understanding our place in the grand tapestry of creation, recognizing our limitations, and acknowledging our dependence on God. This passage is also a beckoning to prioritize love over knowledge. Thomas suggests that too often we search for answers and facts, perhaps even in our spiritual quests, but forget the most imperative commandment: to love. This is an essential reminder that the ultimate goal isn't to accumulate theological knowledge but to foster a loving relationship with God and our neighbors. As we come to the end of this reflection, I'm encouraged to further explore the depth and wisdom of The Imitation of Christ. Thomas a Kempis provides not only a manual for spiritual growth but a gentle reminder of the transformative power of humility and love. Let's allow these insights to permeate our lives, becoming not just a reflection in our minds but a practice in our hearts.

Integrating these advanced ICTs into KM strategies can significantly enhance the ability of organizations to adapt and thrive in this complex landscape. As suggested by authors such as Davenport and Prusak (1998), ICT innovations, including artificial intelligence and machine learning, provide unprecedented capabilities for data analysis and knowledge creation. Organizations, therefore, must embrace digital transformation, leveraging technologies to automate routine processes and free up human resources for more strategic, innovation-oriented tasks. Such technological integration not only supports more robust KM strategies but also facilitates the creation of smarter, more responsive supply chains that are better equipped to meet the ever-increasing consumer demands for transparency and accountability (Ross et al., 2016). In this regard, the strategic use of ICTs complements knowledge management, creating a synergy that drives organizational agility and adaptability. The Internet of Things (IoT), for example, enables organizations to gather real-time data from their operations, which can be used to develop insights that inform continuous improvement processes and contribute to sustainable practices (Atzori et al., 2010). Furthermore, cloud computing enhances collaborative efforts among stakeholders by providing scalable and flexible platforms for sharing and storing knowledge, breaking down silos, and promoting a culture of openness and shared purpose (Armbrust et al., 2010). However, embracing technology comes with its own set of challenges. Organizations must navigate issues related to data security, privacy, and the ethical use of technology (Smith, 2018). Developing comprehensive data governance frameworks, therefore, becomes crucial to ensure the responsible use of data and technology. In addition, organizations must cultivate digital literacy and foster a culture of continuous learning. Employees at all levels should be equipped with the skills and knowledge necessary to effectively use new technologies and adapt to evolving business environments. As observed by Nonaka and Takeuchi (1995), creating a learning organization that values and integrates new knowledge is essential to sustaining competitive advantage and fostering innovation. Moreover, leadership plays a pivotal role in steering the integration of KM with advanced ICT. Visionary leaders need to champion change, setting a clear direction and fostering an organizational culture where risk-taking and innovation are encouraged and celebrated. They must work towards aligning their organizational vision with sustainable development goals, thereby embedding sustainability into the core operational and strategic fabric of the organization (Senge, 2006). Thus, the interplay between knowledge management, technological advancement, and sustainability is becoming increasingly integral in today's business arena. Organizations that can effectively harness and integrate these elements will not only survive but thrive, achieving long-term success and contributing positively to the global challenges of environmental sustainability and social equity. By reimagining business models that prioritize building knowledge-based competitive advantages, such organizations are well-positioned to lead the way towards a future where economic growth harmonizes with ecological preservation and social well-being. Indeed, the future of business lies in the hands of those who can envision beyond the conventional, fostering innovations that redefine success in terms not only of profit but of purpose and progress. In this way, the relentless pursuit of knowledge and its responsible application stand as the bedrock of an enduring and equitable business legacy.

What they did see, however, was Washington Washington lifted from the ground and pitched head first into a clump of laurel, where the light foot of an outraged mule had landed him. "He's killed!" cried Anne, voicing the thought that was in the mind of each of her companions, and a concerted rush was made for the clump of laurel. They found the colored boy somewhat dazed when they dragged him from the bushes. "Wha - whar dat 'monica?" he gasped, referring to the harmonica that he was playing when the mule kicked him. "Maybe he swallowed it," suggested Emma. "I hope not, for he surely would have musical indigestion. Wouldn't that be terrible - for us?" "No great loss if it has landed over in the Cumberlands," observed Tom Gray. "Wash, where did the mule hit you?" "Ah reckons all ovah, 'cept on de bean. Why dat fool mule kick me? Hain't nevah done nothin' laik that befo'. Ah ask yuh why he do dat?" insisted Washington. They glanced at Emma, whose face reddened. "I threw a stone at you and hit the mule, if you must know," she said. "The mule passed it on, hitting you with his foot. That mule must have played tag when he was a child. I'm sorry, Wash - but if you had been attending to your business you would not have been hit." Washington's first thought upon recovering from his daze had been for the harmonica, and his first act, after getting to his feet, was to go in search of it. He found it after considerable effort, and ran the scales on it. "Glory be!" cried the boy. "Dat fool mule ain't done kicked de music out ob it." "Listen to me, Washington," demanded Grace, stepping over and laying a firm hand on the lad's shoulder. "You will put that instrument away - " "'Tain't no inst'ment. Hit's a 'monica," he interrupted. "I am speaking. Put it away, and do not let me see you touch it again until you have finished your work. Do you understand?" "Uh-huh." "See that you do not forget. Unpack both mule packs, but look out for the mules' heels, and remember that we did not hire you for an ornament. Emma Dean, let this be a warning to you," admonished Grace, turning to her companion. "Never trifle with a mule. They are all notoriously devoid of a sense of humor." Washington, in the meantime, had shuffled away and had leisurely begun removing the packs. "Speaking of ornaments, I suppose I am the only real ornament in this outfit," observed Hippy. "You mean the kind that they pack away in the garret with broken chairs and old chromos," suggested Emma. Hippy shrugged his shoulders and walked away, followed by the laughter of his companions. Emma had scored again, as she frequently did, and Hippy, instead of being ruffled, took keen delight, as usual, in her repartee.

Picture this: a guy with an infectious smile and the kind of energy that could convince anyone, even me-a skeptic by nature-to listen with bated breath. Dr. Carmichael launched into a spirited discussion, weaving through a tapestry of nutritional advice, peppered with buzzwords like "metabolic optimization" and "hormonal harmony." It quickly became apparent that his charisma was his strongest tool. But here's where things take a twist. As Dr. Carmichael talked animatedly about why calories weren't the be-all and end-all for weight management, his presentation pivoted to the magical world of ketosis. He painted it as the ultimate, albeit misunderstood, tool for weight optimization, transforming the narrative into a keto crusade. But while the food was delightful, my brain was busy dismantling the information being presented. As the presentation wrapped up, the inevitable pitch arrived. Cue violins. For a moment, it felt like I was inside a carefully orchestrated performance-the crowd was spellbound, eager to sign up for a taste of Dr. Carmichael's magic elixir. Leaving the event, my initial cynicism amused yet empowered, it became clear that such seminars, while educational to an extent, often tread a fine line between information and salesmanship. There was a certain theatricality to the whole affair that, while captivating, underscored the necessity for critical evaluation of health advice. So, I came away, not with a newfound allegiance to the keto gospel, but rather a reaffirmation of the importance of balance and data-driven choices on this weight gain journey. You know, Jordan, there's value in staying open-minded yet discerning, especially when bombarded with the allure of quick fixes. This experience only fueled my mission to share thoughtful, informed guidance through my work. So, there you go, Jordan-my little escapade into the world of Keto Clarity. As the days stretched on in an unbroken chain beneath the relentless sun, the landscape began to wear upon him. To the boy, the horizon seemed not merely a boundary but a mockery of his expectations-a destination that receded even as they approached. He watched the fleecy clouds drift lazily in the expansive sky, and the occasional shimmer of distant heat hung over the earth like a mirage, warping the outlines of the world into an impressionist blur. He often found his gaze lingering on his sister, her laughter ringing out like a bell among the disciplined silence of their companions, brightening the encroaching dust that seemed intent on saturating every cheerful moment. The girl, oblivious to these deeper ruminations, scampered about with an unrepentant curiosity, picking up bits of stone and odd twigs, turning them into treasures that required no currency yet held infinite value in her imaginative grasp. Beyond the wagon, the mixed chorus of creaking wood and the lowing cattle punctuated the air, a rhythmic sound that melded with the hiss of wind over dry grass. At times, the boy would exert his will, trying to languidly lead his thoughts away from the reality of their journey, imagining grand escapades amidst kingdoms of towering rocks and flowing rivers, but always the dream would buckle under the weight of dust and fatigue. The laughter of his sister drew him back, urging him to relinquish the heavy cloak of his worries, however temporary, if only for a moment. They had little in the way of tangible possessions; the dirt at their feet and the vast sky above were their only constants. The oxen plodded on with an everyday patience, their great shoulders rolling with each laborious step. The boy sometimes fancied he shared a kinship with the creatures-bound to this trail as they were, slouching onward into an uncertain future. It was a curious realization, for he had always thought of men as the masters of beasts, but here within this endless stretch of land, equality took on a different form, almost primitive in its simplicity. Each day was a balance between the needs of the men and the burdens of the animals, an intricate dance of survival that ground them deeper into the earth. In the evenings, when the sun sank below the horizon, the sky ignited with colors of orange and violet, and for a fleeting moment, beauty softened the harshness of their existence. The campfires would be lit, casting long shadows as the family gathered round to share their meager rations. The air was filled with the sweet, sharp scent of wood smoke mingling with the sour odor of sweat and toil. They would listen to tired stories, tales spun of fortunes sought and friends lost along the way, the flickering light catching their wan faces, etching in their features the trials of the road. It was during these dinners that the boy often caught sight of the far-off darkness, the low hills rising like sleeping giants against the fading light, and felt the hint of a greater mystery beyond. His heart thudded in rhythm with the crackle of the fire, and he allowed himself a fleeting moment of hope that maybe, unlike those who traversed this seemingly endless expanse, they would be the ones to break through to the other side-into freedom. It was a thought that lingered, as light inevitably gave way to encroaching shadows, and with it the familiar heaviness of the canopy descending once more, wrapping around them in somber embrace as if to remind them that even in the vastness of hope, the reality of their present could not be ignored. It was all the same-yet night after night they gathered, warm in the glow of each other's presence.

But I don't understand why I should not be called to go to sea," I replied; "I have for a long time made up my mind to go, and I intend to try and become as great a man as Howe, or Nelson, or Collingwood, or Lord Cochrane, or Sir Sidney Smith. I've just to ask you, Aunt Deb, what England would be without her navy, and what the navy would be unless boys were allowed to go into it?" "Stuff and nonsense, you know nothing about the matter, Dick. It's very well for boys who have plenty of interest, for sons of peers or members of parliament, or judges or bishops, or of others who possess ample means and influence, but the son of a poor incumbent of an out of the way parish, who knows no one, and whom nobody knows, would remain at the bottom of the tree." "But you forget, Aunt Deb, that there are ways of getting on besides through interest. I intend to do all sorts of dashing things, and win my promotion, through my bravery. If I can once become a midshipman I shall have no fear about getting on." "Stuff and nonsense!" again ejaculated Aunt Deb, "you know nothing about the matter, boy." "Don't I though," I said to myself, for I knew that my father, who felt the importance of finding professions for his sons according to their tastes, had some time before written to Sir Reginald Knowsley, of Leighton Park, - "the Squire," as he used to be called till he was made a baronet, and still was so very frequently, asking him to exert his influence in obtaining an appointment for me on board a man-of-war. This Sir Reginald had promised to do. Aunt Deb, however, had made many objections, but for once in a way my father had acted contrary to her sage counsel, and as he considered for the best. Still Aunt Deb had not given in. "You'll do as you think fit, John," she observed to him, "but you will repent it. Dick is not able to take care of himself at home, much less will he be so on board a big ship among a number of rough sailors. Let him remain at school until he is old enough to go into a counting-house in London or Bristol, where he'll make his fortune and become a respectable member of society, as his elder brother means to be, or let him become a master at a school, or follow any course of life rather than that of a soldier or a sailor."

They banded together, forming militia companies and launching counterattacks against the Indians. John had joined a militia company, and he had quickly risen through the ranks to become one of its leaders. He was a natural fighter, with a keen eye and a steady hand. He had already distinguished himself in several battles, and his comrades looked up to him as a hero. As the war raged on, John found himself at the forefront of the action. He led his men on daring raids against the Indians, and he fought bravely in the thick of battle. He was wounded several times, but he refused to yield. He was determined to see the war through to its end, no matter what the cost. And so the war continued, with John and his comrades fighting valiantly against the Creeks. The outcome was far from certain, but one thing was clear: the settlers would not go down without a fight. They would fight to the death to protect their homes and their way of life, and they would emerge victorious in the end.

This growing concern about NCDs in the global South has led to a surge in research, policy initiatives, and advocacy efforts. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been at the forefront of this movement, publishing numerous reports and guidelines on the prevention and control of NCDs. The WHO's Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases 2013-2020 has been instrumental in galvanizing global action on this issue. The World Bank and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) have also played a crucial role in highlighting the economic and social burden of NCDs in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Their reports and policy briefs have emphasized the need for a comprehensive approach to addressing NCDs, one that incorporates both public health and economic development strategies. Governments around the world have also taken notice of the growing threat posed by NCDs. The Political Declaration on the Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases, adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 2011, represents a major milestone in this effort. This declaration recognizes the devastating impact of NCDs on global health and development and calls for a coordinated response to address this crisis. Public health experts, medical professionals, and civil society organizations have also been vocal in their calls for action on NCDs. The Lancet, a leading medical journal, has published numerous special issues and research articles on the epidemiology, economics, and clinical aspects of NCDs. The NCD Alliance, a global coalition of health charities and patient organizations, has been instrumental in mobilizing support for NCDs as a global health and development priority. The relationship between NCDs and development is complex and multifaceted. On one hand, NCDs can have a devastating impact on economic development, as they can reduce productivity, increase healthcare costs, and burden healthcare systems. On the other hand, addressing NCDs can have significant economic benefits, as it can reduce healthcare costs, increase productivity, and improve overall well-being. The good news is that there are many effective interventions that can help prevent and control NCDs. These include policies and programs that promote healthy lifestyles, such as increasing physical activity, reducing tobacco use, and improving nutrition. They also include healthcare interventions, such as early detection and treatment of NCDs, and prevention and control of chronic diseases. In conclusion, the growing concern about NCDs in the global South is a pressing issue that requires a coordinated response. The WHO, World Bank, UNDP, governments, public health experts, medical professionals, and civil society organizations must work together to address this crisis. By doing so, we can reduce the burden of NCDs, improve health outcomes, and promote sustainable development.

Now, before I go on with this post, I want to emphasize that I am in NO way trying to degrade anyone's belief's or the teachings of anyone's religions or such. I'm simply stating my opinion and the way that I view things. If you view them differently, then that's great. I respect your opinion and would love to hear your take on the topic. So yes, back to the topic at hand. What initially intrigued me is that there are so many instances when something good happens, that we credit it to ourselves and say that we made the right decision, or we earned something, or we went about everything the right way. But when something happens that is detrimental to our lives, we console ourselves by saying stuff like; its what was meant to be, it's the way life goes, that's just fate. This seems interesting...Our accomplishments are of our own doing, but our failures are not due to our decisions, they're due to fate. How does that work? Either you are a stoic and everything that happens is due to fate, or you believe in free will and everything is a consequence of you decisions, or possibly you believe in a mix between the two (like myself). However, what cannot happen is that you believe certain things are solely due to fate, while others are solely due to your credit. That just doesn't work in my view. Seems like a defence mechanism a lot of us have developed in order to help transfer and justify the pain of our failures. You got a scholarship? Good job! You worked hard for it!...You got fire from your job? Don't worry, it's just not what you were meant to do in life. Why isn't it ever the other way around? You got a scholarship? Well that's good, but you were fated to get it anyways. You got fired from your job? Well, you just made some bad choices in your career path....See the difference? The second set seems so cold hearted. Doesn't make you feel good about it at all. But if you belive in fate, then in both cases, you should only believe the "meant to be" answers. If you believe in choice, then you should only belive in the "accomplishment" answers. Either way, you have a case when you have at least 1 cold hearted answer. But this doesn't happen...We alter our mind to create a situation in which we always get rid of the cold hearted answer. Interesting no? I think so. An extension of this, I've never understood how people who belive in "judgement after death" can believe in fate. I mean, doesn't fate mean that everything in your life is written? So how can you be judged (and found guilty) over doing something that you had no control over?

Medicated tampon devices have also been explored as microbicide delivery systems for prevention of HIV transmission (Ball et al., 2012) The approach described in this study is to develop a bioadhesive nanofibrous system which could be processed into suitable dosage forms (particularly, we suggest, as a medicated tampon) for vaginal drug delivery. We believe that such an approach holds several potential benefits including ease and convenience of use, prolonged retention and reduced leakage due to the bioadhesive nature of the carrier polymer and prolonged release due to gel formation of the polymer which provides a diffusion barrier to release. Such a system would potentially allow release over a period of hours which may potentially optimise the treatment regimen and allow daily use for women deemed to be at high risk of early labour. Nanofibrous approaches are attracting increasing interest within the pharmaceutical arena, particularly as the issue of poor yield is now becoming more effectively addressed, thereby rendering large scale production feasible. Pressurised gyration (PG) is a recently developed processing method which involves simultaneous centrifugal spinning and solution blowing to produce polymeric nano- and microfibers (Mahalingam and Edirisinghe, 2013). The laboratory-scale PG equipment consists of a cylindrical aluminium vessel of approximately 60 mm in cross-sectional diameter and 35 mm in height, capable of rotational speed of up to 36,000 rpm. The fibers are rapidly extruded as a polymeric solution under conditions of high rotation and enhanced pressure via a gas input through a series of holes with diameter of 0.5 mm, resulting in rapid evaporation of the solvent and collection of the resulting nano- or microfibers on a surround plate (for more details see Mahalingam and Edirisinghe, 2013). PG has successfully been used to manufacture nanofibers for a variety of pharmaceutical applications including the generation of amorphous drug dispersions (Raimi-Abraham et al., 2014) and microbubbles (Mahalingam et al., 2014). PG represents a promising development for large scale production; while electrospinning remains the most widespread method of producing fibers (Eatemadi et al., 2016), the limitations of scale-up have restricted the use of this approach within the pharmaceutical arena. PG has advantages of simplicity, low cost, high yield and versatility, having already been used for the production of a range of materials from ceramics (Mahalingam et al., 2015) to shape memory 3D mats (Wu et al., 2017). Here we further develop the technique for pharmaceutical applications, with a particularly view to addressing the persistent question of how hydrophobic drugs may be incorporated into hydrophilic polymers. In our previous work, we demonstrated the possibility of generating nanofibers with suitable mucoadhesive properties from a range of polymers using PG (Brako et al., 2015). These included bioadhesive polysaccharides (sodium alginate) and synthetic or semisynthetic polymers (polyacrylic acid and carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC)), using a spinning agent polyethylene oxide (PEO) to elicit sufficient chain entanglement in the liquid state so as to ultimately allow for fiber formation.

A big barn like structure made of corn cobs and grasses. We pushed on to Mitchell, SD where we decided to stop for the night. There is an incredible amount of tourist traps in this state. The most interesting being the Wall Drug Store which offers free ice water, coffee, and donuts. They must give away hundreds of gallons of ice water per day. The place has grown to enormous proportions. What started as a small drug store has now become a giant complex of stores selling everything from t-shirts to hand guns. I think the place has 5 restaurants. And it is quite successful. Just west of wall is the Badlands National Park. This is some really cool stuff. The park is comprised of 244,000 acres of heavily eroded landscape. The formations rise up to 1000 ft above the surrounding plains. The area was once covered by an inland sea. After the waters receded millions of years of erosion created what you see today. The park also has a large concentration of fossils. In fact, it has been called "the richest Oligocene epoch fossil bed in the world". Fossils found include ancient camels, three-toed horses, saber-tooth cats, and other animals. While hiking through the park we saw several prairie dogs. These little guys are pretty cute. They stand guard and make loud chirping noises when danger approaches. One little guy was standing up making the noise while I was taking pictures of him. Then he would duck back down into his hole. He would pop right back up though and continue chirping. He did this several times until I finally walked away. Another cool animal here is the bison. Bison are huge creatures weighing up to 2000 lbs. They are often confused with buffalo, however there are only two species of true buffalo; the African Cape Buffalo and the Asian Water Buffalo. Bison can run at speeds up to 35 mph. We drove around the park on a loop road and then headed north towards Mt. Rushmore. Along the way we stopped at a small town called Scenic. Here we ate lunch at a bar with a couple locals who told us about the local history. Scenic was once a thriving railroad town, but after the railroad left it died quickly. Only a handful of people remain living in the town now. One man named Hank bought up all the buildings in town and turned the whole town into a museum. Everything is set up as if the town were still alive and kicking. The grocery store shelves are full of old food items, the post office still contains letters in the mailboxes, and the barbershop has customers waiting for haircuts. All of this is behind glass though, and visitors aren't allowed inside. Most of the buildings are falling apart, but it's still a pretty cool site. We continued North to Rapid City and stopped for the night. Day 4. On our way to Mt. Rushmore we passed through Keystone, SD. The main street of the town is lined with souvenir shops and places to eat. At one point during the towns history gold was discovered nearby. Prospectors flocked to the area and eventually built the town of Keystone. The town grew rapidly. Today the gold mines are closed and tourism is the primary source of income. We arrived at Mt. Rushmore shortly before noon. The mountain is impressive. Carved into its side are the faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Abraham Lincoln, and Theodore Roosevelt. Sculptor Gutzon Borglum worked on the project for fourteen years beginning in 1927. Originally he wanted to carve the presidents from head to waist, but lack of funding prevented this from happening.

While studies of the Chinese government's approach to managing eco-innovation now commonly appear in the international literature, key neglected areas of research include the political synergies and tensions between the managerialist approach to creating internationally-competitive sectors (requiring the development of technological capabilities, alongside appropriate supply-side and demand-side policy interventions) and the uncertain and unpredictable socio-technical and socio-political reconfigurations and socio-cultural change that are intrinsic to sustainable socio-technical transitions. Western scholars have begun to pay more attention to the role of narratives, institutions, interests and practices as components of the political realities underlying or constraining transitions (Kern, 2011; Verhees et al., 2013; Lockwood, 2013; Smith et al., 2014), however this remains a relatively under-researched area. Responding to this gap in the literature, this article investigates emerging transitions in agri-food systems in China in order to understand how different forms of innovation relate to changing practices among various groups of producers and consumers, as well as how they are supported and constrained by political debates in the country's changing policy-making environment. Mirroring the multiple understandings of 'sustainability' outlined above, China's radically shifting food system not only requires decarbonisation, but also requires innovation to address some of its other associated environmental and social challenges - including nitrogen and phosphorous pollution associated with current agricultural approaches, food safety, food security and food sovereignty. We adopt a 'food practices in transition' framework (Spaargaren et al., 2012) in our analysis, drawing also on insights from the multi-level perspective on socio-technical systems (Geels, 2002; Geels and Schot, 2007) and the pathways approach (Leach et al., 2007, 2010) to understand how different framings of potential transition pathways link socio-technical innovation, governance and, in particular, the role of changing consumer practices in China. Applying these concepts to empirical evidence from China for the first time provides insights into the shifting relationship between consumer practices and transitions to more sustainable agri-food systems, raising important questions for food system governance in the country. Within our focus of sustainable food consumption and production, we analyse two transition pathways that are both linked by maize, a key staple Chinese food and feed grain with a long history in the country. These pathways centre around: The centrally-supported development of genetically modified (GM) phytase maize as a potential component of intensive agri-food (including livestock) systems, and; The emergence of agro-ecological and low external input sustainable approaches to the production and consumption of maize and associated agricultural products. Beyond innovations in maize itself (in terms of seed and cultivation), these pathways incorporate shifts in other components of the agri-food system (Spaargaren et al., 2012) notably in socio-technical innovation, policy and regulation, and the socio-cultural aspects of consumer practices.

As we embrace Ostara, let's strive to be more mindful of our personal growth. Balance, much like in nature, is a theme here. As day and night are equal during the equinox, so can we seek to balance the aspects of our lives, bringing more harmony and renewed purpose as we move forward. All three proteins bind a DNA duplex (in FEN1 this is the helix with the 5' flap strand), with a common element (termed H2TH) that contacts the backbone of the uncleaved strand. In FEN1, a second DNA duplex (that with the 3' flap and connected to the duplex with the 5'-flap by the continuity of the uncleaved strand) is bound, such that the two axes are virtually perpendicular. The active site is centrally located on the platform and comprises a number of conserved carboxylate residues around the - interface that coordinate one or two metal ions in the crystal structures. Mechanistic studies on phage T5 FEN indicate that at least two metal ions participate in the hydrolysis reaction (Syson et al., 2008). Some functionally important helices project above the platform. In all cases, the helix immediately C-terminal to the second section of sheet (counted from the N terminus) projects above the sheet region to abut the end of the DNA duplex, splaying apart the strands; it is thus termed the helical wedge. This helix directs a conserved tyrosine toward the DNA in FEN1 (Tsutakawa et al., 2011). A second section of polypeptide observed in FEN1 and EXO1 is directed above the platform, comprising 1/240 amino acids in two helices. This is termed the helical arch, through which passes the single strand of the substrate thereby selecting substrates with such features. Although sequence homology indicates that GEN1 will contain a number of features in common with FEN1, EXO1, and XPG, we would anticipate that it would have to differ from the other family members in a number of key respects. Given that GEN1 resolves a four-way DNA junction, it must act in dimeric form, in common with all known junction-resolving enzymes (Declais and Lilley, 2008), in agreement with our recent analysis (Freeman et al., 2014). Since the strands of a four-way junction are base-paired and covalently continuous, it would not require the helical arch, so this feature would probably be extensively modified in GEN1. Although the active site would be expected to be conserved in GEN1, the key question of interest is how the enzyme is selective for DNA junctions. To answer this, we require a molecular structure of the protein bound to DNA. Studies of GEN1 from human cells have shown that the N-terminal section acts in dimeric form to resolve four-way DNA junctions (Rass et al., 2010). However, all fragments of the enzyme have been found to be poly-disperse and fail to form discrete complexes with junctions. In contrast, we found that the orthologous enzyme from the thermophilic fungus Chaetomium thermophilum was very well behaved (Freeman et al., 2014).
